About this work

Opera Historica — "Historical Works," Part I — is the collected historical magnum opus of Trithemius's last years, assembling his chronicle of the Franks from their mythical Trojan origins through the Merovingian and Carolingian dynasties to the late medieval period. It follows the universal-chronicle tradition — year-by-year entries assembled from over two hundred manuscript sources — and is an important, if at times credulous, source for early medieval history. (Part II, the Hirsau and Sponheim monastic chronicles, is prdl-70290 in this corpus.) Like much of Trithemius's historical writing it mingles genuine documentary labour with fabricated sources, the most notorious being the invented Hunibald; readers should weigh it against later scholarship, but the breadth of compilation is real.

This is the 1601 Frankfurt edition — printed by Marne, the standard early-modern collected edition of the historical works (dilibri witness). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. The Latin of the Sponheim chronicle source is rougher than most of the corpus — among the worst OCR in the collection — and its tail chunks are the ones graded by GLM-5.2 rather than Claude (see the Methodology honesty note);

Collected Historical Works (Freher ed.), first part

The Historical Works of Johannes Trithemius of Sponheim, first Abbot of Sponheim, then of St. James the Greater at Würzburg, a man most learned in his age: all the works of the first part that have so far been able to be found; partly recalled from old editions now disappearing and corrected according to the authority of the archetypes, partly now first published from manuscripts. A catalogue of them is shown on the reverse page. From the library of Marquard Freher, Palatine councillor. With a very full index. Frankfurt, printed by the Wechel press, at the shop of Claudius Marnius and the heirs of Johannes Aubrius. 1601.

Historical Opuscules Contained in This Volume

  1. Mystical Chronology, on the secondary beings or intelligences that, after God, move the spheres; a book written to Maximilian, Roman Emperor.

  2. Compendium or Breviary of the first volume of the Chronicles or Annals, on the origin of the people and kings of the Franks, over 1189 years, from Marcomirus down to King Pippin; addressed to Laurentius, Bishop of Würzburg and Duke of Eastern Francia.

  3. A compendium on the origin of the people of the Franks, excerpted from Hunibald; in which there is also an enumeration of the bishops of Würzburg.

  4. Chronicle of the succession of the Dukes of Bavaria and Counts Palatine; addressed to Philip, Count Palatine, Prince Elector.

  5. Catalogue of illustrious men who have adorned Germany in every way by their talent and writings; addressed to Jacob Wimpheling of Schlettstadt, theologian, with his prothesis or addition.

  6. Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, addressed to Johann Dalberg, Bishop of Worms, with additions by certain persons.

The Annals of the same author will be published separately in a separate volume.

To the most reverend and most illustrious prince, Lord Julius, Bishop of Würzburg, Duke of Eastern Francia, etc., most gracious lord, greetings.

[unclear]

Since I was about to bring back into the light, for the sake of posterity, the extremely laborious writings of a most diligent writer on German affairs, writings that were almost tending toward oblivion, and was looking around for a worthy patron and defender for them, I did not have to deliberate long, as though faced with a doubtful choice, if I did not wish to change the custom I have carefully observed up to now in publishing and inscribing various monuments of both languages: namely, that I should either dedicate or restore them only to those to whom they seemed especially to belong, and even to be owed. For by how many titles these Trithemian works, belonging especially to the illumination of the Frankish people and of your Church, are most deservedly owed to your name, illustrious prelate, the works themselves declare even if I am silent: since they were both born on your soil and originally inscribed by the author to your predecessors. Nor is it unknown that he, easily the most learned of all abbots after St. Bernard, and of his age, which had for some centuries fallen into barbarism

then, for the first time, had begun to cast them off, when by divine favor good letters had been restored and their most useful instrument, printing, had been discovered, he, no slight ornament, after having won fame for his name through very many writings of every kind, having himself also experienced, by virtue’s perpetual fate, the injustice of fortune and of slander, and yielding to envy, although the protection of the highest princes was nowhere lacking to him, finally chose at your Würzburg a retreat most desired for his old age and his studies. There, holding fast to his purpose to the end of his life and indefatigable in labor, truly dying in the writing of books, he closed his day.

Among these wonders of immense night-labors, works that by their number and their bulk will bring amazement to posterity, those very extensive Annals of Germany or France, divided into three volumes, would easily hold the chief place, if they were extant. These he then left compiled and completed from all the monuments of all ages, by a labor plainly Herculean; but while alive he could not publish them, except for a very brief compendium of the first volume, sent to your predecessor Laurentius de Bibra, from which, as from a claw, one may estimate the lion. This work, certainly, both for the author’s reputation and for the variety of its matter and its own perfection, must be held of any price whatever, and the prayers of learned men have long been seeking it with great desire; so that, if they had it, they would think the loss of the others could easily be borne.

For that man possessed, besides those gifts with which one who is meditating books destined to live ought to be furnished, sharpness of judgment, ease of style, varied reading, accuracy, and endurance of labor; and, for the undertaking of composing history in every form, those further aids which scarcely any others had in such fashion. One, I mean, was the incomparable treasury of various excellent manuscripts in the library of Sponheim, chiefly built up and enlarged by him; that this treasury afterward, partly through the negligence of his successors, partly through the injury of the times amid the disturbances of civil wars, was plundered, carried off, and perished, so that scarcely certain worthless fragments of it now survive preserved at Kreuznach, cannot be lamented enough. The other was his acquaintance with princes and great men throughout Europe, whom in that season God willed to spring up as a good crop, to the great advantage of divine and human letters; they almost vied with one another in courting his familiarity, a companionship bound by true ties of friendship and joined by a shared zeal for virtue and learning. With their help he was able to learn everything concerning serious affairs done at home and abroad, with their causes and circumstances, and thereafter to commit them to papers with no little better trustworthiness [unclear] not only cathedral colleges, but also monasteries [unclear] had appointed for recording annals, were accustomed to do.

This very thought certainly stirs and inflames in the minds of all who are touched by a better care for these letters and by love of their country a marvelous desire to see that outstanding work: since they do not despair that it can be brought forth from some corner of the libraries of your city or jurisdiction; and, to one so judging, it will seem above all a good deed, and worthy of you, so great a prelate and patron of studies, if under your auspices that treasury, rather than book, is restored to the commonwealth. Most reverend prince, if in the public name I should earnestly beseech you to deign to devote some care to this matter, and to allow those Trithemian books, or rather children, demanding with no obscure voice the vindication of their brothers oppressed by an unworthy servitude, to obtain this from you, I have hoped that in accordance with your utmost clemency and humanity you will assuredly take it in good part.

Farewell. At Myrtilletum, on the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1601.

Most devoted to Your Reverend Highness,

MARQ. FREHERUS.

To

To the most reverend and most illustrious prince Julius, bishop of Würzburg, duke of Eastern Franconia.

He to whom the splendid fame of a renowned name befell while he lived and saw the light, him still, after death and a hundred harvests, bright honor follows with undying praise. I speak of great Trithemius, born on the wine-bearing bank of the Moselle, a kind of marvel, because of the hidden arts of his higher intellect, and the godlike knowledge of a thousand matters, which Apollo granted no other mortal to know so equally, or to penetrate to the lofty spirits, with the deity privy to secret things favoring him. But I do not touch the perplexities and winding courses of the Polygraphy, nor the mazes of the Steganography, scarcely to be explained to the sophistical Sphinx if the key is absent. Yet we ourselves have seen this key, and have read the wondrous characters in Hebrew figures.

But let these things be gone. I would commend, duke of Franconia, the plain histories of the very celebrated man; from their recollected books, brought to exactness, behold, today a new edition comes forth into the bright air, under Freher’s guidance. It does not displease you, Julius, that what once pleased the polished intellect of Bibraeus, to whom Trithemius himself dedicated his labors, afterward buried in the church of Saint James as one of heaven’s own. And then would that ancient Mainz, foster-child of the Rhine, or sacred Green Verruca of Pyrcus, born of the Main, would bring forth from papers hidden in shadows that great work on the Frankish people and their renowned kings, whom Hunibald described with truthful pen; even if he is accused of having recorded, in fabulous deeds, some things. Yet it is rash where we suspect that something must be judged of slight credibility; and the smoke of adverse opinion often blinds the eyes.

Let it be recalled, let the ancient enclosed mass of Hunibald’s volumes be brought back from Orcus; what do I wish for more? And, Trithemius, O how great a favor you will afterward enter into among all learned men, and likewise among all Franks throughout the recesses of the eastern boundary and the western, greatest priest of the Rhine, and no lesser priest of the Main, if you readily communicate aid to one another with the graphic promise of Freher, eager thereafter to publish many more things, so that the glory of each learned age may be abundantly enriched, and the storehouse of history increased. For your lecterns in the twofold cave abound in writings, just as Bamberg too is filled with excellent treasures, and with very many a codex throughout its shelves.

Paulus Melissus Francus, Count Palatine and golden knight, Roman citizen.

The Life and Writings of Johannes Trithemius, first Abbot of Sponheim, and afterward of St. James at Würzburg, from the Letter of Johannes Duraclusius, disciple of the same Trithemius, to Nicolaus Hamerius Emelanus.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, was born in the village of Trittenheim, in the diocese of Trier, on the banks of the river Moselle, on the first day of February, at the eleventh hour and thirtieth minute after noon, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1462, in the tenth Roman indiction: his father was Johannes of Heidenberg, and his mother was called Elisabeth of Longuich. This was, namely, the year in which the city of Mainz, in the dissension of two pontiffs, was captured, lost its liberty, and found servitude, many of its citizens having been driven into exile; in the fourth year then running of Pope Pius, the second of that name, and the twenty-second of Emperor Frederick III.

In the year of the Lord 1482, however, in the monastery of Sponheim in the diocese of Mainz, on the first day of February, that is, the day on which he had formerly been born, he laid aside the secular habit and there took up the monastic one under the rule of the blessed father Benedict, according to the observance newly introduced. In the following year, which was 1483, after Johannes of Colenhussen, the abbot, had been transferred by canonical postulation to Seligenstadt, Johannes Trithemius, by the common election of the brothers, was advanced and adorned as abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Sponheim on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and presided for twenty-three years, one month, and nineteen days. When these had passed, not without many labors, provoked by the rashness of certain rivals, he accepted the abbey of St. James at Würzburg, which was being offered to him, and of his own free will resigned Sponheim, full of useless cares.

In both places he wrote several little works, from which he recently set down for me with his own hand in a note the items written below. Since you, my friend, ask me for their titles, I gladly agree to your wishes, so that, from consideration of so many of his labors, you may have the memory of our common friend and teacher [unclear] useless presumptions.

He wrote first the Constitutions of his order, which were made in provincial chapters by command of the presidents, one book. On the manner of holding a provincial chapter, one book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, two books. Homilies and exhortatory sermons to his monks, two books, which he dedicated to his predecessor. On the temptations of cloistered persons and their remedies, two books. To Nicolaus, priest of Münstermaifeld, on the priestly life, one book. Against the private property of monks, one book. A penthic work, that is, a mournful one, on the ruin of his order, one book. On the illustrious men of his order, four books. Praises of the order of the Carmelite brothers, two books. To Gerlacus, abbot of Deutz, praises of manuscript writers, one book. To Johannes Dalburgius, bishop of Worms, on ecclesiastical writers, one book. On the praises of Saint Anne, grandmother of the Lord, one book. To the questions of Autgerus Sicamber, canon of Deventer, one book. A chronicle of his monastery of Sponheim, no small volume, one book. A chronicle or annals of the monastery of Hirsau, two large volumes. [unclear] the prince elector, a single book. The life of Saint Irmina, nun and first abbess in the Horrea at Trier, one book. On the misery of cloistered prelates, two books. Praises of Saint Andrew the Apostle, one book. Praises of Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord, one book. Praises of Saint Benedict the abbot, one book. Praises of the monastic life, one book. Praises

[On the virtue?] of penitence, one book. Praises of the Study of the Divine Scriptures, one book. The Monologion of a Man Devoted to God Addressed to Himself, one book. On the Miracles of Saint Mother Anne, one book. To Ulrich, canon of Cologne, on questions on the Gospel of John, one book. To the same, on questions on the Psalms, one book. To the presidents of the annual chapter, on the Bursfeld observance, he abridged the statutes of the same union, one book. The Spiritual Exercise of Monks, one book. An epitome or breviary of the same, one book. On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. On the Illustrious Writers of Germany, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Schlettstadt, one book. Spanheim letters to various persons, four books. Orations delivered in chapters and elsewhere, twenty-four in number, which make one book. He wrote sermons to the brethren of the monastery of Spanheim, forty in number and very fine, one book. Sermons for feast days to the people, one book. Several supplicatory prayers to God and the saints, one book. From the Greek language he translated into Latin [Maximilianus?] the abbot, On the Incarnation of the Lord; also the anathemas of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, promulgated against heretics in the third synod of Ephesus; and certain letters of the same synod. He also wrote, for the edification of monks, a notable work which he entitled On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, three books. He wrote also certain other smaller works, whose titles he did not indicate to me.

These, dearest brother Nicolaus, are the little works of Trithemius which, during the twenty-three years in which he was abbot, he composed by lamplight at Spanheim, to the honor of God, amid cares and continual occupation with household affairs, reading or writing day and night whenever he was able to steal some leisure for himself. During the years in which he presided, he brought into the library of Spanheim a very great treasure of books in every faculty, not only through the art of printing but also of manuscripts. For when I was with him for the space of [one?] year, to learn Greek and Hebrew letters from him, I counted in the library two thousand volumes which over eighty years had been properly written out with the pen on parchment and paper. I often heard from his mouth that he had spent more than two thousand florins on books; he had received these not from the substance of the monastery, which was always very meager, but, since he was known to and beloved by many princes, he spent the gifts with which he was honored by them for the most part on books. For he is a very great lover and cultivator of books, above all whom I know today living in the flesh. It is said by many, however, that his successor, who is now abbot at Spanheim, has alienated very many volumes; whether that is true I certainly do not know in the least.

In the year of the Lord 1504, when a fierce war had arisen between the kingdom and Philip, count palatine, Trithemius, from fear of the enemy, withdrew with his library and the property of the monastery to Kreuznach, a nearby town, and I likewise returned to my own affairs. But in the year 1506, in the month of October, Trithemius himself, stirred by the envy of certain men, accepted the abbey of Saint James at Wuerzburg and resigned Spanheim. There in quiet he is writing various things, whose titles, when recently asked, he sent to me as follows. To Emperor Maximilian he published a wondrous work, which he entitled Polygraphy, six books. To the same, a key to the same Polygraphy, one book. Responses to eight questions of the same emperor, one book. To the same, On the Seven Intelligences Moving the Spheres, one book. To Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, prince elector, twenty books of various questions, orations, and propositions. To the same, On Forewarnings Permitted and Not Permitted to a Christian, two books. To the same he wrote that wondrous and laborious work of Steganography, in eight books, which that rash Bovillus, not understanding it, criticized most ignorantly and falsely. To the same prince, one book of letters. To the same, Against Malefics and All Arts and Superstitions Forbidden by the Church, five books. To the same, On the Causes and Cure of [broaduci?] and of Malefices, three books. To his brother Jakob Trithemius, The Journey of His Life, two books. To Burkhard of Hornneck, physician, On the Peculium of Nuns, one book. He wrote a history or annals concerning the origin, kings, and deeds of the people of the Franks and Germans, three large volumes, beginning the narrative with King Marcomer, who in the year 433 before the incarnation of the Lord led the people from the borders of Scythia into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine, down to the twenty-ninth year of Emperor Maximilian. To Lorenz von Bibra, bishop of Wuerzburg and duke of Eastern Francia, he wrote an epitome or breviary of those same three historical volumes, three books. To the same, On the Dukes and Bishops of the Franks of Wuerzburg, one book. On the Miracles Shown at the Memorial of Our Lady Saint Mary at Dettelbach, two books. On

On the miracles of the same, shown at Urticetum near Helpruma, six books. An Apology against Charles Bovillus, who slanders things he did not understand, one book. On the Origin and Kings of the Franks, one book. A Chronicle of his monastery, over which he now presides, of Saint James at Wurzburg, one book. To Albert, of the Margraves of Brandenburg, Archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, the Life of Saint Rabanus, arch-prelate, three books. On the translation of the same from Mainz into Saxony, one book. To the same, the Life of Saint Maximus, bishop, one book. To John, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria, and Count in Sponheim, residing at Simmern, On the Origin, Kings, and Dukes of the Bavarians, and likewise of the Counts Palatine and of Sponheim, four books. On Demons and Profane, Maleficent, and Superstitious Arts, a laborious work he has in hand, which will have twelve books, in which he blasts, confounds, and overthrows all the tricks of diabolical arts. Of Wurzburg Letters, which he wrote in that abbey, four books. He also wrote many other smaller works suited to his own devotion and that of his friends, such as a Cursus, a Rosary, an Office of the Mass, and various prayers, together with proses or sequences on Saint Anne, grandmother of our Savior. He also wrote praises, prayers, and a rosary on Saint Mary Magdalene; a rosary on Saint John the Evangelist. At the request of John, Archbishop of Trier, a sequence on Anne, which begins, "Jesus, king of the heavens," to the melody Ave praeclara. Another, to be sung on her feast, which begins: "Let them rejoice on this day." A third to the provincial of the Carmelites at Augsburg, and it begins, "Let us rejoice in honor." A fourth on Saint Hildegard, virgin, which begins thus: "Praise be to you, Lord, king of eternal glory." A fifth on Saint Rupert, leader of the people of Bingen, which begins: "Let them rejoice on this day." A sixth on Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Lord, and it begins thus: "[Let us sing?], illustrious ones." A seventh on Saint Rabanus, archbishop. An eighth on the wounds of Christ, which begins thus: "Let us adore Jesus Christ; let us lament with the crucified." A ninth on the compassion of Blessed Mary ever virgin, and it begins thus: "Ah, let us weep with devout mind, sharing the suffering of the Blessed Virgin Mary," to the melody, namely, Ave praeclara. A tenth on Saint Joachim, father of our Lady, which begins thus: "Let us adore the Trinity; let us praise together the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit." An eleventh on the good proper angel of each human being. A twelfth for the proper Mass of each priest. A thirteenth on Saint Maximus, bishop of Mainz. A fourteenth on Saint Martha, virgin, host of Christ. A fifteenth on Saint Mary of Egypt. A sixteenth on Saint Mary of Egypt. A sixteenth on Saint James the Greater, apostle. A nineteenth on Saint Benedict, abbot. A twentieth on All Saints. And for each of the named commemorations and saints he composed individual new offices of the Mass, conformable to the divine Scriptures. He wrote besides a little work of meditations and prayers on the Lord's incarnation, nativity, life, passion, and death, suited to devotion, two books. The Mirror of Heavenly Doctrine, serving not a little for compunction of mind, one book, which begins thus: "[The beginning?] of human salvation." He also composed, in beautiful variety, many most devout meditations and prayers on our Lord Jesus Christ, on his most holy mother the Virgin Mary, and on various saints, together with many other great works, which all devout posterity will see and admire. These, my dearest Nicolaus, are the volumes of our Abbot Trithemius, which for almost thirty-two years he has worked out in unremitting study, apart from those which, not yet finished, are in hand under the hammer and unknown to me. Farewell from my Duraclusian house, on the fifth day of October, in the year of our salvation 1515.

Johannes Duraclusius.

In the Trithemian chamber (which is still seen intact in the monastery of Spanheim, one mile from the town of Kreuznach), inscribed on every side with elegant letters, red and black, there are read very many poems and sayings of various authors, ancient and more recent, both Greek and Latin: especially of Sedulius, Juvencus, Fortunatus, Bishop Hildebert, Peter of Riga, and Walter of Châtillon. To these Conrad Celtis, his contemporary and friend, added the following:

Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet:

Look, venerable guest, at these little verses, which Trithemius has set here with three marks: how great a cultivator of antiquity he was, or how great a lover of languages, the written wall teaches both.

The likeness of the same Celtis, depicted from life in colors, is seen on the wall, with these words added: Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate, sang these verses in the year of the Lord 1494, when he was here. To the future abbot.

Whoever you shall be as future abbot, I ask that you often be willing to turn over these poems of ours in mindful thought. Be pious, merciful, a lover of religion; and, I advise you, learn to follow my Trithemius.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot, to his successor.

Look: I have set up memorials of learned men, and whatever can greatly adorn you. I exhort and admonish you to follow in our footsteps, you who will come after me and rule my buildings.

From

From the Citicensian Chronicle of Paulus Langaeus Cygnaeus, monk of Bosau, under the year of Christ 1515.

In the same year, when, out of love of letters, with the consent of our venerable abbot Benedict and by leave of dismissal, I was at Wurzburg in the monastery of St James the Apostle, for a time under the instruction and obedience of the reverend and in every respect most learned man, lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the said monastery, while he was then applying himself to setting down the histories of German affairs in three volumes, and while with the same care he wished to continue his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, already produced long ago at Spanheim down to the year of the Lord 1494, down to the present time, namely to connect, by a certain added notice, the illustrious men who in the meantime had written, together with their lucubrations, to the writers of the churches already previously written up and printed in the aforesaid book: in order that he might be able to complete this praiseworthy undertaking more easily and promptly, he sent me, whom he judged suitable to assist him in this, with letters of recommendation to the foundations of all monasteries, yet especially of our order, and also to gather from every quarter throughout all Germany, for the praise of God, giver of all sciences, and for the honor and renown of the whole German nation, the monuments of clear men, as I have said, and, having collected and copied them, to bring them to him. Now the tenor of the aforesaid letters, and likewise of the commissions, was and is as follows.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St James at Wurzburg, of the order of Saint Benedict, to all and singular lords abbots, provosts, priors, and the other rectors, with prayers, ready willingness to obey. We have given in charge to the bearer of these letters, brother Paulus Langius, monk and priest of our aforesaid order, that he diligently inquire after, write down, and report to us, for all monasteries, convents, and churches, of whatever religion they may be, as far as can be done, throughout all Germany, their foundations together with the time and their little works, for the adornment of the Annals or Chronicles of Germany, to which we are applying our labor. Therefore we ask you all and singular, through the Savior of the world, that you kindly admit him to your [unclear], and charitably [unclear], and that in those matters for the sake of investigating which he is sent by us, you not cease to lend him favor and aid according to your strength, being about to receive reward from him who is judge of all [unclear]. [Unclear] on the right hand: Go, blessed of my Father, because when they were strangers [unclear]. Written in our aforesaid monastery at Wurzburg on the first day of the month of April, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1515.

And so I always strove, according to my strength, to carry out the aforesaid embassy or commission, although I was held back and hindered in many places, partly by the difficulty and danger of the roads, partly by fear of robbers and brigands, through mountains and woods, and finally by the unexpected death of Trithemius himself, who had sent me and was my teacher. Nevertheless, while he was still living, several times, when winter was coming on, I returned to Wurzburg to report and consign what had been collected and written, together with various letters and greetings of different wise men. And although many famous, and also very weighty and wholly upright, men praised the aforesaid investigation of antiquities, yet on the other side there were some sycophants and [unclear], and, what is shameful, certain petty religious brethren, biting and Cynical, who quite shamelessly censured that commission and inquiry, not blushing to call me, for so arduous an undertaking, a wanderer and mountebank. But if I am a wanderer, if a circumcellion, who, I ask, was my namesake, the Apostle Paul, of whom it is read in Acts 19: It happened that, when Paul had passed through the upper regions, he came to Ephesus; and who by traveling about from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum sowed the Gospel of Christ, although for a far different and more blessed cause? What, finally, was Jerome, what Rufinus, what Heraclides, what Petronius, Paulus Orosius, Julius Africanus, Severus Sulpicius, Cassianus, Paschasius, and the like, who, on account of pious devotion and the edification of others, crossed seas and most devoutly surveyed the places of the Holy Land? Then, roaming through Egypt, Nitria, Scythia, and Palestine, they most exactly inspected the monasteries of monks, the caves of anchorites, and [unclear], and most religiously and watchfully examined their life and conduct and doctrine; and, generally staying among them for some days and years, and imitating and learning the institutions and morals of the same, and noting down the exhortations of individuals, at last returning to their own country, they elegantly and usefully wrote down what they had seen and heard, for the honor of God and the edification and profit of readers. Had they not gone about the places narrated above, neither monks nor even the world itself would now have the Lives of the Fathers, the Institutions, the Conferences, the Exhortations, the Conversations, and the Itinerary which is ascribed to Jerome, and finally the lives and legends of certain men, and especially of Antony, Hilarion, Pachomius, Onuphrius, Macarius, Romanus, Arsenius, Posthumius, Mary of Egypt, Euphrosyne, Euphrasia, and the like. Happy therefore, and thrice happy, was their travelling about; praiseworthy and holy was their investigation, from which there followed so great a fruit and so great a holiness of morals and of all edification.

Why therefore do envious men make it a charge against me, when it is praised in others; when even heathendom itself extolled it in Ulysses with many proclamations; when the glorious Jerome commended it in the philosophers Plato and Apollonius; when finally the same man extolled it even in women with the highest praises? Well known is that most fervent survey of Saint Paula, by which that most noble one of Roman matrons touched with her own hands, venerated, and kissed countless cells of monks and hermits, and also their beds, garments, hair shirts, and little sweat-cloths. How great a fruit and profit accrued to the world from such journeyings of the holy fathers, neither Cicero himself nor Demosthenes could utter and set forth with their eloquence. For, to pass over others meanwhile, if the holy and most devout fathers of our order, Columbanus, Gallus, Kilian, Boniface, Willibrord, Ludger, and their peers, had remained seated in their monasteries, who would have converted the peoples of the Austrasians, Gauls, Franks, Bavarians, Vindelicians, Thuringians, Saxons, Hessians, and Frisians to the faith of Christ? If finally the most outstanding of our order

[unclear], if Bede, Rabanus, Strabo, Marianus, Claudius, Lampertus, and similar lords had remained: who would have imbued England, Scotland, and Ireland with the rudiments of the faith by preaching? Who, moreover, would have established in Gaul that beneficent and most famous University of Paris? Who would have founded that most powerful and noble bishopric of Wurzburg in Francia? It is indeed most certain that Saint Burghard, the first prelate of that church, established it, just as Alcuin, father of our order, founded the Parisian Academy. Who would have planted the many other bishoprics throughout Europe, whose first bishops, as we proved more fully in the preceding sections under the year of the Lord 978, were of our order and often foreigners? But why do I linger over many things? Why do I try to claim for myself what most excellent men could attain neither by virtue nor by holiness? They, indeed, the more learned and more renowned for sanctity they were, always had all the sharper and more numerous detractors. For, as Jerome says, speaking from experience in these matters, courage always has rivals in public, and lightning strikes the highest mountains, and according to Naso’s similar saying:

Envy seeks the highest things; the winds blow over the loftiest.

But now enough about these matters. Indeed, insofar as both the fruit and the usefulness of the often-mentioned commission and of my survey somewhat— etc.; the rest is missing.

The Much Celebrated Medicinal Powder of the Same Trithemius

Many have always praised up to this point this powder of Trithemius, very useful for the brain and for students. For not a few, by using it, have reached the point that they could easily disregard those inspectors of urine, arteries, tongues, and excrements. Many have extended sound life almost to the hundredth year; finally they have attained such keenness of memory that they easily surpassed any men, even the greatest. And this without pills, electuaries, [unclear], ointments, plasters, electuaries, chewing preparations, gargles, [unclear], fumes, preserves, syrups, waters, theriacal preparations, and the like.

  1. Of aromatic calamus, Of gentian, Of cumin, Of mountain siler, Of anise, Of caraway, Of ammi, Of parsley seed, Of spikenard, of each [unclear]. Of red coral, Of unions or unpierced pearls, [unclear]. Of white ginger, Of bitter-sweet [Chamepitys?], Of senna leaves, Of burnt tartar, of each [unclear]. Of mace, Of cubebs, of each [unclear]. Of cloves, [unclear]. Let a powder be made according to art.

Its dose is [unclear], which should be taken morning and evening, in broth or wine, during the first month; in the second month in the morning only; in the third month [unclear] in the week, and thus thereafter it is continued for life. For indeed it is effective against many illnesses, and is a most proven and efficacious powder. It strengthens the stomach, purges the brain, clears the eyes and sight, sharpens the memory, consumes bad and superfluous humors in the whole body without danger, soothes and opens, drives away constriction, nausea in the [unclear], prevents excessive fatness, preserves from epilepsy and apoplexy, dissolves the matter of stone without pain and does not allow it to harden into stone, and does not permit chiragra, podagra, or sciatica to prevail.

When Paulus Scalichius wished to have the Duke of Prussia, to whom he was then counselor, use this powder, the prince’s physicians forbade it. From this arose a dispute among them, in which they fought in writing for both sides concerning this powder. That inquiry is extant in book two of the Philosophical Satires of the same Scalichius.

Effigy of Abbot Trithemius

Above human comprehension and the senses of the wise, and minds, a genius to whom genius belonged; Could Trithemius not surpass by wondrous art whatever is highest on earth, whatever is in the vault of heaven? Cease to wonder. So great a man, learned in all things, by nature’s instinct was wholly keenness.

Elo-

Eulogy of Johannes Trithemius, from André Thevet of Angoulême, royal cosmographer, Commentaries On Illustrious Men, book III, chapter LXXX.

If any illustrious person has deserved to be honored and to take a place in this book of ours, that man ought chiefly, in this respect, to be esteemed who supplied and depicted for us the first designs and models of this work, and who was able in many places to aid us from his writings and memoirs. Therefore, in order to show and actually display liberality, and not to seem ungrateful, I have not wished to leave behind the natural portrait of Jean Trithemius, a person as learned and as diligent an investigator of all good sciences as any other of his time; I took it from a book printed in Germany, in the same form in which I present it to you here. He was accompanied by [purity?] of life and ardent zeal for the Christian religion, as one who, in a book on the same subject as this one, though not so complete in all its parts and native colors, drew out a brief collection of the learned men who wrote, and whose books came to his knowledge.

Now, since the life of a man, once known, can greatly stir our heart to bear affection toward him, and since at the simple report of virtue we are moved to love those whom we have never beheld with our eyes, we shall say who this Trithemius was, whence he came, and in what time he lived. The town of Trittenheim, on the Moselle in the diocese of Trier, contributed to him two graces not to be despised, namely his birth and the surname which he made so famous, in the year of the birth of our Savior 1460.

While still a child, burning with affection and love for letters, he resolved to seek farther off more solid nourishment to appease his hunger. For this purpose he journeyed through various provinces and studied in the most famous universities then flourishing in both human and sacred learning, so that in a short space of time, by continual labor, he reached the height and perfection of knowledge. For he was a subtle philosopher, an ingenious mathematician, a celebrated poet, an accomplished historian, a very eloquent orator, and a distinguished theologian, endowed moreover with many rare virtues and graces, both of body and of mind.

But since in that time, still not polished, religious men were held in great and good opinion by everyone, both for their singular devotion and for their learning, the monasteries, especially in the order of Saint Benedict, being like public schools where children were taught and where men professed to preach and explain the Scriptures more than is done at present, this Jean Trithemius, desiring to find a place very suitable and peaceful for giving himself to the contemplation of divine things, chose an abbey and monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, where he took the habit of a religious. And because he conducted himself very modestly, two years after his profession he was elected and appointed abbot in the monastery of Saint Martin in the town of Sponheim, diocese of Mainz, which office he administered with very great skill.

And although the charge of governing a number of religious men differing in manners and temperament is very burdensome, indeed as burdensome as a squadron of soldiers of diverse nations is to a good and valiant captain, and although such a charge requires that a man do almost nothing else than give it his eye, ear, and all his senses, especially considering that, although all human actions, both private and public, are subject to the tooth of slanderers, above all the life of a prelate is ordinarily picked over and exposed to the tongues of evil-speakers, whom it is impossible to satisfy, nevertheless this man, with great care, while laboring at the ordering and disposition of external affairs, did not fail to steal some hours, which he carefully employed now in reading and now in composing, as we can easily gather and infer from the works he published, which sufficiently commend to posterity his learning and admirable diligence.

Among his other books, the one which, following the example of Saint Jerome, Gennadius, and others, he entitled On Ecclesiastical Writers is worthy of perpetual memory and praise. In it, with very laborious research, he noted for the most part the authors, the time in which they lived, their profession, the titles of each book, and the prefaces or beginnings of them, by this labor of his providing the brush to many who later imitated him. As for the books of the Polygraphia, even those least well disposed toward him are compelled to admire the ingenuity of the style he used, in which he describes various [unclear].

Key of the city. Steganography. Trithemius too much given over to magic. Regius’s error. Twofold magic. Trithemius’s contemporaneity. Death of Trithemius. The text is erroneous: in the year [1516?]. And this is established from his epitaph.

his ways of writing missives; but this is with such difficulty that those who are best versed in them have trouble enough being able to attain it. For this reason he himself devised a book which he calls the Key of Polygraphy, in order to open the door to it and disclose the secrets, which could not be communicated, seen, or recognized except with inestimable labor.

It would be superfluous to recite here the catalogue of his other books; I will only say that he is to be reproved in this: that, being too curious about the black and occult sciences of magic, he wrote in his book entitled Steganography several superstitious things unworthy of an ecclesiastical man. By this means he furnished many, who were seeking no better bread, with matter for mocking monks, saying that the state of a religious man did not consist in recounting such superstitions and astrological movements; adding that he is thought to have penetrated farther and to have had communication with familiar spirits, which I would not wish to approve.

It is quite true that there have been countless students of this science, which is practiced in many parts of the world, among others in Cambaluh, Malacca, Goa, and even in China, a country of the East Indies. Not that I wish to approve the fable received by Regius in the book he made on the vicissitudes of things, where he says that it is not permitted to those of those countries to attain offices and honors in the commonwealth unless they are learned in this science of magic. This was misunderstood by him, since those who use these sciences are only the sacrificers and priests of their idols, and some other beggarly rogues, most of whom are slaves.

For the rest, I will not occupy myself here in giving you to understand [unclear]; I may call him a beacon illuminating his age, in which letters remained buried, and he is one of those who first revived and clarified them. After having had the occupations I have just recounted, having crossed the forest of this life under the harshness and inclemency of the time, with countless labors and false and wholly unjust calumnies by which he was assailed, he died in the year one thousand four hundred ninety-nine, under Pope Alexander VI and while the Emperor Maximilian was reigning. As for others, it would be too tedious to specify them here; I shall be content, among the others, to choose Josse Badius and Jacques Fèvre, who together produced great fruits throughout all Europe, and especially in our France, and who were for the most part companions in labors, affections, and undertakings.

JOHN-

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, On the Seven Secondary Beings, that is, on the Intelligences or Spirits that move the spheres after God: a little book, or Mystical Chronology.

Comprising within itself many secrets worthy of being known, with marvelous brevity.

The Letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, on the little book concerning the heavenly intelligences that govern the spheres after God.

To the divine Maximilian I, Emperor Caesar, pious and fortunate.

[unclear]

It is the opinion of very many of the ancients, most wise Caesar, that this lower world is governed, by the ordering of the first intellect, which is God, through secondary intelligences. Agreeing with their opinion, the Conciliator of the Physicians says that seven spirits were appointed over the seven planets from the beginning of heaven and earth; each of them governs the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months in sequence. Very many most learned men have hitherto given their assent to this position; I make it known to Your Most Sacred Majesty not by asserting it, but only by reporting it.

I.

The first angel, or spirit of Saturn, is called Orifiel. God entrusted the world to him to govern from the beginning of creation, and he began his rule on the fifteenth day of the month of March, in the first year of the world, and it lasted 354 years and four months. Orifiel, however, is a name of office, not of nature, attributed to the spirit by reason of his action. Under his rule human beings were rude and rustic, living in solitude after the manner of beasts. This does not need proof from me, since it is manifest to all from the text of Genesis.

II.

The second governor of the world is Anael, the spirit of Venus. After Orifiel, he began to rule the influence of his planet in the year of the world 354, in the fourth month, that is, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of June, and he governed the world for 354 years and four months, down to the year 780 from the founding of the world, as is clear to one who calculates the period. Under the rule of this Anael, human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities, to discover manual arts, external work, wool-working, and things similar to these; also to indulge far more in the pleasures of the flesh, and there to take beautiful wives, to forget God, and in many respects to depart from natural simplicity; to invent games and songs, to play the lyre, and to devise whatever pertains to the nature and cult of Venus. This wantonness of life among human beings lasted until the Flood, a sufficient proof of its depravity.

III.

The third, Zachariel, angel of Jupiter, began to govern the world in the year 780 from the creation of heaven and earth, that is, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of October, and governed the world for 354 years and four months, down to the years of the founded world 1063 inclusive. Under his direction human beings first began to usurp lordship over one another, to practice hunting, to make tents, and to adorn their bodies with various garments; and there arose a great [unclear] among [unclear].

Johannes Trithemius

...the division of good and evil, with the good calling upon God, like Enoch, whom the Lord translated, while the wicked ran after the enticements of the flesh. Under the rule of this Zachariel men also began to live more civilly, to endure the laws of their elders, and to grow tame from their former wildness. Under his leadership, too, Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all his posterity the testament of necessary death. Finally, various human inventions and arts emerged at this time, as the historiographers have expressed more clearly.

III.

The fourth ruler of the world was Raphael, spirit of Mercury, who began on 24 February in the year of the creation of heaven and earth 1063, and presided for 354 years and four months; his dominion lasted until the year of the world 1417 and the fourth month. In these times writing was first invented, and letters were first devised after the manner or form of trees and plants; later, however, with time, they both took on a more cultivated ornament, and peoples changed the appearance of the characters according to their own judgment. The use of musical instruments also began to multiply under the rule of this Raphael, and the exchange of merchandise was first invented by men. The rough daring of navigation, too, was first attempted in these times, and many other things of that kind.

V.

The fifth governor of the world was Samael, who began on the 26th day of the month of June, in the year of the world 1417. He governed the world for 354 years and 4 months, until the year 1771, the eighth month. Under his rule men imitated the nature of Mars. Likewise, under the governance of this Samael, the universal flood occurred, in the year of the world 1656, as is clearly evident from the history of Genesis. And it should be noted that the ancient philosophers handed down that whenever Samael, spirit of Mars, is ruler of the world, then a notable alteration of monarchy arises. Religions and sects are varied, laws are changed, and principalities and kingdoms are transferred to foreigners, as we can easily find in the histories in order. But Samael does not at once from the beginning of his rule manifest this disposition of his character, but after he has passed the middle of his governance; the same is to be understood of the spirits of the other planets, as is evident in the histories, all of whom, according to the properties of the nature of their stars, influence and work upon the lower things of this world.

VI.

The sixth governor of the world was Gabriel, angel of the Moon, who began after Samael of Mars, on the 28th day of October, in the year of the world 1771, the eighth month, and governed the world for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 2126. In these times men were again multiplied, and founded various cities. And it should be noted that the Hebrews say that the flood took place in the year of the world 1656, under the rule of Mars. But the Seventy interpreters, Isidore, and Bede confirm that it took place in the year 2242, under the governance of Gabriel, spirit of the Moon, which also seems to me more consonant with truth, by a multiplication which it is not for the present time to express.

VII.

The seventh governor of the world was Michael, angel of the Sun, who began on 24 February, in the year of the world, according to the common reckoning, 2126, and governed the world for 354 years and four months, until the year of the age of the world 2480, four months. Under the rule of the angel of the Sun, as the histories agree with the truth, kings first began to exist among mortals; among them Nimrod was the first, through lust for domination, to seize tyrannical rule over his fellows. The worship of gods, too, was instituted by the folly of men, and the humble began to worship their princes as gods. Various arts were also invented by men at this time, namely mathematics, astronomy, and magic; and the worship of the one God began to be offered to diverse creatures, and the knowledge of the true God gradually fell into oblivion through the superstition of men. In these times, too, architecture was invented, and men began to use more refined customs and institutions.

VIII.

Thereafter, in the eighth order, Orifiel, angel of Saturn, again began to govern the world on the 26th day of the month of June, in the year from the origin of the world 2480, four months; and for 354 years and four months he governed the world a second time, until the year of the world 2834 and the eighth month. Under the governance of this angel, peoples were multiplied, the earth was divided into regions, many kingdoms were established, the Tower of Babel was built, the confusion of languages took place, men were scattered over the whole earth, and men began to cultivate the earth more carefully, to establish fields, to sow grain, to plant vineyards, to set trees in the ground, and to acquire more diligently whatever pertains to food and clothing. From this time first among men

Mystical Chronology.

[among men] the distinction of nobility began to be made, when men excelling the rest both in character and in talent received the insignia of glory from the great men of the earth according to their merits. Hence first the whole world began to come into human knowledge, when peoples had multiplied everywhere, and both many kingdoms arose and various differences of languages followed.

IX.

In the ninth order Anael, the spirit of Venus, again began to govern the world on the 29th day of October, in the year of the creation of heaven and earth 2834, in the 8th month; and he presided for 354 years and 4 months, down to the year of the world 3189. In these times human beings, consigning the true God to oblivion, began to worship and honor the dead and their statues as God; this error occupied the world for more than two thousand years. Introducing elaborate adornments of the body and various kinds of musical instruments, human beings again pursued lust and the pleasure of the flesh to excess; in these times also people established and dedicated statues and temples to their gods. Incantations and malefic arts were devised in those times by Zoroaster, first king of the Bactrians, and by various others; Ninus, king of the Assyrians, defeated him in war.

X.

In the tenth order Zachariel, the angel of Jupiter, again began to govern on the last day of the month of February, in the year of the foundation of heaven and earth 3189; and he governed, as usual, for 354 years and 4 months, down to the year of the world 3543 and the 4th month. These were happy times, which could truly be called golden, in which the abundance of all things both brought increase to the human race and gave the greatest adornment to the world. Likewise at this time God gave Abraham the law of circumcision, and first promised the redemption of the human race through the incarnation of his only-begotten Son. Under the rule of this spirit the patriarchs, founders of justice, were illustrious, and the just were divided from the impious by their own will and deed. In these times also Jupiter was illustrious among the Arcadians; he is also Lisania, son of heaven and of God, a king, who first gave laws to the Arcadians, made them very civilized in their customs, taught the worship of God, built temples, instituted priests, and provided many useful things for the human race. For these reasons he was called Jupiter by them and, after death, was regarded as God. He derived his origin from the son of Eber, namely Jerah, as the histories relate. Prometheus also, the son of Atlas, under the rule of this angel is said to have made men, because from rude people he made them learned, humane, gentle, and refined in morals and knowledge; by art he made images move by themselves. He first devised the use of the ring; likewise he invented the scepter, the diadem, and the royal insignia. Other Jovian persons also were illustrious in these times, very wise men and women, who by their talent handed down many inventions useful to the human race; and because of the greatness of their wisdom, after death they were thought to have been numbered among the gods, namely Phoroneus, who first established laws and judgments among the Greeks; Sol, Minerva, Ceres, Serapis among the Egyptians; and very many others.

XI.

In the eleventh order Raphael, the spirit of Mercury, again assumed rule on the first day of the month of July, in the year of the world 3543, the 4th month; and he presided for 354 years and 4 months, down to the year of the creation of heaven and earth 3897 and the 8th month. In these times, as is clearly evident from the histories of the ancients, human beings devoted themselves more to wisdom; among them were at last very illustrious persons: Mercury, Bacchus, Omogyrus, Isis, Inachus, Argus, Apollo, Cecrops, and very many others, who by their inventions benefited both the world at that time and posterity. Various superstitions also in the worship of idols were established by human beings in these times, and incantations and the arts of diabolical images were wonderfully increased; and whatever subtlety and ingenuity is customarily attributed to Mercury was then augmented. Moses, the very wise leader of the Hebrews, skilled in many matters and arts, worshiper of the true and one God, delivered the Hebrew people from the servitude of the Egyptians into freedom. At this time also Janus first reigned in Italy; after him came Saturn, who taught that fields were enriched with dung, and was regarded as God. Around this time Cadmus invented Greek letters, and Carmentis, daughter of Evander, Latin ones. God almighty, under the rule of this Raphael, angel of Mercury, gave his people the law in writing through Moses, which gives manifest testimony to the future birth of Christ in the flesh. A wonderful diversity of religions also arose in the world. Many Sibyls, prophets, soothsayers, haruspices, magi, and seers also flourished in these times, such as the Erythraean Sibyl, the Delphic, and the Phrygian, with the rest.

XII.

In the twelfth order Samael, the angel of Mars, began to govern the world anew on the 2nd day of the month of October, in the year of the world 3897, the 8th month; and his rule lasted for 354 years and 4 months, down to the year 4152. Under his rule there occurred that great and most famous destruction of Troy in Asia Minor, and a wondrous [unclear] of the monarchy and of many kingdoms was made

Paris. Mainz. Origin of the Venetians. Saul. Homer. Elijah. Elisha [unclear]. Lycurgus. Fall of the Assyrian monarchy. The city of Rome is built. The Seven Sages of Greece. Romulus. Numa. Hezekiah. Nebuchadnezzar. Zedekiah. Jeremiah. The Persian monarchy. The Cumaean Sibyl. Tarquinius Priscus. Change [unclear] of the Roman commonwealth. Pythagoras. Ezra.

Of Johannes Trithemius

...a remarkable change and the new founding of many cities, so that Paris, Mainz, Carthage, Naples, and others arose anew, and kingdoms arose anew, such as those of the Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, Hebrews, and many others. In these times there were very great wars and battles of kings and peoples throughout the whole world, and various changes of empires. From this time the Venetians reckon the beginning both of their people and of their city from the Trojans. And it should be noted that very many other nations, both in Europe and in Asia, claim that they took their origin from the Trojans; to them I have thought fit to grant only as much credence as they themselves can persuade me of the truth by sufficient testimony. Trifling are the things they bring forward about their nobility and antiquity, wishing openly to boast, as though there had been no peoples in Europe before the destruction of the Trojans, and as though there had been no one of ignoble birth among the Trojans themselves. Likewise, under the rule of this planet Saul was made the first king of the Jews; afterward David, whose son King Solomon built at Jerusalem the temple of the true God, most famous in all the world. Hence the Spirit of God, illuminating his prophets with a fuller light of his grace, caused them to foretell not only the future incarnation of the Lord Savior but also many other things, as the sacred histories testify. Among them were Nathan, prophet of King David, Gad, Asaph, Ahijah, Shemaiah, Azariah, Anan, with many others. Homer, the Greek poet and writer of the destruction of Troy, Dares the Phrygian, and Dictys of Crete, who were present at that destruction itself and likewise described it, are read to have been alive in these times.

XIII.

In the thirteenth order, Gabriel, the spirit of the Moon, again took up the government of the world on the thirtieth day of January, in the year from the origin of the universe 4252, and continued in his rule for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 4606 and the fourth month. In this time, moreover, several prophets flourished among the Hebrews, namely Elijah, Elisha, Micah, Obadiah, and very many others. There were also various changes in the kingdom of the Hebrews. Lycurgus gave statutes and laws to the Lacedaemonians. Capetus Silvius, Liberius Silvius, Procas Silvius, and Numitor, kings of Italy, flourished under the guidance of this spirit. Many new kingdoms also took their beginnings under him, such as those of the Lydians, Medes, Macedonians, Spartans, and others. The monarchy of the Assyrians came to an end in Sardanapalus. Likewise the kingdom of the Macedonians was consumed. Various laws were imposed on human beings, and the worship of the true God was neglected; the religion of false gods was propagated exceedingly. The city of Rome was built under the rule of this spirit in the year 1484, which was the 239th year of the government of this Gabriel in order; and the kingdom of the Silvii of Italy failed, and that of the Romans began. In these times also Thales, Solon, Chilon, Periander, Cleobulus, Bias, and Pittacus, the seven sages, flourished in Greece, and from this time philosophers and poets began to be held in esteem. First to rule at Rome was Romulus, founder of the city, for 37 years, a fratricide and cultivator of sedition. After him Numa Pompilius ruled for 42 years; he enlarged the worship of the gods, and in the time of Hezekiah king of the Jews he maintained the kingdom in great peace. Toward the end of the governance of this spirit of the Moon, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took Jerusalem, destroyed King Zedekiah, and led away the whole people captive. Jeremiah the prophet flourished; he foretold this destruction, and likewise the future liberation from Babylon.

XIV.

After Gabriel, Michael, the spirit of the Sun, again assumed the fourteenth rule of the world. He began on the first day of the month of May, in the year of the world 4606, in the fourth month, and ruled the world in his order for 354 years, until the year from the foundation of the world 4960 and 8 months. In the time of this governance Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, restored liberty and a king to the people of the Hebrews, at the direction of Michael, who, as Daniel writes, stood for the people of the Jews, to whom they had been entrusted by God. Likewise in these times the monarchy of the Persian kingdom began. Its first king was Darius, and its second Cyrus; in the days of Belshazzar they utterly destroyed that most powerful kingdom of Babylon, as Daniel and the prophets had foretold. In these times the Cumaean Sibyl flourished; she offered nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus to be bought at a price. In them were contained the sequence of future warnings and the plan of the whole commonwealth of the Romans. But when the king refused the price, the Sibyl burned the first three books in his sight, and for the remaining six she demanded the same price. When he again refused it, she also handed over another three to the fire to be burned; and she would have done the same with the last ones, had not the king, persuaded by the counsel of his men, redeemed them from destruction by paying the price that had been demanded for all. Likewise, after abolishing kings, the Romans appointed two consuls for each year. Phalaris the tyrant occupied Sicily in those times. Magic too, in those times, was held in great esteem among the kings of the Persians. Pythagoras the philosopher and many others then flourished among the Greeks. The temple at Jerusalem and the city were rebuilt. Ezra the prophet [unclear] the burned books of Moses...

Of Johannes Trithemius

from the Chaldaeans, who were also called Babylonians, restored the use of memory as an archetype. Xerxes, king of the Persians, led an army against the Greeks, but accomplished little. Rome was captured, burned, and destroyed by the Gauls, except only the Capitol, protected by a goose, which roused the weary fighters. The very famous wars of the Athenians also occurred in those times. The philosophers Socrates and Plato lived at that time. The Romans, again abolishing the consuls, established tribunes and aediles, and in these times were involved in many disasters. Alexander the Great also, after the rule of Michael had been completed, reigned in Macedonia. He destroyed the monarchy of the Persians in Darius; by his rule he subjected all Asia, together with part of Europe. He lived twelve years and five months; after his death countless wars followed, and many evils; the monarchy was divided into four. Among the Hebrews a contest began over the high priesthood. The kingdom of Syria begins.

XV.

After Michael, fifteenth in order, now for the third time Orifiel, the spirit of Saturn, assumed the rule of the world on the last day of the month of September, in the year 4960, month 8, from the creation of the universe. He presided for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 5315. Under his rule the Punic War began between the Romans and the Carthaginians. The city of Rome was almost wholly consumed by fire and water. The Colossus, a cast bronze image 126 feet high, fell in an earthquake. In this one year there was peace for the Romans after the Punic War; for 440 years they had never been without war. Jerusalem, together with the temple, was burned and destroyed by Antiochus Epiphanes. The history and wars of the Maccabees were carried on. In these times, in the year 606 from the founding of the city, Carthage was destroyed; it burned for 17 continuous days. In Sicily there was a conspiracy of 7,000 slaves against their masters. Great portents were seen in Europe in those times: domestic animals fled to the woods; blood flowed; a fiery globe flashed from heaven with a crash. Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, waged war with the Romans for 40 years. The kingdom of the Hebrews was restored, which had been interrupted for 575 years, from the time of Zedekiah down to Aristobulus. Likewise the German Teutons invaded the Romans; after many battles they are said to have been defeated, and 160,000 were killed, besides innumerable others who killed themselves together with their households, under the consuls Gaius and Manlius. Nevertheless, many of the Romans had previously been destroyed by them. Finally, the civil wars, which lasted 40 years, greatly wore down the Romans. Three suns appeared at Rome, but not for long, and soon they were reduced to one. A few years later Julius Gaius Caesar usurped the empire of the Romans; Octavian Augustus after him enlarged it, and united Asia, Africa, and Europe into one monarchy. He ruled for 36 years; through him God bestowed peace on the whole world. In the year 751 from the founding of the city, the 42nd of Octavian Caesar Augustus, in the 245th year and 8th month of the aforesaid rule of Orifiel, spirit of Saturn, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of December, JESUS CHRIST, Son of God, was born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem of Judaea. Note how beautiful was the ordering of divine providence. For the world was first created under the rule of Orifiel, and under his third rule also was mercifully redeemed, restored, and renewed, so that so great a harmony of events seems to furnish no small credibility to this description of the rule of the world by the seven spirits. For under the first rule of Orifiel there was one monarchy of the whole world; under the second, as we said above, it was divided among many; again under the third, as is seen, it was recalled into unity. It is clear, if we measure rightly, that it is also manifest that under the second rule of Orifiel there was one monarchy of the whole world, when the tower of Babylon was being built. From this time the kingdom of the Jews was taken away, and the victims and continual sacrifice ceased; nor will liberty be restored to the Jews before the third revolution of Michael the spirit; and this will happen after the birth of Christ in the year 1880, month 8, that is, in the year of the world 7170. Sixteenth in order after Orifiel, Anael, the spirit of Venus, [assumed] the rule of the whole world for the third time.

XVI

Sixteenth in order after Orifiel, Anael, the spirit of Venus, [assumed] the rule of the whole world for the third time

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS

... resumed it for the second time, on the last day of January, in the year of the creation of heaven and earth 5315, but from the birth of Christ 169; and he governed the world for 354 years and 4 months, up to the year of the world 5669, 4 months, but of the Lord’s Nativity in the flesh 463. And it should be noted that through almost the whole period of this rule of Anael, angel of Venus, the Church of the Christians flourished and prevailed amid persecutions, countless thousands of men being killed for the faith of Christ. Finally, many heresies in these times began to spring up in the Church, which in time were extinguished not without the labor and blood of good men. In these times there flourished many men most learned and eloquent in every kind of knowledge: theologians, astronomers, physicians, orators, historiographers, and others like them, not only among the nations but also among Christians. At length the persecution of unbelievers against the Church ceased after Constantine Caesar the Great accepted the faith, in the year of the world 5539, after the middle of the rule of this Anael, angel of Venus; although even afterwards it was sometimes disturbed in part by impious men, nevertheless it remained very quiet for a long time. From this time the human race, which from the time of King Ninus had wandered wretchedly in the worship of idols for 2300 years, was mercifully called back to the knowledge of one God. Various arts of subtlety were increased in these times, and through the harmonies of nature received adornment and growth. For the morals of men change with time, and lower bodies are disposed according to the influence of the higher ones. The mind indeed is free, and does not receive the influence of the stars, unless, by reason of the too great commerce which it has with the body, it stains its own affection by inclining itself. For the angels, who are the movers of the spheres, destroy or overturn nothing of those things which nature has established.

A comet of unusual magnitude preceded the death of Constantine. The Arian heresy troubled the holy Church in many places at the end of this rule. In the time of Julian Caesar, crosses appeared on men’s linen garments. In Asia and Palestine there followed wars, plagues, and famines in those places in which the crosses had appeared. In these times also, around the year of the Lord 360, the Franks took their beginning in Germany; afterwards, devastating Gaul, they called the conquered land Francia by their own name. The extent of Francia was long and broad in size; its metropolis was Mainz, but now only Würzburg. The Bavarians, Swabians, Rhinelanders, Saxons, Thuringians, and the surrounding bishoprics today occupy a great part of Francia in Germany. Likewise, in the 280th year of the governance of this Anael, the Roman empire began to decline, when the city was captured by the Goths and burned, the imperial seat having previously been transferred under Constantine to Greece; this was the beginning and cause of the decline of the whole monarchy. For around the end of this rule of Anael there arose Radagaisus, Alaric, and Athaulf, kings of the Goths; likewise afterwards Genseric of the Vandals, and also Attila of the Huns, who, roaming through all Europe, wretchedly tore the empire apart, as is clear in the histories.

XVII.

After Anael, in the seventeenth order, Zachariel, spirit of Jupiter, resumed the universal rule for the third time on the first day of January, in the year of the world 5669, the fourth month, but of the Lord’s Nativity 463, the seventh month; and he presided for 354 years and four months, up to the year of the world 6023 and the eighth month, but of the Lord [unclear]. In these times many, through love of Christian philosophy, betook themselves to the desert; many portents also appeared: comets, earthquakes, rain of blood. Merlin, born in Tumba, foretold marvelous things at the beginning of this rule. Arturus, whom the common people call Arthur, the most famous king of Britain, defeated the barbarians, restored peace to the Church, fought many battles as victor, enlarged the faith of Christ, and subjected all Gaul, Norway, Dacia, and many provinces to his rule. He was the most glorious of all the kings of his time; after accomplishing many outstanding deeds, he appeared nowhere, though the Britons expected for many years that he would return. Of him the mimes once produced marvelous songs. In his reign England was in flower, and thirty kingdoms served him. In these times the orders of monks in the Church of God began to multiply. Theodoric, king of the Goths, an Arian, possessed all Italy and killed the consul Boethius. Everything was full of disturbance, both the empire and the Church. Zeno and Anastasius, Arian emperors in the East, Theodoric and his successors in Italy, and Honorius, king of the Vandals, in Africa, exercised no small tyranny. At length Clovis, king of the Franks in Gaul, having become a Christian, both overcame the Goths and imposed peace on affairs, though not everywhere on earth, in the time of Saint Benedict, in the five-hundredth year of the Christians, or thereabouts, at the beginning of the rule of this angel Zachariel of Jupiter, whose proper function as a spirit is to change empires and kingdoms; that this was done in this revolution the histories declare in many ways. And what he himself could not do, he [left] for Raphael, angel of Mercury, his successor, to do...

Mystical Chronology.

...he ordained that it should be done in Charles of the Franks. For many kingdoms failed in these 350 years: those of the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, Thuringians, Alemanni, Bavarians, and very many others. The emperor Justinian was the first to adorn the commonwealth most splendidly with laws. Under Zachariel several very famous men flourished; Justinian built the church of Saint Sophia [unclear] a tower at Constantinople. The empire was more often divided in two, confused, and full of disturbances. Many signs appeared in these times, as may be found in the histories. Chosroes, king of the Persians, took Jerusalem; Heraclius later killed him. Muhammad the Arab introduced the sect of the Saracens in these times, around the year of Christ 600; through it the Roman empire in Asia is now seen to have been wholly taken away. Dagobert, king of France, overcame and killed the Angles, who were then called Saxons. It should be noted that from this point the Christian faith gradually began to fail in Asia and Africa, as the sect of the Saracens entered in; it has now defiled almost the whole world. Around the year of the Lord 774, crosses appeared on people’s clothing, and not long afterward the Roman empire was divided, the monarchy being transferred to the Franks in Charles, who rescued the Church and the empire from destruction and fought many battles. Under him, after the victory, the name of the [Westphalians?] in Saxony began.

XVIII.

In the eighth place after Zachariel, the angel of Jupiter, Raphael, the spirit of Mercury, took up the government of the world for the third time, on the second day of the month of November, in the year from the creation of the universe 6023, in the eighth month, but in the year of the Lord’s nativity 817; and he presided over the world for [354?] years and 4 months, until the year of the world 6378, but of the Lord 1171. At the beginning of this revolution, as we have said, the monarchy of the Roman empire was transferred to Charlemagne. After Charles, his son Louis ruled for 25 years. When he had died, his sons, fighting among themselves, again weakened the forces of the empire. The Normans devastated Gaul [unclear] Saracens. Under Louis the Second, blood rained from heaven in Italy for three days. In Saxony a certain village, with all its buildings and people, was swallowed up in a moment by a horrible opening of the earth. Around the years of the Lord 910, great disturbances occurred in Italy, and Italy broke away from the empire of the Franks and set up kings of its own; the first of them was Berengar, duke of Friuli, and seven succeeded him in order, for almost fifty years, down to the transfer of the empire to the Germans. Otto became the first emperor, and from this point the monarchy began to be restored; his son Otto and his grandson Otto succeeded him in the empire. Under them the Hungarians were converted to the Christian faith. Otto the Third, dying without children, established the electors of the empire after him, in the year of the Christians 1002, as they remain to the present day. Jerusalem, however, was taken by the Saracens. Many portents were seen in heaven, air, earth, sea, and waters. When Otto the Third had died, Henry was the first to succeed by election of the princes; he ruled for 20 years. He founded the Church of Bamberg, and, dying a virgin together with his wife Kunigunda, shone with miracles. After him Conrad was elected, the first duke of the Franks, and he ruled for 20 years. Likewise Godfrey, count of Bouillon, recovered the Holy Land and Jerusalem from the hands of the infidels. Before the end of the revolution many signs and portents were seen, and after a short time had elapsed the people of the Tartars, going forth from their own borders, did many evils to the Roman empire. Famines, pestilences, and earthquakes occurred in the empire. Three suns were seen in the East, and the same number of moons, in the year of the Lord 1153. Frederick I, called Barbarossa, began to rule, and he ruled for 33 years. The beginning of his rule was in the 336th year of Raphael. He performed many deeds magnificently, enlarged the forces of the empire, and successfully waged many wars; in his time [unclear] and [unclear] were converted to the faith of Christ.

XIX.

In the nineteenth order Samael, the spirit of Mars, took up the universal empire of the world for the third time, on the third day of March, in the year of the world [6378?], and governed for 354 years and 4 months, until the year of the world 6732, in the fourth month, but of the Lord 1525. Under his rule there were many wars throughout the world; in them countless thousands of people perished, and very many kingdoms lost their former boundaries. Between Frederick the First, emperor, and the Roman nobles there were many discords and great battles, and many thousands of Romans perished. The said Frederick overthrew Milan from its foundations. Jerusalem was again taken by the Saracens. The empire of all the Tartars, the greatest in the world at this time, took its beginning in these times; they inflicted a very great scourge on the world, and they do not cease. After Frederick, his son Henry was chosen emperor. When he had died, schism threw the empire into confusion under Philip and Otto, and many endless battles followed in Germany, at Strasbourg, Cologne, Liege, Worms, Speyer, and throughout the whole kingdom. The sect of the mendicants

Three suns in the East. Destruction of Milan. Incursions of the Tartars. Rumors of wars. Decline of the faith.
