Therefore, in the seventh year of Clodomir, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 426, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, on the ninth day of the month of April, by command of the aforesaid king, there went out from the mouths of the Rhine, where the Sicambri had once had their first settlements in Germany, with their wives, children, household goods [unclear], and pack animals, thirty-six armed men [unclear], farmers and craftsmen of various trades, two thousand six hundred eighty-six, setting out for the new settlements promised to the Franks by the Thuringians. They did not all go out together at one time, but successively by bands, beginning on the prescribed day, until at last in the month of September they completed the number previously designated, as Hunibald, the historian of the Franks, attests.

King Clodomir appointed as duke of the people of Eastern Francia his brother Genebald, to whom, according to the custom of the Franks, he entrusted both the army and the administration of the whole duchy on these conditions: namely, that both he himself and his sons, heirs, and successors should remain forever under the authority of the kings of the Franks, should faithfully obey their commands in all things, should go forth with them to war against any adversaries whatever, and, according to the custom of the other dukes of the kingdom of the Franks, should everywhere render to those kings the service and honor owed to them.

When these conditions had been given and accepted, Genebald, duke of Eastern Francia, set out with the people assigned to him for Menigantium, and ruled the principality offered to him for almost thirty years. For he was a prudent, bold, and warlike man, who not only governed and distributed the land of the duchy of Francia prudently, but also greatly enlarged the boundaries of its possession.

When the Suebi heard of the arrival of the Eastern Franks at their borders, they bore it rather ill, fearing that what did happen would come to pass: that, multiplied in number and strength, they would also extend the boundaries of the possession they had received to the Suebi’s ruin. But when they saw that they could in no way resist the undertakings of the Franks, pretending a welcoming gathering for their arrival and sending envoys, they asked for peace, more from necessity, as it seemed to many, than from intention. They also [unclear] every cause of dissension that they alleged against the Thuringians.

Peace is established between the Suebus and Francia. Marcomir, duke of the Eastern Franks. All the Thuringians [unclear].

In the same year, in the month of September, Marcomir, son of Duke Genebald, with the remaining band of Franks which had already earlier been chosen by King Clodomir’s command for migration, by families, households, and persons, came into the southern borders of Thuringia, and around the river Main, with his brothers, to receive the dwellings promised to them: having to the east the Boii and Bohemians; to the south, the Suebi; to the west, the Rhenish people, the people of Mainz, and the Apodae; and to the north, the Fagophagi and Thuringians.

At the entrance of the Franks all the Thuringians fall [unclear].

At the entry of the Franks, the Thuringians, by command of their king Heurolus, withdrew beyond the forest, leaving behind for the new guests all the grain sufficient for the following year. Therefore the newly arrived Franks first settled in the borders of the Thuringians, between the river Saale, as it is now called from Salagaast, and the lower parts of the Neckar, around the banks of the river Main, in that district which was formerly Meningau and was later called Eastern Francia. In it, in the course of time, they built not a few villages and cities in number, and grew in [unclear] and power.

Genealogy of the dukes of Eastern Francia. Faramund, duke [unclear] of the Eastern Franks. Marcomer, son of Faramund, duke.

Duke Genebald begot Marcomir and Dagobert, who ruled over Eastern Francia for twenty-one years. Dagobert begot Clodius, who ruled over the people for ten years. Clodius begot Marcomir. Faramund, however, governed the duchy with his father and alone for fifteen years, and afterward was chosen king of the Franks, as we shall say in its proper order. He entrusted the duchy of Eastern Francia to his brother Marcomir, who held it for eighteen years. Duke Marcomir begot Priamus, who ruled for twelve years. Duke Priamus begot Genebald the second, who ruled for twenty-one years. When he was struck and killed by a boar while hunting, Clodomir, son of the aforesaid Duke Sunno, succeeded in the duchy and ruled for thirty-one years. Clodomir begot Hugbad, who ruled for twenty-six years. Hugbad begot Helenus, who ruled for thirty years. Helenus begot Gotfrid, who ruled for twenty-four years. Godfrid begot Genebald the third, who ruled for twenty years. Genebald begot Clodomir, who ruled for twenty-four years. After him Heribert, his nephew, succeeding in the duchy, ruled for thirty years. When he too had died, Clodoveus, son of his brother, ruled in the duchy

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Annals of Trithemius.

... held office for twelve years. Clodoucus begot Gosvertus, who held office for twenty-six years. In his sixth year Conon, pope of Rome, ordained Saint Kilian, a Scottish monk, as bishop and sent him to the Eastern Franks to preach the faith of Christ. Gosbert begot the younger Gosbert, who held office for nineteen years. The younger Gosbert begot Hetan, who held office for twenty years. When, with him, the male line had died out, in the year of the Lord's nativity 740, in the eighth Roman indiction, the duchy of Eastern Francia remained without a duke for twelve years, under the authority of Pippin, mayor of the palace and afterwards king of the Franks, who entrusted it to his son Charles the Great.

Thus there were in Eastern Francia twenty-one dukes, succeeding one another over 414 years; they make up the sacred sevenfold number tripled in order, and not foreign to mystery. In the year of the Lord's nativity 752, in the fifth Roman indiction, Pippin, raised from mayor of the palace to king of the Franks, as was said above, handed over the often-mentioned duchy of Eastern Francia to Saint Burchard, first bishop of the church of Wurzburg, and to his successors, as perpetual property.

From that time, apart from the bishops of the church of Wurzburg, down to the present day no one by right has been able to claim for himself the duchy of the aforesaid Francia, although by the rashness, not the right, of certain kings and emperors rebellious against the Roman Church and excommunicated, as if in vengeance for themselves, the contrary was sometimes attempted. Among these Conrad, the third of that name, afterwards emperor, since he was Swabian by nation, violently usurped for himself the duchy of Eastern Francia by royal permission; nevertheless, after he had been made Caesar, he restored it to the church with manifold satisfaction.

Let these things, briefly touched upon in a necessary historical digression concerning the origin, genealogy, and succession of the dukes of the people of Eastern Francia, suffice. Let us now return to the order of the kings of the Franks, from which we departed. Clodomir, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely performed, at last died in the eighteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 337, in the tenth Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Seventh.

Richimer, the elder son of King Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned for thirteen years. Throughout all the days of his reign he was always in contention with the Romans and Gauls; with the aid of his uncle Genebald, that is, the duke of Eastern Francia, residing at the city [unclear], and of the other princes of the Franks, as well as the Thuringians, Saxons, and fierce German allies, he fought against them many times as victor and afflicted them with great slaughter.

In the fourth year of his reign, having gathered the support of his allies with a very great multitude of fighters, he entered Gaul and laid everything waste with fire and sword. Against him Tiberianus, prefect of the Romans, also moved a great army of his men to war; when their forces were joined for battle, they fought for a long time with doubtful fortune, and many fell slain on both sides. At last, however, the Gauls were defeated and compelled to seek safety in flight.

In the sixth year of King Richimer, in the fourth indiction, the Romans, gathering in troops into one body with the Gauls, under Constantine the Great, Caesar, declared war on the Franks. King Richimer, since he was a high-souled, strong, and bold prince, was in no way terrified; as usual he summoned as allies the Teutons, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians. When these had been united with the Franks, he set against the Romans and Gauls an army of almost two hundred thousand, with whom he fought vigorously. In the first engagement the Romans were victorious; in the second, defeated and overcome, they fled with loss among their men.

In the last year of his reign, Richimer, king of the Franks, when he was [unclear] about to fight again with the Romans, was killed in battle, namely in the thirteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord's nativity 350, in the eighth Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Eighth.

Theodomir, son of the aforementioned King Richimer, reigned after the death of his father for ten years. Throughout all the days of his reign he lived in contention with the Romans and fought many battles against them with varying outcome. His mother, named Hafila, was the daughter of the king of the Saxons. At that time the kings of the Franks lived in the territories of the Tungri, across the river Meuse, in the fortress which antiquity called Dispargum. From the boundary of the Franks as far as the river Loire the Gauls dwelt under the rule of the Romans; beyond the Loire were the Goths, intermixed with peoples of various nations.

Theodomir reigned ten years.

The seat of the kings of the Franks was among the Tungri at Dispargum.

The duchy of Eastern Francia was vacant for twelve years.

There were twenty-one dukes at [Wurzburg?].

These prelates and dukes of the Eastern Franks Trithemius enumerates in order down to his own age in the Compendium on the Origin of the Franks, published at Basel, vol. I of German Histories, folio 322.

The duchy of Eastern Francia belongs solely to the aforesaid church of Wurzburg.

Conrad [I?], not duke of [unclear], but [unclear].

Richimer reigned thirteen years.

War is joined between the Franks and the Romans.

The Romans again declared war on the Franks.

The Romans are defeated by the Franks in battle.

Theodomir reigned ten years.

The seat of the kings of the Franks was among the Tungri at Dispargum.

Saint Kilian is made bishop.

Compendium, Book I.

The Franks [unclear]. The Eastern Franks cross the Rhine. The city of Trier is destroyed by the Franks.

The boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks at this time were greatly enlarged beyond the Meuse; they had occupied a great part of Gaul, though the Romans were unwilling. Nor did they desist from what they had begun, until at length, reckoning from this point onward, within about seventy years they subjected all Gaul to their rule.

In the times of the aforesaid king Theodomirus, Dagobert, son of Genebald, the first duke of the Eastern Franks, and successor to his father in the principate, gathered a multitude of fighters, crossed the Rhine, and, after carrying off booty, laid waste Cisrhenian Gaul with fire and sword. He plundered and burned the very ancient city of Trier, built in the times of Abraham, prince of the Jews.

But King Theodomirus was at length captured by the Romans inhabiting Gaul, together with his mother Hastila, was beheaded, and died in the tenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 460, in the third Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Ninth.

The reign of Clogio: 18 years. Saint Anthony dies. Julian the apostate fights with the Alemanni. The Franks take the city of Cambrai. The Franks hold Gaul as far as the Saone. The legions of the Romans in Germany. War of the Romans with the Saxons.

Clogio, son of King Theodomirus, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for eighteen years, a spirited, strong prince, and of singular prudence. He fought many battles with the Romans and Gauls, and harshly avenged the death of both his father and his mother in the blood of very many enemies. In his first year, Saint Anthony, abbot and hermit, departed to the Lord on the seventeenth day of the month of January, in the 105th year of his age.

At the same time also the Alemanni had a war with the Romans, not far from the Rhine, in the territories of the people of Strasbourg. In that battle many fell on both sides; yet more of the Alemanni were killed than of the Romans, whose army’s commander was Julian Caesar, despiser of God and apostate.

Clogio, king of the Franks, wishing to avenge his father’s death, gathered a huge army, entered Gaul in force, and stormed the city of Cambrai, where he killed without pity many Romans whom he found there.

Advancing from there, he subjected Gaul to his kingdom as far as the river Saone. Against him the Romans, fighting more with treacheries than with strength, could do nothing.

In the thirteenth year of Clogio, king of the Franks, while the leaders with their armies were laying waste the Gallic provinces, Valentinian, Caesar of the Romans, having secretly and swiftly led legions through Sarmatia into the territories of the Germans, waged war with the Saxons in the territories of the Franks, this side of the Oder, not far from the sea. In it many on both sides fell, killed by the sword. Yet victory at last passed to the Romans, and the defeated Saxons took flight.

But King Clogio died in the eighteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 378, in the sixth Roman indiction, leaving three sons by the queen: Marcomirus, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Dagobert, who after the death of the brother just named held the kingdom under the name of duke, as we say below in its own place; and Hector, surnamed Degenbart, from whom Pippin and Charles, afterward emperor, the Great, derived their lineage, as we have said in the second volume.

The Fortieth.

Marcomirus, Clogio’s elder son, succeeding his father in the aforesaid year in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for fifteen years, a magnanimous, strong, and bold prince, who fought many battles with the Romans.

Indeed, in the first year of his reign the Romans, aided by the forces of the Gauls, stirred up war against him. He met them with the Franks and Saxons in a fearless encounter, fought bravely not far from the city of Cologne, struck down many thousands of the enemy, and divided the spoils among his helpers and friends. This war lasted four years.

But the Franks, spirited with their inborn ferocity, met the Romans for battle, just as a lion is accustomed to tear apart a little dog with extended claws, as men to be handed over at once to death and without pity. At length, after four years had passed, the Romans, considering that they could not tame the Franks and subject them to themselves, recalled by [edict?] the remnants of the legions that had survived, and sent them to other places. Yet the Franks, not ceasing on that account from harassing the Gauls, continued what they had begun.

In the ninth year of Marcomirus, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Maximus, king of Britain, sprung from the lineage of the Caesars, received the name and diadem of the Roman Empire from the soldiers stationed in England.

A few years earlier Octavius, king of Britain, lacking a son, had called him from Rome into Britain with the consent of the nobles; for he was a Briton on his mother’s side, but a Roman on his father’s; and he gave him his daughter

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Annals of Trithemius.

his wife, with whom, after Octavius had died, he obtained the kingdom of the whole island. He had come, however, when summoned into Britain, with an army of Roman soldiers, and the greater part of the soldiers remained with him, a smaller number returning to Italy. Then, after the death of Valentinian and Valens, the Caesars, in the fifth year of his British reign, lifted up in mind into pride and impatient of peace, he had himself made Caesar of the Romans by those soldiers who had remained with him, against Gratian, whom the Romans had set over them. Therefore, as soon as he was hailed as Caesar by the soldiers, he entrusted the kingdom of Britain to be governed by a deputy, and, summoning into one body all the nobility and the military youth of the whole island of Britain, which is now called England, he sailed with them into Gaul, having this intention in mind: that, once the Gauls had been conquered, he would set out for Rome and subject the empire to himself.

Accordingly, in the ninth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 487, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Maximus, king of Britain, entered Gaul by ship with a great multitude of his men and laid waste everything round about the region in hostile fashion. And first indeed he landed with his ships on the shore of the land of Armorica, which from that time thereafter has been called New Britain, or Lesser Britain, down to the present day. The Franks then inhabited it, under the governance of Duke Iubalchus, whom the kings of the Franks had appointed deputy of the kingdom in those places. Duke Iubalchus, not a little disturbed by the entry of so great a multitude of peoples, drew together the forces of his men as best he could, and, advancing to meet those who were coming, joined battle with them. In that battle he himself was killed with fifteen thousand Franks, while the rest sought safety in flight.

Then, in order to strike terror of his name into all throughout the kingdom, he used great cruelty: for he slaughtered without mercy women, virgins, old men, young men, and little children, as many as he found. The kings, dukes, nobles, soldiers, and all the people of the Franks were still blinded and polluted by the empty superstition of idols. Maximus, however, although a tyrant, was nevertheless, with all his soldiery and his people, Christian. After this victory over Iubalchus had been won from the Franks, Maximus bestowed that Armorican principality on Duke Conan, who was the nephew by his brother of Octavius, the aforesaid king of Britain; and, leaving with him a good part of the army of the Britons for protection, he himself departed from there with the remaining multitude of troops and, ranging through all Gaul, made those who resisted his rule obedient by war and arms, no less cruelly than powerfully.

Meanwhile Gratian Caesar at Rome, learning that Maximus had usurped for himself the name and diadem of the Roman empire and, having gone out from Britain with a great army, had begun to lay waste Gaul, himself gathered troops and moved against him into Gaul, entering the city of Paris with his army. Afterwards, engaging with Maximus, he was overcome through the treachery of Merobaudes, master of the soldiers; slipping away in flight, he came to Lyons, where later he was killed.

Conan, however, whom Maximus had established as king in the Armorican region, frequently met [unclear], fought manfully with [unclear], and, after many of them had been killed, turned the rest to flight. Having at last obtained peace and quiet possession of the Armorican kingdom, he began to take counsel with his nobles as to how they might as quickly as possible have their wives and children, whom they had left in Britain, brought to them with all their household equipment, lest the offspring of their race should fail.

The number of soldiers who had come from Britain with Conan into Armorica was thirty thousand fighting men; of commoners and farmers, however, as Geoffrey is the authority, there were one hundred thousand, all of whom had sailed by command from Britain into Armorica. Of these many did not have wives; but the others who did have them had left them in Britain with their little children when they were compelled to follow Maximus. Conan, however, and all his people, since they were Christians, by no reasoning consented to take as wives the daughters of pagans who worshipped mute things. Even if they had been Christians, nevertheless it did not please them to have any matrimonial commerce of mingling with the Gauls.

There was in those days a certain petty king in Britain, which is now called England, named Dionotus, who, after the death of his brother Caradocus, held the principality of Cornwall; to him King Maximus, when about to set out for Gaul, had entrusted the kingdom, as to a most prudent man. He had an only daughter named Ursula, in the judgment of all the most beautiful among all the maidens of Britain, and very devoted to Christ. Therefore Conan, the new king of the Armoricans from Britain, [desired?] Ursula, the daughter of the aforesaid prince of Cornwall, Dionotus, not only

Cornutus, king of Britain, the name, that is, Armorica.

Dionotus, prince of Cornwall, father of Saint Ursula.

Ursula, a most prudent virgin.

30 Compendium, Book I ... knew her very well, but also loved her greatly. Therefore, having sent messengers and letters to him, he asked that she be sent to him as his wife. Secondly he asked that, when the husbands went out by Maximus’s command, they should put on ships the wives and children of the soldiers and common people left in Britain, together with their household goods, and send them to him into the Armorican kingdom. Thirdly he commanded that, according to the number which he had expressed in his letter, virgins should be sent: noble women, for the soldiers of noble lineage; and likewise common women for the commoners, whom each man who then had no wife might take as wives for themselves.

Dionotus, seeing Conanus’s messenger and wishing to satisfy his desire, gathered from the various provinces of Britain eleven thousand daughters of nobles, and from the rest, of lower rank, sixty thousand virgins and women, all of whom he ordered to assemble on a fixed day within the walls of London. He also ordered ships to be brought from all the shores of Britain, sufficient for the transport of so great a multitude. Although this had pleased many in so great an assembly, nevertheless it displeased many also, who loved their parents and fatherland with greater affection. Nor were there perhaps lacking some who, preferring chastity to marriage, would have rather lost their life in any land than be married.

At last, when the things necessary for the transport had been prepared, the women entered the [appointed?] ships and, by the river Thames, passed into the seas. Finally, when they turned their sails toward the Armoricans, that is, from north to south, suddenly a great storm arose at sea, and, the fleet being divided, the ships were separated from one another. Great danger pressed upon all, and the greater part of the ships was scattered into the depth of the sea and was submerged with the women. Those who escaped so great a danger were driven to barbarous nations and islands of the sea, and by an unknown people were either slaughtered or consigned to perpetual slavery. For they had fallen upon the army of the impious princes Wanius and Melga, who, hired for pay by Caesar Gratian, were devastating Britain first, and then the maritime nations and the surrounding islands, out of hatred for Maximus; by them they cruelly perished for the love of chastity.

Wanius, moreover, was king of the Huns, or, if you prefer, Gnauius in the manner of the Gauls; Melga was king of the Picts. The emperor Gratian had hired them for pay and sent them into the borders of Germany and Gaul together, so that they might afflict those who followed the party of Maximus. Around [unclear] regions they encountered [the women] cast there by the wind; and since they were both beautiful and Christian, they solicited them to intercourse with themselves. But when the women, faithful in Christ, refused to consent to the shamefulness of the wicked men, they were miserably slain by the impious.

This lamentable history of the holy seventy-one thousand virgins and women, besides infants and little children, Hunibald does not relate; but the aforesaid author Geoffrey of Monmouth records it at the end of the fourth book, on the origin of the people and the deeds of the kings of the island of Britain, which was first called the Island of Giants; then from Brutus the first king it was called Britain; afterward it was named Albion; and finally, having obtained the name of England, it retains it to this day.

But Marcomirus, the above-mentioned king of the Franks, because he was a prudent man, so governed the reins of his principality that he followed neither the party of Maximus nor that of Gratian, because the former had taken Armorica away from the Franks, after many of them had been cruelly and without reason killed; and they cruelly slew an innumerable multitude of the people. When this had been reported to King Maximus, who at that time was staying at Trier, he sent a certain Gratian, a citizen, with two legions into Britain, to drive the enemies from there. With the Huns and Picts, however, were Scots and Norwegians, all of whom Gratian, after an engagement had been made, put to flight into Ireland.

In these times Maximus, king of the Britons and usurper of the Roman empire, after all Gaul had already been conquered and Caesar Gratian had been killed at Lyon, established the seat of his kingdom in the city of Trier; there he also called a synod of bishops, at which Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, appeared in person and shone forth with many signs and miracles. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, was also present, and Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux,

Conanus asks from Dionotus noble boys. That he should also seek wives for the soldiers and common women.

12,000 noble women. But 60,000 of the common sort, virgins and women. He took up the number of girls as 71,000.

95,000 girls placed on ships are imperiled at sea.

The greater part of the girls was submerged; the rest, captured in Barbary. Wanius and Melga, Huns and Picts, seized them.

Annals of Trithemius

[Burdigalensis?], who wrote a metrical work on the praises of his homeland and of the city of Trier, which he entitled Mosella, from the river flowing past. Jerome also, the priest of Bethlehem, at the same time copied out at Trier the book of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, On the Synods.

Maximus, moving from Trier with a very great army, appointed his infant son Victor king of the Gauls, and deputed Quintinus and Nanneus, princes of the city of Trier, as his guardians. Then he himself set out with the army into Italy and was killed by Theodosius, in the thirteenth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks. Not long afterward his son Victor also perished by the sword, to win the favor and goodwill of Theodosius.

After the death of Maximus, Marcomir king of the Franks assembled forces and sent a great army of his men into Gaul under the leaders Sunno, Genebald, Priam, and Antenor, so that they might not only recover what had been lost but also make all Gaul subject to the Franks. In a short time, recovering many things which Maximus had taken away, they also added no small part of Gaul to the kingdom of the Franks. Yet the kingdom of the Armoricans, which the Britons inhabited, as we have said, under Conan, they could not obtain on that occasion; nevertheless they afterward recovered it.

Meanwhile, while these leaders were intent on the Gallic war, the Romans, under Valentinian Caesar, who ruled with Theodosius, sent a great army into Germany, hoping to destroy the Franks utterly. Marcomir, king of the Franks, advanced against them to battle with Germans and Saxons; when the engagement was fought, he fell, slain by the enemy with many others, while others slipped away in flight, in the fifteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth Roman indiction. Valentinian, wishing to advance farther and desiring to subjugate to his rule the whole kingdom of the Franks that was in the Cisrhenane regions, was compelled to withdraw into Italy because of an incursion of the Lombards. But, craftily concealing the necessity of going back, he sent messengers to those Franks who had remained in the kingdom, through whom he commanded that they either choose war anew or pay tribute to the Romans. But the Franks, now deprived of their king, and with the strength of their soldiery [unclear] with the leaders in Gaul, since they did not know the emperor’s necessity for withdrawal and thought nothing other than war was threatening, saw that they were unequal in strength and promised tribute to the Romans. Yet they could neither promise it without the consent and will of the princes, then, as we have said, far absent, nor pay it. When Valentinian the emperor had carried out these matters with the Franks as he wished, he set out against the Lombards.

Meanwhile all the things that the Romans, under Valentinian, had done with the Franks were reported to the leaders of the Franks, Dagobert, Sunno, Genebald, Priam, Antenor, and the other elders who were directing the wars of the people in the region of the Gauls: how they had condemned the king to death and bound to tribute a people which had always been free and had been subject to no one since its Trojan origin. They were angry, they were moved, they were greatly disturbed, and many deliberated in councils as to how they might prudently avenge this injury.

After much and long consultation, therefore, they finally came to one opinion: that they ought rather to preserve their ancestral fatherland in liberty than to press on with Gallic affairs. Therefore, leaving Duke Priam in the Gallic territories with a sufficient [unclear], [unclear] was ruler of the kingdom for almost five years, as Hunibald indicates, a magnanimous and warlike man. In his time Marcomir, son of Clodius, held the duchy among the Eastern Franks for sixteen years. Dagobert took up the government of the kingdom under the name of duke in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth indiction.

Dagobert, brother of Marcomir king of the Franks, who was killed by Valentinian, son of the aforesaid king Clogio, after the death of his brother was, by the consent of the Franks, interim king or governor of the kingdom for almost five years, as Hunibald indicates; he too was magnanimous and warlike. In his time Marcomir, son of Clodius, held the duchy among the Eastern Franks for sixteen years. Dagobert took up the government of the kingdom under the name of duke in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth indiction.

In the second year of Duke Dagobert, Valentinian Caesar, after sending messengers to the people of the Franks in Germany, demanded the tribute imposed in the preceding year. To him the leaders and people of the kingdom sent back word through the same messengers as follows: The everlasting liberty of the Franks is accustomed to impose tribute on other nations, not to pay it. But you, who fought with an unarmed few when the strength of the Franks was absent, conquered by war, not by courage. If you trust that you have the right to exact tribute from the Franks, come whenever you wish; by the sword we shall show [unclear] that we are, and have always been, utterly free. We make this known to you, so that you do not send anything unarmed to us on this matter, since we contend to give up life rather than lose liberty.

Valentinian demands tribute from the Franks. The Franks neglect tribute.

[unclear] that we both are and have always been utterly free, and [unclear] we shall show you. We make this known to you: do not send anything unarmed to us on this matter, since we contend to give up life rather than lose liberty.

Compendium of Book I

When Valentinian received this news, he wondered at the constancy of the Franks, and said to those standing around: “Frank, Frank, you are a hard people, to be named rather from ferocity than from liberty.” And the matter rested in the current year, because at that time the Roman commonwealth was suffering many and varied hostile incursions from different nations.

But in the following year Valentinian, misled by the counsel of his own men, again sent Sisinnius, a count of the court, to the Franks, so that by good persuasions he might induce them to the payment of tribute and to the very firm friendship of the Romans. But the Franks, not forgetful of what they had previously sent back to Valentinian, and desiring to avenge the death of Marcomir, their most beloved king, killed with the sword the count sent to them, together with the whole company that he had brought, in contempt of Valentinian and of all the Romans.

After this the Franks, having united a very great army of their men into one force, under the leaders Sunno and Genebald, whom the Gauls called Gundebaud, crossed the Rhine with violence and, breaking into the territories of the Romans, devastated everything, and even struck fear into the people of Cologne. For they were striving to subject to their own rule all that lay between the rivers Rhine, Meuse, and Tabula. But after the incursion of the Franks became known among the Treveri, Nannenus and Quintinus, leaders of the Treveri, who, like the people of Cologne, followed the Roman side, gathered an army and resolved to make attacks upon them. For meanwhile the Franks, after laying waste the region of the Gauls and killing many of them, sent the spoils on to their ancestral seats with part of the army, while they themselves proceeded farther.

When Nannenus and Quintinus of the Treveri had come with the aforesaid army to that same place, the Franks, as we have said, already laden with plunder in good number, had crossed the Rhine, intending to return to their companions, to lay waste with all their strength whatever remained untouched among the Gauls. Great confusion followed the Franks because of the ill-considered and insufficiently cautious division of the army. For the first seats of the Franks, as we have often said, were around the borders and mouths of the Rhine, where now are Holland, Zealand, the peoples of Utrecht, Gelderland, and the Frisians. Part of these later received the name Westasen, that is, western Gauls, by comparison with the others, who in the region of Münster were called Ostualen, that is, eastern Gauls. And the Franks had to the east the Saxons, Teutons, Germans, and Marcomanni; to the south, the Gauls of Cologne; to the west, the Tungri and Morini, who inhabited the seacoast; but to the north, the Scots, the Orkneys, the Danes, and likewise the sea.

Therefore, when Nannenus and Quintinus had arrived with the army of the Treveri at the places where the remainder of the Franks had stayed, awaiting the return of their companions, they drew up a battle line and pursued them as they fled as far as the Carbonarian Forest, forcing them to retreat, after slaughtering not a few of them. From this arose the hatred of the Franks toward the Treveri, because of which they later crossed the Rhine and began to winter in the region of the Treveri and to devastate everything.

After these things had been done, it seemed useful to Quintinus that they should lead the whole army of the Treveri across into Francia and, by a sudden incursion, seize the Franks while they were unprepared. But Quintinus’s counsel did not please Nannenus, who did not doubt that the Franks would be bolder in resisting on their own soil. Therefore Nannenus withdrew from Quintinus with his men and returned to Mainz.

But Quintinus, persisting in his purpose, crossed the Rhine near the fortress of Musium and led out the army. He was planning to destroy the Franks at the first attack, with a spirit prouder than his strength for victory. But the Franks, not sluggish, met the Gauls with a manly encounter; and when battle had been joined, many thousands of the Treveri perished, with few saved by flight. In that encounter fell Heracleus, tribune of the Roman legion; almost all who were in command of the soldiers perished with him by the missiles and sword of the Franks. For, with a few exceptions, to whom the black night gave safety and the woods afforded the opportunity of hiding, the whole army of Quintinus perished by sword, bow, and marsh.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, in the seventh indiction, the emperor Valentinian perished at Vienne, a city of Gaul, by trickery and by the severity of Arbogast, master of the soldiers, by a noose. A certain Roman, Eugenius, by the machination of the same Arbogast, seized the kingdom of the Gauls and reigned for three years; afterward, when war was joined with the emperor Theodosius, he was killed by him.

When the Franks heard of the death of Caesar Valentinian, they resolved to cross the Rhine and invade Gaul. Arbogast, understanding their plan, anticipated it; at Cologne Agrippina, in the harsh winter, when the Rhine was frozen, he led an army across and began to devastate, by hostile incursion, the Franks nearest to the Rhine.

14 Compendium, Book I.

To Alaric, after prior deliberation with his own men, he granted the Gauls, otherwise agitated by the fury of shifting peoples, to be inhabited by the Goths.

The Vandals, however, who had remained in the Gauls, hearing of the coming of the Goths, although they had been produced from one Scanzian nation, nevertheless, terrified by fear, abandoned Gaul; and with the Alans and Suebi they occupied part of the Spains, where, after remaining for almost thirty years, they afterwards sailed into Africa and destroyed the city of Hippo.

But Alaric, by permission of Honorius Caesar, intending to seek Gaul, departed from Italy with his men. Against him Count Stilicho, commander of the Roman army, without orders rushed upon him on the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, when he suspected no evil, and provoked him, unwilling, to battle. And in the first assault he indeed proved victor; in the second encounter, defeated, he was compelled to seek safety in flight. King Alaric, who believed that this deed had been contrived by Honorius, immediately broke the treaty which he had made with him, and, changing his route, returned into Italy and cut down everything round about.

Stilicho the count is killed by Spain.

Rome is captured and overthrown by Alaric, king of the Goths.

King Alaric captured the city of Rome, overthrew many buildings, and gravely harmed the citizens in their goods. Yet he refrained from bloodshed and the slaughter of men, and spared those fleeing to the basilicas of the saints. On the third day he departed from Rome of his own accord, and, as he was about to sail to Sicily, he endured [unclear]; and not long afterward, having fallen gravely ill, he suddenly exchanged life for death.

While these things were being done in Italy by the Goths, the Franks, thinking that the time had come when they might subject all Gaul to themselves, gathered forces and assembled a great army; and under the leaders Pharamund, Marcomir, Sunno, Priam, and Antenor, they entered the Gallican borders. First they engaged with the Vandals, who were again raiding the Gauls, and killed their king Godgisith, whom some call Godogisil, with twenty thousand men. And unless Respendial, king of the Alans, had come in timely aid to the Vandals from Spain, where he was then reigning, they would all have been killed by the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 419, Genebald, inter-king of the Franks, son of Dagobert and grandson of King Marcomir, died in the twenty-first year of his rule and beyond; after his death the Franks, as we shall say, again had kings.

For in the same year, immediately after the death of Genebald, the nobles and elders of the Franks, coming together as one, held mature counsel among themselves, judging it useful that, after the custom of the ancients, they should appoint for themselves as king one of the dukes. And the proposal seemed good in the eyes of all, and the following dukes came together for the purpose of this business at another assembly: namely Pharamund, duke of the Eastern Franks; Marcomir, duke, and Sunno, duke, brothers of Pharamund the Easterner; Clodius, duke, son of Pharamund; Dagobert, duke, son of Marcomir; Nicanor, duke; Pharabert, duke; Richimer, duke; Antenor, duke of the Menapians; Priam, duke, his brother; Berther, Gallican duke; Hieribert, duke of the Islanders; Sunno, duke, and Richer, duke, sons of Genebald, the deceased duke and inter-king of the Franks; Diocles, duke, and Meroveus, duke; Adelhard, Richer, and very many others, both from the common people and from the nobles.

All these, after sharing among themselves the counsel of mature deliberation, at last by unanimous consent elected Pharamund, duke of Eastern Francia, at Würzburg as king of the Franks; he had been the son of Duke Marcomir, who, as we said above, died in the year of the Lord 404. This Marcomir was the son of Clodius, who was the son of Dagobert, who was the son of Genebald, the first duke of the Franks and brother of King Marcomir, whose father was Clogio, king of the Franks, who, as we said above, died in the year of the Lord 478.

Pharamund [unclear] third.

The duchy of Eastern Francia he entrusted in the same year to his brother Marcomir to govern; he ruled it vigorously for eighteen years. His lineage and successors in the duchy, continuing in order down to the last duke, Heranus, and Charles the Great, son of Pippin, we described above, when we set down beforehand the genealogy of the first duke. Against him, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the dukes of the Franks moved a powerful army, and, when the enemies had been gathered, they killed more than twelve thousand of the Gauls and put the rest, with Arbogast, to flight.

After this, in the year of the Lord 397, the emperor Theodosius came from the East into Gaul with a great army against Eugenius. When Eugenius learned this, he was afraid; and, coming to the Rhine, with great entreaties and promises he implored the aid of the Franks and Saxons, which nevertheless he could not obtain. And so Theodosius, coming into Gaul, joined battle with Eugenius, gained the victory, and killed him with many [unclear]. Arbogast, however, the inventor of all evils, in despair killed himself with his own sword. Theodosius, victorious, died on his return at Milan. His body was taken back to Constantinople and buried with due honor. After him his two sons succeeded in the empire: Arcadius ruled in the East, Honorius among the Romans.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 398, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, died Dagobert, interrex of the Franks, son of the late most noble king Clodio, brother of King Marcomir.

The Forty-Second.

Genebald, the elder son of the already mentioned duke Dagobert, succeeding his father in the government of the kingdom of the Franks, was set over the people with the dukes for twenty-one years. Yet he neither wrote himself king nor was called king by others, but, content with the name of duke, usurped nothing of royal dignity for himself. He had two brothers, Marcomir and Sunno, who, together with the other dukes of the Franks, faithfully administered the commonwealth of the people and its wars by common counsel and care.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 404, in the second indiction of the Romans, died Marcomir, duke of the Eastern Franks, who dwell at Würzburg among the Thuringians [and] Suebi, a vigorous man, but a pagan, buried, according to the superstition of his homeland, on the mountain called Frankenberg.

In the duchy of the Franks [unclear], his elder son by birth, named Pharamund, succeeded him: a prudent, bold, warlike man, who was set over his people for fifteen years, and afterward, as we shall say, was elected king of the Franks by the unanimous consent of the dukes and nobles of the people.

After these things, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 410, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, while the Franks were concealing their hatred of the Romans and Gauls, Carocus, king of the Vandals, with an innumerable multitude of people, set out from the Scansian islands, or, as they are now called, the Gothic islands, made his way through Germany and the borders of Saxony, crossed the Rhine with the consent of the Franks, and entered Gaul; after laying waste the region through [unclear], he grievously afflicted the natives of the land.

He had a mother upon whose will he depended, who said to him: “If you seek an everlasting name, hear and follow my counsel. Destroy all the buildings that other kings and princes have built; kill the men whom they spared. For you will not be able to build better or more beautiful buildings than those they long ago built, nor by piety, moderation, or mercy, by sparing those whom you have conquered, make for yourself a glorious name.” Following the evil counsel of his impious mother, Carocus crossed the Rhine, erased the city of Mainz, on this side of the Rhine, together with all its inhabitants, burned it, and utterly destroyed it. Then with similar fury he attacked Worms, and afterward Speyer, and, after killing all the citizens whom he found, overthrew them. Moving from there, he besieged, captured, and destroyed the most ancient city of Trier, on this side of the Moselle, scarcely recovering a little from the slaughter inflicted by the Franks. From Trier he moved to the city of Metz; when its wall fell by a wondrous divine command, he captured and overthrew it, after all its inhabitants had been killed. For all people of either sex and of every age whom he found on the way, Carocus, that most savage enemy of nature, killed cruelly and without mercy. Having advanced from the city of the people of Metz, the savage man entered inner Gaul. After the devastation of many cities, he finally besieged the city of Arles, where he was captured by a certain soldier named Marius, bound in chains, and led about in mockery through all the cities he had devastated. He ended his excessively impious life by a worthy death.

The Vandals, however, who had remained in Gaul with the Alans, after the death of Carocus set over themselves as king Godgifith, a man notorious for crimes.

Alaric also, king of the Visigoths, devastating Italy with a great army, sent word to Caesar Honorius that either he should engage him in battle, or grant the Goths a suitable place in his kingdom to remain in peace. But Honorius, not daring to fight with [unclear].

Annals of Trithemius.

In the third year of his reign, Pharamund, king of the Franks, in order to restrain by laws a people uncultivated in customs and fierce in spirit, summoned to himself certain nobles of the kingdom and began to take mature counsel concerning the establishment of new arrangements. For the condition of the times did not admit in every respect the constitutions of the ancient kings; these, moreover, through the varied unrest of the nation, had for many years now come not only into disuse, but also utterly into oblivion and contempt. For this reason it seemed altogether necessary either to alter them by correction or to abolish them by novelty.

Now in that assembly of the Franks there were many men prudent in their generation. From their number four of the more eminent were chosen, to whom the king, together with the nobles, had entrusted full power for making laws. Their names were said to be these: Salagast, Wesogast, Wyndegast, and Batogast. The first of these built a village beside the banks of the river Meuse, which he called Salagastat after his own name; Wyndegast, however, founded in Eastern Francia the village Wyndesheim, named from his own name.

Therefore these four, meeting together, carefully handled the origins of cases through three assemblies, and, striking out a judgment on each matter, issued a new volume of legal constitutions. This received the name of the Salic Law from its chief author, Salagast, who was supreme priest of Jove; afterward King Clodoveus added chapters of interpretation to it.

In the same year the Vandals, Alans, and Suevi, having divided the region of the Spains among themselves in three parts for habitation, and having been separated into three kingdoms, assail one another with mutual and civil war. The Vandals, Alans, Suevi or Suedi, and also the Goths, Lombards, and Normans are equal in origin, so far as concerns the first homeland of their nation, having arisen at the beginning of their migration from the borders of Germany and the Scanzian or Scandian islands, which are now called Gothia under four or five divisions.

In the third year of Pharamund, king of the Franks, blessed Jerome the priest, renowned in signs, after fifty-six years with his books published and completed, so cast down in the chest by asthmatic suffering that he could not rise from bed unless he grasped with his hands a rope which hung from a beam for this purpose, died at Bethlehem, in the ninety-first year of his age, on the last day of September.

In the sixth year of Pharamund, in the year of the Lord’s birth 425, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, Saint Theonestus, bishop of Philippi in Greece, driven from his church by the violence of heretics, came into Italy, and then into the territories of Germany, with Albanus the priest, Ursus the deacon, and Abraham the subdeacon. Of these Albanus suffered at Mainz for the faith of Christ.

Pharamund, king of the Franks, died in the seventh year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s birth 426, in the ninth indiction of the Romans.

The Forty-Fourth.

Clodius, son of King Pharamund, succeeding his father in the same year, reigned twenty years: a magnanimous, strong, and warlike prince, who powerfully crushed the Gauls and Romans by his valor, extended the kingdom of the Franks far and wide through Gaul, and was to be feared by all nations throughout all Europe on account of his famous power.

At once at the beginning of his reign he commanded all the Franks by edict to grow long hair, so that the Franks might at first sight be distinguished from the Gauls, whom they were either going to attack, or had already previously permitted, after their defeat, to dwell with them. For this reason thereafter King Clodius himself was called the long-haired or the hairy, since he let his hair and beard grow long. But he ordered the Gauls defeated by him to have their hair shorn, as a sign of servitude. From this it will be permissible to infer that the Franks, Germans, subjected the Gauls to servitude; the Gauls, nor any other nation, ever conquered the Germans. For it is manifest, as Hunibald testifies, that from that time when the Franks first entered Germany until the death of King Clodoveus, who first received the faith of Christ, as we shall say, for not less than nine hundred forty years, under forty-seven kings and petty kings, they always both were and remained most free, nor did they ever serve any man, even for a moment. But after Clodoveus, since all Franks have remained free down to the present day, both those who are in Gaul and those who remained in Germany, no proof is needed, since this is known to those skilled in histories without envy.

Clodius, king of the Franks, in the eighth year of his reign, which was the 434th year of the Lord’s birth, in the second indiction of the Romans, having gathered forces, moved the army into Thuringia. The Franks, as we said far above under King Franco, in the thirty-seventh year before the birth of Christ, with the Thuringians, Saxons, Teutons, and Ger[unclear]

Pharamund, king of the Franks, caused laws to be restored. He corrected the old laws. Four Frankish lawgivers: Salagast, Wesogast, Wyndegast, Batogast. The laws of the Franks, founded, are approved by King Clodius. The Salic Law. The Vandals with the Alans and Suevi devastate Spain. The priest Jerome. Saint Theonestus. Saint Albanus is martyred at Mainz. Clodius the Long-Haired reigned twenty years. The Franks, as free men, wore long hair. The Gauls, as slaves, had their hair shorn. It was not the Gallic people who subjected the Franks to themselves, but the Franks who subjected the Gauls. All Franks, both Gallic and German, were always most free. King Clodius moved the army of the Franks into Thuringia.

had contracted a perpetual treaty with the [unclear], which was kept inviolate by all for almost 430 years, down to the death of King Marcomir. But when Marcomir, king of the Franks, had been slain by Valentinian Caesar, as was said earlier, in the year of the Lord 393, the Doringi and the Saxons, together with the Germans and the Teutons, withdrew from alliance with the Franks, matters having been managed under the dukes without sufficient foresight.

On the occasion of this dissension King Chlodio powerfully entered Doringia, defeated the king and the people, and compelled them to pay annual tribute to the Franks and thereafter to obey his commands, so that those who had refused to remain free allies under the right of the ancient treaty were forced to be their servants, subjects, and tributaries. The same thing later happened to the Germans and to the Saxons, who, after breaking the treaty of alliance, thereafter found the Franks no longer, as before, friends, but kings and lords. Then King Chlodio, crossing both the Rhine and the Meuse, set an expedition in motion into Gaul; and devastating the whole region of the Tungri and powerfully taking possession of it, he subjected it to the kingdom of the Franks. And for the confirmation of the new possession, once lost but then recovered, he settled there for some time; then, advancing as far as the Tabula, he recovered everything.

After this, in his eleventh year, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, Chlodio, king of the Franks, considering that the power of the Romans had declined not a little, sent scouts into farther Gaul, so that they might diligently reconnoiter the [unclear] of the land, the strength of the people, the [unclear] of the cities, and the guard of the fortifications, and take care to report back to him as quickly as possible. At that time the Burgundians lived in the province of Lyon, and the Goths in Aquitaine; together with the Spaniards and Gauls they were occupying the land.

When the scouts returned to Chlodio, they reported that the regions were excellent, the land thoroughly fruitful, and the site also very pleasant; that the people were unarmed, fearful, and weak, and that the Roman guard in the cities was small. Hearing this, King Chlodio, whose mind was set on nothing more than extending the name, glory, and kingdom of the Franks, gathered a great army of his men and, moving beyond the river called the Tabula toward the sea into Gaul, besieged and took the city of Cambrai, killing all the Roman soldiers whom he found in it.

Moving from there through the Carbonarian forest, he hastened swiftly and directed his course to the city of Tournai, which was fortified by a Roman garrison. The Roman soldiers who were in the garrison, when they heard of the coming of the Franks, advanced outside the city against them for battle; in that battle they were all killed by the Franks to the last man, so that not even one remained from all of them to carry news of the others’ destruction to the Romans. They subjected the city of Tournai, with the whole region, to themselves.

Then, advancing farther, the Franks received the Morini, the Taravani, and whatever remained of the Gauls as far as the sea into their complete power, and they possess all of it down to the present day, which the Romans thereafter neither recovered, nor indeed will they be able to recover it forever. For that which once flourished has withered.

But Chlodio, distinguished king of the Franks, after he had magnificently enlarged the kingdoms and had powerfully subjected to the kingdom of the Franks the whole land of the Gauls which lay between the Rhine on the east, the Morinian Sea on the west, the British Sea on the north, and the Seine toward the south, that is, the Batavi, the Menapii, the Tungri, the Taravani, the Morini, the Ambiani, the people of Cambrai, the people of Tournai, the Atrebates, the Bellovaci, and whatever lies between these regions, and beyond the Seine as far as the Loire, died in the twentieth year of his reign, and in the year 446 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the fourteenth indiction.

Forty-fifth.

Merovech, the eldest son of the aforesaid King Chlodio, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twelve years: a prince inferior to none of the preceding kings in power, courage, and greatness of deeds, who crushed the Roman Empire and, following in glorious imitation the footsteps of his father, enlarged the kingdom of the Franks not moderately in the few years in which he reigned. For all the territories of the Gauls which his father had joined to the kingdom of the Franks he not only kept under his subjection throughout all the days of his reign, but also, with the Romans wherever found either killed or put to flight, he wonderfully extended far and wide the boundaries of the acquired possession.

In the eighth year of his reign, earthquakes were almost continual, and many fearsome signs were shown in the sky. For as evening was drawing on one day, the sky appeared red as fire from the north, with [unclear] intermingled through the fire

Annals of Trithemius.

fell, and many other prodigies were seen, which the evils that followed show not to have been wholly without meaning.

For in the following year, which was the ninth of King Meroveus and the 453rd from the Lord’s Nativity, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, Attila, king of the Huns; Walamir, king of the Ostrogoths; Ardaric, king of the Gepids; and other northern peoples, conspiring together as one, came forth from the borders of Pannonia, and with five hundred thousand fighters invaded the western empire and at the same time the kingdom of the Franks in the regions of Gaul. They carried out immense slaughters and spared no one.

And first, indeed, throughout all Gaul their fury, God permitting it, raged so greatly that no fortification, strength, or power could defend a city, town, or castle from their assault. Against their insolence Meroveus, king of the Franks, and Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, and Aetius, patrician of the Romans, advanced to war with the military forces of various other peoples in a common array. With them, in the Catalaunian plains, they fought from morning until night. The Franks, with their allied companions adhering to them, defeated the enemy, although Attila was not altogether destroyed.

In that battle one hundred and eighty thousand fighters were slain, among whom also fell Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, a most warlike man. When the Franks, together with the rest who had assembled against the Huns, withdrew, King Attila took his army and returned to his homeland, so that, once his army had been restored, he might continue his foolish fury and reduce Gaul together with Italy to desolation.

For in the following year King Attila entered Italy and either plundered or utterly overthrew almost all its cities. Leo, the first pope, came to him clothed in pontifical vestments, and not only obtained safety for the city and the people, but also secured that he should leave Italy behind and depart. When he was asked by his own men why he had been so gentle toward the pontiff, he answered that he had not revered him, but rather a certain old man, venerable in appearance, standing beside him, who, with sword drawn, threatened death to the king if he either saddened the pontiff or denied anything that he asked. Not long after, King Attila, having drunk to excess at his wedding, died from a stroke of apoplexy.

In the eleventh year of Meroveus, king of the Franks, and the 457th from the Lord’s Nativity, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, the Franks captured the city of Trier on the following occasion; Attila, king of the Huns, had taken it in war a few years before and crushed it with heavy devastation.

After the death of Valentinian, whom the friends of the patrician Aetius had killed in the same year, and who had ruled after Theodosius together with Marcian, Avitus was appointed emperor by the Romans; under him the city of Trier was captured. At that time there was in the city of Trier a certain senator named Lucius, who had a wife, in the estimation of many, most beautiful; Avitus languished in shameful love for her. For this reason, feigning illness, he took to his bed at an appointed time, and, as if to obtain relief from his sickness, ordered all the matrons of the city to come to visit him in succession. Among others came the wife of Lucius, suspecting no evil; Avitus immediately violated her. When the crime had been committed, the woman silently returned home to her husband. On the next day Caesar Avitus, rising from his bed healthy in body but polluted in conscience by his crime, said to Lucius as he met him: “You certainly have baths beautiful enough, Lucius, but you wash in cold water,” hinting at his wife’s foul flow, contrary to nature. But Lucius, understanding the figure, bore it gravely; and, sending messengers with letters in deepest secrecy to the Franks, he promised that if they came as quickly as possible, he would hand over the city of Trier into their power, without doubt, delay, or difficulty.

For up to that point the Trier people had, for many years past, held fast to the Romans and their kings with stubborn adherence. But the Franks, not forgetful of the slaughter and injuries which they had once suffered from Nannenus and Quintinus, princes of Trier, near the Carbonarian forest in the times of Duke Dagobert, the interking, soon gathered forces and hastened gladly to the destruction of the Trier people. When the city was taken, the Franks plundered everything and subjected it to their own kingdom.

In these times the kingdom of the Franks gradually took on great increases and expanded its borders in many ways throughout Gaul. Therefore the kings of the people, who from their first entrance into Germany had held, for nearly eight hundred and seventy years, their seats near the Rhine, where Holland now is, with the peoples who are called Gelders, Westphalians, Cleves people, and Frisians, at Nijmegen, Duisburg, and other places and castles on this side of the Rhine, transferred the dwelling place of their habitation into Gaul, rarely resting from wars, until at last they subjected all Germany and also Gaul, together with Italy, to the kingdom of the Franks.

Thus the kingdom of the Franks, which took its beginning from one small people, with much labor,

Attila of the Goths, Walamir, Ardaric.

Abridgment, Book I. The kingdom of the Franks, greater than all the kingdoms of all Europe, at last grew immeasurably through most bloody wars and through a very great shedding of the blood of kings, dukes, nobles, soldiers, and common people over about nine hundred years, and took increase above all the kingdoms of all Europe, so that it ruled with power over many kingdoms and peoples; and from several kingdoms there came to be one, which, gathered by the sword, should be called in honor of the victor, and should be, by the name of the Franks.

The kingdom of the Franks today is, and remains, divided in two. The Franks, with [unclear] among whom they [unclear], are counted [unclear]. From this it is manifestly clear that, just as the Franks who remained with the Germans use both the language and the customs of the Germans, so also those who, entering the Gauls with their kings, remained with the Gauls changed both their customs and their manner of speaking along with their settlements; and those whom nature had made Germans from the beginning of their birth, a change of places in the midst of the Gauls likewise made Gauls in speech and customs. Indeed, when they were in Troy, they also practiced Trojan customs and tongues among the Scythian ones; in Germany, German ones; and in Gaul they learned and kept Gallic ones. So too Aeneas, coming from the Trojans into Italy with his people, gradually forgot the speech of his fatherland and began to use the customs and language found at Rome.

After this Meroveus, king of the Franks, seized by illness, died in the paganism of idols, as did all his forefathers, in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord's nativity 458, in the eleventh Roman indiction.

The Forty-Sixth.

Childeric reigned 23 years. Childeric the king, out of fear of the Franks, fled into Thuringia. For after only one year had passed in his reign, the nobles of the kingdom, conspiring against him, wanted to kill him, because, living too insolently and wantonly, he had defiled by his shameful conduct several daughters and wives of theirs and of the nobles. When he learned this, he fled with a few men into Thuringia and remained with Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, his kinsman, for three years. He withdrew, deposed by the Franks, in the year of the Lord 459, in the twelfth indiction. After his departure from the kingdom, in that same year the princes of the Franks at once set over themselves as king a certain Aegidius, a Roman prefect among the people of Soissons, who, while Childeric was in exile, occupied the kingdom of the Franks for three years. He, continually raging against the princes and magnates of their kingdom, slaughtered many, having no reasonable cause apart from empty suspicion. Hence the rest, fearing that similar things might at some time threaten them, unanimously arranged a conspiracy against the tyrant, judging that it would be more tolerable to suffer that man to preside over the kingdom who abused the daughters and wives of his subjects, than to endure any longer the one who thirsted for nothing more than the blood of princes.

Therefore in the year of the Lord's nativity 462, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Childeric, by the industry and loyalty of his friend Wimbald, who was one of the more powerful princes of the kingdom, was recalled from Thuringia into the kingdom of the Franks, and with the favor of all the nobles and of the people was restored to his father's kingdom, and Aegidius, hated by all, was driven from it. And thereafter Childeric reigned most moderately for another twenty-two years. And when Basina, wife of Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, had heard that Childeric had been restored by the Franks to the kingdom, she left her husband and followed him into Gaul, stirred by excessive love for him, which she had contracted from the long familiarity of living together among the Thuringians. Childeric, receiving her as she came with a cheerful face, took as his wife the woman known to him, the wife of Bisinus the king, by whom he had been kindly received as a guest for three years, badly repaying this kindness.

But as the first night of the marriage approached, Basina advised Childeric to postpone intercourse for a little while, and to watch the doors of the bedchamber, and to report to her, who would prophesy faithfully in all things, what portents he should see in the courtyard for the third time. The king, trusting the woman, obeyed as she commanded; and after watching the buildings three times, he returned to her, saying that first he had seen in the palace courtyard rhinoceroses, that is, unicorns, and also lions and leopards. Secondly, wolves and raging bears, attacking one another. Thirdly I saw, he said, many dogs, but small ones, which were tearing one another with their teeth, and biting fiercely; but what they signify, you must say.

Compendium, Book I.

[in the] times of the aforesaid Childeric, king of the Franks. After Odoacer’s departure from the Rugii, the Lombards invaded Rugium; over them at that time a fifth king, named Gudeoch, held rule, and they lived in that kingdom for some time.

But Childeric, king of the Franks, after he had performed many deeds bravely, died in the twenty-third completed year of his reign, but the twenty-sixth if the interruption is counted, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 484, in the seventh Roman indiction.

The Forty-Seventh.

To this the woman, a seer, said thus to the king: “Behold, we shall beget offspring, differing in various habits with time. For the first that is born from us will be very noble, to be compared in its nobility with lions and noble unicorns. From the first generation, with time, a second will arise, which, after the manner of wolves, despising nobility, will practice plunder and oppression of the poor. The generation after this, the third and last from us, will, after the manner of dogs, tear, bite, and strike one another, until at last in the final days the kingdom will fail.” That same night the woman conceived, and bore a son, named Clodoveus, as we shall say.

In the following year, which was the 463rd from the Lord’s nativity, a son named Clodoveus was born to Hilderic. He afterwards succeeded his father in the kingdom of the Franks and was the first to receive the faith of Christ, as we shall say below. At almost the same time Hilderic, king of the Franks, having gathered a great army of fighters, made war against the people of the Alemanni, who lived between Italy and Suevia, where the cities of Chur and Sitten and Valais now are. When battle was joined, the Alemanni were defeated and brought under the tribute of the Franks. In these times also, when Vtherpendragon, king of Britain, which is now called England, had died, his son, named Arthur, was raised to his kingdom. Concerning him not only the history of the Britons, as Geoffrey of Monmouth relates, but also the voices of the peoples of England sound forth wonderful things down to the present day, although many of them are more fabulous than in accord with truth. This Arthur, endowed with great uprightness of conduct, prudence, gentleness, and at the same time kindness, strove with all zeal to make himself beloved and venerable to all, because, along with virtue of soul, he also abounded in marvelous generosity toward everyone, and especially toward ecclesiastics, on whom for the love of Christ he bestowed many small gifts as well as offerings.

He expelled the Saxons and Picts from Britain; he powerfully subjected to his kingdom the Scots, the Irish, and the Orkneys. When the kings of Dacia, Norway, and [unclear] heard this, they came of their own accord and submitted themselves to his dominion. Merlin, the seer of the English, foretold to his father Vtherpendragon wonderful things about this Arthur’s birth as well as his future deeds; we made mention of these in the first volume of the annals.

In these times also Odacar, by nation a Rugian, or a Saxon Teuton, armed with a multitude of Turcilingi, Heruli, and also Sueti, or those whom we now call Swedes from the island, having come out from nearly the farthest boundaries of Saxony, came into Gaul and entered the city of Orléans as victor. Afterwards he also received Angers into his power by the surrender of its citizens.

Against him Hilderic, king of the Franks, led out his army on the following day, joined battle, killed Count Paul, and took the city. Odoacar, making peace with King Hilderic, left Gaul and entered Italy to conquer it. He compelled Orestes, patrician of the Romans, who did not dare to meet him in Liguria, to flee back; and when he was hiding in the city of Ticinum, which is now called Pavia, he besieged, captured, and killed him. After this he obtained all the cities and fortifications of Italy, with no one resisting at all, and possessed them very peacefully; and, having placed the diadem of the kingdom on his own head, he reigned in Italy for fourteen years according to his own pleasure. Afterwards, however, he was killed by the king of the Goths.

Hilderic, king of the Franks, having gathered a very great army of his own men, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 475 ranged with a powerful hand through all Gaul, subjected to his kingdom everything that remained, and killed those who dared to resist; but those who made surrender voluntarily he received with favor. In that disturbance he killed many of the Romans and freed Gaul from their dominion.

At the same time the Franks, seizing Cologne Agrippina from the power of the Romans with a strong hand, also subjected it to their own dominion. Then Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and not long afterwards Strasbourg, together with all the towns and fortifications throughout the whole region [Cisrhenana?], from the city of Constance in Alemannia as far as the sea; and thereafter among the Treveri and Mosellani they set Heribert, among the vicars of the city of Metz, after the custom of the ancient kings of France. Clodoveus the king, however, afterwards had nearly all of them killed because of his ambition for sole rule.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 369, in the second indiction of the Romans, [unclear]

Sabinus is recorded [unclear] the established peace of the aforesaid kingdom that was to be. The condition of the kingdoms of the Franks. In the year of the Lord [unclear], Clodoveus is born from Basina; in the year of the Lord 462, [war?] of the Franks with the Alemanni. Vtherpendragon’s son. Arthur becomes king of Britain. Aristarchus first was above Galileo [unclear]. Odoacar the king expelled the Saxons and Picts from Britain. Merlin. Odoacar, defeated by Fridic, goes into Italy. Odoacar reigned in Italy fourteen years. The Franks, taking Cologne from the Romans, subjected it to themselves. Here the kingdoms of the Franks were multiplied [unclear].

Annals of Trithemius.

... the Sicambri, not among the Scythians, but among the Germans. Thus Clovis, first of all the kings of the Franks, received the faith of Christ, and was baptized by Saint Remigius in the thirty-sixth year of his age, the fifteenth of his reign, and the 499th of the Lord's nativity, in the seventh Roman indiction.

On the same day, after the king, three thousand of the courtly chief men and nobles of the Franks were baptized. And in the days that followed, the bishops and priests of the Lord baptized all the rest of the people with great joy, giving thanks for the mercies of almighty God, who by his grace, that he might give peace to the Church, subjected a most fierce people to the yoke of faith.

Thereafter great things were done for the honor of Christ, not only by Clovis but much more by his successors, the kings of the Franks: churches were built, several monasteries of those serving God were founded throughout Germany, Italy, and Gaul, and the ministry of divine worship was in many ways increased at that time. King Clovis, however, although he was a most dutiful man toward his subjects, is nevertheless read to have been excessively cruel toward his own blood-relations, since he had many very noble men sprung from the ancient stock of the kings of the Franks, kings, dukes, and princes, cruelly and treacherously killed, so that he alone might have the kingdom.

But love of historical truth impels us to commend a few examples out of many to posterity. At that time there was ruling at Cologne Agrippina an old man, born of the seed of the kings of the Franks, named Sigebert, whom Clovis's father Childeric, after Cologne had been acquired, had placed there as vicar of the kingdom. He had a son named Ludovicus, to whom King Clovis wrote thus in cunning deceit: "Your father is now old and useless for the kingdom. If he were to die, his kingdom would come to you, with our friendship, and not to another."

The young man, led astray by desire for the kingdom, resolved to kill his father. And when King Sigebert on a certain day, suspecting nothing of the sort, went out from Cologne, crossed the Rhine, and was hunting through the forest of Buronia with a few men, the son had his father killed by assassins sent against him while he was sleeping in his tent at clear midday, as if he were going to possess his kingdom according to Clovis's promise.

When the murder, indeed the parricide, had been most wickedly carried out, Ludovicus wrote to King Clovis: "My father is dead; I hold his treasures in my possession, together with the kingdom. Send men, therefore, and whatever of my father's treasures pleases you I shall send to you with good will." King Clovis wrote back to him: "I give thanks for your good will. I ask that you show everything to our men when they come, since you are henceforth to possess your father's kingdom alone, with our friendship."

When the envoys of King Clovis came, Ludovicus showed them his father's treasures. While they were looking at the various different things, the young man said, "In this chest my father was accustomed to put back his gold coins." "Put your hand," said one of those standing by, "down to the bottom, so that you may test whether it is all gold." When he had done this, and was bent far down, that one who had given the order raised his hand and swung an axe into his brain; he was dead at once in that same place.

When these things had been wickedly done, King Clovis came to Cologne, as if unaware of the crimes, and, after summoning all the people of the city, said: "Hear, best citizens, the unspeakable evil that recently happened. Ludovicus, the son of my kinsman Sigebert, misled his father with false words, saying that I was plotting against his life. And when he was fleeing through the forest of Buronia, Ludovicus sent brigands against him and killed his own father. He too, while brooding over the treasures, was struck down by someone I do not know and perished. But in these matters I am in no way complicit. For I cannot shed the blood of my kinsmen, since that is a crime. But since these things have happened so, I give you counsel, if it seems acceptable: turn to me, so that you may stand under my protection." But they applauded with hands and voices, and, after he had been raised on a shield according to the custom of the people, they set him as king over themselves. And thus he received into his own power the kingdom of Sigebert with all his treasures.

For God was daily casting down his enemies beneath his hands [unclear]; afterward he had both their heads cut off.

He also killed King Riuacharius, who was ruling the Franks at Cambrai and living very wantonly and luxuriously, together with his brother Richarius, after they had been treacherously captured while fleeing from battle, striking them with an axe by his own hand.

He also had Lingomirus, their brother, who was ruling in the region of Le Mans, killed with similar cruelty.

After their deaths, he usurped their kingdoms with their treasures for himself. He killed other kings ...

Three thousand Frankish nobles are baptized on the same day.

The Franks all begin to be attached to their faith.

The young man, believing Clovis, hastens to his father's kingdom.

Ludovicus the parricide invites the king.

The parricide is killed by the machination of King Clovis.

The fictitious exculpation of King Clovis.

Riuacharius, king of the Cambrai region of Francia, is killed with his brother.
