in the times of the aforesaid Hilderic, king of the Franks. After Odoacer’s departure from the Rugians, the Lombards invaded Rugium; at that time their fifth king, named Gudeoch, ruled over them, and they dwelt in that kingdom for some time.

Hilderic, king of the Franks, after he had performed many brave deeds, died in the twenty-third completed year of his reign, but the twenty-sixth interrupted year, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 484, in the seventh Roman indiction.

The Forty-Seventh.

Clovis, son of King Hilderic by Basina, when he was twenty-one years of age, succeeded his father and reigned thirty years. Of these he spent fifteen as a pagan, like all the kings of the Franks before him, in vanity; and the remaining fifteen, reborn in the faith of Christ, he passed faithfully. He was a prince of outstanding beauty and distinguished by strength of spirit. Soon, at the beginning of his reign, he put to flight the son of the former Roman duke Aegidius, named Syagrius, who was ruling at Soissons, and added the city to the kingdom of the Franks.

Then, advancing, he took the city of Reims, whose church at that time was governed by Saint Remigius, a most learned bishop; and his wife, that is, the mother of Clotildis, with a stone tied to her neck, he cast into the water. But Clotildis was a faithful Christian woman, who earnestly admonished the king to believe in the Lord Jesus and to renounce the vain worship of idols. Although he despised this at the beginning, nevertheless, after fifteen years had passed in his reign, having obtained victory over the Alemanni, as we shall say in its place, he afterwards believed in Christ.

He took as wife Clotildis, daughter of Hilderic, king of the Burgundians, whom King Gundebald, his brother, had slain; and his wife, that is, the mother of Clotildis, with a stone tied to her neck, [unclear], and he divided the plunder among the soldiers according to law. Whatever in all Gaul belonged to the jurisdiction of the Romans, Clovis in a short time subjected wholly to the dominion of the Franks, as it remains even to the present day.

In the ninth year of his reign, King Clovis made war in Thuringia, because they were accustomed insolently to despise the tribute formerly imposed on them, and openly accused his mother Basina not only of adultery but also of theft. Coming therefore into the region of the Thuringians, he devastated everything with sword and fire, defeated the king, and compelled him to pay tribute.

In the eleventh year of his reign King Clovis, having gathered forces, led an army against Alaric, king of the western Goths. He met him ten miles from the city of Poitiers and killed him, together with many others; and he added all his treasures and the city itself to his kingdom.

In the fifteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 499, in the seventh Roman indiction, when the Alemanni again grew proud, and were unwilling either to be subject to the Franks or to pay tribute any longer, Clovis summoned a great army of his men and set in motion a strong expedition against the Alemanni for battle. At the beginning of the conflict the fighting was fierce and long uncertain, with Mars divided between both sides, and many fell on both sides.

At last, by the ordering of divine providence, while the Alemanni fought bravely, the Franks gradually began to give way; and when it already seemed near that they would flee, the king, suffused with tears, prayed silently within himself, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, whom my wife proclaims to be the Son of God and able to grant all things asked to those who believe faithfully in you, if you give me victory today over these my enemies, I shall believe in you and shall have myself baptized in your name, and I shall be a faithful and devoted servant to your name as long as I live.”

And while, praying thus, with hands and eyes raised to heaven, he groaned, the help of Christ was suddenly present. At its presence the Alemanni were turned to flight; and those who before had fought immovably like a wall now suddenly fled, as the most fearful women are wont to do. The king of the Alemanni fell in that battle, together with many. But when the Franks did not cease to pursue the fleeing Alemanni more insistently, they cried out to King Clovis: “Do not pursue us any further, most victorious king, because we are yours; from now on we promise that we shall serve you forever.” Moved by these prayers, he forbade the pursuit, received the Alemanni in surrender, and returned to Gaul.

And when he had come to the palace, on the advice of Queen Clotildis he summoned to himself Remigius, the most holy bishop of the church of Reims. Having been more fully instructed by him in the Christian faith, in public confession, while all the nobles of the Franks looked on, he prepared himself with the greatest reverence and humility for the mystery of holy baptism. When he was now entering the baptistery to be washed, Saint Remigius, a most eloquent bishop, said to him: “Gently, Sicambrian, lower your neck. Adore what you burned; burn what you adored.” From this it is manifest that the Franks had somewhat earlier been called Sicambri—

Annals of Trithemius. The Forty-Eighth.

[unclear]

Lothar, therefore, the third-born son of King Clovis, from whom the line of the kings of the Franks descending in direct succession is continued down to Childeric, the last of the stock of Pharamond, reigned after his father in the Frankish city of Soissons for fifty years. When his brothers and all their sons had died, he at last brought the kingdom, divided into four parts, back into one monarchy; each of his brothers had reigned for a time in his own place.

For Theodoric, the firstborn of King Clovis, whom he had begotten not by Queen Clotilde but, before his marriage to her, by a certain concubine, received Austrasia in the division of the kingdom of the Franks, in which is the city of Metz, together with other cities belonging to it. At that time it was called the kingdom of Austrasia, or of the Austrasians, in which he reigned twenty-three years. After him his son Theodebert reigned over the Austrasians fourteen years. When he too had died, his son Theodebald reigned over the people of Metz for nine years. When he died without children in the year of the Lord’s Nativity [unclear], in the eighth Roman indiction, his paternal uncle, the aforesaid Lothar, received the kingdom of the Austrasians, or of the people of Metz.

Clodomir, however, the third son of Clovis, but the firstborn by Queen Clotilde, reigned at Orléans in Gaul for seven years. In the year of the Lord’s Nativity [unclear], after he had slain Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, with his wife and sons, and had again engaged his brother Godomar, he was killed by him. He left three young sons, Theodebald, Gunther, and Clodoald; after their father’s death, their most pious grandmother Clotilde, living at Tours, kept them with her and reared them as a mother. But a few years later Lothar and Childebert, the kings and brothers of the said Clodomir, summoned to themselves their nephews Theodebald and Gunther and, devising wicked things out of ambition to rule, killed them with their own hands. The third, however, named Clodoald, snatched away with the help of courtiers, escaped by flight; exchanging worldly nobility for divine service, he became a cleric.

Childebert, the fourth son of Clovis king of the Franks, received the kingdom of Neustria in the division of the monarchy and reigned at Paris for forty-five years. When he at last died, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity [unclear], in the seventh Roman indiction, his brother Lothar received the kingdom of the Parisians into his own power. Thus, when his three brothers and their sons and grandsons had died or been cruelly killed, Lothar alone obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter, after all his brothers, reigned still another five years.

In the second year of King Lothar, Sigismund, king of Burgundy, who had built the monastery of the martyrs of Agaune, killed his son Sigeric, following the evil counsel of the boy’s stepmother. Moved by great repentance, he devoted himself wholly to the holy martyrs of Agaune; frequent miracles after his death testify that he was worthy of pardon, and in his honor health is given to those suffering from fever.

In the fourth year of King Lothar, Theodoric, king of Austrasia, having been asked [with the promise of] half of his kingdom, treacherously killed Bertharius and Balderic, his brothers, on the road, while they were returning toward Thuringia from the city of Metz, which they had approached for the sake of greeting him, suspecting no evil. But when the crime had been committed, and Theodoric demanded from Ermenfrid the half of the kingdom of Thuringia promised to him, Ermenfrid neither gave what he had promised nor sent a fitting reply to the petitioner, deceived by the counsel of his wife, who was the sister of Theodoric and Lothar. This matter, afterward, as we said in the first volume of the Annals, brought on the final destruction of all Thuringia and extinguished the royal name and title in it. In the same year the holy virgin Brigid, dying in Scotia, ascended to Christ.

In the seventh year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Boethius, the Roman consul, worn down by a long imprisonment, was killed by Theodoric, king of the Goths, who had occupied Italy after Odoacer had been slain. He wrote many useful works for the faith of Christ. In these times also there flourished in Italy our lawgiving father, Saint Benedict, the first founder and abbot of the monastery of Cassino. He became the chief of all western monks, to whom he handed down a rule of life preeminent in every discretion, and he showed forth to all, by his most holy works, the lucid teaching of his words as worthy of imitation. Under his Rule many thereafter served the almighty Lord in a spirit of humility, distinguished by the names of orders or congregations. Among these, first and principal of all is our own order, which, having received an honorable name from its founder, is called by the name of that Saint Benedict himself. The Order of Cistercian monks also professes the same Rule, and likewise the Order of the Celestines,

Lothar reigns for fifty years.

Compendium, Book I.

[unclear] several [kings?] of the Franks, all of whom had been begotten from the blood of his parents, especially those of whom he was excessively and suspiciously afraid, lest they seize the kingdom before him; sparing no one, and in this way, after almost all his kinsmen had been extinguished, he extended his kingdom throughout all Gaul. But let Hunibald praise Clovis as much as he wishes, as though he acted well in these matters; for my part, in this respect I cannot praise a parricide, and one who killed so many innocent men.

For on a certain day, in the presence of many of his courtiers, he is said to have spoken about these relatives and kinsmen of his whom he himself had destroyed: “Woe is me, because I remain alone like a stranger among foreigners, and today I have no one of my relatives or kinsmen still living who, if adversity should come upon me in any matter, could help me as friend is wont to help friend.” He said this deceitfully, thinking that someone among those standing by would reply by way of consolation: “Look, you still have this man or that man of your people living,” so that any who survived among his kinsmen might also themselves be killed as soon as possible.

In the seventeenth year of his reign, King Clovis, at the continual urging of Queen Clotildis, who desired the cruel death of her parents to be avenged upon her uncle, declared war on Gundebald, king of the Burgundians. After he had been defeated, Clovis subjected Burgundy to the tribute and subjection of the Franks.

But Clovis, king of the Franks, after his kingdom had been extended through all Gaul and a great part of Germany, and after many deeds had been bravely accomplished both in war and in peace, at last died in the thirtieth year of his reign, but in the fifty-first year of his age, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 514, in the seventh indiction of the Romans, and was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Peter.

He left four sons: Lotharius, Clodomirus, and Hildebertus. These divided their father’s kingdom in equal portion. But because thereafter more kings were born from these, and because at one time the kingdom of the Franks was subject to one monarch, while at another time, divided into parts, it was ruled by many, we have thought it worthwhile to continue in order the names of those kings, marked beforehand chapter by chapter in red, who carried the line of the royal stock in a direct line down to King Hildericus, the last. For Lotharius was not the firstborn among the sons of Clovis; rather Theodoricus was older by birth. Clodomirus was born second, and Lotharius himself, from whom the genealogy of the kings is continued, was born third. After King Clovis had died, Hunibald also finished his own history concerning the origin of the Franks, distinguished into eighteen books, comprising a period of not less than 950 years, during which there were forty-seven kings from Marcomirus, son of Antenor, who first led the people from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the river Rhine in Germany, down to the death of King Clovis. The things that follow, however, in this second volume of our annals, we have taken from authors whose names are these:

Einhardus, abbot of Saint Amand; Flodoardus, priest of the church of Reims; Richerus, monk of Reims; Gregorius, archbishop of Tours; Lampertus, abbot in Hasungen; Regino, abbot of Prüm; Eghardus, first abbot in [Vraugia]; Lampertus, monk of Hersfeld; Freculfus, from monk made bishop of Lisieux; Strabus, monk of Fulda; Windekindus, monk in Corbie of Saxony; Rupertus, monk of Saint Alban near Mainz; Ioannes, monk of the same monastery; Adelbertus, monk of the monastery of Saint Vincent of Metz; Meginfridus, monk of Fulda; Golstherus, monk of Saint Matthias, in the deeds of the Treveri; Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda; Sigebertus, monk of Gembloux; Richardus, monk of Cluny; also Robert Gaguin, formerly minister general of the Order of the Holy Trinity; Ado, bishop of Vienne; Galfridus Brito; Saxo Dacus; Ptolomaeus Lucensis; a Saxon by homeland, in the Rudimentum novitiorum; Wernherus, Carthusian monk of Cologne; Hartmannus Schedel from Mount Noricus; Iacobus Bergomensis, hermit of Saint Augustine; Marcus Antonius Sabellicus. From the aforementioned and various other writers of histories I wrote the two volumes of our annals that follow, not without very great labor, because there is much diversity among historiographers, not only in years, but also in deeds and in the names of persons: what is narrated as having been done by me in one year is narrated as having been done in this one, and a deed done, which by this one is told thus, by another otherwise. Since, therefore, it is not within my powers to be able to reconcile so great a discordance of histories, I follow the opinion of those whom I find to have differed less from one another, something that could be observed not uniformly in every individual case, but in some.

Trithemius [unclear] the following, disagreeing in name.

Compendium, Book I.

The Order of Saint William, the Order of Monte Oliveto, the Order of the Slavs, the Order of Vallombrosa, the Order of Saint Paul the First Hermit, the Order of the Humiliati, with certain others, which for the sake of brevity we have passed over here. Saint Pope Gregory set forth the life of this saint.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 624, in the seventh indiction of the Romans: when Theodoric, king of Metz, demanded from Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, what had been promised because of the murder of his brothers, as we have said, and did not obtain it, he was stirred to anger; and, having summoned to his aid his son Theobert and his brother Lothar, kings, he launched an expedition into Thuringia, captured King Ermenfrid with his wife and children, killed him, and subjected the whole kingdom to himself. From that time the Thuringians had no king of their own.

Among the others taken captive was Radegund, daughter of the former King Berthar, whom his brother Ermenfrid, as we have said, had caused to be killed through Theodoric, king of Metz. King Lothar joined her to himself in marriage; she shone with great holiness, and afterwards, having become a nun, was resplendent with very many signs and miracles. Concerning this destruction of the Thuringians, Fortunatus the archbishop wrote more fully in verse and prose.

In the twelfth year of his reign, Lothar, king of the Franks, with his brother Hildebert, besieged Autun, a city of Burgundy, and, after King Godemar had been put to flight, powerfully subjected the whole province of the Burgundians to his dominion.

In the sixteenth year of his reign, Lothar, king of the Franks, powerfully wrested from the hand of Athalaric the king whatever his grandfather Theodoric, king of Italy, had possessed in the Gauls.

In these days Saint Nicerius flourished, from abbot of the monastery of Limoges made archbishop of Trier, a man of many virtues in Christ, whose deeds are extant. Theodoric, king of Austrasia, who ruled over the people of Metz, Trier, Liege, Cologne, Mainz, and all those on this side of the Rhine, brought many clerics from the citizens of Auvergne, whom he ordered to be enrolled in the church of Trier to serve the Lord.

In the twenty-sixth year of King Lothar, in the ninth indiction, King Hildebert rose up against this same Lothar, his brother in Christ, together with his brother’s son Theodobert; but, when their mother Clotilde acted with prayers before God that there should be no war among her sons, they were restrained by a dreadful storm, while upon Lothar not even a sign of so great a terror appeared. Compelled by manifest necessity, Hildebert withdrew from his brother in peace.

In the twenty-eighth year Lothar and Hildebert, the aforesaid brothers, having besieged in Spain the city of Zaragoza, while the citizens prayed to God and carried around the tunic of the holy martyr Vincent, accepted from them, as a gift of that martyr, his stole, and returned in peace, after the greater part of Spain had been acquired by war. At the same time Saint Maurus and Faustus, disciples of Saint Benedict, flourished in Gallican France, distinguished in conduct, learning, holiness of life, and miracles.

In the fortieth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 654, in the second indiction of the Romans, Queen Clotilde died, formerly the wife of the great Clodoveus, king of France; she was buried with him at Paris in the church of Saint Peter. In the same year Bucellinus and Amingus, leaders of the Franks, engaged in war with Narses, patrician of the Romans. For these two leaders, Bucellinus and Amingus, had seven years before entered Italy with King Theobert of the Franks with a strong force, and they did not cease to disturb it with varying fortunes of war. Then, sailing into Sicily, they subjected it to tribute to the Franks, and, after many spoils had been acquired, occupied it.

In the fortieth year of his reign, Lothar, king of the Franks, having gathered forces, moved into Saxony. For the Saxons, who until then had been tributary to the Franks, rose in rebellion, with the Thuringians bringing aid; they themselves bore the yoke of the Franks heavily, and with equal firmness refused all tribute. Therefore, coming into Saxony with a great army, Lothar subdued the Saxons in a severe battle.

In the forty-sixth year of his reign, Lothar, king of the Franks, pursued with an army his son Granus, long rebellious and doing many evils in the kingdom, when he was a leader in Brittany. When an engagement had taken place, he killed Duke Conober, obtained Brittany, and captured his son, whom, consumed by fire together with his wife and daughters, he reduced to ashes.

In the year

ANNALS OF TRITHEMIUS

In the following year, namely the fiftieth of his reign, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 563, in the twelfth indiction of the Romans, Lotharius himself, king of the Franks, died, leaving four sons, Heribertus, Gunthramus, Sigebertus, and Hilpericus, who again divided their father’s kingdom among themselves. The aforesaid King Lotharius built the abbey of Saint Medard, first bishop of Noyon and Tournai, at Soissons; into it he placed, with the greatest reverence and honor, the body of the same saint, translated from Tournai. But King Hildebertus, his brother, built the abbey of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, in which he deposited the stole of Saint Vincent the martyr together with his dalmatic. But the order of this abridgment now requires that we pursue the division of the kingdom.

THE FORTY-NINTH.

Hilpericus the younger, son of Lotharius king of the Franks, is for this reason placed by us before his brothers in this abridgment of the kings: because through him the line of kings descending in the direct line is continued down to Hildericus. He reigned for two years before his father’s death in the city of Soissons, and, succeeding his father, reigned for twenty-one years. And thus the whole time for which he reigned was twenty-four years. The name of his first wife was Andovera. By her he begot two sons, Clodoveus and Meroveus, both of whom, slain in adolescence by the deceit of their stepmother, perished, as we said in the first volume.

When Andovera had borne a child while the king was absent, and when no one was at hand to lift the boy from the sacred font for baptism, the queen mother herself, deceived by the wicked counsel of Fredegundis, fulfilled the office of godmother, and lifted from baptism the infant whom she had borne. Fredegundis, contriver of the deceit, soon reported this gladly to the king when he came, saying: “You will no longer have Andovera as your wife, O king; she has preferred to be your co-mother rather than your spouse. Now I am yours.” For this reason King Hilpericus repudiated Andovera his wife, asserting that by decree of the canons it was forbidden him to have his co-mother as wife. Thus, seduced by the crafty deceit of Queen Fredegundis, she was thrust into a monastery; and her fraudulent deceiver Fredegundis was taken by King [Heribertus?] as wife, by whom he begot the successor of his paternal kingdom, as we shall say later.

Herbertus, however, the eldest son of Lotharius, in the division of the monarchy of the kingdom of the Franks received Neustria, holding the seat of his kingdom at Paris; and he reigned for nine years, and, doing nothing worthy of memory, died in the year of the Lord 573, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, leaving the kingdom to his brothers.

Gunthramus, the second-born son of King Lotharius, reigned at Orleans for thirty-three years, a prince excellent in his own condition, but he obtained a most wicked wife, named Austrigildis. Among the many evils that she committed, when she was sick unto death and could not be helped by the physicians, she circumvented the king by crafty persuasion, so that he confirmed by oath that he would unquestionably grant her the effect of her petition while she was still alive. “Before I die, therefore,” she said, “have the heads of my physicians, who have vainly tortured me with their medicines, cut off while I look on.” What more? Men are sent at once to bring in the physicians. When they had entered the bedchamber, the witch said: “Ah, you are not physicians, but liars, who compel me to die before my time by your medicines, though I have prepared a rich reward for you, so that, compelled to death, you may pass on before me.” Soon, that the executioner might satisfy the desire of the impious woman, by order he cut off the heads of two innocent physicians while she herself looked on and laughed as witness. King Gunthramus died in the year of the Lord 597, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans.

Sigebertus, however, the third-born son of King Lotharius, reigned at Metz in Austrasia, and also over the Treveri, the people of [Londium?], Cologne, Mainz, and the remaining cities and provinces on this side of the Rhine, for fourteen years. He had a Spanish wife, named Bruna, whom writers have more often been accustomed to call Brunihildis, the slayer of ten kings. She was so hateful to the Franks that they said the prophecy of the Sibyl was fulfilled in her: “Bruna will come from the regions of Spain; before her sight peoples and kings will perish, but she herself will perish by the heels of horses.” By her Sigebertus begot a son named Theodobertus, who reigned after him for twenty-one years and died in the year of the Lord 599. His son, named Theodoricus, succeeded and reigned for sixteen years; he expelled Saint Columbanus from Gaul at the instigation of his Brunihildis in the year of the Lord 613, and died shortly afterwards, leaving three sons, as is read, born out of wedlock. The eldest of these, Sigebertus, was put to flight in battle by Lotharius, son of the aforesaid king, and thereafter appeared nowhere. Corbus, the second-born, was slain by the same Lotharius. But Meroveus, the third-born, whom he had in fact lifted from the font, the same Lotharius kept alive. Brunihildis, however, the slayer of ten kings, he put to death.

Lotharius king of the Franks dies.

[unclear] of Saint Medard is built at Soissons. The monastery of Saint Germanus of the Meadows is founded.

Hilpericus reigned for 24 years. He had reigned at Soissons two years earlier. Andovera, wife of King Hilpericus; Queen Fredegundis, the deceiver. Hilpericus repudiated Andovera and his co-mother.

Heribertus reigned 9 years.

Gunthramus reigned at Orleans for 33 years. A cruel queen, [unclear] indulgence, physicians’ heads are cut off at the queen’s persuasion. King Gunthramus dies.

Sigebertus reigned in Austrasia. Brunihildis, wife of Sigebertus, cruel. The prophecy of the Sibyl concerning Queen Brunhilda. Theodoricus king of Austrasia, his son. The three illegitimate sons of Theodoricus.

Compendium, Book I.

The Huns, ravaging Thuringia, are cut down by the Franks.

In the third year of King Hilperic, the Huns went forth with a great army and began to ravage the territories of the Franks in Thuringia in hostile fashion. Against their insolence Sigebert, king of the Franks of Austrasia, brother of King Hilperic, under whose kingdom the Thuringians were contained, brought out his forces, joined battle, laid low many thousands of the Huns, and turned the rest to flight. Meanwhile, while Sigebert was occupied in Thuringia with the Huns, his brother King Hilperic besieged the city and received it in surrender.

In the same year spears were seen in the air, and battle-lines of soldiers; at the same time the din of conflicts was heard, portending the irruption of the Lombards into Italy, about which Pope Gregory the Great speaks in a homily.

For in the following year, namely in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 568, in the first indiction of the Romans, Alboin, king of the Lombards, entrusted Pannonia, in which he had previously settled with his people, to the Huns, friends of the Lombards; and, taking as auxiliaries Saxons, Marcomanni, and other neighboring peoples, with all his people, he occupied part of Italy, which from the name of the people is called Lombardy down to the present.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 583, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans, the Saxons who were with the Lombards in Italy, no longer enduring the pride and unjust domination of the Winuli, for so the Lombards were formerly called, returned with their children and wives, under the guidance of Sigebert, king of the Franks, through Austrasian Gaul to Cologne Agrippina; there, crossing the Rhine, they returned to their former seats of Saxony, which they had abandoned.

In the same year Sigebert, king of the Franks, who dwelt at Metz in Austrasia, brother of Hilperic, surveying the land of Saxony empty of inhabitants, who had gone with the Lombards, as we have said, into Italy, lest it should be reduced entirely to desolation, handed it over to the Suevi to inhabit. And so, while the Saxons dwelt with the Lombards in Italy, the Suevi lived in Saxony for fourteen years. When these had passed, since the Saxons saw themselves in the lowest place among the Lombards, in the condition of slaves, they considered returning to Saxony.

But the Suevi, to whom King Sigebert had given the land to inhabit, at first denied the Saxons entry; secondly, they agreed to restore a third part to them. But when the Saxons demanded back not a part but the whole, the Suevi offered half the region. The Saxons remained constant in their resolve, demanding back not a part, not the half of the land, but the whole entire. At last the matter was committed to the sword, and both armies fought most fiercely for possession of the seats. At length the Suevi were defeated; more than twenty thousand of them perished in that battle by the sword of the Saxons. And so the Saxons recovered by war the land which, at the persuasion of the Winuli, they had abandoned rather imprudently, in the fourteenth year after their departure, some of the Suevi being slain and others expelled.

Whence the name. From that time the aforesaid Saxons, returning from Lombardy into Germany, are called Westphalians, that is, western Gauls, down to the present day, although they are in fact true Saxons and Germans. They built a new city in the middle of their region, which they named Milan, in remembrance of another Milan in Lombardy; in it now is the episcopal see of the church of Münster. Hence some writers have also called these Saxons or West-Gauls Lombards, because they carried their customs and rites into Saxony.

In the fifth year of King Hilperic, the king of Austrasia, his brother, mindful of the injuries which he had received from him when in the previous year he was absent from the kingdom fighting with the Huns in Thuringia, gathered a great army and advanced against him for battle. He occupied the city of Soissons, the seat of the kingdom of his brother Hilperic. He took Theodobert, his son, captive and condemned him to exile; he defeated Hilperic himself in battle and put him to flight; he recovered for himself again everything which he had previously taken away, and usurped a great part of his kingdom.

In the same year King Sigebert took as wife Bruna or Brunhild, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, as was said above, who was reigning in Spain.

In the seventh year of Hilperic, king of the Franks, the Huns again devastated Thuringia, doing great things by magical arts. Against them Sigebert, king of the Franks, advanced to battle; by their incantations he had almost been deceived and defeated, but, the name of Christ having prudently been invoked, he stood firm bravely, fought manfully, and finally conquered. With him the Huns made a treaty and returned to their own land.

In the following year the Winuli, who are the Lombards, after the city of Pavia had been taken by surrender following a siege of three years, soon obtained almost all Italy except Rome and Ravenna; with no one resisting, they ruled powerfully everywhere. In the year

Annals of Trithemius, 47. In the ninth year of King Hilperic, in the sixth Roman indiction, his brother Heribertus, king of the Franks, who was reigning in Neustria in the city of Paris, died without children. Heribertus, king of Neustria, dies at Paris. In the tenth year of Hilperic, king of the Franks, Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed by one of his own armor-bearers on the following occasion. Alboin, king of the Lombards, is killed. In the 547th year of the Lord's nativity, in the tenth Roman indiction, in the time of Lotharius the Great, king of the Franks, this same King Alboin had a war with Chunimundus, king of the Gepids, in which sixty thousand men fell on each side. The king of the Gepids, Chunimundus, is killed. There Alboin slew Chunimundus and had a drinking-cup fitted for himself from the bone of his head, which he was especially accustomed to use on days of rejoicing and feasting. He also took his daughter captive as his wife. And when, in the aforesaid year of Hilperic, on a certain solemn day, he had become rather merry over his cups and offered his wife her father's [cup?], saying, 'Drink with your father,' she, kindled with womanly fury, had the king killed at night while he was asleep by his own armor-bearer. Alboin, king of the Lombards, is killed. After his [death?] Cleph was again set in the kingdom and reigned for two years; after he died at the end of the two-year period, the Lombards were under dukes for ten years.

Hilperic, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the tenth Roman indiction, pressed, harassed, and disturbed his brother Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, very greatly, both in person and through his son Theodobert. Hence in the following year, the fourteenth of King Hilperic, and the 578th of the Lord's nativity, a cruel war arose between them, in which Theodobert, son of Hilperic, was slain, and many Franks on both sides [were killed]. Sigebert, king of the Franks among the Austrasians [unclear]. Conspiracy of the Franks against King Hilperic. After this the Franks over whom Hilperic held dominion, hating their lord the king himself, [unclear] Sigebert, brother of [unclear], over themselves [unclear]; with hatred of [the woman?] almost all the Franks were troubled; and although she abused very much with insolence, nevertheless she honored the churches of God. She established many new [buildings?] from the foundations. King Sigebert [is killed] by the treachery of Fredegund. [unclear] had King Sigebert treacherously killed, in the year of the Lord's nativity [unclear]. [Brunhild: unclear].

War of the Franks [unclear]. In the following year, the seventeenth of Hilperic, king of the Franks, the dukes of the Lombards began to devastate the territories of Gaul. The Franks met them with a great and strong multitude of troops and fought many battles with them at the risk of death, sometimes defeated and sometimes also victorious. Finally, however, the Franks triumphed. Gregory, from a monk [became?] pope. [unclear], in the [unclear] Roman indiction, leaving a single son named Lotharius the Younger, an infant of four months, who succeeded in the kingdom. Lotharius, son of Fredegund the husband-slayer, reigns as an infant. Lotharius, when he was an infant of four months, was placed in his father's stead and reigned forty-four years, beginning under the guardianship and governance of his mother. In the second year of his reign Antharius, king of the Lombards after the dukes had been driven out, [unclear], in the 58[unclear] year of the Lord's nativity, took as wife Theodolinda, daughter of Garibald, king of Bavaria; to her the blessed Pope Gregory afterwards sent the four books of the Dialogues, as to a woman of singular devotion. Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards. King Hilperic is slain by the treachery of his wife.

In the same year also, when Antharius, king of the Lombards, had died without children, the Lombards, having granted Queen Theodolina the choice of selecting for herself a husband and king of Italy, [she] wanted Agilulf to be king for them and at the same time her husband; he thereafter reigned vigorously over the Lombards for twenty-five years. Agilulf is appointed over the Lombards for twenty-five years. Thassilo, king of Bavaria under [unclear] of the Franks. In the fifth year of Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, Garibald, king of the Bavarians, father of the aforementioned Theodolina, queen of the Lombards, died. After him Hildebert, king of the Franks, appointed as king in Bavaria a certain duke named Thassilo, born from the race of the Franks, who defeated in war the Sorbs, who are Slavs but afterwards were called Bohemians.

Compendium, Book I.

In the following year King Agilulf entered to lay waste the borders of the Romans, but through the action of Theodolinda, queen of the Lombards, who was the wife of Agilulf himself, as we have said, not long afterward he made a treaty of friendship with them. Yet they entered, plundered, and destroyed the monastery of our holy father Benedict, abbot, on Monte Cassino, while at the same time the monks fled to Rome.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans, Gunthram, king of the Franks, the second-born son of Lothar the Great and nephew of King Clovis, died at Orleans in the thirty-third year of his reign, not without a reputation for holiness; his kingdom passed to his cousin Childebert by the embassy of one making a testament.

In the following year Richard, king of the Visigoths, entered into a treaty with the kings of the Franks, and joined to himself in marriage the sister of the aforesaid King Childebert. In the same year, on the twenty-first day of the month of November, Saint Columbanus died, abbot, priest, and teacher of the Scots and Picts, who left to his successors many memorials of holiness, except that, in rustic simplicity, he neither learned nor taught that Easter ought to be celebrated on the Lord’s day, and never on any other day.

In the fourteenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Childebert, king of the Franks, died at Orleans; he was the son of King Sigebert, who was the son of Lothar, who was the son of Clovis, the first Christian king. He left two sons, Theobert and Theodoric, who divided their father’s kingdom between themselves; their grandmother Brunichild sowed manifold dissensions.

Therefore in the six hundredth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, which was the eighteenth year of Lothar’s reign, Theobert and Theodoric, the aforesaid brothers, with their grandmother Brunichild stirring up their fury, she being a supporter of Theodoric and laboring under incredible hatred of Theobert, waged a most savage war against one another, in which more than thirty thousand fighting men fell. The angel of the Lord also was seen by many who were present, holding and brandishing in his hand a drawn sword in the air above the people.

At last Theobert, having been defeated, when he could do otherwise, sought safety at least by flight. His brother Theodoric, pursuing him as far as Cologne, caused his soldiers, likewise fleeing, to wander without cease along the whole road. But Theobert entered Cologne and immediately ordered the gates of the city to be closed. Theodoric his brother, pursuing him, as has been said, surrounded Cologne all around. The citizens, hastening to the city walls, asked from Theodoric those things that belonged to peace. He answered them: “You shall never have peace from me unless you first cut off my brother’s head and throw it out to me from the wall. But if you refuse to do this, I shall not depart from here until, when the city has been violently taken, I destroy all of you with your lord, your little children, and your wives.”

When they heard this, the citizens were exceedingly terrified, and, after holding counsel among themselves, at last, lest it happen that all should perish, they cut off the head of King Theobert their lord and threw it out over the wall to Theodoric, his impious brother, as he had ordered, while his own men were then present, shamefully purchasing peace in the blood of their own king. Thus made victor in his brother’s blood, the bloodthirsty king Theodoric entered Cologne in peace, and received that city and its citizens, together with the whole kingdom of his brother’s Austrasians, in surrender. He himself also at last perished by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild, as we shall say in its place, deprived of heirs.

But King Theobert, pursued by a miserable fate, left three sons and one, as is read, exceedingly beautiful daughter: namely Sigebert, Gunthram, and Lothar. I have nowhere found the daughter’s name. But King Theodoric, having entered Cologne, sent as captives to the city of Metz the aforesaid two younger sons of his brother, Gunthram and Lothar, and their sister. Their cruel grandmother Brunichild met them, and, inflamed with excessive fury, in hatred of their slain father rushed upon them and killed with her own hand the grandsons who were still little children; she herself also died badly a little later. But Sigebert, the elder son of Theobert by birth, having been let down through the wall by the help of certain citizens and having very secretly crossed the Rhine, fled away in the dress of a scholar; and coming into eastern Francia, he lay hidden for some years, unknown, among his kinsmen Godfrid and his son Genebald III, dukes of the Franks, who ruled around the Main and Würzburg. At length, after the death of King Theodoric, through the intervention of the princes, he received by the gift of King Lothar a duchy in Upper Alemannia, which is now called Helvetia; but he was not permitted to bear either the royal name or the diadem in the manner of his parents. And he remained under the subjection of the kings of the Franks. He begot a son named Theobert after his father.

In the forty-first year of King Lothar, and in the 618th year of the Lord’s nativity, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, Theodoric, king of Austrasia, died at Metz by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild.

Compendium, Book I

All these were descended from the ancient kings of the Franks: he was of King Anthenor; he was of King Clodius; he was of King Nicanor; he was of King Cloodomir; he was of King Basangot; he was of King Diocles; he was of King Helenus; he was of King Priam; he was of King Antenor; he was of King Marcomir, who led the Franks from Scythia into Germany. But Pippin the elder begot Charles Martel; and he begot Pippin the younger, mayor of the palace of the Franks, and king after Childeric. Thus from King Marcomir the first down to King Pippin, son of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, father of Saint Gertrude, there are counted fifty-one generations over the course of one thousand fifty-nine years.

But King Lothar, in the forty-first year of his reign, which was the six hundred twenty-eighth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the first Roman indiction, appointed Dagobert, his son by Queen Bertrude, king of Austrasia, subjecting to him Metz, Trier, Cologne, Liège, Tournai, Arras, Tongeren, Thérouanne, the Morini, and whatever lay between the western sea, the English sea, the northern sea, and also the Rhine. He very earnestly entrusted him to Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and to Pippin, count of Namur and most noble duke of the Brabanters, to be instructed and directed. Dagobert established the seat of his kingdom, according to the custom of the old kings of Austrasia, in the aforesaid city of Metz, and governed the kingdom of the Franks well, both by himself and through dukes and counts.

In the following year the Saxons rose in rebellion and refused the customary tribute to the Franks. Therefore King Dagobert, having gathered the forces of his men, moved his army against the rebels and fought with Berthulf, duke of the Saxons, by whom he was gravely wounded in the first encounter. When his father Lothar, who was then in the Ardennes, heard this by a swift messenger’s report, he immediately crossed the Rhine at Neuss and hastened to his son’s aid. The battle was renewed; hard and fiercely it was fought on both sides. At last, however, the Saxons, after their duke Berthulf had been slain by the Franks, were defeated and sought safety in flight.

But King Lothar, pursuing the fugitives with the Franks, laid them low in a miserable slaughter, sparing no one, but killing with the sword all who exceeded the length of his sword. The people who remained throughout Saxony he brought back under subjection to the Franks, and imposed on them a tribute of five hundred oxen.

After this, in the six hundred and first year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the fourth Roman indiction, the aforesaid Lothar, king of the Franks, died in the forty-fourth year of his reign, leaving by his first wife, who was called Bertrude, a son named Dagobert, who succeeded to the kingdom. After his first wife had died he had taken a second, named Sighild, who bore Heribert.

The Fifty-First.

Dagobert, the elder son of King Lothar, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the Lord’s Nativity noted above, reigned three years while his father was still living; thus the whole time during which he reigned was seventeen years.

Heribert, however, Dagobert’s brother by the same father but born of another mother, as has been said, received in the division of the kingdom Aquitaine, Toulouse, and the other cities contained between the Pyrenees and the Loire as the possession of his inheritance, on this condition, namely, that in the other kingdoms of the Franks he should claim no right for himself. He established the chief seat of his kingdom at Toulouse. In the fourth year after this, having seized an occasion for war, he received the Gascons into surrender.

King Dagobert constructed anew from the foundations the monastery of Saint Denis the martyr, which he enriched with many estates, goods, and possessions, though not without injury to certain churches, which he despoiled by force of many things, as if all things acquired for the services of Saint Denis, both by right and by wrong, were owed to him. He built the wholly most beautiful church of the same monastery, which was roofed with solid silver; into it he transferred from the village of Catulliacum the bodies of the aforesaid martyr and his companions and placed them in a golden shrine. He most beautifully adorned the walls of the church itself on the inside with tapestries very fittingly interwoven with pearls and large pearls, and gave the place to be inhabited by monks of our order.

Dagobert first had a wife named Gertrude, whom he repudiated because of sterility, and he married another in addition, whose name was Nanthild. Finally, he is read to have had very many

Annals of Trithemius.

he died, in the nineteenth year of his reign. His kingdom Lotharius, the already mentioned son of Hilperic, received; and so, according to the prophecy which Saint Columbanus had once foretold to him, he became monarch of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter reigned alone for thirteen years. Against him the sons of King Theodoric, at the instigation of Brunichildis, raised an army; they were defeated, and Brunichildis herself, instigator of all evils, was captured and, together with Eudolina, daughter of King Theodoric, presented to Lotharius. Condemned by decree of the nobles, she received the sentence of a dreadful death. For, deprived of one foot and the other arm, and tied to the tail of an untamed mare, she was torn apart limb by limb by violent dragging; they said that she had destroyed ten kings.

Lotharius, therefore, having been raised to monarchy over the whole kingdom of the Franks, which previously had been divided into four parts, since he could not govern so broad a dominion effectively by himself, entrusted the provinces to counts descended from the ancient stock of kings. He appointed Guarnerius, a noble and very eminent man, count or prefect of the royal palace. Burgundy, however, he entrusted to a certain Harpo to govern; he too was a count sprung from the most ancient race of the kings of the Franks.

To Rado also, a most noble count, he entrusted Austrasia, in which are the very famous cities Trier, Metz, Liege, Cologne, and the peoples of the Moselle region, the Luxembourgers, the Austrasians, the [Euphalij], the people of Namur, and many others.

To Genebaldus, third duke of the Franks in the east of that name, at Marcopolis, which is now called Wirtzburg from the castle of Saint Mary adjoining it on the mountain, he entrusted Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and the people of those regions; he built the town of Frankfurt beside the Main.

But to Pippin, who was the son of Duke Ansegisus and brother of Saint Arnulph, bishop of Metz, and also count of Namur and duke of Britain, from whom the Palatine counts of the Rhine and the dukes of Bavaria, who today live to the number of eighteen whom I have known, apart from the women, all descended on the mother’s side, namely from Gertrudis, daughter of Henry, count palatine, residing at Heidelberg, who, married to Otto, duke of Bavaria, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1225, joined together the principality of Bavaria and the Palatinate, King Lotharius entrusted all lower or northern Francia, that is, the people of Tournai, Arras, the Morini, the Taravani, the people of Cambrai, and whatever lies between them, except the county of Namur and the duchy of Brabant, which belonged by right to the aforesaid Ansegisus. To Duke Sigebert, son once of Theodobert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, whose head, as we have said, the people of Cologne had cut off, King Lotharius, when he had been made duke through the intervention of the nobles, entrusted the cities of Germany: Chur, Lausanne, Sion, Constance, Basel, and the surrounding peoples, the Alemanni, Rauraci, Helvetii, and those dwelling at the source of the Rhine.

Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirty-second year of his reign, in the seventh Roman indiction, after making an alliance, remitted to the Lombards the tribute of twelve thousand gold florins which they were bound to pay yearly to the Franks.

In the thirty-eighth year of Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, Guarnerius, count of the palace or mayor of the house of the Franks, died. After him Ansegisus, son of Saint Arnulph, bishop of Metz, monk, hermit, formerly married, was made mayor of the house of the Franks; with his son Pippin, and at the same time Saint Arnulph himself, faithfully helping him, he held the principate. Pippin, later mayor of the house, who was also called the Elder, was the son of the aforesaid Ansegisus, who was son of Saint Arnulph. He was son of Ansegisus, or, as others write, of Arnold the Elder. He was son of Ambertus, surnamed Nicanor, born from Blidehildis, daughter of Lotharius, the first king of Clovis. He was son of Duke Priam. He was son of Duke Diocles.

Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirty-eighth and also the thirty-third year of his reign, in the fourteenth Roman indiction, Guarnerius, count of the palace, died; [unclear], brother of Saint Arnulph, bishop of Metz, monk, hermit, formerly married, was made mayor of the house of the Franks; Pippin the son, together with the son and Saint Arnulph himself, faithfully helping him, held the principate. Pippin, later mayor of the house, who was also called the Elder, was the son of the aforesaid Ansegisus, who was son of Saint Arnulph. He was son of Ansegisus, or, as others write, of Arnold the Elder. He was son of Ambertus, surnamed Nicanor, born from Blidehildis, daughter of Lotharius, the first king of Clovis. He was son of Duke Priam. He was son of Duke Diocles.

He was son of Duke Sunno. He was son of Duke Genebaldus. He was son of Duke Dagobert. He was son of Marcomir, king of the Franks. He was son of King Clogio. He was son of King Theodomer. He was son of King Richimer. He was son of King Clodomer. He was son of King Dagobert. He was son of King Walter. He was son of King Clodius. He was son of King Barther. He was son of King Hilderic. He was son of King Sunno. He was son of King Pharabert. He was son of King Clodomer. He was son of King Marcomer. He was son of King [Oodomar]. He was son of King Richemer. He was son of King Anthenor. He was son of King Clodomier. He was son of King [Marcomeius]. He was son of Siccamber, from whom the Franks are said to have been named. He was son of King Antharius. He was son of King Cassander. He was son of King Clodemer.

Lotharius becomes the monarchy of the kingdom [unclear]. Brunichildis, slayer of ten kings, is killed.

Lotharius, elevated to the same monarchy, since he could not govern so broad a dominion effectively by himself, entrusted the provinces to counts descended from the ancient stock of kings. Of the royal palace, count or pre-

Annals of Trithemius.

[he] had concubines, and troops of mistresses accompanied him wherever he went, besides those whom he maintained in several places, dressed and adorned after the manner of queens. Yet Pippin, mayor of the palace, or count palatine, who had been duke of Brabant and at the same time count of Namur, nephew of Saint Arnulf and father of Saint Gertrude, the virgin nun of Nivelles in Brabant, resisted his shameful deeds to no small degree; nor did he in every respect allow the king to sink so freely, at his own pleasure, through so many vices.

In the second year of King Dagobert, which was the six hundred thirty-third year of the Lord's nativity, his wife Nanthild bore him a son, who was named Sigebert. This infant, forty days old, when he was baptized by Saint Amand the bishop, while all were silent, himself answered Amen in a clear voice. His uncle [Charibert?], who reigned at Toulouse, lifted this Sigebert from the holy font of baptism. But after King [Charibert?] died some years later, and not long afterward also his son, named Chilperic, the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks returned to Dagobert, many parts always tending into one, and again, by the plurality of sons, confounding unity.

After King [Charibert?] died, the Gascons, [unclear] the Franks, scorned to be subject; King Dagobert attacked them in war and compelled them to submission.

At the same time Nidachil, who held the dukedom of that same Brittany, terrified by the threat of imminent war, subjected himself and all the people of Armorican Brittany to Dagobert, king of the Franks, and to his successors forever. King Dagobert also attacked in war the Slavs, the Sorbs, who are now called Bohemians, conquered and overcame them, and made them subject and tributary to the Franks.

If this Dagobert, the great king of the Franks, founded that once distinguished, exempt, and royal monastery of our order in the town of Wissembourg in the diocese of Speyer, concerning which I have heard many persons expressing doubt, it seems to me that, if this deed accords with history, it was done in the third year after his father's death, not the twenty-third, since he reigned only fourteen years, although certain uncertain authors seem to have thought otherwise. With this reckoning of times agrees the number of the years of the Lord's nativity, six hundred thirty-four, which was the third year of the aforementioned Dagobert, king of the Franks, but the sixth of his reign over Austrasia, not the twenty-fourth, as we read in Dagobert's own rescripts. Whether these are true or false, how shall we be able to know unless we see their archetype? Desiring to untie the knot of this doubt, let us set down a copy of the letters.

Dagobert, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, to all the chief men of his kingdom, indeed to all who profess the Christian faith, both future and present. A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God or to the saints cannot be made void without the stain of guilt: the greater and more worthy he is to whom the vow is made, by so much the heavier judgment will strike the presumption of the one who vows and does not pay. Therefore we too ought, and we wish, to pay what we have vowed to the Lord, to the terrible God, to him who takes away the spirits of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth. How he terrified us by the arm of his power, how, by striking, he again visited us with [unclear], we have thought should be made known to all as an example of correction, especially so that every faithful person, hearing of our danger, may abstain from devastation of the churches of God and may show fitting honor to things dedicated to God. First, therefore, we shall briefly set forth the dreadful examination of God held over us, and afterward the devout payment of our vow. After my father Chlothar, of most blessed memory, died, I undertook the care of my father's kingdom; but, led by frivolity of life and distracted by desire for rule, I neglected the duty of the royal office, showing no diligence, or [unclear], toward what had been entrusted to me, making little of or judging lightly the zeal of gentleness or institution. Among my other excesses, I had begun to be a destroyer and dissipator of the churches of God, of which I ought to have been the defender and exalter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At last the kindness of God, breaking the pride of an obstinate mind, visited my iniquities with the rod of correction, and, when I had been chastised, did not deny me pardon. For, snatched up on high and brought more immediately before the divine majesty, seated among the choirs of saints in the aspect of one judging, I was gravely and steadfastly accused by the most holy patrons of the churches for the ecclesiastical goods taken away by robbery and consumed by me, especially by the most holy Mary, mother of God, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles. And since, burdened by conscience, I did not dare defend my crimes, I was brought from the judgment of the presiding one to punishment, and when [unclear] had been cut off and I had been overwhelmed by little savage [unclear], there came to meet me at last [unclear] that I should build a monastery of special service. This promise I gladly vowed, and, dismissed from those above, returned. Therefore, under a certain [unclear] remission of indulgence for sins, by our zeal, the vow which we made, [unclear]

King Dagobert exceedingly given to lust.

Pippin, mayor of the palace of the Franks.

An infant of 40 days, when he was baptized, answers Amen.

The monarchy of this kingdom of the Franks is assigned to Dagobert.

The Gascons are overcome by the Franks.

Brittany [unclear] is subjected to the Franks also.

The Slavic Sorbs, who now are called Bohemians.

Discussion concerning the foundation of the monastery of Wissembourg.

The calculation of years does not agree with the history.

A copy of the letters of foundation of the said monastery is compared.

He narrates according to [unclear] whether there had been [unclear] in the church.

King Dagobert enumerated his excesses.

He asserts that he was presented before God as judge.

He comes to build a monastery.

Compendium, Book I

...the church, in honor of the Holy Trinity, and of holy Mary, ever-virgin, and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, in the place called Wyssenburg, which we have built, and which we have resolved to exalt and enrich with royal munificence. Therefore we give to it, and wish it to have been given forever, from the possessions of our fisc lying adjacent there, whatever pertains to us, as much in villages as in bondsmen, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, and all their courses; and all these things we bring by free conveyance to the use of the brethren there serving God under monastic profession. And so that the authority of this our donation might remain stable and firm for all time, we have taken care to note below the boundaries and the names of the surrounding places. Toward the eastern region the march which we have conveyed extends to Aldenburg, and thence to Geboldesvege, and thence below the ford of the Lutra, and thence to Buozdingenhorste, and thence to the boundary which stands on the summit of the valley Inuenesdal, and thence it leads toward the southern region above Warspach, and thence to Bodemlose stompha, and thence to Sebach, and thence to Ingeldeshaere, and thence to the wooded mountains as far as Beedebur. But toward the western region, as far as Lautenbach and Bernbach, and thence to Belebach, and thence to Gruneburnen, and thence to Otterichesheyt. Toward the northern region, as far as Eichenberg. And the place itself, which we embrace with singular affection, now and henceforth under royal will free from every oppression of servitude, namely in such a way that no public judge, no one by judicial license, may presume to exercise or have [authority] there; nor to constrain the men of that place, or [summon them] for hearing cases, or paying fines or tributes; finally, to exact absolutely nothing from them...

He wishes the monastery to be exempt.

...of the other bishops, should have any power of ruling there, or of conducting any causes whatever; but under the protection of our immunity, let the father of the monastery with his brethren possess freely and quietly everything belonging there. In addition, we grant to the same place a coinage having on it images and letters expressed in the likeness of the coinage of Nemetum, and we wish it to be valid and firm by the gift of our authority, so that the men of the same church may freely attend to their business throughout all the bounds of our kingdom, namely in such a way that no toll is owed by them. And no judge, or any person of whatever order, may presume to inflict any violence on them in a matter of this kind. But to the brethren there serving God, so that they may keep the order of holy conduct the more devoutly and peacefully, we grant free power of choosing an abbot for themselves from among themselves. To this abbot, and to all who succeed him, we grant this special privilege of dignity: that he may advance into the order and right of ministerials whomever from the household he shall judge worthy of such honor. Also all the ministerials of the same church by gift of the abbot...

Coinage in the manner of Speyer is granted to the monastery.

The men of the monastery are to be free. Freedom of the monks in choosing an abbot for themselves.

...from the lord abbot.

The ministerials are to obey the abbot alone. The right of advocacy over the household is expressed from the first [unclear].

In the year of the Lord 714, in the twelfth indiction.

Discordance of the time gives rise to doubt.

Lotharius was still living in the year 624.

Works of Trithemius kept for use by our [unclear].

St. Eligius, goldsmith, formerly a bishop. St. Remaclius, from a monk, a bishop of our order.

I find nothing in these letters that introduces doubt for me concerning the aforesaid foundation; but because, except those who are in the immunity. But if the advocate has been absent in these pleas, nothing of the denarii from these is owed, unless he is proved to be in the king’s service. And so that this our conveyance and the institution of the dignity granted may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have signed this written charter, strengthened by the affixing of our seal. Given, as we did, in the monastery itself, in the month of May, on the eleventh day, in the twenty-third year of our reign, in the name of Christ, happily, Amen.

You will find several foundations and donations of this kind made by this King Dagobert in Franciscus de Rosieres, in the Stemmatum Lotharingiae, among the prefixed diplomas of kings and princes; and also in Brusch’s work on monasteries.

At the same time Saint Eligius, powerful in the court of Lotharius and Dagobert, kings of the Franks, and from being an admirable goldsmith, founded, with expenses both royal and his own, the abbey of our order which is called Solignac; in it he himself became a monk and innocently carried out the office of abbot, where also Saint Remaclus, coming from Britain, trained himself under him in the holy soldiery of Christ. Saint...

Compendium, Book I.

under the same rule of Saint Benedict, over whom he set Adela, another daughter of King Dagobert.

But the same bishop Modoaldus built a third holy congregation of girls on the bank of the Moselle, near the walls of the city of Trier, in honor of the divine martyr Symphorianus, under the standard of Saint Benedict, where he set his sister, named Severa, as mother and abbess over the holy women. Living in every purity of mind and body, she in no way fell short of the holiness of her brother. At length, when the course of the present race had been most holily completed, she passed to the Lord and was buried in the same monastery of Saint Symphorianus the martyr, whom she had served most devoutly. This Modoaldus, whom others write as Rodoaldus, was the brother of Itha, wife of Pepin the Elder, and the maternal uncle of the blessed virgin Gertrude. This Itha founded in Brabant the monastery of Nivelles for nuns, in which, after Pepin’s death, she thereafter served Almighty God most holily with her daughter.

But the most holy Modoaldus, prelate of Trier, not long after his sister’s death, himself also resting in the Lord, was buried beside her in the church of Saint Symphorianus. Numerianus succeeded him in the archbishopric.

Nor should it have been passed over in silence that Dagobert, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 627, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans, began to found the Dologiense monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, by the counsel and aid of the blessed archbishop Modoaldus; Sigebert, king of Austrasia, his son, completed it. And the holy prelate Pirminius, a monk, afterward adorned it more beautifully.

In these times, in the diocese of Trier, men of great holiness were illustrious. One of their number was Paul, who on Mount Gebenna, opposite the city of Trier, across the bridge of the river Moselle, led an eremitic life. Then, coming to the aforementioned Dologiense monastery, he became a monk; finally, ordained bishop of Verdun, he faithfully kept in all things the little rule of his former holiness. The mountain previously called Gebenna, taking its name from him, is called Paulimons, commonly Paulsberg, down to the present day, and shines with countless miracles. At his tomb in the aforesaid little town there is a frequent gathering of peoples out of devotion.

There was another, at almost the same time, Wandalinus, a monk and priest, a disciple of Saint Columbanus, companion in pilgrimage of the divine monk Walaric, a holy man, an outstanding preacher, who converted many by the word and example of his manner of life, who, dead to the living, down to the present day shines with countless miracles. At his tomb in the aforesaid little town there is a frequent gathering of peoples out of devotion.

Wandalinus also, a monk and priest; Carilephus, a monk and priest; Wolffrichus; Bantus his brother; Beatus; monks and priests; Wolff, a layman, most holy men, with many others in the diocese of Trier, in these times led a solitary life in the wilderness. Saint Disibotus also, a monk and priest, in the diocese of Mainz, in the county of Spanheim, two miles from Kreuznach and one from a certain monastery of mine, Spanheim, leading an eremitic life, built a monastery of monks in that place, Sobernheim, where the Nahe and the Glan flow together; it exists today under his name.

In the first year of Clodoveus, king of the Franks, Saint Remaelus is ordained bishop of the church of Maastricht, a man of much learning and great holiness.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 647, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, Pepin the Elder died: count of Namur, duke of Brabant, mayor of the palace, palatine count of Sigebert king of the Franks, who held the seat of the kingdom at Metz in Austrasia; father of the holy virgin Gertrude. He left a son, Grimoald. Grimoald succeeded his father in the leadership of the royal household for eleven years; afterward he was killed, as we shall say in its place. He had a son named Childebert, of whom we shall also speak, namely how he made him king after his own lord had been driven into exile.

In the year noted above, Radulf, duke of the Thuringians, lifted up in pride, refused to pay the accustomed tribute to the Franks. Therefore Sigebert, king of the Franks of Austrasia, having gathered forces, moved an army into Thuringia; and, when battle was joined, he defeated the duke and compelled him to pay the tribute.

In the same

Annals of Trithemius

Saint Dado, also called Audoenus, bishop of Rouen and chancellor of King Dagobert, likewise built within the forest of Brie a monastery of our order, which they call Resbac, and appointed over it as first abbot Saint Agil, a man beloved by Christ and renowned for many virtues.

King Dagobert, in the ninth year of his reign, designated his son Sigebert, a boy of seven years, as king over the Austrasians, under the guardianship and direction of Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, and of Pippin, duke of Brabant and count of Namur.

In the same year, which was the six hundred and fortieth from the Lord’s Nativity, in the thirteenth indiction, Saint Arnulf died: Pippin’s grandfather, formerly mayor of the palace of the Franks, bishop of Metz, and from bishop a solitary hermit. Clodulf, after his father, was ordained bishop of Metz, and imitated his holiness.

Doda, formerly the lawful wife of Saint Arnulf before his episcopate, mother of the aforesaid bishop Clodulf, was enclosed at Trier for love of Christ, whom she had chosen as her spouse; separated from her husband, she shone with [unclear] holiness.

In the eleventh year of his reign, Dagobert, king of the Franks, led an army against the Wends. The Saxons came to his aid with all eagerness. When battle was joined, the Wends were defeated by the Franks and were forced under tribute into servitude to the Franks. But the Saxons, who annually paid the Franks five hundred oxen as tribute, seized the opportunity and, approaching King Dagobert after the victory, asked him to remit the tribute to them. The king, wishing to repay their voluntary service with favor, remitted the tribute.

After this Dagobert, king of the Franks, died on the first day of the month of February. He was buried in the church of Saint Denis, which he himself had built, in the fourteenth year of his reign, and in the six hundred and [forty-]fifth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the third indiction of the Romans.

The Fifty-Second

Clovis, son of King Dagobert, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned seventeen years. His mother’s name was Nathildis. His mayor of the palace, or count, or prince of the palace, was an energetic and most noble man named Erchenwald, [unclear].

Clovis reigned seventeen years over Neustria, that is, over Paris, Amiens, Beauvais, Blois, Reims, Orleans, Tours, and also Aquitaine, in the whole kingdom that had belonged to his father.

But his brother Sigebert, as we have said, reigned in Austrasia: over the people of Metz, Trier, Cologne, Liège, Maastricht, where Saint Amandus was then bishop, over Tongeren, also the Morini, the Hollanders, Frisians, Saxons, Thuringians, Bavarians, Suevi, Alemanni, those on this side of the Rhine, Strasbourg, Worms, Mainz, the [Cynonoti?], and the Burgundians. His mayor of the palace, or prince of the palace, was Pippin the Elder, son of Ansegis, grandson of Saint Arnulf, count of Namur, duke of Brabant, father of Grimoald and of Saint Gertrude, abbess of Nivelles, in the paternal duchy of Brabant.

The chancellor of Sigebert was Saint Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne. In very many of the places or provinces already named, under the dominion of King Sigebert and of Mayor of the Palace Pippin, there were appointed petty kings, dukes, counts, and prefects, by whose administration the people was governed.

Irmina, a virgin of most holy way of life, was one of the daughters of King Dagobert, sister of the kings mentioned before. For her, while he was still living, her father built in the city of Trier, in his very ancient palace which was called the Horrea, a monastery of girls under the rule of Saint Benedict, and a church in honor of blessed Mary ever virgin. In it he placed a congregation of nuns, to whom he gave as mother and abbess that same daughter of his. She was renowned for many virtues and miracles in life and after death; her venerable head is held in the abbey of Sponheim. After this Irmina in the governance of the nuns of the aforesaid monastery succeeded Modesta, a pupil of the monastery of Romaric, daughter of the sister of blessed Modoald, archbishop of Trier; after her Anastasia; in the fourth place Basilissa. All these have been numbered among the saints.

At the same time the aforesaid bishop of Trier, Modoald, at whose urging the monastery in the Horrea already mentioned had been built, also built another monastery in the old palace, which was situated in the suburbs of Trier, in which nuns

Saint Modesta, Saint Anastasia, Saint Basilissa, abbesses in the same place.

Saint Modoald, confirmer of many monasteries.

Annals of Trithemius.

In the same year Saint Furseus, abbot, came from Ireland into Gaul as a pilgrim for the love of Christ, and was honorably received by King Clovis. He founded the monastery of Latiniacum, now of our order, and established monks there. Not long afterward two brothers of his, Foillanus and Vitanus, monks, following him with an equal vow of pilgrimage, enlightened Gaul by the word and by the example of their life.

Of these, Foillanus, by the gift of Saint Gertrude the virgin, later founded the monastery of Fosses, where also, crowned with martyrdom, he rests in the Lord.

In the sixth year of King Clovis, Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, despairing of offspring in posterity, built here and there twelve monasteries of the order of Saint Benedict in honor of God, with Grunwald, mayor of the palace, and Saint Remaclus, bishop of the people of Maastricht, working with him in these matters. Among them Stavelot and Malmedy were preeminent, which are governed under one abbot. This Remaclus, not long afterward, became a monk in the same monastery of Stavelot, resigning the episcopal office, full of cares, and at last happily rested.

In these times also, in Gallic France, Saint Landelinus, confessor of Christ, and Morotius built four monasteries of the aforesaid order: Lobbes, [Alciense], [Wafariense], and Crespin, where he rests bodily in the Lord with his disciples Adolenus and Domitianus.

At the same time the monastery of Fleury was founded by Abbot Leodeboldus; to it, not much later, the body of our divine father Benedict the abbot is said to have been transferred from Monte Cassino by the monk Agilulf, after his monastery, as we said above, had been laid waste by the Lombards. The Italians contradict this.

In the seventh year of Clovis, which was the six hundred fifty-second year of the Lord’s Nativity, Sigebert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, adopted Hildebert, son of Grunwald the mayor of the palace, as his son, [unclear].

In the following year Saint Judocus, son of the king of the Britons, despising the kingdom and the world, as a pilgrim and hermit in the district of Ponthieu, rested in Christ.

In the eleventh year of King Clovis, Sigebert, king of Austrasia, his brother, died, after commending his son Dagobert, still very small, to the trust of Grunwald, mayor of the palace, so that by his help he might be advanced to the kingdom. In the following year Grunwald had him tonsured by Dido, bishop of Poitiers, and sent him into Scotland; against good faith he raised up his own son Hildebert as king of the Austrasians. But the Franks, grieving over such great faithlessness on Grunwald’s part, captured him and presented him for the judgment of King Clovis at Paris. Clovis caused him, bound in chains, to be consumed by a bitter death in prison; and, after casting down his son, he appointed his own younger son Hilderic king of the Austrasians and avenged his nephew’s injury.

Clovis, king of the Franks, because of his insufficiently reverent contact with the body of Saint Dionysius, died after two years insane and out of his mind, in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 662, in the fifth indiction.

The fifty-third.

Lothar, the elder-born son of King Clovis, reigned after his father over the Franks for four years. His mayor of the palace was Eberwinus, whom the French, not understanding the property of the name, since it is Teutonic, wrongly write as Ebroin: an impious and wicked man, a destroyer of the Church, a persecutor of the clergy, a most abominable murderer of bishops, [unclear] and they returned home.

In these times Queen Balthildis, mother of Lothar, formerly the surviving wife of King Clovis, founded two distinguished monasteries of our order in Gallic France, of which one is named Corbie and the other Chelles; in them many most holy and most learned monks flourished. At the same time also many other monasteries of the aforesaid order of our divine father Benedict were built in the Gallic kingdom, among the number of which these are recorded: the monastery of Chelles, [unclear].

Saint Furseus, abbot and pilgrim.

Foillanus and Vitanus, monks, [unclear].

Twelve monasteries of our order were founded.

Saint Remaclus, bishop in Maastricht.

Landelinus, confessor of the Lord.

The monastery of Fleury is founded.

Hildebert is adopted as son by Sigebert.

Saint Judocus dies in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Sigebert, king of Austrasia, died, [unclear] son.

Grunwald, mayor of the palace of Austrasia, is captured and [unclear].

The Lothar kings of the Franks reigned in name only.

The whole administration of the kingdom was in the hands of the mayors of the palace.

The monasteries of Corbie and Chelles were founded.
