They remained in that land for a long time, retaining the name of Franks, until at last they were called Marcomeri from a certain duke Marcomerus, whose son Brand built the city of Brandenburg.

On the Origin of the Franks

In the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar of the Romans, the younger brother of Titus, after Nero stirred up the second persecution against the Christians; he also, first of all the Caesars, in his sixth year, ordered himself to be called Lord and God.

King Richimer, in the eleventh year of his reign, waged war with the Roman Gauls not far from the city of Basana, which is now called Aachen. At the same time the legions of Roman soldiers at Cologne, after a war with the Franks had been engaged not very successfully, on receiving news of the death of Caesar Cocceius Nerva, made Ulpius Trajanus Crinitus, a Spaniard by nation, emperor. He stirred up the third persecution against the Christians. Later, having been instructed, he ordered that Christians should not be sought out, but that only those who presented themselves voluntarily ought to be killed. Afterwards, however, changed again, he raised a fourth persecution against them. Richimer, king of the Franks, died in the year of the Lord 113, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.

Odemar, the first-born son of Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for thirteen years, a prince very beloved by the people of the Franks. He abstained from wars as far as could be done. He made truces, that is, truces or assurances, with the Gauls and Romans, and showed himself so much a friend of both that all lamented his death. Therefore, having peace with everyone, he devoted all his zeal to the dignity and adornment of the nation, renewing laws and establishing new cities and fortifications. Among many cities he founded one in his own name, in the land that was called Tuendia, which lies between the Saxons and the Franks, bordering near the little river Vecht; he ordered it to be called Odemarshesin, in the fourth year of his reign, and in the 117th year of the Lord’s nativity. King Odemar died in the fourteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 128.

Marcomer, son of Odemar, reigned after his father for twenty-one years. He had as wife the daughter of the king of Britain, named Athildis, by whom he begot seven sons, whose names are these: Clodomer, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Marcomer, who was duke among the Nitriones and founded a city of his own name, called Marcoburg; Clogio, who perished in Britain; Franc, who was duke among the Hogian peoples from Coblenz as far as the Main, toward the east between the people of Mainz and the Saxons, who, restoring the old city Helenopolis beside the bank of the Main, ordered it to be called Frankfurt; Merodac, who died when struck by a boar in the hunt; Nicanor, who was duke of the island of Holland; and Odemar, whom his father appointed pontiff of sacred rites. At that time Doracus, counsellor and philosopher of the Franks, flourished, a man eminently learned in all the sciences of the world, who presided over songs and annals. The Franks had peace all the days in which Marcomer reigned, and under him they greatly increased in wealth and power, augmented in number and dignity. Doracus writes in the annals, as Hunibald reports, that the Romans always regarded the Franks with suspicion both in war and in peace, as though [unclear] by name Hasildis, by whom he begot three sons, Farabert, Nicanor. The elder by birth succeeded his father. The second was king of Phrista. The third, Rorich, was drowned in a river, from whom the name Rora has remained for the river down to the present day, between the castle Neocum [unclear] for the most part happened under Paramund and his followers. King Marcomer died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 148.

But in the year of the Lord 165.

Clodomer, the first-born son of King Marcomer, reigned after his father for seventeen years. He was a prudent, modest, and active man. He had as wife the daughter of the duke of the Rugii, named Hasildis, by whom he begot three sons: Farabert; the third, Rorich, was drowned in a river, from whom the name Rora remained for the river down to the present day between the castle Neocum. The elder succeeded his father. The second was king of Phrista. The third, Rorich, was drowned, from whom the river Rora [unclear] down to the present day between the castle Neocum. For the most part it happened under Paramund and his followers. King Marcomer died in the twentieth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord 175.

But in the year of the Lord 185.

Farabert, son of Clodomer, the elder by birth, reigned after his father for twenty years. Of his [unclear]

Suimo reigned eighteen years and fought many battles with the Gauls and Romans. For in his time Severus Caesar of the Romans brought Britain, which is now England, back again into subjection to the Romans, which did not please Suimo and his princes. Therefore, when Severus had died in Britain, Suimo laid waste Gaul in the penultimate year of his reign and returned victorious. He died in the 148th year of his reign, and in the 223rd year of the Lord’s nativity.

Suimo reigned 28 years.

Johannes Trithemius. Hilderic reigned 40 years.

Hilderic, the elder son of Suimo, succeeding his father, reigned forty years, a man powerful in arms and of great prudence. On an island of the Rhine he built a very strong castle, not far from Neoco, which he called Hildeburg from his own name. In his time flourished Hildegast, the wisest philosopher of the Franks, counsellor and seer, or prophet, born of royal seed, who succeeded Odemar in the highest pontificate. For forty-six years he was of such opinion and reputation among the Franks that he was heard by all as though he were some divine power, and gave commands both to kings and dukes and to the whole people of the Franks as if he were God and Lord.

The prophecy of Hildegast concerning [arvosa Friderum], that is, the lion and the serpent.

On the birthday of King Hilderic, standing in the temple of Jove at Neopagus before the image of that very god, after prayers poured forth for prophecy, he began to rave, as is the custom with those prophesying; and with head shaken and hands curved back, he prophesied thus: “Victory comes to the Franks from the western god, whom the ancient Dardanian fathers worshipped. Whatever the Gaul possesses, whatever all Germany possesses, all will yield to your right, warlike Sicambrian. When he has given you the first king from the name, whom the princes and dukes without a king shall establish, while he reigns the Frank will reign without end.” Concerning the Romans too he added these words: “Behold, the great god will give the Frank the brothel-camps, and the lion will break the eagle, the serpent [unclear].”

For they had been more accustomed to live in fields than in cities or in beautiful or elaborate dwellings. Often, indeed, by command of their kings they were compelled to change their seats and homes, and therefore they did not care for beautiful buildings. But Hildegast taught them more cultivated speech and manners, and to build houses divided into different apartments. For whatever they had constructed before, through excessive simplicity, was contemptible. Hence the Germans, taking up a proverb, when they see anything made or painted with ancient simplicity, are accustomed to say down to this day: “This is an old work of the Franks.” Das ist ein alt Fränckisch Werck. The rest concerning Hilderic is in Hunibald. He died in the fortieth year of his reign, and in the 253rd year of the Lord’s birth.

Bertherius, son of King Hilderic, reigned after his father for seventeen years. In his time the Romans, who were staying in legions in Gaul on this side of the Rhine, waged war with the Suevic Alemanni, leading their army to Augusta, the city of the Raetians, which is now in Swabia, in the seventh year of Berther, king of the Franks, where Valerian was created Augustus by the soldiers in the army, and Gallienus was called Caesar by the senate at Rome, Gallus and Volusianus having been killed by Aemilianus.

The Franks devastated Italy, Gaul, and Spain.

In Berther’s tenth year, Germans, with the aid of the Franks and Saxons, entered the territories of the Romans as enemies, and, devastating everything, came as far as Ravenna.

Clodius reigned 27 years.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. Proceeding from there, they reached as far as Italy and inflicted many losses on the Romans. In the following year the Franks, having the Germans and Saxons as allies, by order of King Berther, under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons, ranged through Gaul with a great army and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through the [Belucaci?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 261.

The Franks went again into Gaul.

Clodius reigned 27 years.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. As they proceeded from there, they reached as far as Italy and inflicted many losses on the Romans. In the following year the Franks, having the German Saxons as allies, by order of King Berther, under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons, ranged through Gaul with a great army and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through [Belucae?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 351.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. As they proceeded from there, they reached as far as Italy, having the German Saxons by order of King Berther under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons; with a great army they ranged through Gaul and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through [Belucae?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 361.

Clodius, son of Berther, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years. In his eighth year the Romans expelled the Franks from the territories of Spain and inner Gaul, many being slain on both sides. For the Franks withdrew as far as their old seats on the Meuse.

Thereafter, in the twelfth year of his reign, King Clodius, desiring to avenge himself on the Romans, again invaded Gaul through his dukes, and many thousands of the Romans were killed by the Franks. And so

The Franks held a great part of inner Gaul for seven years.

In the nineteenth year of King Clodius, the Romans came again under the commander Probus, and again expelled the Franks from Gaul, with not a few of their own men killed and destroyed in war on both sides.

In these times of Clodius also the Roman empire was variously governed, because not

50

On the Origin of the Franks.

...suffered no small loss from the Franks, Germans, Suebi, that is, Alemanni, and Saxons. But in the eleventh year of King Clodius, Claudius Caesar led the Roman army against the Suebi; the Suebi, meeting him not far from Lake Benacus with thirty thousand men, fought fiercely. At length the victory fell to the Romans, and more than twelve thousand of the Suebi fell, the rest seeking safety in flight.

King Clodius died in the seventeenth year of his reign, and in the year 288 of the Lord’s Nativity.

Walther, son of King Clodius, reigned after his father for eight years. In his first year Diocletian began at Rome and ruled for nearly twenty years; he was of such arrogance and pride that he ordered himself to be publicly worshipped as God.

In the first, second, third, and fourth years of King Walther there were great disturbances in Britain, which is now England. For, after Lucius, king of the Britons, had died some years before, he who first had received the Christian faith from Pope Eleutherius in the time of Suimon, son of Pharabert, king of the Franks, in the year of Christ 188, the Romans appointed Severus, a senator, in his place and sent him into Britain with two legions; when he landed, the Britons received him at the shore with war.

After he was at length slain at York, Carausius, born in Britain of the lowest rank, was declared king with the consent of the Romans and exercised much tyranny. When he at last had been killed, in the times of Walther, king of the Franks, the Romans sent Alexius in his place with three legions of soldiers. But the Britons, unable to bear the rule of the Romans any longer, themselves appointed Asclepiodotus as their king, and killed Alexius with two legions of Romans. But they besieged Gallus the prefect with the third legion at London; when he saw that he could not resist, after receiving permission to depart, he surrendered the city. Asclepiodotus began in the eighth year of Walther and reigned ten years.

The Romans were powerful in these times and ruled many nations. The Franks, however, were afflicted by the utmost hatred of the Romans; nevertheless they remained quiet, silently awaiting the prophecy of their prophets, which had not yet arrived. King Walther died in the eighth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 296.

Dagobert, son of King Walther, reigned after his father for eleven years. He was very gentle toward his subjects; hence it came about that great and small revered him as a father, each pursuing him with great reverence and honor.

In the fourth year of Dagobert, king of the Franks, Coel, duke of Gloucester, rising against his lord Asclepiodotus, king of the Britons, induced by the promises of the Romans, killed him in war. Rejoicing at this news, the Romans sent Constantius, a senator, who had previously subdued Spain for them, a man no less prudent than bold. When Coel heard that he had landed on the shore, he sent messengers, sought peace, and promised tribute to the Romans, provided only that he might have the kingdom. Constantius agreed. These terms having been settled, Coel died within forty days; soon afterward Constantius took his daughter, named Helena, to whom no maiden in the land was equal in beauty, knowledge of the liberal arts, and skill with musical instruments. [unclear] afterward succeeded in the kingdom, and prevailed not only over the Britons but also against Maxentius for the empire of the Romans.

For Constantius, having been made emperor, made Constantine Caesar and entrusted Gaul to him. At that time the Alemanni occupied Gaul in great power; Caesar Constantine waged war with them in the fourth year of the aforesaid Dagobert, king of the Franks, at the city of Langres in Gaul, and killed sixty thousand of them. Dagobert, king of the Franks, died in the eleventh year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 307.

Clogio, son of Dagobert, succeeding his dead father, reigned only two years. For in the second year of his reign the Romans fiercely invaded the kingdom of the Franks around the Meuse and the Rhine, namely in that year in which Constantius, dying at York in Britain, commended the kingdom and empire to his son Constantine with his mother.

When therefore Clogio, king of the Franks, fought rather incautiously, he was intercepted by the Romans and killed, leaving two sons, of whom the elder by birth was then in his thirtieth year, while the younger by birth, Richimer, was eighteen. But by the law of the Franks it was forbidden for anyone to be advanced as king unless he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it came about that neither of Clogio’s sons could come to the kingdom, but their paternal uncle, by election of the princes, was crowned king. King Clogio was slain in the second year of his reign, and in the year of Christ 309.

The Alemanni, that is, the Suebi, are cut down by the Romans.

Walther reigns for 8 years.

The Romans occupy Britain, England.

The Britons [unclear] of the Romans [unclear].

The Franks’ and Romans’ accustomed hatred.

Dagobert reigned 11 years.

Asclepiodotus, king of Britain, is killed.

Constantius the Roman becomes king of Britain, afterward Caesar.

Clogio reigned for 2 years.

Killed by the Romans.

The law of the Franks.

Johannes Trithemius

Clodomer reigns for 18 years. Genebald, duke of the Franks, fights against the Romans.

Clodomer, the brother of Clogio, reigned after him for eighteen years. In his second year the Alemanni, who are also Suebi, having been severely afflicted by the Romans, called the Franks, Thuringians, and Saxons to their aid, warning and entreating them not to delay in coming swiftly to help them, considering that, if the Romans, as they had conceived in their minds, should prevail, the Franks, Saxons, and Thuringians would without doubt soon be attacked by them. When these matters had been recognized, King Clodomer appointed his brother Genebald commander of the army, and placed under him eighty thousand men. The other kings also did likewise; having been called to their aid, they joined auxiliary soldiers to the Alemanni and formed a great army, and, assembling against the Romans, fought fiercely and killed more than forty-six thousand of them; the rest sought safety in flight.

When the Germans had obtained this victory and were dividing the spoils in the camp according to their accustomed manner, there arose between two soldiers, one of whom was a Thuringian, a certain disturbance, which grew so great that a dangerous sedition followed. For each had many men of his own people adhering to him. Nevertheless, through the intervention of the authority of the dukes and princes, they ceased from tumult on that occasion. The cause of the disturbance was that the Suebian soldier, named Adelbert, had said that a Thuringian named Gunther had secretly taken away something from the booty common to all. But when the Thuringian denied the theft, the Suebian offered to prove his statement by duel. When the princes allowed this, the combat of single battle was undertaken, and the Thuringian was killed by the Alemannian in the second encounter. When his body had been stripped of its arms and clothing, the theft too of which he had been accused was found in his possession. At this shame the Thuringians were stirred in mind beyond measure. Yet, concealing their anger, one hundred and twenty men afterward held counsel apart as to how they might avenge Gunther, who had been slain, upon Adelbert the Suebian, and ordered everything to be kept most secret.

Therefore, on the following night they rushed upon the tent in which they suspected Adelbert the Suebian to be, and cried out, “Hand over to us the murderer, that he may die.” What more? They run to arms. The Suebi determined to defend their innocent soldier, or to die with him, and, rushing against those one hundred and twenty Thuringians, almost all were slaughtered. When this was announced in the camp of the Thuringians, at once driven to fury, at daybreak they rushed upon the Suebi, shouting in madness, “Ogyverrederß hoeß vwichi.” But the Suebi, not sluggish, seized their arms and defended themselves bravely. A fierce battle was joined between friends, in which more than twelve thousand Thuringians were killed by the Suebi; the rest, slipping away in flight, came to the camp of the Franks, who were distant from them by about two leagues. For the matter had become known neither to the Franks nor to the Saxons until it had been carried out, because they had pitched camp not in the same place, but far from one another.

After this, the princes and dukes of the Franks and Saxons labored with great efforts for peace and concord between the Alemanni and the Thuringians; but since both sides complained that they had been gravely injured, they could not restore full peace. They did, however, obtain truces for three years, during which the parties were to abstain from war, until in the meantime, as the disturbance of the commotion cooled, it should be allayed. From that time down to our age there remains a perpetual hidden discord between the Suebi and the Thuringians, although many do not know the cause, and they pursue one another mutually.

In the sixth year of Clodomer, king of the Franks, when the truces or agreements between the aforesaid peoples had ended, the Alemanni declared war on the Thuringians. But the Thuringians, distrusting their own resources, sent noble and distinguished messengers to King Clodomer and the nobles of the Franks, asking with great urgency that, as friends, they would deign to send forces to their aid against the Alemanni. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the surrounding islands. The king of the Franks, because the settlements of his people were not far distant from Britain, was in great anxiety, fearing the treacheries of the Romans, lest perhaps they should make an incursion by land and harass the borders of the Franks, as indeed they had often done before.

Therefore, after taking counsel with his men, he answered the envoys of the Thuringians in a public assembly of the magnates, saying: “Through Duke Genebald, my very dear brother, I have long understood what was the cause, friends Thuringians, of the discord between you and the Alemanni, and of those disturbances which today are at the gates. But you yourselves know very well that the Romans with the Gauls press upon us daily and observe most diligently whether by any occasion they might be able to destroy our kingdom. Therefore I do not judge it prudent for us in these perilous times to divide the people and, with our own affairs neglected, to guard those of others. If we could do this without danger to ourselves, as we have often done before, we would do it now also with friendly service. For the distance of the places is too great for us to fight against the Alemanni, since they hold the beginning and source of the Rhine, while we hold its farthest mouths.”

When these things had been heard from the king of the Franks, the envoys of the king of Thuringia answered: “Lord king of Francia, and you nobles of the Franks, listen. We have a broad, fertile, and pleasant land; wherefore, if it pleases you, it is

On the Origin of the Franks.

[unclear] our king, with the whole people of the Thuringians, [is ready?] to give to your people an excellent land, which is by the banks of the Main and among the Alemanni, so that it may be a wall for us and the destruction of the Alemanni. At the petition of the Thuringians, the Franks gave their consent and accepted what was offered.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 316, which was the seventh year of Clodomir, king of the Franks, on the nineteenth day of April, there went out from Cismarine Francia, where now are Utrecht, Holland, Guelders, Zeeland, part of Frisia and Westphalia, and also Brabant with many adjacent lands, thirty thousand armed men and two thousand six hundred eighty-six farmers and craftsmen of various trades, with their wives, children, and possessions, chosen and approved by the king to go up into the land which the Thuringians had promised to give to the Franks; and they received it with great joy.

The king appointed as duke over the people sent out and the whole army his brother Genebald, who in earlier years had fought with the Alemanni. He was a man of great prudence, bold and warlike, who not only held well the borders given to him and his people, but in a short time greatly enlarged them. And when the Franks had left their ancestral hearths, Duke Genebald advanced with twenty thousand fighters to the place assigned to him by the Thuringians; the remaining ten thousand, for the protection of the people following behind, he left on the road after him with his son Marcomer.

When the Alemanni learned that the Franks had received new settlements from the Thuringians beside the banks of the Main, in their midst, they were greatly afraid, and, sending envoys to Duke Genebald, they begged for peace, and [unclear] every cause of quarrel [with?] Thuringia and Saxony. At their entry all the Thuringians, by command of their king Herol, withdrew into Thuringia and received the dwellings assigned to them, leaving, by order of the king, provisions sufficient for the Franks for a whole year. But the Franks, newly arrived, settled in the land now their own; first in that [unclear] they send. The Thuringians did likewise. And so the great discord between them was extinguished by Genebald’s prudence.

In the same year, in the month of September, Marcomer, the son of Duke Genebald, came with the remaining people of the Franks into southern Thuringia, and they received the promised settlements around the river Main, having Bohemia on the east, Alemannia on the south, the Rhine and Mainz on the west, and Thuringia and Saxony on the north. At their entry all the Thuringians, by command of their king Herol, withdrew into Thuringia and received the dwellings assigned to them, leaving, by just command, provisions sufficient for the Franks for a whole year. The Franks, impatient [unclear] and very ready for wars. Yet he could not restrain them because they were more than usually occupied in many provinces.

Duke Genebald, however, [unclear] with Clodomir, king of the Franks, who reigned in western Francia around the sea, the Meuse, and the Rhine, entered into an alliance with the Alemanni and Thuringians, so that he might be stronger to attack the Romans and Gauls, who threatened the borders of Francia on the other side of the Rhine at Mainz and Strasbourg. Against them he often fought after crossing the Rhine, and killed many of them.

Duke Genebald begot Dagobert, who ruled the people for twenty-one years. Clodius, however, begot Marcomer, and he begot Clodius, who ruled for twenty-three years. Clodius begot Faramund, who in the second year of his dukedom was elected king of the Franks, as is written below in its proper order. The aforesaid four leaders of the eastern Franks, presiding over the people for ninety-four years, extended the borders of the possessions they had received as far as the river Rhine, and did great damage to the Gauls and Romans. But now what remains concerning the succession of the kings of the Franks must be continued. King Clodomir died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 328.

Richimer, son of Clodomir, reigned after his father for fourteen years, and throughout all the days of his reign was in conflict with the Romans and Gauls, and joined many battles with them. He had also in his father’s lifetime fought with Caesar Constantius, the father of Constantine, namely in the year of the Lord 218. For Constantius, about to enter Britain by command of the Romans, made a hostile attack on the people of the Franks dwelling along the borders of the Rhine by the sea and the Meuse, and compelled them to retreat, many of them being slain in battle. When he at last died in Britain [unclear].

Where now is Eastern Francia.

Thirty thousand armed Franks, and two thousand six hundred farmers, [unclear] from Holland, go up to Würzburg.

Genebald, the first duke of the eastern Franks, etc.

In the year of Christ 1379.

Genebald, duke of the eastern Franks, [unclear] thirty.

The eastern Franks, with the Alemanni and the aid of Thuringia, against this [unclear].

Genealogy of the dukes of the eastern Franks, ruling under the kings.

Richimer, son of Clodomir, reigned over Francia for 13 years.

On the Origin of the Franks.

Genebaldus, the second duke, first-born son of Dagobert, the first duke, held for nineteen years the principate assigned to him by his father. Moreover his two brothers, Marcomerus and Suimo, were dukes in the places marked out for them by their begetter: one, that is, on that side of the Rhine which faces the Saxons, and the other on the other side, where the Sea divides Gaul, Holland. Genebaldus, however, held Tongres and a great part of Gaul, together with Brabant.

This division of the principate did not please the nobles of the Franks, by which they did not doubt that they would become weaker day by day; yet it was quite pleasing to the Romans. At that time Marcomerus, son of Chlodius, fourth in the order of dukes from the time when the Franks had received seats from the Thuringians in that place, ruled over the eastern Franks. His dominion extended from the borders of Bavaria and Bohemia in the east as far as the Rhine, having under him the [Hogii?], the [Meneganii?], and the [Caraganii?], as far as the baths of Alsace. The Romans were never able to subdue this duke, although they tried more than once.

In the second year of Duke Genebaldus, which was the 387th year of the Lord’s Nativity, Maximus, of the stock of the emperors, who had drawn his origin from Britain, whom Octavius, then king, had called from Rome into England and had made his son-in-law and successor to the kingdom, was made emperor through a mutiny of the soldiers, against Gratian. For after he had reigned in Britain for five years in good peace, lifted up in pride by the Roman soldiers whom he had brought with him, he commanded that he be made emperor, and soon sailed with all his soldiery into Gaul against Gratian, in order to subject it to his rule.

First, therefore, he invaded the kingdom of the Armoricans, which is now called New or Lesser Britain, and with the Franks who inhabited it he joined battle under the aforesaid Duke Genebaldus. Iubalchus had been appointed by Genebaldus as commander of the Franks’ war; meeting Maximus with the whole army of Franks that he had, he fought with him, and victory fell to Maximus. In that battle fifteen thousand of the Franks fell, and the duke Iubalchus himself perished. The rest fled; with the little children, [unclear], the old men also, and all the young men, as many as he found throughout all Armorica, he cruelly killed. But he gave that kingdom of New Britain to Iunanus, who had been the nephew of Octavius, king of the English, leaving with him a great soldiery, after, that is, he had made all Gaul subject to himself.

For after Maximus had subjugated all Gaul to himself, Gratian, fleeing from Paris, was captured and killed at Lyon. Maximus set the seat of empire in the city of Trier, where he made his son Victor, still a boy, his associate in the empire; later, when he was about to set out for Italy, he entrusted him to Nannenus and Quintinus.

Meanwhile Conamus of the Armoricans, king of the Britons, wishing to give wives to his soldiers who had none, and to bring over with their children those who had left their own in England, so that they would have no cause for intermingling with the Gauls, sent messengers into England to Dionotus, king of Cornwall, who had succeeded his brother Coradocus in the kingdom. He asked of him that his daughter, named Ursula, a beautiful virgin, be given and sent to him as wife. Likewise, secondly, he asked that he similarly send to him, placed on ships, the wives with the children of the soldiers and nobles who were then in Armorica. Thirdly he asked that, for the soldiers who did not yet have wives, he send virgins.

King Dionotus, wishing to satisfy the prayers of Conamus, gathered from the whole island eleven thousand daughters of nobles, and sixty thousand from the stock of the lower order, that is, in sum, eighty-one thousand; among these were likewise counted the wives of nobles and soldiers with their children. He also ordered ships to be brought from different shores, in which he placed everything necessary for those sailing. And although the voyage pleased many in that company of women, it displeased many others, who loved their parents and fatherland more intensely with greater affection. But the king’s command prevailed.

When the ships had been prepared, the women, together with the virgins, boarded around the river Thames. While they directed the fleet toward Armorica, a great storm arose on the sea, and the ships were separated from one another. The greater part of that whole assembled multitude perished in the clouds on the sea; when the ships collided, it went down into the deep.

But the remaining women and virgins, who were able to escape so great a danger, were driven to barbarous nations and were either slaughtered by an unknown people or consigned to perpetual servitude. A great part of them fell into the army of Gnanius, king of the Huns, and Melga, king of the Picts, who, hired for pay and defending Gratian’s party against Maximus, were laying waste the maritime regions from Spain as far as England with a pitiable destruction by land and sea. Refusing their lust, all were killed along the shore, in the ships, and destroyed to the last one. For they were all Christians.

[page 107]. 76. JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS.

The Franks immediately recovered their former borders, and compelled the Roman garrison to flee. At last, however, the emperor Constantine, son of Constantius and Helena, slew Richimer in battle, in the 13th year of his reign, [and] of the Lord 340.

[Margin: Theodomerus reigned 10 years.] Theodomerus, son of Richimer, after [his] father reigned ten years, who also himself waged many battles with the Romans. At that time the dwelling of the kings of the Franks was in the region of the Tungri, not far from the river Meuse, in a fort which was called Dispargum. But from the border of the Franks up to the river Loire the Gauls dwelt, and beyond the Loire the Goths. At the same time the duke of the eastern Franks, Dagobert, the Rhine being crossed, devastated Gaul, and burned with fire the despoiled cities of the Treveri. But king Theodomerus, together with Astila [his] mother, was captured by the Romans occupying Gaul, and slain by the sword, in the 10th year of his reign, [and] of the Lord's nativity 350.

[Margin: Clogio reigned over the Franks 18 years.] Clogio, son of Theodomerus, succeeding [his] father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned eighteen years, in whose time Constans, son of Constantine the Great, Caesar, joined many battles with the Franks, more often vanquished than victor. For king Clogio, a great army of the Franks having been gathered, in the first year of his reign stormed the city of Cambrai, and cruelly killed many of the Romans in vengeance for [his] father's death; thence advancing, [he subjected] Gaul up to the river Somme to the kingdom of the Franks.

[The source here repeats, with scribal variation, the passage above:] "Dagobert, the Rhine being crossed, devastated Gaul, and burned with fire the despoiled cities of the Treveri. But king Theodor[inus], together with Astila [his] mother, was captured by the Romans occupying Gaul, and slain by the sword, in the 10th year of his reign, and of the Lord's nativity 367." [end of the duplicated passage]

Meanwhile, while these [things] were being done in Gaul, Dagobert, duke in eastern Francia, crossing the Rhine by a bridge built [for it], at the village of Altrip between Speyer and Worms, devastates the Gauls and Romans in hostile fashion. The Goths also, at the same time, invading Spain, were tearing [it] apart. Constans, therefore, seeing that, set in the midst of danger, he could not resist all, made peace with the Franks. And Constans, without delay, leads an army into Spain against the Goths, whom he compelled to retreat; and not long after, in the third year of Clogio, he was slain, in the 30th year of his age, [and] the 13th of [his] reign, the Roman commonwealth being left in disturbance. Clogio, king of the Franks, dies in the 18th year of his reign, [and] of the Lord's nativity 367.

Marcomerus, son of Clogio, after [his] father reigned four years. Against him the Romans moved war in his first year, which lasted four years; for they bore [it] very ill that the Franks inhabited Gaul. But the Franks stood firm. At last, however, king Marcomerus, in the fourth year of his reign, was killed by the Romans in battle, in the year of the Lord's nativity 381.

But the Franks, their king having been slain, considering that they could not on that occasion resist the Romans, sought peace from them; which [the Romans] gave on such a condition, that the Franks should thereafter not have a king, but, the kingdom being reduced to a province, should be governed by dukes, and should pay tribute yearly to the Romans, [and] keep faith. And although it seemed too grievous to the Franks—who had hitherto always been free—to give tribute, yet, compelled by the malice of the times, they did otherwise than they would have wished.

In the year, therefore, 711 from the first coming of the Franks into Germany, that nation, hitherto always unconquered and feared by all nations—[its] kings being lost and [it] committed to dukes—is compelled to pay tribute to the Romans for 20 years.

[Margin: Dagobert, duke or viceroy of the Franks, 13 years. Valentinian emperor.] In the eighth year of the same duke Dagobert, the Romans, under [their] duke Gratian, joining battle with the Alemanni not far from Argentaria [Colmar], slew thirty thousand of them. But duke Dagobert had three sons—Genebald, Marcomerus, and Suno—to whom, while he yet lived healthy, with all the people favoring, he divided the princedom. In the eleventh year of duke Dagobert, Clodius, duke of the eastern Franks, died, to whom Marcomer his son, succeeding, governs the upper Franks for 20 years. But the aforesaid Dagobert of the western Franks dies, in the 12th year of his dukedom, [and] of the Lord's nativity 385. Gene[bald]…

On the Origin of the Franks.

advancing, they joined battle; in it twelve thousand Gauls were killed, and the rest were turned to flight. These things were done in the year of the Nativity 314.

Eugenius obtains the aid of the Franks.

In the following year Eugenius, king of Gaul, who was seeking the Roman empire, when he learned that Theodosius, emperor of the East, was going to come from Constantinople into Gaul against him, grew afraid; and, coming to the Rhine, he called upon the aid of both the eastern and western Franks, together with the Alemanni, against Caesar. In the same year he was killed by Theodosius, because he did not fear the aid of the Franks. Arbogast, chief of the evil men, killed himself with his own sword. Theodosius died at Milan; his corpse was taken back to Constantinople and buried, and his two sons succeeded in the empire: Arcadius in the East, and Honorius among the Romans in the West.

Pharamundus succeeds Marcomer.

In the eighteenth year of Genebaldus, great duke of the western Franks, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 403, Marcomer, duke of the eastern Franks, died on the mountain called Franckenberg, and was buried according to the custom of the gentiles. After him his son Pharamundus succeeded in the duchy; after two years he was elected king of all the Franks.

In the same year Marcomer and Sunno, dukes and brothers of Genebaldus of Lower Francia, died without male children and were buried at Neopagus.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 404, Genebaldus, great duke of the western Franks, died in the nineteenth year of his principate, leaving two sons, Sunno and Richer; the elder of them was lame in his feet, while the younger was not sufficiently fit for the kingdom.

At that time the Franks greatly extended their borders, and were subject to many dukes, all of whom nevertheless obeyed one greater man as though a king. It seemed to them, however, that this division of rule was not good for the people of the Franks; but, judging that it would be better, in contempt of the Romans, to appoint for themselves their own king, as they had had thirty years before, they took counsel.

Assembly of the nobles of the Franks for the election and institution of a new king.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 406, in the third Roman indiction, all the dukes, magnates, and nobles of the Franks came together in the month of March at Neopagus for the election of a new king. Among them these men were more eminent than the rest: Duke Pharamundus of the eastern Franks, and his two brothers Marcomer and Sunno with their sons, Clodio, Dagabert, Nicanor, Farabert, and Richimer; Duke Anthenor, prince of the Franks among the Hogii and the inhabitants of Frankfurt on the Main, with his brothers Priamus and Dagabert; Duke Bertherus the Gallican; Duke Heribertus the Islander; Duke Sunno and Richer, brothers and sons of Duke Genebaldus. Among many magnates were Salagast Philippus, Gasthald the secretary, Herhald, Wisogasthald, Rutwich, Adelhardet, and Rieherus. All these, with the rest, by one consent unanimously elected as king Pharamundus, born of royal stock and duke at Marcopolis among the eastern Franks.

Pharamundus, king of the Franks, [unclear].

Pharamundus the king, son of Duke Marcomer, who was [unclear] of Clodius, who was [unclear], in the year of the Lord [407?]. Pharamundus was magnanimous and a most daring fighter, who crushed the Roman legions in battle.

Johannes Trithemius

In the sixth year of Genebald, duke of the Franks, Maximus the tyrant, at the third milestone from Aquileia, after being stripped of his royal garments by the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, was beheaded and died. His son, named Victor, was killed not long afterward by Arbogast.

In the same year, after the death of Maximus became known to the Franks, they at once united and raised a strong army. With Genebald, Marcomer, and Sunno as leaders, they recovered all the land which they had lost while he was raging, whether in Germany or in Gaul, many thousands of Gauls, Romans, and Britons being slain as enemies. For the Britons, after the departure of all the nobility with Maximus, had become wholly weakened, and therefore were no longer to be feared by the Franks. The Gauls and Romans were being battered by mutual seditions; this circumstance gave the Franks the greatest hope of reclaiming the freedom of their homeland.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 392, the Franks, conspiring as one, scorned any longer to be subject to the tribute of the Romans. At that time Valentinian the Younger held the empire of the Romans; Theodosius had restored him after he had been driven from Italy by Maximus. Sending messengers to the Franks, he demanded the promised tribute. But when Valentinian’s envoys came to them, the Franks expelled him with disgrace in place of tribute, saying that they had been born free and were prepared even to die in defense of liberty. And at once, taking up arms, they moved against the Romans and Gauls; as has been said, after many of their adversaries had been cruelly slain, they recovered everything they had lost. In the twentieth year after they had paid tribute to the Romans, by fighting bravely with arms they reclaimed and recovered their former freedom.

For under the dukes Genebald, Marcomer, and Sunno, with a huge army, advancing from Lower Francia, which is around the mouths of the Rhine, near the sea, they soon occupied everything between the Meuse and the Rhine, after the Gallic inhabitants had either been killed or driven away in flight, and the spoils were sent back to their ancestral seats. Then, moving upward, they began to devastate the territory of the people of Cologne, striking great fear into the townsmen who were still with the Romans.

When the incursion of the Franks was heard of among the Treveri, who themselves had sided with Victor, the son of Maximus, namely that they were devastating the territory of Cologne, Nannenus and Quintinus, masters of the soldiers, to whom Maximus, when about to set out for Italy, had entrusted his son Victor and the defense of Gaul, drew together their forces and went down to aid the people of Cologne against the Franks, intending to fight if opportunity were given. But before they came to Cologne, the Franks, already laden with booty, had crossed the Rhine and returned to their own territory. They had nevertheless left behind not a few on the other side of the river, because they had conceived in their mind to return to them and proceed farther into Gaul. The first seats of the Franks, as has been said, had previously been within the three mouths of the Rhine, where Holland now is; from there on the eastern side of the Rhine toward Saxony and Frisia, where now is the inner part of Westphalia together with Frisia. To the west also beyond the Rhine as far as the Meuse they likewise once lived, where now are the people of Guelders and Jülich, and sometimes even farther, advancing to the Morini and the maritime regions.

Nannenus and Quintinus, coming with their army, attacked the remnants of the Franks that had remained in Gaul and joined a most savage battle, in which, though often defeated, they sometimes also emerged as victors. At last, however, the Franks were overcome near the Carbonarian Forest; some of them were killed, others were saved by flight.

When this had been done, it seemed useful to Quintinus that they should carry the whole army over into Francia and forestall the unprepared by an incursion. But such a plan did not please Nannenus, who did not doubt that the Franks would be stronger on their own soil.

Therefore, after Nannenus returned to Mainz, Quintinus crossed the Rhine around the fortress of [Musium?], brought the army over, and strove to bring war upon the Franks. But the Franks, not sluggish, received the Gauls manfully. In this battle many thousands of Gauls and Romans were slain by the Franks, with very few saved by flight. In that battle Heraclius, tribune of the Roman legion, fell; with him almost all who were in command of the soldiers perished by the sword and missiles of the Frankish people. For, except for a few to whom deep night and the dense hiding-place of the woods gave shelter, the army of Quintinus was destroyed, either by the sword of the Franks or by the marshes.

In the seventh year of Genebald, duke of the Franks, the emperor Valentinian died at the city of Vienne in Gaul, by the treachery and harshness of Arbogast, the master of the soldiers, by a noose. Eugenius, by the machination of Arbogast, was [unclear]. They resolved to invade Gaul, but before they could bring this to effect, Arbogast anticipated their plan: near Cologne Agrippina, having led his army across beyond the Rhine in the harsh winter, he devastated the Bacteri nearest the Rhine, the Chamanni, and others subject to the Franks. Against him Genebald and Marcomer, dukes of the Franks, [unclear].

Maximus the tyrant is killed.

The Frankish dukes recover what they had lost through the tyrant Maximus.

The Franks scorn to give tribute to Valentinian and the Romans.

The Franks cross the Rhine and devastate the territory of the people of Cologne in Gaul.

Nannenus and Quintinus of Trier move the army against the Franks.

The first seats of the Franks in Holland and the regions of Guelders.

The Franks are defeated near the Carbonarian Forest.

The Franks defeat Quintinus and kill many thousands of Romans.

The emperor Valentinian is strangled by the treachery of Arbogast. Eugenius becomes king.

Johannes Trithemius

... had been [unclear] in Westrasia, and he received the Gauls in surrender. He and his father were the first among the dukes to be Christians. He died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 571.

  1. Gotfridus succeeded his father for twenty-four years. He was a pious prince, yet he was not able to convert all his subjects to the faith of Christ. For at that time the Franks were stiff-necked in accepting the faith, and the greater part of them was still pagan in the duchy. Duke Gotfridus died in the year of the Lord 695.

  2. Genebaldus succeeded his father for twenty years. In his time Saint Gregory the Pope sent preachers into England. This duke died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 665.

  3. Clodomirus succeeded his father in the duchy of the eastern Franks for twenty-three years. In his first year Anastasius the Persian, a monk, was martyred. He died in the year of the Lord 639.

  4. Heribertus, nephew of Clodomirus, succeeded in the duchy for thirty years. In his time Saint Furseus, abbot in Ireland, flourished. This duke died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 668.

  5. Clodoveus succeeded Heribertus his uncle for twelve years. In his time Clodoveus was king of the Franks in Gaul. Duke Clodoveus died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 680.

  6. Gosbertus succeeded his father for twenty-six years. In his sixth year, Pope Canon ordained Saint Kilian, a Scot by nation and a monk by profession, as bishop, and sent him into eastern Francia to preach the faith of Christ. After he had spent two years at Herbipolis in preaching, together with his ministers, Colman the priest and Totnan the deacon, he was martyred by order of Geilana, the duke’s wife, in the year of the Lord 689. Duke Gosbertus died in the year of the Lord 806.

  7. Hetanus succeeded his father in the duchy for thirteen years. In his time Saint Aegidius, abbot, flourished in Gaul. This duke died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 320.

  8. Hetanus succeeded his father in the duchy for twenty years and died without sons, in the year of the Lord 761, leaving one daughter named Immina, who was a nun and of holy conduct. And so Pippin, mayor of the palace and afterward king of the Franks, took the vacant duchy to himself and entrusted it to his son Charles to administer for ten years. Then, in the year of the Lord 751, when Pippin was already king, with the consent of his son Charles and of all the nobles of the whole kingdom of the Franks, he gave the duchy as perpetual property to Saint Burghard, first bishop of the Wirtzburgers, and to his successors.

  9. Therefore Burghard, established by Pippin as duke and bishop of the eastern Franks, presided for forty years. He was upright in morals and most holy in conduct; from a monk of Saint Benedict he was ordained bishop by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. Burghard resigned the episcopate, together with the duchy of the Franks, to the church and to his successor, in the eleventh year of his rule, but in the year of the Lord 791; and in that same year the same Saint Burghard died.

  10. Megengaldus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for four years; he too was a monk. Others, in the manner of the Hollanders, turning I into V, call him Mergingaudus, a holy man. He died in the year of the Lord 752, on the third day before the Kalends of March, under Charles the Great, emperor.

  11. Bernwolphus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for six months, one month, and twenty-three days, and died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 800, under Emperor Charles.

  12. Ludericus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for five years. And he died in the year of the Lord 753, on the third day before the Kalends of March, under King Arnulf among the Saxons, killed in time of war during the solemnities of the Mass.

  13. Agilvardus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for five years, one month, and eighteen days, and died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 715, under Emperor Lothar.

  14. Wolfgerus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for twenty-two years, six months, and twelve days, and died on the day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Lord 931, under Louis.

  15. Hunibertus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for ten years, three months, and seven days. He died on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 822, under Emperor Lothar.

  16. Rodulphus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for [unclear] years, and died on the third day before the Nones of August, in the year of the Lord 1108, under Louis III.

  17. Gosswaldus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for thirteen years, five months, and eighteen days, and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord 756, under Emperor Louis II.

  18. Arno, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for thirty-six years, six months, and twelve days. Famous for miracles, he died on the third day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord 792, under King Arnulf among the Saxons, in time of war, killed during the solemnities of the Mass.

  19. Dracolfus, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for five years and four months. Sent by Emperor Conrad I into Greece, he died on the journey, in the year of the Lord 913.

  20. Theodo, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for nineteen years, two months, and fourteen days. He died

  1. Adelbero, bishop and duke, presided for forty years. In that dissension which occurred between Henry III and his son, the fourth Henry, he was driven from his see by the elder emperor, in the year of the Lord 1085. Meginhard was substituted for him by that Caesar himself. Adelbero, however, having been expelled, died in Bavaria on the day before the Nones of October, in the fifth year of his exile, and in the year of the Lord 1090, in the monastery of Lambach, which his father had built; he was buried there.

  2. Megenhard II presided for three years and twenty-five days. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1098, under Henry IV.

Emehard.

  1. Erlung, bishop and duke of the Franks, appointed by the emperor, presided for two years. In the year of the Lord 1105, the emperor's son, Henry V, deposed him again because he adhered to his father Henry IV. He caused Rupert to be ordained in his place. The father, soon following, restored Erlung of Würzburg and drove out Rupert. But not long afterward Erlung was deposed by Caesar's son, and Rupert was restored to the bishopric, in the year of the Lord 1105.

  2. Rupert, bishop and duke of the Franks, presided for not fully two years. While he was making his way to a general council in Lombardy in the month of September, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord 1106, under Henry IV [or V?].

Rupert.

  1. Erlung, again bishop and duke, was taken up by the consent of all, and thereafter presided for sixteen years and eleven days. For four continuous years before his death he was afflicted with elephantine disease, and at last died on the second day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord 1122, under Henry V. Because the schism forbade it, he was buried not in the city but in the monastery of Schwarzach.

Gebehard the intruder.

  1. Gebehard was appointed as bishop of the Franks against the will of all by the emperor, while he was still a layman, less suitable because he was young. But the clergy and the procurators of the people elected Ruger the deacon as pontiff for themselves; Gebehard drove him from the city in the year of the Lord 1032.

  2. Ruger, bishop-elect and duke of the Franks, lawfully prevailed against the intruder Gebehard, and was consecrated in the monastery of Schwarzach by the hands of the archbishop of Mainz, in the presence of the legates of the Apostolic See and of certain princes. He held for his own use that part of the bishopric which lies around the river Neckar. Gebehard, however, securely possessed the city of Würzburg and the places adjacent to it. Ruger presided for four years and three months, and died in the year of the Lord 1126.

On the Origin of the Franks.

  1. Gerhardus of Schwarzburg, prelate and duke, presided for 31 years, and died in the month of November around the feast of Saint Martin, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1403, under Rupert, king of the Germans, in the eleventh indiction.

  2. Johannes of Egloffstein, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for 9 years, and perished by poison at Forchheim in the year 1412, under King Sigismund.

  3. Johannes of Brunn, prelate and duke, presided for 28 years, and died in the year of the Lord 1440, under Frederick, then the third king, in the third Roman indiction.

  4. Sigismund, from the dukes of Saxony, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for three years and ruled in the year of the Lord 1443, under Frederick III.

  5. Gotfridus IV of Limpurg, prelate and duke, presided for 13 years, and died on Tuesday after Palm Sunday, in the year 145[unclear], under Emperor Frederick III.

  6. Johannes of Grumbach, prelate and duke, presided for 11 years, and died in the year of the Lord 1466, under Emperor Frederick III, in the fourteenth indiction.

  7. Rudolf II of Scherenberg, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for 29 years less one day; he relieved the Church, which was burdened with another’s debt. He died, the last in his lineage, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1495, under Maximilian, king of Germany.

  8. Laurentius of Bibra, elected on the fourth day before the Ides of May in the year noted above, a peaceful prelate and duke of the Franks, holds rule today in his nineteenth year.

But now, after this necessary digression, let us return to the above-mentioned Pharamund, king of the Franks, for the continuation of the history which we have begun.

In the fourth year of King Pharamund, on the last day of the month of December, the Vandals and Alans, under the leader Modigiscus, crossed the frozen Rhine and led an army into Gaul with their children and wives, and afterward passed on into Spain.

In the eighth year of Pharamund, the Goths under King Alaric captured and overthrew Rome. In the same year King Pharamund, under the command of Clodius his son, sent a great army of the Franks into Gaul against the Romans. When the Franks entered Gaul, some of the Romans sought safety in flight, others were killed by the Franks. And thus the Franks obtained a great part of Gaul, the Romans having been utterly wiped out.

Hearing this, the king of the Vandals [unclear], and fearing that he might one day be driven from Gaul by the Franks, undertook war against them. Hence a fierce battle was joined, in which the victorious Franks killed more than twenty thousand Vandals. And unless Respendial, king of the Alans, who was already then ruling in Spain, had intervened in time, all the Vandals would have been slain by the Franks.

The Vandals, like the Goths, originated from the island of Scandia, and after the defeat received from the Franks they remained in Spain for 22 years; after this they sailed to Africa. The Franks, however, greatly increased in number and power. And King Pharamund died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord 431.

Clodius the Long-Haired, son of Pharamund, succeeding his father in the same year, reigned for 20 years. In his first year, Aetius, after hearing of the death of King Pharamund, led the Roman army into Gaul, and, after many Franks had been slain, recovered [unclear].

In these times Salagastus flourished, a wise man and philosopher of the Franks, and from the ancient line of kings, drawing his origin from dukes. Since he was most learned in every literature, by order of King Clodius he wrote down the laws of the Franks, which he named Salic laws after his own name. Later King Clodoneus, converted to the faith, had these laws enlarged.

The same Salagastus, by permission of King Clodius, founded a new city on the bank of the Main not far from Frankfurt, which he named Salagast after his own name, and which ignorant authors today call, by a corrupted term, Seligenstadt. In this same city of his, Salagastus died and, after being burned, was placed in an urn, in the sixteenth year of Clodius.

In the eleventh year of his reign, King Clodius, [unclear] the power of the Franks to be greatly diminished, sent scouts into Gaul, who were to investigate secretly and carefully the situation of the land, the strength of the people, and the guard of the cities. At that time the Burgundians lived in the region of Lyons, and the Goths in Aquitaine.

The scouts returned and reported that the region was excellent, the people weak, and the guard of the Romans small. Therefore King Clodius gathered a great [unclear] of the Franks

Siegfried. 53. Siegfried, prelate and duke, presided for five years and six months, and died in the year of the Lord 1155, under Frederick the first emperor, in the second indiction.

Gebhard. 54. Gebhard the second, prelate and duke, presided for six years, five months, and twenty-four days, and died in the year of the Lord 1161, under Frederick the first emperor.

Henry. 55. Henry the second, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for six years and four months, and died in the year of the Lord 1167, under Frederick the first emperor.

Herold. 56. Herold, prelate and duke, presided for seven years, ten months, and eleven days, and died in the year of the Lord 1174, under Frederick the first emperor.

Reinhard. 57. Reinhard, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for four years, ten months, and fifteen days, and died in the year of the Lord 1189, under Frederick the first emperor.

Gottfried. 58. Gottfried of Pistenberg, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for five years, eight months, and twenty-four days. Having set out for Jerusalem, he died in the army of the Christians and was buried at Antioch, in the year of the Lord [unclear], under Frederick the first emperor.

Henry. 59. Henry of Biebelrith, the third of that name, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for six years, eight months, and as many days. He died in the tenth indiction of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1162, under Henry the sixth.

Gottfried. 60. Gottfried of Hoenlo, prelate and duke, a lover of the clergy, presided for six years, four months, and eleven days. He died in the year of the Lord 1198, in the last year of King Henry.

Conrad. 61. Conrad, prelate and duke, chancellor of King Philip, presided for five years, three months, and twelve days, and was killed on the public road at Würzburg by Bodoner and Henry, knights of Rabenspurg, and by Herold and Conrad, their servants, on the third day before the Ides of December.

Henry. 62. Henry the fourth, a doctor of Paris, called de Taseo, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for four years, seven months, and seven days. And he died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1210, in the third indiction, under Otto the fourth emperor.

Otto. 63. Otto of Lodenburg, prelate and duke, presided for thirteen years and five months, and died on the fifth day of the month of December, in the year of the Lord 1223, under Frederick the second emperor.

Theodoric. 64. Theodoric, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for one year, two months, and sixteen days, and died in the year of the Lord 1124, under Frederick the second emperor.

Hermann. 65. Hermann of Lodenburg, prelate and duke, presided for nineteen years, and died in the year of the Lord 1240, under Frederick the second, in the thirteenth indiction of the Romans.

Eringus. 66. Eringus of Reinstein, prelate and duke, presided for thirty-six years, and died in the year of the Lord 1276, under Emperor Rudolf, in the fourth indiction.

Berthold. 67. Berthold of Sternberg, prelate and duke, presided for thirteen years. He died in the year of the Lord 1288, under Emperor Rudolf, in the first indiction.

Manegold. 68. Manegold, prelate and duke, presided for fifteen years, and died in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1303, under Albert the first king, in the first indiction.

Andrew. 69. Andrew of Gundelfingen, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for fifteen years and died in the year of the Lord 1322, under Louis the fourth emperor.

Gottfried. 70. Gottfried the third of Hoenlo, prelate and duke, presided for four years, and died in the year of the Lord 1322, under Louis the fourth, in the seventh indiction.

Wolfram. 71. Wolfram of Grunbach, prelate and duke, presided for two years, and died in the year of the Lord 1333, on the octave of the Apostles, under Louis the fourth.

Otto. 72. Otto Wolffskell, prelate and duke of the Franks, presided for twelve years, one month, and three days. Against him Hermann of Lichtenberg, a canon of Speyer, promoted by the emperor, violently occupied the episcopate for the first four years. Otto died on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 1343, under Louis the fourth emperor.

Albert. 73. Albert of Hoenlo, prelate and duke, presided for four years: not elected, but appointed by Pope Clement the sixth against Albert of Hoenlo, who had been canonically elected. But afterwards, when the pope was better informed about the case, he transferred his Albert to the church of Freising in the year of the Lord 1349, and confirmed Albert of Hoenlo, the provost, previously canonically elected, to his own church.

Albert. 74. Albert of Hoenlo, prelate and duke, presided for two years, and died on the Sunday after the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1352, under Charles the fourth emperor, in the tenth indiction. After him Albert of Hesberg, canon, was unanimously elected by the chapter, but Pope Gregory the eleventh, at the emperor’s request, annulled the election and installed Gerhard of Svvartzenburg.

Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] an army, and, moving into Gaul, he besieged and took Cambrai. Moving on from there through the Carbonarian Forest, he directed his hurried march toward Tournai, a city which had been fortified with a garrison of Romans. Therefore, when the Roman soldiers heard of the arrival of King Clodius, they advanced against him to battle; they were all slain by him, and not one remained. Thus Clodius for a second time subjected a great part of Gaul to the Franks, which the Romans were never thereafter able to recover, down to the present day.

Now after Clodius, king of the Franks, had magnificently extended the boundaries of his kingdom and had subjected to the rule of the Franks all the land of the Gauls which lies between the Rhine on the east and the sea on the west, and likewise from the sea on the north as far as the Seine toward the south, that is, the Batavians, Menapians, Tungrians, Taravanians, Morini, Ambiani, people of Cambrai, Atrebates, Bellovaci, and Crusi, who are now the Hollanders, Gelderlanders, Brabanters, Zeelanders, Picards, people of Louvain, people of Traiectum, Namurians, people of Beauvais, people of Noyon, and whatever adjoins these, he died in the twentieth year of his reign, and in the year 451 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the fourth Roman indiction.

Meroveus, son of Clodius, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for ten years. In the third year of his reign, in the month of June, assisted by the support of Helenus, duke of the eastern Franks, he besieged, took, plundered, and subjected to his rule the city of Trier, still at that time subject to the Romans. He killed a Mosellan leader named Sabinus, and powerfully obtained the whole region on this side of the Moselle from Mediomatricum, which is now Metz, as far as the Rhine. And lest the people of the land be able to rise in rebellion, he transferred twelve thousand Mosellans, with their children, wives, and possessions, into eastern Francia under Duke Helenus; in their place he set twelve thousand eastern Franks along the banks of the Moselle, in cities as well as in castles and villages. And from that time the use of the wine which is called that of the Franks first began to exist among the Mosellans. For the Franks, cultivators of wine, transferred to the Moselle, were the first to bring with them from eastern Francia that kind of vine.

In the eighth year of King Meroveus the Huns were devastating Gaul; against their insolence King Meroveus himself led a great army of Franks. Battle having been joined on the Catalaunian fields, the Franks slew one hundred eighty thousand of the Huns.

In his time the Franks added almost all Gaul to their kingdom, the strength of the Romans now diminished and failing, especially after the death of Aetius, whom Valentinian had killed out of envy. Therefore the Franks, mingled with the Gauls, took wives for themselves from their daughters, and begot sons and daughters, who all learned their language, and likewise their customs; with them they have henceforth lived together down to the present day. But those who remained in eastern Francia, and also the Mosellans this side of the Rhine, the people of Wurzburg, Mainz, the Hangones, Neometae, Argentorates, Helvetii, Alsatians, Westerasians, Treveri, Agrippinenses, Holgii, Batavians, Menapians, Hollanders, and Brabanters, differing only in dialects, all use the German language.

King Meroveus, however, after the kingdom of the Franks had been greatly enlarged, died a pagan, in the tenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 461, in the fourteenth indiction.

Hilderic, son of Meroveus, succeeding his father, reigned for six years. Then, driven from the kingdom, he fled and lived in exile in Thuringia for eight years, while a certain Roman, Aegidius, meanwhile occupied the kingdom of the Franks. After eight years had passed, Aegidius was cast out of the kingdom by the Franks; Hilderic was recalled, and thereafter reigned for another nine years. And all the years in which he reigned amounted to fifteen. For in the sixth year of his reign, the princes and nobles of the Franks conspired against him because, living insolently and too luxuriously, he had violated many wives and daughters of the nobles, and they wished to kill him. When this became known to him, he secretly fled with a few men into Thuringia to King Basinus, and there he remained for eight years. He fled in the year of the Lord 467, in the fifth Roman indiction.

When Hilderic had been put to flight and was living in exile with Basinus, king of Thuringia, who was joined to him by blood, the Franks set over themselves as king a certain Roman named Aegidius, who ruled over the Soissons; he reigned for eight years. The Franks at length, no longer able to endure him as he tyrannized excessively and cruelly killed all the nobles, cast him out, judging that the shame of daughters and wives should rather be endured or disregarded than that they should be so cruelly slain by a tyrant.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 475, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, Hilderic, through the loyalty and industry of Wimbald, returned from Thuringia into Gaul; Aegidius having been put to flight, he was restored to the kingdom of the Franks by the consent of all, and thereafter reigned for nine years, and changed the former habits of his youth for the better. Hearing

ON THE ORIGIN OF THE FRANKS. 85.

Basina, wife of Basinus, king of the Thuringians, hearing of the prosperous successes of Childeric, leaving her husband, came to him in Gaul, and he took her as wife—forgetful of the hospitality of king Basinus, and recompensing [it] with an evil exchange.

On the first night of the marriage now at hand, Basina admonishes Childeric to abstain from intercourse, and to watch the doors, and to report to her what he should see three times in the courtyard. The king believed the woman, and, the house having been gone round three times, returned to her, saying that he had seen, first, in the courtyard of the palace, rhinoceroses—that is, unicorns—and lions and leopards; secondly, bears and raging wolves, biting one another mutually; thirdly, small dogs, attacking [each other] with alternate bites, and tearing one another in turn.

To these [things] the prophetic woman foretold to the king that there would issue from [their] intercourse offspring of various morals, diverse with time: the first, which would be noble by nature, would imitate the rhinoceroses and lions in nobility; the second, which by the habit of bears and wolves would bend [its] mind to plunder; but the third, which, by deadly biting, would imitate the rabid dogs, and would fall away from [its] pristine nobility.

In the year after these [things], Childeric led an army into the Alemanni—who are now the Suevi—and subjected them to his kingdom, and made [them] tributary to the Franks, namely in that region which is nearest to Italy, which the Alemanni or Suevi had earlier invaded.

In the third year of his resumed reign, Odoacer, a Rugian by birth, relying on the throngs of the Turcilingi, Sciri, and Heruli, going out from the farthest borders of Saxony, with a strong band of his [men] entered Gaul, and occupied the city of Angers; against whom Childeric, arriving the following day, slew Count Paul, put Odoacer to flight with the Saxons, and subjugated the city to himself. Thence moving, Odoacer—a treaty having first been made with Childeric—led [his] army toward Italy, slew Orestes, patrician of the Romans, met in battle in Liguria, obtained Pavia and all the Roman fortifications round about, and in a short time, with none resisting, subjected all Italy to his dominion. The diadem having been placed on his head, he reigned in Italy fourteen years, with no one disturbing him.

But Childeric, king of the Franks, after many [things] bravely done in paganism, like his fathers also, died, in the year of the Lord 484, in the seventh Roman indiction.

Clovis, son of Childeric, after [his] father reigned thirty years, who was the first of the kings of the Franks afterward made a Christian, as we shall say. Clovis was outstanding in form, and renowned in greatness of mind, who straightway in the beginning of his reign put to flight Syagrius, son of Aegidius the former king, whom [his] father had left as prince of Soissons, and obtained the city; and proceeding further, [he obtained] also the city of Rheims, and several others. [The source here repeats, within this paragraph, the Odoacer passage above:] "…a treaty having first been made with Childeric, he led [his] army toward Italy, slew Orestes, patrician of the Romans, met in battle in Liguria, obtained Pavia and all the fortifications of the Romans round about, in a short time, with none resisting, subjected all Italy to his dominion, and, the diadem [placed] on his head, reigned in Italy fourteen years, with none disturbing him." [end of the duplicated passage]

Clovis was admonished to assume the faith of Christ, and to renounce the superstitious and vain worship of idols. But before Clotilde was his wife, he had a son from a concubine, by name Theodoric. Moreover Gunderic, king of the Burgundians, had four sons: Gundebald, Godegisil, Chilperic the father of Clotilde, and Bodemar. Gundebald, therefore, killed his brother Chilperic with the sword, and his wife, the mother of Clotilde—a stone having been tied to [her] neck—he sank, cast headlong into the water; whose two daughters, Mucurina and Clotilde, he condemned to exile. But Clotilde, Clovis asking [for her], is sent by [her] uncle into Gaul.

In the tenth year of his reign, king Clovis moved [his] army into Thuringia, to whose aid came Clodomer, duke of the eastern Franks, with twelve thousand warriors. The cause of the war was that Basina, formerly wife of Basinus, going into Gaul to Childeric (as was said a little before), had carried off with her many treasures in gold, silver, and pearls, which the son of king Basinus, demanding [them] back, when he had not obtained [them], declared war on Clovis. But he, not slothful, forestalling the king of the Thuringians in his own kingdom, conquered [him], and made [him] tributary to the Franks.

[Marginal notes summarize: Basina came, leaving her husband, to Childeric, and shows [him] a vision of [their] future offspring; the Franks subject the Alemanni; Odoacer subjected all Italy to himself as king; Clovis despoiled the churches of the Christians; Clotilde, wife of Clovis, daughter of the king of Burgundy; Chilperic killed by [his] brother; Clodomer subjected Thuringia.]

Johannes Trithemius.

In the eleventh year of Clovis, Theodoric, king of the eastern Goths, sent into Italy by Zeno, emperor of the East, killed Odoacer of Saxony, the tyrant, and thereafter himself occupied the Roman Empire for thirty-one years.

Clovis, king of the Franks, killed Alaric, king of the western Goths, an Arian, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, together with many others in battle, and took the city of Poitiers, with all its land and his treasures, into his own power.

The king had war with the Alemanni. And it happened that, when both armies engaged, the Franks were violently cut down and began to fail badly. When King Clovis noticed this, raising his eyes to heaven, he prayed with tears, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, whom my wife proclaims to be the Son of God, if you give me victory over these enemies of mine, I shall believe in you and receive baptism in your name.” And while he was saying these things in prayer, the Alemanni at once turned in flight; and when they saw that their king had been killed by the Franks, they submitted themselves to Clovis, saying: “Do not, we pray, pursue the people any further; now we are yours, and we shall serve you faithfully forever.” But he, forbidding the war to continue, accepted the Alemanni in surrender and imposed tribute upon them.

Having returned into Gaul, he summoned to himself Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims; fully instructed by him in the Christian faith, he prepared himself with great humility to receive the sacrament of baptism. When he entered for baptism, Saint Remigius said with eloquent mouth: “Gently bow your neck, Sicamber; worship what you burned, burn what you worshiped.” On that day three thousand of the Franks were baptized, and in the following days many more also of the rest of the people.

At that time there reigned in the borders of Gaul, at Cologne, Sigebert, an old and wealthy man. He had an only son named Ludovicus, who, seduced by desire of reigning, had his father killed in a certain grove; because of this crime he himself, a little afterward, by a certain Frank under the direction of Clovis [unclear] three thousand, in the following days of the rest, of the people completed. When he had been killed, King Clovis, by the consent of all at Cologne, obtained the whole kingdom of Sigebert.

Ragnachar also, who was reigning at Cambrai, and also Chararic, another king, with brothers and sons, all of whom were of the race of the Franks, he caused to be killed after they had been deceived either by war or by trickery, and subjected the whole kingdom of the Franks to himself.

He held under suspicion all who reigned throughout Gaul, whether they were Franks of his own stock or foreigners, lest perhaps he should be killed by them. Therefore, after many kings had been killed, including his own kinsmen, concerning whom he feared lest they take the kingdom from him, he extended his kingdom throughout all threefold Gaul: Celtic, Aquitanian, and Belgic. Sitting one day among his courtiers he said: “Woe to me, who have remained alone like a stranger among foreigners; no one of my kin lives who could help me in necessity.” He did not say this with the intention that he was either sorry for the cruelty he had committed against his kinsmen, or grieved for those killed, but in deceit, so that if perhaps anyone of his stock were still hidden, he might be betrayed by some incautious disclosure of one of those listening.
