In these two she relates the marvelous and secret things of nature by subtle exposition to a mystical sense, so that, unless from the Holy Spirit, a woman could by no means know such things.

She wrote another large volume whose title is Divine Works, one book; to the clergy of the city of Trier, on the future calamities of the Church, one book; also to the people of Cologne on the same subject, one book. In these she foretells wonderful things, yet without determining the time. She also wrote, at the request of certain priests, an exhortatory book for secular persons, one book; to her sisters, a book of exhortation, one book; to the gray monks, one book. Various songs composed with sweet melody. To Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, one letter. Also a book of letters to various persons, of which I have read one hundred thirty-five; in all of them Catholic doctrine shines forth, by which she either confirms faith or instructs discipline. [unclear] in the same volume, stirred by the fame of her sanctity and divine revelations from regions of the world [unclear], commended themselves to her prayers through messengers and letters, and sought from her the solution of various questions.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180, indiction 14, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninety-first year of her age, and was buried in the middle of the choir of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Rupert, before the high altar.

Werner, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise.

Theodoric, an abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, most chaste, a man practiced and learned both in sacred Scriptures and in secular letters, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, wrote for the edification of many the life of the same Hildegard, bride of Christ, one book; also various letters to diverse persons, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Cae[unclear]

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters: a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and very celebrated poet. Under the name of Peregrinus he published many excellent volumes, in which the adorned arrangement of the thoughts and the pleasing elegance of the language show that their author was inferior to none of the ancients. Among these the following are reported: a notable work of dialogues under the names of Peregrinus the priest and Theodota, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled The Mirror of Virgins, 8 books; on the Gospels through the cycle of the year, a large volume, 1 book; On the Life of the Spirit, the Fruit of Death, 1 book; and another which is entitled The Matricularius, 1 book; another, Didascalon, 1 book; On Music, the Difference of Tones, 1 book; On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, 1 book; various sermons, homilies, 1 book. He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come into our hands. Whatever he wrote in prose, however, apart from sermons and letters, he arranged for the most part in the manner of a dialogue. There was another preacher who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, not to be despised, but much inferior to our Peregrinus in learning and eloquence. For that man, in the manner of the declaimers of this time, content with simple speech, introduces frequent quotations from the Scriptures; but our author, echoing Ciceronian eloquence in the manner of the ancients, was not accustomed to make his discourse scarred with superfluous citations. He flourished under the emperor Conrad, the third of that name, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Dudechinus, priest of the church in Lobenstein, a studious and learned man, for the hope of eternal life went with many others to Jerusalem under the emperor Conrad III. Often fighting with the Saracens in naval battle, he shone forth with great devotion and steadfastness for the faith of Christ. Having returned to his homeland, at the request of Cuno, abbot of Mount Saint Disibod, then still [unclear] of our order, he [unclear] the history of his pilgrimage and how great things [unclear] with the unbelievers. And he published some things on various matters to different persons, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under the emperor Conrad, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Christian, archchancellor of the emperor Frederick I, afterward the thirtieth archbishop of Mainz, appointed by him, sat for eighteen years. He was a man most learned in secular literature, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, brilliant in talent, eloquent in speech; even Italy was amazed at him when he spoke. Among other monuments of his ability he wrote: The Deeds of the Emperor Frederick I, 1 book; also very elegant letters to various persons, and certain other things still unknown to us. Leo Tuscus, notary of Emmanuel, emperor of the Greeks, and a contemporary of this Christian, mentions him with praise in the book On the Prevarications and Errors of the Greeks. He flourished in the times of the same Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180.

Eckebert, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florin at Schoenau, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, was the brother of the blessed Elisabeth, abbess and virgin of Christ. He wrote: on the Magnificat, 1 book; on the life and death of his holy sister, 1 book; Meditations on Jesus and Mary, 1 book; On the Praise of Our Savior, 1 book; also sermons, in the manner of the ancients, uncorrupted by citations of chapters, 2 books; letters to various persons, 1 book. He also published some other works which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1160.

Elisabeth, a nun, sister of the aforesaid abbot Eckebert, abbess of the convent of virgins of Christ which likewise is called Schoenau, is seen to be almost adjacent to the aforesaid monastery of men. A virgin of most holy manner of life, consecrated to the Lord from her infancy, she deserved to be divinely illuminated by many approved revelations, which, for the edification of the faithful, she duly committed to writing. Of these the following are read: she wrote a very beautiful work, namely, on martyrs, confessors, and virgins, 1 book; on the eleven thousand virgins crowned with holy martyrdom at Cologne Agrippina, 1 book; of her revelations, 2 books; to her brother Eckebert, still a canon at Bonn, 1 book; of letters to various persons, 1 book; to Saint Hildegard, virgin of Christ, one letter. She dies under

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Caesarius, monk in Heisterbach. Caesarius, a monk in Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Cologne, a devout man and an outstanding lover of regular discipline, and trained by long study in the divine scriptures. For the edification of novices, whose instructor he was by office, he wrote in simple and plain speech several little works, the reading of which is not to be despised by devout people. Among them I have found the following: a large volume of dialogues concerning miracles and various visions that occurred in his time in Germany, in [twelve?] books. Also homilies on the Sunday Gospels, two books; likewise on the Gospels concerning the saints, one book; many varied sermons pertaining to the instruction of novices, one book. The other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to my knowledge through reading. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Peter de Vineis, archchancellor of Emperor Frederick II. Peter de Vineis, archchancellor of Emperor Frederick II, a man very learned and eloquent in secular letters. He wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor, six books of letters to various persons; also one book on imperial power, and certain other things. He always defended Frederick’s party against the Roman Church and the supreme pontiff, the vicar of Christ; often in a public council, in the presence of the pope and the prelates, he tried by pleading with such eloquence to excuse his emperor’s rebellion that he turned everyone to admiration. But at last he was repaid by Frederick with a fitting reward, when he expelled him from his court and tore out the light of his eyes. This is the reward of those who defer to princes against obedience to the Roman see of the vicar of Christ; afterwards, unless they repent, they go down wretched to the lower regions. He flourished under the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Jordan of the Order of Preachers. Jordan, of the Order of Friars Preachers, after Saint Dominic master general, a man sufficiently trained and learned in the divine scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, who by word and example converted many to the way of righteousness. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote many useful exhortatory letters to the brothers, in which the whole integrity of the spiritual life is seen. He is also said to have composed very useful sermons. He is reported also to have written a book on the institution of his order, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished at the same time as Saint Dominic, under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Simon, monk of the monastery of Affligem. Simon, a monk of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, distinguished in speech. He so turned into practice the counsel of our holy lawgiver Benedict, by which we are enjoined especially to love the divine scriptures in the monastery, that nothing in this life was sweeter to him than to devote himself to holy study, and he always turned over the little works of the holy fathers. Among other things he wrote: sermons on the Song of Songs, [unclear] books; also the admirable vision of a certain lay brother, one book; also several sermons and letters. He also abbreviated the Moralia of the blessed Pope Gregory in ten books, extracting all the better things that suited his purpose. The other works which he wrote have not come to my knowledge. From the time when the orders of the mendicant friars began, the study of letters perished in our order, and down to the present day it scarcely revives. For from the times of Emperor Frederick II down to the last year of Frederick III, in which we wrote these things, for nearly two hundred and seventy years, scarcely anyone appeared in our order who, after the example of the ancients, [unclear] knowledge and holiness of life [unclear], who because of knowledge and usefulness composed anything worthy for the edification of posterity, as is clear in what follows. But these things do not pertain to the matter.

John, bishop of Strasbourg and Bosnia. John, called from his fatherland the German, from the town of [Freiburg?], of the Order of Friars Preachers, of the convent of Strasbourg and afterwards bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, a man much trained and learned in the divine scriptures, and singularly learned in secular philosophy and canon law; later, abandoning that office, he returned to his own order. After Raymond he was appointed master general of the whole order. He wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among them there is extant a notable summa on cases, which they call the Summa of Confessors, in five books. On the decrees of Gratian also, the first among the named doctors, he produced an apparatus. The other works which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250; he was buried in his own convent at Strasbourg, once famous for many miracles.

Otto, bishop of Freising. Otto, bishop of the church of Freising in the Noric province, which is now called Bavaria, as some write, nephew of Emperor Frederick I, a man in the divine scriptures

142 [unclear] of Johannes Trithemius

Heinrich of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, easily the most learned of all men of his time, and very well instructed both in secular philosophy and in divine scripture, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, a most acute disputant of written questions, who, because of the great glory of his learning, deserved to be called the Solemn Doctor. Among the many small works of his intellect he wrote: an outstanding Summa of Theology, 1 book; On the Sentences, 4 books; Quodlibets, 2 books; On holy virginity, 1 book; On penance, 1 book; also various sermons, and diverse lectures on sacred scripture; On Aristotle’s Metaphysics, 14 books; also on the books of the Physics, 8 books; and on many other books of Aristotle. He wrote many other things besides, which have not come into our hands. He died under the emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the third indiction, on the day of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was buried at Tournai in the church of the Mother of God.

Emicho, abbot of the monastery of Schönau, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, once a hearer and disciple of the above-mentioned abbot Eckbert, a man studious and learned in divine scripture, and not ignorant of secular literature, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, notable no less for life than for knowledge. He wrote many excellent small works, both in verse and in prose, though few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read his little work On the Praises of the blessed virgin Elisabeth of Schönau. Also many and various sermons, and certain other smaller works, not without usefulness. The rest that he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Abbot Eckbert, in the year of the Lord 1200, or thereabouts.

Conrad of Media Civitas, commonly Halberstadt, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned to no low degree both in divine writings and in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and an excellent disputant. He wrote On the Sentences, 4 books; also a Summa for students, 3 books; On the trivium, 1 book; a noteworthy lecture on the books of the holy abbot, 1 book; also many and various sermons, 1 book. He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to me. For he is said to have made lectures and explanations on many books of the Bible. Finally, he is reported to have been the first to arrange the concordances of the New and Old Testament in alphabetical order.

Nicolaus of Bibra, master of the gymnasium of Erfurt, nobly learned in secular writings and not ignorant of divine scripture, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote volumes in both styles that are not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I find only: a work mixed of verse and prose, On Avoiding Evil, which he entitled The Hidden, 1 book; also Letters to various persons, 1 book; and diverse poems. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Hugo of Strasbourg, of the Order of Preachers, a doctor of Paris, studious and learned in holy writings, and excellently learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. Among other exercises of his intellect he wrote: On the Sentences, 4 books; also a Compendium of Theological Truth, a work not to be rejected, 6 books; also many sermons; quodlibets, questions, disputations, and various explanations in the divine books; and he is said to have written not a few other things, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Gerard, of the same Order of Preachers, lector of the convent of Liège, a man studious and learned in divine scripture, an excellent declaimer in making sermons to the people, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech. Among other things he wrote a very useful treatise On God and the Persons, which he entitled On the Doctrine of the Heart, teaching the seven dispositions to be made concerning the heart, and sagaciously gathering here and there from divine scripture many things pertaining to edification. Also sermons, as they say, on the season and on the saints, very noteworthy, 2 books. But he is said to have written several other things, which have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Alan of Lille, master of Paris, a man most learned in divine writings, second to none in his time in secular letters, an outstanding theologian, a distinguished philosopher, and a most celebrated poet, who for a long time presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris, where he shone brightly in every science, divine and likewise human, so that he deserved to obtain the name Universal Doctor. He wrote almost countless small works in verse and prose; not all, but only a few of these have come to my knowledge: On the Sentences, 4 books; Quodlibet, 1 book; To the abbot of Saint-Gilles, on the words of sacred scripture, a work of no small size, which he entitled The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book; On the Doctrine of Moses, the same number of books; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On Penance, to the patriarch of Bourges, 4 books; On Mystical Equivocations

Of Johannes Trithemius

learned, and by no means poorly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote a certain history of the deeds of the time past, which is very greatly commended by learned and erudite men. Other things, if he wrote any, have not yet come to my knowledge. Aeneas Sylvius, also Pope Pius II, mentioned this bishop Otto in a certain oration delivered at Frankfurt, not without praise. But in the Description of Europe, when setting forth the location of Frisia, led astray by the similarity of the words, he took “Frisian” for “Freisingian.” He flourished under Frederick II in the year of the Lord 1260.

David, of the Order of Friars Minor, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and venerable no less in life and conduct than in knowledge, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the edification of simple brothers, little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: On the Instruction of Novices, 2 books; also Various Sermons to the People, and certain similar things, the reading of which is judged very useful for devout brothers. He was buried in the convent at Augsburg.

Walter, bishop of [Maguelonne?], born from Lille, a town of Flanders, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, who in his time was held in great esteem because of his learning and erudition. At the request of the provost and clerics of the church of Lille, he wrote a work, elegant in polished speech, On the Psalter, 1 book; and, as they report, certain not inelegant letters to the rich. He also published some other works, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading.

Albert, surnamed the Great, of the Order of Friars Preachers, bishop of the church of Regensburg in Bavaria, born from Lauingen, a village of Swabia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular philosophy, second to none in his time; subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, devout and most holy in life and conduct. He publicly taught the divine letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years, first at Paris, then at Cologne Agrippina, where among others he had Saint Thomas Aquinas as a pupil. Afterwards assumed to the episcopate of the church of Regensburg, after he had governed it for some time he left it, and out of love for saving study returned to his convent at Cologne, where he remained teaching and writing until the end of his life.

He wrote almost countless little works, of which the following are reported: A Notable Summa of Theology, 4 books; also On the Sentences of Master Lombard, 4 books; On the Four Coeval Things, 1 book; On Man, 1 book; On the Good, 1 book; On the Spiritual Life, 1 book; On the Office of the Mass, 1 book; On the Body of Christ, 1 book; Ten Sermons, 32; On the Strong Woman, 1 book; On the Books of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, 5 books; On Manifold Fear, 1 book; On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book; A Defense on Behalf of the Orders of Mendicant Friars, 1 book; On the Formation of Man, 1 book; On the Birth of Man, 1 book; On the Origin of the Soul, 1 book; On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book; On the Manner of Preaching, 1 book; On the Restoration of the Fallen, 1 book; On Cleaving to God, 1 book; On the Pentateuch, 5 books; On Joshua, 1 book; On Judges, 1 book; On Ruth, 1 book; On Kings, 4 books; On Chronicles, 2 books; On Ezra and Nehemiah, 3 books; On Tobit, 1 book; On Judith, 1 book; also On Esther, 1 book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book; On Ecclesiastes, 1 book; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book; On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book; On the Books of Maccabees, 2 books; On Job, 1 book; On the Prophet Isaiah, 1 book; On the Prophet Jeremiah, 1 book; On the Prophet Ezekiel, 1 book; On Daniel, 1 book; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 12 books; On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book; On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book; On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book; On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On All the Epistles of Paul, 14 books; On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book; Sermons for the Season and on the Saints through the Cycle of the Year, 2 books; On Souls, 1 book; Paradise of the Soul, so titled, 1 book; Orations on the Sentences; also Orations on the Gospels; On the Difference between Spirit and Soul, 1 book; On Divination and the Prophet, 1 book; Of Various Questions, 1 book; On the Causes of the Elements, 1 book; On Death and Life, 1 book; On Plants and Vegetables, 1 book; A Certain Summa of Philosophy, 1 book; On the Unity of the Intellect, 3 books; Questions against the Averroists, 1 book; On the Unity of Form, 1 book; On Moral Philosophy, 16 books; On Monastic Philosophy, 5 books; On Economics, 4 books; On Politics, 8 books; On Arithmetic, 1 book; On Geometry, 1 book; On Music, 1 book; On Astronomy, 1 book; On the Stars, 1 book; On the Sphere, 1 book; Mirror of Astronomy, 1 book; On the Ancient Authors of Astronomical Science, 1 book; On Minerals, 1 book; On the Nature of the Gods, 1 book; On the Secrets of Nature, 1 book; On the Twelve Alphabets, 1 book; On Choosing Masters, 1 book; On Universals, 1 book; On Dreams, 1 book; On the Categories, 1 book; On the Six Principles, 1 book; On Definitions, 1 book; On Causes, 1 book; On Grammar, 1 book; On Rhetoric, 1 book; also On Medicine, 1 book; On Wool-working, 1 book; On Agriculture, 1 book; On Ploughing, 1 book; On Navigation, 1 book; On Metaphysics, 13 books; On Perspective [unclear].

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[unclear], one book; On the Astrolabe, two books. He also wrote commentaries on all the books of Aristotle. He is said to have written many other things as well, but they have not come to my knowledge. As for the fact that he is commonly accused of necromancy, this is frivolous and fictitious, since it is known that he lived most religiously to the end of his life, and it seems incredible that so good and holy a man devoted himself to evil arts. That he is said to have done certain marvellous things, I do not doubt. For many astonishing things can be done naturally, and the hidden matters of men can be subtly uncovered by certain conjectures, and some future things also predicted; all these are judged by the inexperienced to be above nature. This Albert the Great died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, in the eighth indiction, in the eightieth year of his age. He was buried in his convent at Cologne, in the middle of the choir, not without a reputation for sanctity. And after him there did not arise in that order, in all letters, sciences, and subjects, a man so learned, educated, and experienced.

PHILIPP, abbot of the monastery of Otterberg of the Cistercian order, a man in the divine scriptures more studiously skilled through long practice, ready in talent, devout in life and conduct. He wrote for the edification of readers some little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: On the Song of Songs of Solomon, one book. Also various sermons through the cycle of the year, on feasts, to the brothers, two books. He is also said to have written several letters to [various persons?]. He composed some other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

WALTER, called de Castellione, originally from the town of Lille in Flanders, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and learned, and also excellently instructed in secular letters, a most renowned philosopher, poet, and theologian, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, very ready and skilled in verse. He wrote in elegant verse the deeds of Alexander the Great, a work certainly not to be rejected, which in the schools of the grammarians had for a long time been of such authority that the reading of the ancient poets themselves seemed neglected. But he composed many other things, which have not come to me.

THOMAS of Cantimpre, of the order of Friars Preachers, a Brabantine by country, once, as they report, a disciple of Albert the Great, certainly a most learned man, highly educated both in secular philosophy and in the divine scriptures, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, venerable no less for honesty of conduct than for knowledge. He wrote some little works not to be despised, by which he commended his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a volume no less useful than delightful to all Christians, on the mystical bees, which he entitled The Universal Good, one book. He also composed another volume, On the Nature of Things, one book. The life of a certain holy woman in Spain, who was called Christina, one book. He also wrote the life of Saint Lutgard, a nun, one book. He published many other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge. There are some who write that he had skill in the Greek language and translated the books of Aristotle which are now used in the schools. He flourished while living at Louvain, in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

GERARD, monk of Saint-Quentin in Lille, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and skilled through constant practice, not ignorant of secular letters either, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to those then living and to posterity. Among these the following are reported first: The History of the Translation of the Crown of Thorns and of Part of the Cross of the Lord from Constantinople into France, one book. Also On the Miracles of Blessed Elizabeth, Done by Divine Grace after Her Death in Thuringia, one book. He composed the office of chant for the feast of that same saint. He also published many various sermons. But he is said to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

ULRICH of Strasbourg, of the order of Friars Preachers, once a hearer and disciple of Albert the Great, a man excellently learned both in canon law and in the divine scriptures, ready in talent, scholastic in speech. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with praise to posterity. Among these the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books. A very notable Summa, six books. Also On the Soul, one book. Various sermons as well. He composed many other things too, which have not come to me. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1282. HEIN-

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

On mystical [matters], one book; On the Six Wings of the Cherubim, one book; The Complaint of Nature, one book; a Summa of Virtues and Vices, one book; On Parables, one book; Anticlaudianus, one book; On the Maxims of Theology, one book; On the Natures of Animals, one book. He is also said to have written many sermons and various letters to various [recipients]; whether all these can be found I do not know. Finally, he is reported to have composed commentaries and elegant lectures on many books of the Bible, especially on the prophets, the Gospel, and the Apostle, but I do not remember that any of them has come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in A.D. 1300.

William, monk of Affligem of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in verse and prose, published in both genres, that is, in alternating style, little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity: Sermons, not useless, to the people and the brothers, one book; also the Life of Saint Lutgard, one book; also Visions of a Certain Nun, one book. He also published many other things which have not come to my notice.

Henry of Brussels, monk of the same monastery of Affligem, of the Order of our holy father Benedict, skilled in the holy Scriptures through long practice, not ignorant of secular literature, an excellent philosopher and computist, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote On the Method of Computus, one book; likewise a Calendar on [indictions?], one book; also On the Astrolabe, one book. Moreover he is said to have written many other things, which have not yet come to the notice of our reading.

Eckardus, of the Order, as some maintain, of Preachers, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and a most diligent preacher of the divine word. He wrote many subtle volumes by which he commended his memory to posterity; among them I have found the following: On the Sentences, three books; On Genesis, one book; On Exodus, one book; On the Book of Wisdom, one book; Of His Positions, one book; The Gospel of John, one book; On the Lord's Prayer, one book; Positions in Defense, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book; various Collations delivered at other times in chapters of the Preachers. The rest that he composed have not come to the notice of our reading. We made mention, in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, of certain of his sayings that were condemned. He flourished in his time especially in Austria, where by preaching, teaching, and writing he was held in great esteem by the people.

Peter of Saxony, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, a man of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote a summa On Cases, not useless for preachers and confessors, which in its time was in the greatest esteem. Likewise, sermons on the temporal cycle [unclear]. Finally, [unclear] on many books of the Bible; Sermons for Lent, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book; the Rule of his order, one book. Also many various sermons. He corrected the ordinal of his religious order with discerning attention. But he is said to have written several other things, which have not come to my notice. He flourished in the convent of Cologne in the times of Louis IV of Bavaria, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in A.D. 1320.

John of Blomendale, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, was excellent in delivering sermons to the people. Among other things he wrote elegant Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book; also Sermons for Lent, one book; also Sermons on the Saints through the cycle of the year, one book. He is also said to have written some other things, which

Of Johannes Trithemius ... have not come to my notice. He flourished under Emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

JOHANNES Danckonis of Saxony, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and astronomer, the most erudite of all his time, distinguished in talent and eloquence, taught the science of the stars for a long time to the French at Paris, among whom he was held in the highest honor. He wrote certain excellent little works, of which I have found only the following: Canons of the First Mover, one book; Tables of the same, one book; On the Plane Astrolabe, two books; also On [incensions?], [unclear] book[s]; On Eclipses, one book; On the Truth and Usefulness of the Science of Astronomy, one book. The other things that he composed have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter of Lutra, monk of the monastery of Lutra.

Johannes Danckonis of Saxony. JOHANNES Danckonis of Saxony, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and astronomer, the most erudite of all his time, distinguished in talent and eloquence, taught the science of the stars for a long time to the French at Paris, among whom he was held in the highest honor. He wrote certain excellent little works, of which I have found only the following: Canons of the First Mover, one book; Tables of the same, one book; On the Plane Astrolabe, two books; also On [incensions?], [unclear] book[s]; On Eclipses, one book; On the Truth and Usefulness of the Science of Astronomy, one book. The other things that he composed have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1430.

PETER of Lutra, a monk of the Premonstratensian order of the monastery of Lutra, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, a most distinguished philosopher and jurist, subtle in talent, scholastic in eloquence. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Sentences, three books; On the Gospel of John, one book; To Baldwin the Archbishop, On the Prerogatives of the Church of Trier, one book; The Sevenfold [Candelabra?], On the Eminence of the Supreme Pontiff, three books; Against Brother Michael of the Order of Minors, formerly general, and those adhering to him, who were attacking the Supreme Pontiff, one book; On the Form of Marriages, one book; To Cardinal Colonna, On the Mystical Columns, one book; On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; also various Sermons on the Season and on the Saints through the circle of the year, two books. He also published many other things, which have not yet come to the notice of our reading. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis the Bavarian and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Lupold of Bebenburg, bishop of Bamberg, formerly a hearer and disciple of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, a jurist most celebrated by the praise of all, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, cautious in talent and ready in speech, wrote certain little works of great learning by which he consecrated his name to immortality: A distinguished volume On the Zeal and Fervor of the German Princes and Nobles for the Catholic Faith, the Honor of the Roman See, and the Prelates, one book. Likewise On the Rights of the Roman Empire, one book. He also elegantly composed many letters to various persons. But he is said to have written some other things, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1341.

CONRAD of Monte Puellarum, canon of the church of Regensburg in Bavaria, a man learned in the divine writings, most learned in secular philosophy, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech. In the gymnasium of Erfurt he first learned the rudiments of the liberal arts, and then, betaking himself to the French, he devoted himself to sacred letters. Raised to the doctorate at Paris, he instructed many in saving knowledge for eight years with glory. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote: On the Sentences, four books; also To Lupold, the above-mentioned bishop of Bamberg, a very distinguished Oeconomica, three books; to the Duke of [Austria?], a Monastica, one book; also a Politica, one book. He determined various disputations and questions at Paris. But he published many other things, which have not yet come to the notice of our reading. He flourished under Emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, in the year of the Lord 1341.

HEINRICH of Urimaria, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man from boyhood most devoted to the holy writings and much learned, and in the philosophy of the Peripatetics second to none in his time among the Parisians, since, having ascended the doctoral chair, he publicly taught theology and philosophy for many years in the same gymnasium. He wrote not a few volumes for the edification of readers, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books; quodlibetal questions disputed at Paris, one book; On the Ten Precepts, one book; An Epitome of the Conferences of the Saints of John Cassian, twenty-four books; On the Perfection of the Human Word, one book; On Instincts, one book, which is ascribed by some to Heinrich of Hesse; On Exemption, one book; Exposition of the Decretal on the Celebration of Masses, one book; Sermons on the Season and on the Saints, two books. He is also said to have written commentaries on many books of the Bible and of Aristotelian philosophy, and to have composed various other treatises, which have by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1341.

LUDOLPH of Saxony, a Carthusian monk of the house of Strasbourg, a man devoted to the divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, mild in talent,

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[unclear], sweet and well-composed in speech, worthy of reverence no less for his life than for his learning. He wrote certain little works of great devotion and erudition, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the following: a great volume, a distinguished work, on the life and teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, which, drawing from the Gospel, he entitled The Life of Jesus, in two books; likewise, on the whole Psalter, a very celebrated work, one book. He is also said to have written several other things, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Simon of Speyer, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Germany, of a certain [unclear] church, a man most learned in divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, who taught theology with distinction for a long time in the school of Cologne, acquired great glory for his learning. He wrote On the Sentences, four books; Against the Jews, one book; also various postils on the Scriptures, which he read at Cologne; also sermons not to be rejected, one book. He also published several other things which I have not yet been able to see. He died at Cologne, buried in his own convent, in the year of the Lord 1340, in the eighth indiction, on 6 January, under Pope Benedict XII.

John of Saxony, of the order of Friars Minor, studiously learned in holy Scriptures, excellently instructed both in canon law and in Peripatetic philosophy, and a man of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote several distinguished volumes, by which he commended his name to the memory and knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a notable summa on cases of conscience, not useless to hearers of confessions, one book; also sermons for the seasons and for the saints, two books; but certain other works are unknown to us. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian in the year of the Lord 1340.

John Eligerus of Gondersleuen, formerly a hearer of lord John of Saxony, the very distinguished astronomer, a man learned in holy Scriptures, the most celebrated among all astronomers in his time, a philosopher and astronomer [unclear] among all, and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote volumes in astronomy not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Construction of the Astrolabe, one book; On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, one book; On the Usefulness of the Quadrant, one book; also On the Magnet, two books; On the Astrogemeter, one book; and certain other works unknown to us. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John de Beka, cleric of the Church of Utrecht, a man learned in holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters. He published certain little works of his talent not to be despised; of these I have seen only [unclear], a volume bringing [unclear] to the knowledge of John, bishop of the Church of Utrecht, and William, duke of Holland, concerning the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and of the counts and dukes of Holland, beginning from the time of Willibrord, the first bishop, down to the year of the Lord 1346. Concerning the rest I have seen nothing; they also have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1348.

Thomas of Argentina, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of [unclear], [unclear] of Rimini, prior general of the whole order, a learned and erudite man, a preacher and a distinguished interpreter of secular philosophy, notable in life and conduct, since he vigorously governed his order by word and example. He wrote certain excellent volumes in divine Scriptures, by which he transmitted his memory with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, four books; Constitutions of the Order, one book; also various sermons to the people, two books. But he is said to have written certain other things also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1366, in the third indiction, on 10 February, under Charles IV, emperor.

Henry of Erfurt, studiously learned in holy Scriptures, and in

Johannes Trithemius [unclear]

... excellently learned in [secular?] letters, a philosopher, jurist, theologian, and very celebrated chronicler, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence. He wrote little works of authority not to be despised, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity; among them the following are reported: A notable work of histories concerning memorable deeds, one book. Also a noteworthy Summa on cases of conscience, one book. Many sermons, and various other treatises; from these we conjecture that he was a religious, although we do not know the distinction of his order. He flourished under Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Johannes of Erfurt, of the order of Friars Minor, an enlightened doctor in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, a most learned interpreter of philosophy and of both laws, subtle in intellect, ready in eloquence. He wrote several volumes of great usefulness, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these, however, few have come into our hands: Table of Law, one book. Also a Summa on cases of conscience, not useless for hearers of confessions, two books. Popular sermons, not inelegant, on the season and on the saints, three books. The other things which he composed have not come into our hands.

Thilmannus of Aachen, of the order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, after Heinrich of Dolendorp provincial prior of Lower Germany, a distinguished doctor of the divine scriptures, presiding over the theological school first at Paris and then at Cologne, acquired great glory for his learning both by teaching and by writing. Among the other works of his talent he wrote: On the Sentences, four books. Also a noteworthy reading on the Gospel of Matthew, which he read publicly at Cologne in his convent, one book. He also disputed various questions. He likewise composed many elegant sermons, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Jacobus of Altavilla, by homeland of the Rheingau, fifteenth abbot of the monastery of Eberbach of the Cistercian order, which is situated in the Rheingau almost two miles from Mainz, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, an ornament of the Parisian school, a distinguished doctor, wrote a noteworthy work on the Sentences, four books. But also various questions disputed at Paris, one book; likewise many sermons to the brothers, which are partly extant, but partly have been lost through negligence. He also published elegant letters to various persons, and other things unknown to us. He flourished under Charles, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes of Ymenhusen, doctor of Paris, studious and learned in the holy scriptures, and excellently learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, an acute disputant. Among other things he wrote a distinguished volume on the Sentences, four books; also sermons, and various questions of the scriptures. Finally, he is said to have made elegant commentaries on certain books of the Bible, and to have written many other things, but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands. He flourished under Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes of Tambach, of the order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, [unclear], much practiced and learned, not ignorant also of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, composed with the polish of scholastic speech. He published certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity; among these they report the following: A large work, not to be rejected, against the darts of flattering fortune, no less useful than pleasant, which he entitled Consolation of Theology, four books. On the sensible delights of paradise, one book. Also sermons on the season and on the saints, two books. Certain other things. He flourished under Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes of Hildesheim, of the order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, bachelor of sacred theology, lector, prior of Kassel, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, in secular letters by everyone’s opinion the most learned of his time; a theologian, rhetorician, philosopher, and very celebrated poet. In declaiming homilies to the people he was of excellent talent. He wrote many outstanding volumes, by which he commended his name to posterity; among them the following are extant: On the Sentences, three books. To Florentius, bishop of Münster, On the Translation of the Three Kings, one book. Also a Chronicle of the Times, one book. A Defense of the Mendicant Orders against Richard, archbishop of Armagh, one book. A metrical work On Monsters in the Church, one book. The work entitled Fountain of Life, one book. On Antichrist, one book. Against the Jews, one book. Against a certain man painting shameful things, one book. Sermons on the season and on the saints, one book. Of letters to various persons, number 80, one book.

CATALOGUE OF ILLUSTRIOUS MEN.

…a book of Epigrams: 1 book. He published also many others, which have not come to my knowledge. This John was once hearer and familiar friend of blessed Peter Thomas, patriarch of Constantinople, formerly master general, [then] residing at Avignon. He flourished under Charles IV. In the year of the Lord 1360.

Albert of Rickmersdorp, a Saxon by country, thirty-first bishop of Halberstadt in order, a man studious and erudite in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, a doctor of Paris. He wrote many illustrious volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity, of which these are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books; he published commentaries on many books of Aristotle; and he unfolded various questions in the holy Scriptures. But he composed also many others, which have not come to my knowledge. He received the bishopric of the aforesaid church of Halberstadt from Pope Urban V, in the year of the Lord 1365, in the third indiction, and presided twenty-four years. He was buried in his greater church of Halberstadt.

Matthew of Cracow, doctor of Prague, bishop of Worms, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, and excellently learned in secular philosophy, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, who, on account of [his] inestimable learning, [was] constituted president of the theological school first at Prague [and] then at Paris, [and] obtained great glory among the doctors by reading and writing. He wrote many illustrious little works, of which, however, I recall few to have come into our hands: On the Sentences, 4 books; to Heinrich, bishop of Worms, a beautiful volume on predestination, and that God has done all things well, whose interlocutors are the Father [and] the Son, which he entitled the Rationale of the divine works, 7 books; On contracts, 1 book; On the frequenting or intermitting of [the] celebration [of Mass]; a Dialogue of the reasoning of conscience, 1 book; Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; also various sermons. The rest which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He dies in the year of the Lord [1410?], the fifth day of March; he is buried at Worms.

John [Klenkok?], of the order of the hermit-brothers of Saint Augustine, sprung from Saxony, doctor of Prague, most learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent [and] eloquent in speech. He wrote certain illustrious little works, by which he commended his name to posterity, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books; Questions of various positions disputed at Prague, 1 book; also sermons on the [seasons of the] year [and] on the saints, 2 books; Of letters to various [persons], 1 book. The rest which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

John Fust, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, first lector of the convent of Kreuznach in the county of Sponheim, and then Prior of Strasbourg, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in eloquence, devout in life [and] conversation, a most wonderful declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote, among the other monuments of his talent: Questions of the Sentences, 1 book; he published also some sermons, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in his convent of Kreuznach, where he first put on the habit of [his order], under the emperor Charles IV. In the year of the Lord 1370.

Gerard Groot, called also Magnus, of Deventer, a man most learned both in the divine and in the human writings, especially in canon law, subtle in talent, scholastic in eloquence, devout in life [and] conversation. He wrote several little works of no contemptible reading, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory, of which these are reported: On contracts [and] usuries, 1 book; On the instruction of novices, 1 book; On the taking-up of the pastoral care, 1 book; On the inner conversation, 1 book; On the governance of nuns, 1 book; On the inconveniences of matrimony, 1 book; also Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; he published, besides, various sermons [and] many [things], which have not come to the notice of our reading. He dies under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1384, in the seventh indiction.

Conrad of Alzey—a town of the duke Palatine [and] count, in the diocese of Mainz, situated three miles from Worms—a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned in secular letters, a most celebrated philosopher [and] poet, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, exercised in meter [and] prose. He wrote in either kind certain volumes not to be cast away, by which he obtained great praise of erudition first among the Prague-men and then at Erfurt; but few of them have come to my knowledge, for [I read] only…

Of Johannes Trithemius

also a little work which he elegantly composed in verse and rhythms on the most pure Virgin Mary, Mother of God, entitled The Book of Figures, 1 book. He also wrote many elegant letters to various persons, and many poems of various kinds, 1 book, and several other things. He flourished under Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Bertrammus, bishop of [unclear], of the order of the Friars Preachers of the convent of Koblenz, and vicar in pontificals of the bishop of Metz, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most famous among the doctors of his time, outstanding in talent and renowned in eloquence, also an excellent declaimer of sermons. He wrote On the Sentences, 4 books. Likewise, to Cuno, archbishop of Trier, On the Illusions of Demons, 1 book. To the same man, On the Schism, 1 book. He also issued various sermons to the people and to the clergy, and besides many other things, which have not come into our hands. He died under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1387, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth indiction. He was buried at Koblenz in the diocese of Trier, in his own convent of Preachers, where, after having once received the order, he had been prior.

Heinrich of Kalkar, monk of the Carthusian order and prior of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man whose understanding was illumined in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, sweet in eloquence, and devout also in life and conduct. He issued little works of reading not to be despised, the use of which is judged not unprofitable for devout brothers. Among these the following are reported: Monastic Exercise, 1 book; Speech on Rhetoric, 1 book; Song on Music, 1 book; On the Origin and Progress of the Carthusian Order, 1 book. He also composed sermons to the brothers not to be despised, and certain other things especially pertaining to the cleansing of consciences. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390.

John Ruusbroec, of the order of the regular canons, prior of the monastery of Green Valley in Brabant, a studious and devout man. He wrote, among the other works of his talent: On the Adornment of Spiritual Marriage, 3 books; On the Progress of Religious, 2 books; also many sermons to the brothers; also several letters to various persons, 1 book. He also issued some other works, which have not come into our hands. This man’s writings in the third book On the Adornment of Spiritual Marriage are to be read cautiously, as John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, warns us in the book issued by him on this matter. He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, not without a reputation for sanctity, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Conrad, monk of the monastery of Fons Salutis in Swabia, of the Cistercian order, a man most studious in the divine writings, not moderately learned in secular letters, renowned in talent and plain in eloquence. He wrote On the Sentences, 4 books; also sermons on the season, 2 books; sermons on the saints, 2 books. But he issued some other works which have not come into our hands. This man’s sermons are commonly called “sermons of juice,” because they were extracted with sagacious study from the juicy marrow of the Scriptures. Yet there are some who pretend that the reason for this word took its origin from footwear, because he used to carry with him to the choir or elsewhere slips enclosed in his boots for composing sermons. He is said to have flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390.

John of Schoonhoven, of the order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Mechelen, a man studiously learned in the holy writings, not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote, for the usefulness of simple preachers, volumes not to be rejected, by which he commended his memory to posterity: a distinguished work On Vices, Virtues, and Every Preachable Matter, according to the order of the alphabet, in two volumes, which he entitled with the Greek word Polypodium, 2 books. He also wrote sermons, not inelegant, through the circle of the year on the season and on the saints, 2 books. But he is said to have written several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Conrad of Zutphen, by homeland a Gelderlander, of the order of the regular canons of the monastery of Windesheim in the diocese of Utrecht, a man more studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence. He wrote many excellent volumes for the instruction of simple brothers; yet only a few of these have come to the knowledge of our reading, for I have found only the following: On Spiritual Ascents, a very useful treatise on notable men, 1 book; also On the Reformation of the Inner Man, a work not to be rejected, 1 book. He is also said to have composed many elegant sermons, the reading of which is judged necessary for religious. The rest which

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

149

The things which he wrote, although they are many, nevertheless have by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1400.

William of Oppenbach, a Parisian doctor, most learned in the sacred Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, quite capable in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote On the Sentences, four books; also Various Questions, which he disputed at Paris and Cologne, one book; Sermons to the People and Various Collations to the Clergy. But he also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. It is established that he was a religious, but of what order he was I have not yet been able sufficiently to discover.

Gerard of Zutphen, another distinct from the first, the ornament of the Cologne school and a formed bachelor of sacred Theology, a learned and very venerable man, subtle in intellect and a very acute disputant of difficult questions. He wrote notable Questions on the Sentences, four books. He also arranged quodlibetal questions, in which he determines many matters for the instruction of students. He also published some other works, which have not come to me. He flourished around the times of the emperors Wenceslaus and Rupert of Bavaria, in the year of the Lord 1400.

John of the little town of Wittlich, of the diocese of Trier, which is about four miles distant from the city of Trier, a man judicious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not moderately learned in secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, who once taught sacred letters publicly in the Cologne school. He wrote On the Sentences, four books. He also published a notable lecture on the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul. He also publicly recited [unclear] questions to many hearers. He also published some other works, which have not come to me. He flourished under Emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Henry of Langenstein, called of Hesse, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters, outstanding in intellect, scholastic in speech, abundant and expansive, since, after spending many years in lecturing on Genesis, he scarcely reached the fourth chapter of the book, and completed as many volumes. For he was resolved for everything and copious in speaking and writing, so that for him it was a matter of greater difficulty to repel things worthy of remembrance that occurred to him of their own accord than to find new things to say. This man, as I discovered from a certain letter of his, I would believe to have been a canon of the church of Worms. He flourished first in the Parisian school, where he also earned the laurel of the doctorate; then, for the honor of the new planting, he betook himself to Vienna, where by teaching and writing he obtained great glory for learning. Of his little works the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books; On the Helmeted Prologue of the Bible, one book; On the Beginning of Genesis, four books; To the Bishop of Freising on Antichrist and Schism, one book; On Contemplation, one book; On the Contemplative Soul, one book; Mirror of the Sinful Soul, one book; On the Seven Canonical Hours, one book; Against the Predictor of the Thelenses [unclear], one book; On the Lord’s Prayer, one book; On the Ave Maria, one book; On the Creed of the Apostles, one book; On Contempt of the World, a notable volume, one book; Against a Certain Wycliffite Heretic, one book; To the Canons Regular, one book; On the Property of Monks, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; Sermons for the Season and on the Saints, two books; Letters to Various Persons, one book. He also published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. There are some who write that he was bishop of Worms, others bishop of Warmia in Silesia, and that Matthew of Krakow wrote to him seven very learned little books on predestination. The name indeed agrees, not the time; we leave the truth to be investigated by the studious. He flourished under Emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1400.

John Gluel, born in the imperial city of Aachen, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Cologne, a man exceptionally learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent intellect in delivering sermons to the people. Among the other works of his study he wrote a volume On the Origin and Progress of His Order, which he entitled Mirror of the Carmelites, one book; also Sermons for the Season and on the Saints throughout the cycle of the year, one book; also Sermons through Lent, one book. He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished at Cologne, where he was also buried.

Henry of Cuta, or Oyta, Parisian Doctor.

Henry of Cuta, or Oyta, Parisian doctor, studious and learned in the sacred Scriptures, and nobly learned in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an excellent deliverer of sermons, the singular ornament of the Viennese school in Austria and its primary co-planter. He wrote certain excellent things in volumes of writings

Of Johannes Trithemius [unclear], by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Among these I found the following: on the Sentences, book I; also Quodlibets, book I; on contracts, book I; on the conception of blessed Mary ever virgin, book I; various sermons. Of the rest which he wrote I have seen nothing. He flourished under Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1490.

Heinrich of Andernach, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Cologne convent, a man trained by long study and learned in the holy Scriptures, and subtly imbued with Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, who adorned first the Parisian and then the Cologne academy by his learning and presence. He wrote a distinguished work on the Sentences, books IV; Notable Questions of Philosophy, book I; sermons on the season and on the saints through the cycle of the year, books II. The other things which he composed have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo in Ghent, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, an outstanding doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, venerable no less for religious conduct than for knowledge. He wrote a notable little book on the eating of meat, in which, disputing subtly, he concludes according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the sanctions of law that the eating of meat is unlawful for a healthy monk, and therefore wholly forbidden. He also wrote explanations on our Rule, book I; also questions of the Sententiary, book I. In addition, he is said to have written various and many treatises, which have by no means come down to us.

Johannes of Werden, of the diocese of Cologne, of the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man studious and learned in the holy divine Scriptures, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in speech, the most celebrated of all in his time as a declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote very notable sermons on the season and on the saints, which today are commonly called the sermons “Sleep securely,” because any preacher can make progress in them without labor. Also sermons for Lent, book I. He also published some other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the Cologne convent under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Johannes of Duren, of the Order of the Friars Minor, of the diocese of Cologne, a not idle preacher of the divine word, renowned in talent, eloquent in speech, studious and learned both in the divine writings and in secular letters. He wrote for the use of simple brothers certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to those present and to posterity; among these I found the following: On the Seven Sins, book I; on the hidden sins of vice, book I; on the manifest things of vice, book I; also sermons for Lent, book I. The other things which he composed have by no means come into our hands.

Arnold of Austria, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Vienna convent, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, an outstanding disputant of questions. He wrote a distinguished volume on the Sentences, books III; also elegant sermons and various questions in Scripture. But he is said to have composed some other things, which have not come into our hands.

Thomas of Haselbach, learned in the holy writings, well taught in secular philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in speech, but in many things overly diffuse and prolix, and for that reason subject to the judgment of certain people; for when he was ordinary lector of the Vienna academy, he was subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many volumes on the prophet Isaiah, which I do not know whether all are to be found. Also on the Sentences, books IV; on the Ten Commandments of the Decalogue, book I; on the five senses of man, book I; also many sermons on the season and on the saints, books II; and many other things. He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Johannes Brammart, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Aachen convent, provincial prior of Lower Germany, doctor of Paris, studious and learned in the holy writings, and excellently learned in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, devout in life and conduct. He wrote a distinguished work on the Sentences, books III; also many sermons, various questions, and certain other things which have not come into our hands. Finally, after many good things bestowed upon his province, he died under Rupert the Bavarian, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1307, in the fifteenth indiction. He was buried at Cologne in the middle of the choir of his convent.

Thomas

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Thomas de Kempis, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, of the Mount of the holy martyr and virgin Agnes near Zwolle in the diocese of Utrecht, a man zealous and learned in the Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding venerator of blessed Mary, Mother of God, formerly, as they say, a disciple of Gerard the Great of Deventer, about whom marvelous things are told. He wrote certain devout volumes, of which the following are reported: On Contempt of the World and the Imitation of Christ, 4 books; sermons to novices, 3 books; Dialogue of Novices, 1 book; sermons to the brothers, 1 book; On the Solitary Life, 1 book; [On] Tabernacles, 1 book; Alphabet of True Compunction, 1 book; Little Garden of Spiritual Roses, 1 book; Valley of Lilies, 1 book; Alphabet of the Monk, 1 book; Consolation of the Poor, 1 book; Epitaph of the Monk, 1 book; What Sort of Man a Monk Ought to Be, 1 book; Manual for Little Ones, 1 book; Doctrinal for Youths, 1 book; On the Vanity of the World and Contempt of It, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book; and others. He flourished in the times of Rupert of Bavaria, the most renowned emperor, in the year of the Lord 1410. And it should be noted that two men are reported to have had this name: both from Kempen, both regulars on the Mount of Saint Agnes, both outstanding in talent, and both composing various little works. The first of these, converted to religious life in the times of Master Gerard the Great and deemed worthy of divine revelations, is said to have written the things which we have listed above. The second, however, still lived almost in our own times among men, and composed various things which have not come into our hands. And perhaps some things have been ascribed to the first which the second is thought to have made. The little book On the Imitation of Christ, however, is reported to be by the first author; our elders say that, many years before, their elders read it, although I know that some think the contrary in this matter. This elder Thomas flourished under Emperor Rupert of Bavaria, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Michael Herbrant of Düren, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Kreuznach in the diocese of Mainz, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished by experience in many matters, ready in talent, lucid in speech, and also an excellent preacher or declaimer of the divine word. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity; among these there are many elegant sermons, 1 book, also conferences and many [unclear]. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Rupert, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Peter of Speyer, of the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, an excellent declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote things not to be rejected [unclear] zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice. I have found the following: a mystical exposition on Exodus, 1 book; on the epistle of Saint Paul the Apostle to the Romans, 1 book; On the Three Monastic Custodies, 1 book; On the Annunciation of the Lord, 1 book; Eulogy of Paul the First Hermit, 1 book; sermons on the season and on the saints, 1 book; also several letters to various persons. Surveying with remarkable industry the difficult work of William of Paris on the whole corporeal and incorporeal universe, he beautifully reduced it into a brief compendium. He wrote also some other things which have by no means come to our knowledge. He died in the house of the Valley of Grace near Bruges, while being beneficially occupied in the act of visitation, on the seventh Ides of July, in the year of the Lord 1410, in the third indiction.

Of Johannes Trithemius

HEINRICH of Hachenberg, of the order of Friars Preachers, of the convent of Koblenz, a studious man, practiced in the Scriptures, of excellent talent and great reputation in delivering sermons to the people. Among other works of his exercise he wrote: Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1; also Sermons on Lent, book 1. But he is said to have written several other things which have not come to my knowledge.

JORDAN, of the order of the Friars of Saint Augustine of the Hermitage, of Strasbourg, a devout man, an excellent expounder and interpreter of the divine Scriptures, of most excellent talent in delivering sermons. He wrote several elegant treatises useful to devout brethren, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, however, few have come into our hands: On the Apocalypse of John, book 1; An Apology for his order, book 1; On the Passion of the Lord, book 1; Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1; Sermons throughout Lent, book 1; and many other things. He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410.

VINCENT Gruner of Zwickau, doctor of Prague, founder of the Leipzig school, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, published some little works not contemptible in their reading, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant: A notable lecture on the office of the Mass, which he publicly read at the new planting of the aforesaid Leipzig school, book 1; also On the Sentences, books 4; Various Disputed Questions, book 1. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished at the time of the transfer of the Prague school to the city of Leipzig, in the province of the Margraviate of Meissen, around the year of the Lord 1410, under Emperor Rupert.

JOHN, bishop of Lombariensis, of the order of Friars Preachers, born in the city of Basel in Germany, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and a most celebrated deliverer of sermons. He published several distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant an outstanding work On the Sentences, books 4; also various sermons; and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished around the times of the emperors Rupert and Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410.

JOHN, monk of the monastery of Kastl, of the order of our divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Eichstatt, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, a theologian, philosopher, and notable rhetorician. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which I have found only those set down below: On the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, a very celebrated work in two large volumes; likewise A Breviary of the Bibles, book 1; elegant Sermons on the Temporale and on the Saints, books 2; also forty-two sermons On the Passion of the Lord, book 1; Letters to Various Persons, book 1; On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, book 1. But he published many other things which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished at about the time when the reform of Kastl was vigorous, under the emperors Rupert and Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

JOHN Zacharias of Erfurt, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, an acute disputant, who adorned the Erfurt school with the majesty of a Sententiary. He wrote: On the Sentences of Peter Lombard, books 4; also On Genesis, book 1; On Exodus, book 1; On Leviticus, book 1; On the Epistles of Paul, books 14; many sermons; various determinations of questions. But he is said to have composed several other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund; in the great Council of Constance he was magnificently praised for disputing against the heretical Hussites, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

NICHOLAS of Dinkelsbuhl, doctor of Vienna, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, well instructed in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, keen in talent, scholastic in speech, outstanding in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which I have found only those set down below: On the Sentences, books 4; also Questions on the Sentences, book 1; On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, book 1; On the Ten Commandments, book 1; On the Lord’s Prayer, book 1; On the Eight Beatitudes, book 1; On the Three Parts of Penance, book 1; On the Eight Capital Vices, book 1; On the Seven Mortal Sins, book 1; On the Commandment of Charity, books 2; On the Sins of the Tongue, book 1; Sermons on the Temporale and on the Saints, books 2; also other moral sermons, book 1. But he is said to have written many other things which have not come to my knowledge. This man, sent by the University of Vienna to the great Council of Constance, one of the highest

154 Of Johannes Trithemius and often an envoy to princes. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading; of these I have found the following: Against the Hussites, Bohemian heretics, 1 book; against the scabini of the secret judgment, called Feymeri, 1 book; On Contracts, 1 book; On Predestination, 1 book; Popular Sermons, 2 books; an oration delivered before the king of France; also an oration before the king of England; an oration before the duke of Savoy; many other varied orations, 1 book. He also wrote several questions disputed in the schools, 1 book; various letters; and certain other things still unknown to me. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

HENRICUS of Gulpen, abbot of the monastery of Saint Giles at Nuremberg, of the order of our holy father Benedict, doctor of decrees, studious and learned in both divine and secular writings, and venerable no less for his religious manner of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, whose readiness of mind and foresight in counsel Johannes Nider, having once experienced it, commends in the book On Ants, wrote elegantly on [unclear] concerning penance, 1 book; likewise on the distinction On Consecration, 1 book; On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; and certain other things. He was personally prominent at the Council of Constance, when he was still held to be a secular master of arts and a student of law; and at the Council of Basel, already doctor and abbot, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1435.

RUDOLPHUS of Bruxella, from a village in Swabia, in the diocese of Speyer, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently taught in the secular philosophy which they call Aristotelian, a distinguished professor of sacred letters, who in the Heidelberg gymnasium acquired great praise for his learning by teaching and writing, wrote in that faculty certain excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among them these are reported: Questions on the Sentences, 1 book; many very useful sermons; various questions disputed in the schools; many orations to the fathers of the same gymnasium. The rest that he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished at the Council of Basel in the year 1435.

HENRICUS of Gauda, a man skilled in the holy Scriptures through long study, subtle in intellect and a very keen disputant of scholastic questions, earned the chair of mastership in the Heidelberg gymnasium both by teaching and by writing.
