He wrote certain excellent monuments of his intellect, by which he showed himself useful to those present and memorable to those to come. Of these I have found only: on the third book of the Sentences, 1 book; also On the Celebration of Masses, 1 book; various orations delivered in the university; also many questions excellently disputed in the schools. But of the rest that he composed, nothing has reached our hands. He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1435.

NICOLAUS of Susato, by birth a Westphalian, the ornament and pillar of the Heidelberg gymnasium, a distinguished doctor of sacred theology, held in esteem by Ludwig, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, and at the Council of Constance joined, from the German nation, with the remaining cardinals for electing the supreme pontiff, wrote certain excellent monuments of his intellect, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have found only: notable questions on the Sentences, 1 book; several elegant sermons and orations; and various questions on diverse subjects disputed in the schools. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the aforesaid Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1417 and thereafter.

JOHANNES Gritsch, of the order of Friars Preachers, by birth from Basel, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and skilled through long exercise both in canon law and in the other letters of secular philosophy, an excellent declaimer of popular sermons, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, wrote for preachers of the divine word little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there are extant: sermons on the temporal cycle and on the saints, 2 books; sermons through Lent, 1 book; also On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; and many other things. He flourished, as his own people report, in the times of Emperor Sigismund and of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1435.

JOHANNES Nider, of the same order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and well instructed in scholastic philosophy, of excellent intellect in declaiming sermons to the people, for a long time an inquisitor of heretical depravity, and a most keen persecutor of the poor women whom the common people call witches, wrote in a clear style indeed, but volumes not to be despised. Of these the following are extant: On the Contracts of Merchants, 1 book; On Moral Leprosy, 1 book; On Ants, [unclear] books; in whi-

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

...by appointment of the supreme pontiff he was constituted Elector on behalf of the German nation, as is contained in the acts of that council. He flourished under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Peter of Rosenheim, a monk of the monastery of Melk in the regions of Austria, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and magnificently instructed in secular letters, an excellent philosopher and poet, ready in intellect and renowned in eloquence. He wrote, in verse and prose, little works not to be rejected, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these I have read a metrical volume which, at the persuasion and request of Nicholas Dinkelsbuehl, he composed for lord Branda, cardinal of San Clemente, apostolic legate in Austria, on all the chapters of the Bible, which he entitled Roseate Memorial of the Divine Utterances, book 1. Also a History, or Chronicle of the Times, book 1; many various sermons, book 2; letters to various persons, book 1. He also published many other works which have not yet come at all to the notice of my reading. He flourished in the times of the Council of Constance and of the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Nicholas, monk of Holy Cross.

Nicholas, a monk of the monastery of Holy Cross in Austria, of the Cistercian order, a man learned in the holy divine Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, excellent in intellect and renowned in eloquence. He wrote certain little works of no contemptible usefulness, by which he showed to posterity the liveliness of his intellect. Among these the following are extant: a work in praise of blessed Mary, mother of God, not useless to preachers of the divine word, which he entitled Image of Holy Mary, book 1; various sermons, book 2; also many letters to various persons. The rest which he composed [unclear] did not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the Council of Constance and of the most clement Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420. He composed various treatises on the holy Scriptures.

Hermannus Petra of Studorp, a monk of the Carthusian order, prior of the house [unclear].

Hermann Petra of Studorp.

...devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, vicar and rector of the house of the nuns of the divine mother Anne near Bruges in Flanders, where for nine years [unclear]. On the Lord's Prayer, sermons [unclear]. The following are also extant: On the Government of Nuns, book 1; sermons [unclear]. Suitable volumes, of which the following are extant: On the Government of Nuns, book 2; fifty sermons, book 3; sermons on the saints, book 4; on Genesis [unclear]. He died under the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction.

Henry of Hesse the Younger, a monk of the Carthusian order, prior of the house [unclear].

Henry of Hesse the Younger.

...of the monks of Saint Mary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence. He published many outstanding volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Many of them he read publicly, before his entry into religion, in the universal schools. Among these the following are reported: on the Sentences, book 1; on the Apocalypse of John, book [unclear]; also book 2; on the Proverbs of Solomon, book 3; on the Apocalypse, book 4; various sermons [unclear]. He died under the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, in the sixth indiction.

John called Plaeth, doctor of Heidelberg, most learned in the holy Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and venerable no less for the integrity of his conduct than for his knowledge of letters; also sufficiently apt and eloquent in delivering sermons to the people. Among the other works of his intellect he wrote [unclear] a great and distinguished work on the Catholic faith, on the chapter Firmly we believe, which he read publicly in ordinary course in the aforesaid school of Heidelberg. Likewise he wrote various questions on the Sentences, book 1; against the errors of the Bohemians, book 2; sermons to the people [unclear]. Devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, renowned in intellect, clear in speech, an acute disputant, a declaimer of popular sermons, renowned in intellect, most eloquent in speech because of his singular learning; chaplain and secretary to Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, because of his singular learning and prudence, and in many difficult affairs [sent] to kings [unclear]. He flourished under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

John of Dieburg.

John of Dieburg, called of Frankfurt, doctor of Heidelberg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, renowned in intellect, clear in speech, an acute disputant. A declaimer of popular sermons, renowned in intellect, most eloquent in speech because of his singular learning; chaplain and secretary to Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, because of his singular learning and prudence, and in many difficult affairs [sent] to kings [unclear]. He flourished under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

in which he relates many and various miracles that occurred in his own times; Consolatory Work for a Fearful Conscience, 1 book; Mirror of Perfection, 1 book; sermons for the season and on the saints, 2 books; sermons through Lent, 1 book; and many other things. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund at the time of the Council of Constance [and] Basel, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Heimericus de Campo, vice-chancellor of the Cologne gymnasium. Heimericus de Campo, vice-chancellor of the Cologne gymnasium, a man most learned in divine Scripture, second to none in his time in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, and a most acute disputant of difficult questions. He wrote many distinguished volumes by which he commended his memory to posterity, though only a few of them have come into our hands. On the Sentences, 4 books. To Nicholas of Cusa, later cardinal, he wrote a Compendium of Questions, 1 book; On Being and Essence, 1 book; [unclear].

Nicholas [Lackman?], subtle and a most acute disputant of difficult questions. He wrote many distinguished volumes; [Lackman?], subtle, also had skill in discussing a difficult question. But because he could not do this, he wrote many varied questions from the schools, 1 book; he also composed many sermons and various orations; finally, in which superfluous memorial material was present, namely: On Truth, On Faith, On Grace, On Free Will, On Predestination, On the Will of Omnipotence, On the Soul, On the Body, On the Nature of Heaven, On Creatures, On Providence, On the Resurrection, On Purgatory, On Indulgences, On Penitentiaries, [and repeated corrupt forms concerning indulgences]. He wrote on the Sentences, 4 books, of questions; volumes in which the memorial material was superfluous, namely: But because he could not do this, he wrote on many various orations composed from the schools; he also expounded many and various matters concerning sermons, which are held in esteem in the Cologne gymnasium. He flourished at the Council of Basel, sent by his university; they came into our hands, in the year of the Lord 1538, under Emperor Albert.

He wrote a Compendium of Questions, 1 book; On Being and Essence, 1 book; [unclear]. Nicholas Lackman, of the Order of Friars Minor. 4 books; On the Authority of a General Council, as it is above the pope, 1 book; various questions, subtle, and also had skill in discussing difficult questions; but because he could not do this, he wrote on many various orations composed from the schools; he also explained many and various sermons, which are held in esteem in the Cologne gymnasium. He flourished at the Council of Basel, sent by his university, where he wrote and disputed many things, in the year of the Lord 1438, under Emperor Albert.

Nicholas Lackman, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, provincial minister of Saxony, a profound doctor learned in divine Scripture, and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; renowned in intellect, [unclear] in disputation, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons. He wrote on the Sentences, 4 books, of questions; [several corrupt repetitions of the same notice about writing on the Sentences and being a celebrated declaimer of sermons]. He wrote on the Sentences, 4 books; he is also said to have composed many things, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished at the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Johannes de Schonhouia. Johannes de Schonhouia, of the Order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of Groenendaal in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, a man learned in divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, whose reading is judged very useful for devout brothers: a spiritual exhortation to his nephew, 1 book; On the Course of a Monk, 1 book; also [several corrupt repetitions of the same titles]; he published various sermons, and several letters to various persons, and many other things.

Hugo Sletflaminus. [A man] learned in divine Scriptures, a most celebrated interpreter of Bonaventure, renowned in intellect, scholastic in speech. He wrote a distinguished work on the Sentences, 4 books; also various sermons on Scripture; [unclear].

He published various sermons, several letters to various persons, and many other things. He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1520.

Hugo Sletflaminus.

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Dominic, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Alban near Trier, by nation indeed a Prussian, a learned and most devout man, lived laudably in his order for more than fifty years. He wrote certain volumes, not to be despised for devotion, in which he usefully exercised his talent. Of these I have found the following: a volume entitled The Sound of One Feasting, because he produced it in the solitude of his cell while eating and almost ruminating. Another, which he wished to entitle The Crown of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, in which he compares her life to precious stones. Likewise a third work which he wrote, he entitled The Book of Experience, in which he inserts various revelations divinely made to him. I once saw also certain little works of his, whose titles oblivion has taken from my memory. He died, not without a reputation for holiness, in the year of the Lord 1360, in the eighth indiction, on 31 December, and was buried at Trier in the common cemetery of his brethren, as he had requested.

Bartholomew, Prior of Bethlehem, Carthusian monk.

Bartholomew, a monk of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Bethlehem in the town of Roermond in Guelders, a man zealous and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and an acute, devout, and highly reputed interpreter of them, wrote for the edification of his brethren certain excellent little works, of which the following are current: Exercise of Devotion, one book; Summary of Vices, or the Destruction of Vices, a notable work, one book; On Abstinence from the Eating of Meat, one book; On the Proclamations of the Brethren in Chapter, one book; On Rash Judgment, one book; On the Oath, one book; and On the Vow, one book. The rest that he wrote have not come to my knowledge.

At length he died, after many holy exercises, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1446, in the ninth indiction, on 12 July.

John Rode, abbot of the monastery of Saint Matthew the Apostle near Trier, of the order of the divine father Benedict, born from the city of Trier, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in canon law, devout in life and conduct, who was a most celebrated restorer of regular observance; from his labor and foundation the latest Bursfelde reform of our order began in Germany. He devoted some effort to letters at the University of Heidelberg, where, becoming a bachelor of sacred theology and a most learned licentiate of canon law, he already seemed in mind and body to despise the world. For although he was a canon of the church of Metz, dean of Saint Simeon’s at Trier, and official of the court of Trier, he despised all things for the love of Christ and, having entered the order of Carthusian monks near Trier, was not long afterward unanimously elected prior. Finally, at the instance of lord Otto, archbishop of Trier, he was drawn out of the Charterhouse by apostolic mandate and appointed abbot of the aforesaid monastery; by his diligence many monasteries were reformed. He wrote, for the restoration of regular discipline, Notable Constitutions, one book; On the Governance of an Abbot, one book; and certain other things. He died in the year of the Lord 1439, in the second indiction, on the first day of September, in the twentieth year of his abbatial office, under Emperor Albert.

Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen.

Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen and cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, born in the diocese of Trier in a village by the Moselle called Cusa, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and easily the foremost theologian of his time; also exceptionally learned in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated mathematician of all; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; wholly upright in life and conduct and singularly devout; a sincere and fervent lover of the salvation of souls; a most fluent preacher of sermons; a most bitter enemy of all vices; unchangeable in constancy of mind; most patient, even in old age, of honorable labors; eloquent beyond expectation. He retained all histories in memory; in the mathematical disciplines no one in his time was more learned than he. He recited from memory civil and pontifical law and the decrees of the fathers; he was a most acute disputant in Aristotelian philosophy. Indeed he was the highest interpreter and master of Christian theology, as Johannes Aleriensis, secretary of the Apostolic Library, testifies at length in a certain place. This Nicholas, sent into his Germany as apostolic legate, did and established many useful things for the reform of the Church and of monastic religion. He wrote the following little works: On the Vision of God, one book; On the Peace of Faith, one book; On the Correction of the Calendar, one book; On Mathematical Complements, one book; A Sifting of the Alcoran, three books; On the Hunt for Wisdom, one book; On the Game of the Sphere, a mystical work, two books; Compendium, one book; Trialogue on Possest, one book; On Mathematical Perfection, one book; Against the Heresy of the Bohemians, one book; On the Gift of the Father of Lights, one book; On Seeking God, one book

156. JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS. [page 187]

…[he wrote], of which I have seen a volume which he entitled On definitive votes in a general council, in which he concludes that all who have had a place in the council ought also to have definitive votes. Item, On the authority of the pope and of the council, 1 book; also On the nature of schism, 1 book; On neutrality, 1 book; of the rest (although he wrote much) nothing has come to me. He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440, under the beginning of the reign of Frederick III.

[Johannes Gower.] Item, On the concord of the Evangelists—which work he entitled "One out of four"—1 book; sermons on the [seasons of the] year and on the saints, 2 books; also triple sermons through Lent, [several] books. But he is said to have written also several others, which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1461.

[Margin: Gerard de Stredam.] GERARD DE STREDAM, monk of the Carthusian order, Prior of the house of the Apostles near Liège, a man exercised and erudite by long study in the divine Scriptures, mild in talent and sweet in eloquence, venerable no less for conversation than for knowledge. He wrote, for the edification of [his] readers, certain illustrious volumes, of which the following are reported. To a certain abbot of our order, of the monastery of Saint Adrian of Geraldsberg, on the care…

[Johannes?] Benedicti, learned in the sacred Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, endowed with singular charm in speech, and also an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity; among their number the following are reported. Questions on the Sentences, one book. Various Questions, one book. Speeches, one book. On the Power of the Virtues, one book. On Abstinence from Meat, one book. On the Use of Flocks in God, one book. On Progress, one book, under which are contained the following. The Soliloquy of a Man to God, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Various Sermons and Speeches, one book. Various Poems or Epigrams, one book, and certain other brief works, but not unpleasing. He died in the year [unclear].

[Blank page in the source scan.]

one book. On the Summit of Theory, 1 book; On Learned Ignorance, 3 books; On Conjectures, 2 books; On the Filiation of God, 1 book; On Genesis, 1 book; Idiota, On Wisdom, 4 books; On the Squaring of the Circle, 1 book; On Fortune, [unclear] book; Directory of the Speculator, 1 book; also very fine sermons for the whole year, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book; and he published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1463, in the twelfth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of August, in the sixty-third year of his age.

Heinrich Kalteisen, by homeland a man of Koblenz, of the order of the Friars Preachers of the convent of his native city, archbishop of the churches of Nidaros and Caesarea in Norway, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, a most eloquent declaimer of sermons. He wrote certain distinguished volumes of his talent, of which the following are extant: On the Magnificat, 1 book; various questions, almost without number, disputed in the schools and elsewhere, 1 book; sermons on the season and on the saints, 2 books; sermons through Lent, 1 book. He is also said to have written on the Sentences of Master Peter Lombard a great and notable volume, which I have not yet seen, and other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1465, in the twelfth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, buried at Koblenz.

Heinrich of Gorkum, a learned doctor of sacred theology, an outstanding interpreter of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, an acute disputant, presiding from the master’s chair in the University of Cologne, by teaching, writing, and explaining earned great praise for his learning. He wrote works not to be despised in reading: Against the Hussite Heretics, 1 book; Summary of the Sayings of Saint Thomas, 1 book; sermons and various collations. He is also said to have written various questions, determinations, lectures, books, verses, and treatises, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes Kanneman, of the order of the Friars Minor, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have thought otherwise than he should have concerning ecclesiastical power, whence he provoked the talents of many against himself. When he was sought by the minister of Saxony for imprisonment, he escaped by flight and betook himself to the Observance; thereafter he amended his error together with his life. Long before, Johannes of Hagen, a most learned Carthusian monk, had reproved him and recalled him to the paths of justice. Among many writings indeed unknown to us, he also wrote the following: A Defense of His Propositions, 1 book; a very notable treatise On the Passion of the Lord; sermons on the season and on the saints, 2 books; also various letters and questions. I have found nothing about the rest. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Jacobus of Jüterbog, a monk of the Carthusian order of the house of the Savior at Erfurt, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, a very eminent interpreter of canon law, ready in intellect, clear in speech, devout in life and conduct. He is said previously to have been abbot of a certain monastery of the Cistercian order; for the hope of amendment of life he gave up the dignity of pastoral care together with the order and obtained a place on the aforesaid Mount of Saint Savior, where, made famous by writing and disputing, he gained the name of Doctor to such a degree that his words and writings were held almost as the oracle of Apollo. Among his works these are reported: On the Jubilee Year, 1 book; On the Causes of Many Passions, 1 book; On the Morals of Christians, one book; On the Threefold State of Men, 1 book; Consolation of the Evils of This Age, 1 book; On the Manner of Observing an Interdict, 1 book; Apologeticus of Religious, 1 book; On the Cautions of Diverse States, 1 book; On the Knowledge of Secret Events, 1 book; On Truth to Be Spoken or Kept Silent, 1 book; On Thoughts, 1 book; On Contracts, 1 book; On the [unclear] of This Age, 1 book; On the Obedience of Monks, one book; On the Stability of Monks, 1 book; On the Art of Dying, 1 book; On the Restraining of Thoughts, 1 book; Soliloquy of a Man to His Soul, 1 book; On the Art of Curing Vices, 1 book; On the Seven Deadly Sins, 1 book; and On Actual Sins, 1 book; On the Seven Mental Deadly Sins, 1 book; On the Power of Demons, 1 book; On the Dignity of Prelates, 1 book; On the Priesthood, 1 book; On the Observance of the Commandments, 1 book; On the State of the Safer Life, 1 book; On the Sabbath, 1 book; On the Direction of Intention, 1 book; On the Progress of the Spiritual Life, one book; On Indulgences, 1 book; On the Good Moral Remedy against Temptations, 1 book; On the Two Cities, namely Jerusalem and Babylon, 1 book; Directo-

A Directory of his order, 1 book; On the confirmation of the statutes of the Carthusian order, 1 book; On those who celebrate frequently or rarely, 1 book; A method of resisting temptations, 1 book; sermons for the season and on the saints, 1 book. He also published many other things, which have not come into our hands. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1466, in the fourteenth indiction.

Goswinus de Hex, a Brabantine by birth, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Vlissingen, bishop of [Ieropolis?], vicar in pontifical matters of the bishop of Utrecht, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and notably instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, also a very celebrated preacher of popular sermons. He wrote On the Ten Commandments, 1 book; also A Directory of a Troubled Conscience, 1 book; sermons for the season and on the saints, 2 books. But he is also said to have written several other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1475, in the eighth indiction, on the Kalends of April.

Johannes de Aurbach, priest and canon of the church of Bamberg, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an excellent doctor of decrees, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who for a long time adorned the University of Erfurt by his learning and presence, both in teaching and in writings. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity; of these I have found only the following: Judicial Process, 2 books; also On the Sacraments, 1 book. The rest that he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Henricus de Herp, of the Order of Friars Minor of the Observance, of the province of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of pontifical law, ready in intellect, clear in speech, devout in life and conduct; and among his sermons the following are extant: On the Ten Commandments, a great and distinguished volume, 1 book; On the Three Parts of Penance, 1 book; sermons for the season and on the saints, 2 books; sermons through Advent, 1 book; also sermons through Lent, 1 book. Concerning the rest, however, I have found nothing. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes de Mechilinia, trained by long study in the holy Scriptures and not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in intellect and clear in eloquence, taught the divine Scriptures with distinction for many years at the University of Cologne, and acquired great renown for his learning. He wrote On the Sentences, 4 books; On the Whole Psalter, 1 book; Various Questions Disputed in the Schools, 1 book; also sermons. Besides these he is said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Dionysius Rikel de Lebis, monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Bethlehem at Roermond in Gelderland, a man most devoted to the divine writings and thoroughly learned by continual exercise, also not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, singularly devout in life and conduct, so much so that he was even held worthy of divine revelations. He wrote so many and such great works that, in number of volumes among the Latins, apart from Augustine, he had no equal. He was accustomed to devote himself to contemplation and prayer with such fervor that he seemed never to have been able to write anything. Again, he was so continually engaged in the study of reading and writing that one would have thought he could neither pray nor contemplate. He slept very little, was admirable in abstinence from food and drink, and, after the example of Saint Jerome, judged it sweet to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, always either reading or writing something useful, so that prayer often interrupted reading, and reading continued prayer. Of the works of this most studious man I have found the following: On the Sentences, four books; On Genesis, 1 book; On Exodus, 1 book; On Leviticus, 1 book; On Numbers, 1 book; On Deuteronomy, 1 book; On Joshua, 1 book; On Judges, 1 book; On Ruth, 1 book; On Kings, 4 books; On Chronicles, 2 books; On Ezra, 3 books; On Nehemiah, 1 book; On Tobit, 1 book; On Esther, 1 book; On Judith, 1 book; On Job, 1 book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book; On Ecclesiastes, 1 book; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book; On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book; On Isaiah the Prophet, one book; On Jeremiah, 1 book; On the Book of Baruch, 1 book; On Ezekiel, 1 book; On Daniel, 1 book; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 12 books; On the Books of Maccabees [unclear].

Johannes Trithemius

[unclear], 2 books; on the Psalter, 3 books; on the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book; on Mark, one book; on Luke also, 1 book; on John, 1 book; on all the epistles of Paul, 14 books; on the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book; on the canonical epistles, 8 books; on the Apocalypse of John, one book; an exposition of hymns, 1 book; on the seven penitential psalms, 1 book; On Authentic Documents, 1 book; an exposition of the Mass, 1 book; a dialogue on the celebration of Masses, 1 book; on holy communion, one book; a Compendium of Philosophy, 1 book; a Compendium of Theology, 1 book; a dialogue between a philosopher and a theologian, 1 book; on the books of blessed Dionysius the martyr, 4 books; on eleven epistles of the same, 1 book; on the book of John Climacus, 1 book; on Boethius, On the Consolation of Philosophy, 5 books; a summary of the parts of Saint Thomas, 1 book; sermons for the seasons and on the saints, 2 books; likewise sermons for religious, for the seasons and on the saints, 2 books; six sermons on the venerable Sacrament, 1 book; an exposition of the Lord's Passion, 1 book; meditations on the Lord's Passion, 1 book; On the Praises of the Most Praiseworthy God, 1 book; On the Praises of Saint Mary, 4 books; On the Fountain of Salvation and the Paths of Life, 1 book; On the Light of Christian Theory, 1 book; On the Beauty of the World, 1 book; On the Nature of the True and Eternal God, 1 book; On the Divine Essence of Divine and Human Perfection, 1 book; On the Happiness of the Soul, 1 book; On the Benefits of God, 1 book; On the Mutual Recognition of the Saints in the Fatherland, 1 book; On the Gifts of the Holy Spirit, 1 book; The Cordial, 1 book; On the Guarding of the Heart, 1 book; On Inner Joy and Peace, 1 book; On the Purgative Way, 1 book; a dialogue on the Catholic faith, one book; a dialogue between a Christian and a Saracen, 1 book; Against Magicians and Waldensians, 1 book; Against Various Superstitions, 1 book; On Vices and Virtues, 1 book; Against Ambition, 1 book; Against the Saracens, 3 books; On the Gravity of Sin, 1 book; On Contempt of the World, 1 book; On the Method of Judging and Correcting, 1 book; On Remedies for Temptations, 1 book; The Mirror of the Sinner, 1 book; On the Four Last Things, one book; On Internal Reformation, one book; On Particular Judgment, 1 book; On the Passions of the Soul, 1 book; On the Discernment of Spirits, 1 book; On the Progress of Charity, 1 book; On the Perfection of Charity, 1 book; The Kindling of Divine Love, 1 book; On Contemplation, 1 book; On Prayer, 1 book; Meditation, 1 book. He also set down another, The Sound of One Feasting, 1 book; On the Processions that Take Place in the Church, 1 book; On the Elevation of the Mind to God, 1 book; On the Power and Authority of the Pope, 2 books; On the Authority of a General Council, 3 books; On the Reformation of the Universal Church, 1 book; Against Simony, 2 books; On the Reformation of Cloistered Religious, 1 book; Against Plurality of Benefices, 1 book; On the Rules of Life of Christians, 1 book; On the Reformation of Nuns, 1 book; On the Life of Nobles, 1 book; On the Rule of Princes, 1 book; a dialogue between Christ and a prince, 1 book; a dialogue between Christ and the wife of a prince, 1 book; On the Governance of the Polity of Cities, 1 book; a dialogue between himself and a boy, 1 book; On the Life of Widows, 1 book; On the Life of Married Persons, 1 book; On the Life of Enclosed Women, 1 book; On the Solitary Life, 1 book; On the Office of Merchants, 1 book; a dialogue between Jesus and a priest, 1 book; Against the Vice of Property among Monks, 1 book; Revelations Divinely Shown to Him, 1 book; an annotation of his works, 1 book; three collations for various chapters. He published many letters to Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal, and to various others. But he is also said to have written many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He recast the little works of John Cassian into an easier style, also for the sake of the simpler brothers. He died under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the fourth indiction, on the day of blessed Gregory, which is the twelfth of the month of March, and was buried with his brothers in the common cemetery of the aforesaid house of Roermond, not without a reputation for holiness.

Johannes de Hagen, otherwise de Indagine, a monk of the Carthusian order of the house of Mount Saint Savior at Erfurt, prior in Eisenach and in Stettin, was a man most devoted to the study of the divine Scriptures and very learned, and excellently taught in canon law; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, ready and provident in counsel, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished volumes to kings, princes, bishops, and other prelates of churches, when he was asked about various and diverse matters and questions. Of these, however, few have come into our hands, namely: On the Praise of Poverty, one book; On the Life of Religious, 1 book; On the Case of Religion, 1 book; On the Life of Young Men, one book; On Humility and Pride, one book; On Interior Adornment, 1 book; On the Approach to the New Man, 1 book; On Grace and the Free Will of Man, 1 book; On Rebuke and the Grace of God, 1 book; On Nature and Grace, 1 book; On Perseverance, 1 book; On Spirit, Body, and Soul, 1 book; On the Commands of the Prelate-

of prelates, one book; On Charity, one book; On the Love of God, one book; On the Search for the Highest Good, one book; Against the Errors of the Bohemians, one book; To the Bishop of Regensburg, Against the Same, [one?] book; To the Margrave of Brandenburg, one book; To the University of Erfurt, one book; On the Rule of our holy father Benedict, one book; On [unclear], one book; On Knowledge of Future Things, one book; On the Vision of Tundal, What Should Be Thought of It, one book; On the Vision of Daniel, chapter seven, one book; On the Apparition of a Certain Deceased Woman, one book; On Future Prodigies, one book; The Lament of [unclear], one book; On the Crusade against Heretics, one book; On the Removal of the Bridegroom from the Church, one book; On the Time of Schism, one book; On the Authority of the Pope in a General Council, one book; On Ecclesiastical Power, one book; What Is to Be Held concerning Little Children Dying Unbaptized, one book; On a Judge Judging against Conscience, one book; Against the Heretical Flagellants, one book; On Whether Someone Is to Be Considered a Religious without Profession, one book; On the Fast of the Fifth Feria, one book; On Just and Unjust War, one book; On the Teaching of the Church, one book; On Hearing Mysteries, one book; Against Brother Johannes Kanneman of the Order of Minors, one book; On the Spiritual Life, one book; On the Discernment of Thoughts, one book; On True and False Penitence, one book; On the Manner of Confessing, one book; On Hearing Confessions, one book; On the Spiritual Art of Memory, one book; On the Four Senses of Sacred Scripture, one book; On Contemplation, one book; On the Interdict, one book; To Rudolph, Bishop of Lavant, one book; On False Prophets, one book; On Communion under Both Kinds, one book; five sermons At the Dedication of a Church. Many sermons On the Season and On the Saints, two books; On the Books of Kings according to the Fourfold Sense of Sacred Scripture, two books; Letters to Various Persons, one book. Finally, he composed useful commentaries on many books of the Bible, which have by no means come into our hands, but also more than three hundred other treatises on various questions.

... is said to have written on sacred matters, on logic, and on philosophy, works which have not yet at all come to my knowledge. He flourished at Erfurt under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Sifridus of Mainz, of the order of Friars Preachers, titular bishop of Cyrene, vicar in pontificals of the archbishop of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, skilled in the Hebrew language, an acute disputant, and an outstanding preacher of the divine word. He wrote to Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, On the Usury of the Jews, one book; On Taxes and Redemptions, one book; various questions; also many sermons and certain orations to the clergy. And certain other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1473, in the sixth indiction, on the sixteenth day of the month of May. He was buried in his convent at Mainz.

Godescalcus Gresemundus of Meschede, a Westphalian by country, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, sharp in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct, a profound doctor of sacred theology, who taught it gloriously for many years in the gymnasium of Erfurt. He wrote notable questions on the Sentences, four books; moreover various questions disputed in the schools, one book; many sermons and diverse conferences. And certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480. And almost ten years before this he died.

Stephanus Hoest of Ladenburg, priest and canon of the church of Speyer and preacher of the word of God in the castle of Heidelberg, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, excellent in verse and prose, acute in intellect, composed in speech, in delivering sermons to the people no less learned than eloquent. He wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, of which, however, few have come to my knowledge. For I found a distinguished volume on the new translation of Aristotle’s Ethics, ten books; various sermons and orations to the people, clergy, and princes. And certain epigrams. Concerning the rest I have as yet found nothing. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the fourth indiction.

Heinrich of Cologne, called de Piro, namely from his father’s house, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man rather studious in the divine Scriptures and, before his entrance into religion, a subtle doctor of both laws and very celebrated in reputation. He wrote and lectured in that faculty many distinguished volumes, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Yet few have come into our hands, namely a notable work on the Institutes, four books; To Novices on Internal Reform, one book; various counsels in diverse cases; quite a number of sermons on the season and on the saints. Concerning the rest nothing is known to me. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Nicolaus Donis, monk of the order of the divine father Benedict, of the monastery, as they say, of Reichenbach, a man certainly studious and learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher and astronomer, a most vigilant discoverer and most diligent restorer of the Cosmography of Ptolemy, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence. He wrote volumes not to be contemned, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there survives a marvelous and very celebrated work, most elegantly arranged with pictures and new tables, on the Cosmography of Ptolemy, addressed to Pope Paul II, four books; also On Wondrous Places, one book; he also composed letters, and many, in my judgment not inelegant, to various persons. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Georgius of Peuerbach, most skilled in the knowledge of secular letters and not ignorant of the holy Scriptures, the philosopher and astronomer easily the most learned of all in his time, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, who in the gymnasium of Vienna for a long time publicly taught philosophy and the science of the stars, where, among countless other pupils, he instructed Johannes of Regiomontanus, a most learned man. He wrote New Theories of the Planets, one book, and several other works on astronomy, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1480.

Johannes Tinctoris of Cologne Agrippina, a man rather studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, an acute disputant, publicly taught sacred letters for many years in the gymnasium of Cologne, and [unclear] the praises of learning

163 acquired great praises. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity; and, first of all, he indeed strove to reconcile the disagreements of Thomas and John Scotus in one volume, which, overtaken by death, he did not complete. He also wrote notable questions on the Sentences, [unclear] book; sermons to the people; various orations to the clergy; and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes de Beetz.

He acquired great praises. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity; and, first of all, he indeed strove to reconcile the disagreements of Thomas and John Scotus in one volume, which, overtaken by death, he did not complete. He also wrote notable questions on the Sentences, [unclear] book; sermons to the people; various orations to the clergy; and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes de Beetz.

Johannes de Beetz, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Tienen, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and most skilled in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and devout also in life and conduct, teaches as a declaimer of popular sermons no less than as an eloquent man. He wrote On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book; also On the Precepts of the Divine Law, ten books; On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book; Various Questions Disputed in the Schools, one book; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; Sermons on the Season and on the Saints, two books. Finally he published many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Frederick III, Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the ninth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of [unclear].

  1. And he died a few years ago.

Arnoldus de Busco.

Arnoldus de Busco, canon regular of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of Windesheim in the diocese of Utrecht, for some time prior in Sulta in Saxony, in the diocese of Hildesheim, a man studious in the holy scriptures, of honorable morals and devout conduct. He wrote, in a plain style, little works not to be despised, the reading of which is judged useful for devout brothers who love their salvation. Of these, however, I recall that few have come into our hands. I have read that volume which he wrote On the Lives of the Illustrious Men of his Order, of the Monastery of Windesheim, one book; also On the Origin of the Modern Devotion and the Reform of his Order, [unclear] book; a lengthy letter On the Manner of Making Progress in Religion. The other things which he wrote have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1470. And he died a few years ago.

Rudolphus de Rudesheim.

Rudolphus de Rudesheim, a Rhenish countryman from the diocese of [unclear], first dean of Worms and afterward bishop of Wroclaw, doctor of sacred letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, honorable in life and conduct, flourished gloriously for many years in the academy of Heidelberg, both by reading and by teaching. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which the following are extant: On Genesis, one book; On Exodus, one book; on Leviticus, one book; also on Numbers, one book; on Deuteronomy, one book; on Joseph, one book; on Judges, one book; on the prophet Isaiah, [unclear] book; on the Sentences, four books; many various sermons on the Season and on the Saints, one book. He also delivered several orations, which it would be too long to describe one by one. But he published some other things, still quite unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes de Regiomonte, once a disciple of the astronomer Georgius Burbachius, a man most learned in every respect, no less than Anaximander of Miletus or Archimedes of Syracuse, most learned in Greek and Latin eloquence, the glory of the Germans, on account of astronomy and the other mathematical disciplines endowed by Matthias, king of Pannonia, with a consulship and perpetual stipend among the citizens of Nuremberg, attained great praise for his learning not only among our Germans but also among the Italians and the French. For, summoned to Rome by Pope Sixtus IV to correct the Paschal computation of Dionysius, while he was preparing many things for posterity, he died of disease or plague, not without the very great loss of students. He wrote a very fine Calendar with [unclear], [unclear] book; likewise Ephemerides on the disposition of the heavens for individual days over certain years, one book; Against Gerardus Cremonensis, one book; various orations; many letters to different persons; for Lord Johannes, archbishop of Esztergom, Tables of Directions and Profections, useful in nativities, one book; also Tables of the Right Sine, one book; On the Composition of the Astrolabe, one book. Also other things

Gerardus de Elten, of the order of the brothers preachers, of the convent of Cologne, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and exceptionally skilled in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, acute as a disputant, who, after he had publicly taught theology for many years in the academy of Cologne, not without great praise from all, despised the world and, already an old man, put on the monastic habit, not without the admiration of many. He wrote, as is reported, Questions on the Sentences, one book; also other various questions disputed in the schools; sermons to the people; several orations to the clergy. And he is said to have written certain other things, [unclear]

Gerardus de Elten.

[Of] Johannes Trithemius

[unclear] studious and learned, an outstanding lover of regular discipline, devout in life and conduct. He wrote, in a clear and plain style, certain little works not to be despised for the edification of his brethren, with which he usefully occupied his talent. Of these he once showed me: On the Spiritual Vineyard, a work not to be rejected, one book; likewise On the Fuller Instruction of Novices, one book. He also wrote certain other small but useful exercises for religious, which have not yet come to the knowledge of my reading. He died old and full of days and good works, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1485.

Heinrich Arnoldi, a Saxon by nation, by profession a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Basel, a man devout in religion, distinguished in talent, sincere in affection, grave in character, sweet in speech, affable in conduct, pious, humble, gentle, bright in example, very much exercised in sacred letters, and not ignorant of pontifical law. When he held the office of notary for many years in the holy Council of Basel, he was approved by the testimony of all as faithful, just, and prudent. At length, seeing that all things are vanity, having chosen all things for the love of Christ, he governed the monks subject to him for many years in great peace and tranquillity. He wrote many very devout and wholesome little works, among which the following are reported: Many Prayers on Various Saints, one book. Also Many Sermons, one book. Histories of Many Saints, one book. The Passion of the Lord Harmonized from the Four, one book. Meditations on the Life of Christ, one book. On the Immaculate Conception of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, one book. On the Instruction of Novices, one book. Dialogue between Jesus and Mary, one book. Dialogue between Saint Margaret and Her Little Servant on Spiritual Exercises, one book. Another Dialogue between the Same on the Cross, one book. On the Commendation of Charity, one book. On Holy Humility in the Form of a Prayer, one book. Again, On Humility, one book. Chronicle of His Carthusian House in Basel, one book; and certain other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1487, in the fifth indiction.

Jodocus Eichman of Calw, born in a village of Swabia, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and also not moderately instructed in secular philosophy, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, was held in esteem for many years in the Heidelberg gymnasium by reading, teaching, and preaching. There also, according to custom, he held for some time the office of preacher in the church of the Holy Spirit. He wrote certain treatises, as they say, not to be rejected, but they have not come to the knowledge of my reading. There are extant many learned sermons of his, two books. Also various disputed questions. Also some orations to the fathers. He also wrote A Vocabulary for Preachers, one book, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1485, and died under Pope Innocent.

Heinrich of Gelnhausen, a monk of our monastery in Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, bachelor of the Erfurt gymnasium, and once rector of scholars in his native town, a man learned in secular philosophy, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, with which he occupied his talent usefully enough. To the novices of the monastery of Porta Mariae of the Order of Saint William he wrote a long and learned letter On Spiritual Progress and Instruction, one book. The Life of Saint Benedict the Abbot in elegiac verse, one book. Sermons on the Temporale and on the Saints, one book. Against the Plurality of Benefices, one book. And certain letters to various persons. He died under Emperor Frederick III, at the age of fifty, in the year of the Lord 1488, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, buried in the southern part of the cloister.

Peter le Kyrslaken, of the order of the Friars Preachers, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, a famous declaimer of sermons. He wrote to the bishop of the church of Regensburg in Bavaria a treatise against the faithless Jews On the Conditions of the True Messiah, that is, Christ. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Philipp Kersbeele, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, philosopher and theologian, [wrote?] against Vincent of Newcastle, of the order of Preachers, who was barking against the most pure conception of the divine Virgin Mary, which Carolus Fernandus, a monk of the divine order of Benedict in France, reshaped into a more elegant style. He died while studying at Paris almost three years ago,

Nico-

Of Johannes Trithemius unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

JOHANNES of the little village of Lutra, called de Lutrea, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned and excellently taught in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, honorable in life and conduct, singularly devout, a lover of virtues, an enemy of vices, a most steadfast despiser of greed, who abhorred plurality of benefices and scorned the title of a bishopric offered to him, first taught theology gloriously for many years in the school of Erfurt, and afterward vigorously performed the office of preacher in the church of Mainz. He wrote On the Sentences, four books; also various Questions; Sermons on the season and on the saints, two books; and certain other things unknown to us. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction.

ALANUS de Rupe, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of most excellent reputation in declaiming sermons to the people, devoted to God in life and conduct, a special lover of blessed Mary ever virgin, and a venerable [unclear] promoter of her Rosary, deserved to be refreshed by a very singular gift of heavenly consolation, and, as they say, to be honored with frequent revelations and miracles. He wrote, among other little works of his talent: A Compendium of the Psalter of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, one book; also On the Miracles of the Rosary of the same glorious Virgin, one book; many various Sermons, one book; On the Fraternity of the Rosary, one book; and many other things. He died in his convent of Zwolle, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the seventh indiction, on the vigil of the Assumption of Mary.

CONRADUS de Zabernia, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, an excellent musician, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, honorable in life and conduct. He wrote in plain speech certain little works not to be rejected, by which, exercising his talent usefully and fruitfully, he also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: On the Monochord, one book; On the Manner of Singing Well, one book; On the Conclusions of the Collects, one book; many various Sermons, one book. The rest that he composed have not at all come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1475, under whom he died.

JOHANNES de Dorfftein, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, of the convent of Erfurt, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, sufficiently suited to disputing and resolving difficult questions of the Scriptures, and also of excellent eloquence in declaiming sermons to the people. In the school of Erfurt he excelled in teaching and preaching. He wrote little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: Questions on the Sentences, one book; On the Vice of the Tongue, one book; Sermons on the season and on the saints, two books; and certain other things. He flourished at Erfurt under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1475.

THEODERICUS de Herxen, visitor and rector of the congregation of the Brethren Clerics Living in Common, a devout man, zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech. He wrote for the edification of his brethren many excellent little works, by which, exercising his talent usefully enough, he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Whole Psalter, three books; On the Lord’s Prayer, one book; On the Angelic Salutation, one book; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; also On the Desire of Dying, one book; several Sermons to the brothers, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

ANGELUS de Brunsuco, a Saxon, who was commonly called Master Engelinus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, eloquent in declaiming sermons to the people, who shone out very brightly in teaching and lecturing in the school of Erfurt. He wrote a notable work On the Canon of the Mass, which he is said to have read at Mainz before the clergy; many various Sermons, one book. He also disputed diverse Questions in the schools, and certain other things. He died at Strasbourg and was buried in the monastery of the penitents, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the thirteenth indiction.

CRODENBERG, abbot of the monastery of Mount Saint John the Baptist of Rheingau, in the diocese of Mainz, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a devout and learned man, a most upright guardian and lover of the newly introduced regular observance, one of those who by our reformation

Johannes Trithemius not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, venerable no less for the integrity of his life than for his learning. He wrote several excellent little works, by which, usefully occupying his talent, he commended his memory to posterity. Of these, in the aforesaid gymnasium at Erfurt, he is said to have lectured in ordinary course: On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. He delivered various orations in praise of Saint Jerome. He is said to have written many sermons and diverse questions, together with certain other things, which have as yet by no means come into our hands. He died in the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt, where he was buried, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493, indiction 12.

Johannes Frytag of Dufeldorp, a town of the diocese of Cologne, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Mainz and prior of Strasbourg, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, a doctor of Cologne, sharp and forceful in intellect, no less eloquent than learned in delivering sermons to the people, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover of regular discipline. He wrote: On the Observance of Feast Days, 1 book; On the Places of the Holy Land, which he traversed with his own feet and saw with his eyes, 1 book; various sermons on the season and on the saints, 2 books; and many other things. He died under Maximilian, Emperor, in the year of the Lord [1494?], indiction 12, and was buried at Strasbourg.

Sebastian Murrho of Colmar, priest and canon in Colmar, the town of his birth, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, orator, poet, and astronomer-cosmographer of very celebrated reputation, distinguished in knowledge of laws and canons, most skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole Quadrivium, subtle in intellect, rich in eloquence, mature in life and conduct. He wrote to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat a brief indeed, but very fine, epitome on the history and praises of the German princes and peoples, 1 book; also many most elegant poems, 1 book; also many letters to various people, 1 book; and various orations. He began commentaries on Baptista Mantuanus the Carmelite, but, overtaken by death, did not bring them forth. Conrad Leontorius, monk of Maulbronn, undertook to finish them and will shortly permit them to be printed. He died, to the very great loss of scholars, carried off by plague, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13.

Rudolf Langius, canon of the church of Münster in Westphalia, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a distinguished orator and poet, subtle in intellect, rich in eloquence. He wrote many excellent little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he made himself useful to those present and memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported: To the Dean of the Church of Cologne, a book of diverse poems, 1 book; On the Siege of the Town of Neuss by Charles, Duke of Burgundy, 1 book; On the Three Kings, a Sapphic poem; On the Praises of Albert the Great, a poem; many poems; various letters to various people; and certain other things unknown to us. I hear that he is still living, an old man, although there are some who say that he departed this life in this year of the Lord 1495.

Jacob de Stralen, priest of the church of Cologne, a man learned by long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who once for some time held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many little works indeed worthy of commendation, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he is said to have read some publicly in the gymnasium at Erfurt: On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book; On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; Itinerary of the Holy Land, 1 book; various questions disputed in the schools, 1 book; many sermons; and several other things. He is still living in [unclear].

Wilhelm of Aachen, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, excellent in life and conduct, who once for some time held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many little works indeed worthy of commendation, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he is said to have read some publicly in the gymnasium at Erfurt: On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book; On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; Itinerary of the Holy Land, 1 book; various questions disputed in the schools, 1 book; many sermons; and several other things. He is still living in [unclear].

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[unclear] laid the foundations for the Bursfeld reform. Since he was an outstanding lover of blessed Mary ever virgin, he wrote in her honor, in plain discourse, a very celebrated volume, taking the material of praise from each of her members under the figure of a cluster of grapes; he entitled it On the Vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, one book. The Exercise of Novices, one book. On the Preparation of the Priest for Mass, one book. He delivered various addresses in our chapters, one of which begins: “The crown of our head has fallen”; another: “Catch us the little foxes”; a third: “Blessed is the servant,” etc. He also composed various sermons for the brothers, which are partly extant and partly have been lost through negligence. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Innocent VIII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. He was buried in the right apse of the choir toward the south side, before the altar of the holy father Benedict.

Georgius Molitoris of Neuenburg, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned, and not moderately instructed in scholastic philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; subtle and acute in intellect, honorable in life and conduct. In the school of Erfurt he taught theological science gloriously for not a few years. He wrote On the Sentences, three books; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; also many sermons and various questions. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1490, in the second indiction.

Nicolaus of Wachenheim, doctor of Heidelberg, skilled in the holy Scriptures through long and sustained practice, an acute interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, mature in life and conduct. In the school of Heidelberg, for almost fifty years, in teaching, lecturing, and writing, he was held in the highest esteem as a prince among theologians. He wrote works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity; of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. He flourished at Heidelberg under Frederick III, emperor. Questions on the Sentences, one book. Several sermons; speeches not useless to the clergy, [unclear]. He died at Heidelberg under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1480, a very old man, under Sixtus IV, pope; he died almost [seven years?] before this.

Heinrich, surnamed Prudent, a monk of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the Valley near Bruges in Flanders, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in intellect, devout in life and conduct, singularly devoted to God. For the instruction of religious he wrote several devout little works, by which he commended his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a very celebrated work, especially suited to devotion, which he entitled Tetralogue of Devotion, three books. He also wrote many devout letters to various persons, and many other things not yet seen by me. He died in the new house of Saint Sophia of Constantinople near ’s-Hertogenbosch, in which he held the office of prior for some years, under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the second indiction.

Rudolphus Agricola of Groningen, a Frisian by birth, a man the most learned of all in secular letters in his time, not ignorant of divine letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech; formerly the teacher of Johann Dalberg, bishop of Worms, a man equally most learned. In the school of Heidelberg, by teaching and writing, he easily held first place in Latin. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have found the following: a heroic poem On Saint Anne, one book; Life of Francis the Patriarch, one book; also a very subtle Dialectic, three books; also many letters to various persons, several poems and epigrams, and various treatises. He composed an epitaph of this kind: “Envious fates have shut beneath this marble Rudolph Agricola, the hope and glory of Frisian soil; in this one man, namely, Germany earned whatever praise Latium has, whatever Greece has.” He was buried at Heidelberg in the convent of the Friars Minor.

Thilmann, prior or provost of the monastery of Saint Christopher at Ravengiersburg, at the edge of the diocese of Mainz toward Trier, in the place that from antiquity was called the retreat of the Huns, of the order of regular canons of Saint Augustine, a man in the divine Scriptures

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Nicolaus of Crutzenach, from a town of the county of Spanheim, in the diocese of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life, an acute disputant and an excellent preacher of sermons, taught theology publicly for many years in the university of Vienna. Both among the scholars there and before Emperor Frederick III he won great [unclear] and profit from his learning. He wrote certain distinguished volumes of his talent, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books; On the Most Pure Conception of the Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, one book; Sermons on the Season and on the Saints, two books; many orations to [unclear]; various questions disputed in the schools; and certain other works unknown to us. He died at Vienna in Austria, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Petrus Schot of Strasbourg, priest and canon of Saint Peter in Strasbourg, a man whose intellect was practiced in the divine Scriptures, most learned in both laws, and very learned in the other arts of humanity, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, excellent in intellect, mature, honorable, and distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote certain beautiful little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. On Saints John the Baptist, the Evangelist, and Chrysostom, he wrote a learned and delightful work in elegiac verse, one book; Diverse Poems, two books; Letters to Various Persons, one book; Brief praises of Andrew the Apostle in verse; Praises of John Gerson. Before the first [unclear] in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Petrus Schot of Strasbourg.

[unclear] a part of his works printed. He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1492, in the ninth indiction, in the thirty-first year of his age. He was buried at Strasbourg in his church of Saint Peter; Jacob Wimpheling described his life, character, and intellect.

Nicasius of Voerda, by nation a Brabanter, having been deprived of his eyes from the third year of his life by the bitterness of measles, was made entirely blind, and for that reason utterly ignorant even of all letters. As if a second great miracle, in our time he showed himself a Didymus of Alexandria, since he appeared most learned in every doctrine and science, both divine and human. For in the university of Cologne, where he died, [unclear].

[unclear] delightful works in elegiac verse, two books; Diverse Poems, three books; Letters to Various Persons, five books; Brief praises of Andrew the Apostle in verse; Praises of John Gerson. Before the first [unclear] in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Nicasius of Voerda.

He recited [unclear] from memory. In the University of Louvain he first received the degree of master in arts; afterward he directed schools for some time in Mechelen; then, having returned to Louvain, he was appointed licentiate in sacred theology. He does not celebrate the divine rites by himself at the altar. Finally, using his memory as a book, he recites. [unclear] through the age, he was made doctor of canon law by the consent of all the doctors in the Cologne Academy, and at Cologne was a cautious interpreter of imperial laws. He published a very celebrated work which he read extraordinarily in that same University of Cologne, with more than one hundred students taking it down by the pen: On the Institutes, four books. Likewise at Louvain he published On the Sentences, four books. He disputed various questions in the schools, which are partly extant and partly have been taken away. He also gave many sermons to the people. He gave me several rather elegant letters, in one of which, quite full, he wove together the whole story of his fortune, when questioned by me; [unclear] that he had made little works, he was humble. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the tenth indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, at Cologne, in [unclear].

Third, in the year of the Lord 1590. For there was an error about him in [unclear]. He was buried in the church of Saint Columba, not in the major church. For there was an error about him in the Catalogue of Writers.

Johannes Pheffer of Widenberg, by nation an East Frank, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long study, excellently taught in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, devout, gentle, and distinguished in life and conduct. Sent from the University of Heidelberg, he illuminated the beginning of the university of Freiburg by his learning; there he taught sacred letters for many years with great glory, and thoroughly instructed many of his hearers. He wrote an outstanding volume on the Epistles of Paul, which, when read publicly, he entitled; Priestly Directory, thirteen books; also Questions on the Sentences, one book; sermons; and various treatises on the Scriptures, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III in the year of the Lord 1490. And he died almost two years before this.

Johannes of Mylbach, doctor of Erfurt, learned in the holy Scriptures, and [unclear].

Johannes of Mylbach.

Nicolaus of Crutzenach.

Johannes Pheffer of Widenberg.

Johannes of Mylbach.

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

in good old age under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Gabriel Biel, of the order of clerics living in common, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, distinguished in talent, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct, presided for many years over the school of Tübingen from the beginning of its foundation, where he trained notable pupils both in philosophy and in sacred letters. He wrote certain works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Among these, in the aforesaid academy, he ordinarily lectured on the Canon of the Mass, a large and very beautiful volume, one book. He also wrote On the Passion of the Lord, ten books; also many sermons, [unclear] book[s]. He is now said to be writing on the Sentences, a singular and useful work, which he now lectures to his pupils. He is also said to have written several other things, which have not come to our knowledge. He is still living, nearly seventy years old, and persists vigorously in the study he has undertaken, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction XIII.

Johannes de Lapide, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the Basel house, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, who formerly, in the school of Paris, obtained the mastership in the faculty of arts, governed there for several years, and, diligently pursuing the study of sacred letters by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, deserved to be adorned with the dignity of doctor in the school of theologians. He first transferred to the university of Basel the teaching of those Parisians who are called Realists, and there planted, strengthened, and enlarged it. He was also one of the principal founders of the Tübingen school. Finally, after the free resignation of several benefices, he was called to the canonry and office of preaching of the distinguished church of Basel; and at length, after a few years had passed, leaving all things for the love of Christ, he assumed the habit of the sacred Carthusian order. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made himself memorable as one who would be useful to those now living and to those to come; yet only a few of these have come into our possession. An Introduction to Grammar, one book. A Dialogue on the Art of Punctuation, [unclear] book[s]. On Expoundable Propositions, one book. On the Art of Solving Sophistical Arguments, one book. An Explanation of All the Books of Aristotle’s Logic, ten books. An Explanation of the Books of the Physics, [unclear] and one book. On Those Things Which Pertain to a Worthy Priest, one book. A Resolutory Work on Doubtful Dangers Occurring around the Mass, one book. A Summary of the Passion of the Lord, [unclear] book[s]. On the Ascension of the Lord, among the sermons of Meffret, one sermon. Likewise among his sermons he wrote a treatise, one book. And many other things unknown to us. Moreover, he divided the books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which the intention [unclear]. Always of the Virgin, not less holily than learnedly, stopping the mouth of those who speak wicked things. This treatise, with the aforesaid sermons, will be found printed in most copies. He also wrote several sermons both to the clergy and to the people, one book; also various prayers and letters, one book; and many other things unknown to us. Moreover, he divided many books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which their intentions may be clearly recognized. Among these are Cicero’s books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, and On the Dream of Scipio; likewise Aristotle’s books of Logic, the same author’s books On the Soul, and the books of the Metaphysics; likewise the books of blessed Ephrem the deacon, of John Chrysostom, and of Augustine, the same author’s book of letters, almost all the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop, and many others. He is still living in good old age in the Basel Charterhouse, composes various works, and by his writings and example summons many to holy studies. Under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we have written this, 1495, indiction XIII.

Conrad, called Hensel, by country a Hessian, pastor and rector of the church of Frankfurt, doctor of sacred theology and canon law, a very celebrated interpreter, most subtle in talent, composed in speech, who first, after absorbing letters in the school of Erfurt, publicly taught philosophy for some time, then in the school of Greifswald, and, having obtained the church of the imperial city of Frankfurt, vigorously governs to this day, and has for many years governed, by word and example the common people committed to him. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant. On the Sentences, [unclear] book[s]. Also On the Canonical Epistles, seven books. On the Song of Songs, one book. On Penance, Fasting, and Prayer, one book. On Faith, Hope, and Charity, one book. On the Four Virtues Which They Call Cardinal, one book. On the Sanctification of the Sabbath, one book. On the Gospels and Sunday Epistles through the cycle of the year, one book. Many various sermons, one book. Also On the Precepts of the Church and Evangelical Truth, one book.
