Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, a man very venerable in morals, life, and doctrine, suffered many injuries from the Arians for the faith of Christ. For, through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, after being banished from the synod of Beziers to Phrygia, for four years he bore hard exile with a constant spirit, where by his prayers he is read to have called a dead man back to life. Since he was a man most learned in every respect, he composed many short works. Of their number the following are reported.

Against Dioscorus, one book. Against Valens and Ursacius, one book.

On the Holy Trinity against the Arians, two books, “As I look around...”

One book, “God who everywhere...”

Defense of the Catholic Faith, one book, “To the most beloved brothers...”

One book, “The degree which Matthew...”

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book.

To the Emperor Constantius, three books, “Now is the time to speak...”

One book, On the Book of Job.

One book, “To the most blessed and glorious...”

One book, On the Song of Songs, one book.

Mysteries, four books. Letters to various persons, one book.

One book, On the Canonical [unclear] concerning fasts and abstinence.

Against Auxentius, one book, [unclear]. “In the first sermon...”

On Heresies, one book, [unclear]. “Logos, or...” etc.

Chronicle, one book, [unclear]. “He lives and [unclear]...”

Two books, [unclear]. “Be present, true light...”

He also published some other works, which have not come into our hands. At length, having returned to his city from his exile, he died under the emperor Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 371, in the fourteenth indiction; his feast is celebrated on the Ides of January.

Victorinus the African, a man of consular rank, the most celebrated rhetorician of all in his time, taught rhetoric for a long time in the city of Rome under the emperor Constantine; there, because of the excellence of his learning, he earned a bronze statue in the Forum of Trajan. Converted to the faith of Christ in his old age, he published many treatises on the holy Scriptures in a dialectical manner, obscure enough and scarcely accessible even to the most learned men. Of these the following are extant.

Against the Arians, two books, [unclear]. “In the first sermon...”

On the Holy Trinity, one book, [unclear]. “Homoiotypos...”

Against the heretics, one book, [unclear]. “He lives and [unclear]...”

On the homoousion also, one book, [unclear]. “Be present, true light...”

On the letters of the apostle Paul, four books, [unclear].

And certain other things.

He was distinguished at Rome under the emperor Constantine, in the second year, 360.

Titus, bishop of Bostra, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, sharp and vehement in talent, is said to have fashioned many short works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported.

Two books. Commentaries on the Gospel, one book.

Against the Manichaeans. And many other works besides.

He was distinguished in the year of the Lord 349, and died under the emperor Valens.

Damasus, pope, a Spaniard by nation, sat after Liberius in the chair of Peter for eighteen years; a man most learned in divine matters and excellently instructed in secular letters, a rhetorician and most celebrated poet, and most skilled in composing verses, subtle in talent,

life

Abbot of Spanheim.

...devout and most holy in life, a very great lover of the blessed priest Jerome. He wrote various little works in both kinds. Of these the following are extant.

The deeds of the supreme pontiffs, 1 book. “The blessed apostle Peter...” On the faith, against heretics, 1 book. “Since after the Nicene council...” Letters to various persons, 1 book. “Bishop Damasus...” Various poems. And other works.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and by far most learned in grammatical training, sharp and forceful in talent, distinguished in speech, wrote certain notable volumes in defense of the Catholic faith; among them there is extant the very celebrated work:

Against the mad Porphyry, 30 books. And certain other works.

He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Didymus of Alexandria, deprived of his eyes from early childhood, and for this reason wholly ignorant even of the elements, displayed so great a miracle of himself that he perfectly learned dialectic and geometry, which especially require sight. In the divine Scriptures he was very learned, the teacher of the blessed Jerome and a very close friend of Saint Antony, sharp in talent, distinguished in life. He wrote the following works in Greek:

Against the Arians, 2 books. Also On Doctrines, 1 book. On the canonical epistles, 7 books. “James, etc. [unclear]...” On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. “All indeed which are divine...” On the books of Saint Job, 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet, 10 books. [unclear], 3 books. On Zechariah, to the same, 5 books. On Hosea, to Jerome, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Also On the Psalter, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished as an octogenarian under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 395.

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, an African by nation, a man learned in the study of the divine writings, outstanding in talent, devout in life, a Catholic, is said to have written certain notable little works in defense of our faith, in which he magnificently exercised his abundant talent. Among these there is said to be extant a great and distinguished volume which he wrote:

Against the Donatists, 6 books. And several letters. And many other works.

He flourished under the rulers Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a learned and most holy man, had such authority among the Greeks that no one, however slightly learned, ever dared to contradict his teaching or writings in any matter. He wrote many notable little works in Greek, but few of them have come into our hands.

On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. Against Eunomius, 9 books. “In the beginning, etc. [unclear]...” A rule for monks, 1 book. “The human race...” An exhortation for monks, 1 book. “Hear, my son, the admonition...” On the education of boys, 2 books. “Indeed of God, without [unclear]...” On faith, 1 book. “Every scripture [unclear] by divine...” Several homilies, 4 books. “It is time to cry out...”

In addition he composed other treatises, sermons, and letters to various persons.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year 380.

Ephrem the monk, a distinguished inhabitant of the desert, deacon of the church of Edessa, ordained priest by the blessed Basil, because of humility never approached to perform the divine mysteries, although before God and men he was considered worthy. Nevertheless, so far as belonged to his office, in admonishing the people he delivered innumerable homilies. This man, as is read in the Lives of the Holy Fathers, was seen by an angel to have received a book written in golden letters; from this, soon on the next day and thereafter, with the Holy Spirit speaking in him, he had so great a grace of declaiming that he found no one like himself in his time. He wrote in the Syrian language

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] certain little works for the instruction of readers. Of these the following are found among the Latins, namely:

On the Holy Spirit, book 1. “Grief compels me.” On Compunction of Heart, book 1. “Come, dearest beloved.” On Contrition of Heart, book 1. “Our Lord Jesus Christ.” On Penitence, book 1. “In the struggles of this...” On the Struggles of the Age, book 1. “Come, most beloved.” On the Day of Judgment, book 1. “Glory to almighty God.” On the Resurrection, book 1. “Blessed is he who has hated...” On the Blessedness of the Soul, homily 1. “In the holy Scriptures.” On Thoughts, homily 1. “As often as, brothers...” On Severe Preaching, homily 1. “I ask you, brothers.” On the Celebration of the Mysteries, book 1. A Lament over the City of Edessa.

He also published not a few other works, especially sermons and homilies to the people, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, a very close friend of blessed Basil, as you will be able to find in his legend. In the year 380.

Book 1. “I understand man from the soul...”

Gregory, bishop of Emesa, brother of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, stirred also by his brother’s zeal, himself wrote several little works in Greek. Of these, among our writers, I have found only:

On the Image and Condition of Man, book 1. Against Eunomius, 2 books.

He flourished, younger than his brother, under the princes Valentinian and Valens; he composed various works. In the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, formerly a monk, bishop of Nazianzus, a man of such learning, integrity, and eloquence that not even his adversaries dared in any way to contradict what was said by him, so that, for the confirmation of authority, it sufficed merely to say that Gregory had said something. He was a cultivator and lover of the monastic life; when, because of the excellence of his teaching and the holiness of his life, he was called to the episcopate, he fled and hid himself, preferring to be abject in the house of the Lord than to be exalted in a crowd by fleeting honors. But almighty God did not wish so bright a radiance to be hidden under the bushel of the aforesaid way of life, since it could be extended to the salvation of many. Found therefore by divine indication, he was led by the people to the episcopal see, and immediately, in excuse for his flight, a solemn homily was delivered, in which the government of souls is shown to be the art of arts. On account of his distinguished learning and holiness of life he was called Gregory the Great before the blessed pope of the same name. He wrote many little works in Greek. Of these the following are extant:

Book 1. On the Praise of Maximus the Philosopher, book 1. Against the Same, in Reproach, book 1. On the Death of His Brother Caesarius, book 1. On Virginity, in hexameter. On the Praise of Cyprian the Martyr, book 1. “I have been overcome, I confess.” On the Holy Spirit, 2 books. “Christ, being born, [unclear] glory...” Apologetics, When He Had Fled, book 1. “Again Jesus [unclear].” On the Nativity of the Lord, book 1. “I was longing for you.” On the Second Epiphanies, book 1. “My belly grieves me.” On the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost, book 1. “Our tongue alone...” On Himself, Returned from the Country, book 1. “What praiseworthy thing alone...” On Jeremiah, with the Emperor Present, book 1. Against Julian the Apostate, book 1. On the Reconciliation of a Monk, book 1. On the Devastation by Hail. Against Eunomius.

He published several sermons and homilies, and various treatises on diverse subjects, which have not come to my knowledge. At length, worn out by old age, when he saw that he could no longer be equal to the government of the people, after another bishop had been ordained in his place, he returned to the pursuit of the solitude he had left behind.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius. In the year of the Lord 390.

Eutropius, monk and priest, a man of a very religious manner of life, in the divine

ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.

very devoted to and learned in [unclear] scriptures, and fully instructed in secular letters, he is said to have composed several little works. Of these the following alone are extant for us, known by title:

To two virgins, sisters, 2 books. Of Chronicles down to his own times, 1 book.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370. There are also those who write that he was a disciple of Augustine and flourished in the year of the Lord 430.

[Hesychius?], priest and monk, formerly hearer and disciple of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, bishop, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, admonished by the example of his teacher, is said to have written many little works of explanations on the divine books, and to have labored over various volumes on both the New and the Old Testament, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that notable and very large work which he wrote to Eutychianus, the venerable deacon.

On Leviticus, 1 book. To the venerable deacon.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a Roman by country, a man most celebrated for faith and holiness, easily the most learned of all in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, perfectly instructed in the Greek and Latin tongue, whose merit the whole world proclaims, whose works Holy Mother Church confirms as books with a great commendation of authority. In expounding and explaining the divine scriptures he surpassed all doctors, so that, although many bishops were banished into exile for the faith, no one ever dared to touch Ambrose. For he was a most steadfast hammer of heretics, whose tongue, speaking in the faith of Christ, no human authority could ever impose silence upon. Always ready to undergo any dangers for the faith, with the Lord protecting him he escaped everywhere free and unharmed. He wrote many distinguished little works, of which I have found only those set down below.

On Duties, 3 books. “Not to seem arrogant.”

On the Calling of the Gentiles, 2 books. “Among the defenders [unclear].”

Hexaemeron, 6 books. “Only lest of opinion.”

On Human Dignity, 1 book. “Let us make man.”

On Paradise, 1 book. “Concerning Paradise [unclear].”

On Cain and Abel, 1 book. “Concerning Paradise in the preceding.”

On Noah’s Ark, 1 book. “Of holy Noah we undertake.”

On Abraham the Patriarch, 2 books. “Abraham, of this book.”

On Isaac, or the Soul, 1 book. “In the father of holy [unclear] for us.”

On the Good of Death, 1 book. “Since concerning the soul above.”

On Flight from the World, 2 books. “Frequent for us concerning [unclear].”

On Jacob and the Blessed Life, 1 book. “Necessary for learning.”

On Joseph the Patriarch, 1 book. “The life of the saints to others.”

On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, 1 book. “First of all, how great.”

On Naboth the Jezreelite, 1 book. “The story of Naboth [unclear].”

On Elijah and Fasting, 4 books. “Many disturbances for us.”

Apology of David, 1 book. “The apology of the prophet.”

On Interpellations, 5 books. “The queen of the South came.”

On Solomon, 3 books. “[Jeroboal?] under the tree.”

On the Mysteries of Those Being Initiated, 6 books. “Concerning morals daily.”

On the Sacraments, 1 book. “I wish, brothers, [unclear].”

On Pastoral Care, 1 book. “The mystery of Passover concerning.”

On Faith, to Gratian, 2 books. “We have brought down, brother.”

On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. “In the preceding book something.”

On Faith, the Creed, 2 books. “If that is the end of virtues.”

On the Incarnation of the Lord, 1 book. “I admonish you, brothers.”

On the Mystery of Passover, 2 books.

On the Death of His Brother, 1 book.

On Penitence, 1 book.

An Exhortation to Penitence, 1 book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On virgins, three books: “If, in accordance with the heavenly [unclear].”

On widows, one book: “It has happened well, brothers.”

An exhortation to virgins, one book: “You who to the great banquet.”

To a devout virgin, one book: “Hear, daughter, and see,” and one book: “Hear me now, you who.”

To a fallen virgin, one book: “Ambrose, bishop, [unclear].”

Against Symmachus, one book: “And if the increase.”

A consolatory work for Valentinian, one book: “Dalmatius [unclear] me.”

Against Auxentius, one book: “I see that you, beyond what is usual.”

On the handing over of the basilicas, two books: “You entrust me with a pledge.”

On the instruction of a virgin, one book: “This movement [unclear] for us.”

On the death of Theodosius, one book: “You have undertaken the office, sacred [unclear].”

On the instruction of priests, one book: “No ordinary [unclear].”

On circumcision, one book: “An army always with continual [unclear].”

On the synagogue, to Theodosius, one book: “To the lady sister of life and [unclear].”

The revelation of Gervasius and Protasius, two books: “Ambrose to the virgins.”

On the passion of Saint Agnes, one book: “Concerning judgments.”

On choosing a pontiff, one book: “Into the Epistles of Paul.”

On Saint Job, one book: “Although also mystical [things].”

Of hymns and prefaces, one book: “You warn well, brother.”

On the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” ten books: “As we are about to write into the book of the Gospel [unclear].”

On the Gospel of Luke, one book: “The Simonians from Simon.”

Of many sermons, one book: “On the forty-two stopping-places.”

On certain psalms, two books.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally, he is said to have made Hegesippus and certain others Latin from the Greek.

He flourished under the most merciful emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

PHILASTRIUS, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, known and familiar to blessed Ambrose of Milan, whom Saint Augustine mentions in a certain letter to Quodvultdeus, wrote for the common benefit certain distinguished little works, none of which I remember to have come into our hands. His notable work, which he wrote, is reported, with blessed Augustine bearing witness in the place cited above:

On 156 heresies, one book: “The Simonians from Simon.”

The rest I have not seen.

He flourished under the most Christian emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

EVAGRIUS, monk and disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, and afterwards bishop of Antioch, a man most learned from every point of view, instructed in both secular and divine writings, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, preserving even in the episcopate the austerity of his former life, was of such abstinence that he was held to be a miracle. He was the first to commend to writing the life of the holy fathers; from his own vein he published many little works. Of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. The following are reported as his:

To anchorites, very useful, one book.

On the eight principal vices, one book.

Also to cenobites, one book.

An exhortatory work to a virgin, one book.

He made the Life of Antony Latin, one book: “The presbyter Evagrius.”

On the life of the holy fathers, one book.

He also wrote many other works, and translated from Greek into Latin works unknown to us. He flourished under the prince Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

MAXIMUS, bishop of Constantinople, an Alexandrian by nation, a distinguished philosopher and theologian, in whose praise Gregory Nazianzen published a book, enduring many injuries from the Arians and at last driven from the episcopate, wrote many things against them. He composed explanations, which among the Greeks at that time were held in great esteem. Of these the following are reported among us:

Against the Arians, one book. The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished in Greece under the prince Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

AMBROSIUS, a presbyter, an Alexandrian by nation, once a hearer and disciple of Didymus the Blind, from whose exposition of the divine Scriptures he learned magnificently, composed various explanations on them.

Commentaries on Job, one book.

Against Apollinaris of Laodicea, one book.

The Abbot of Spanheim

He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Arcadius in the year 400.

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a monk in his manner of life, very learned and eloquent in the divine Scriptures, and no less worthy of reverence for holiness than for knowledge, shone with many miracles in life and after death, as is read in his history. Among other things he wrote:

On the Life of the Holy Fathers, book I. On the Ordination of a Bishop, book I.

And other things unknown to us.

He died under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 385, in the thirteenth indiction.

Pachomius, abbot, a most magnificent founder of the monks of his time, founder of many monasteries, and a man of most holy life, shining with many miracles in life and after death, was a learned man, instructed in the divine Scriptures. For the edification of the brothers he wrote many letters, of which the following are reported:

To Abbot Cornelius, letter I. To the provosts of the monasteries, letter I.

To Abbot Syrus, letter I. To the working brothers, letter I.

Also a Rule of Monks, book I.

He flourished under the princes Valentinian and Theodosius in the year 390.

Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man most learned in secular letters, sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in meter and prose, was held fast for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world; he read and expounded many little works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems. At last, however, in old age, having rejected the vanity of the world, he betook himself to the sacred Scriptures, and in verse and prose expounded many hidden things of both Testaments. He wrote many excellent little works, of which I found the following made in metrical measure:

Against Symmachus the Idolater, book I. “Paul, herald of God.”

On the Conflict, book I. “The faithful old man first.”

On Divinity, book I. “God is three, the highest.”

Against the Patripassians, book I. “There are very many, but.”

Against the Sabellians, book I. “Yield, profaner.”

Against the Jews, book I. “These things, if [unclear] Jewish [unclear] in 30.”

Against the Homuncionites, book I. “There are those who [unclear].”

Against the Phantastics, book I. “It is worth the trouble [unclear].”

On the Origin of Sins, book I. On the Hexaemeron, book I.

On the Holy Trinity, book I. “The winged herald of the day [announces] the light.”

Of Various Hymns, book I. “Blessed martyr, near.”

Praises of Saint Vincent, book I. “Ancient [unclear].”

Praises of Saint Lawrence, book I. “Roman, of Christ [unclear].”

Of Histories, book I. “Behold, there was a dove.”

On the Nature of the Soul, book I. “A doubtful person meets here.”

On the Resurrection of the Flesh, book I. “I ask with me in Christ.”

On the Martyrs, book I. “They have been written in heaven.”

On the State of the Soul, book I. “Whoever [says] souls [unclear] errs.”

Hamartigenia, book I. “Brothers, [unclear] the digger.”

On the Hope of Pardon, or a Prayer, book I. “O God, parent of [unclear].”

Against the Marcionites, book I. “As often as [unclear] rage hurls down.”

Peristephanon, book I. “Pious, faithful, innocent.”

He also wrote not a few letters.

He also published some other works which have not come into our hands.

He flourished under the emperor Gratian in the year of the Lord 380.

John, monk and priest of Damascus, a learned and holy man, of whom wondrous things are told on account of the excellence of his teaching and the sincerity of his life, held in high esteem at Constantinople and appointed prelate of the monks, turned many away from iniquity. In the Greek language he wrote little works of profound meaning, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read only that famous work:

On the Tradition of the Orthodox Faith, book I. “No one has ever seen God.”

The History of Barlaam and Josaphat, book I. I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under the most devout prince Theodosius in the year of the Lord 390.

[unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Ticonius the African, whom blessed Augustine, in the third book of On Christian Doctrine, records as having belonged to the Donatist party, although in some matters he disagreed with them, was certainly a keen man and much practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote not a few short works. Of these the following are reported, namely:

On Internal War, three books. An Expository Work on Various Questions, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. The Rules of Sacred Scripture, one book. Several letters to various persons. And many other things. He flourished when Theodosius and his sons were ruling, in the year of the Lord 390.

Heraclides the monk, a man holy in conduct, distinguished for learning in the divine Scriptures, a most diligent investigator and imitator of the holy fathers, anchorites and monks, who, like a resourceful bee, gathered the flowers of virtues from the way of life of each into the little cell of his breast and produced the honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other things, for the edification of readers, he wrote a notable work on the life and conduct of the holy fathers living in the desert or in monasteries under a rule, whose title is:

Paradise, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures [unclear], wrote, among other things, a useful work:

On the Holy Spirit, one book.

Of the other works which he is said to have composed, nothing has come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the devout emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

The Abbot of Spanheim ... not unaware of the Luciferian party, and for that reason deservedly blameworthy. He wrote many excellent [unclear]. He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390. One book.

Jerome, priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius from the town of Stridon, a man very learned in secular letters and, among all the doctors, most learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished by skill in many languages, interpreter of the sacred law, hammer of heretics and most powerful assailant. This is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasury new things and old, and giving to his fellow-servants in due season the measure of spiritual wheat, despoiled the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. This is the eminent doctor of the Church of Christ, who, with his pious mother Rebecca, that is, the grace of God, brought forth the garments of Esau, wandering astray through the byways of errors, laid up unused for the Lord, and clothed the meek Jacob, faithful and serving Christ. This is Jerome, sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who, passing no time in idleness, meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, and, scarcely granting his body the sleep it required, always by days and nights wrote, read, taught, or prayed, as the almost countless books which he published bear witness. This defender of truth, cultivator of virtue, and most bitter enemy of vices, when he was priest of the Roman Church and constantly reproved the crimes of the clerics, [unclear] from the city through their envy; and, coming into Judaea, he visited the glorious sepulchre of the Lord, and, establishing for himself a dwelling-place beside the manger at Bethlehem, became renowned throughout the whole world, this no doubt being arranged by divine providence, so that the light of the world should rest there where the true sun of justice had become known to men by being born. A holy and fitting inhabitant of a most holy place, firm in faith, kindled with charity, mature in conduct, who could not be led astray by prosperity, whom no adversity ever cast down from his holy purpose. But why do I, a foul praiser, touch the holy head of the man with impure lips? It would have been more fitting for me to keep humble silence than to speak inadequately about so most holy a man. Now therefore let us set down in order what we have found concerning his writings and little works. Among these are:

On Daniel, 2 books. On the prophet Hosea, 3 books. On Joel, 3 books. On the prophet Amos, 1 book. On Obadiah, 1 book. On Jonah, 1 book. On Micah, 2 books. On the prophet Nahum, 1 book. On Habakkuk, 2 books. On Zephaniah, 1 book. On Haggai, 1 book. On Zechariah, 3 books. On Malachi, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 5 books. On the Song of Songs, 3 books. On the Gospel of Matthew, 4 books. On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. On the Gospels anagogically, 4 books. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 7 books. On the Epistle to the Thessalonians, 6 books. On the Epistle to Titus, 1 book. On the Epistle to Philemon, 3 books. On the Epistle to the Hebrews, 1 book. An apologetic work addressed to Pammachius, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Several sermons, 1 book. On the priestly vestment, 1 book.

These are the works among the writings of the most blessed doctor Jerome which have occurred to us at present to record. Nor do we doubt that he wrote more which are not contained in this catalogue, chiefly for the reason that they have either remained unknown to us or scattered among many things. For among all the doctors of the Church no one was of more benefit than Jerome, who, besides innumerable small works, translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, corrected the New according to the Greek truth, and faithfully offered it to be read by the Church. He also made many volumes of the Greeks into Latin: namely those of Origen, Josephus the Jew, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus of Alexandria, Victorinus the martyr, and others.

At length, after many labors, full of days, he died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the last day of the month of September, at the hour of Compline, in the ninety-ninth year of his age. He was buried at Bethlehem, shining with many miracles; Eusebius, his disciple, described his life.

Audentius, a Spanish bishop, a man possessing a mind trained in the divine Scriptures, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, but with his principal intention against the Photinians, who afterward were called Bonosiacs, a notable work which he is said to have [unclear].

On the faith, against heretics, 1 book.

He also published some other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

Rufinus, a monk and presbyter of the church of Aquileia, an eloquent man, very learned in the divine Scriptures and skilled in Greek and Latin speech, was of no small reputation among the ecclesiastical doctors. Although his writings are many, nevertheless they are counted among the apocrypha, Distinction 15, Sancta Romana, because he wrote invective letters against the most holy man Jerome, as can be understood from reading them. But po-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

But afterward, returning to the harmony of brotherly love, Rufinus’s little works were made authentic, insofar as they were not contrary to the statements of Jerome. Concerning the writings of Rufinus, therefore, the following are reported.

On the prophet Hosea, one book. On the prophet Amos, one book. One book: “To me indeed, most faithful [unclear].” On his faith, to Bishop Laurentius, one book: “I have read your writings.” Two books: “I have heard that certain men, when...” Invectives against Jerome, one book. On the sacraments, one book. One book. Additions to the Ecclesiastical History, two books. On his faith, to Anastasius. On the blessings of the patriarchs, one book. An exhortation to Proba, two books. Letters to various persons.

He is said besides to have composed many other works, but they have not come into our hands. He also translated the volumes of many Greeks into Latin, namely Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory the Great the bishop, Pamphilus the martyr, Eusebius of Caesarea, Evagrius, Sixtus the philosopher, and many others; all these he marked beforehand with his own prefaces and letters. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, and wrote many things. In the year of the Lord 400.

John, bishop of Constantinople, formerly at Antioch a hearer and disciple of Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, while he was still a priest, who because of the charm of his eloquence is called Chrysostom, that is, Golden-Mouth, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in declamations and homilies to the people was of excellent talent; he was distinguished no less for holiness than for learning, and was held by the people in great reverence and love. This most blessed prelate suffered many wrongs from Theophilus of Alexandria, and by his fraudulent and deceitful contrivances was driven from his bishopric into exile, as is found in his Life and in the Tripartite History. He wrote many volumes in Greek. Of these I have seen among the Latins the following.

On compunction, one book: “When I look upon you, blessed...” One book: “I know that by thicker...” That no one is harmed except by himself: “Who will give to the head...” “As they report Matthew...” On the Gospel of John, 87 homilies, one book: “He who [unclear] the contests...” Two books: “In many portions and in many ways...” On the Gospel of Matthew, one book: “There is undoubtedly nothing...” He is also said to have written many homilies, sermons, and innumerable letters, which have not come into our hands. At last, after many labors and holy exercises, through the deceit of Theophilus of Alexandria and Eudoxia Augusta, he died in exile in Pontus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 411, in the ninth indiction. 50.

Severianus, bishop of Gabala, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and an admirable teacher in delivering homilies to the people, was of incredible eloquence; for this reason he was summoned to Constantinople for a sermon. Saint John entrusted his people to him when he was being driven into exile, venerating not only his doctrine but also the merit of his life. But Severianus, recommending himself to the people more than he ought, supplied kindling for discord between himself and John. But when the patriarch returned from exile, they returned to the covenant of fraternal love, as the homily delivered on this matter in the church of Constantinople testifies. Of the writings of Severianus, a most learned man, few are possessed among the Latins; still fewer have come into our hands. 134. In the ep-

There are also extant among us certain other homilies of his, brief indeed, but very useful. Concerning his other little works, although many are reported, I have so far found nothing. He flourished under Arcadius and Honorius, at the same time as John Chrysostom. In the year of the Lord 400.

Vitellius, an African, defending the schism of the Donatists, was indeed a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, and, if he had remained in ecclesiastical unity, he would have composed sufficiently useful doctrine. But because he accused the true Catholics as betrayers and persecutors, he was deservedly held in contempt, together with his volumes. The following volumes are extant from his writings.

Against the nations, one book. That the servants of God are hated by the world, one book.

Against our people, a book of complaints, one book.

He is said besides to have composed many volumes, which have not come to my knowledge.

On the incarnation of the Lord, [unclear] books.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Constans, son of the emperor Constantine the Great. In the year of the Lord 360.

He flourished under [unclear], a presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and eloquent man; and in reading the old authors he wrote against the Apollinarists and Eunomians a most elegant volume, in which by very clear reasoning and authority he confuted the perverse doctrines of the heretics.

He gave this magnificent and distinguished work the title:

Theodore, a presbyter, and afterwards, in the city of Rome, a hidden bishop of the Donatists. While he was still a presbyter in the Church of God, he wrote to confessors and to virgins of Christ a volume of moral, yet very necessary, doctrine. In it he especially treats and discusses:

On the preservation of chastity, one book.

He flourished first among our people in Africa, then among his own Donatists at [Montefes?], afterwards at Rome.

Heliodorus, a certain presbyter, zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, sufficiently keen for disputation and of a forceful intellect in the scholastic manner, so that he might show there to be one principle of all things, and nothing [unclear] hand, a governor, and venerable no less for holiness than for learning. He wrote clear sermons on the holy Scriptures for monasteries.

[Unclear], three. Of exhortation [unclear].

He flourished under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 420.

On the natures of original things, one book.

He is also said to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Theodore, a monk, disciple of the blessed Pachomius, and after his death [unclear]’s colleague, a man perfectly instructed in the divine writings, and notable both in life and in learning. For the edification of monks he wrote a work seasoned with divine salt and furnished with all the instruments of monastic discipline, which we may entitle:

Orsiesius, a monk and disciple of Saint Pachomius and of his successor Theodore, [unclear] of the preservation of monks, one book. Whether he wrote anything more I do not know.

On the instruction of monks,

He flourished under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius. In the year 420.

John Cassian, a Scythian by birth, formerly a hearer and disciple of the blessed John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, and ordained deacon by him, after some years was expelled by the same man, for what cause I do not know. Consecrated presbyter at Marseilles, he founded two monasteries, one of men and one of women, in which great fervor of regular discipline remained for many years. With experience as his teacher he wrote several little works, in which even in translation elegance of speech is apparent. They are reported in the following number. At the request of Leo the archdeacon, afterwards bishop of the city of Rome, he wrote against Nestorius the heretic:

On the incarnation of the Lord, two books.

On the institutes of monks, three books. On the institutes and [unclear].

218 The Abbot of Spanheim

On the eight capital vices. 8 books. “The fifth, with [unclear] helping us.” Conferences of the holy fathers. 24 books. “When in the desert of Scete.” In these Conferences of the saints there is useful and necessary instruction for monks; but because in certain matters he is criticized by blessed Prosper concerning freedom of choice, his little works are reckoned among the apocrypha. At length he died, after the publication of many books, at Marseilles, not without a reputation for holiness, when Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning. In the year of the Lord 435.

LUCIAN, priest of the Church of Jerusalem, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, to whom, in the times of Honorius and Theodosius, almighty God revealed the place of the tomb and relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen. He is said to have written some little works.

Epistle. Lucian the priest. On the discovery of Saint Stephen. 1 book. Of the other things I have seen nothing.

He wrote this revelation in the Greek language; Avitus, a priest of Spanish birth, translated it into Latin speech, and, with his own letter added, sent it through Orosius to be read by Easterners. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, around the years of the Lord 410.

SEVERUS the priest, surnamed Sulpicius, born from the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and letters, and conspicuous for his love of poverty and humility. Dear also to the holy men Martin of Tours and Paulinus of Nola, bishops, in his old age he was deceived by the Pelagians; and, recognizing the fault of loquacity, he kept silence until death, so that the sin which he had contracted by speaking he might healthfully amend by keeping silent. He wrote little works not unworthy of reading, of which the following are reported.

“Most mortals.” On the life of Saint Martin the bishop. 3 books. “When I into one place.” Conference of Postumianus and Gallus. 3 books. Letters to his sister. 1 book. Letters to various persons. 1 book. To Paulinus, bishop of Nola. 2 books. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished with Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours, under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. In the year of the Lord 420.

AUSONIUS, bishop of Bordeaux, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters second to none in his own time, excelling in verse and prose, shone forth no less famous for content [unclear] than for learning. At Trier, in a council under the emperor Maximus, together with the saints Martin, Ambrose of Milan, and Jerome the priest, he did many splendid things. While there, among other things, he wrote in verse the distinguished little work that is entitled:

On the praise of the same homeland. 1 book. Mosella. 1 book.

But he is also said to have written many other little works which have in no way come down to us. He flourished under Maximus. In the year of the Lord 410.

AUGUSTINE, bishop of Hippo, by nation a Carthaginian in Africa, a man most learned of all the doctors both in the divine writings and in secular letters, eloquent in speech, renowned in expression, profound in understanding, most holy in life and conduct. He wrote so many little works that I would believe no one could either read or possess them all. Hence without doubt he is convicted of lying who professes that he has thus found the whole of Augustine. For he surpasses all writers both in the number of books and in usefulness, since he composed more than a thousand distinguished treatises. No one explained sacred Scripture so profoundly as Augustine; no one so usefully instructed Christian morals; nor did anyone defend the catholic faith more ardently than he. The king brought him into the wine-cellar, and clothed him with such strength that with the sword of his mouth he powerfully laid low the obstinate adversaries of the faith. If you had him as teacher, even if the others were lacking, he alone would suffice for you. Now therefore, from the many books which he published, let us record at least a few.

On the deposition of the bishop of Carthage, one book.

On the last day, one treatise.

On voice and word, one treatise.

On hunters of mercy, one treatise.

On the woman with an issue of blood, one treatise.

On the deposition of Restitutus the bishop, one treatise.

On the usefulness of fasting, one treatise.

On the drunkenness of Noah, one treatise.

On the works of the six days, two treatises.

On choosing a bishop, one treatise.

On the rod of Moses turned into a serpent, two treatises.

On the dead raised by the Lord, one treatise.

On the strong woman from Proverbs, two treatises.

On the Nativity of the Lord, seven treatises.

On the Epiphany also, two treatises.

On Lent, five treatises.

On the Passion of the Lord, two treatises.

For the vigils of Easter, one treatise.

On greed also, one treatise.

Of exhortation to the candidates, twenty-three treatises.

On the ordination of a cleric, one treatise.

On Saints Perpetua and Felicity, three treatises.

On the Ascension of the Lord, two treatises.

On spiritual almsgiving, one treatise.

On Saint Vincent, two treatises.

More than 200 letters, [unclear].

On bodily alms, one treatise.

He also published many other things; if anyone desires to know them more fully, let him read the index of his books published by Possidius, from which we have taken many items. Jacobus de Voragine, bishop of Genoa, writes in his treatise which he composed on the books of Augustine, that the number of his books, treatises, sermons, and letters rises above one thousand and thirty. And he concludes:

One book. One book. One book. Two books. One book. One book. Two treatises. Four [unclear]. One treatise. One treatise. One book. One treatise. Two treatises. Ten [unclear]. One treatise. Thirty treatises. Six treatises. Seven treatises. Eight treatises. Nine treatises. Ten treatises. Eleven treatises. Twelve treatises. Thirteen treatises. Fourteen treatises. Fifteen treatises. Sixteen treatises. Seventeen treatises. Eighteen treatises. Nineteen treatises.

One book. One book. [Unclear] book[s]. One book. One book.

One book. One book.

One book. One book.

One book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and [unclear]. And therefore no one has ever been found who could discover all the books of Augustine. And Possidonius says: “He lies who declares that he has read all of you, Augustine.” But in this work I have, not without deliberation, omitted certain treatises which are ascribed by many to blessed Augustine. Among these is the book On Spirit and Soul, in the thirty-seventh chapter of which Boethius is cited, who was born long after Augustine. Moreover the style itself does not savor of Augustine. Likewise the book which, under Augustine’s name, has now been printed On True and False Penance is falsely ascribed to him, since in the seventeenth chapter, near the end, Augustine himself is cited. The book On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices, which begins “The apostolic voice,” echoes the style of Pope Gregory and agrees with the older copies. Likewise the book On the Ladder of Paradise, whose beginning is “When on a certain day,” is in the old copies inscribed to blessed Bernard, whose spirit and phrasing it seems to express. Why should I labor over many examples? So many are the treatises and sermons falsely inscribed to blessed Augustine that a review of them would require its own volume. Nor is it mine to sit as judge and deprive of their titles works that belong to others. Let the prudent reader consider what he ought to do or hold in these matters.

The holy doctor Augustine died in the city of Hippo, when it was being besieged by the Vandals, in the year of the Lord 430, in the thirteenth indiction, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his priesthood, according to Marianus Scotus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the third month of the city’s siege. While the attacks of the besieging Vandals were underway, at the very end of his days, he was replying to the books of Julian the Manichaean, and gloriously persevering in defense of the Christian faith. He made no testament, because he had nothing from which to make one, except the library of the church, which even in death he commended to the brothers to be guarded most diligently. Poor in possessions, rich in merits and learning, Augustine the bishop rested in the Lord; Possidonius, bishop of Calama, wrote his life.

Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople after blessed John Chrysostom, a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, was nevertheless blameworthy in this: that he allowed himself to be ordained in the place of a living bishop who had been unjustly expelled. From this many scandals arose in the Church of God. He wrote, as works not to be despised: To the Queens, Daughters of the Emperors of Constantinople, to Be Guarded Most Diligently, two books. And not a few other things.

He flourished under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 420.

Paulinus the presbyter, disciple of Saint Augustine of Hippo, and afterward bishop of Nola in Campania, to whom many letters and various treatises of Augustine and Jerome are said to have been sent, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular letters, shone forth no less clearly in holiness than in learning. Concerning him blessed Pope Gregory writes in the third book of the Dialogues that he was of such great piety and compassion that, after he had spent all his possessions for the use of the poor and the liberation of captives, he even handed himself over into servitude for the son of a certain widow; from this at last, together with many captives, he was released on account of the merit of his life. He wrote many volumes, both in meter and in prose: The Life of Saint Felix, Bishop of Nola, one book; To Severus Sulpicius, four letters; Letters to Various Persons, one book; also On the Sacraments, one book; On the Death of a Baptized Infant, one book; Panegyric of Theodosius, one book; Hymns in Various Meters, one book; On Contempt of the World, one book; On Penance, one book; On the Praise of Martyrs, one book; To a Fallen Virgin, one book; Letter-collection to Various Persons, [unclear] books; To a Fallen Virgin.

He flourished in the time of the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year 420. [unclear]

Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, acute in talent, open and polished in speech, wrote little works for the edification of readers, of reading not to be despised. Among them the following are reported: A Preparation for Candidates Who Are Being Made Ready for Baptism, one book; On the Errors of Paganism, [unclear] books; On the Faith of the One Majesty, one book; Against the Genealogy, one book; also On the Creed, one book; The Division of the Paschal Lamb, one book; To a Fallen Virgin, one book; and certain other things.

He flourished in the time of the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year 420.

224 The Abbot of Sponheim

SIMPLICIANUS of Milan, bishop after Saint Ambrose, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, a lover of poverty, urged Augustine, while he was still a presbyter, in many letters to exercise his talent and devote himself to expositions of the Scriptures, so that he might seem, like another Ambrose, an instigator of Origen’s work. Hence Augustine resolved many questions in letters addressed to him. But he himself wrote useful letters to Augustine and various others, which are found partly here and there. He flourished under the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

ISIDORE the elder, bishop of Cordoba, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, quick in talent, sufficiently eloquent in speech, distinguished no less by the conduct of his life than by knowledge of the Scriptures, whose learning was held in great esteem among the ancients, wrote not a few small works in various volumes. Of these, however, I have found an excellent work which he published for Saint Orosius, the Spanish presbyter:

On the Four Books of Kings, 4 books.

Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished under the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

OROSIUS, presbyter, Spanish by nationality, once a hearer of blessed Augustine, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in secular letters, and very renowned in life and conduct. Blessed Augustine sent him, when he came to him from Spain to learn the question concerning the nature of the soul, to Saint Jerome at Bethlehem of Judea; there, after staying for some time, he clearly learned the question for which he had come, and, returning to Hippo, carried with him relics of Stephen the protomartyr. To this most studious man there are extant several works of blessed Augustine, varied resolutions of questions of the Scriptures. He himself wrote the following volumes:

Apologetic, 7 books. Against the Pelagians, 1 book. Chronicle on the Hormesta of the world, 1 book. On the Reason of the Soul, 1 book. Several Letters to Augustine, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

He flourished, illustrious in life and doctrine, with Saint Augustine, in the year of the Lord 420.

JOHN, bishop and patriarch of Jerusalem, devoted and learned in the holy Scriptures, but too intent on the teachings of Origen, stirred up writings of the fathers against himself, namely of the most holy presbyter Jerome and of Bishop Epiphanius, as is found in the letters sent among their acts. But John himself, giving an account of his own study, says that he imitated not the faith of Origen but his talent. For this reason especially he wrote a noteworthy work:

Against the Detractors of His Study, 1 book.

And certain letters to various persons, and certain other things. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

MAXIMUS, bishop of Turin, most learned in the holy Scriptures, second to none in his time in delivering homilies to the people, was distinguished not only in doctrine but also shone most brightly in holiness of life. He wrote many excellent small works, which holy mother Church has received to be read with great authority. Among these the following are reported:

On Chapters of the Gospels, 1 book. On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. In Praise of the Apostles, 1 book. Incipit: “The most glorious solemnities of Christ to us.” In Praise of John the Baptist, 1 book. Incipit: “Of the holy fathers my.” On the Life of Eusebius of Vercelli, 1 book. Incipit: “Concerning the words of Isaiah.” On Saint Cyprian the Martyr, 1 book. Incipit: “The feast of Saint Cyprian.” On the Grace of Baptism, 1 book. Incipit: “On avarice. The waning of the moon.” On Hospitality, 1 book. Incipit: “On the tradition of the judge.” On Alms, 1 book. On the Lord’s Sepulcher, 3 homilies. On the Office of the Mass, 1 book. On the Accusation of the Lord, 1 homily. On the Resurrection of the Lord, 4 homilies. Incipit: “Not undeservedly, brothers.” On Saint Lawrence, 1 homily. Incipit: “It is holy, brothers, and God.” Reading of the Acts of the Apostles. On Ca-

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Kalends of January, 1 homily. On the Nativity of the Lord, 3 homilies. On the Epiphany of the Lord, 2 homilies. On Easter, 3 homilies. On Pentecost, 3 homilies. On the penitence of the Ninevites, 1 homily. On not fearing fleshly enemies, 1 homily. On giving thanks after food, 1 homily.

He also wrote many other things: sermons, treatises, letters, homilies, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420. And he died under Theodosius the Younger.

Julian, a Campanian bishop, a man of sharp and vehement intellect, learned in the Holy Scriptures, schooled in Greek and Latin speech. Before he revealed in himself the impiety of Pelagius, he was distinguished among the doctors of the Church. Afterwards, however, wishing to defend his heresy, he wrote little works against the holy doctors, in conformity with his own opinion. Of these there survive:

Against Saint Augustine, 4 books. Against the same, another 7 books. A dialogue of disputation between the parties, 1 book.

And many other things, all of which, because of the author’s errors, have rightly been cast out from the ecclesiastical library. In a time of the hardship of famine he distributed all his possessions in alms to the poor; he associated with his heresy many noble religious men, deceived under the appearance of piety. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord [420?].

Innocent, the first pope of that name, a learned and most holy man, Alban by nation, the forty-second after blessed Peter, presided over the universal Church for fifteen years, and gloriously ordained many things for its benefit. To him, while he was still a priest, blessed Jerome composed the history of the woman struck seven times, as the prologue of the same work shows. Since he was most learned in the divine Scriptures, he wrote some excellent little works for the edification of the faithful. Of these I have found only the following:

A decree against the Pelagians, 1 book. Against the Bonosiacs, 1 book. It begins: “I have long greatly wondered.” Letters to various persons, 1 book. It begins: “In inquiring about these things.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He died in the year of the Lord 417, indiction 15, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Eusebius of Cremona, monk, disciple of blessed Jerome the priest, a studious and learned man, venerable in life and conduct, continually devoted, after the example of his most reverend master, to holy prayers and divine readings, [unclear] a great reputation for holiness [unclear]. Having lived on familiar terms for many years with Saint Augustine, he shone forth, distinguished in life and doctrine among ecclesiastical prelates. Among other things, he wrote for the edification of the faithful:

On the passing of Saint Jerome, 1 book. It begins: “To the most reverend Da-.”

He flourished in the time of Saint Jerome, in the year of the Lord 430.

Possidius the African, bishop of Calama, formerly a hearer and devoted disciple of blessed Augustine, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters,

An index of his books, 1 book. It begins: “With the true inspirer of all things.”

[unclear] he found, condemned with the help [unclear]. Those who were converted, however, he relegated to a monastery for the doing of penance until the end of life. Among other things he wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona:

A decretal little work, 1 book. It begins: “Against the pagans concerning.”

He flourished under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 450.

Siricius, pope, Roman by nation, sat after Damasus in the pontificate for 15 years; a learned and holy man, a very keen defender of the catholic faith, all the Manichaeans whom he found in the city [unclear].

He died under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 398, indiction 6, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March.

Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, distinguished also in life and conduct, notable in speech and intellect, wrote some devout little works. Among these, a certain volume addressed to Fatalis is said to have been written with sound doctrine.

On Christian doctrine, 1 book. On preserving widowhood, 1 book.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 420.

Celestine, the first pope of that name, Roman by nation, a learned and holy man, by whose order blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, held at Ephesus a synod of two hundred fathers, in which Nestorius and Pelagius, together with their wicked doctrines, were condemned. There also

The Abbot of Sponheim

it was also decreed that the most blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, should thereafter be so called. Blessed Celestine wrote, among other things, a solemn decree:

Against Nestorius, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He died under Theodosius the Younger, prince, in the year of the Lord 433, in the tenth year of his pontificate, in the first indiction, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

THEODORETUS, bishop of the city which from its founder, Cyrus, king of the Persians, was called Cyrus, a man very learned in the divine scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, is said to have composed some little works on the sacred volumes, but they have not come into our hands. His notable work, published after Jerome, is reported to be:

Ecclesiastical History, one book. On the Incarnation of the Lord against Eutyches, one book.

He flourished in the times of the most sacred prince Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390. His history is now inserted in the Tripartite History.

EVODIUS, bishop in Africa, disciple of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to whom Augustine wrote that same treatise On the Soul of Christ among the Dead, and many letters, was a man learned in the holy scriptures and most upright in the conduct of his life, who deservedly should be placed in the catalogue of the saints. He is reported to have written certain devout little works. Of these there is extant a volume concerning miracles performed in Africa through the relics brought by the priest Orosius:

Of St. Stephen the Martyr, one book. And several letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Saint Augustine, in the year of the Lord 420.

PALLADIUS, the first bishop ordained by Pope Celestine for the Britons or Scots of the island of Ireland, Greek by nation, a learned and holy man, by his most sweet preaching converted the people committed to him to the faith of Christ. After him Saint Patrick, a Briton by birth, consecrated by Saint Pope Celestine as archbishop of Ireland, shone with signs and miracles for forty-nine years and converted the whole island to the faith. Palladius wrote:

The Life of Saint John Chrysostom, one book.

He was sent into Scotland by Pope Celestine I in the year of the Lord 432, in the fifteenth indiction, according to Marianus Scotus.

CYRIL, bishop of Alexandria, Greek by nation, once the ornament and notable inhabitant of Mount Carmel, a learned and holy man, by order of Pope Celestine I presided in the council of two hundred fathers at Ephesus. There, condemning Nestorius and Pelagius with their errors, he uttered many elegant judgments. Since he was most learned in the holy scriptures, he wrote many little works. Of these, the following are reported:

On Faith against the Heretics, one book. Against Nestorius, one book.

On the Failing of the Synagogue, one book. On the Origin and Praise of Saint Mary, one book.

On the Paschal Cycle of 95 Years, one book. Commentaries on the Gospel, four books.

In addition he composed several letters, homilies, and sermons, and various other treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished while presiding at the Council of Ephesus under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 432, in the fifth indiction.

THEODORE, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and very learned in secular letters, especially strong in dialectic, eloquent in speech and an acute disputant, being quite eminent in the Council of Ephesus, wrote there in a dialectical manner, very obscurely:

Against Nestorius, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the prince Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

SOZOMEN, Greek by nation, an outstanding cultivator of secular letters and sufficiently learned in the divine scriptures, is reported to have written some little works for the edification of the churches. Of these there is extant a notable work addressed to Theodosius the Younger, prince, from the third consulship of Crispus and Constantine Caesars down to the seventeenth year of that same Theodosius:

Ecclesiastical History, nine books. “Thoughts sometimes to me.”

The rest of what he composed has not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the aforesaid emperor Theodosius, in the year 430.

SOCRATES, a certain Greek by nation, a learned and eloquent man, a notable historiographer and renowned for experience of great affairs, wrote from the time of the first Constantine the Great, emperor, down to the reign of Theodosius the Younger, a volume:

Of Ecclesiastical History, one book.

Other

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come into our hands.

And it should be noted that three Greek authors, namely Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, Sozomen, and this Socrates, each wrote histories of ecclesiastical affairs at almost one and the same time; Epiphanius Scholasticus translated them into Latin, as they stood, and from them Cassiodorus Senator, the monk, made one continuous history, which he called the Tripartite.

Vigilius, deacon and monk, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, guardian and ruler of monastic discipline, is said to have composed certain small works for the edification of monks, which the distance of places and times has prevented from coming down to our memory. The priest Gennadius says, however, that he wrote a very useful rule:

On the Conduct of Monks, one book. He says nothing of the rest.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year 420.

Hosius, bishop of Corduba, before Isidore, to whom Chalcidius the grammarian is recorded to have translated Plato’s Timaeus, was indeed a learned and eloquent man. In the council of Sardica, as president, he delivered many excellent opinions, as is contained in the acts of that same synod. In his old age, however, greatly terrified by the Arian emperor Constantius, and fearing that, as a rich old man, he would either suffer exile or be condemned, he soon consented to the Arian impiety. But, as he deserved, he ended his life not long afterward by a cruel death. For after his impious defection, when Saint Gregory, bishop of Elvira, had come to Corduba by imperial decree and refused to communicate with Hosius, Hosius, angered, asked Clementinus, the vicar of the prefect of Constantius, to drive Gregory into exile. The vicar said to him: “I do not dare send a bishop into exile unless you have first deposed him from the episcopate.” Hosius, unable to endure the delay, mounted the chair as judge. He summoned Gregory by royal edict; when Gregory appeared in the sight of the multitude, and Hosius, proud in arrogance, tried to pronounce the sentence of deposition, Gregory appealed to Christ with all his strength, that he should not allow so unjust a presumption on Hosius’s part to go unpunished. And behold, while the impious Hosius was sitting and wished to deliver the sentence, his mouth turned awry, twisting his neck likewise, and, falling to the ground, he suddenly expired. From this fear seized everyone; after this no one dared touch Gregory. Hosius, while still Catholic, wrote to his sister:

On the Praise of Virginity, one book. In the aforementioned council: eighteen opinions, two books.

And several letters. He flourished under Constantius, already a very old man, by whom he was also deceived and perished, around the year of the Lord 390.

Idacius, bishop of Lemice, a city of the Spains, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and renowned in speech and eloquence, who, with Bishop Ursacius, because of the death of Priscillian, whom they had accused at Trier, was separated from the communion of the Church and driven into exile, died there. He wrote, however, works not to be despised, of which the following are reported:

Against Priscillian, one book. Chronicles from the time of Theodosius, one book.

And certain other works. He flourished under the venerable emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Leporius, priest and monk, zealous in the divine writings, but presuming too much on the purity of his life, taught dogmatically that he lived religiously by his own judgment and effort, not by the grace of God, defending the Pelagian error. But, admonished by the Gallic doctors and corrected in Africa by Saint Augustine, he yielded to the truth and later sharply attacked the heresy which he had formerly preached. Giving thanks, therefore, for his correction, he wrote:

A Corrective against Heresy, two books. And certain other works.

He flourished under the younger emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 430.

Sedulius, priest, a Scot by nation, a disciple from early youth of Hildebert, archbishop of the Scots, a man practiced in the divine writings, most learned in secular letters, excelling in verse and prose, left Scotland out of love of learning and came into France; then he travelled through Italy and Asia, and finally, leaving the borders of Achaia, shone forth in the city of Rome, renowned for his admirable learning. He wrote several small works in metre and in prose; of these I have found only the following. To Abbot Macedonius, an excellent work following the sequence of the whole Gospel, which he entitled:

Paschal Song, in metre, three books. “Paschales quicunque da.”

On all the Epistles of Paul, in prose. “Antequam Apostolica verba.”

On the Miracles of Christ, one book. “A solis ortus cardine.”

To the emperor Theodosius, two books. “Romulidum ductor cla.”

On the Greater Volume of Priscian, one book. On the Second Edition of Donatus, one book.

An Exhortation to the Faithful. “Cantemus socii domino.”

Episto-

228 The Abbot of Sponheim

Several letters to various persons, one book.

Sedulius Scotigena.

On the miracles of Christ, in prose, two books.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. This man at last, as Sigebert writes, was ordained bishop, but he does not state in what church or city. He flourished under Theodosius, in the year 430.

VICTORINUS, a rhetorician of Marseilles, a man most learned in secular letters and very devoted to the Holy Scriptures, attempted to expound the Holy Scriptures; but, occupied with secular literature, and having entered the field of the divine utterances without a teacher, he did not accomplish what he wished. Hence the little works that he wrote are indeed excellent in Christian sense and pious zeal, but are shaped by a lighter weight of judgment. He published, addressed to the person of his son Etherius, commentaries from the beginning down to the death of the patriarch Abraham:

On Genesis, four books. And certain other things which are hidden from us.

He flourished under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year 430.

PHILIPPUS, monk and priest, once a hearer and disciple of blessed Jerome, a studious and learned man, a notable lover of voluntary poverty, who by word and example instructed many toward piety, after the death of his master published certain commentaries on the divine Scriptures. Of these there is extant, as they say, an outstanding work:

On Job, one book. Letters to various persons, two books.

He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 430. And he died under Marcian.

VINCENTIUS, monk and priest of the island of Lérins, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in life and morals. There is extant his notable work, which he composed under the name Peregrinus, very celebrated and praised by the ancient doctors, on avoiding the errors [unclear] of heretics:

Against all heretics, two books.

He is also read to have written some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, in the year of the Lord 430.

PAULUS, priest, a Pannonian by nation, which is now called Hungary, a man devoted to sacred letters, sufficiently learned, venerable no less for the practice of religion than for knowledge of the Scriptures, a zealous defender of the Christian faith, is said to have written not a few volumes, the reading of which is held to be quite suited to confuting heretics. There are extant his works addressed to Constantia, a virgin dedicated to Christ:

On virginity and contempt of the world, two books.

Concerning the others I have as yet found nothing. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

ISAAC, from being a monk a priest of the church of Antioch, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of very celebrated reputation for delivering homilies to the people, beloved by God in life and conduct, venerable to men, wrote in the Syriac tongue, in imitation of Saint Ephrem, several devout little works, the reading of which is judged very useful for religious men.

Of these I have found among our holdings the following:

Against the Nestorians and Euty[ches?], two books.

An exhortation to the spiritual life, one book.

On the battle against vices, one book.

On access to God, one book.

On the difficulty of virtues, one book.

A dialogue on spiritual progress, one book.

On the order of the monastic life, one book.

On humility, one book.

On the three orders of those making progress, one book.

On the solitude of monks, one book.

On diverse temptations, one book.

On the instruction of novices, one book.

On penitence, one book.

A poem on the desolation of Antioch, one book.

He delivered many homilies to the people, but they have by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

EUCHERIUS, bishop of Lyon in Gaul, a learned man, imbued from youth with the discipline of monks, ready in talent, ordered in speech, in life and conduct

The soul that loves God. The honor of many [unclear].

When someone into some ruin. However much virtue without.

By what bond he is held. From violent operation.

Blessed is the man who knows [his] infirmity. There are three orders in.

A man of much anxiety. The virtues one another.

This is the sober order. The strength which [unclear].

50 40

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear], pleasing to God and to men, since by both word and example he turned many away from iniquity. He wrote several distinguished volumes, but as yet only a few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only these:

On Contempt of the World, one book.

Expositions of the Divine Names, one book. Formulas of the Spiritual Life.

To the Sons Salonius and Veranus, one book. Epitome of Cassian, one book.

Certain letters to various persons, one book. To Bishop Hilary, on the Praise of the Wilderness, one book.

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Hilary, bishop of Arles, to whom Eucherius [wrote] one book when he was seeking the deserts of the wilderness.

The Life of Saint Honoratus, Bishop, and certain other things.

Almost countless homilies.

He flourished under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440. He died, however, under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

Zosimus, pope, Greek by nation, sat in the pontificate after Saint Innocent for one year and eight months; a learned man, holy, beloved of God; by word and example [unclear], eloquent in speech, whose merits of holiness the Catholic Church proclaims. He was of such great piety toward the poor that, after all his possessions had been cheerfully distributed for their use, he was thereafter called and was the father of the poor. Among other things, in quite distinguished style, he wrote [letters] of his predecessor:

Letters, one book. From the report of our brother.

On Easter, to Hilary, one book.

On the Priesthood, to Esychius, one book. Your affection requires, etc.

He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 419, in the second indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

Boniface, the first pope of that name, succeeding blessed Zosimus, presided over the Church for three years and four months; a man of great learning, quite fit for the governance of souls, who established many things for ecclesiastical usefulness, which are found scattered in the canons of the holy fathers. For the edification of the faithful, as they say, he wrote some small works. Of these I have found only:

Decretal Letters, one book. The Roman Church, to which, etc.

He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

Proba, a most elegant woman, wife of Adelphus, the Roman proconsul, a woman most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, burning with wonderful zeal, surpassed her sex by her learning. Perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin letters, and excelling in verse and prose, since she held Virgil word for word in her mind, she conceived the idea of describing the New and Old Testament from his words, as if he had intended to demonstrate it in his poems. Therefore, boldly undertaking the work stored up in her mind, carefully going through all the books of Virgil, taking now this verse, now that one, sometimes half a verse, sometimes smaller portions of verses, with wonderful industry and with the measure of the feet everywhere preserved, she described the Catholic volumes in the poet’s verses, and marked this work with a Greek term in about seven hundred verses:

Virgilian Cento, one book. Long ago [I began] to profane, etc.

Whether she wrote anything more I do not know.

Nevertheless this work is counted among the apocrypha, because, even if a devout woman undertook the study of pious things, nevertheless Virgil never considered that his little words should be referred to the honor of Christ or to our faith. For this is not a proper interpretation of the matter, but a fictive one assumed by Proba. She flourished, as some think, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, a woman most devout in the Christian religion and most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, returning from Jerusalem, brought with her the relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen and honorably placed them in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Since she was very learned, excelling in verse and prose, she is said, in imitation of Proba, wife of Adelphus, to have turned back the poems of Homer

The Abbot of Sponheim

... herself to the Christian faith, likewise prefixing to the published little work a title such as this: Homeric Centos, one book. But this too is apocryphal.

She also wrote certain other things. Since Saint Jerome, in a certain letter, states that he had read Homer-centos and Virgil-centos, they must necessarily have been composed before his death.

She flourished with Theodosius her husband, who took up the empire. In the year of the Lord 423.

Primasius, an African bishop, as some maintain once a disciple of blessed Augustine, a man indeed learned in the Holy Scriptures, splendidly imbued with the disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, is said to have composed many little works, which among the ancients were held at a high price. Of these I have found only:

Against Heresies, to Bishop Fortunatus, three books.

On the Apocalypse of John, to Castorius, five books. Concerning the book of the Apocalypse of blessed John.

The rest, however, which he composed have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Theodosius II, in the year of the Lord 440.

Junilius, bishop of a certain city in Africa, but I have not been able to discover the name of the city, a man certainly very learned in the sacred Scriptures, in my judgment sufficiently instructed in secular disciplines, profound in understanding, sweet and ornate in speech, is said to have written many little works; but I have seen only the distinguished work which he wrote to Primasius, the above-mentioned bishop, which he entitled:

On the Parts of the Divine Law, one book. To the holy and most blessed bishop.

Of the rest I have seen none.

He flourished at the same time as Primasius, in the year of the Lord 446.

Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, a man most learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a distinguished theologian and computist, whom in the times of Leo Augustus the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, after making a sedition with Timothy as author, cruelly killed. And they set up that same Timothy, like an idol, in his place as bishop of Alexandria. Among other things he wrote to Saint Leo the pope:

On the Celebration of Easter, three letters.

To Hilary on the same matter, one letter. Since your holiness has arisen.

Several letters to various persons.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

Pascasinus, a Sicilian bishop, learned in divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, venerable no less for his conduct than for his knowledge, is said to have presided in place of blessed Pope Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, in which, together with the holy fathers to the number of two hundred, he condemned the heretics Eutyches and Dioscorus.
