He published, besides, many others, which have not come to the notice of our reading. His little works, even while he yet lived and was always writing new [ones], were of such great authority that, by the ordinance of the prelates of England, they were publicly read in the churches. And since, in the heading of [his] homilies, they wrote by custom the name of "the venerable author Bede the presbyter"—not being able, while he lived, to call him otherwise—the title attributed once from the beginning has prevailed up to the present day, that he is called Bede the Venerable rather than Saint. For while [he was] living it was not permitted to name [him] otherwise (even if he were a saint). There are [those] who invent other reasons for this title "Venerable"—some from the inscription of [his] epitaph, others dreaming that Bede was blind. But they err, since Bede was neither blind, nor do we know such an epitaph inscribed on his tomb. And indeed, were I not consulting brevity, I would most easily refute these ravings. He dies under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 732, in the 15th indiction, in the 72nd year of his age, the day before the Kalends of June.

GREGORY, pope, the second, a Roman by country, sat in the chair of Peter after Constan[tine]…

249. ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

[Gregory II] …Constantine the pontiff, for 16 years [and] 9 months, a man otherwise learned and most holy, who ordained Boniface—an English monk, a Mainzer by nation—bishop. He wrote certain little works full of erudition, of which the following are reported: To the questions of Justinian, of Responses, 1 book; Against Leo Augustus, 1 book; To John, bishop of Constantinople, 1 book; Of letters to various [persons], 1 book. He dies under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 731, in the 14th indiction, the 3rd [day before] the Ides of February. To whom Gregory III succeeded.

BONIFACE, the first archbishop of Mainz, a Scot by nation, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, when he was a boy of five years, was offered by his parents to a monastery in England which is called Michael's; in which, devoting [his] study to letters and morals, he turned out a man both learned and most holy. Ordained presbyter, for love of pilgrimage for Christ, he came to Germany, and there, preaching the word of God, was ordained bishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory [II], and by his successor Gregory III was raised to archbishop and primate of Germany. Who, being an erudite man, taught the people committed to him not only by word but also by writings. Of his little works I have found only: Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; the Life of certain saints, 1 book. He dies preaching in Frisia, crowned with martyrdom, in the times of Pippin the emperor, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the 36th year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. Whose body blessed Lullus—whom he had ordained archbishop after himself—caused to be brought back to the monastery of Fulda, situated in Buchonia, and honorably buried.

VERUS, bishop of Seville, of the province of Baetica, where Isidore once held the prelacy, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, [subtle] in talent, [wrote]: Of letters to various [persons], 1 book; the Life of Saint Gallus in prose, 1 book; the same afterward in meter, 1 book. [He flourished under the same period.]

[The source here degenerates: the Boniface and Verus entries above are repeated several times over, with progressively worsening OCR and drifting dates (755, 750, 742, 740, 730); this is a print/scan loop, not distinct content, and is not re-translated.]

The Abbot of Spanheim ... of the Church for ten years, a most learned man, who, because of his learning and holiness of life, is rightly judged comparable to the best pontiffs. He translated the four books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory, the great pope, from Latin into Greek, and enlightened many who were ignorant of the Latin language by their reading. He also wrote, in his own vein, works in Latin that were very elegant and useful.

Letters to various persons, one book.

Among these there are several addressed to Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. He died under Pippin, two years before the martyrdom of the same Saint Boniface, in the year of the Lord 752, in the fifth indiction, on the Ides of March.

Alcuinus, or Albinus, monk and deacon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, English by nation, formerly a pupil of Saint Bede the priest, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in knowledge of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, was summoned from Britain by the emperor Charlemagne. He was held in such intimacy by him that he was called the emperor's beloved master; under his instruction the emperor himself strove to be initiated in all the disciplines of the liberal arts. He wrote many distinguished volumes, among which are reported:

On the Holy Trinity and the Faith, one book. To the glorious lord Charles, emperor.

To the Questions of Fredegisus, one book. To the most desired son.

To Eulalia, On the Nature of the Soul, one book. Dearest in Christ [unclear].

To Count Guido, On the Virtues, one book. To the most beloved son Guido.

Sentences on Genesis, one book.

On the Song of Songs. On Ecclesiastes, one book.

On the Gospel of John. On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.

Mirror of Little Ones, one book. To the venerable and in Christ.

Life of Saint Vedast the Bishop, one book. We believe in one God.

Letters to various persons, one book. In the writing of divine [unclear].

He is also said to have written many other things, which, however, have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the rule of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 770.

Isuardus, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, French by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, quick in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, by order of the emperor Charlemagne, after Eusebius, Jerome, and Bede, gathered from the writings of the ancients the deeds and passions of the holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins into a single volume of no small size, which we are accustomed to entitle:

Martyrology, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the same emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 790.

Paulus, monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the Order of Saint Benedict, Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, was held in great esteem by the emperor Charles because of his knowledge of letters. Formerly, before his conversion, he had been a deacon of the church of Aquileia and chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards; and, captured with him by Charles and taken into Gaul, he at length became a monk. He wrote not a few volumes, both in verse and in prose. Of these I have found only the following. At the request of Aldeburga, daughter of King Desiderius, he added:

To the Chronicle of Eutropius, one book.

The Deeds of the Bishops of Metz, one book.

The Life of Pope Gregory the First.

The Life of Saint Arnulph the Bishop, one book.

The Life of Saint Benedict, [unclear].

The Deeds of the Lombards, one book. The northern region.

Many hymns in various meters, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

By order of Charles he arranged histories and readings throughout the whole year, suitable for the several feasts of the saints. And he arranged and wrote many other things.

He flourished in the times of the same Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 780.

Adrian, the first pope, Roman by nation, after Stephen III sat in the pontificate for twenty-three years, a learned and most holy man, held in the greatest honor by the emperor Charles, established many things for the benefit of the Church, and the Felician heresy

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He condemned the heresy in a synod of three hundred and fifty bishops, by order of Emperor Charles, at Frankfurt. Since he was devoted to study and learned in the divine Scriptures, he abridged the thirteen books of letters of Saint Pope Gregory into two, selecting the more useful parts. He also wrote from his own [unclear] to Leo the Younger and Constantine his son, emperors at Constantinople.

On the veneration of images, one book. To Emperor Charles, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He died under Emperor Charlemagne in the year of the Lord 795, indiction 3, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, 7 Kalends of January.

Ruggandus, bishop of Metz, nephew by his sister of King Pippin, ennobled the nobility of his lineage by holy morals and by the study of the Scriptures; he was an outstanding venerator of the bodies of the holy martyrs, desiring to instruct in justice, by word and example, the clergy and people committed to him. For the clergy of the church of Metz he wrote a sufficiently instructive and useful

Rule of canons, one book. And certain other things.

He transferred from Rome into Francia the bodies of the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius. The body of Saint Nazarius was laid up in the monastery of Lorsch, then of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Worms.

He flourished under King Pippin, father of Emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 760.

Leo, the third pope, a Roman by nation, sat after Pope Adrian for twenty years; he was a man very learned in both divine and secular writings, and also most renowned for the holiness of his morals and life. He bound Charles, great both in name and deed, to the empire of the Romans, and transferred this dignity from the Greeks to the Franks. Among other things he wrote:

Letters to various persons, one book.

He died under Charles on the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord 816, indiction 9.

Haymo, third bishop of the church of Halberstadt in Saxony, formerly abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, once a hearer of the monk Alcuin, to whom Rabanus, then abbot of Fulda, composed twenty-two books On the Universe, was certainly a most learned man in every respect, a most acute interpreter of the divine Scriptures, and of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people. He was first a monk of the monastery of Fulda with Rabanus; afterward he was made the third abbot of Hersfeld; finally he was consecrated the third bishop of Halberstadt. He governed that church vigorously by word and example for thirteen years. He wrote almost innumerable little works; among them the following which we have set below are reported.

On the five books of Moses, one book. On Joshua, one book. [unclear], one book. On Ruth, one book. On Kings, one book. On Chronicles, one book. [unclear], one book. On Ezra and Nehemiah, one book. On Tobit, one book. On Esther, one book. On Judith, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On Job, three books. Isaiah the prophet, [unclear] one book. And it came to pass, says the blessed [unclear]. On Isaiah the prophet, one book. The word which came. [unclear], one book. The Lord, consulting for human [unclear]. On Jeremiah, one book. From Corinth, the metropolis [unclear]. On Ezekiel, one book. We read in Ecclesiastes [unclear]. On Daniel, seven books. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On the truth of books, one book. Since you are the only most holy [unclear]. On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the memory of Christian matters, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, letters, sermons, and various treatises, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 834, indiction 12. He was buried in the church of Saint Stephen at Halberstadt.

Claudius, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, once, as they say, a disciple of Bede in England, colleague of Albinus the Levite and abbot, a Scot by nation, a man very devoted to study and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular learning, practiced in verse and prose, composed many little works on the sacred volumes. Among these are reported:

On the five books of Moses [unclear]. On Judges also [unclear] one book. On

The Abbot of Sponheim, book I.

On the book of Ruth. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. And many other things. He flourished in Gaul under Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 800. Seven books.

Freculphus, bishop of Lisieux, in the province of Rouen, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, toward whom Rabanus, while still abbot, exercised his talent in many volumes, a man most devoted to and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and quite fit for teaching the people, distinguished no less by his conduct than by his learning, is said to have written certain excellent little works. Of these I have read only a large and distinguished volume, containing from the beginning of the world down to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ.

A history of deeds done, “While some [unclear] of time.”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He wrote the aforementioned work to Helisachar; in it he also unraveled the more difficult questions of the Scriptures, and in lucid speech wrote down the deeds of both the Jews and the Gentiles from the beginning of the world down to the Virgin’s giving birth. One book. He flourished under Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, of a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and instructed from youth in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He is said to have composed several little works in both styles, but they have not yet come into our hands. He, having been innocently sent into prison by the Emperor Louis on account of I know not what suspicion, composed the hymn “Gloria laus”; when, on Palm Sunday, as the emperor was passing by, he had sung it in a loud voice, it so pleased the emperor that he immediately allowed him to go free. He wrote, among other things, in various meters:

Hymns. Letters, one book.

He flourished under the empire of Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Einhard, chancellor of the Emperor Charlemagne, a German by nation, and afterward a monk of the Order of the holy father Benedict, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading; of these the following are reported. Imitating Bede, who abridged the Hebrew Psalter by extracting from it all the verses containing words of prayer, he himself abridged the Gallican Psalter, extracting from it all the verses containing words of prayer. He also wrote in his own person [unclear] of the emperor.

Letters to various persons. The Life of the Emperor Charles, one book. A history of the times. And certain other things.

He flourished under Charles and his son Louis, in the year of the Lord 820.

John Scotus, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, formerly hearer and disciple of the monk and most famous doctor Bede, colleague of Albinus, coming with the same [unclear] into Gaul, was held in great esteem by the Emperor Charles. Since he was a man most learned in all the Scriptures, he published very famous little works in clear speech, of which these are reported:

On the Gospel of Matthew. On human duties, one book. On the division of nature. He also composed many other things, which have not come to my notice.

He flourished in the times of the Emperor Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 800.

Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis at Paris, of the Order of the holy father Benedict, archchaplain of the sacred palace, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, published commentaries on the four books of Kings, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, excellent both in verse and in prose. He wrote to the Emperor Louis in both styles:

The Life of Saint Dionysius. And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis, son of the Emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 840.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, formerly a monk of Saint Denis at Paris, a man singularly learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular letters, conspicuous for wisdom and uprightness of morals, and most eloquent. He wrote several little works of authority not to be despised, of which I have found only the following. In the person of the Emperor Charlemagne he wrote very instructively:

To the church of Ravenna. The Life of Saint Remigius, bishop, one book. To Walo, bishop of Metz, one book. Of many letters, one book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis his son. Year [unclear]. Year [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 800. And he wrote many doctrinal works.

Amalarius Fortunatus, archbishop of Trier, German by nation, a monk of Luxeuil, and cardinal of the Roman Church, a learned and most eloquent man, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, was sent by Charles the Great, emperor, to Constantinople to the emperor Michael, and by his remarkable diligence and eloquence confirmed peace and friendship between them, as is contained in the deeds of the Treveri. He wrote, among other things:

On ecclesiastical offices, 1 book. “Satis et nimium quidem.” To Louis on the same matter, 4 books. On the mysteries of the Mass, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under the emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 813, in the sixth indiction, in about the sixteenth year of his episcopate.

Angelomus, a monk of Luxeuil, of the order of St. Benedict, a man endowed with a noble talent for expounding the divine Scriptures, so that, in comparison with him, the ancients seem not to have expounded what he himself expounded, and not ignorant of secular writings either, at the command of Drogo, bishop of Metz, who was the son of Charles the Great and brother of the emperor Louis, wrote a most excellent work, of such a kind as I do not remember having read elsewhere in the holy Scriptures:

On the Books of Kings, 4 books. “Igitur cum a quampluribus.” To Lothar on the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Priusquam augustale decus.” On the divine offices, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis and his son Lothar, in the year of the Lord 830.

Rabanus Maurus, sixth archbishop of Mainz, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fulda of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, from the city of Fulda in Buchonia, once a hearer of Albinus the Englishman, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, and most subtle poet, to whom, that I may speak without envy, neither Italy bore anyone similar nor Germany an equal. For while still a young man he put on the monk’s habit in the monastery of Fulda, and advanced wonderfully both in morals and in knowledge; whence he was consecrated the fourth abbot of the same monastery, and for twenty-four years presided by word and example over the sheep committed to him, and composed almost innumerable little works of Scripture. At length, offended by the wickedness of his monks, who said that he was too intent upon writings and neglected temporal matters, the devil doing this among them, they conceived displeasure against him, scandalized by him in that by which they ought most of all to have been edified. Therefore, giving place to anger, and not consenting to remain longer with ungrateful sheep, he abandoned the monastery and its inhabitants and moved to the emperor Louis, with whom he also remained for many days. But the monks, led by penitence, sent a delegation to him and begged that he return to the monastery, but they did not obtain it. He therefore remained with the emperor until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz; appointed in his place, he was in charge of the aforesaid church of Mainz for nine years. Having also held a synod, he established many things for the [unclear] of the faithful. He wrote while still established in the monastery of Fulda, both in verse and in prose:

On the book of Ruth. On Chronicles. On Ezra and Nehemiah. On Judith. On Esther. On Job. On the Proverbs of Solomon. On the Song of Songs. On the book of Wisdom. On Ecclesiasticus.

4 books. “In principio,” etc. [unclear]. 4 books. “Exodus exitus dici.” 4 books. “Numerorum librum multi.” 4 books. “Sequentis libri.” 1. “Levi.” 4 books. “Filii Israel castra mo-.” 2 books. “Domino beatissimo vereque.” 2 books. “Post mortem Iosue.” 1 book. “Scrutantibus ergo histo-.” 4 books. “Fuit vir,” etc. “Dicamus.” 3 books. On Tobit, 1 book. 7 books. “Domine electe et merito.” 1 book. “Liber Hester quem he-.” 1 book. On the Psalms, 1 book. 10 books. On Ecclesiastes.

[unclear] On Isaiah-

254 The Abbot of Sponheim

On Isaiah the prophet, 8 books. On Jeremiah, 20 books. On Ezekiel, 3 books. On Daniel, 12 books. On Maccabees, 3 books. On the Gospel of Matthew, 8 books. On the Gospel of Luke, 3 books. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. On all the epistles of Paul, 23 books. On the canonical epistles, 7 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. On the praise of the holy cross, 2 books. To Bishop Haymo, On the Universe, 22 books. On universal nature, 1 book. On the instruction of clerics, 3 books. On the divine offices, 1 book. On computus, a dialogue, 1 book. To Bishop Reginbald, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book. “Because you, venerable father.” On questions of the canons, 1 book. On the blessings of the patriarchs, 1 book. Of sermons, almost innumerable, 1 book. 19

He also published many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under the princes Louis and Lothar, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban near Mainz, not without a reputation for holiness; I have read his epitaph in nearly twenty ornate verses.

Bellator, a priest of a certain church, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, distinguished in talent and speech, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters. He is said to have expounded many volumes on the holy Scriptures, in which he splendidly displayed his talent. Among the rest there is extant an outstanding volume of his, which he published at the request of friends:

On the Book of Wisdom, 7 books. I have found nothing concerning the others.

He is said to have flourished in the times of the emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Strabus, a monk of Fulda, a German by nation, formerly the pupil and scribe of Abbot Rabanus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in the studies of secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in speech. He wrote not a few little works in exposition of the sacred volumes, in which, showing himself a learned man, he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Therefore, imitating his master, Abbot Rabanus, he wrote:

On Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book. On Leviticus, 1 book. A very brief work on the Book of Leviticus.

And many other things. Finally, this Strabus is remembered as the first to have compiled, from the sayings of the holy fathers, the gloss on the whole Bible which is now called the Ordinary Gloss; others afterward enlarged it by adding many sayings of the fathers.

On Three Questions, 1 book. And certain letters, as well as other things.

He flourished under the emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Lupus Servatus, priest, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, is read to have written eight books on the epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans, was a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and, according to the age of his time, abundantly skilled in secular letters. He wrote some little works of his talent, of which very few have come to my knowledge. There is extant a volume of his:

The Hierarchy, the books of Dionysius, 4 books. He wrote on the same, 4 books.

And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 830.

John, called Erigena, a monk, learned in the divine writings, most learned in the discipline of secular letters, fully instructed in Greek and Latin speech, subtle in talent, ordered in discourse, at the command of Charles, son of Louis and brother of Lothar, emperors, [unclear] the laws of Charles the Great and Louis, which I have seen as follows, namely:

Ansegisus, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, afterward archbishop of Sens, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in speech and talent, arranged and compiled, for the use of the catholic Church, the imperial [unclear]:

Ecclesiastical Statutes of Charles, 2 books. “Our Lord Jesus reigning.”

Laws

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Secular laws of the same, 2 books. “Concerning peace we admonish ...” Ecclesiastical statutes of Louis, 2 books. “To all of you either by sight ...” Secular laws of the same, 2 books. “If slaves through contumacy ...” Besides these he published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Lothar, son of Louis, in the year 840.

Amulus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, learned from reading the ancients, and also not moderately instructed in secular letters, distinguished in both the Hebrew and the Latin tongue, keen and forceful in intellect, scholastic and orderly in speech. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which I have read only the notable work to Charles: Against the Jews, 1 book. “Concerning detesting the Jews ...” Of the rest I have as yet seen none. He flourished under Louis, son of Charlemagne, in the year 830.

Bertram, priest and monk, very skilled in the divine writings and excellently learned in the letters of the secular disciplines, subtle in intellect and renowned in speech, and no less distinguished in life than in doctrine. He wrote many excellent little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. To King Charles, brother of the emperor Lothar, he wrote a commendable work: On the Body and Blood of the Lord, 1 book. On Predestination [unclear]. He flourished in the times of the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 830. Letters to various persons, 2 books.

Turpin, archbishop of Reims, friend and secretary of the great emperor Charles, a man learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular letters, having an intellect exercised in verse and prose, advocate of the poor, beloved by God in life and conduct; he declares that, together with Charles, with his own hands and arms he often fought against the Saracens [unclear], 1 book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 860. The Deeds of Charlemagne, 2 books. He flourished under the same Charles and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 830. The same, 1 book.

Anastasius, keeper and most sagacious restorer of the apostolic library, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, very skilled in Greek and Latin expression, is said to have composed some little works, but nothing has come into our hands. He translated many volumes of the Greeks into Latin. For, by order of Nico[laus?] [unclear], 1 book. And many other things. Lives of Many Fathers, 1 book.

Nicholas, the first pope, Roman by birth, sat in the pontificate after Benedict [unclear], 1 book. The seventh universal synod [unclear]. One hierarchy of Dionysius, 1 book. A book of letters to various persons. Lives of Many Fathers, 4 books. He wrote, among other things, an excellent volume in the person of his pontificate. He died under Lothar or Louis II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 869, in the second indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of December. And also other things. The Life of St. Gregory, the first pope, 2 books. He flourished under Charles the Bald, emperor, in the year of the Lord 870.

Notger, bishop of Liege, formerly abbot of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the holy father Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, among all of his time, most learned in the disciplines of secular letters; a distinguished philosopher, poet, and musician, and no less venerable for holiness than for knowledge. He wrote many little works, both in meter and in prose, of which few have come into our hands. For I have read only the volume that he entitled Sequences, which he had written while still a monk, in a distinguished style, a large volume, which contains: “The sum of holiness [unclear] ...” Prologue or preface, 1 letter, 1 book. Sequen-

Abbot of Spanheim

The Sequentiary, however, thus, one book. On music and symphony, one book. On the expositors of sacred Scripture, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Of the other works which he composed, nothing has come to the notice of our reading. Pope Nicholas I approved the Sequences of this most learned man and ordered them to be sung at Masses. Because of the distinction of his learning and life he was first made abbot, and then, in his old age, consecrated bishop; tenth in order, he presided over the government of the church of Liège, under the emperor Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 850. Under him he also died, not without a reputation for sanctity.

CHRISTIANUS, also called Druthmarus, monk and priest of Corbie, of the order of Benedict of holy memory of Cassino, an Aquitanian by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and imbued with Greek and Latin speech, coming from Aquitaine into Gaul, made his name known by writing. Of his little works I have thus far merited only a great and distinguished work, written in plain language to the monks of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, standing under one abbot in the diocese of the church of Liège:

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. He did not make this title: “Euan.” Of the others I have seen nothing.

In the prologue to the exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew he also promised that he would write on the other Evangelists, and this he is said to have done, but it is unknown to us.

WANDELBERT, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm, of the order of St. Benedict, of the diocese of Trier, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently instructed in secular letters, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote not a few volumes both in metre and in prose, of which I have seen only a certain one addressed to Abbot Marcuard:

The Life of St. Goar the priest, one book. The Miracles of the same, one book. A Martyrology in metre, one book. He flourished under the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 860.

ALMANNUS, monk of the monastery of Hautvillers, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote various little works both in metre and in prose, by which he made his name known also to posterity. And because in his time Francia was being laid waste by the Normans, after the example of the prophecy of Jeremiah he lamented the desolation of that same land and of his monastery in a fourfold alphabetic composition, one book. The Life of St. Vinardus the bishop, one book. The Life of St. Helena Augusta, one book. The Translation of the same. On Sobriety, in metre, one book. The Life of St. Amandus, in metre, one book. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Charles III, in the year of the Lord 890.

MILORD, monk of the monastery of St. Amand, of the order of the divine Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in every respect, an orator, poet, and distinguished musician, and no less venerable for honorable conduct than for knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote not a few volumes both in verse and in unbound discourse. Of these the following especially are current, addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald:

Letters to various persons, one book. The Life of St. Amandus, in metre, one book. He flourished in the times of Charles the Second, emperor, surnamed the Bald, in the year of the Lord 870, and composed many excellent works.

HUGOBALD, monk of the monastery of Elno, of the order of St. Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned both in divine writings and in secular letters, in music, poetry, philosophy, and the other arts of humanity second to none in his time, as the many works written by him in both styles testify. Of these I have so far found only the following: addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald, a remarkable work of 136 verses, in which all the words begin with one letter, C: “Carmina clarisone Calvis cantate camenae,” as it is entitled.

On the Praise of Bald Men, one book. Carmina clarisone cal., one book. On the Art of Music, one book. The Deeds of St. Lebuinus. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also described the lives of many saints in ornate eloquence, and composed songs in their honor with sweet and regular melody. He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles the Bald, 880.

REMIGIUS, monk of Auxerre, of the order of St. Benedict, and afterwards, as they report, bishop of the same city, a man most learned in divine and human writings, a distinguished writer in verse and prose, teacher of St. Odo, the first abbot of Cluny, renowned in life and doctrine. He published many volumes in both styles, of which the following are current.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Song of Songs, one book: "Divine prophecy [unclear]." On the whole Psalter, one book. On the canon of the Mass, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the festivals of the saints, one book. On the divine offices, one book. Also several sermons, one book. To the Bishop of the Aedui, one book. He also composed other works, both on sacred letters and on secular writings, expounding Donatus and the old authors, which are held by many. He flourished under the emperor Charles the Bald, in the year of the Lord 880.

Constantinus, a monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, an African by nation, a man very zealous in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, especially in philosophy and medicine, fully instructed in Greek, Latin, and Arabic expression. He wrote many small works in medicine, which are valued among physicians. He also translated many volumes of the ancient physicians from Greek and Arabic into Latin, which he prefaced with his own prefaces and letters. Of his small works I have seen these:

Universal diets, one book: "What first compelled." Particular diets, one book: "More fully in the first book." On medicinal weights, one book: "Medicinal weights." Also on urines, one book. As for the rest of his volumes, which he both wrote and translated in great number, I do not recall that any has come into our hands. They are better known to physicians.

Ambrosius Ansbertus, monk and priest of the order of Saint Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, gentle in disposition and sweet in speech, published many commentaries on the sacred volumes, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to posterity. Yet few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following:

On the Song of Songs, one book: "The gift of wisdom with Sa[unclear]." Also on the Psalter, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, ten books. On cupidity, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished under the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 890.

Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, nobly instructed in Greek and Latin expression, acute in intellect, composed in speech. He wrote not a few small works in verse and prose, of which I have found only the following. To Placidus, abbot of our order, a distinguished work:

On the sacrament of the altar, one book: "Whoever among Catholics." The life of Saint Adalhard the bishop, one book. On the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah, one book. He also translated some things from Greek into Latin, and composed many others.

Ericus, monk of the order of Saint Benedict, of the monastery of the city of Auxerre, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, was an outstanding teacher in delivering homilies to the people. He wrote clearly in verse:

Homilies to the people, one book.

Several sermons and letters. He also composed many other works in both styles, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished around the times of the emperor Charles the Fat, in the year of the Lord 880.

Otfridus, a monk of the monastery of Weissenburg, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, once a hearer and disciple of Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished poet, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote many splendid small works both in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. After the example also of the great emperor Charles he attempted to reduce the barbarousness of the German tongue to grammatical rules, which he partly accomplished. Hence those things which he wrote in his native language cannot easily be read and understood in our age, even by a man however skilled in the German tongue. Of his small works the following survive. To Luitbert, the eighth archbishop of the church of Mainz, a great and distinguished work on the Gospel, which he entitled:

The grace of Theotista, one book: "By the height of dignity, grace." To King Louis, one book: "To Louis of the easterners." To Bishop Solomon, one book: "To Solomon the bishop, Otfrid." To the monks of Saint Gall, one book: "Otfrid of Weissenburg." On the Psalter, three volumes, one book. On the Last Judgment

Abbot of Sponheim

On the joys of the heavenly kingdom, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Poems of various kinds, one book. Lost through the negligence of copyists, and erased and torn by the ignorance of monks, they have not come down to me. He flourished under the emperors Louis, Lothair, and Charles, succeeding one another, in the year of the Lord 870.

Adrevald, also called Albert, a monk of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man distinguished on every side and most learned, made his name known by writing, when for the edification of simple brothers he composed many volumes on the holy Scriptures. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, from the time of the translation of the body of St. Benedict from the monastery of Cassino to the monastery of Fleury down to the time of Odo, king of the Franks, a history containing the matter in lucid speech. The Miracles of St. Benedict, one book. And many other things, which, however, I have not seen. He flourished in the times of the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 890.

Odo, first abbot of Cluny, of the Order of St. Benedict, once a pupil of Remigius, monk of Auxerre, a man diligently trained and learned in the holy Scriptures, an outstanding restorer of the fallen order of the father Benedict, shone forth no less renowned for holiness than for erudition. He was a notable musician, arch-cantor of the church of Tours, who, after hearing the fame of Berno, the most holy abbot of Gigny, entered the order under him; afterwards appointed abbot of Cluny, he adorned the order with great holiness. Since he was an outstanding preacher of homilies, he composed many sermons for the brothers. He also wrote, among the other works of his talent: The Life of Saint Gerard, one book. Praises of St. Martin, one book. A brief chronicle, one book. He also composed various hymns and chants in honor of the saints in a sweet, regulated melody. At the request of the brothers, too, he abridged the books of blessed Pope Gregory on Job and brought them together into one volume. He flourished in the times of the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 920.

Rathbod, the fourteenth bishop of Utrecht, a German by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, and most holy in life and conduct, shone with many miracles both while alive and after death. Nanno, a most learned philosopher, had instructed him in all humane letters; he was advocate in the palace of King Charles the Fat, afterwards entered a monastery, and finally, as we have said, was consecrated bishop. He governed the church of Utrecht energetically for seventeen years during the heavy persecution by the Danes. He wrote several excellent little works, of which these are reported: Praises of Saint Martin, one book. Praises of St. Boniface the bishop, one book. On Saint Amalberga, one book. Homiletic sermons, one book. Flowers on St. Willibrord, one book. He also composed a complete office on the translation of St. Martin, and various chants in honor of the saints. He died under Louis, son of the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 917, in the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate. He was buried at Deventer, where previously he had been accustomed to reside in his episcopate.

Aurelian, a cleric of the church of Reims, very diligent in the holy Scriptures, nobly learned in secular letters, an excellent and notable musician in his time. He wrote to Bernard, arch-cantor and later bishop, an outstanding volume on the rules of modulations, which they call tones or tenors, and on the names of [unclear], whose title is: The Regular Tonary, one book. He wrote certain other things. He flourished around the times of the emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 900.

Regino, abbot of the monastery of Prum in the diocese of Trier, of the Order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular letters, easily held the first place among the teachers of Germany and Gaul in his time. He wrote little works of great authority, of which I have found only the following. To Albero, first bishop of Metz, containing especially the deeds of the Franks and Germans from the nativity of Christ down to the year 98 of the same. He wrote a History or Chronicle, [unclear] books. On Ecclesiastical Discipline, [unclear] books. “First one must inquire.” Of the rest I have as yet seen nothing. He wrote the aforesaid work, which is entitled On Ecclesiastical Discipline and the Christian Religion, at the command of Rathbod, archbishop of Trier, which

On Ecclesiastical Writers

which he compiled from the decrees of the holy fathers and of the general councils in two books, and clearly distinguished, according to custom, into nearly nine hundred chapters by rubrics. He flourished under Emperor Arnold, in the year of the Lord 910.

Hildovinus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the order of St Benedict, was first bishop of Liège; then, driven from there, he came to Hugh, king of Italy, to whom he was joined by a line of kinship. By him he was made bishop of Verona, and finally, after Lambert, was made archbishop of Milan. He ordained Ratherius the monk as bishop for the church of Verona. He was a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures. While he was still abbot, at the request of the brothers, he wrote [unclear], one book; Sermons to the Brothers, one book; and certain other things. He flourished under Hugh, king of Italy, in the times of Conrad, emperor of the Romans and Germans, in the year of the Lord 920.

Ratherius, formerly a monk of the monastery of Lobbes, after Hildovinus bishop of Verona, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in the arts of humanity, which they call liberal; simple in spirit, gentle in disposition, and scholastic in speech. With Bishop Hildovinus he came to King Hugh in Italy, and after Hildovinus’s transfer to the archiepiscopate of the church of Milan, he was appointed bishop of the city of Verona. Not long afterward he was expelled from there by Hugh, for the reason that he had admitted Arnold, duke of Bavaria, Hugh’s enemy, into Verona; driven out, he was banished to Pavia. At length, having returned to his church, again [unclear]; I do not know whether they will be able to please readers no less than to profit them. Of these, the following are reported: On His First Exile, one book; another, concerning the second, entitled Phrenesis, one book; another, which is called Inefficax, one book; On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book; Against the Anthropomorphites, one book; Agonisticon, that is, of Preliminaries, six books; also a Confession, one book; Life of St Ursmar of Lobbes, one book. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge. And finally, as Sigebert the monk writes, he was made bishop of Liège, and was also driven from there. He flourished in the times of Henry, the first emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 950.

Stephen, formerly a cleric of the church of Metz, bishop of Liège after Franco, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, magnificently skilled in secular letters, and venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge. He wrote several little works of no contemptible usefulness, through which his name became known to posterity: To Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, Life of St Lambert, one book; To Rupert, bishop of Metz, one book; and certain other things. He also wrote the chant on the Holy Trinity from Alcuin, which we use on the octave of Pentecost; on the finding of St Stephen; and the nocturnal chant on St Lambert, bishop and martyr. All these, together with certain others, he composed in an authentic and sweet melody. He flourished in the times of Louis, son of Emperor Arnold, in the year of the Lord 910.

Radulphus of Flavigny, a monk of the order of St Benedict, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in his time, most learned in all letters of humanity; subtle in talent, profound in judgment, sweet, adorned, and eloquent in speech; acute and very distinguished in expounding sacred volumes. He wrote two great and distinguished volumes: On Leviticus, twenty books, “When at one time there was speech concerning Judah”; On the Epistles of Paul, one book; History of the Franks, one book; also a brief Chronicle. Besides these he published many other things, which had not come to my knowledge. There are some who write that he was a monk of the monastery of Fulda in Germany.

Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of St Michael, of the order of our lord father Benedict, a man [unclear], acquired a reputation for his knowledge and conduct. For he wrote many distinguished little works. Of these I have found only the following: On the Rule of St Benedict, one book, “When the crowds of very many”; Diadema of Monks, one book, “This little book”; On the Whole Psalter, one book; On the Epistles and Gospels throughout the Year, two books; also Several Sermons, one book. But concerning his other little works I have nowhere been able to find anything. It is said, however, that he published many commentarial treatises on the divine Scriptures. But he expounded Donatus Major and explained many authors of secular letters.

Abbot of Sponheim

Widukind, a monk of the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very well instructed in secular letters, quick in talent, clear in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote many distinguished little works in an alternating style. Of these I have so far found only the following. From the beginning of the Saxons down to the death of Otto, the first emperor, he wrote to Mechthild, his daughter:

A History of the Saxons, 3 books. Flore virginali cum ma [unclear]. The Deeds of Otto I, 1 book. The Passion of Thecla the Virgin, in verse, 2 books. The Life of Paul the First Hermit, 1 book.

He flourished under Otto, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 950.

Liutprand, deacon of the church of Ticinum, Italian by nation, born from the city of Pavia, formerly scribe and secretary of Berengar, king of Italy, a man very learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, sharp and forceful in talent, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, no less excellent in verse than in prose. He is said to have written several distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Driven out of Italy by King Berengar, he came into Germany and stayed at Frankfurt. He wrote a notable historical work on his own time, containing the tyranny of that Berengar; this, as if in recompense for the injuries received from him, he entitled:

The Antapodosis, that is, Retribution, 7 books. Regnantibus, imo senien [unclear].

Of the others I have seen nothing. He wrote the aforesaid volume to [Recemund?], bishop of the church of Elvira in Spain; in it he sometimes uses verse, sometimes Greek speech, interspersing many things about the deeds of the Germans.

He flourished under Otto I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 950.

Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures by constant reading and study, exceptionally learned in secular disciplines, and also distinguished in life and conduct, was proved worthy even to the crown of martyrdom: while he was preaching the word of God in Vasconia, he was made a witness of the Christian faith by the shedding of his blood. He wrote:

On the Reckoning of Victorius, 1 book. Additions to the same, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Otto I, in the year of the Lord 970.

Robert, king of France, noble, brave, just, learned, and religious, rightly receives a place among ecclesiastical writers, since he composed chants and sweet responsories in regular melody for the honor of the catholic Church. In humane letters, especially in music, he was most learned; and he was of such religion that he sang the canonical hours in church with the clerics, and outside, at home, read them with his own people. He was of such compassion and mercy toward the poor that, sometimes stripping himself of his own garments, he many times covered their nakedness. A book never left his hands, so much so that, sitting on the tribunal amid the noise of judicial cases, he would have the Psalter open in his lap. Hence he is read to have shone with miracles after death. His is that well-known sequence which is sung on the days of Pentecost:

On the Holy Spirit, namely, “Come, Holy Spirit.” A responsory on Saint Peter, namely, “Cornelius the Centurion.” On the Nativity of the Lord, namely, “Judaea Jerusalem no” [unclear]. And that Alleluia, namely, “Deliver me from my enemies.” And many other things which I do not know.

The responsory “Cornelius the Centurion,” when the supreme pontiff was celebrating Mass at Rome, he offered with great devotion to Saint Peter on the altar at the time of the offertory. The ministers of the altar, hurrying up, thought that the rich king had offered gold of great weight; but, finding a written and notated sheet, they marveled, praising the talent and devotion of the prince. Therefore the pope decreed, at the request of the clerics and in memory of the most holy king, that this responsory should thereafter be sung in honor of Saint Peter.

He flourished under Otto II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 980.

Ammonius, a monk of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, French by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters. He is said to have composed several little works both in verse and in prose, but they have by no means come into our hands. He afterwards wrote one volume to the monk Renald:

On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. Berno the abbot

On Ecclesiastical Writers

the abbot of Reichenau mentions [him] in a certain book to Archbishop Aribo. He wrote a notable dialogue under the person of his Adelbold, a cleric and monk then living at Rome and later bishop of Utrecht, of whom we must speak presently, entitled [unclear].

On the [unclear] of the Church, one book. The Life of St. [Ursmar?], in verse, one book. To Hugh, on Questions, one book. On the Divine Offices, one book. The Deeds of the Bishops of [Liège?], one book. On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. And many other things. He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Flodoardus, a monk of Reims of the Order of St. Benedict, learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by study of which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these there is said to be a distinguished work from the founding of the city of Reims, which, they record, the soldiers of Remus, [after Remus had been killed by?] his brother Romulus and [they had been] driven out, built in memory of their lord and so named, down to his own times; in it, interweaving many things about the holy martyrs and other matters and deeds, he chose to give the volume this title:

The Deeds of the Bishops of Reims, one book. Also Lives of Many Saints, one book. Other [lives] of several saints, one book. Songs in honor of the saints. And certain other things. He flourished in much religious discipline in the times of the emperor Otto [unclear], in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, the nineteenth after St. Boniface the martyr, for whom Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, wrote a treatise On the Advent of the Lord, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures: after holding a synod at Seligenstadt with Burchard, bishop of Worms, he established many useful things, which are contained in authentic writings. He also wrote, among other works of his talent:

On the Fifteen Gradual Psalms, one book. To Abbot Berno, one letter. And certain letters to others. He died under the emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1023.

Burchardus, from a monk of the monastery of Lobbes of the Order of St. Benedict [became] bishop of Worms, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters. While he was still a monk, he kept a public school of monks at Lobbes, in which he instructed [unclear], together with others, in both literatures. He wrote, from the opinions of the holy Fathers, of general councils, and of various pontiffs, a great and notable work after Isidore, namely:

Decrees, which he divided into twenty books. “In the New Testament first...” Letters to Various Persons, one book. He flourished under the holy emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very nobly instructed in secular letters, a musician and poet second to none in his time, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote certain excellent volumes both in verse and prose; of these I have found only the following. For Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, he composed an excellent and useful volume:

On Music, or on Tones, one book. “Every regular [unclear]...” On the Instruments of Music, one book. “The musician is not to be content...” On the Advent of the Lord, to Aribo, one book. “Of the highest dignity...” Also On the Office of the Mass, one book. On the Fast of the Four Seasons, one book. On the Saturday Fast, one book. On the Measurement of the Monochord, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He published many other things besides, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of St. Henry, the first emperor but the second king, because the first did not receive the crown of empire, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Adelboldus, bishop of Utrecht, formerly, as they say, a monk of Lobbes of the Order of St. Benedict, under whose person Abbot Heriger composed the dialogue On the Advent of the Lord, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, held in great esteem at the court of St. Henry the emperor; no less by arms than by learning he [unclear] the unbelievers. He wrote,

The Life

The Abbot of Sponheim

The Life of St. Henry the Emperor, one book. On the praise of the holy cross. On the praise of blessed Mary. But he also published some other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1027, in the tenth indiction, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

Osbert, a monk of Canterbury, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in the art of music, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published various treatises in both kinds of literature, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to posterity. He wrote, among other things: The Life of St. Dunstan, archbishop, one book. Also On Music, one book. He flourished in the times of St. Henry the emperor, in the year of the Lord 1026.

Odilo, fourth abbot of Cluny, of the Order of St. Benedict, a holy and learned man, presiding over the monastery for fifty-six years, led the souls of many to Christ by word and example; Peter Damian, bishop and cardinal of Ostia, described his life, full of virtues and miracles, in a lucid discourse. He composed for the edification of his brothers: Elegant Sermons, one book. He died under Henry II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1048, in the first indiction, in the eighty-seventh year of his age, on the first day of the month of January.

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned of teachers in all his time, a distinguished poet and dialectician, presiding for many years over the public school, produced very many highly learned hearers. In life also most holy, he is read to have shone with many miracles. Among other things, he is said to have written: Letters to various persons, one book. In Praises of St. Mary, one book. Various hymns and prayers. And certain other devotional works. He flourished in the times of Henry, the first king, in the year of the Lord 1016.

Bruno, bishop of Wurzburg, paternal cousin of Conrad II, emperor, German by nation, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, who, because of the excellence of his merits, was inscribed in the catalogue of the saints and is held to be the special patron of East Francia. He gathered from the writings of the ancient fathers a fine exposition: On the Whole Psalter, one book, "Blessed is the man who has not gone away." Whether he wrote anything else I do not know. He died under Henry II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1045, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, zealous for regular discipline and an active governor, so that he could be considered a useful shepherd of the sheep committed to him by word and example. He wrote for the edification of his brothers fine and elegant Sermons, one book. He also published some other works, which have not yet come to our knowledge.

Guido, monk and abbot of the monastery of the Cross of St. Leufredus, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, by homeland an Aretine, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular disciplines, an outstanding dialectician and musician. In this too he is to be preferred to the rest: that even boys and girls may learn unknown songs more easily by themselves through his rule on their hand than through the voice of a master or by any instrument. He wrote, among the other little works of his intellect, against Berengar, cleric of the church of Tours: On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. Also On Music, two books, "Therefore those who [unclear] our discipline." And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Egelnoth, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, most holy in life and conduct, a most merciful advocate of the poor. At his exhortation Cnut, king of England, made many alms, especially to the church of Chartres, over which the most learned man Fulbert, bishop, then presided, of whom we have made mention above. He is said to have written, to the honor of almighty God, a fine work: In Praise of St. Mary, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1039.

Adelmann the grammarian, from a cleric of Liege bishop of Brescia, formerly a hearer of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, a philosopher and dialectician famous in his time, excelling in verse and prose. He wrote in both

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and certain little works worthy to be commended for their style, of which few have come to our knowledge for reading. He wrote to Berengar of Tours, formerly his fellow pupil under Fulbert, then beginning to err and to teach dogmatically, correcting him at great length and in friendly fashion.

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. “I call you a collector.” One book of letters to various persons. He is said besides to have written many other things, both in verse and in prose, which I have not seen. He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Hermann, who was called Contractus, a monk of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, son of the count of Veringen in Swabia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most thoroughly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, astronomer, rhetorician, musician, second to none in his time, and highly skilled in the three languages Greek, Latin, and Arabic. He wrote many distinguished volumes in verse and prose, of which I have found only the following, namely:

On Music, one book. On the Monochord, one book. “In considering the mono-.” On the Six Ages of the World, one book. “The first is of this world.” On the Construction of the Astrolabe, one book. “Therefore in measuring under-.” On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, one book. “Whoever of astronomical-.” On Eclipses, one book. On Computation, one book. On the Squaring of the Circle, one book. On the Conflict of Rhythmomachy, one book. “He who is skilled in arithmetic-.” On Physiognomy, one book. “Of a distinguished prudent man.” Lives of Several Saints, one book. Various hymns and sequences. He also composed, in sweet and regular melody, most beautiful chants and sequences. Among these is that very sweet one concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, “Salve regina,” and “Alma redemptoris mater,” and others, of which the number is abundant. He also translated into Latin some volumes of Greek philosophers and Arab astrologers. In his limbs he was, in accordance with his name, contracted, but always persevering in thanksgiving; hence he deserved to be inwardly wonderfully consoled and enlightened by the most blessed Virgin, Mother of God. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord [1040?].

Guimundus, archbishop of Aversa, formerly a monk of the monastery of the Cross of St. Leufredus, of the order of the most holy father Benedict, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, perfected in secular letters, and also not ignorant of secular literature. He wrote certain volumes in Latin [unclear] in the time of the astronomers. In his limbs he was, in accordance with his name, [unclear]. I have found only the following prose works, namely:

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. “To the matter in these times.” And certain other works unseen by us.

Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, formerly a monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the order of St. Benedict, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfected in secular letters, and also of very celebrated reputation among secular writers. He wrote certain little works [unclear], by which he made known to posterity the name also of profound understanding and his talent [unclear]. Of these there survive:

On the Union of the Word of God and Man, one book. On the Four Humors of the Body, one book. He also composed other volumes in every branch of literature, which have by no means come down to us.

Campanus, a Lombard by nation, philosopher and astronomer, in the opinion of all most celebrated in his time, keen in talent, scholastic in speech, and also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, an outstanding calculator and computist. He published not a few works of his talent, of which I have read the following, a great and distinguished work:

On Ecclesiastical Computation, one book. “One of [them] asked me from-.” On the Construction of the Quadrant, one book. “You must know that the circle.” He also composed many other things in astronomy, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Helpericus, a monk of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, most instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, distinguished astronomer, subtle in talent, composed in speech. He wrote both in verse

The Abbot of Spanheim some little works in verse as well as in prose. Of these I have been able to find only a distinguished work:

On ecclesiastical computation, one book. “When with our brothers [unclear]...” Also On Music, one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1069.

Berthorius, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and nobly educated in the discipline of secular letters, an eminent philosopher and physician. Before his conversion he is said to have written many little works in his own faculty. But afterward changing his study, and having been made a physician of souls, he wrote for the edification of his brothers:

Elegant Sermons, one book.

He also published other various treatises, knowledge of which has not reached me.

Rogerius, a monk of the Order of St. Benedict, to whom Guimundus of Aversa, bishop, while still established in the monastery, is said to have written three books Against Berengar; a learned man, educated both in divine and in secular letters, described, for the edification of many, in a sufficiently lucid style:

The Life of Bruno, Bishop of Cologne, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year 1040.

Algerus, from a scholastic a monk of Corbie in Saxony, German by nation, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man trained by constant study in the sacred writers, rich in reading of the ancients, and magnificently learned in secular books, cautious in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, strong in verse and prose. He wrote in a very polished style a notable volume:

On the Sacrament of the Altar, two books. “Because the saints concerning the body...” On Grace and Free Will, one book. “It must be known that free...” And certain letters.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come into our hands.

Albertus, a monk of Metz, of the Order of St. Benedict, French by nation, a man skilled in the Holy Scriptures through continual exercise, and not ignorant of the arts of humanity, which we call liberal, in order to transmit his name to posterity, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised. Of these there is said to be a short but useful work, containing the history of the events of his own time, which he dedicated:

To the Bishop of Metz, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Eckebertus, cleric of the church of Liege, German by nation, elegantly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters. He wrote some little works both in verse and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives a volume composed in elegant verse, which he entitled:

On Rustic Riddles, one book. “On the same matter, greater than others...”

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Leo, Pope IX, formerly bishop of the city of the Leuci, which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, sat in the chair of Peter after Damasus for seven years. Previously called Bruno, a learned and holy man. He wrote some distinguished little works, in which the grace of expression and sublimity of thought are deservedly commended. Of these, to Constantine the monk [unclear]:

Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book. To the Patriarch of Constantinople, two books. Letters to Various Persons, three books. To the bishops of Africa and Egypt.

He died under Henry the third king, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the seventh indiction, shining with many miracles.

Humbertus, a monk of Toul, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular letters, lofty in intellect and eloquence, whom Pope Leo IX, because of his knowledge of letters, brought forward and ordained cardinal bishop. Sent by him to Constantinople to refute the heresies of the Greeks, by God’s aid he refuted and defeated Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk, in the presence of Emperor Constantine and Patriarch Michael, so that he anathematized his book which he had written against the Church of the Latins and with his own hand threw it into the fire to be burned. And whatever he said or did there in disputation, he wrote out lucidly under the name of the Roman and the Constantinopolitan:

In the Manner of Dialogues, one book. He also wrote certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Ansel-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

ANSELM, a monk of Reims, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Frenchman by nationality, a man having a mind trained in the divine scriptures, wrote certain small works of his own study, which have not yet come into my hands. And among other things he gathered into one volume the deeds of Pope Leo IX performed throughout Gaul in councils and assemblies, in order to make known with how great authority he held a synod at Reims, or in other cities; with how great industry and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what apportionment he corrected sinners; and how divine power worked together with him, as was sufficiently clear in one case of the Synod of Reims, where, when the bishop of Freising acted contumaciously against apostolic authority, by God’s vengeance he suddenly became mute before the eyes of all. He wished this work to be entitled:

The Itinerary of Pope Leo, one book.

He flourished under Henry III, king, in the year of the Lord 1050.

LANFRANC, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Caen, of the Order of St. Benedict, an Italian by nationality from the city of Pavia, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, and in secular letters, especially in dialectic, by the opinion of all the most learned of his time, famous no less for holiness than for knowledge, left outstanding monuments of his intellect. Of these I have found only the following, a distinguished work:

On All the Epistles of Paul the Apostle, four books. Commentaries on the Psalter, one book. Against Berengar, one book, “Lanfrancus misericor.” The Deeds of Count William, one book. Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

PETER DAMIAN, formerly a monk of the holy father Benedict, bishop of Ostia, cardinal of the most holy Roman church, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle and keen in intellect, pleasing and polished in speech, sufficiently capable in persuasion, shone forth as distinguished and famous no less for holiness than for learning. Following the example of the great bishop Gregory, through love of solitude and quiet he abandoned his episcopate, and after he had governed it strenuously for some years he returned to his monastery, thereafter spending his life with his brothers in tranquility of mind. But when he was reproved by the supreme pontiff with a charitable rebuke as to why, being a useful and suitable man, he had relinquished the episcopate through love of private salvation, he issued apologetic writings to the Roman pontiffs who succeeded one another, Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII; in these, humbly excusing his action by authority, reason, and example, he appeased their minds. Of his small works the following are reported: To Leo the Hermit, whether a solitary person praying the canonical hours ought also to say “The Lord be with you,” when there is no one to answer; an instructive little work, entitled:

The Lord Be with You, one book, “To Lord Leo, with love.” Apologetics, one book, “To his lord Nicholas alone.” On the Incontinence of Priests, one book, “Recently, having with some.” On the Wives of Clerics, one book, “I address you, O [unclear].” Rule of Solitaries, one book, “While the fervor of holy [unclear].” Exhortation to Monks, one book, “To the brothers in Gangra.” Miracles of His Own Time, one book, “To the most beloved Gerard.” On the Progress of Monks, one book. Antilogion against the Jews, one book. one book, “Hugh, abbot of Cluny.” Life of Abbot Odilo, one book, “To Blanche, formerly countess.” On the Terror of Death, one book, “Indeed it must be considered.” On Meditation on Death, one book. Against a Certain Bishop, one book. Against Simoniacal Bishops, one book. On the Insolence of Wicked Men, one book, “To Lord H. of Ravenna.” Most Pleasing or Most Approved, one book. On the Natures of Certain Animals, one book. Of Rhetorical Declamation, one book, “Still, most beloved men.” On Flora Lucilla, one book, “Admirable, glorious.” On Cassian the Martyr, one book, “The glorious [unclear] of blessed Boniface.” On St. Boniface, one book, “To the fair, brothers, [unclear].” On St. Anastasius, one book. And many other things which I have not seen. Sermons and homilies [unclear].

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1050.

BRUNO, archbishop of the Ruthenians, formerly a monk, of the Order of St. Benedict, an Italian by nationality, a man learned in the divine scriptures, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, holy, and finally

The Abbot of Sponheim

...and finally worthy of God, since, preaching the Catholic faith in Prussia, he is read to have been crowned with martyrdom by the enemies of Christ. He wrote some distinguished little works of his talent. Of these there survive, of commentaries:

On Genesis, 2 books.

And certain others. He suffered at the hands of the Prussians under St. Henry of Bamberg, who was the second king of this name and the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1008, indiction 6. After afflicting him with many tortures and cutting off his feet and hands, they at last made him a martyr of Christ by beheading.

Erhard, a monk of the order of St. Benedict, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and learned by continual exercise, subtle in intellect and ready in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering homilies to the people. By expounding the divine Scriptures he made his name known, and by frequent study of them became an outstanding teacher. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which there are reported:

Commentaries on Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book.

On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book.

On Deuteronomy, 1 book. Also of homilies, 1 book.

He also published some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Bernold, priest of the church of Constance in Swabia, a German by nation, a devout man, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and [unclear] in eloquence, left some little works of his study, which nevertheless have not at all come to the knowledge of our reading. He is said to have composed, for the usefulness of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, a volume which he entitled:

The Roman Order, 2 books.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Marbod, bishop of Rennes, very zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned by reading the ancients, and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, which could no less please readers than profit them. Among these there excels a notable work which he composed in elegant meter with a threefold sense:

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. The Passion of the Theban Martyrs, in verse, 1 book.

And certain others. He flourished in the times of Henry III, in the year of the Lord [1050?].

Marianus, a monk of Fulda, of the order of St. Benedict, a Scot by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a historian and distinguished computist, left his homeland and came into Germany as a pilgrim for the love of Christ. First, at Cologne, he was made a monk at St. Martin's, and, from desire for solitude, was enclosed; he remained there for two years. Afterwards, however, transferred to Fulda, he remained enclosed there for 12 years, until at length, on account of his learning and sanctity, by order of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda, he moved to Mainz and, staying again enclosed at St. Martin's for 17 years, was held by all in great honor. He wrote from the beginning of the world down to his own times:

A notable Chronicle, 2 books. We are instructed by the divine.

On the Harmony of the Evangelists, 1 book. It was in the days of Herod.

Also On Computus, 1 book.

And certain others. He died under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1086, indiction 9, in the 58th year of his age, and was buried at Mainz at St. Martin's, in the greater church, not without a reputation for sanctity.

Weneric, bishop of Vercelli, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, made his name known to posterity by writing, although his little works have not come to the knowledge of our reading.
