And he left after him many distinguished disciples, nobly learned in the imperial laws as well as in other disciplines of humane letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, a doctor of great authority among the old professors of this faculty. He wrote certain excellent volumes in that discipline, of which I have seen only:

On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus.” On [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers, book I. It remains now that concerning the office.

On the Office of a Notary

Various questions of law.

The other things which he composed have not yet at all come into our hands.

FRANCIS, founder and head of the Order of Minors, an Italian by nation, sprung from the city of Assisi in Italy, a man of most holy conduct and a most ardent follower of evangelical poverty, who by word and example converted many from iniquity and directed them into the way of Catholic justice, was so great a lover of Christ that in contempt of the world and of transitory consolation he scarcely had an equal. In his order many very learned men have already flourished, who for the usefulness of the faithful have composed almost innumerable little works. Francis himself, however, wrote a brief work:

The Rule of the Minors, book I, "The rule and life of the Minors."

A brief Testament, book I, "The Lord gave to me, brother."

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

CAESARIUS, a monk in Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, of the diocese of Cologne Agrippina, a devout man, outstanding in regular discipline, and by long practice devoted to the divine scriptures, composed for the instruction of the novices, whose instructor he was, some little works in a simple and open style, the reading of which is not to be despised by more simple devout brothers. Of these I have found only the following.

A lengthy work on miracles and diverse visions made in Germany in his own time, which he entitled in imitation of the holy Pope Gregory.

Dialogues on various matters, 12 books, "Gather up the fragments, lest."

On the Sunday Gospels, book I, "The cluster of Cyprus, beloved."

On the Gospels for saints, book I, "Our Lord and Savior Jesus."

Sermons to novices, book I.

Besides these he published several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

WILLIAM, monk of the monastery of the divine martyr Dionysius of Paris, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man skilled in the divine scriptures by constant study and excellently learned in the disciplines of secular letters, clear in talent and eloquence, and a distinguished knower of times, not ignorant, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which, writing and teaching various things, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant:

A volume of Histories, 3 books. And many letters to various persons, book I.

He is said, moreover, to have published commentaries on the divine scriptures, which I have not yet seen.

JACOBUS de Vitriaco, bishop of Acre, afterward cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, bishop of Tusculum, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity.

The Eastern History, book I. The Life of Mary of Oignies, 3 books.

Against the Saracens, book I. On the holy women of Liege, book I.

Letters to various persons, book I. Besides these he composed some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

BONAGUIDA of Arezzo, a man in both laws the most learned of all in his time, of great authority among the ancient professors of this faculty, subtle in talent, clear in eloquence. He wrote for the usefulness of students of law certain splendid volumes, by which he made himself useful to those present and known to those to come. Among these there is extant the noble summa which he entitled:

The Introductory Work for Advocates, 2 books, "Since the office of advocacy."

The Pearl of Law, book I, "Since after the invention."

Explanations of various cases. But he is said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

PETER de Vineis, a German by nation, scribe and chancellor of Emperor Frederick II, a learned and eloquent man, but especially blameworthy in this, that adhering to that same Frederick and relying on his favor he foolishly barked against the Roman Church; by him at last he was worthily rewarded, when he had offended him in certain matters, and lost the light together with his eyes. He wrote certain little works of his talent, of which I have found only these:

Letters in the person of the Emperor, 6 books, "The pontiffs gathered."

On imperial power, book I.

He flourished in the times of the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

ANTONIUS, called of Padua, but a Spaniard by nation, sprung from the city of Lisbon, of the Order of Minors, disciple of blessed Francis, a man most learned in the divine scriptures

Abbot of Sponheim

[unclear], since before entering the order he taught theology gloriously for a long time at Toulouse, Bologna, and Padua, and left distinguished disciples after him. He was of such holiness that, living and dead, he shone with many miracles. He was moreover a most excellent preacher, so much so that the supreme pontiff was accustomed to call him the ark of the covenant. And St. Francis used to call him his bishop. Among other little works of his talent he wrote very elegant and most ardent works:

Sermons on the season, 2 books. “There shall be signs [unclear].” Also sermons on the saints, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And because of the frequency of miracles after his death he was at once enrolled in the catalogue of saints by Pope Gregory IX, together with Saint Dominic and Elizabeth, landgravine of the Thuringians.

Jordan of the Order of Preachers, after Saint Dominic, as they say, master general, a German by nation, a man sufficiently trained and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, by his own example and honey-flowing teaching instructed many in piety. He is said to have written some little works, the reading of which is judged not unprofitable for declaimers and devout brothers. Of these, from the office of the priorship, there are said to be, to the brothers of his order:

Several exhortatory letters, 4 books. Sermons to the people. On the institution of the order.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, at the same time as blessed Dominic, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Hubert of Bobbio, professor of both laws, a most sagacious interpreter, subtle in intellect, clear in expression after the scholastic manner, who among the old professors of this science was regarded as one of the foremost doctors, handed down his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity by teaching and writing, giving to others both an example of learning and an aid to advancement. For he wrote a notable summa, which he entitled:

On the order of judges, 3 books. “Because paternal piety.” Questions and determinations.

And not a few other things, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands.

Bernard Dorna, a Provençal by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of the very famous Azo of Bologna, professor and most learned interpreter of both laws, stirred by the example of his most learned teacher, applying himself wholly to letters, wrote various little works, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Of these there survives a distinguished volume:

On the conceptions of libels, 1 book. And other things which I have not seen.

Accursius, an Italian by nation, born in the city of Florence, formerly a hearer and disciple of Azo, a man most skilled in both laws, and not among the least learned in the other disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and famous in eloquence. How great his authority is at this time among professors of the laws, no one even moderately learned is unaware. He wrote many distinguished little works; he was the first to gloss the whole civil law:

On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Code. On the Institutes, 4 books. “Since by imperial command.”

He published besides not a few other things, which are very well known to students of the laws. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Hubert of Bonacursus, an Italian by nation, a man skilled in both laws and not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech, who among the old expounders of law was of no obscure reputation. He composed in that faculty certain distinguished little works, of which I do not recall that any has come into our hands. There is said to be his:

On the preludes of cases, 1 book. Other useful and distinguished works.

We believe, however, that both these and his other works are not unknown to skilled jurists.

John of Abbeville, archbishop of Besançon, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a Frenchman by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, a very famous interpreter of those same sacred letters, who in the Parisian studium taught theology excellently for many years, most excellent in declaiming sermons to the people; for this reason especially, from a master at Paris he was made archbishop of Besançon. He wrote:

Sermons on the season, 2 books. Sermons on the saints. Other things.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He also published many other works, which have come to my knowledge. He also wrote the aforesaid sermons through the cycle of the year: first, brief readings from the Gospel and the Apostle, expounding them briefly; afterwards he published other sermons, both on Sundays and on festivals, so lengthy, introducing so many testimonies of the Scriptures, that they can scarcely be committed to memory; yet these have now, with newer ones coming in, partly lost their value.

RAYMUND of Pennafort, a Catalan by nation, [was?] provincial and third master general of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in knowledge of canon law; by writing various things he made his name immortal, and by his little works bound the church to be perpetually, so to speak, his debtor. For at the command of Pope Gregory he compiled the Decretals of law, in 5 books: “The peace-making king, by pious mercy.”

A Summa on cases, in 3 books: “Since, as Jerome says.”

The Constitutions of his order, in 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

ALBERTUS Galioti, a Parmese by homeland, a professor and famous interpreter of canons and laws, subtle in talent, cautious in counsel, scholastic in eloquence, who because of his learning and experience in affairs was held among the foremost doctors by the old jurists. He wrote certain little works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with immortal praise. Among these there is extant a summa:

The Pearl of Questions, in 10 books: “When I, Albertus Galio.”

And Declarations of Judgments, in 1 book.

And certain other unknown works are held by various persons.

ODOFREDUS of Benevento, a hearer of Azo of Bologna, afterwards the teacher of Jacobus Balduini, a man most skilled in both laws, very subtle in talent, clear in eloquence, who left many distinguished disciples after him; on account of his learning and erudition, both in law and in the other letters of humanity, he was held in great authority among the ancients. Many little works of his are reported, by which he made his name known to posterity.

On the Formation of Libels, in 1 book: “After the work of notarial art.”

On Judicial Order, in 1 book: “In what manner Christ’s.”

On the Art of the Notariate, and other things which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

JOHANNES de Blanosco, a Burgundian by nation, a man most learned in both laws, sufficiently instructed in the precepts of secular philosophers, keen and ready in talent. He wrote in plain speech little works not to be scorned by professors of this faculty, by which the fame of his name became known then to those present and afterwards to those to come far and wide. Among these there is extant a volume of great usefulness, which he entitled:

“I, Johannes de Blano.”

On the Actions of Advocates, in 1 book. But the rest of what he composed has by no means come to my knowledge.

And Various Questions. A Genoese by origin, from the city of Fribourg by origin, John by name, a German by nation, much [unclear] from the divine Scriptures; bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, of the Order of Preachers, a man [unclear] in the divine [unclear] by the consensus of the fathers, much practiced and learned in secular law, excellently skilled in philosophy, who, because of his learning and holiness of life, had been taken from the order to the episcopate; later abandoning it, he returned to his order and, after Raymond, was made general master of the order [unclear]; he did many good things. He wrote a notable work:

Summa of Confessors, in 5 books: “Since the newness of doubts.”

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. He was buried in his convent at Strasbourg, once shining, as they say, with many miracles.

INNOCENT IV, pope, formerly called Symbaldus, an Italian by nation, [unclear] city.

On Ecclesiastical Power, in 1 book: “It is read in Ezekiel.”

Apparatus on the Decretals, in 5 books.

Rule of the Poor Clares, in 1 book: “The form of life of the order.”

Authen-

288 The Abbot of Spanheim

Also the Authenticae, one book, and certain other works. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250. [unclear] books.

Rolandinus de Romantiis, a professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, was not among the least of the old jurists. In that faculty he wrote certain excellent opuscula, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a summa, one book. It begins: “A little book begins: On the order of crimes”; Determinations and Questions.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Bernardus, priest of Compostella, familiar and chaplain of Pope Innocent IV, a man most learned in law, prompted by the zeal of the same pontiff, wrote certain excellent opuscula in law, which in these times are held in great authority among jurists. Of these I was able to find a few, namely an outstanding apparatus:

On the Decretals, five books. It begins: “At the beginning of this book.”

Cases of the Decretals, five books. It begins: “The peace-making king, by pious [mercy?]...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Guido de Suzaria, a most skilled doctor in law, and sufficiently instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, had great authority among the old experts in these matters. He is said to have composed certain excellent opuscula in law. Among them there exists a notable summa which he entitled:

On the Actions of Cases, one book. It begins: “On the ordering of cases.”

Also Various Declarations, [unclear] books. It begins: “Since, with [unclear] supporting...”

And many other works, which have not yet come into our hands at all.

Bartholomaeus Brixianus, a professor and very learned interpreter of canon law, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote various excellent opuscula both in law and on other matters, by which he gave his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported:

A Repertory of the Decretum, three books.

A Chronicle of Italy, one book.

Disputations on the Decretals, five books.

And certain other works.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Johannes de Deo, a professor and outstanding expounder of both laws, and sufficiently learned in the disciplines of philosophy, subtle in intellect and scholastic in speech, by the memory of his name came to the knowledge of many. Of his works only a few have come to my knowledge; for I found only the following:

A Summa of Cavillations, seven books. It begins: “To the honor of the highest [Trinity?].”

Another, entitled Judgment, [unclear] books. It begins: “May he be present at our beginning.”

A Table of the Decretum, [unclear] books. It begins: “The book of decrees, distin[ction]...”

A Concordance of the Decretum and the Decretals, [unclear] books. It begins: “For those wishing readily...”

Various Questions. A tractate on constitutions.

He taught in the city of Bologna, where he composed the aforesaid works and others.

Hugo Barchinonensis, of the Order of Preachers, made cardinal priest of the holy Church of the title of St Sabina, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who before entering the order had been a master of sacred theology and had many distinguished disciples. He wrote several outstanding opuscula, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. No less shining in conduct and religion than in learning, he remained in dignity the same man he had been before. The following books are attributed to him:

On Genesis, [unclear]; On Exodus, one book.

On Leviticus, [unclear]; On Numbers, [unclear] books.

On Deuteronomy, [unclear]; On Joshua, [unclear] books.

On Judges, [unclear]; On the Book of Ruth, [unclear] books.

On Kings, [unclear]; On Chronicles, [unclear] books.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, [unclear]; On Tobit, one book.

On Judith, [unclear]; On the Psalter, one book.

On the Book of Job, [unclear]; On Ecclesiastes, one book.

On Proverbs, [unclear]; On the Song [of Songs], one book.

[unclear] books. 10.

One book. 49.

One book. 39.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Book of Wisdom, one book. On Ecclesiasticus, two books. On Isaiah the prophet, one book. Book 3. On Ezekiel, one book. Book 4. On the twelve minor prophets, twelve books. Book 5. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. Book 6. On the Gospel of Luke, one book. Book 7. On the epistles of the Apostle Paul, fourteen books. Book 8. On the canonical epistles, seven books. Book 9. A Summa on cases, one book.

He also composed several other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Jacobus Baldewini, once a hearer of Odofredus Beneventanus, a most distinguished man, a professor of civil law and an eminent interpreter, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, wrote in that faculty certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, twelve books. On the old Digest, twenty-four books. Book 13. On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

And certain other works. He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor: 1240.

David, of the Order, as they say, of Minors, German by nation, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, notable in life and conduct, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works in plain speech, whose reading is not to be despised by devout brothers; of these the following are extant. To novices.

On the formation of the outward man, one book. The progress of the religious man, 7. My conferences, which, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. On the new Digest. And certain other works. While I was thinking about [unclear], one book. A Summa for preachers, Every man is to be exhorted, one book. The deeds of the friars preachers. On the offices of his order, one book. To the sons of grace and coheirs.

And certain other works. He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Letters to various persons, While I was thinking about [unclear], one book.

Humbert, the fifth master general of the Order of Preachers, Viennese by homeland, once a hearer of the theologian Hugh of Barcelona, a man learned in the divine writings and an outstanding preacher, evangelical in life, pure in conscience, outstanding in action, sweet in eloquence, and fit for persuasion, who once drew Hugh, his own teacher in sacred theology, into the order, wrote certain devout little works, by which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the rule of St. Augustine, Every man is to be exhorted, one book. A Summa for preachers. On the offices of his order, one book. To the sons of grace and coheirs. The deeds of the aforesaid brothers. On the offices of his order. On the three substantial things of the religious [unclear]. While I was thinking late about [unclear]. Letters to various persons, all [unclear]. On the offices of his order.

And certain other works. He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Vincent, a Gaul by Burgundian nation, of the Order of Preachers, called of Beauvais, a man studious and practiced in the divine writings, and rich from reading the ancients, subtle in talent and composed in speech, applied so much zeal to letters that he could never be called away from their cultivation by any labors, vigils, or occupations, without always either reading, writing, or preaching. Therefore he was so great that after him he has not yet had an equal, if we weigh in an even balance with the others the lofty little works which he wrote, laboriously collected from many sources. For at the request of the king of the Franks, and with him providing the expenses, he brought together, with very great labors, the great and admirable work of the Mirrors, concerning everything knowable, so to speak, in many volumes, which he prefaced and divided in this way:

The Historical Mirror, thirty-two books. God is substance in [unclear]. Book 33. Since the multitude of books. The Natural Mirror. In all things, the multitude of books. Book 1. Since the multitude of books. The Moral Mirror, The book of generation, and. Four books. If God by the prophetic mouth [unclear]. On the grace of God also, Blessed John the Evangelist. Book 1. Sons have been instructed for you [unclear]. On the praises of St. John the Evangelist. First, therefore, take note. Consolation over the dead, one book. Letters to various persons. Other [unclear].

Abbot of Sponheim

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Alexander of Hales, English by nation, of the Order of Minors, teacher of Cardinal Eustachius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and second to no one in his time in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence: when he was doctor of sacred letters in the Paris school, in order that he might become a true disciple of heavenly philosophy, he entered the order of the poor of Christ, which he wonderfully adorned by his learning and holiness. At the command of Pope Innocent IV he wrote a distinguished work, in four volumes of parts, usefully comprising many things, which he entitled:

A Summa of Theology, 4 books. “Since, as Boethius says...” A Declaration of the Rule of the Minors, 1 book. “To the reverend in Christ...”

The rest of his works I have not seen. It is said, however, that he postilled both the Old and the New Testament in great part, and that he subtly discussed many things concerning the concord of divine and human law, and composed various other works, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

John of La Rochelle, of the Order of Friars Minor, master of sacred theology at Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures, and splendidly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, who together with Alexander of Hales subscribed himself in the declaration of the Rule of the Minors to the minister general. He published certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 1 book. A Summa of Virtues and Vices, 1 book. Also On the Soul, 1 book. “Alpha and Omega are one in...”

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Henry, archbishop of Embrun and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, commonly called Hostiensis, a man most skilled in both laws, who, because of the excellence of his intellect and learning, was held in esteem by Pope Alexander IV. He wrote certain little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work known to all:

On the Title of the Decretals, 5 books.

The rest that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge at all. He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1150.

Galerius, bishop of Poitiers, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent industry in sermons delivered to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported. For at the command of Pope Alexander IV he arranged in style very useful sermons through the cycle of the year:

Sermons, 1 book. “It is asked how virtue...” Quodlibets, 1 book. On the Sentences, 4 books.

He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Galerius, bishop of Maguelone, born from the town of Lille in Flanders, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, who in his time, on account of his learning and erudition, was held in great repute. At the request of the provost and clerics of the church of Lille he wrote:

On the Psalter, 1 book. And certain letters.

He also published some other works, which have not come to our knowledge at all.

Alexander, called de Villa Dei, of the homeland of Dol, of the Order, as they say, of Friars Minor, certainly a man practiced in every respect, a grammarian, philosopher, astronomer, and notable calculator. He wrote not a few little works both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have so far found only the following: a volume written in leonine meter on grammar, which today is in constant use in boys’ schools; I do not know whether it is so useful, because of the defect of weaker age and the sloth of teachers. He entitled this same work:

The Doctrinale of Boys, 1 book. “To write for little clerics...” On Ecclesiastical Computation, 1 book. “Although now at the end...” On the Sphere, 1 book. On the Art of Numbering, 1 book.

He is also said to have written many other things: sermons, letters, and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands at all. He flourished in great religion and learning under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Eustachius, who is also Bonaventure, born at Bagnoregio, of the Order of Friars Min--

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[of the Friars Minor?] general minister, and thereafter bishop of Albano, and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church; formerly a hearer and disciple of Alexander of Hales; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, devout and most holy in life and conduct. His teacher Alexander, considering the gift of his intellect and the purity of his life, used to say: "In Brother Bonaventure Adam does not seem to have sinned." He wrote many profound and most devout little works, in which, putting forth burning words, he kindles the reader's affection in the love of Christ no less than he illumines the intellect with holy teachings. For he easily surpasses all the doctors of his time in the usefulness of his works, if you attend to the spirit of divine love and Christian devotion speaking in him. He is profound, not wordy; subtle, not curious; eloquent, not vain; putting forth flaming, not inflated, words. Hence he is read more safely, understood more easily by one who loves, frequented more usefully, retained more sweetly and fruitfully. Many put forth doctrine; many preach devotion; few by writing books have taught both. But Bonaventure surpassed many few, while his devotion instructs doctrine and his doctrine devotion. Therefore, if you wish to be learned and devout, be intent upon his little works. These are:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Profunda fluutorum [unclear]. A Breviloquium, 7 books. Flecto genua mea ad. A Soliloquy, 1 book. Dic queso o homo si. The Itinerary of the Mind into God, 1 book. In principio primum. 1 book. Christo confessus sum. An Exhortation to a Brother, 1 book. Quoniam dilecte mi frater. On the Reduction of the Arts, etc., 1 book. Omne datum optimum et. The Rule of Conscience, or A Little Good, 1 book. Ecce descripti can tibi [unclear]. A Compendium of the Scriptures, 1 book. The Itinerary of the Mind into Itself, 1 book. Malum considerare occur [unclear]. On the Instruction of Novices, 1 book. In conversionis mea pro a [unclear]. A Quiver, or Spark-book, 1 book. Questio est de pauper. On the Five Feasts of Christ's Infancy, 1 book. Cum secundum virorum venera [unclear]. On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, 1 book. Primum omnium necesse ha. On the Excellence of the Eucharist, 1 book. On the Six Wings of the Seraph, 1 book. To Blanca the Duchess, 1 book. In medio ecclesia ape [unclear]. A Notable Work of Illuminations, 1 book. Tres sunt ternarii pec [unclear]. On the Three Ternaries of Breasts, 1 book. Contemplativorum aquili [unclear]. On the Seven Degrees of Contemplation, 1 book. Si vis in spiritu proficere. On the Progress of Religious, 1 book. Si vis ad vitam ingredi. On the Ten Commandments, 1 book. Summi legislatoris. An Apology of the Poor, 1 book. Pater noster. Oratio hec praeni [unclear]. The Legend of Saint Francis, 1 book. On Genesis, seven visions, 1 book. The Constitutions of His Order, 1 book. In principio, etc. Circa. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Spiritus Domini super me. Confi [unclear]. On Three Questions, 1 book. In nominato magistro. On the Feasts of the Apostles, 1 book. Quoniam secundum apostolum Iohan. On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book. Currite gentes undig [unclear]. Sermons through the Year, 1 book. Several Letters to Various Persons.

He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He died while the Empire was vacant, under Pope Gregory X, in the Council of Lyons, in the year of the Lord 1283, indiction 1. He was buried in the cathedral church of Lyons. At length, on account of his holiness and miracles, in our days he was canonized by Pope Sixtus IV, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1482, indiction 15.

Philip, chancellor of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular philosophy, since he was a famous master of sacred letters, presided gloriously for a long time over the theological school at Paris, where he magnificently instructed disciples by lecturing and peoples by preaching. He wrote two or three sermons on each of the Psalms.

Elegant Sermons, 1 book. A Summa of Theology, 1 book.

He also published many other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Albert, bishop of Ratisbon, a friar of the Order of Preachers, German by nation, Swabian by homeland, originally from Lauingen, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular philosophy second to none in his time, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct, who because of his doctrine and learning was called “the Great,” taught sacred letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years: first at Paris, afterward at Cologne, where among others he had Thomas Aquinas as an outstanding disciple. Then, having been taken up to the bishopric of the church of Ratisbon, after he had governed it for some years he left it, and out of love for salutary study returned to his convent at Cologne, where he persevered in teaching and writing until the end of his life. He wrote many, indeed almost innumerable, little works, of which the following are reported.

The Summa of Theology, 4 books. “Knowledge has become wonderful...” On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Four Coevals, 1 book. On Man, 1 book. On the Good, 1 book. On the Spiritual Life, 1 book. On the Body of Christ, 1 book. On the Office of the Mass, 1 book. “Behold, I shall turn aside into [unclear],” 1 book. On the same: 32 sermons, 1 book. On the Most Sacred Body, 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Writers 293

The Age of Astronomy, one book. On Sleep and Waking, one book. On the Nature of the Gods, one book. Questions, 15, one book. On the Twelve Alphabets, one book. On Minerals, one book. On Dreams, one book. On the Secrets of Nature, one book. On Wounds, one book. On the Choosing of Masters, one book. On the Six Principles, one book. On the Categories, one book. On Causes, one book. On Definitions, one book. On Grammar, one book. On Rhetoric, one book. On Medicine, one book. On Agriculture, one book. On Wool-working, one book. On Metaphysics, two books. On Ploughing, one book. On the Heavens and the World, three books. On [unclear], one book. On the Science of Meteors, four books. On Aristotle's Physics, five books. On Nourishment and the Nourishable, one book. On Generation and Corruption, one book. He commented on the books of Aristotle, and composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. On the Soul, one book.

He died under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, in the eighth indiction, in the eightieth year of his age. He was buried in the middle of the choir of his convent at Cologne. And after him there did not arise a man like him, who was so learned, erudite, and experienced in all letters, sciences, and matters. As for his being accused of necromancy, the man beloved by God suffers an injustice.

SIMON of Tournai, priest, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly trained in secular philosophy, a very acute dialectician and highly skilled in all the liberal arts, became master of the theological school and taught for many years in the Parisian gymnasium, where he instructed very many hearers. But while he follows Aristotle too much, he is found to have erred in certain matters. He wrote certain little works of his own talent, of which the following are reported.

His Sentences, one book. Various Questions, one book. On the Creed of Athanasius, one book. He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

THOMAS of Aquino, of the order of Friars Preachers, hearer and disciple of Albert the Great in the convent at Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, notable in life and conduct, easily obtained first place among all the doctors of his time. Like another Augustine, he gave himself wholly to the study of the Scriptures, spending day and night in love and practice of it; he wrote so many and such great volumes that among the moderns he has few equals either in number or in usefulness.

On the Sentences, two books. I, wisdom, have poured forth. Summa of Theology, three books. Since Catholic truth. Against the Gentiles, four books. He will meditate on truth. Book five. The little book from excellence. Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book. Blessed Peter the Apostle. Compendium of Theology, one book. The Word of the eternal Father. On the Precepts of Charity, one book. Three things are necessary for man. On Faith and the Sacraments, one book. Your [unclear] asks of me. On the Lord's Prayer, one book. Our Father. Among other things. On the Ave Maria, one book. Ave Maria, etc. In [unclear]. On the Creed of the Apostles, one book. I believe, etc. The first thing which is. On the One Hundred Eight Articles, one book. First it must be considered. On the 42 Articles, one book. To the reverend in Christ. On the 36 Articles, one book. Having read your letters, in them. On the Six Articles, one book. To his dearest in Christ. On the Difference between the Divine Word and the Human Word, one book. For the understanding of this. On the Nature of the Word, one book. Since concerning the nature of the word. On Separated Substances, one book. Since concerning the holy [unclear] of the angels. Against the Averroists on the Intellect, one book. As all men by nature. Against Detractors of Religion, two books. Of the Christian religion. On the Perfection of the Spiritual Life, three books. Since certain persons of perfection. Against the Assailants of the Order, four books. Behold your enemies [unclear].

On the judgments of the stars, 1 book. On the eternity of the world, 1 book. On fate, 1 book. On the principle of individuation, 1 book. On being and essence, 1 book. On the principles of nature, 1 book. On matter and dimensions, 1 book. On the mixture of the elements, 1 book. On the hidden works of nature, 1 book. On the motion of the heart, 1 book. On instants, 1 book. On the four opposites, 1 book. On demonstration, 1 book. On fallacies, 1 book. On modal propositions, 1 book. On the nature of accident, 1 book. On the nature of genus, 1 book. On the principles of the soul, 1 book. On time, 1 book. On the plurality of forms, 1 book. On the nature of syllogisms, 1 book. On sense and intellect, 1 book. On the discovery of the middle term, 1 book. On the nature of place, 1 book. On universals, 2 books. On the intellect and the intelligible, 1 book. A concordance of his sayings, 1 book. “As I was thinking what.” “Having read the little book from you.” “To your excellency [unclear].” “Our Savior [sent] the disciples.” “Therefore we condemn [unclear].” On Jeremiah, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “But just as in things which.” “To the most holy and most reverend.” On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. “He has made a memorial of wondrous things.” “Christ Jesus came.” “Master, what is commanded.” “Be perfect, as.” “Blessed are they who dwell in the Lord.” “Since the foundation.” “Because of the priest’s office.” “In the power of the holy cross.” “There are four [unclear] of virtues.” “I have received your letters in.” “What is truth?” “The question is concerning power.” “To the illustrious lady Alheidis.” “It has been asked of God.” “From the beginning of the nativity.” “Run ahead first in the Lord.” “Your [unclear] requested of me.” 10 “Because you asked that for you.” “Granted according to faith.” “It is asked concerning fate, whether it is.” “Since there are two in man.” “Because a small error in.” “Since something can be.” “After, concerning the principles [unclear].” “A doubt among many.” “Since in certain natural things.” “He who [says] everything that moves,” 40 “Since every duration.” “Since there are four works.” “For having knowledge.” “Because logic is reason.” “Because a modal proposition.” “Since all human knowledge.” “Since every generic nature.” “As an aid to man.” “As the philosopher wishes.” “Since the holy thing is man.” “Since to know is [to know] the cause of a thing.” “About the consideration.” “Since the principle of the syllogism.” “One must consider concerning the nature.” “For knowing the nature.” “Concerning universals [unclear].” “It must be known that, concerning the account.” “Many shall pass through and.” Sermo-

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

[Thomas Aquinas, continued:] …Many sermons, 1 book; Against William of Saint-Amour, 1 book. By command of Pope Urban IV he composed the office of the feast of Corpus Christi. He commented on all the books of Aristotle and Porphyry. He published also many other [things], as much in the divine Scriptures as in secular philosophy, which have by no means come into our hands. He dies under the emperor [Rudolf], in the year of the Lord 1274, in the 2nd indiction. And he was canonized by Pope John XXII.

THOMAS of Cantimpré, a Brabanter by nation, of the order of Friars Preachers, once (as they report) a disciple of Albert the Great, a devout man, and excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, prompt in talent, scholastic in eloquence. He is reported to have written certain illustrious volumes, by which he brought his name to the notice of posterity. Of these there is extant a work on the mystical bees, which he entitled: The Universal Good: 2 books. ["To the reverend in Christ…"] On the nature of things: 1 book. The Life of Saint Christina: 1 book. And the rest, which I have not seen. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270. And there are [those] who write that he had skill in the Greek tongue, [and] translated the books of Aristotle which are now in use in the schools.

ALPHONSO, king of Castile [and] León, the most distinguished philosopher [and] astronomer among all of his time, [flourished] in the time of the vacancy of the empire, in the year of the Lord 1170.

[A Dominican,] of the order of Friars Preachers, a Gaul by nation, provincial prior of the same religion in France, a man learned by long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, acute in talent, prompt in eloquence, in declaiming sermons to the people [outstanding]; [who], when the brother of the king of England had been elected king of the Romans, [and] was a good [and] prudent man—Richard being dead—in the fifteenth year of his election, for the sake of peace voluntarily ceded before Pope Gregory X, [and] spontaneously renounced all his right which he had had in his election. He wrote very useful [and] elegant [works]: In Astronomy, Tables: 1 book; Of letters to various [persons]: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book; also Sermons on the saints: 1 book. But he is said to have written some others, which have not come to my knowledge.

PETER of Tarentaise, of the order of Preachers, after Gregory X, pope—canonically consecrated under the name of Innocent V—sat in the supreme pontificate only five months, a man certainly most erudite in the divine Scriptures, nobly learned in Aristotelian philosophy, who taught theology excellently for many years, [and] acquired great praise of his erudition. He wrote many illustrious little works, by which he made his name known to those then present, [and] afterward to those to come. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences: [—] books; On the Song of Songs: 1 book. On all the Epistles of Paul: 1 book; And certain others. He wrote also other lectures on the Bible, [and], as is said, several, which I have not yet seen.

PETER of Russia, of the order of Friars Minor, after Saint Bonaventure, sent to Constantinople by Pope Gregory X, brought back the Greeks to the obedience of the Roman church by his exhortations, [and] persuaded [them] to come with him to the Council of Lyon. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, [works] not to be despised: Several letters to various [persons]: 1 book; Sermons on the Saints: 1 book. He flourished, the empire being vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270. And certain others.

JOHN Esculanus of Ascoli, of the order of Friars Minor, minister general, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, a distinguished declaimer of sermons, not ignorant of secular literature, since indeed he taught theology excellently for many years, [and] left after him many distinguished disciples. He wrote some illustrious little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant, to Haymo the Englishman, minister general of his order, an equally most learned man, a Declaration: On the Rule of Saint Francis: 1 book; also On the Sentences: [—] books. Various sermons: 1 book; And certain others. He flourished, the empire being vacant, in the year of the Lord 1170. [VDAL—]

296 The Abbot of Sponheim

ULRICH of Strasbourg, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, once a hearer and disciple of Albert the Great, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, composed little works of reading not to be despised, through which he became known to those present and to those to come. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Summa of Theology. Also On the Soul, 1 book. And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

HAYMO, an Englishman by nation, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man trained by long study in the holy Scriptures, since, having attained the master's chair of the faculty of theology, he instructed many pupils in it; at the command of Pope Alexander IV he corrected and rubricated the Roman Breviary. He is said, among other things, to have written compendiously:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And certain sermons, 1 book. And certain other things. He flourished when the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord [1270?].

OTTO, bishop of Freising in Bavaria in Germany, as some write a nephew of Emperor Frederick I, a German by nation, whom Pope Pius II cites and commends in a certain oration, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not meanly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant an outstanding work, to be praised with every commendation:

Histories, 1 book. And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished when the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

PETER the Spaniard, a Portuguese, bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff after Hadrian V, a man very learned in medicine, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, sat in the pontificate for only eight months. As a physician he wrote little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported:

Treasury of the Poor, 1 book. On Problems, 1 book. Canons of Medicine.

And certain other things. He flourished in the pontificate under the name John XXI, in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord [1275?].

WILLIAM, a citizen of Piacenza, a learned doctor of the art of medicine, not ignorant of other humane letters, who, hired on a public salary at Verona, held a school in that faculty for many years and instructed several excellent pupils. He wrote little works not to be despised for professors of this science, by which he made his name known both to those present and to those to come. Of these there is extant an outstanding volume which he wished to be entitled:

On All Medicine, 4 books. Also On Surgery, 1 book.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing. He flourished under Emperor [Arnolph?], in the year of the Lord [1270?].

WILLIAM, bishop of Paris, by native land an Auvergnat, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence, and venerable no less in manner of life than in learning, composed not a few works of his erudition, by which, showing himself a learned and devout master, he made the memory of his name immortal. Of these the following are reported: an outstanding volume entitled:

On the Holy Trinity, 1 book. On the First Principle, 1 book. On the Sacraments, 1 book. I shall add still four. Why God Became Man. Summa of Vices, 1 book. Summa of Virtues. In the order of divine things, holy, 1 book. On Faith and Laws. On Good and Evil, 1 book. On Human Souls. On the Profession of Novices, 1 book. On the Thirty Remedies for Temptations. On the Works of the Virtues, 1 book. The Cloister of the Soul. Against Plurality of Benefices, 1 book. [unclear] On Divine Rhetoric. In sacred things and [their] signification. On Penance. The second plank after [shipwreck], 1 book. On Demons. After which, by the help of God, [unclear], 1 book. On the Psalter. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Letters to various persons. He also published some other works, which have come to my knowledge, 1 book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

John Valeis, otherwise Galensis, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who for a long time gloriously taught theology in the Parisian school, was of such learning and eloquence that he was called the tree of life. He wrote many excellent small works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come into our hands. For I found a distinguished volume which I judge very necessary and useful for preachers of the word of God, which many commonly call the Commoniloquium, because it contains something concerning every estate; but he himself entitled it:

Summa of Collations, 7 books. “Since the doctors are [unclear].” On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Ordering of Life, 1 book. “Since in every business [unclear].” Handful of Flowers, 1 book. “Abstinence is good in [unclear].” On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. On Various Subjects, 1 book.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

And note that this John began the book called the Handful of Flowers, whose prologue begins, “Poor little Ruth,” but, overtaken by death, did not finish it; afterward Brother Thomas of Hibernia completed the same work. The book itself begins thus according to alphabetical order: “Abstinence is good: to receive food with thanksgiving,” etc. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William Duranti, bishop of Mende, once hearer and disciple of Henry of Susa, whom they call the Speculator, a most skilled doctor in law and very zealous for ecclesiastical observance, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote for Ottobono, cardinal of Saint Hadrian and afterward supreme pontiff Hadrian V, an outstanding work divided into three volumes, which he entitled:

Mirror of Law, 3 books. “To the reverend in Christ.” Rationale of Divine Offices, 8 books. “Whatever in ecclesiastical [unclear].” Repertory of Law, 1 book. “By the rust of the first-formed man.”

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Rudolph. And he completed his work, the Rationale of Divine Offices, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1286.

Jacobus de Belvisio, a most distinguished doctor of both laws and a careful interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in counsel and knowledge, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, is said to have written certain excellent small works in law, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have not yet been able to see any. The following, however, are said to be his:

On the Authentics, 1 book. On the Use of Fiefs, 1 book. Additions on the Novels, 1 book. And various disputations. And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Lyon, of the Order of Preachers, as they say bishop of the same church, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in intellect and subtle, not affected in speech yet well composed, was quite outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have written several small works, by which he greatly instructed both the powerful of that time and those who would come afterward. Of these there are said to be:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Summa of Virtues, 5 books. “Since concerning individual useful things.” Summa of Vices, 8 books. “About to speak concerning the individual vices.” Sermons to the People, 1 book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

“Since, as blessed Augustine testifies.”

William, monk of the monastery of Saint Quentin on the Island, a man [unclear] in the holy Scriptures, [unclear] of John Scotus of the same order, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures and, by long study, very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy after the manner of the modern theologians. Prompt in intellect and clear in speech, he wrote certain small works not of contemptible reading, [unclear] certain small works not to be spurned, by which he made himself known to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. “Since, as blessed Augustine testifies.”

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Gerard, monk [unclear]. King Louis of France, having obtained [unclear] from the emperor of Constantinople, transferred [it/them] to Paris. He also wrote of blessed Elizabeth, landgravine, [unclear].

298 The Abbot of Spanheim

Miracles after death, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270. And in both branches of learning he composed various little works.

William de la Mare, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long use and practice, and sufficiently skilled in secular philosophy according to the custom of that time, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, composed various little works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them these are reported:

On the Sentences, four books.

Additions to Bonaventure, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Richard, archbishop of Reims in France, of the Order of Friars Minor, excellently learned in the holy Scriptures, inferior to none of the doctors of his time in delivering sermons to the people, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written many excellent volumes, by which he made himself useful to those then present and known to those to come; but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands. These are reported as his:

Sermons on the Season, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Samuco, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, French by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, and venerable no less in conduct than in doctrine. He published several little works of great usefulness, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them the following are reported: a certain little work, not useless for spiritual persons, which he entitled:

Decretals of Religious, one book.

On the Rule of His Order, one book.

And many others. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Also Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Chronicle of His Order, one book.

Giles of Rome, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, prior general, and afterwards archbishop of Bourges, formerly a student of blessed Thomas Aquinas, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many, indeed almost countless, little works, of which few have come into our hands. The following, however, are reported as his:

On the Hexameron, two books.

Let your voice sound in my ears, one book.

For it is the brightness of light, fourteen books.

We firmly believe and, one book.

From the royal and most sacred, one book.

Questions proposed, one book.

On the Possible Intellect, one book.

On Divine Wisdom in the Blessed, one book.

On Good Fortune, one book.

What among the other things which, one book.

To the noble knight, lord, one book.

Question: Whether an angel, one book.

Distinction of the Articles of Faith, one book.

Every being either is, etc.

The soul, as the philosopher testifies.

I [unclear] and.

In which are set forth, etc., one book.

Of Theological Truth.

It will not please him when, one book.

Why have you disparaged the sermon, one book.

He flourished

Notable Letters. And not a few other things.

He flourished

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

[Goffredus?] of Trani, subdeacon of the Roman church and, as they report, chaplain of the supreme pontiff, a man nobly learned in canon law and secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, who among the doctors of this faculty was not considered the least in his time. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a notable and quite widely circulated summa:

On the Titles of the Decretals, 5 books. The Diversity of Glosses, in 1 book. Various Questions.

Other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Guido de Baysio, archdeacon of Bologna, a man very skilled in both laws, sharp in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, whose authority among the professors of this science has remained great even to the present day. He wrote many notable volumes, by which he rendered the memory of his name, so to speak, immortal. Of these only a few have so far come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following: a large and very notable volume which he entitled Rosarium.

On the Decree, 3 books. “To the reverend in Christ.” On the Decretals, 5 books.

He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Thaddaeus, Florentine by nation, a very skilled doctor of the medical art, who taught that science excellently at Bologna for certain years, being hired at a public salary; and, gathering an almost incredible treasure, he acquired a great reputation for his experience. For when he was summoned by some prince, he wished to receive no less than fifty gold pieces as his daily wage. Once summoned by Pope Honorius IV, he refused to come before those stated gold pieces had been fixed for each day; and the pope, cured by him of a very grave illness, bestowed ten thousand gold pieces on him. He wrote:

On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, 1 book. On the Prognostics of the same, 1 book. On the Work on Acute Diseases of the same, 1 book. On Galen’s Tegni, 1 book. On the Isagoge of Johannitius, 1 book. On Preserving Health, 1 book. Various Consilia, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280. And at last he died at Bologna, an octogenarian.

John of Parma, born from the territory of Bologna, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and a notable lover of holy poverty, who was elected general in his absence from the Parisian school, where he had taught the sciences. He is said to have written many and various treatises, by which he [unclear] his name to our memory; only these have been found:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Conduct of Religious, 2 books.

He flourished when the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

John Christophori, of the Order of Friars Preachers, trained in the scriptures by long and continuous study, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, of ready intellect and scholastic in speech, is said to have published many little works on the holy scriptures; the publication of these made him, useful then to those present, known to those to come. For over a long time he expounded the divine letters by public lectures, and explained them with subtle understanding. From his commentaries the following volumes are reported, namely:

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On Mark, 1 book. On Luke, 1 book. On John, 1 book. On all the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. And many others.

He flourished when the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

Hannibaldus, Roman by nation, professor of sacred theology and an excellent interpreter of the scriptures, subtle and forceful in intellect, and sufficiently fit for disputing and resolving the difficult questions of the same, is said to have written certain excellent little works for the instruction of his disciples, by which he made his name known. Among them there are extant:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Quodlibets, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Henry of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, German by nation, a man among all the doctors of his time most learned in the divine scriptures, and very subtle in Aristotelian philosophy, was of such reputation and authority in the Parisian school that he was called the Solemn Doctor throughout the whole Christian world. For he was subtle in intellect

The Abbot of Sponheim

[He was] subtle and very acute in scholastic disputations, as his distinguished works attest: [unclear], 1 book; On the Sentences, 4 books; On Virginity, 1 book, “For holy virgins [unclear]”; Quodlibets, 2 books; On Penance; On the Metaphysics, 14 books; On the Books of the Physics, 8 books. He composed many other things indeed, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died under the Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the sixth indiction, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was buried at Tournai in the church of Mary, the holy Mother of God.

Hugolinus, patriarch of Constantinople, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently learned, of [subtle?] intellect. He composed many other things indeed, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died under the Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290, in the sixth indiction, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was buried at Tournai in the church of Mary, the holy Mother of God. Among these the following are reported, among others, as the more important: On the Sentences, 4 books; Quodlibets, 1 book; Sermons on the Season, 1 book; Various Sermons, 2 books.

Arlotus, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, Tuscan by nation, a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, a subtle dialectician and very acute disputant, who by writing various things attained great [unclear] of learning and praise. In declaiming sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He is said to have composed the New and Old Testament into one. He flourished under the Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290. Concordances, 1 book; Various Sermons; and certain other things. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Jacobus, bishop of Genoa, of the Order of Preachers, a man trained in the divine Scriptures, who because of his frequent citations of them is called Vorago, ready in intellect and clear in speech, was sufficiently suited to declaiming sermons to the people. For the use of readers he wrote not a few little works, by which he made his name known. Of these a few have come to my knowledge, and they are set down below. A volume of great size on the life and deeds of many saints, which he entitled The Golden Legend or Mirror of Saints, but it is now commonly called the Legend or Lombard History, 1 book, “The whole [unclear] of the present time.” A Mariale on St. Mary, 1 book, “As I was considering, [unclear] day [unclear].” A Chronicle of the Genoese, 1 book, “Holy Scripture of the divine [unclear].” On the Little Works of St. Augustine, 1 book. Lenten Sermons, 1 book, “He followed in his footsteps.” He also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Lucas, of the Order of Friars Minor, Italian by nation, born at Padua, a man trained by constant study in the holy writings, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, clearer in intellect and open in speech, taught the peoples the way of God in truth no less by deed than by word, and, with the Holy Spirit working together, converted the hearts of many to the love of Christ. He wrote certain little works, not to be despised, in both branches of knowledge, by which his name was brought down to the memory of posterity. But few of them have become known to me. For I have found only: Sermons on the Season, 1 book; Sermons on the Saints, 3 books, “This little work into three”; A Summa for Students, 1 book, “In three things [unclear]”; also On the Trivium, 1 book, “Until the time [unclear]”; A Reading on Job, 1 book, “In plu-”

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

He is also said to have written commentaries on several books of the Bible, which, however, have not yet come into our hands at all. This man is also reported to have been the first to arrange concordances of the whole Bible, of the New and Old Testament.

Richard of Middleton, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed both in philosophy and in canon law, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, subtle and ready in resolving doubtful questions of the Scriptures. He is reported to have written many distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

On the Sentences, one book. “He brought forth hidden things,” in one book. “All our fathers under the [cloud?],” one book. On the Four Gospels, one book. On the [distinctions?] of the Decretum, one book. It is also said that he published elegant commentaries and lectures on several parts of sacred Scripture, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Adolf and Pope Nicholas IV, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Nicholas of Bibera, a German by nation, a man nobly learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and notable poet, who, being valued in his own time among the [unclear], acquired very great glory for his learning. He wrote not a few short works both in verse and in prose, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have seen only the work whose title is hidden, which he composed at Erfurt in verse and in prose.

On Avoiding Evil, one book. “Listener of the poem, read,” one book. Letters to various persons. It is also said that he published elegant commentaries and lectures on several parts of sacred Scripture, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Adolf and Pope Nicholas IV, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Nicholas the Frenchman, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a theologian most learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, since he was [unclear] in both kinds of learning, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, who, being valued in his own time among the [unclear], acquired very great glory for his learning. He wrote not a few short works both in verse and in prose, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only a little work whose title is hidden, which he composed at Erfurt in verse and in prose.

A work not to be despised. A work not to be despised, four books. Of the rest I have found nothing. A work not to be despised, On the Sentences. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1390.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

John of Paris, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, of Mount Carmel, the seventh prior general, a learned and holy man, who, after he had governed his order for almost twenty years strenuously, as far as he could, resigned his office for the love of Christ and returned to the quiet of the hermitage, where he persevered in holy conduct until death. He wrote [works] by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant, after [unclear], which he entitled:

The Fiery Arrow. The Fiery Arrow. On the Sentences, one book. An Inventory of Sentences, one book. Several sermons. On the Sentences, four books. An Inventory of Sentences, one book. Several sermons. On the Sentences, one book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf and [unclear].

[Nicholas?] of Aquasparta, of the Order of Friars Minor, the twelfth minister general, afterwards bishop of Porto, cardinal of the most holy Church, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy according to the custom of this time, composed certain distinguished short works of excellent intellect, by which nevertheless he made his name known far and wide. Of these there are extant:

Matthew of Aquasparta, of the Order of Friars Minor, the twelfth minister general, afterwards [unclear] of Porto, cardinal of the most holy Church, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy according to the custom of this time, composed certain distinguished short works of excellent intellect, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these there are extant:

William Perault, a Frenchman by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and especially in secular letters, sufficiently and excellently learned in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He published in both faculties several instructive volumes, by which he made his name known not only to those then present, but also to future generations. Of these there are extant:

Summa of Virtues and Vices. Summa of Virtues and Vices, one book. On the Instruction of Religious, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Sermons on the Saints. Garstas, a Spaniard by nation, a man very practiced in both laws, subtle in intellect, [unclear].

The Abbot of Spanheim

ready and cautious in counsel, and acute in resolving questions of cases, was held in esteem in his own time among the professors of this faculty, and by teaching and writing spread his name abroad. For he is said to have written several small works both on the laws and on canon law, which have not come into our hands. Of his there are extant:

On the Decretals, 5 books. And several works on the laws.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Nicholas IV, pope, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly called Jerome, a Picene by nation, born from the city of Asculum, sat after Honorius IV in the chair of Peter for four years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and not at all poorly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, and no less venerable in life and goodness than in learning. He wrote a quite distinguished work:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And certain sermons.

He is also said to have published useful commentaries on several books of the Bible. He died at Rome, the Empire being vacant after the death of Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1291, indiction 4.

Boniface VIII, pope, a Campanian by nation, formerly called Benedict, sat after the resignation of Celestine V in the chair of Peter for eight years and nine months. He was indeed learned, but excessively arrogant and ambitious; the chroniclers have not kept silent about the means by which he acquired the pontificate. Since he was highly skilled in law, and saw that new varieties of cases were arising daily in the contentious forum which could not be determined by the Decretals, he composed, through three men most learned in law, new constitutions, which he wished to be called:

The Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. “The sacrosanct Roman...” Letters, several, to various persons, 1 book.

He died under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1303, indiction 1. Of him it had previously been prophesied: “He entered like a lion; he died like a dog,” etc.

William Mandagot, archdeacon of Nimes and afterward archbishop of Embrun, and finally cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was a man most skilled in both laws, one of those who, by order of Pope Boniface VIII, published the Sixth Book of the Decretals, as is clear at the beginning of that same volume. He wrote in that faculty small works not to be despised, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Of these I have seen only a notable work, which he wrote, while he was still holding the office of archdeacon in the Church of Nimes, to Berengar, succentor of the Church of Béziers, later bishop:

On the Election of Prelates, 1 book. “Since while elections in...” An Exposition of the same, 1 book. “Since I am not the author of that...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Berengar, succentor of the Church of Béziers and afterward bishop, and finally cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, to whom the aforesaid William Mandagot, while both were still established in minor offices, composed the book On the Elections of Prelates, was another of those who, at the command of Boniface VIII, composed the Sixth Book of the Decretals. A man most learned in the same juridical faculty, while he was still succentor he wrote to the same William, then archdeacon of Nimes, a notable work on the Summa of Hostiensis according to alphabetical order, which, since it is as it were an elucidation of that same Summa, he entitled:

The Eye, 1 book. On the Sentence of Excommunication, 1 book.

He is also said to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1301.

Richard of Siena, vice-chancellor of the Roman Church and afterward cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Eustachius, doctor of both laws, most celebrated in his time by the praise of all, was the third of those who by order of Pope Boniface VIII put together the Sixth Book of the Decretals; his name is expressly contained at the beginning of that same volume. He is said to have written some small works on law, but I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands. Let my studious reader seek them out. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year 1300.

Dinus Mugellanus, professor of both laws and a notable expounder, subtle in intellect, and very ready and acute in disputing and resolving doubts and questions of law, acquired great glory for himself among all the doctors of Italy by teaching and writing. He published in his faculty many excellent small works, of which the following are reported. At the command of Lord Pope Boniface VIII he was the first after the Archdeacon to write elegantly:

On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Sixth of the Decretals, book 1. On the Code, 10 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. Many counsels, book 1.

Besides these he published not a few other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

John Duns, a Scot by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, once a pupil at Paris of Alexander of Hales the Englishman, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and most learned in Aristotelian philosophy, and so profound that his writings are penetrable by few, and for that reason also less commonly used. He published certain well-ordered volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books, “Desiring concerning the prologue.” Book 1, “All things are difficult.” Book 1, “Because the highest thing for us.”

Quodlibets also, book 1, “There shall be signs,” etc. “In this.”

On the knowledge of God.

Questions on the Metaphysics.

Sermons on the season, book 1.

Sermons on the saints, book 1.

He is said to have written commentaries on the Gospel and the Apostle, and to have composed various other treatises, which have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1308, indiction 6. He was buried at Cologne among the Minorites.

Simon, monk of Hasungen, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, so turned into practice the counsel of our divine lawgiver Benedict, by which the monk is commanded to love the divine Scriptures, that nothing in this life was sweeter to him than to read sacred literature and to turn over with diligent study the little works of the holy fathers. He abridged:

The Moralia of Pope Gregory, book 1. He wrote sermons on the Song of Songs, book 1.

The vision of a certain convert, book 1. Several sermons, book 1.

Letters also to various persons, book 1. And many other things.

He also collected excerpts from the sermons of blessed Pope Gregory on Ezekiel; likewise from the Conferences of the holy fathers, from Richard of Saint Victor on the twelve patriarchs and contemplation, and various things from various sources, not to be despised.

Peter de Bella Parthica, a Burgundian by nation, a man most skilled in both civil and canon law, subtle and sharp in intellect, and most ready in disputing and resolving doubts and questions of law. He wrote many distinguished volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among them these are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Institutes, book 1. On the Old Digest, book 1. One hundred disputations, book 1.

24 books. And certain other things.

On the Infortiatum, 14 books. Pope Octavus. In the year of the Lord 1500.

He flourished at the same time as Saint Mugelanus, under Emperor Albert and Boniface [unclear].

Absolution. Concerning absolution.

Reiner of Pisa, an Italian by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and sufficiently skilled in canon law, prompt in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, cautious in counsel, venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, and certain other things.

Gerard of the Order, On the Teaching of the Heart, book 1, “Prepare your hearts.”

Sermons on the season, book 1. Sermons on the saints.

Besides these he published certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

James de Arena, Parmensian by nation, a very celebrated jurist of both laws, in intellect

The Abbot of Spanheim

profound, scholastic in speech, whose opinions in explaining the laws, as Bartolus bears witness, were so proper and fitting that he always seemed to be writing from the mind of the founder of the law. He published many distinguished little works on civil law, by which he transmitted his name to the perpetual memory of posterity.
