On the Code, 9 books. On the New Digest, 24 books. On the Old Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On Excusations, 1 book. Various Disputations, 1 book.

But he also published some other works that have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

JOHANNES of San Gimignano, of the Order of Preachers, a man zealous and very learned in the divine writings, of clear talent and plain eloquence, of excellent diligence in delivering sermons to the people, gained great praise and fruit from his learning in the salvation of souls. He wrote, among other things:

On the Similarities of Things, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Various Collations, 1 book.

He is said besides to have written certain other things, which have not come to me.

PETRUS of Dacia, philosopher, calculator, and astronomer, most excellent and very celebrated among all men of his time, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures and the Greek language. He is reported to have written many little works in astronomy and the art of calculation, which are judged not useless for ecclesiastical computation, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge.

On Calculation or Computation, 1 book. Also a Calendar, 1 book. And of his Tables, 1 book.

The rest, even if there are many works that he composed, have nevertheless not come to me. He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

NICOLAUS of Naples, a man skilled and very learned in civil law, nobly instructed also in other secular letters, whose authority among the professors of this faculty flourished in no small degree in his time. He wrote several little works on the laws, by the publication of which he bestowed his name upon immortality. But I have been able to find only the titles of the following.

On the Code, 9 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books.

Concerning the other works that he is said to have composed, I have as yet been able to find nothing certain. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1305.

HUBERTINUS of Casale, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of Johannes of Parma, the minister general, a devout man and sufficiently learned in the Holy Scriptures, when he saw that his order was falling away from its first institution, began certain new separations under the appearance of reform, and obtained that they be confirmed by the supreme pontiff. These, however, at the petitions of the custodians and ministers, were immediately revoked by the same pope, because they seemed to have been undertaken to the grave scandal and division of the order. Moved by this, Hubertinus entered the Carthusian order. He wrote a very distinguished and notable volume, useful to religious and devout persons, which he entitled:

The Tree of the Life of the Crucified, 5 books. To all who are truly Christ’s. Sermons and Letters. And certain other things.

Certain Catholics warn us that Hubertinus, in the aforesaid volume, in certain places, especially where he takes up the canticle of Simeon, must be read cautiously, because on certain articles he thinks otherwise than the Church, the mother of us all. Yet the author himself is to be excused, because it had not yet been determined, etc. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

JACOBUS of Ravenna, sprung from the province of Lorraine, a man very learned in civil law and the sacred canons, and in his time easily the most skilled of all in both the divine Scriptures and secular letters, professor of sacred Scripture, philosopher, and notable dialectician, who, as Cinus says, converted what had been handed down by the elders in simple meaning to the dialectical mode of argument. He wrote many little works in both laws. Of these there are reported:

On the Code, 19 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Digest of the Infortiatum, 14 books. Various Disputations, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Alanus of Insulis, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular letters, a most celebrated theologian, philosopher, and poet, who for a long time gloriously presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris, where, shining clearly in every divine and human science, he deserved to be called universal. He wrote, in verse and prose, almost countless little works, by which the memory of his name has been made immortal among posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following under their titles.

On the Sentences, 4 books. Quodlibeta also, 1 book. The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book. “To the most reverend father and [unclear],” 5 books. “Every science rests upon its own [unclear].” On Doctrine also, 1 book. “Since many, for adorning...” On the Five Books of Moses, 4 books. “By the grace of God, [to the] Bituricensian father...” On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Concerning the six wings of the Cherubim,” 1 book. On Penance, to the Bituricensian, [unclear]. On Mystical Equivocal Terms. On the Lament of Nature. On Parables. On the Art of Preaching. On the Natures of Animals. Letters to various persons.

Finally, he is said to have published distinguished commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, especially on the Prophets, on the Gospel, and on the Apostle. Concerning these I have so far been able to find nothing. Certain marvellous things are told about him; I neither affirm their credibility nor rashly undermine it.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Sermons, not without usefulness, 1 book. Visions of a Certain Nun, 1 book. On the Life of Saint Lutgardis, 1 book.

But other works which he composed have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

Guilhelmus, a monk of the monastery of Affligem, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, and for some time prior in the same monastery, a man devoted to studies of divine writings, learned by long practice, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, published in both kinds of writing certain little works not to be despised, by which he perpetuated the memory of his name.

Glosses on the Laws, 1 book. Disputations also, 1 book. And several other things. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Franciscus of Fano, professor and interpreter of both laws, most celebrated among all in his time, teacher of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, most acute in pleading judicial cases. He wrote excellent volumes in his faculty, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have found only:

On Actions, 1 book. “I indeed, Martinus...” On the Judgment of Cases, 1 book. “Since many principal...”

I have seen nothing of the others. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

On Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book. On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book. On Deuteronomy, 4 books. On the Gospel, 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Sermons Through Lent, 1 book. And certain other things. [unclear] many distinguished volumes, by which he made himself useful then to his parents and memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

306 | The Abbot of Sponheim | I

Dinus de Garbo, by country a Florentine, a most expert doctor of the art of medicine, and nobly learned in the rudiments of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. In his own faculty he published for students some works not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported:

Commentaries on Galen. On the Malignity of Various Complexion, 1 book. On Hippocrates, On the Nature of the Fetus. Various Questions, 1 book. Also on Avicenna. Also various works in philosophy, 1 book. And certain other things. His father Brunus was a most expert physician in the art of surgery; he handed this Dinus over to Thadaeus, the Florentine physician, to be instructed in that science. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Guilhelmus of Cumae, a Gaul by nation, a most learned interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; in that faculty in his own time he had few more learned than himself, and by teaching and writing he magnificently adorned the school of Orleans. He published for professors of law some works not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity:

On the Old Digest, 24 books. Also on the Code, 9 books. And various other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Jacobus of Viterbo, archbishop of Naples, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote, for the edification of readers, some works not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with glory. Of these I have not yet deserved to see any. There is, however, said to be his work addressed to Pope Clement V:

On the Government of Christians, 1 book. On the Sentences, 4 books. Also quodlibets. And some other things, 1 book. He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and of Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Henricus of Brussels, a monk of the monastery of Affligem of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man devoted to the divine writings, skilled through continual exercise, an outstanding philosopher and computist, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote some commendable works, by which in his time he became known far and wide. Among these are reported:

On the Method of Computus, 1 book. Calendar on Incensions, 1 book. And certain other things, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

Alexander of Alexandria, sixteenth minister general of the order of the Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in sense and understanding. He composed certain works in both branches of knowledge, by which, exercising his intellect, he brought his name down to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Various questions, 1 book. 40. On Aristotle’s Metaphysics. On the books On the Soul, 3 books. He also commented on other books of Aristotle and wrote various things. He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1319.

Eckardus, a Teuton by nation, of the order, as some will have it, of Preachers, a man learned in the divine writings, in Aristotelian philosophy the most learned of all in his time, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; but, pursuing philosophy too much, he introduced [unclear] novelty, among which there survive seventeen articles condemned by the supreme pontiff and retracted at the end of his life by the same Master Eckardus, many of which are contained in his exposition on the Gospel of John. Finally, the masters of the theological faculty of the school of Heidelberg, in the year of the Lord [1430?], publicly declared the same errors, together with certain others, to have been condemned. Eleven articles, however, were left as suspect; [unclear] he wrote in Catholic fashion and gave sufficiently profound and useful doctrines. Of his books I have found:

On the Sentences, 1 book. On Genesis, 1 book. The beginning: “This Scripture,” 1 book. On Exodus, “These are the names, because.” On the book of Wisdom, “Love,” Index [unclear]. On Can-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Song of Songs, one book.

On the Gospel of John, one book, “In the beginning,” etc. “Of the Lamb.”

On the Lord’s Prayer, one book, “Our Father.” “Before the Lord’s day.”

A sermon in the chapter of preachers, one book, “I like a vine have borne fruit.”

Of his own positions, one book, “Blessed be God and the Father.”

Sermons on the season, one book, “The God of peace and love.”

Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in his own time especially in Austria, where by teaching and preaching he was held most famous; and he wrote many other volumes.

Richard Malumbra, by native land a Cremonese, once the hearer and disciple of Jacobus de Arena, a man not moderately learned in imperial law and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, publicly taught law for many years in the university of Bologna, where he acquired no small praise for his learning. And although he was the most learned of all the doctors of his time, nevertheless he is read to have been condemned for heresy. He wrote many volumes in explanation of civil law.

On the Code, nine books. On the Institutes, forty-three books.

On the Digest, fifty books. Various Questions, one book.

And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Lampertinus de Ramponibus, a man most learned in both laws and nobly educated in the other arts of humanity, distinguished in intellect and speech, and notable for the practice of many virtues. In that faculty he wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise. Of these are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books. On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Guilhelmus de Monte Laudinio, as they report, abbot of the monastery of Poitiers, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man excellently learned in the divine scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, especially Aristotelian philosophy and pontifical law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech. He published several little works of great authority, by which he made the memory of his name known to posterity. Of these the principal are reported:

On the Sacraments, one book. A Summa on Cases, one book.

Various Declarations. Moreover he published many other little works, especially in law, and arranged various glosses of the canons, concerning which I have nowhere been able to find anything.

Guido, priest of the church of Ferrara and afterward, as they report, bishop, a man practiced by long study in the divine scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, and nobly learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and poet. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, several little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these I found only one written in verse, to Pope Clement V,

on the New and Old Testament, imitating Petrus de Riga, which is entitled:

The Pearl of the Bible, one book, “A noble beginning three times.”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, Emperor VII, and Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Petrus de Saxonia, by nation a German, of the Order of Friars Minor, learned in the holy scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, and nobly learned in canon law, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher of the divine word. He wrote certain excellent volumes of his intellect, which in his own time were held in esteem. Among these there survives a notable work useful to confessors:

A Summa of Cases, one book. Sermons on the season, one book.

Sermons on the saints, one book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Cruslanus, by nation an Italian, by native land a Florentine, once the hearer and disciple of the physician Thaddaeus, a man indeed learned and educated in philosophy and medicine, but by no means fortunate; and for this reason, bidding farewell to the world, he entered the order of the Carthusians and usefully commended the art of the flesh to the medicine of the spirit. He had previously written some little works in his own faculty, by which he made his name known. Of these there survives a commentary.

The Abbot of Sponheim

On Galen’s Tegni. One book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the Carthusian order in the times of Albert, Roman emperor, in the year of the Lord 1300. And thereafter he is said to have written various treatises for spiritual edification.

Peter of Verberie, called Aureolus, of the Order of Friars Minor and archbishop of Aix, a doctor of the Parisian school, most learned in the divine Scriptures, and very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy according to the custom of this time, subtle in intellect and an acute disputant, was outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he greatly spread his name. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences. Four books. “Quia disciplinati hominis.” A Breviary of the Bible. One book. “Venite ascendamus.” On the Conception of Saint Mary. One book. “Nondum erant abyssi.” Sermons on the Season. One book. Sermons on the Saints. One book.

And other things which I have not seen. He flourished before his pontificate, lecturing on the Sentences at Paris, in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317.

Gentilis Fulgin[as?], a distinguished professor of medicine and magnificently learned in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, had no small expertise in that faculty. He wrote in medicine many excellent volumes, as they say, by which his name became known with praise not only to those then present but also to posterity. But I have seen none of them. They are said, however, to be twenty:

Commentaries on Avicenna. Five books. Against Pestilence. One book. Also On Fevers. One book. On the Degrees of Medicine. One book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord [1310?].

Dante Alighieri, an Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man most devoted to study in his time both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and very learned, a philosopher and a poet inferior to none in his age, subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence, the keenest disputant of all, wrote in meter and prose many distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Driven from his homeland, he lived in exile all his days, for some time in Gaul and afterward with the king of Aragon; concerning his misfortune he composed various things. Of his little works these are reported:

Of Comedies. One book. On the Monarchy of the World. One book. Several letters.

And certain other things.

At last he died in exile at Ravenna, under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Michael of Cesena, of the Order of Friars Minor, the seventeenth minister general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, clear in eloquence, and venerable no less for religion than for learning, published in the holy Scriptures little works of exposition not to be scorned, by which he became known far and wide, both to those then present and now to posterity. Of these I have so far been able to find very few, namely:

On the Sentences. On the prophet Ezekiel. One book. Sermons on the Season. One book. Sermons on the Saints. One book.

He published readings and commentaries on many books of the Bible, which I have not yet seen. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bertrand, of the Order of Friars Minor, Milanese by homeland, born from a noble family, according to some a priest cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was certainly a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures, not moderately instructed in secular philosophy, and of outstanding talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote several little works of great usefulness, of which I have found:

On the Sentences. Four books. Sermons on the Epistles. Sermons on the Gospels. One book. “Videbunt filium,” verse. Sermons on the Saints. One book.

The rest that he composed have as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1325.

Gerard of Bologna, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, the eleventh prior general, a doctor of Paris, most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect

On Ecclesiastical Writers

book 4. Quodlibets, one book. Ordinary Questions, two books. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, three books. And many other things.

He began an excellent Summa of Theology, which, however, overtaken by death, he left unfinished. He died under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317, indiction 15. He was buried at Avignon.

John de Columna, a Roman by birth, of the Order of Friars Preachers, archbishop of Messina, a man whose mind was practiced in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a most acute investigator of the histories of past time, wrote, with noble talent, works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there is extant the volume which he entitled:

The Sea of Histories, ten books. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published some other works, which have not at all come to my knowledge.

Martin, of the Order of Friars Preachers, penitentiary of the lord pope in the city of Rome, and afterwards, as they say, bishop of a certain city, was a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A Table of the Decretum, one book: “Among all things whatever, if ...”

A Concise Chronicle, two books: “Since to know the times is of the highest ...”

Sermons for the season, three books: “Knowing that it is the hour ...”

Sermons on the saints, four books: “With mouth confessed it becomes unto salvation ...”

On Various Miracles, five books: “A certain householder ...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

There are those who write that this Martin was of the Order of our divine father Benedict; in my judgment they have been deceived by the similarity of the name of Marianus Scotus, of our Order, whom I mentioned above, and who himself also wrote a chronicle. There are likewise some who think he should be added to the fellowship of the Cistercian Order; these either ignorance of the facts or spite has obscured.

Gerardus Odonis, of the Order of Friars Minor, eighteenth minister general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear in speech, and sufficiently fit for disputation, is said to have worked at certain writings on the holy Scriptures and other little works, of which few have become known to me:

On the Sentences, two books. On Logic also.

On the Books of the Ethics, ten books.

Various Questions, three books. On Moral Philosophy.

He also composed the office of the stigmata of Saint Francis, founder of the Order of Friars Minor. Finally, he is said to have published commentaries on many books of the Bible, which have still by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, emperor 4, and Pope John 22, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Nicholas de Lyra, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most devoted to the study of the holy Scriptures and, through long practice, [unclear]. Perfectly instructed in the Hebrew language, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, he wrote many distinguished little works on the sacred volumes, through which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. How useful and how necessary they are to all who desire to learn sacred Scripture, no one knows better than he who has exercised himself in reading them. For there are some who think he should be despised because of the simplicity of his eloquence; they seem to me vain and unskilled, and unworthy of sacred knowledge and saving philosophy, since they both disparage ecclesiastical simplicity and embrace words, not things. Of the works of this devout and learned man the following are reported:

On the Sentences, one book: “In the beginning,” etc. [unclear].

On Genesis according to the letter, two books: “According as Isidore says ...”

On Leviticus, three books: “And he called Moses,” etc.

The Abbot of Sponheim

On Numbers, 1 book. On Deuteronomy, 1 book. On Joshua, 1 book. On Judges, 1 book. On Ruth, 1 book. On Kings, 4 books. On Chronicles, 1 book. On Ezra and Nehemiah, 1 book. On Tobit, 1 book. On Judith, 1 book. On Esther, 1 book. On Job, 1 book. On the Psalter, 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet, 1 book. On Jeremiah, 1 book. On the Lamentations of Jeremiah, 1 book. On the book of Baruch, 1 book. On Ezekiel, 1 book. On Daniel, 1 book. On the twelve minor prophets, 1 book. On Maccabees, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On Mark, 1 book. On Luke, 1 book. On John, 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul, 1 book. On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. On the canonical epistles, 7 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. He expounded the following morally, 1 book. On Genesis again, 1 book. On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book. On Deuteronomy, 1 book. On Joshua, 1 book. On Judges, 1 book. On Ruth, 1 book. On Kings, 1 book. On Chronicles, 1 book. On Ezra and Nehemiah, 1 book. On the book of Esther, 1 book. On the book of Job, 1 book. On the Psalter, 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet, 1 book. On Jeremiah, 1 book. On the Lamentations of the same, 1 book. On Ezekiel, 1 book. On Daniel, 1 book. On the twelve Prophets, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On Mark, 1 book. On Luke.

“The Lord spoke,” etc. “An explanation of the discourses.” “You shall bring them in and [plant them?].” “The Lord raised up judges.” “In the days,” etc. Here [unclear]. “Through me kings reign.” “Gather up the fragments.” “The priest will be over [unclear].” “These things it was necessary to do.” “Arphaxad,” etc. After [unclear]. “In the days,” etc. After. “Have patience with me.” “A great prophet has arisen.” “Behold, I have described it to you.” “The words of Ecclesiastes.” “Let him kiss me,” etc. [unclear]. “After the historical books.” “All wisdom,” etc. “Jerusalem [unclear].” “A prophet among the nations.” “How she sits.” In [unclear]. “These words,” etc. After. “The heavens were opened,” etc. “But to Daniel God gave.” “Of the twelve prophets.” “And it came to pass,” etc. After. “Four faces to one.” “The face of a lion on the right.” “The face of an ox on the left.” “The face of an eagle above.” “Behold, I have described them to you.” “They were all filled with the Spirit.” “James,” etc. This book. “You must prophesy again.” “I saw in the right hand [unclear].” “These are the names,” etc. Through the sons [unclear]. “He called,” etc. In this book. “The Lord spoke.” “These are the words.” It follows. “And it came to pass,” etc. [Allegorically?]. “After the death,” etc. [Allegorically?]. “In the days of one judge.” “There was one man.” [Allegorically?]. “Adam, Seth,” etc. In this [unclear]. “In the year,” etc. This Cyrus. “The words of Jeremiah,” etc. Through [unclear]. “How she sits.” Here begins. “There was a man,” etc. [unclear]. “Blessed is the man,” etc. As. “The vision of Isaiah.” In this. [unclear], etc. It follows. “The word which,” etc. It follows. “The book of the generation of Jesus.” “The beginning of the Gospel,” etc. “There was in the days,” etc. Among. On Jo-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On John, book 1. On the Acts of the Apostles, book 2. On the Apocalypse, book 3. On Tobit also, book 4. On the Book of Judith, book 5. On Maccabees, book 6. On the Song of Songs, book 7. Sermons on the saints, book 8. Against the Jews, book 9. He also published a number of other works besides, which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Guido of Perpignan, a Catalan by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, the twelfth prior general, and afterward bishop of the churches of Majorca and Elne, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and pleasing in eloquence, an acute disputant, and distinguished no less in manner of life than in knowledge. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he commended his name to posterity, and among them the following are reported: a polished and distinguished work in three parts.

On the Perfection of the Catholic Life. To Pope John XXII, book 1. Six Quodlibets, book 2. Ordinary Questions, book 3. On the Concordance of the Evangelists, book 4. To the cardinal of Albano, book 5. Questions on the Soul, book 6. On the Sentences, book 7. In our first [unclear], book 8. Whether the Word in [unclear], book 9. Correctory of the Decretum, book 10. On the Books of the Physics, book 11. He also composed several other works,

To Jo- [unclear]

he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Pope John XXII: a work of no small size.

On Ecclesiastical Power, book 1. On the Sentences, book 2. On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks, book 3. On the Entry into the Land of Promise, book 4. On the Resurrection, book 5. On Mark, book 6. On John, book 7. On the Magnificat, book 8. On the Canonical Epistles, book 9. On the Apocalypse, book 10.

He began a distinguished work from the writings of the holy father Augustine, which he entitled the Milleloquium, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; afterward Bartholomaeus of Urbino, of the same order, completed it. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, emperor IV, and Pope John [unclear], in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter of Abano, an Italian by nation, a Paduan by homeland, a man devoted to and learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and a physician of most celebrated reputation, subtle in talent and renowned for knowledge of many languages, is said to have worked through many little works both in philosophy and in medicine, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. There are some who write that he was a magician and displayed many marvels by that superstitious art; whether this is true, I would not dare affirm, since indeed I know nothing certain about it. For I do not recall either having read anything of his little works or having seen them anywhere. Yet among them the following are reported: a distinguished work divided into one hundred and ten distinctions, which he entitled:

On Medicine of Every Kind, book 1. On John Mesue, book 2. And certain other works. He translated Galen on black bile and on the regimen of health, together with many other works. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year 1320.

Sibertus de Beka, a German by nation, from Guelders by homeland, of the order of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Lower Germany, a man in

most learned in divine writings, and excellently taught both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence; in his own time he shone no less for his manner of life than for his learning. He wrote certain commendable little works, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Summa of the Censures of the New Law, 1 book. On the Rule of His Order, 1 book.

And certain others. He also corrected the ordinal of his order with sagacious intent. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

CLEMENT, the fifth pope, originally from Gascony, previously called Bernard, bishop of Bordeaux, sat after Benedict XI in the chair of Peter for eight years and ten months; a learned and vigorous man, at whose command the order of Templars was destroyed on one day throughout the whole world. He celebrated the Council of Vienne, in which he established many things for the utility of the Church. He composed the seventh book of the Decretals, which John XXII, his successor, published, as is contained at the beginning of the same. It is commonly called:

The Code of the Clementines, 1 book. The foundations of the Catholic faith. Also Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Clement, bishop, servant...

He died while Henry VII governed the Roman Empire, in the year of the Lord 1314, indiction 11.

PETER of Perpignan, called Rimi, a Catalan by birth, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the holy scriptures and a subtle expounder of scholastic philosophy, ready in intellect and an outstanding declaimer. He published many little works of reading not to be despised, by which, exercising the abundant vein of his intellect, he made his name known also to posterity. Among them are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. On the Whole Psalter. Various Sermons, 1 book.

But concerning the other things that he composed, nothing has ever come to my knowledge.

ODERIC, of the order of Friars Minor, a holy and learned man, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, on account of his most fervent love for which he undertook a pilgrimage and penetrated Asia and India, where, by preaching and teaching, evangelizing the faith of Christ, he converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. His most holy life was confirmed by many signs both in the flesh and after death. Among the other little works of his intellect he wrote:

The History of His Pilgrimage, 1 book. Also Various Sermons, 1 book.

And certain letters. He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

FRANCIS of Meyronnes, of the order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in divine writings and nobly taught in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, composed in style, constant in study, sufficiently acute and very fit for debating and resolving questions of the scriptures. He wrote not a few distinguished volumes of his intellect, in which he showed himself most learned and transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Concerning the proemium of the first. On Formalities, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

It is also reported that he composed certain commentaries on the divine volumes and other various treatises, which have not yet come at all to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

BONAVENTURA of Padua, of the order of Hermits of St. Augustine, formerly prior general, and afterward priest-cardinal of the holy Church of the title of St. Cecilia, a man learned in divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect and clear in eloquence, reverend no less for his manner of life than for his learning, of great reputation in delivering sermons to the people. When he was defending the liberty of the Church most vigorously against tyrants, he was at last pierced by an arrow by the lord of Carrara and crowned with martyrdom. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. The desired one will come with... Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. But far be it from me to glory...

And certain others. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

WILLIAM Ockham, an Englishman by birth, of the order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of John Scotus, a man learned in divine writings, nobly [unclear] in Aristotelian philosophy

Concerning Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] learned, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain small works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Acting and writing against John the Twenty-second, who condemned the heresy of the Fraticelli, together with Peter of Picenum, whom Emperor Louis had set up as an idol and had caused to be called Nicholas the Fifth, and declaring him to be a heretic, he was excommunicated by him. Fleeing to Emperor Louis, likewise excommunicated, he said to him: “O Emperor, defend me with the sword, and I shall defend you with the word.” And so he remained excommunicated with the excommunicated man until the end of his life, and at length at death he was absolved. He was a very fierce opponent of Scotus his master, and attacked almost all his sayings. He wrote:

Against John XXII, on the poverty of Christ and the apostles. An Apology, one book. On the Sentences, four books. Also Quodlibets, one book. On the Supporters of Heretics, seven books. In all curious matters. On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320. And he was buried in a convent of his order in the Norican province, which is now called Bavaria, of which Emperor Louis had formerly been duke.

Alpharus, of the order of Friars Minor, a Spaniard by nation, a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by John XXI, acted in writing and in words against William Ockham the Englishman. He published certain distinguished volumes of his intellect, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is a great and notable work describing the defects of ecclesiastical persons, which he entitled:

On the Lamentation of the Church, one book. On the Sentences, In the name of our Lord Jesus, four books. An Apology, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished at the same time as Ockham, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Matthaeus Sylvaticus, a Mantuan by homeland, noble by birth, a physician by art and profession, in which faculty in his time he was held before many others both learned and experienced, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote in that science volumes not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable work addressed to Rupert, king of Sicily, and physician, on all simple medicines and their properties, which he entitled:

Pandecta, one book. Aaron in Greek, in Arabic. I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Johannes Canonicus, of the order, as they say, of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer and disciple of John Scotus in the school of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly learned in secular philosophy, and also not ignorant of both pontifical and imperial law. He is said to have composed certain distinguished small works, by which, exercising his intellect, he also made his name known to posterity. But I have seen none of them. They are said to be:

On the Sentences, four books. Disputed Questions, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, of the order of Friars Preachers, and afterwards, as they say, bishop of the church of [Anciensis?], a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not meanly learned in secular philosophy, ready in intellect and eloquence, an excellent declaimer of sermons, at first a defender of the writings of St. Thomas Aquinas, but afterwards, as we see, an opponent; a certain wavering reason for this change is reported, to which I [unclear] belief. [unclear] by which he made his name known. Of these are reported:

On the Sentences, one book. Dearest brothers and sa[unclear]. On the Instruction of the Clergy, one book. Various Questions, one book. A Notable Summa. Different Sermons, one book.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

Herenus of Boyo, a Breton by nation, of the order of the brothers of the ever-Virgin Blessed Mary of

The Abbot of Spanheim

of Mount Carmel, a man in every respect most learned, an eminent professor of sacred Scripture, of keen and vigorous intellect, quite suited to resolving questions of the Scriptures. He is said to have written some excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is found an outstanding work, as his own report:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And various questions.

But he is also said to have composed certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Rupertus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long practice, and a subtle and profound interpreter of scholastic philosophy, an acute disputant and outstanding declaimer, keen in intellect, scholastic in speech. He published certain works not to be despised, by which, exercising his talent fruitfully and usefully, he made his name known not only to those then living but also to those to come. Of these I have seen only the necessary one:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Sermons on the season, 1 book.

Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

Moreover, he adorned many books of Aristotle with very elegant commentaries. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Astesanus of Asti, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man nobly learned in divine writings, a philosopher and distinguished jurist, renowned in knowledge, profound in intellect, cautious in counsel, firm in judgment, composed in speech. He is said to have fashioned various little works of his excellent talent, by which he made his name known both to those then living and to those to come. Of these I have seen only the necessary one:

A Summa on cases, 8 books. “Since, therefore, we are about to speak in this first...”

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes de Alerio, by nation a Toulousain, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the thirteenth prior general, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and venerable no less for the fervor of religion than for learning, governed the Carmelite order energetically for nine years. He published several excellent volumes, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent. Of these there survive:

On the Sentences, [4?] books. A Reading on Ecclesiasticus, [1?] book.

And many others. He was elected general of his order at Montpellier, in the general chapter, on the day of Pentecost, under Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1321, indiction 4.

Johannes de Regno, by nation a Frenchman, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, from the convent of Toulouse, a man learned in the sacred Scriptures and not ignorant of secular learning, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He published many excellent volumes, by which he made his name known even to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 1 book.

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. Lenten sermons, 1 book.

Sermons on the holy [unclear]. But the other things which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

1 book. Various questions, 1 book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

Stephanus de Provincia, professor and exceptional interpreter of both laws, and sufficiently instructed both in divine writings and in secular letters, renowned in intellect and eloquence; his learning was approved among his contemporaries. He wrote certain volumes not to be neglected, by which, exercising his talent gloriously, he also transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these is an outstanding work:

On the Clementines, 1 book. “Because [unclear] is...”

Various questions, 1 book. “[unclear]”

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 2 books. On the Novellae, in two ways. “[unclear]”

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Additions to the Speculum, one book. I, Johannes An[unclear]. The work entitled Mercuriale, one book. Since frequently in the forum, A Summa on betrothals and marriage, one book. Johannes: Gracious. On the Clementines, one book. Jerome constantly [unclear]. On the praises of Saint Jerome, four books. Of the rest I have seen nothing. On the tree of consanguinity, one book. He finally died of the plague and was buried at Bologna, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1348, indiction 1.

Cinus of Pistoia, born from the noble family of the Symbaldi, formerly a hearer and disciple of Dinus Mugellanus, a very distinguished man, and a close friend of Johannes Andreae, was certainly the most learned of all men of his time in civil law, subtle in intellect, ready and very abundant in knowledge. He published many little works in that faculty, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported.

On the Code, nine books. On the first part of the Old Digest, one book. On the second part, one book. Additions on the remaining parts, one book. And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Monaldus, of the order of Friars Minor, a most learned theologian and jurist, subtle in intellect, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, a man of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He published, for the benefit of the simple, little works not to be scorned even by the learned, by which he provided both for those then present and for those who would live long afterward. Of these the following necessary and very beautiful works are reported.

A Summa of canon law, one book. Since one who is ignorant [unclear]. Questions on the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book. And several other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Oldradus de Laude, an Italian by nation, formerly a hearer of Dinus Mugellanus, a most learned man, and the very close friend of Johannes Andreae, a man most skilled in both laws, also a student of philosophy and excellently imbued with the disciplines, who for many years was a consistorial advocate and acquired great praise and glory for his erudition. He wrote several distinguished little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A volume of Counsels, one book. In the name of the Lord, Amen.

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He is said to have left many selections in civil law afterward, which I have not yet seen. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Johannes de Blomendal, a German by nation, of the order of Friars Minor, a man studious and learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, was an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, volumes not to be scorned, by which he made his name known to posterity; of these I have so far found only:

Sermons on the season, one book. Take up your arms, quiver [unclear]. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Guido de Monte Rocherii, a man very studious in the sacred writings and rich in reading of the ancients, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech. He wrote little works of his intellect not to be despised, by which he made the memory of his name known even among posterity. Of these I have seen only that well-known work, circulated in print, which, composing it for the instruction of simple and upright priests, he wished to be entitled:

The Manipulus curatorum, three books. Since, as the prophet says,

I could not find any others. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Johannes de Lignerii, a philosopher and astronomer the most celebrated of all in his time, who magnificently restored this discipline, already almost erased from human memory, acquired erudition in the Parisian gymnasium, where he had as collaborators and associates in this faculty men most learned in mathematical science: Johannes de Saxonia, Johannes de Muris, and Bernardus, distinguished philosophers and astronomers.

Canons of the first movable, one book. Of any arc I have set [unclear].

Dd 2

The Abbot of Sponheim, Book I.

Tables of the same man. Also On the Sphere, one book. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the times of Louis IV the Bavarian, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes Danck of Saxony, a German by nationality, a contemporary of the aforesaid Johannes de Ligneriis and companion in his studies, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and astronomer, very celebrated among all men of his time, subtle in intellect and eminent. He produced many distinguished and admirable little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. But thus far I have found very few:

Eclipse Canons, one book: The quantity of an eclipse of the sun. Canons of the Tables, one book: The time of the fourth aspect. On the Astrolabe, one book. On Incensions, one book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Petrus de Palude, a Frenchman by nationality, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, an excellent disputant and declaimer. He produced certain distinguished volumes on the holy scriptures, by which he bestowed his name upon immortality. Among these are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Various Questions, one book. And various sermons, one book. And many other things.

He is also said to have adorned and expounded many books of the Bible with his commentaries.

Johannes Calderini, an Italian by nationality, from Bologna, once a hearer and disciple of Johannes Andreae, a professor and very celebrated interpreter of canon law, not ignorant of secular philosophy and the divine scriptures, prompt in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote not a few volumes in his faculty, by which, proving his ability through diligent exercise, he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Among these I found a great and distinguished work, divided into three not small volumes, which he entitled:

Repertory of Law, one book: A. This word sometimes from... On the Decretals, one book. On Ecclesiastical Interdict, one book: Although there are several doubts concerning... Many Counsels, one book. Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis IV the Bavarian, emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Paulus de Liazariis, a hearer of Johannes Andreae of Bologna and fellow student of Johannes Calderini, a man most skilled in both laws and nobly instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, distinguished in intellect and speech, who was by no means the least among the doctors of law in his time. Among the other little works of his ability he wrote a distinguished volume, which is called:

On the Clementines, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV the Bavarian, emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lupoldus of Bebenburg, bishop of Bamberg, a German by nationality, once, as they report, a hearer of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, and nobly learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech. He produced little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great glory. Among these there is extant a distinguished work on the zeal for the Christian religion of the ancient princes:

Of the Germans, one book. On the Rights of the Roman Empire, one book. And certain other volumes on diverse subjects, which have come to me.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Nicolaus of Modena, a man nobly learned in both laws and especially in the laws, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel, so that he might leave memorials of his ability to posterity. He wrote certain distinguished volumes in civil law, by which he had made himself useful to those then living and known to those to come. Among these are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books. On the New Digest, eleven books. On the Infortiatum, three books.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV the Bavarian, emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1348.

Lapus de Castellione, abbot of San Miniato, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[He was] learned in law, among all the men of his time one of the most learned, and imbued from his earliest age, [as they say?], with the disciplines of the philosophers; distinguished in talent, scholastic in expression, and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions. His authority among jurists is to be considered by no means slight. In his own faculty he wrote several little works, of which there survives an excellent work:

Of his allegations, one book. On the Clementines, one book.

And many other things. He flourished in the time of the emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Guerricus, abbot of Igny, a man by no means poorly learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in talent, sweet and well-ordered in speech, and quite fit for persuasion; distinguished no less for his manner of life and love of regular observance than for knowledge of the Scriptures. For the edification of simple and devout brothers he wrote little works not to be despised, in which, showing himself a useful and faithful shepherd of Christ’s sheep, he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have found only a work of sermons on the season and on the saints throughout the cycle of the year, which he delivered:

To his brothers, one book. We await the Savior.

He also wrote letters.

But concerning the rest which he is said to have composed, I have nowhere been able to find anything.

Henry of Urimaria, of the order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, by nation, as they say, a German; a man from boyhood most zealous and very learned in the holy Scriptures, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy. For many years he was an outstanding doctor in the school of Paris and shone forth as distinguished for celebrated learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are said to exist:

On the Sentences, four books. Quodlibets, one book.

Flowers from the conference of the fathers, one book. Hear, O Israel, the commandments.

On the perfection of man, two books. Because many [unclear].

On the fourfold impulse, one book. On the incarnation of the Word, one book.

On exemption, one book. Behold, other seed fell in.

Sermons on the season, ten books. Exposition of the decree On the celebration of Mass, one book.

On the books of the Ethics, sixteen books. Sermons on the saints, one book.

And many other things. He flourished in the time of the emperor Louis IV, surnamed the Bavarian, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Bartholomaeus de Osa, a native of Bergamo, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and historiographer, [unclear] in the eloquence of preachers. He is said to have fashioned some volumes of excellent learning, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following work excels:

A notable Histories, sixteen books.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Bartholomaeus of Pisa, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, very skilled in both laws, and nobly instructed in philosophical knowledge; distinguished in talent, clear in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel. He is said to have written certain excellent little works, of which I have seen only the summa which they call the Pisan, truly a work not to be rejected. A few years ago it was in use among confessors of the common people. The author entitled it:

A magisterial summa, one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, and completed his summa, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1338.

Albertus of Brescia, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and by no means poorly learned in both laws; also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, and no less holy than learned, since he is said to have shone with miracles even in life. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote a notable work:

Various sermons, one book.

A summa on cases, [unclear].

And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Ludolph, of the Carthusian order in the house of Strasbourg, by nation a German, born from the land of Saxony; a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters; gentle in talent, sweet and well-ordered in speech, and distinguished also in life and conduct. He published certain excellent little works of great devotion and profound learning,

The Abbot of Spanheim ... by which, nobly exercising his talent, he consigned his name to immortality. Of these I have seen only the following: a large and distinguished volume on the Gospel, which he entitled The Life of the Lord Jesus, in 2 books, “No other foundation ...”; also On the Psalter, 1 book, “As once manna ...” Other works of his are also reported. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Hermann of Schildis, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most devoted to and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, and distinguished no less in life than in learning and knowledge, published many excellent volumes, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent and transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise and glory. Of these the following are reported: On the First Book of the Sentences, 1 book; A Lecture on Genesis, 1 book; A Double Hexaemeron, 1 book; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On the Lord’s Prayer, in two treatments, 2 books; On the Matter of the Song of Songs, 1 book; Brevilogue, 1 book; An Exposition of the Mass, 1 book; On the Four Senses of Scripture, 1 book; On the Capital Vices, 1 book; A Manual for Priests, 1 book; On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book; The Cloister of the Soul, 1 book; Introduction to Law, 1 book; On True and False Friendship, 1 book; On the Canonical Hours, 1 book; An Exposition of the Mass, 1 book; Against the Flagellants, 1 book; On the Forty-Two Stations, 1 book; On the Comparison of the Mass, 1 book; The Division of Philosophy, in verse, 1 book; On the chapter Omnis utriusque, 1 book; various sermons, 1 book; preachable conferences, 1 book; Various Questions, 1 book; On Aristotle’s Rhetoric, 1 book. He also published many other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Guilhelmus of Kayothus, of the Order of Preachers, provincial prior in France, a man learned in the divine writings, and nobly instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, of excellent ability in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote certain works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with praise. He abridged the Summa of Johannes Teutonicus, which is called The Confessors’ Summa, 1 book, “What is simony ...”; various sermons, 1 book. The rest which he composed have by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter of Casa, a Limousin, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fourteenth prior general, then bishop of [Basionia?], and finally, as they report, patriarch of Jerusalem, a man most learned in the divine writings, ready in talent and clear in eloquence, learned and eloquent in declaiming sermons to the people, published certain excellent volumes by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books; sermons for the season, 1 book; sermons on the saints, 1 book; and certain other works. He flourished, and was elected prior general of his order from the convent of Limoges, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1350, indiction 13. He ruled his order energetically for twelve years.

Paulus of Perugia, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent and scholastic in speech, published several works of great authority, by which, exercising a brilliant talent, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with great glory. Of these there survives a very celebrated and almost divine work, which he recited in the University of Paris: On the Sentences, 1 book, “Concerning the first book of the Sentences ...”; also Quodlibets, 1 book; and certain other works. He flourished at Paris and completed his lecture under Louis the Bavarian, Emperor IV, and Pope Clement VI, in the year 1344, indiction 12. Not long after this same lecture of his, he died at Paris and was buried there in the convent. Bernar-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

BERNARDUS Parentinus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, skilled through long practice, and not moderately learned in scholastic disciplines, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the instruction of simple priests, certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant:

An exposition of the Mass, 1 book: “Since the Wise Man cries out.” Various sermons, 2 books. And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

OSBERTUS, English by nation, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man certainly very learned in the holy Scriptures and excellently taught in secular philosophy, of sharp and forceful intellect, of scholastic eloquence, subtle in disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity; of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books: “One conclusion having been proposed.” Various determinations, 5 books: “It is asked whether [unclear].” Also various sermons, 6 books.

The rest that he composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

JOHANNES Estuidi, English by nation, a man easily the most learned of all in secular letters in his time, a philosopher and astronomer second to none, outstanding in intellect and sweet in eloquence. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant an outstanding work of judicial astrology, on the accidents of the world, which is commonly called:

The English Summa, 2 books: “My intention in this book.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished and completed the same summa, as is stated at its beginning, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1347, the fifteenth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

BERNARDUS, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in life, and a notable cultivator and propagator of regular observance. He wrote, for the edification of monks, certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant:

Mirror of Monks, 1 book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book: “It is read in Proverbs.” On regular precepts, 2 books. Sermons to the brothers, 1 book.

He is also said to have composed many other things, which have by no means reached us.

SIMON of Cremona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, quite excellent in delivering sermons to the people, since for a long time among the Venetians he labored at this office, where by word and example he instructed very many. He wrote, for the instruction of simple preachers, little works not to be despised, of which there are extant:

On the Gospels, 1 book: “Lift up your heads, because.” Also on the Epistles, 1 book: “Let us cast off the works of darkness.”

The rest that he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

PETRUS Raymundi of Insula Grassa, French by nation, of the Order [unclear], who after Petrus of [unclear], of Mount Carmel, the fifteenth prior general, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, vigorously governed his order for fifteen years. He wrote elegantly:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And certain other things.

He flourished and was elected general from the convent of Carcassonne in the province of Narbonne, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1343, the eleventh indiction.

REINHERUS Foroliviensis, the most celebrated jurist of all in his time, teacher of Bartolus of Sassoferrato, a man distinguished in intellect and eloquence. He is said to have composed various little works in civil law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. But I have not been able to find any of them anywhere. He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1358, the third indiction.

320 The Abbot of Sponheim

Simon of Cascia, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, and venerable no less for holiness of life than for knowledge. Indeed, he is said to have been illumined by the spirit of prophecy in the Florentine convent. He published excellent volumes of great usefulness, in which he shows himself a learned and devout man. Among these I have found a notable work on the whole Gospel, which is commonly entitled:

The Deeds of the Savior, 15 books. “From the good, concerning the good.” On Christian Doctrine, 1 book. On Patience, 1 book. An Exposition of the Creed, 1 book. On the Mirror of the Cross, 1 book. On the Discipline of Spiritual Persons, 1 book. And certain others. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340. On the Sentences, 4 books. Also Against the Jews, 1 book. A Postil read at Cologne, 1 book. In addition he published several other works, but they have by no means come to our knowledge.

Sertorius, whom some call Fortanerius, of the Order of Friars Minor, the nineteenth minister general, English by nation, Welsh by homeland, afterward Archbishop of Ravenna, and finally Patriarch of Grado, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man [unclear] in divine Scripture, won from all men great praise for learning. He wrote a notable volume:

On Augustine’s City of God, 22 books. I have found nothing about the rest.

Finally, he is also said to have composed various treatises on the books of the Bible. He flourished when he was elected minister general of his order in the chapter at Marseilles, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1356, indiction 9.

Albericus of Rosate, from Bergamo by homeland, a distinguished professor of both laws, a most renowned interpreter, excellently learned also in the other secular letters, ready in intellect and polished in speech. He published many well-ordered volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, 12 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 1 book. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On Dante’s Comedy, 1 book.

He also composed several other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

John of Saxony, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently learned both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, published certain excellent volumes of his talent, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these there is extant:

A Summa on Cases, 1 book. And other works which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerard of Siena, Italian by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man not moderately learned in the holy Scriptures, skilled through long practice in both laws, subtle and sharp in intellect; John Andrea, his contemporary, often commends and cites his learning. He wrote several excellent little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported as the more important:

On the First Book of the Sentences, 1 book. On Contracts of Usury, 1 book. On Prescriptions, 1 book. I have found nothing about the rest.

He flourished with John Andrea, under Louis the Bavarian, Emperor IV, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

John of Rupescissa, of the Order of Friars Minor, very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, seduced by I know not what spirit (not to say induced), [began] to predict the desolation of the Catholic Church and other terrible things

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Having begun as if a prophet, he was cast into prison by the ministers of his own order, and a lying spirit was found in his mouth. He wrote in chains to a certain cardinal: His Revelations, one book, “Most reverend in Christ.” Also On the Sentences, four books. And certain other things. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerard, bishop of Savona, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, by homeland of Bergamo, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in canon law, subtle in intellect and renowned in speech, distinguished no less by life than by doctrine, composed for the benefit of readers some little works not to be despised, by which, usefully exercising his talent, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported: On the Sentences, four books; Two Quodlibets, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Sixth of the Decretals, concerning [unclear], one book; On the Epistle to the Hebrews, one book; and certain other things. He is also said to have written many other little works, which have not come to my knowledge. A Summa of Medicine, one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, fourth emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Thomas de Garbo, by homeland a Florentine, son of Dino, once a physician, a man learned and skilled in medicine and nobly instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, adhering to the footsteps of his most learned father, published in his own faculty little works not to be scorned by physicians, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these there exists a very notable [work], four books. Of the rest I have learned nothing.

Alphonsus, bishop of Seville, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most learned both in divine writings and in secular letters, and in his time most celebrated among ecclesiastical doctors, renowned in intellect and speech. He published several volumes of great [unclear], by which he also made his name known to posterity; of these I [unclear] volumes of such authority, by which he transmitted his name, present in usefulness and distinguished, to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, one book; On the Gospel of Mark, one book. He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340. On the Gospel of Matthew, seven books; On the Apocalypse, one book.

John of Bacon, an Englishman, of the order of the friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine writings and excellently taught both in canon law and in secular philosophy, in the Parisian school no less in conduct than [unclear]. The Example of His Order, four books; Various Quodlibets, one book; The Mirror of His Order, one book; “You are sons of the saints [unclear],” one book; The Defense of His Order, one book; On the Poverty of Christ, one book; Against the Jews, one book; and many other things.

John Eliger of Gondersleuen, by nation a German, once a hearer of John of Saxony, a most renowned astronomer, a man most learned in secular letters, exercised himself magnificently in [philosophy?]. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Clement VI, pope, in the year 1350. On the Rule of His Order, two books, “About to treat of the great [unclear].” Moreover he published explanations on the books of blessed Augustine On the Holy Trinity and On the City [unclear], one book, “While [unclear] prays for us.” On the Composition of the Astrolabe, one book, “The uses of the new [unclear].” On the Usefulness of the Quadrant, one book, “The king of the stars, Ptolemy [unclear].” On the Magnet also, one book, “With zeal the principal [unclear].” On the [astrogetrum?].

The Abbot of Spanheim

And many other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Rupert, French by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent, clear in speech. He published various little works on the Holy Scriptures, in which, magnificently exercising his talent, he also made the memory of his name known to posterity. He was an excellent preacher of the divine word, and wrote many things useful to declaimers of sermons. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Epistles of Paul, 19 books. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, [unclear].

He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Clement VI, pope, from Limoges by country, previously called Petrus Rogetius, abbot of Fécamp of the order of St Benedict. He sat in the chair of Peter after Benedict XII for ten years and six months; a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, an eminent doctor of canon law, venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge, and of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. He published certain distinguished little works, in which he showed the liveliness of his talent. Of these the following are reported:

Various sermons, 1 book. At the canonization of Ivo, 1 book. Exult and praise [unclear]. At the approval of King Charles, 1 book. Solomon shall sit upon. Many conferences, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book.

And certain other things. He died at Avignon and was buried under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1332, in the fifth indiction.

Gregory of Rimini, of the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine, prior general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and much instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent and speech. In the Parisian school he earned from all men great glory for his learning, since he shone forth as most celebrated in life and doctrine. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which these are reported as the more important:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Epistles of Paul the Apostle, [14?] books.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Philip of Bergamo, prior of the monastery of Saint Mary of [Avantia?] in Padua, of the order of our holy father Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and distinguished in speech. He wrote several little works of holy doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found only a large volume:

On the Ethics of Cato, 1 book. To the glory and praise.

He is also said to have written sermons, 1 book.

The rest which he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading.

Johannes de Beka, German by nation, cleric of the church of Utrecht, a man very studious and learned in the sacred Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, published certain little works of his talent not to be despised. Of these I saw only one work, written in a simply clear style, addressed to Lord John, bishop of the church of Utrecht, and William, duke of Holland, concerning the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and the counts of Holland. Carrying it down from the time of Saint Willibrord, the first bishop, to the year of the Lord 1346, he wished it to be titled:

Chronicle of the Church of Utrecht, 1 book. Therefore from the year [unclear].

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of Louis IV and likewise Charles IV, emperors, in the year of the Lord [1350?].

Francis Petrarch, Tuscan by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and by far the most learned of all in secular letters in his own time, a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, who after a long silence called the dead letters of humanity, so to speak, back from the underworld to those above; he shone forth as distinguished no less in holy conduct than in knowledge. For love of Christ and of saving philosophy he undertook the solitary life, in which, persevering until death in meditation, prayer, and writing, his fame was borne throughout the whole world. Of his little works I found:

On the Solitary Life, 1 book. I have known few men. On re-

ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

[Petrarch, works list:] On the remedies of fortune: 2 books.
