["Since [you ponder your] affairs and fortunes…"]; On the seven penitential psalms: 1 book; On the conflict of cares: 1 book; On the present world: 1 book; On the history of Griselda: 1 book; Bucolics, in meter: 1 book. ["Monicus, in [the] tranquil…"]; Of letters to various [persons]: 8 books; The Africa, to King Robert: 1 book; the Life of Scipio Africanus: 1 book; On memorable matters: 1 book; On orchards, to Sagremor: 1 book. He published also many others, which have by no means come into our hands. He dies in his hermitage of the Paduan territory, under Charles IV, emperor, and Gregory [XI], pope, in the year of the Lord 1374, in the 12th indiction.

Michael de Massa, of the order of the hermit-brothers of Saint Augustine, a man studious and erudite in the divine Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, and nobly learned in secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, and a distinguished declaimer of sermons, distinguished also for the honesty of [his] life [and] conversation. He published many illustrious volumes for the edification of the faithful, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the notice of posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books; On Isaiah; On Matthew; On Mark; On Luke; On John; On the life of Christ; On the passion of the Lord; On the four virtues; Various sermons. And many others. He is said, finally, to have elaborated elegant commentaries on many books of the Bible. He flourished in the times of the emperors Louis IV [and] Charles IV likewise, and of Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Richard de Bury, bishop of Durham, chancellor of Edward III, king of the English—to whom there is extant a letter of Francis Petrarch inquiring about the island of Thule—a man most studious [and] very erudite in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, a singular [and] most celebrated lover of books, who at great expense [and] labors founded a distinguished Library in the University of Oxford, which he established, for the public benefit of those studying there, with incredible zeal. He wrote, on the love of books [and] the institution of the said Library, a most beautiful treatise, which is now printed, which he entitled with a Greek name: Philobiblon: 1 book. ["A desirable treasure…"]; Several letters: 1 book. And certain others. He flourished under Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John Walsgram, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, nobly learned in secular philosophy, subtle [and] acute in talent, adorned with the master's infula in the gymnasium of Paris, [and] most celebrated in reading [and] disputing. He wrote certain illustrious volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a distinguished work: On the Sentences, 1 book; Various questions, 1 book; Sermons on the [seasons of the] year, 1 book; A Summa of law, 1 book; Sermons on the saints. The rest which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, [and] Clement VI, pope, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Thomas of Strasbourg, a Teuton by nation, of the order of the hermit-brothers of Saint Augustine, after Gregory of Rimini prior general, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures, a distinguished cultivator of secular philosophy, renowned for the honesty of [his] life [and] conversation, who wonderfully exalted his order by word [and] example. He wrote some illustrious volumes on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the notice of posterity. Of these there is extant a most luminous work: On the Sentences: [—] book[s]. ["The abyss gave [its] voice…"]

324 Abbot of Sponheim

The Constitutions of his order, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John Brãmart of Aachen, German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Lower Germany, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of the scholastics of this time, a most celebrated expounder of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent and eloquence, an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote for the no small profit of the faithful some minor works, by which, exercising his talent, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Various sermons, [unclear].

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henry of Erfurt, German by nation, exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned, and excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote for the edification of the Church a number of volumes, by which he made his name and fame known to many. Among these is reported a work of histories:

On memorable deeds, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John of Erfurt, German by nation, a Thuringian by homeland, of the Order of Friars Minor, an enlightened and skilled doctor in the divine Scriptures, and nobly and excellently learned both in each law and in secular philosophy. He published several works of great authority, in which he showed also to posterity the power of his outstanding talent. Of these I have seen only a large volume which he entitled:

Table of Law, 1 book. Since, as it is written, 12.

Summary on cases, 1 book. Asked by the brothers that.

Of the others I have seen nothing. He is said, however, to have composed elegant sermons, but they have not come to me.

John Tacephale, English by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a learned doctor of the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, very subtle in talent, composed in speech, the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time. He published works of no contemptible reading, by which, exercising his talent [unclear], he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences. On the Apocalypse of John.

Sermons on the saints, 4 books.

And certain other things.

Sermons on wisdom, 1 book.

Rupert Holcot, English by nation, of the Order of Preachers, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and also an excellent preacher of sermons. He wrote many distinguished works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Whether any wayfarer.

On the Book of Wisdom: The Lord is my rock and ro[unclear].

On the seven mortal sins: This is the way, walk in it.

Moralizations: Theodosius concerning life.

On the immortality of the soul. On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

He died of the plague, after he had begun a lecture on the Book of Ecclesiasticus, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1346, in the second indiction.

On the Sentences. And many other things.

Determinations of questions, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the school of Oxford and wrote many various volumes.

Pav-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

PAUL of Perugia, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and also excellently learned in other humane letters, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, was for a long time keeper and master of the library of Rupert, king of Sicily, a most learned and zealous prince. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survives a notable volume, in which there are many things both pleasant and useful concerning the gods of the gentiles and others, which he entitled Collections, 1 book. And certain other things. He flourished in the time of the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

BONOMINUS, [Bergomensis?] by nation, born in the town of Clusone, a learned physician and easily the most skilled of all in his time, and in the other disciplines of philosophy not moderately learned, most expert in healing human bodies. He wrote in that faculty little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But I do not remember having seen any of them. The following, however, is reported as his: On Poisons, 1 book; Diverse Questions, 1 book. He is also said to have composed works On the Sentences and various commentaries on the Bible. Concerning these and certain other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

TILMANNUS of Aachen, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a distinguished professor of sacred letters, outstanding in intellect and an excellent preacher, and also quite sufficiently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, wrote works not to be despised for the use of readers [unclear]. Of these there is reported one especially notable lecture, which he delivered publicly at Cologne: On the Gospel of Matthew, 24 books. He is also said to have composed sermons and various commentaries on the Bible. Since I am uncertain about these, I can judge nothing certain.

BARTOLUS de Saxoferrato, formerly a hearer and disciple of the learned Cino and Jacobus Butrigarius, a very celebrated jurist, one like whom earlier ages had not had in that faculty, subtle and keen in intellect, elegant and eloquent in speech. He published certain distinguished volumes, especially on the laws; how great their authority is today among jurists no one even slightly learned and experienced is unaware. Among these are reported the following notable commentaries of civil law: On the Code, 9 books; On the Old Digest, 1 book; [unclear], 2 books; On the Infortiatum, 4 books; On the Institutes, 4 books; also Tiberiadis, 1 book; also Counsels, 7 books; On the Guelphs and Ghibellines, 1 book. And many other things. He flourished under the emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1355, in the eighth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

PETRUS Thomas, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Car-[unclear], patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in divine writings, in life and conduct [unclear], in the year of the Lord 1350. And buried in Cyprus.

BARTHOLOMAEUS, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, English by nation, [unclear], was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, 19 books; [unclear] The Properties of Things, 1 book; [unclear]; On the Properties of Things; various sermons. He is also said to have written many other things, but they have by no means come into our hands.

Petrus Boherius, abbot of Saint Avianus, of the order of our lord father Benedict, a jurist and an excellent cultivator of the sacred Scriptures, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, a very celebrated director of monastic discipline. He published for the edification of his brothers a number of little works, in which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these I have found only [unclear].

The Abbot of Sponheim

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. On the Mirror of Monks, one book. On the Signs of Speech, one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

Since he was a very celebrated doctor of the decretals, he commented on the Rule of the holy father Benedict in a new and unusual kind of exposition, comparing with pontifical law not only all its chapters, judgments, and teachings, but also, what is the work of greater diligence, its words, counsels, and precepts; with admirable subtlety he confirmed them by the canons of the fathers. He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

JACOBUS of Altavilla, a German by nation, by homeland of [Rinaugia?], of the diocese of Mainz, a most learned professor of sacred letters, nobly educated in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech. He published some notable little works on divine writings, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have thus far been able to see only an excellent volume.

On the Sentences, one book. Various Questions also, one book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

JOHANNES of Imenhufen, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, an outstanding teacher no less by example than by word. He wrote certain excellent volumes, of reading not to be despised, by which, magnificently exercising his talent, he also made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences, one book. Elegant Sermons.

Of other things I have seen nothing. He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year 1360.

PETRUS Berchorius, a Frenchman by nation, from Poitiers by homeland, prior of the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man most zealous and very learned in divine writings, and excellently learned in secular letters, of outstanding talent in delivering sermons to the people, a philosopher, historian, and distinguished cosmographer. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Johannes de Pratis, bishop of Palestrina and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, he wrote a great and distinguished work, which has now been printed in three volumes, not unuseful to simpler preachers, which they call the Dictionarium, etc.; but he himself wished it to be entitled:

Moral Repertory, one book. To the Reverend [Christopa.?], one book.

Moral Reductory also, one book. “See, since not only in.”

Moral [Inductorium?], one book.

Breviary of the Histories of the Bible, one book. “Considering the history.”

He wrote a Cosmography, one book. Various Sermons.

And many other things. Finally, at the urging of John, king of France, he translated Titus Livy into the French language. And it should be noted that of the three moral works which we assigned the first place, one, which consists of three large volumes, of which one part of the Moral Reductory, embracing morally all the historical books of the Bible, has been printed, begins from Genesis thus: “God in the creation of the world.” There follows his Letters to various persons, small but many treatises. He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

JOHANNES of Tambach, a German by nation, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a man much practiced and learned in divine writings, and also not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, composed with the brilliance of scholastic eloquence, published certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: a large work not to be rejected against the darts of fortune favoring adverse things, no less useful than pleasant, which he wished to be entitled:

Consolation of Theology, one book. “Whatever things have been written,” one book.

On the Sensible Delights of Paradise, one book. “In the delights of the paradise of God.”

He published Sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 1350.

LEONARDUS of Chifano, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, the twenty-fourth minister general, and afterwards priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, a man most learned in divine writings, very skilled in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence. He is said to have left many monuments of his talent, of which I have found very few.

On the Sentences, one book. On the Song of Songs,

Sum:

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

A notable summa, one book. Various sermons, one book. He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Johannes Balistatii, a Catalan by homeland, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the seventeenth prior general, was a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, who governed his order strenuously in deed and word for sixteen years. He composed distinguished monuments of his talent, of which the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. On the War of the Church Militant, one book. Various sermons, one book. And certain other works.

The aforementioned notable work on the fierce war of the Church Militant and of Antichrist attacking her he sent dedicated to Pope Gregory XI. He died in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year 1374, in the twelfth indiction, in his convent of Majorca.

Johannes Boccatius of Certaldo, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a man easily the most learned of all his time in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated poet, philosopher, and astronomer, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, published many distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Robert, king of Sicily:

On the Genealogy of the Gods, fourteen books. “If sufficiently from the things related, lord...” On Illustrious Men, one book. “When I was seeking...” one book. “The day before, of women sick...” On Famous Women, one book. On the Victories of Sigismund, one book. On the Heresies of the Bohemians, one book. “Degeneration signifying...” On the Wars of the Emperors, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. On Springs, one book. “I had indeed risen weary...” On Mountains, one book. “After concerning mountains and...” On Springs, one book. “By a poetic fiction...” On Rivers, one book. “Tyndarus, not sufficiently...” On the Wars of the Florentines, one book. “And if sometimes from pools...” On the Victory of the Tartars, one book. “Having undertaken a modest labor...” On Marshes and Swamps, one book. On the Rebellion of the Lands of the Church, one book. On the Names of the Sea, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Bucolics, one book. “When of the most venerable...” On the Capture of Constantinople. And many other works.

In the vernacular language, moreover, many books of his are extant, full of jokes and vanities, such as the book of the Hundred Novellas, Corbaccio, and Philostratus. He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1375, in the thirteenth indiction, at the age of 62.

Johannes of Hildesheim, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly educated in secular letters, an eminent theologian, philosopher, and poet, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He was formerly at Avignon the familiar and devoted servant of blessed Peter Thomas, the general, a most holy man, of whom we made mention above. He wrote in verse and prose many distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Florentinus, bishop of Münster, he published a lengthy volume:

On the Three Holy Kings, one book. “When of the most venerable...” A Chronicle of Histories, one book. A Defense of His Order, one book. one book. On the Fountain of Life, one book. On Monsters in the Church, one book. Against the Jews, one book. On Antichrist, one book. Eighty Letters, one book. Against One Painting Shameful Things, one book. And certain other works. Various sermons, one book. Against the Wycliffites, one book. A Table of Originals, and certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Johannes Maronis, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly trained in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and an excellent disputant of scholastic questions, composed certain distinguished little works commending his talent, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these there is reported the notable work which he entitled:

[unclear] The archbishop of Canterbury were condemned.

The Abbot of Sponheim

John of Mount Carmel, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Rouen, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently trained in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote some little works of no contemptible authority, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives an excellent work:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the office of the Mass, 1 book. “Sing to the Lord a song.” Various Questions. He also published some other works besides, which have not come into our hands.

Henry of Dolendorp, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of worldly philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; acute in intellect, and very well suited to debating and resolving scholastic questions. For the instruction of readers he wrote certain excellent volumes. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the time of the Emperor Charles IV and Pope Urban V, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Gallus, abbot of the monastery of Aula Regia in Bohemia, of the order, as they say, of the Cistercians, a German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and rich in his reading of the ancients, an outstanding contemplator of divine things, subtle in intellect, clear and ordered in eloquence, also distinguished in the conduct of regular life, published for the edification of his brothers certain excellent volumes, by which he directed his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives a large and notable dialogue between father and son, which he entitled:

Malogranatum, 3 books. “Son, approaching to the service.” Sermons to the brothers, 1 book.

This volume of the Malogranatum is today much used among religious and truly devout persons, because it is suitable for beginners, the progressing, and the perfect.

Richard, archbishop of Armagh and primate of Ireland, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in discourse, of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, from his own talent, several little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. When he once preached to the people on the subject of mendicancy, he set forth nine conclusions; offended by these, the brothers of the mendicant orders appealed before the people to the Apostolic See. Therefore, when both the archbishop and the brothers appeared at Avignon before Pope Innocent VI and the cardinals, in the year of the Lord 1357, on the eighth day of the month of November, Archbishop Richard publicly set forth, read, and pronounced:

Of his Propositions, 1 book. “Do not judge according to.” He also wrote Sermons, 1 book. Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Matthew of Cracow, a Pole by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in eloquence; having been raised to a master’s chair in the university of Prague, he earned great praise from all for his learning. He wrote many excellent little works, of which, however, few have come into our hands. I have seen his work, not to be rejected, addressed to Henry, bishop of the church of Warmia, on predestination, and on the fact that God made all things well; the speakers of this dialogue are father and son, and he entitled it:

Rationale of Divine Works, 7 books. “I should wish it to be declared by what.” Also On Contracts, 1 book. “On the transfer of things [unclear].” On the celebration of Mass, 1 book, to the bishop of Warmia. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Sermons and Collations.

He flourished first in the university of Prague; then, when he was driven out with the other Germans by the Hussites, he taught letters for a time in the university of Paris.

John Fust, a German by nation, originally from the town of Kreuznach in the county of Sponheim, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters,

On Ecclesiastical Writers 329

[unclear], excellent in talent in delivering sermons to the people. While he was still lector in the Kreuznach convent, he wrote for the instruction of simple preachers some little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Weekday Sermons through Lent, one book.

Of the other things, however, which he composed, nothing anywhere has come into our hands. He is said to have flourished at Kreuznach around the time of the emperor Charles IV. The originals of his sermons are said to be held [unclear] in the Kreuznach convent.

Gerard the Great of Deventer, German by nation, of the diocese of Utrecht, excellently learned both in divine Scripture and in canon law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was the first to establish at Deventer the house of the brothers whom they call “of the common life.” He wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, by which, exercising his intellect, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. For he was renowned throughout all Germany not only for learning, but also for religious life and praiseworthy conduct. Among his little works these are reported:

On Contracts and Usury, one book. On the Instruction of Novices, one book. On the Leasing of Pastoral Care, one book. It is asked whether anyone can? On Internal Conduct, one book. On the Governance of Nuns, one book. On the Disadvantages of Marriage, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And many other things.

He died under the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1384, in the seventh indiction, in the forty-fourth year of his age.

William of Calford, English by nation, of the order of the brothers of the most blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, very learned in the divine writings, an excellent cultivator of secular philosophy, of powerful and excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote for preachers of the divine word little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to many. Of these there are extant, notably:

A Certain Lecture, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished in the Cambridge school in England, where by writing, teaching, and disputing he acquired great glory for his learning.

Francis Martini, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, Catalan by nation, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, an excellent expounder. He published a splendid volume, prepared with much diligence, on the holy and most pure conception of the glorious virgin Mary, mother of God, which he entitled:

Compendium.

And certain other things. He flourished in the convent of Barcelona, where at the beginning of the aforesaid golden work he states that he compiled it in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord [1390?].

James of Lausanne, of the order of the Friars Preachers of St. Dominic, bishop, as they report, of a certain city, a man most devoted to the divine writings, skilled by long practice, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, and quite excellent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote little works of utility not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these are reported:

On Genesis, one book. In the beginning God created, one book. On Leviticus, one book. I shall come to you [unclear], one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. On the Book of Numbers, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. As in the day honorably. Sermons on the Saints, one book. I am fixed to Christ. Lenten Sermons, one book.

Besides these he published many other lectures on the sacred books, conferences, determinations, and various treatises, which have not come into our hands.

Conrad of the town of Alzey, of the diocese of Mainz, a man learned in the divine writings, in secular [unclear], distant from Worms, German by nation, a man learned in the divine writings, excellently learned in secular letters, a philosopher and mathematician among [unclear] in his time

The Abbot of Sponheim Most celebrated among the Germans, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose. In both styles he wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there survives a volume, in verses with rhymes, painted with beautiful variety, on the most holy and most pure Mary, Mother of God, entitled On the Redemption of the Human Race. A figured work, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Poems also, one book. And many other things. He flourished around the times of the Emperor Charles IV. In the year of the Lord 1370.

Stephen [Petringon?], English by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, a most acute disputant, and very distinguished in delivering sermons to the people, published little works not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Among these are: Against the Wycliffites, one book. A Repertory of Arguments, one book. A Certain Notable Lecture, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. He flourished in the University of Oxford at the time when John Wyclif was burned.

Bertramus, bishop of [Thefelicensis?], of the Order of the Brothers Preachers, German by nation, vicar in pontificals of the bishop of Metz, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very famous among the doctors of his time, excellent in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and also an outstanding preacher of sermons. He wrote to Cuno, archbishop of Trier, a distinguished work entitled On the Illusions of Demons, one book. “Most reverend in Christ.” To the same, On the Schism, one book. “The wise [unclear] glory.” Various Sermons, one book. And several other things. He died under the Emperor Wenceslas and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1387, on 20 January, in the tenth indiction. He was buried in his convent at Koblenz.

Thomas Lombe, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, a man learned in the sacred Scriptures through long exercise and continual study, well instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle and keen in talent, who, having obtained the magisterial chair in the Oxford school, earned praise for his learning. He wrote an outstanding work: On the Sentences, four books. Against the Lollards, one book. Sermons also, one book. On the Incarnation of the Lord. And various Questions. And certain other things. He flourished in the University of Oxford especially at the time when John Wyclif in England was exhumed and publicly burned.

Philip Riboti, Catalan by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior of Catalonia, a man studious and learned in the sacred Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, venerable also in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover and guardian of the Carmelite Order. For the edification of his brothers he wrote little works not to be scorned, in which, showing the fervor of spiritual zeal toward his religion, he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives a volume which he entitled On the Particular Deeds of the Carmelites, ten books. “When the people of Israel.” On the Illustrious Men of Carmel, one book. Sermons. Letters. He composed several other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Nicholas Ritzonis, from Toulouse by homeland, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, provincial prior in the kingdom of Sicily, a learned man, distinguished in life and conduct, an outstanding preacher of sermons, subtle in talent and lucid in speech, published some little works in writing, the reading of which will not be contemptible for preachers of the word. Among these are reported: Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. A Double Lenten Collection.

Henry of Kalkar, German by nation, of the Carthusian Order, prior lord of St. Barbara in Cologne, a man having an enlightened talent in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, notable in life and conduct, published not

On Ecclesiastical Writers

minor works of reading not to be despised, whose use is judged very useful for religious and devout brothers. Among them these are reported:

Exercitatorium monachale, book I. Loquagium de rhetorica, book I. Cantuagium de musica, book I. On the Origin of His Order, book I.

And certain other works, pertaining especially to the cleansing of consciences. He flourished under the Emperor Wenceslas, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Richard Maidstone, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, a man very learned in the divine scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; distinguished in ability, rather scholastic in speech, and an eminent declaimer. He wrote many commendable minor works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found:

Against the Lollards of Wyclif, book I. Sermons on the Season, book I. Sermons on the Saints, book I. The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished at the school of Oxford, especially at that time when the heresy of John Wyclif began to sprout in England, and he wrote various works.

Marsilius of Inghen, English by nation, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and most nobly instructed in secular philosophy, the first planter of the school of Heidelberg, which Rupert, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, established and magnificently endowed, and which Pope Urban VI confirmed on the model of Paris; also, as Wimpheling testifies, canon and treasurer of the church of St. Andrew at Cologne. He published minor works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these, in the library of Heidelberg today, written in his own hand, are held:

Questions on the Sentences, book II. Notable Dialectic, book I. Commentaries on Aristotle, several books. And certain other things.

He died under the Emperor Wenceslas and Pope Boniface [unclear], in the year of the Lord 1384, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction. He was buried at Heidelberg in the church of St. Peter. There are those who write that he was German; to them I freely concede their judgment. But it is established that he was called from the school of Paris to Heidelberg for the beginning of the university.

John, monk of the monastery of Castell, in the diocese of Eichstatt, of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters; excellent in ability and eloquent in speech, an eminent theologian, philosopher, and rhetorician. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a great and very distinguished work, divided into two volumes, which he published with great and commendable study.

Conrad of Monte Puellarum, German by nation, canon of the church of Regensburg, a man learned in the divine scriptures and very learned in secular philosophy, subtle in ability and distinguished in eloquence. First in the school of Erfurt [unclear] the rudiments of the liberal arts; then [unclear] to the university of Paris, where, drawing in philosophy and sacred letters, he then betook himself to the university of Paris, where, publicly reading philosophy and sacred letters to students for eight years, he attained the insignia of the doctorate. He wrote for Lord Lupold, bishop of Bamberg, a great and noble work, which he entitled according to the Greeks:

Economics, book II. All of moral philosophy. Monastics, to the duke of Austria, book I. Politics also, book I. Various Questions, book I.

And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the Emperor Wenceslas and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Henry Boyc, Breton by nation, from the diocese of Leon, as he testifies at the beginning of his work on the Decretals; a man most learned in canon law, nobly instructed in scholastic philosophy, outstanding in ability, distinguished in eloquence, eloquent and abundant in judgment. He wrote in that faculty volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Decretals, book II. Venerabilibus et dif. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, book I. On the Clementines, book I.

It is also reported that he published commentaries on the Decrees, and various other treatises on different subjects, which have by no means come into our hands.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Johannes Rusbrock, prior of the regular canons of the Green Valley in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, a German by nationality, a man, as they say, devout but little learned. In his native tongue he wrote certain little works for the edification of the simple; after his death they were translated into Latin by another, and are said by doctors to be excellent in some respects, but erroneous in others. And concerning these, Johannes [Gerson], chancellor of Paris, composed advisements. Of them these are reported:

On the Adornment of Spiritual Nuptials, 3 books. “Behold, the bridegroom comes,” etc. On the Progress of Religious, 1 book. Exhortatory Letters, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes Schodehouen, a German by nationality, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Mechelen, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote, for the use of preachers of the word of God, volumes not to be despised. Of these the following are extant: a notable work on vices and virtues and on every preach-able subject matter, according to alphabetical order, in two volumes, which he entitled:

Polipodium, 2 books. “They hide themselves much.” Various Sermons, 2 books. He also produced a number of other works, which have by no means come into our hands.

Michael Angrianus of Bologna, an Italian by nationality, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular philosophy and canon law; Pope Urban VI first appointed him vicar of the whole order, and, finally elected general in the year of the Lord 1381, he governed the order under the obedience of Pope Urban for nine years. He wrote many excellent volumes. Of these the following are reported: to the cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere, a notable and excellent work.

On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book. On the Whole Psalter, 5 books. On the Sentences, 4 books. Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. A Table of the Sentences, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. “They were both,” etc. [unclear]. A Table of Gregory’s Moralia, 1 book. A Table of the Decretum, 3 books. A Lenten Book, 1 book. He began a Dictionary, 1 book. On Valerius Maximus, 1 book. On Aristotle’s Ethics, 1 book. And certain other works. Overtaken by death, he did not complete this divine work of the new dictionary, but carried it through from A to C inclusive in three volumes. He died in the last year of Emperor Wenceslaus, under Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1416, on the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction. And, honorably buried before the high altar of his own convent at Bologna, he rests in the peace of Christ.

Philippus Ferrariensis Tholosanus, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, learned and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, ready in talent and clear in eloquence; formerly preaching in the kingdom of Sicily, he converted many from iniquity and brought forth for God great fruits of his learning. He wrote elegant:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other works. There are those who write that, because of his exceptional learning and uprightness of life, he was raised to the honor of the cardinalate; of this I am not certain.

Galterus Differ, an Englishman by nationality, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, nuncio and legate of Pope Boniface IX in the kingdoms of England, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, Aragon, and in the regions of Gascony, and in the other lands and kingdoms, preaching the cross against infidels and schismatics; a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons. He wrote little works not to be despised, by which he made known only his name. Of these there are extant:

Against the Lollards, 1 book. On the Schism also, 1 book. On Some Psalms, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Gerardus Zutphanensis, a German by nationality, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

learned, also not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, to be preferred no less for his way of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published certain small works pertaining to the instruction of devout brothers, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

On Interior Reform, 1 book. A certain man went down. On Spiritual Ascent, 1 book. Blessed is the man whose is. Various Sermons, 1 book. Of the rest I have found nothing.

From his writings it appears that he was a devout, religious man, of some order, although it is unknown to us. There are indeed those who write that he was a canon regular, which we pass over as probable. He flourished in the school of Cologne. He wrote various works.

John of Hesdin, of the order of the brothers of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, an eminent doctor of the sacred page, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, keen in talent and orderly in speech, published many distinguished volumes; at the University of Paris he delivered many elegant lectures. Of these the following are extant:

On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. He was made like a lion. [unclear], 1 book. On the Epistle to the Romans, 1 book. [unclear], 2 books. On the Epistle to the Galatians, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Ephesians, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Philippians, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Colossians, 1 book. On the Epistles to the Thessalonians, 2 books. On the Epistles to Timothy, 2 books. On the Epistle to Titus, 1 book. Train your son, because as. On the Epistle to Philemon, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Hebrews, 1 book. On the Lord’s Annunciation, 1 book. Hail Mary, full of grace. Various Sermons, 1 book. And many other things.

He is also said to have written commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, which have as yet by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Philip of Monte Calerio, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man practiced in the sacred writings, a great and excellent preacher of the word of God. For the use of those who devote themselves to declamations he wrote small works not to be despised, by which, nobly exercising his talent, he also destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

Sermons on the Temporale, 1 book. There will be signs in the sun, [and in the moon?]. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Lenten Sermons, 1 book.

He is said besides to have composed various other treatises and to have explained several books of the divine writings, but none of them has come to me.

John, surnamed Grossus, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, nineteenth prior general, others have it twenty-first, a Toulousain by country, a studious and learned man. In clear speech he wrote volumes not to be scorned, by which, having splendidly exercised his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work which, containing the foundation and progress of the Carmelite order, is entitled:

Viridarium, 3 books. By what things [unclear]. His Sermons, 1 book, are reported. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1406.

Nicholas of Gorran, of the order of the Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures, nobly learned, outstanding in talent, published in scholastic and clear speech many volumes, the reading of which will not be to be rejected by those who desire to be initiated in the holy Scriptures; of these I remember that few have come into our hands. Among the many, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the five books of Moses, 5 books. On Isaiah the prophet, 1 book. On Jeremiah also. On Ecclesiasticus, a large work, 1 book. He will give a blessing. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke

334 The Abbot of Sponheim

On the Epistles of Paul, one book. He brought genius to light. Various sermons, one book. And certain other things. He is also said to have published commentaries and notable lectures on almost the whole Bible, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

JACOBUS de Theramo, an Aprutian canon and Archdeacon of Aversa, a very celebrated jurist, a distinguished doctor of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear and ordered in speech, whose authority among professors of this faculty was great in his own time, published in that discipline certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the dialogue on the redemption of the human race, commonly called Belial, which the author entitled:

The Consolation of Sinners, one book. After through the tree of knowledge. On the Clementines he is said to have written one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

GUILIELMUS de Oppenbach, a German by nation, an eminent doctor learned in the Holy Scriptures and nobly practiced in scholastic philosophy, keen and forceful in intellect, sufficiently suited to disputing and unraveling questions of the Scriptures. He wrote in the theological faculty some little works not to be rejected, by which he made his name known in the Parisian school; of these I have found:

On the Sentences, four books. Disputed questions. He is also said to have written certain sermons and other treatises, and to have labored over ten lectures in the schools, which have not come to my knowledge.

HENRICUS de Langenstein, called de Hassia, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, abundant and expansive, since after spending many years in lecturing on Genesis and scarcely reaching the fourth chapter of the book, he completed as many volumes. For he was ready for everything, and copious in speaking and writing, so that for him it was a matter of greater difficulty to repel things worthy of mention that came to him of their own accord than to find new things to say. As I have found from a certain letter of his, I would believe that he was a canon of the church of Worms. He flourished first in the University of Paris, where he earned the laurel of the doctorate; then, for the honor of the new planting of the University of Vienna, he betook himself there, and by both teaching and writing acquired great glory for his learning. Of his little works the following are reported:

On the Sentences, two books. In the beginning God created. A prologue on Genesis, three books. To the reverend in Christ. On the schism of Antichrist, one book. I shall give you the keys of the kingdom. On the instruction of the priesthood, one book. On contemplation, one book. On the contemplative soul, one book. Seven times in the day praise. The Mirror of the Soul, one book. Many princes [unclear]. Against the Astrologers, one book. Divine wisdom in things. On the Lord’s Prayer, one book. Hail Mary, full of grace. On the Hail Mary, one book. I believe in God the Father. On the canonical hours, one book. To the reverend lord John. Against brother Thelefforus, one book. Against a certain Wycliffite, one book. To the regular canons, one book. Behold, we have left behind. On the property of monks, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. H. de Langensteyn di[?]. Various questions. He also published many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Rupert the Palatine, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year 1400.

JOHANNES de Bromyard, of the Order of Preaching Friars of Saint Dominic, a man devoted to the divine writings, learned by long practice, not ignorant also of secular letters, excellent in intellect, an outstanding declaimer. He wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he established the memory of his name among posterity. Among their number the following are reported: a great and most lucid work, very useful to preachers, which he entitled:

The Summa for Preachers, one book. The life of preachers c[unclear] Sum-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

A summary of moral law, one book. Which in the following little work [unclear]. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. He is said to have written many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes Gluel, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior at Cologne, born in the imperial city of Aachen, a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people. Among the other little works of his study he wrote a volume not to be rejected by the followers of this order, on the origin and progress of his order, which he entitled:

The Mirror of the Carmelites, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Lenten sermons, one book: “Lay up treasures for yourselves.” Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in his convent at Cologne, writing and composing various little works, where at last, failing and meeting his day, he was buried in peace.

Henricus Eutafiuue Oyta, a German by nation, the singular ornament and co-founder from the beginning of the school of Vienna in Austria, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, and an excellent preacher of sermons. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which very few have thus far come into our hands. I have read only:

On the Sentences, four books. Concerning the prologue of the first, one book: “Love justice, you who...” On contracts, one book. “Conjurator virgo de Isra[el?].” And certain sermons. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the school of Vienna, under Emperor Wenceslaus, with Henricus de Hassia, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Henricus of Andernach, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an excellent interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, outstanding in talent and, among all men of his time, famous as a preacher of sermons, published little works of no negligible authority, of which the following are reported: a distinguished work:

On the Sentences, four books. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Questions of philosophy, one book.

And certain other things which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished chiefly in the convent of Cologne, where he is also said to be buried.

Blasius Andernarius, a Frenchman by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly practiced in the arena of scholastic discipline, distinguished in talent and an excellent disputant. He wrote several distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among their number there stands out a lucid and notable work:

On the Sentences, one book. On the Institutes, one book. On the Code, one book. He is also said to have written some things in moral philosophy, but they have not come to me. And very many other things.

Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, jurist, most celebrated of all men of his time, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, whose sayings are held in great authority among professors of civil law, published certain lucid little works on the laws, by which he consecrated the memory of his name to immortality among posterity, of which the following are reported.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of St. Bavo, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, an excellent doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and polished in eloquence, distinguished no less by religious conduct than by knowledge of letters. He is said, moreover, to have written various and numerous treatises, but I do not remember that any of them came into our hands, except the little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which he beautifully sets forth [unclear].

One book. Declarations on the Rule, one book. Questions on the Sentences, one book.

He is said, moreover, to have written various and numerous treatises, but I do not remember that any of them came into our hands, except the little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which it is beautifully set forth [unclear].

THE ABBOT OF SPONHEIM and he soundly concludes that, for a healthy monk professed according to the Rule of St. Benedict, the eating of meat is unlawful, and therefore altogether forbidden.

RICHARD LAVINGHAM, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, a man exceptionally learned in the sacred Scriptures and an outstanding interpreter of secular philosophy, and also of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He also wrote some volumes, among which these are reported:

Against the Lollards, one book. On the foundation of his order. For the book of Bridget, one book. Various sermons. Also on logic, one book. And various questions.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, especially at the time when the heresy of John Wyclif and of the Lollards began in Bohemia.

JOHN OF WERDEN, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the sacred Scriptures, rich from reading the ancients, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy; of excellent talent, composed in scholastic simplicity of speech, and in his time a very celebrated preacher of sermons to the people. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote little works very necessary for preachers of the word of God, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

Double sermons on the season, two books. “Let us put on,” etc.; see. Double sermons on the saints, two books. Also sermons throughout Lent, [unclear].

But the other things that he composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

JAMES, who is called the Great, of Toledo by homeland, of the order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished for knowledge of natural philosophy, and well supplied with reading of the ancients. He is reported to have published various treatises and commentaries on the divine books, which have not yet come into our hands. I have found one excellent, notable volume of his, entitled On Speech, Inquiry, and Wisdom.

Sophologium, three books. “Of the most illustrious prince.”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

JOHN CAMPSEN, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, long exercised in the sacred Scriptures by study and rich in talent through continual reading of the ancients, an excellent preacher of sermons. He is reported to have published certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of persons. Of these number the following very noteworthy works are said to be extant:

Sermons on the season, two books. Sermons on the saints, [unclear].

But of the other things that he composed I have not been able to find the titles of the works.

On the whole Psalter, one book. “Blessed is he who [unclear].” On the Proverbs of Solomon, three books. “In hidden things I shall prepare.” On Augustine’s City of God, ten books. “The force of the river [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, one book.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, where he is said to have composed many volumes, especially various lectures on several books of the Bible. A distinguished and notable work.

PHILIP, abbot of the monastery of Otterberg, in the diocese of Worms, of the Cistercian order, German by nation, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and learned through long practice, not ignorant of secular literature, published volumes not to be despised for the edification of readers; by these, properly exercising his talent, he also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these number the following are reported. If he published anything further, it has by no means yet come to my knowledge.

NICHOLAS, a physician of outstanding learning, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man most learned not only in medicine but also in other letters of philosophy, renowned in talent

On Ecclesiastical Writers

... distinguished, adorned with eloquence; how highly his learning is esteemed among the physicians of this time is proved not by my words, but by their testimonies. He published certain excellent little works in that faculty. Among these an outstanding work is reported:

Summa medicinae, one book. And certain other things.

He died in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1412, indiction 5.

Johannes de Duren, of the Order of Friars Minor of St Francis, a German by nation, a studious man and nobly practiced in the sacred writings, of great and distinguished reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He is said, for the guidance of simple priests [unclear], [unclear], by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there are extant:

Sermones de tempore, one book. Sermones de sanctis, one book. “Sanctificate [unclear].”

Quadragesimale, one book. “Cum confessor idoneus.”

De septem peccatis mortalibus, one book. “Est via quae videtur ho[mini].”

De occultis vitiis, one book.

De confessione, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Tilmanus de Hachenberg, of the Order of Friars Minor, a German by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man studious in the divine scriptures, learned by long practice, having a language polished by use in speaking, shone forth as great and most renowned in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised by simple people; by profitably applying his talent to these, he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there are extant:

Sermones de tempore, one book. “Erunt signa hic praedicti.”

Sermones per quadragesimam, one book.

Sermones de sanctis.

And certain other things.

He flourished in his convent at Koblenz, where he was buried when he died.

Johannes de Ligniano, a very celebrated jurist, thoroughly instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence. He is said to have published certain excellent little works in canon law; by applying himself to these he spent his time usefully, and also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, as Franciscus de Zabarellis testifies in the prologue on the Clementines, there are extant collections:

Super Clementinis, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Hugo de Slestadt, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and excellently taught in the disciplines of the philosophers, subtle in talent, a distinguished disputant of scholastic questions. He wrote, as they report, certain excellent volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a work:

Quaestionum sententiarum, four books. And certain other things.

He was, moreover, a follower in his determinations of the divine father Bonaventure, of the Order of Friars Minor, [unclear] most learned in Aristotelian philosophy, second to none in Italy in his time, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, an excellent declaimer. He composed many little works, especially in philosophy, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these are reported:

Contra Iudaeos, one book. “Plurimorum astrictus.”

Summa de naturalibus, one book. Sermones de sanctis, one book. “Omnis doctrina.”

Sermones de tempore, one book. “Naturali philosophia.”

Sermones de quadragesima, two books. “Tecum sapientissime re[x?].”

Super librum Posteriorum, eight books. “Tanta literarum [unclear].”

Super Physicorum, twelve books.

Super Metaphysicam, two books. “Conspiciens [unclear].”

Super de anima, one book. “Humanarum divinarumque.”

Summa philosophiae, two books. “Maxima forti[?] [unclear].”

Logica duplex, one book.

Super de generatione et corruptione.

Super librum Porphyrii.

338 THE ABBOT OF SPONHEIM

On the book of the Categories, one book. “When I was asking,” etc. On Strode’s Consequences, one book. “That God was a man.” And many other things. He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1400. And, dying young, he was buried at Venice in the sacristy of his order.

JACOBUS of [Cessolis?], of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in sacred writings, not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in intellect, polished and well arranged in speech, second to none in his time in delivering sermons to the people, produced certain distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity the praiseworthy memory of his name. Among these there is extant a notable work, entitled On the Manners of Men, the Duties of Nobles and Commoners, setting forth as its subject: On the game of chess, one book. “Among all kinds of signs.” Various sermons, one book. But other things which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

THOMAS of Haselbach, a German by nation, learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, scholastic in speech, but too diffuse and prolix, and for that reason liable to the criticism of some. For when he was ordinary reader in sacred theology in the university of Vienna, lecturing on the prophet Isaiah for twenty-one years, he did not reach the end of the first chapter. He wrote several little works on the divine Scriptures; among these the following many volumes are reported. On the prophet Isaiah, one book. On the Sentences, On the Ten Commandments, one book. On the five senses of man, one book. “After, by God’s gift, thus.” Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

THOMASINUS, by homeland a Ferrarese, of the Order of Friars Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer in correcting the sins of peoples. He is reported to have fashioned certain excellent little works for the instruction of simple priests, by which he transmitted the knowledge of his name with praise to posterity. Of their number especially the following are reported. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book. But the rest which he composed have not come to our knowledge up to this point.

THOMAS à Kempis, a German by nation, of the Order of Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the mount of the blessed martyr and virgin Agnes, near Zwolle in the diocese of Utrecht, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, a special lover of the blessed Mary ever virgin. He wrote, for the instruction of simple brothers, little works not to be despised. Among these the following are reported. On contempt of the world, one book. “He who follows me, not.” Sermons to novices, one book. “Behold how good and how pleasant.” Sermons to the brothers, one book. “He who has not renounced.” Dialogue of novices, one book. “I ask you, dearest Father.” On the solitary life, one book. “Dearest, when you were in.” On the three tabernacles, one book. “It is written in the Prophet.” On true compunction, one book. “Weep with me, all friends.” Little garden of roses, one book. “With the holy you will be holier.” Valley of lilies, one book. “I am the flower of the field, the lily.” Alphabet of a monk, one book. “Your ways, O Lord, [unclear].” Consolation of the poor, one book. “Be comforted, be comforted.” Epitaph of a monk, one book. “The way of the just is straight.” What a monk ought to be like, one book. “Listen, religious monk.” Manual for little ones, one book. “Let the little ones come.” Instructional book for youths, one book. “My son, from your youth.” Letters to various persons, one book. “The Lord rules me; nothing.” And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

NICOLAUS, monk of the monastery of Holy Cross in Austria, of the Cistercian Order, by nation

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in divine studies, rich in his reading of the ancients, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain small works of no contemptible usefulness, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a work not to be rejected, in praise of the most blessed mother of God and virgin Mary, useful to preachers, which he entitled:

The Image of Saint Mary, 3 books. The name of the Virgin Mary. Various Sermons, 1 book. The rest, although many works are reported which he composed, have by no means come down to us.

BARTHOLOMAEUS of Urbino, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man zealous in divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, is said to have composed many distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity; of these he brought together [unclear] little works into one alphabetical order, to which he gave the title:

Milleloquium of Augustine, 1 book. Milleloquium of Ambrose, 1 book. Also On Spiritual Warfare, 1 book. And very many others. He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

FRANCISCUS de Plataea, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man learned in the divine scriptures, instructed both in law and in secular philosophy, excellent in talent, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, is said to have composed many distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity; of which [unclear] he brought together into one alphabetical order, to which he gave the title:

A distinguished and excellent work, which he entitled: On Restitutions, 1 book. Whether restitution is to be made concerning the man. On [censuitis?], 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. The other works, however, which he composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Petrus de Candia, a Cretan by nation, of the order of the Friars Minor, first bishop of Novara, then archbishop of Milan, afterwards cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, finally supreme pontiff named Alexander V, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, magnificently instructed in scholastic philosophy, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, who once presided over a public school in the university of Paris, acquired great and immense praises by teaching and writing. Among his most elegant little works there survive clear and useful commentaries:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Also On the Sentences, 1 book. And certain other works. He died in the last year of Rupert, king of the Romans, and was buried in the convent of the Minorites at Bologna, in the year of the Lord 1410, indiction 3.

FRANCISCUS de Bachone, a Catalan by country, of the order of the brothers of the blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Girona, a man learned in the divine scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, had such power in teaching and disputing in the university of Paris that he was surnamed the Sublime Doctor. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a great and distinguished work from the writings of the holy fathers, sufficiently useful for declaimers of sermons to the people, which we can title:

Repertory of Preachers, 1 book. Also Repertory of Preachers, 1 book. He is said besides to have written certain other works, but they have not come to our hands.

Michael Herbrant of Duren, of the order of the brothers of the blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a Teuton by nation, lector of sacred theology, prior of the convent of Creuznach in the diocese of Mainz, a learned man and so distinguished a declaimer that he was summoned not only nearby but also to distant places and cathedral churches, and preached while being held in admiration by all. He was of great familiarity and authority with Johann, the last count of Spanheim, and obtained from him many goods for his convent. Among other things he wrote elegant works:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Synodal Collations, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Petrus de Spira, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a Teuton by nation, a man zealous in divine writings, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote certain excellent little works by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these are reported:

The Abbot of Sponheim

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book. On the books of the Ethics, eight books. have not yet come to my reading. one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. But the other things which he composed, to the knowledge

Reinhardus of Fronthoven, a German by nation, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Preachers, a man studious in divine Scripture, sought out by long practice, not ignorant of secular literature. He wrote works not to be rejected by preachers of the word of God, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only:

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book.

I have seen nothing of the others. He flourished, as his own people say, in the convent at Koblenz, where he died.

Johannes Capreolus, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a Toulousain by homeland, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures, excellently instructed in the disciplines of Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect, quite suited for disputation, a defender and most vigorous champion of the sayings of Saint Thomas Aquinas. He wrote very pleasing monuments of his intellect, by which he made his name known. Of these many volumes are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. And Various Sermons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1415.

Henricus of Coesfeld, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Saint Mary near the mount of Saint Gertrude in Holland, a man very learned in divine Scripture, devout in life and conduct, of great fame, subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence, and also a very celebrated declaimer of sermons. He wrote many excellent volumes, the frequent use of which is judged useful for devout brothers who love their own salvation. Of these the following are reported:

On Exodus Mystically, one book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book. On the Three Substantial Vows, two books. Do not love the world. Against the Vice of Property, one book. On the Three Monastic Custodies, one book. On the Instruction of Novices, one book. The Mystical Circumcisorium, one book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. On the Annunciation of the Lord, one book. Eulogy of Paul the Hermit, one book. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book, 30.

And many other things. With remarkable industry he examined the difficult work of Guilhelmus, bishop of Paris, On the Whole Corporeal and Incorporeal or Spiritual Universe, and beautifully brought it to a close in a brief compendium. He died in the house of the Valley of Grace near Bruges, while being healthfully occupied in the act of visitation, in the times of the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410, in the seventh indiction, on the Ides of July.

Henricus of Hachenburg, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a man magnificently exercised and well instructed in the divine writings, of excellent intellect and very celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote volumes not to be rejected for the direction of simple priests. Of these there are extant:

Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book. I will take care to come, Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished, as his own people report, in the convent at Koblenz; he composed various things.

Jordanus, of the order of the Friars of Saint Augustine of the Hermitage, a German by nation, a devout man, an excellent expounder and interpreter of the divine Scriptures, of most excellent intellect in declaiming sermons. He wrote several elegant treatises useful to devout brothers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Yet only a few of these have come into our hands. These, however, are reported:

On the Apocalypse of John, one book. Apology for His Order, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Cause to inspect according to [unclear]. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle Sermons on the Saints, one book. Behold, he will give to his voice [unclear]. Lenten Sermons, one book. Various Questions, one book.

And many other things. He flourished under King Rupert, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Petrus, bishop of Cittanova, an Italian by nation from the town of Bruniquelli, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man very learned in divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, clear in eloquence, published several works of great usefulness, by which, with magnificently exercised intellect, he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a certain notable work in which he reduced all the histories of the New and Old Testament to alphabetical order, and arranged them under individual subjects. Su-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Sentences, 4 books; On the Proverbs of Solomon; also On Ecclesiastes, 1 book; On the Song of Songs; and many other things. Moreover, he is said to have adorned almost the whole Bible with excellent commentaries. He flourished under Rupert, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Laurentius Justinianus, Venetian by nation, of the Celestine order, and afterward patriarch of Venice, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in character and life, although he could have possessed the greatest riches and honors of this world, entered the aforesaid order for love of Christ and contempt [of the world]. In that order, [unclear] in great religion and abstinence, he published very devout little works for the edification of the simple. Their titles are given below.

The Tree of Life, 1 book; On Monastic Discipline, 1 book; On the Marriage of the Word and the Soul, 1 book; On the Struggle of Christ, 1 book; On Interior Conflict, 1 book; On the Lamentation of the Church, 1 book; On the Sacrament of the Altar, 1 book; On the Solitary Life, 1 book; On Contempt of the World, 1 book; On the Lord’s Discourse at Supper, 1 book; On the Pastoral Office, 1 book; also On Obedience, 1 book; On the Degrees of Perfection, 1 book; Forty Sermons, 1 book.

He flourished in the time of Rupert, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410. He was buried at Venice in the cathedral church. At his tomb many miracles are divinely performed. [unclear]

Augustinus of Rome, of the order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, prior general, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and also nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and renowned for eloquence, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survive:
