On the Sentences, 4 books; On All the Epistles of Paul, 14 books; On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book; On Free Will, 1 book; On Original Sin, 1 book; On Christ and the Church, 1 book; On the Love of Christ toward the Elect, 1 book; On the Perfect Righteousness of the Church, 1 book; On the Power of the Pope, 1 book; On the Books of the Ethics, 8 books.

He is said besides to have written many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Baldus of Perugia, once hearer and pupil of Bartolus of Saxoferrato, the most celebrated jurisconsult of all his time, and also nobly learned in secular philosophy, acute in intellect, profound in understanding, cautious and steady in counsel, wrote many distinguished little works in both laws, by which he won eternal memory for his name among posterity. Of their number the following are given:

On the Code, 9 books; On the Old Digest, [24?] books; On the New Digest, 12 books; On the Infortiatum, 1 book; On the Institutes, 1 book; On the Second Book of the Decretals, 1 book; Additions to the Speculum, 1 book; Many Legal Opinions, 1 book; and several other things.

He died in the time of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1423, in the first indiction. He was buried with honor at Pavia, in the convent of the Friars Minor of St. Francis, in the month of July.

Angelus of Perugia, brother of the aforesaid Baldus and his companion and associate in studies, most learned in civil law, renowned in intellect, and very celebrated in fame and reputation among jurisconsults, also composed many volumes in his own faculty. By establishing monuments of excellent talent through them, he sent the memory of his name to the knowledge of many. Of their number the following very elegant commentaries are reported:

On the Code, 9 books; On the Old Digest, [24?] books; On the New Digest; On the Institutes, [unclear]; On the Infortiatum. Indeed, he is said to have labored over the whole body of civil law, and certain other things. He died in the time [unclear]. [unclear] former hearer, a man very skilled in both laws and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, who, although he was bound by the bond of a wife and occupied with family affairs, nevertheless always in the first lecture [unclear].

Petrus de Ancharano, Italian by nation, Bolognese by homeland, once a hearer of Baldus of Perugia, a man very skilled in both laws and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, who, although he was bound by the bond of a wife and occupied with family affairs, nevertheless always in the first lecture [unclear].

Abbot of Spanheim

... engaged in the study of [unclear], he published many little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among them are reported:

On the Decretals, 1 book. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the rules of law, 1 book. On the old Digest, 24 books. On the new Digest, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410, a close associate of Franciscus de Zabarellis.

Vincentius Gruner, a German by nation, a man learned in sacred writings and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech. He published little works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is an important lecture, which, in the new planting of the Leipzig gymnasium, he publicly wrote and read before the scholars.

On the office of the Mass, 3 books: To the honor of the blessed ... Disputed Questions, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished at the time of the transfer of the University of Prague to Leipzig, in the province of the margraviate of Meissen, which Pope Alexander V confirmed and endowed with privileges, in the year of the Lord 1410.

Johannes de Auerbach, a German by nation, priest of the church of Bamberg, a man learned in sacred writings and in secular studies, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech. He published little works of authority not to be regarded as worthless, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only a distinguished work, 1 book: To the praise of God and of souls.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the city of Bamberg and composed various little works.

Dionysius de Burgo Sancti Sepulchri, of the order of the hermit brothers of the divine father Augustine, a man learned in sacred scriptures and most learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech. He wrote, in both branches of literature, little works not to be despised, by which he left to posterity perpetual memorials of his talent. Among these the following are reported: very beautiful and elegant commentaries, 1 book. On Valerius Maximus, 1 book. On the Metamorphoses, 1 book. On the tragedies of Seneca, 1 book. On the Rhetoric, 1 book. And certain other things. Moreover, he reduced all the fables to a pleasing tropological sense.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Petrus de Aliaco, bishop of Cambrai and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, once chancellor of the Parisian gymnasium, teacher of Johannes de Gerson, a man most learned in sacred writings, nobly instructed in secular letters, especially in Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and also an outstanding declaimer of sermons. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name and talent. Of these I have found the following: 4 books: Whether this doctrine ... 1 book: Upon this rock I shall build ... 1 book: This certain doctrine ... 1 book: Whether of Peter, of the Church [unclear]. 3 books: Whoever, who from the world ... 1 book: Since many wise men ... 1 book: There are four spirits. 1 book: A shortened word [unclear]. 1 book: The Lord God terrifies me.

On the General Council, 1 book: Charity has requested. 1 book: Highest priest, you ... 1 book: Let them kiss, etc. This book ... 1 book: True repentance, as it were ... 1 book: Thus therefore you shall pray: Father. 1 book: Our Father who, etc. O Father. 1 book: As I was thinking, O most holy ...

On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Magnificat, one book. The Sum of the Trinity. On the Canticle of Zacharias, one book. “About to speak of the canticle of Zacharias.” [unclear], one book. “Finally there is added a canticle.” On the election of the pope, one book. [unclear], one book. “A devout soul desiring to.” On spiritual exercise, one book. “If we gather into one.” [unclear], one book. “The old [unclear] hands down to the author.” On the twelve honors, namely of Joseph, one book. On the concord of theology. On the soul and its accidents, two books. A concord of theology and astronomy, one book. “Since you have very often asked me.” On the sacraments of the Church, one book. Several letters to various persons, one book. Sixteen various sermons. And certain other things. He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, at which he was also present in person. In the year of the Lord 1416.

Nicholas of Clemanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, a man learned in the divine scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, [who attained] the mastership of sacred scripture in the school of Paris, [wrote] volumes in which he left the memory of his most brilliant talent. Among these the following are reported: to Lord Peter of Ailly, bishop of Cambrai, the aforesaid cardinal, the distinguished work which he entitled: On the Fruit of the Hermitage, one book. On the Corrupt State of the Church, one book. On New Festivals, one book. On the Matter of the Schism, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of the Council of Constance. In the year of the Lord 1417.

John Dominici, cardinal of the title of Saint Sixtus, commonly called “of Ragusa,” by homeland a Florentine, of the order of the Friars Preachers, who was sent by Pope Gregory XII to the Council of Constance for the sake of unity, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain excellent volumes by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these the following are reported: On Ecclesiastes, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. The work entitled The Little Light of Night, one book. The Itinerary of Devotion, one book. “If I speak with the tongues of men.” Sermons of Charity, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Sermons through Lent, one book. “Blessed is the man who has not gone away.” And certain other things. He died at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund. In the year of the Lord 1418, indiction 11.

John, bishop of [Lombaria?], German by nation, Basel by homeland, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, and distinguished in eloquence, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, produced little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number the principal ones are reported: On the Sentences, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And certain other things. Moreover, he is said to have delivered many speeches and collationes before the clergy, and also before the supreme pontiff and the assembly of cardinals, which I have not seen.

John Zacharias, German by nation, Erfurt by homeland, a man very studious and learned in the divine scriptures, also an outstanding interpreter of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, a very acute disputant, highly suitable in delivering sermons both to the clergy and to the people, wrote certain excellent little works by which he made his name known. Among these are reported: On the Sentences, one book. On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, one book. Various sermons. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Sigismund; in the Council of Constance he was magnificently praised for disputing against the heretics. In the year of the Lord 1426.

Antonio da Butrio, Italian by nation, Bologna by homeland, easily the most celebrated jurist of all in his time, in other writings, both divine and human, excellently learned,

Abbot of Spanheim ... renowned for [unclear] and eloquence, and venerable no less for honorable conduct than for learning, he published several little works in law, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Decretals, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book. Repertory of Canon Law, 2 books. Repertory of Civil Law, 1 book. Most elegant Consilia, 1 book. And certain others. He flourished in the time of Emperor Sigismund and of the general Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Gabriel of Spoleto, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in divine Scripture and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent and an outstanding declaimer of sermons. He wrote some commendable little works, by which he showed to posterity too the knowledge of his lively talent. But I have not deserved to see any of them up to this point. Nevertheless, these are reported as his principal works:

Against the Heretics, 1 book. Against the Fraticelli, 1 book. And certain others. He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year 1417.

Franciscus de Zabarellis, a Paduan by nation, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, a man most learned in canon law, and nobly taught both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence. He wrote little works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Decretals, 1 book. On the ten books of sermons [unclear]. [unclear] On the Clementines, 1 book. That there is nothing new [unclear]. On the Canonical Hours, 1 book. About to repeat the decretal. Various Repetitions. And many other things. He flourished in the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418. There he also died, and was buried among the Friars Minor. Poggio delivered an oration in his praise.

Petrus Maurocenus, a Venetian patrician, bishop-cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man most learned in divine Scripture and in canon law, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent, composed in speech, notable in life and conduct. He is reported to have fashioned many excellent little works, in which the liveliness of his talent is known to shine forth. But I, up to the present, have not deserved to see any of them. There is reported as his an outstanding volume:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. And various determinations. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

Nicolaus Dinckelspule, a German by nation, the ornament and rector of the Viennese school in Austria, most learned in the holy Scriptures and much instructed in secular philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in discourse, notable in life and conduct. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 2 books. Questions on the Sentences, 3 books. [unclear] On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, 1 book. It is written, Matthew 22. On the Ten Commandments, 4 books. If you shall ask the Father anything. On the Lord's Prayer, 6 books. In the Gospel where it is read [unclear] On the Eight Beatitudes, 6 books. On the Eight Capital Virtues [unclear] On the Three Parts of Penance, 4 books. It must be noted that, as is said [unclear] On the Seven Mortal Sins, 9 books. There are two precepts of char[ity] [unclear] On the Commandment of Charity, 10 books. Consequently it must be said [unclear] On the Sins of the Tongue, 3 books. Sermons on the Saints [unclear] Sermons on the Season, 3 books. And many other things. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, sent by the University of Vienna, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Petrus of Rosenheim, monk of the monastery of Melk in Austria, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in divine writings, and magnificently taught in secular letters; a philosopher and an excellent and renowned poet, he published, both in verse and in prose, little works not to be rejected, by which he well exercised his talent. Among these is the metrical work which he wrote, at the persuasion and request of Nicolaus Dinckelspule, to the lord Branda, cardinal of Saint Clement and apostolic legate in Austria, on the chapters of the whole Bible, which he entitled Ro

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] memorial of divine things, one book. “Astripotens [unclear] terram.” A notable history of the times, one book. Various sermons, one book. He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420, and composed many and various works.

Raphael Fulgosius, by nation a man of Piacenza, very learned in both laws and well instructed in the precepts of secular philosophy, excellent in talent, cautious and steady in counsel, published certain distinguished volumes on civil law, by which he showed the force and liveliness of his talent also to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, one book. On the New Digest, twelve books. Many legal opinions. And certain other works. He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

Johannes de Palomar, archdeacon of the church of Barcelona, a distinguished doctor of decretals, and nobly learned both in sacred scripture and in secular letters, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, excellent in life and conduct, published little works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a distinguished treatise addressed to Johannes, abbot of the Scottish monastery of the order of Saint Benedict at Vienna.

“The sons will rise in judgment.” Sermons and questions. On abstinence from meats, one book. And several others. He flourished under Sigismund. The rest of what he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. Famous in the university of Vienna in Austria, he composed many works in the time of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Raphael Cumanus, a distinguished professor of civil law and a very celebrated interpreter, excellent in talent and outstanding in counsel, whose authority among jurists is by no means slight, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books. Also one book of legal opinions. And several others. He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

Johannes de Teneramunda, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Sillimacum in Savoy, a man devoted to sacred scripture and very learned, devout in life and conduct, famous in talent, composed in speech, published works very useful for the edification of religious brothers:

On the Christian faith, one book. On the nature and fall of man, one book. On the conception of Saint Mary, one book. On the love of God, one book. He also elegantly composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Gasparinus, a very celebrated grammarian, by homeland a man of Bergamo, born of Barziza Rusculus, a man most learned in secular letters, a philosopher and most outstanding rhetorician, subtle in talent, eloquent and articulate, who raised from the dead the elegance of Latin speech when it was half-dead. He wrote many distinguished little works in that faculty, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On orthography, one book. “I rejoice very greatly and [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. On the letters of Cicero, one book. Various orations, one book. On the same author’s On the Orator, one book. On the same author’s On Duties, one book. And certain other works. He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Antonius of Genoa, of the order of the hermit friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in sacred scripture and a professor of canon law and very celebrated interpreter, outstanding in talent and famous in eloquence. He wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which [unclear] his name with [unclear].

Of Moral Figures, one book. “To religious men in Christ.” The rest have not come to me. He flourished in person at the general Council of Constance, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

Jo-

346 Abbot of Spanheim

Johannes de Imola, by birth a Bolognese, a most celebrated doctor of both laws, excellent in talent and renowned in eloquence, whose learning and eloquence in his own time magnificently illuminated all Italy. He is said to have published many distinguished volumes in both laws, whose authority is raised with the highest praise among the professors of this faculty. Among these the following in particular are reported:

On the three books of the Decretals, 3 books. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book. On the Digestum Infortiatum, 14 books. Before we come to. On the Digestum Novum, and certain others.

He died at Bologna in the times of the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1436, indiction 14.

Antonius of Parma, prior general of the Camaldolese order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, composed in speech, sufficiently suitable in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the direction of preachers of the word of God some distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Of these the chief are reported:

Sermons on the season, 1 book. When he had approached. Sermons on the saints, 1 book. Sermons for Lent, 1 book.

And certain others. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Leonardus Aretinus, philosopher, orator, and distinguished historian, and a man most learned in every respect, skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, first secretary of the Roman pontiffs Innocent VII, Gregory XII, Alexander V, and John XXIII down to the Council of Constance, and then, after chancellors had been summoned by the Florentine senate, was appointed general chancellor; in this office he remained until the end of his life with great fidelity and authority. He wrote, among other things:

A distinguished work of dialogues, 1 book. A history of his own time, 1 book. On the good deeds of the Florentines, 12 books. On the praises of Florence, 1 book. A history of the Goths, 4 books. A history of the First Punic War, 2 books. The life of Aristotle, 1 book. On the life of Cicero, 1 book. A volume of letters, 1 book.

He also composed some other things most elegantly, which have not come to my knowledge. Moreover he translated many things from Greek into Latin, namely the treatise of the blessed priest Basil on the instruction of pupils; he also translated from Plutarch the lives of Tiberius and Gracchus among the Greeks, and of Paulus Aemilius, the later Cato, and Sertorius among the Romans. He likewise translated Xenophon’s little book on the tyrant, Plato’s Gorgias and Phaedo, and certain letters, and Aristotle’s Economics and the books of the Ethics and Politics. And other things which have not come to me. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1426. He died, however, under the Emperor Frederick III and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, indiction 6, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, at almost the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Poggio the Florentine, a philosopher and eloquent rhetorician, perfectly instructed in the Greek and Latin languages, for many years a most eloquent writer of apostolic letters. He is said to have composed some little works of excellent talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Laurentius Valla was a very keen rival of this Poggio, and wrote various things against him. He himself published:

On the situation of the region of India, 1 book. Against Laurentius Valla, 2 books. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Various orations, 1 book.

And very many other things. He made Dionysius Siculus and many other Greek authors Latin. Moreover, at the Council of Constance he delivered very many funeral orations. The work of obscenities which he entitled Facetiae we have judged rightly to be rejected from this catalogue of illustrious men, because the reading of it offends the devout, harms the unwary, and infects the carnal. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Laurentius Valla, a Roman patrician, by far the foremost of the grammarians of this age, a most outstanding philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian, subtle in talent, sharp and vehement, preferring Latin eloquence to Greek, composed many things for its adornment. Most skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, he published little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported. Ele-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Six books of Elegances, beginning, “When often with myself [unclear] of the ancestors...”

On the reciprocal use of sui and suus, one book, beginning, “You, John, are singular...”

Many letters, one book. Also On Quintilian, 12 books.

Dialectic, one book, beginning, “As I was undertaking, Paul...”

Panegyric on the True Good, 3 books, beginning, “I should very much wish, Garcia...”

On Free Will, one book, beginning, “I hear that Poggio [unclear] another...”

Apologue against Poggio, one book. And many other things.

Against Antonius Raudensis, one book. He flourished at the Council of Constance in person, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

He translated into Latin Homer, Thucydides, and several others.

Of him a certain man says as follows: What did that most biting censor of the Latin language, Laurentius Valla, gain for himself by his harsh and exact criticism? What praise, I ask, did he obtain after death, except that the fine epigram composed about him according to his deserts is read and proclaimed everywhere? “Now, after Valla, dead, has sought the shades, Pluto does not dare to speak Latin words. Jupiter would have deemed him worthy of the honor of heaven as censor of language, but he fears him as censor of his own.” But what he thought concerning the Donation of Constantine, by which Constantine endowed the Church, his book clearly shows; I wish so great a man had never published it.

John Tortelli, by nation an Aretine, a very close friend of Laurentius Valla, to whom [unclear]. Two books of grammatical commentaries, beginning, “The Greek letters by which...” He also published On Dialectic, one book, and various letters, and many other things. He translated the life of Athanasius of Alexandria into Latin for Pope Eugenius. He was chamberlain of Eugenius, and afterward a household companion of Pope Nicholas and his most intimate companion in studies, fully instructed in Greek and Latin letters, a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a large and distinguished volume which he entitled [unclear].

Hermannus Petra of Stutdorp, of the Carthusian order, by nation a German:

Sermons on the Temporale, 3 books.

Sermons on the Saints, 3 books.

Fifty sermons on the Lord’s Prayer, one book.

On the Governance of Nuns, one book.

And many other things. He died under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction.

Omnibonus Leonicenus, a man most learned in humane letters, fully instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, the most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician of all in his time. He was once a student at Venice of Manuel Chrysoloras of Constantinople, who brought Greek letters back into Italy. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On Cicero’s Orator, 3 books, beginning, “How much of Cicero’s speech...”

On the poet Lucan, one book, beginning, “In expounding this...”

On Quintilian, one book.

In Praise of Eloquence, one book, beginning, “How much admiration...”

Many orations. And he published many other things, which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1426.

Henry of Hesse the Younger, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the monks of Mary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, published many most elegant volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity; and before his entrance into religion he publicly lectured on many of them in the universities. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books.

On Genesis, one book.

On Exodus, one book.

On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book.

On the Apocalypse of John, one book.

Dialogue between a Bishop and a Priest, one book.

Useful sermons, and certain other things.

348 The Abbot of Spanheim He dies under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, indiction 6.

Johannes de Gerson, a Frenchman by nation, chancellor of Paris, [unclear] of Peter de Ailly the cardinal, not ignorant of philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, firm in judgment, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, a most distinguished interpreter of sermons, notable in life and conduct, by far the foremost of the theologians of his time. He wrote in verse and prose many very excellent little works, by which his name will always obtain immortality among posterity; the reading of them is no less useful than pleasant to devout and religious men. Of these there is extant:

On the Praise of Scribes, one book, “To search the Scriptures.”

On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book, “That the Gospel was broad.”

On Ecclesiastical Power, one book, “Ecclesiastical power [unclear].”

On the Removability of the Bridegroom, one book, “But the days will come when.”

On the Manner of Conducting Oneself in Schism, one book, “For removing certain people’s.”

On Ecclesiastical Unity, one book, “The unity of the Ecclesiastical [unclear].”

On Ecclesiastical Estates, one book, “The peace which all.”

On the Manner of Living of the Faithful, one book, “The first rule which.” “Perhaps it is said to me,” etc.

On Ecclesiastical Defects, two books, “In the inquiry of truth.”

On Schism, one book, “About to give occasion.”

On a General Council, one book, “It is asked whether this.”

A Trialogue on Schism, one book, “Very often [unclear].” “The marriage was made in.”

On the Marriage of the Church, one book, “A compendious declaration.”

What Things Must Necessarily Be Believed, one book, “A protestation or renewal.”

On Various Heresies, one book, “But he who blasphemous [unclear].”

On Appeal from the Pope, one book, “And first it is clear,” etc.

Against Peter de Luna, Thirty Articles, one book, “About to offer, according to himself.” “And first it must be noted.”

Against the Same Man, Eight Articles, one book, “Most reverend in Christ.”

On the Assumption of the Humanity of Christ, one book, “As it is written in.”

Two Lectures on Mark, one book, “Beware of false pro-[unclear].”

On the Literal Sense of Scripture, one book, “The wisdom which from the Lord God.”

Against the Heresy of the Bohemians, one book, “Recently one from the readings.”

On the Testing of Spirits, one book, “The Apostle blames those who.” “Recently praising me.”

On the Errors of Magic, one book, “Recently praising me.” “Most reverend in Christ.”

On True and False Visions, one book, “A certain master in the [unclear].”

Against Matthew Grabon, one book, “This has as proper to art [unclear].”

Against the Flagellants, one book, “The law of Christ is called the law of love.”

Moral Rules, one book, “Let us act now meanwhile.”

On the Precepts of the Decalogue, one book, “Of Christianity, what sort for his own [unclear].”

On the Difference of Sins, one book, “He who considers well.” “And if the virtue which,” etc.

On the Confession of Softness, one book, “Since Christ has given.” “It is asked whether to speak ill.”

Remedies for Those Relapsing, one book, “Grace to you and peace, brother.”

On Sacramental Absolution, one book, “On the matter of simony.”

On Contracts, one book, “Do not be anxious what.”

On Indulgences, one book, “Blessed is that servant whom.”

On Four Questions, one book, “Someone recently doubts whether.”

On Various Questions, one book, “Because they wish the rich to become [unclear].”

On Simony, one book, “On the matter of simony.”

On the Solicitude of Ecclesiastics, one book, “Do not be anxious what.” “Blessed is he whose name,” etc.

On Making a Will, one book, “It has been doubted by me.”

The Testament of a Pilgrim, in verse, one book, “De pol-[unclear].”

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On nocturnal pollution, one book. “Long ago I wrote certain things.” On the chastity of ecclesiastics, one book. “There are eunuchs who [unclear].” One book. “It is a great and wondrous thing.” On abstinence from meats, one book. “Already in one earlier reading.” On the temperance of prelates, one book. “Repent, believe.” On the life of clerics, one book. “So far has it gone out to [unclear].” One book. “A certain noble man.” On humility, one book. “O Jesus, king of kings, graciously.” On nobility, one book. “Soldiers in the wilderness.” On the prince’s consideration, one book. “Whatever things have been written.” Dialogue of two soldiers, four books. “Let us inquire into the matter, O monk.” One book. “They have been the source.” On the Consolation of Theology, one book. “Conceived of the Virgin.” Apologetic dialogue, one book. “I baptized you with water.” Josephina, in verse, one book. “He has put down the mighty from.” Centiloquy on concepts, one book. “Repent, believe.” One book. “Treating in the readings.” On the spiritual life, one book. “To you it has been given to know.” Centiloquy on impulses, book [unclear]. “Grace to you and peace.” On Mystical Theology, one book. “The meditation of my heart.” The practical Decade, one book. “In simplicity of heart.” Elucidation of the same, one book. “I will confess to you in [unclear].” One book. “The kingdom of heaven is like.” On the perfection of religion, one book. “[Unclear] were the disciples.” Against faintheartedness, one book. “He who is of faintheartedness.” On the meditation of the heart, one book. “But we, under the hand of God.” On simplicity of heart, one book. “God wills that it be [unclear].” On the direction of the heart, one book. “Passion, fervor.” On the illumination of the heart, one book. “You shall love the Lord your God.” On the eye also, two books. “Perhaps some will wonder.” On the mountain of contemplation, one book. “O my poor infirm [unclear].” On spiritual diversity, one book. “One must always pray.” On the value of prayer, three books. “We have sung to you, and [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, one book. “My soul magnifies.” On the Magnificat, twelve books. “I bear passion, true [unclear].” A poem on the same, one book. “Glory to God in the highest.” On the Angelic Hymn, one book. “I love you; to make order [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, four books. “[Unclear] the bride [unclear].” On the nuptials of Wisdom, two books. “And John was clothed.” To the teachers of boys, one book. “Let the little children come.” Sermons in the Council of Constance, one book. “Walk while you have the light.” Sermons to the clergy, one book. Sermons to the people, one book. Dialogue on quodlibetal questions, one book. Many letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other smaller works besides, indeed, but very useful ones, of which no certain knowledge has come down to us. He was personally prominent in the Council of Constance, in which, laboring gloriously for the extirpation of heresies, at length, when that council was dissolved, he was deprived, for defending the truth, of home, country, relatives, friends, dignities, and his own possessions, and was sought by many hostile persons. Hence, compelled by necessity, he went to the city of Lyon, and there after a few years he died, under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1429, the seventh indiction, in the sixty-sixth year of his age, on the fourth day before the Ides of July. He was buried there with honor among the Celestines.

VINCENT Ferrer of Valencia, of the Order of Friars Preachers, to whom some letters of John Gerson are extant, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, devout in morals and manner of life, the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time, shining with miracles both alive and dead, wrote elegant

Sermons on the season, one book. “Blessed is he who comes in.” One book. “He is rich toward all who [unclear].”

The Abbot of Sponheim

Sermons for Lent, one book. Certain letters.

He was present in person at the Council of Constance in the year of the Lord 1418. After his death, because of frequent miracles, he was canonized by Pope Calixtus III in the year of the Lord 1455, in the third indiction. His feast is in April.

Boniface Ferrer of Valencia, a Catalan by nation, of the Carthusian order, the twenty-fifth prior, brother of the aforesaid blessed Vincent the preacher, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and an outstanding doctor of canon law, not falling short of his holy brother in life and conduct, governed the Grande Chartreuse energetically by word and example. Among other things he wrote a notable treatise on why few in the Carthusian order have been canonized and why they do not perform miracles publicly.

To Boniface of the same order, one book. On the approbation of the order, one book. Certain letters. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Lupus of Oliveto, a Spaniard by nation, of the order of the hermit-monks of Saint Jerome, prior general, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and an outstanding restorer of his order, wrote several excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported, from the sayings of Saint Jerome:

The Rule of his order, one book: “Dearest brothers, not...” Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain other things. Martin V confirmed this newly compiled rule in thirty-two chapters. He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1426.

Dominic of San Gimignano, a most distinguished legal consultant, learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other letters of the secular disciplines, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, wrote certain excellent volumes in canon law, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is an eminent and very celebrated work, divided into two volumes, two books: “Because the first gloss without...”

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals. And various declarations. The other works which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Paul of Saint Mary, Jewish by birth, Christian in faith, first bishop of Cartagena and afterwards bishop of Burgos in Spain, arch-chancellor of the king of Castile and Leon, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine writings, and master of sacred theology, having been converted in his mature age to the Catholic faith, advanced so far in life and doctrine that among all the doctors of Spain he had no equal in his time. He wrote for his son Alfonso, dean of Compostela and doctor of laws, on the Postils of Nicholas of Lyra:

Notable Additions, one book: “What do you wish for yourself, that living...” Scrutiny of the Scriptures, two books: “Search the Scriptures...” And certain other things.

He flourished and completed this Scrutiny of his under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1434, in the twelfth indiction, in the eighty-first year of his age.

Petrus Paulus Vergerius, by homeland a Justinopolitan, a man devoted to the divine writings and most learned in secular letters, and a very celebrated rhetorician, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech, formerly a hearer of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher who taught Greek letters at Venice, wrote certain excellent little works of excellent talent, which he left to posterity. Among these there is an eminent work containing the deeds of the Carrara lords, one book: “A very beautiful history...”

In Praise of Saint Jerome, one book. And many other things. On Liberal Manners, one book. He flourished at the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Maffeo Vegio, by homeland of Lodi, datary of Pope Martin V, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, outstandingly learned, and in secular letters most learned, a very celebrated orator and poet, distinguished no less in conduct than in knowledge: through his care and expense the relics of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, were translated from Ostia Tiberina to Rome and deposited in a new chapel, expensively built by him, in which he himself is buried. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, certain excellent volumes, among which there is a very celebrated work, necessary for all religious, composed from divine and human letters, addressed to certain sisters, which he entitled:

On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On perseverance, seven books: “Since grave matters often, as happens...” On the penitential Psalms, one book. In praise of Saint Monica, one book. A thirteenth book of the Aeneid in heroic verse, one book. Several epigrams, one book. On military affairs. A dialogue, which is called Philaletes. Many letters. And very many other works. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Plaeth, German by nation, the ornament and pillar of the school of Heidelberg, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, insofar as the secular state allows, an excellent doctor in delivering sermons to the people. Among other things he wrote a great and distinguished volume, which he read in ordinary and public lectures at the aforesaid University of Heidelberg.

On the first chapter of the Decretals, one book: “Venerable fathers...” Against the Bohemians, one book: “As the wise man says...” Questions on the Sentences, one book. Several sermons. Various questions. And certain other things. He flourished under the Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Dieppurg, called “of Frankfurt,” German by nation, a doctor of Heidelberg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, an acute disputant and an excellent declaimer of sermons, formerly chaplain and secretary of Ludwig, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, and often an envoy in many difficult cases. He wrote little works not to be scorned in reading, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

Against the Hussites, one book: “When recently, in the year of the Lord...” Against the Feymeri, one book: “The law of the Lord for external [unclear]...” On contracts, one book: “As in the forum of the soul, where in...” On predestination, one book: “Glory to God in the highest...” Many sermons, one book: “I have a word for you...” An oration before the king of England, one book. An oration before the king of France, one book. An oration before the duke of Savoy, one book. Several letters. Various questions, one book. [unclear] Various orations. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Raymundus Sebeide, Spanish by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, who by teaching and writing in the school of Toulouse gave great proof of his learning. He is reported to have written many splendid little works; of these I have seen only a large volume, which he had read publicly in the aforesaid university, and at its beginning he promises many and glorious things, concerning the truth of which some applaud themselves as experienced men, because he set it forth beforehand.

Of creatures, or On man, one book: “To the praise and glory...” Disputed questions, one book. The rest are unknown to me. He flourished in the times of the Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Franciscus Barbarus, a Venetian patrician, a pupil in Greek letters of the Byzantine philosopher Chrysoloras, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a famous philosopher and a supreme orator in both languages. While still a young man he wrote certain little works not unworthy of reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives the work which he entitled:

On wifely duty, one book. A collection of letters to various persons, sixteen books. And certain other things. From Plutarch he translated into Latin, for his brother Zacharias, the life of Aristides and of Cato, and of many illustrious men. Likewise also other things. He died in the times of the Emperor Frederick III and Pope Nicholas V, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the second indiction.

Thomas Walden, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, and general prior of the English province, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect and for disputation

352 The Abbot of Sponheim

[unclear] sufficiently qualified, distinguished no less in conduct than in learning, and also an excellent declaimer of sermons, and formerly confessor-secretary of Henry V, king of the English.

Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a notable work, divided into three large volumes, against the mad Wycliffites and Hussite heretics; Martin V, pope, after it had been examined, confirmed it by apostolic authority. This work is entitled:

The Doctrinal of the Church, 3 books. Let God arise, let him scatter. Also, On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Books of the Physics, 8 books. On Generation and Corruption, 2 books. On the Books on the Soul, 4 books. On the Books of the Ethics, 10 books. On the Book On the Heavens and the World, 4 books. On the Books of the Meteorology, 4 books.

He is said to have written many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He died at Rouen, honorably buried in his convent, under Emperor Sigismund, in the last year of Pope Martin V, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430, indiction 8, on the third day of the month of November, that is, 3 Nones.

Paulus of Castro, the most celebrated jurist of all his time, a man of great learning and eloquence, who for many years, hired at a public salary, taught civil law with distinction at Siena, Florence, and Padua, composed many little works on the laws, known and dear to the professors of this faculty, by which he left to posterity the memory of his very celebrated name. Among these the following are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. Most elegant Counsels, 1 book. And many other works.

He died in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1437, indiction 15.

Ambrosius the Florentine, general abbot of the Camaldolese order, once a pupil of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher teaching Greek letters at Venice, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular studies, a most brilliant philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian, left to posterity many distinguished monuments of his talent. He was the nuncio and orator of Pope Eugenius to the Council of Basel, where he delivered a solemn oration on his behalf to the fathers. He wrote a notable volume:

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Various Orations. And many other works.

He also translated from Greek into Latin the four books of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, in a rather elegant and easy style. Also the original Life of Blessed John Chrysostom, to Emperor Sigismund. Likewise Basil On Virginity, to Cardinal Gabriel, afterward Pope Eugenius IV. Likewise Laertius On the Life of the Philosophers, to Cosimo de’ Medici. But he translated the three books of divine John Chrysostom to the monk Stagirius [Arrepticius?] in clear and ornate eloquence. And many other works still known to us. He flourished in the times of the Councils of Constance and Basel, and adorned both by his presence, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Caietanus, by homeland a Vicentine, a Paduan canon, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and physician, a very celebrated theologian, who taught sacred scholastic letters publicly in the Paduan gymnasium, acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote, as they report, several little works in both literatures, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Books of the Physics, 8 books. On the Book On the Heavens and the World, 4 books. On the Books on the Soul, 4 books. And

On Ecclesiastical Writers

And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Henricus Gulpen, abbot of the monastery of St. Giles in Nuremberg, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, an eminent jurist, and excellently learned both in divine Scripture and in secular philosophy, venerable no less for his religious way of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures; Johannes Nider, having had experience of him, commends the readiness of his talent and the foresight of his counsel in his little work On Ants. He wrote elegantly on the seven distinctions:

On Penance, one book. On Consecration, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished at the Council of Constance in person, while he was still a secular master of arts and student of law, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Jacobus Forliviensis, a philosopher and physician of very celebrated reputation, who is said by many to have far surpassed all the professors of philosophy and medicine of his time, distinguished not only for learning but also for experience in curing human illnesses. In his faculty he wrote works very useful for students, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these the principal ones are reported to be:

On the Extension of the Degrees of Forms, one book. On the First Canon of Avicenna, one book. On the Aphorisms of the same, one book. Also on the Tegni, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Sigismund, most Christian emperor, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430.

Rudolphus of Buxella, a village of Swabia, a German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, and excellently trained in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, an eminent professor of sacred theology, who acquired great praise for his learning in the Heidelberg academy. In that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity, namely:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Very Useful Sermons, one book. Various Questions, one book. And if holy mother [unclear] Several Orations to the Fathers, one book.

And many other things. He flourished in the Heidelberg academy at the time of the Council of Basel and thereafter [unclear] left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these are reported:

On the First Book of Avicenna, one book. On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book. On the Tegni of Galen, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Henricus de Gauda, a German by nation, magnificently learned in the holy Scriptures, subtle in talent, and a most acute disputant of scholastic questions, easily held the first place in the Heidelberg academy in his time, both by reading and teaching, and then by composing. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, of which few have so far come to my knowledge.

Fount of Gardens, Well, On Celebration, one book. Various Orations. Disputed Questions. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Sanctes de Arduinis, born from the city of Pesaro, a man most learned in philosophy and medicine, and most experienced in healing human bodies, held in great esteem among the Venetians in his time, published certain distinguished little works in this faculty, by which he transmitted the memory of his very famous name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a notable work on all natural and artificial poisons, one book.

Also On Odoration, one book. On Prolification, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

354 The Abbot of Spanheim

NICHOLAS de Susato, a German by nation, a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, and most learned both in secular philosophy and in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by Ludwig, duke of Bavaria, count palatine of the Rhine, and in the Council of Constance joined with the cardinals from the German nation, together with the others, for electing the supreme pontiff, as is found in the acts of that council, wrote several distinguished little works of his talent, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Many sermons, one book. Various questions. And many other things. He flourished at the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

JOHANNES de Marliano, a very celebrated philosopher and physician, excellent in talent, renowned for experience in this art, and not among the least of the physicians of his time, published certain distinguished and lucid little works both in philosophy and in medicine, the reading and study of which are said to be of no little use to students of these matters, namely:

On reaction, etc., one book. On the heat of bodies, one book. On antiperistasis, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Sigismund, most Christian emperor, in the year of the Lord 1430.

JOHANNES Gritch, a German by nation, from Basel as his native place, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and clear in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote little works not to be despised for preachers of the word of God, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons throughout Lent, one book. “When you fast,” etc., second. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. And certain other things. He flourished, as his people say, in the times of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

JOHANNES Nider, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently taught in scholastic philosophy, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people, an inquisitor of heretical depravity and a most keen investigator of the little women whom the common people call witches, wrote in plain speech several volumes by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the contracts of merchants, one book. “Since the office of merchants.” On moral leprosy, one book. “Once, while we read in Levi.” On the precepts of the Decalogue, one book. “The most sacred law of the Decalogue.” On ants morally, one book. “Often traversing those which.” On the consolation of a fearful conscience, one book. “Among the disciplines I found.” Mirror of Perfection, one book. “Behold your king,” etc. Three. Sermons on the season, one book. “Come after me,” etc. Sermons on the saints, one book. “Turn to,” etc. Lenten sermons, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and of the Councils of Constance and Basel, in the year of the Lord 1430.

NICHOLAS Siculus, abbot of Monacen. of the Order of Saint Benedict, sprung from the city of Catania, called de Tudeschis, first auditor of the cases of the lord pope and of the Rota, afterward archbishop of Palermo, and finally cardinal of the sacrosanct church, the most celebrated of all [unclear] in law, subtle and acute in talent, ready and firm in counsel, open and orderly in speech, who is deservedly called the lamp of the law. He wrote many distinguished volumes by which he made his name known to posterity; of these the following are reported:

On the Decretum, incomplete, one book. On the Decretals, one book. On the Clementines, one book. For the Council of Basel, one book. One hundred four counsels, one book. “Since every reason of the heavenly.” “Since the truth of words.” “A peaceful matter of all.” “The contingency of the fact is such.” Dispu-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Various disputations, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1435. And on behalf of the authority of that council, before the princes at Frankfurt, he publicly read the aforementioned treatise and delivered an elegant oration there.

Ludovicus Pontanus of Rome, an Italian by nation, a most distinguished jurist, and no less zealous in the sacred Scriptures than in secular philosophy, excellent in talent, concise and weighty in judgment, published volumes not to be despised for those wishing to make progress in the faculty of law, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number I [have seen] only the work entitled:

Notable singular points, one book: “A word is wholly understood.”

Johannes Noblet, of the Order of Friars Minor of blessed Mary ever virgin, in the times of Sigismund, the most excellent emperor, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of Sigismund, the most excellent emperor. Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

On the Canonical Epistles, one book: “Her husband is noble in the gates.”

A Centiloquy of Enigmas, one book. Various sermons, one book. And many other things. Moreover he is said to have written wondrous and most elegant commentaries on many books of the Bible, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Johannes de Ragulio, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, published certain excellent little works of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have read a work addressed to the fathers of the Council of Basel:

Against the Hussites, one book: “Most reverend, venerable...”

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, where he publicly pronounced the said treatise against the heretics before the fathers, under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1438.

Blondus Flavius of Forli, secretary of Pope Eugene IV, a man skilled in every discipline of the good arts, a most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, and a distinguished historiographer, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, and second to none in grace of speaking, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Three decades, so entitled.

On the Deeds of the Romans, [unclear] books: “Of the Roman empire...”

On Rome Triumphant, ten books. On Rome Restored, one book.

On Italy, [unclear] books. Letters to various persons, one book.

And many other things.

Various orations, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund, under Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1455. He left five sons from a legitimate marriage, cultivators of the good arts.

Heymericus de Campo, a German by nation, vice-chancellor of the University of Cologne, a man learned in the divine writings and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent and excellent in disputing difficult questions, wrote many excellent little works, of which, however, few have so far come into our hands. He was present in person at the Council of Basel, sent by the University of Cologne, where at the urging of master Nicolaus of Cusa, later cardinal, he published:

A Compendium of Questions, one book: “After very many, the occasion...”

On the Sentences, [unclear] books: “As Augustine says in the book...”

On Being and Essence, one book: “Being and not-being are opposed.”

A Compendium of Divine Matters, two books: “In this little work [unclear]...”

Various Questions, one book. Many sermons, one book. And many other things.

On the Authority of the Council,

He flourished at the Council of Basel, where he wrote and disputed many things, in the year of the Lord [unclear], under Emperor Albert.

Gregorius Trapezontius, apostolic secretary, a man most learned in every respect [continues].

The Abbot of Sponheim

...a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, who, placed by Pope Eugenius in charge of the public school at Rome, taught rhetoric and poetics for many years, and left after him many pupils most skilled in every science. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these are extant:

A Very Beautiful Rhetoric, one book. On the Orations of Cicero, one book. And certain other things, one book. A Singular Dialectic, one book. Various Orations and Letters, one book.

He flourished at Rome in the time of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1435.

Florianus of San Pietro, an Italian by nation, from Bologna by homeland, a man easily the most learned of all his time in civil law, not ignorant of either the divine Scriptures or secular philosophy, acute in intellect, clear in speech, a subtle disputant, a cautious adviser. He wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he commended to posterity the memory of his very celebrated name. Of these there are reported:

On the Code, two books. On the New Digest, three books. On the Infortiatum, four books.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Nicolaus Lackman, a German by nation, of the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, minister of Saxony, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, outstanding in intellect, fit for disputation, and of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote little works not to be rejected in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number the following are reported as the more important:

On the Sentences, nine books. Sermons on the Season, ten books. And very many other things, one book. Various Questions, two books. Sermons on the Saints, three books.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Johannes of Schonhouen, a German by nation, of the Order of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine, of the monastery in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, which in the vernacular is called Groenendael and in Latin Viridis Vallis, in which Johannes Rusbrugh once held the office of prior; a man studious and learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, cautious in intellect, composed in speech, and no less distinguished in manner of life than in knowledge. He wrote to Simon, his nephew:

A Spiritual Exhortatory, one book. “Great joy to me...” On the Course of a Monk, one book. “That to you, dearest...” A Defense of Johannes Rusbrog, one book. “Fight the good fight...” Various Sermons, one book. “Since a certain doctor...” one book. Letters to Various Persons, two books. And very many other things.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Petrus de Colle, of the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally taught in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, eloquent and clear in delivering sermons to the people, published for the edification of readers several volumes, by which he transmitted the memory of his distinguished name to posterity. Among these there is extant an instructed work which he recited to the fathers at the Council of Basel:

On the Authority of a Council, one book. “The Church fought many...” Questions on the Sentences, one book. Various Sermons, two books. And very many other things.

He flourished at the time of the same Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Hermann, a monk in Camp, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Münster, a German by nation, from Westphalia by homeland, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, [unclear], excellently learned both in law and in Aristotelian philosophy, prompt in intellect, open in speech, wrote several little works of his exercise, by which for the defense...

On Ecclesiastical Writers

In the [unclear] of the Council of Basel he labored by no means slightly. Among his works I found a small treatise which he entitled On Definitive Terms.

In a General Council, one book. “Now, by very often repeated vi...” On the Power of the Pope and of the Council, one book. “Blessed Athanasius.” On a Schismatic, one book. On Neutrality, one book.

Of his decretals, although many things are reported which he composed, nothing has come down to me. He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Johannes Gauwer, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, lector of sacred Scripture in the convent of Mainz, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and quite fit for delivering sermons to the people. He wrote some not-to-be-despised little works of his practiced intellect, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. “To the praise of almighty God.” On Exodus, one book. “The law for the common utility.” Harmony of the Evangelists, one book. “Because God sent his Son.” Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. A Threefold Lenten Work, three books. “When you fast,” etc., “knowing...” And many others.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

Bernardinus, of the order of the Friars Minor, an Italian by nation, from Siena as his homeland, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, the most celebrated preacher of all his time, and most holy in life and conduct, since both alive and dead he showed by countless miracles the force of his practiced intellect also to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Apocalypse of John, one book. “Blessed is he who reads,” etc., “threefold...” On the Eternal Gospel, one book. “For I came not to destroy the law.” On the Christian Religion, one book. “Now remain faith, hope.” On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book. “The depths were not yet,” and... On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain other works.

He died at Aquila, a city of Abruzzo, in the reign of Emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, in the sixty-third year of his age. Because of his frequent miracles he was inserted by Pope Nicholas V into the catalogue of the saints, in the year 50, and the seventh after his death. His feast is observed on the twentieth day of the month of May.

Antonius Gayerus, from Pavia by nation, a very celebrated doctor of the art of medicine, nobly learned in the precepts of the philosophers, excellent in intellect, and by no means slightly renowned for skill in his profession, wrote in that discipline certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On Disease of the Stomach, one book. On Fever, one book. On Diseases in General, one book. On Pleurisy, one book. On the Womb, one book. On Fluxes, one book. On Arthritis in the Joints, one book. On the Ailments of Stone, one book. On the Third Book of Avicenna, one book. And many others.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Gerardus Stredam, a German by nation, of the order of the Carthusians, prior of [unclear]; the following works are reported as [unclear]. To the abbot of Saint Hadrian of Giraldi Mount.

On Pastoral Care, one book. On the Ten Commandments, one book. On the Seven Sacraments, one book. Mirror of Religious, one book. Dialogue on Virtues, one book. Dialogue on Vices, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain other works.

He died at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction.

Matthaeus Palmerius, an Italian by nation, from Florence as his homeland, a historiographer,

The Abbot of Sponheim

...a philosopher and a most eloquent orator, who in the Council of Florence, which Pope Eugenius IV held against the Synod of Basel, was numbered among the distinguished men. He wrote a book full of error on the angels; defending it obstinately, he was condemned as a heretic and burned at the city of [unclear]. Carefully examining the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, he corrected it and, completing it down to the year of the Lord 1448, gave it a title.

To Peter, [son] of Cosimo de' Medici, one book: Innate in our minds. Letters to various persons, one book. Also various orations. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

Johannes Ernesti, a German by nation, once the ornament and rector of the Heidelberg school, learned in the Holy Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech with singular charm, an outstanding disputant of questions. He wrote, as they say, certain distinguished little works, by which the memory of his name is transmitted with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported.

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Disputed questions, one book. Many sermons, one book: Although of speaking concerning the greatest... 26. An oration on the Nativity of the Lord, one book: Most sacred desires.... On fasting, to the university, one book. On the authority of a council, one book. Many and various orations, one book. And very many other works. He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Bartholomaeus, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Bethlehem in the town of Roermond in Guelders, a German by nation; an acute, devout, and celebrated interpreter of sacred letters. He wrote for the edification of his brothers certain distinguished little works, in which he magnificently exercised his talent and left the memory of his name to posterity. Of their number the following are reported.

Exercise of devotion, one book. Summary of vices, one book. On abstinence from meats, one book. On the proclamations of the brothers, one book. On rash judgment, one book. On an oath, one book. Also on a vow, one book. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord [unclear], on the fourth day before the Ides of July. On the Sentences, one book. And very many other works. 36. Also various sermons, one book: Having perhaps gone out from the cubit.... He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1490.

Henricus de Werlis, a German by nation, of the order of Friars Minor, of the province of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, an excellent scholastic in talent and speech, an acute disputant and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, composed certain lucid volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there survives a notable work.

...the Rhine and the Hercynian forest, which, called the Saonus, extends toward Trier to the west; certainly a studious man, learned in the divine writings and not ignorant also of secular letters, outstanding in talent and clear in speech. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant.

Soliloquies of man to God, one book: When once by the divine calling.... On the progress of virtues, one book: Of your fraternity.... On the use of flocks, one book: Reverend father, recently from.... Letters to various persons, one book: Although among all who sinisterly.... Various conferences, one book: Although there is nothing in me that.... Poems and rhythms. And certain other brief works. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Sponheim, before the introduction of the most recent Bursfelde reform, in the year of the Lord 145[unclear].

Anto-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Antonius, of the Order of Friars Preachers, archbishop of Florence, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, famous in preaching sermons to the people and of celebrated reputation, and no less venerable for his life and conduct than for his learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, in all of which he labored magnificently for the edification of the Church militant. Of these there is extant a great and very celebrated work, divided into four not small volumes, which is entitled:

Summa of cases of conscience, 4 books. “How magnified are...”

A great and noteworthy Chronicle, 3 books. “I shall speak propositions from...”

Guidebook for confessors, 1 book. “Those who search have failed...”

On ecclesiastical censure, 1 book. “Turn to the Lord...”

Sermons on the season, 1 book. And certain other things.

Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

He died, after many labors in sacred study, not without a reputation for holiness, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1459, indiction 7, on the sixth day before the Nones of May. He was buried at Saint Mark’s, the convent of his order.

Sermons on the season, 1 book. “Interpreter of divine things...”

Sermons on the saints, 1 book. And certain other things.

On laws during Lent, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year 1445.

John of Capistrano, from a town of Abruzzo not far from the city of Aquila, of the order [unclear], studious and learned in the Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of outstanding talent and very high reputation in preaching sermons to the people. For the use of preachers he wrote certain excellent little works, by all of which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Sermons on the season. “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves...”

3 books. Various sermons, 1 book.

On laws during Lent. Certain letters.

Against the Hussites, 1 book.

Certain letters.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1450, and not without [unclear]. He converted many from iniquity by word and example, and wrote certain little works of no small usefulness, of which few have come down to me.

On cupidity. “I shall now disclose what to you...”

1 book. “He was among those who at...”

Against the Hussites. “Take, most holy father...”

1 book. “To the praise of the Almighty...”

On the Passion of the Lord. “So great is the power...”

“It has been proposed, my...”

Most upright in life and conduct and singularly devout, a sincere and fervent lover of the salvation of souls, who, sent as legate into Germany, did and established many useful things for the reform of the Church, and especially of our order; he wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant:

On the Vision of God, 1 book. “Receive a brief compendium...”

Correction of the Calendar. “Since to us [unclear]...”

1 book. “The noble mind is solicitous...”

The Sifting of the Qur’an, 1 book. “Nicholas, by the mercy...”

1 book. “Whoever shall have read those things which in...”

On the Hunt for Wisdom. “And if already before P.V.NO. ...”

Compendium, 1 book.

Dialogue of Three on Possibility, 1 book.

On Mathematical Perfection, 1 book.

Against the Bohemians, 1 book.

On the Beryl, 1 book.

On the Gift of the Father of Lights, 1 book.

1 book. 1 book. 1 book. 1 book.

1 book. 1 book. 3 books. 1 book. 1 book.

1 book. 1 book. “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves...” Various sermons. Certain letters.

1 book. 1 book. “He was among those who at...” “To the praise of the Almighty...” “So great is the power, my...” “Since to us I grant...” “The nobility, my...” “Nicholas, by the mercy...” “Whoever shall have read that which in...” “And if already before P.V.NO. ...”

1 book. 1 book. “I shall now disclose what to you...” “Receive a brief compendium...” “Since to us grant...” “The solicitous thing is of the noble soul of mine...” “Nicholas will show mercy...” “Whoever shall have read those things which in...” “And if already before Peter the Venerable Nonon.”

360 The Abbot of Sponheim

On Seeking God, 1 book.

On the Summit of Theory, 1 book.

On Learned Ignorance, 3 books.

On Conjectures, 2 books.

On the Sonship of God, 1 book.

On Genesis, 1 book.

The Layman, on Wisdom, 4 books.

On the Squaring of the Circle, 1 book.

Directory for the One Contemplating, 1 book.

Sermons for the Whole Year, 1 book.

And many other works. Near Cusa, the village of his birth, on the banks of the Moselle opposite Bernkastel, he built a very famous hospital in honor of Saint Nicholas the bishop, which he richly endowed with estates and revenues, and adorned with many books in every science, Greek, Latin, and others. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on the eleventh day of the month of August, in the sixty-third year of his age. He was buried at Rome; his heart was sent to the aforesaid hospital, and there buried beneath marble in the middle of the choir.

Johannes Rode, abbot of the monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, from Trier by homeland, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, and outstandingly learned in canon law, devout in morals and manner of life, and a very famous restorer of regular observance, from whose labor and foundation the most recent Bursfeld reform of our order in Germany takes its beginning. He formerly devoted himself to letters in the school of Heidelberg, where, becoming a bachelor of sacred theology and a most learned licentiate of canon law, he already seemed to despise the world in mind and body. Afterwards made canon of the church of Metz, dean of Saint Simeon, and official of the Trier curia, he despised all things for love of Christ, and entered the Carthusian order outside Trier, to the amazement of all; and for some years before, though refusing and unwilling, he had taken up the office of prior.
