But Otto, archbishop of Trier, perceiving that this man was learned, experienced, and zealous, drew him out of the Charterhouse by authority of the supreme pontiff and appointed him abbot in the aforesaid monastery; through him he reformed many monasteries in his diocese. He himself also, by authority of the Council of Basel, magnificently extended the reform. He wrote, for the reform of monks:

Useful Constitutions, 1 book. “When the divine office which...”

On the Quality of an Abbot, 1 book. “In what way from on high proceeds every...”

And certain other things. He died under Emperor Albert and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1439, the twentieth of his abbacy, in the second indiction, on the first day of the month of December. He was buried in the said monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle at Trier, before the altar of Stephen the protomartyr, in the right apse of the choir, beneath a stone inscribed with his name.

Guarino of Verona, once a hearer of Chrysoloras the Byzantine philosopher, in secular writings easily the most learned of all in his time, and not ignorant of divine letters, most skilled in Greek and Latin speech; by his labor the studies of the good arts, which seemed weakened and already almost extinct, were stirred up and recalled into the light. He taught first at Venice, afterwards at Ferrara, and in both places had very famous pupils. He wrote to Prince Leonello a work entitled:

On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend, 1 book.

Also a brief Grammar, 1 book.

A Comparison of Scipio and Gaius, 1 book.

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

Many Orations, 1 book.

Many poems.

And not a few other things. By order of Pope Nicholas V he translated into Latin the Geography of Strabo, a work no less [unclear] than delightful. From Plutarch he made Latin versions of the lives of many illustrious men. But he also translated Plutarch himself On the Education of Children, with many other works, most elegantly; these are partly extant. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460, in the eighth indiction, on the day before the Nones of December. He was buried at Ferrara in the convent of the Carmelites, honorably granted a marble tomb.

Henricus Kaltysen, archbishop of the churches of Nydrosia and Caesarea, of the order of the Friars Preachers, a German by nation, from Koblenz by homeland, where also he entered the order; first made lector of the sacred palace, preacher of the Holy Cross, and inquisitor of heretical depravity, and afterwards, as we have said, consecrated arch-prelate of two provinces by apostolic authority, he became renowned throughout the whole world for his learning and preaching. Since he was a very famous doctor of sacred theology, he wrote, among other things, notable:

Sermons

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book. Various questions, one book. And many other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1465, indiction 13, on the sixth day before the Nones of October. He was buried in his own convent at Koblenz.

JOHANNES Berthachinus of Fermo, a very celebrated jurist, and exceptionally diligent in that faculty, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain excellent little works on law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there is an outstanding work, divided into three large volumes, which he compiled with much labor, most diligently and in fine order, and entitled:

Repertory of both laws, three books. “Princes are accustomed [unclear].” Various questions.

He also published many other things besides, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

PIUS, the second pope, Tuscan by nation, of Siena by homeland, previously called Aeneas Sylvius, sat in the supreme pontificate after Calixtus III for six years. A man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, orator, and distinguished poet, he left many monuments of his talent to posterity. He once, poor, served a certain prelate at the Council of Basel. Then, taken on as a scribe of the chancery of Emperor Frederick III, and created poet by him after receiving the laurel, he was first bishop of Trieste, afterward of Siena, then cardinal, and finally was elected pope by the vote of all. Concerning his writings, the following are reported, composed with great powers of eloquence:

On the miseries of courtiers, one book. “That those are fools who [serve] kings.” On the education of children, one book. “To all who [advance] toward virtue.” Solution of questions, one book. “The imperial [unclear] was recently present.” One book. “The city [unclear] whence to you.” Against the Taborites, one book. “Although among the Bohemians.” To Nicholas of Cusa, one book. “It came to me on this very [day].” One book. “About to write something to you.” On faith to the Turk, one book. “Of the prophet Ezekiel.” Abridgments of Blondus, one book. “Heraldus of Alphonsus [unclear].” On the expedition against the Turks, one book. On the source of the river Nile, one book. To the bishop of Krakow, one book. “But there was in the city of Con[stantinople?].” On the Council of Basel, one book. “That all things are perishable.” Europe, to Cardinal Antoninus, one book. “It would be well, illustrious man.” On the study of hunting, one book. “When I was recently suffering from gout.” On grammar, one book. A dialogue against the Turks, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. An unfinished work of histories, one book. On the fall of Constantinople, an oration, one book. “Necessity does not compel me.” On the calamity of the universal Church, one book. “The Constantinopolitan [unclear].” An oration at the Mantuan assembly, one book. “Unwilling indeed, most blessed [fathers].” An oration to Pope Calixtus, one book. “Since today the war against [unclear].” On the deeds done by himself, one book. “Most people are accustomed.”

He is said to have written many epigrams and certain other very elegant little works, which I have not seen, by which he made his name known to posterity. He died under Emperor Frederick III, at Ancona, as is said, in the year of the Lord 1464, indiction 11, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, likewise in the sixty-fourth year of his age. He was buried at Rome in the church of Saint Peter, beside the altar of Saint Andrew.

LANFRANCUS of Oriano, a very celebrated jurist and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote in his profession certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity; and in study he proved himself in many ways and splendidly. Of their number the following exist:

Repetitions. “Since against these decrees.” Commentary on the Clementine Saepe, On the Meaning of Words, one book. On the chapter Dispendiosam, On Judgments, one book. “Since against these decrees.” “This Clementine contains in itself.” “It is not necessary to divide.”

The Abbot of Sponheim

A repetition on “Raynucius,” On Testaments, one book. In the text where “Raynucius” occurs: “This law is divided into two: for a clearer understanding...”

On the law “Admonendi,” On Oaths, one book: “This law is famous...”

On the Interpretation of Statutes, one book.

A repetition on the rubric On the Cause of Possession and Property, one book.

He also published many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...he transmitted his glory, and in the school of Poitiers, both by disputing and by writing, earned great praise for his learning. Of his little works the following are reported: a distinguished and very celebrated work, almost divine, pleasing for its singular usefulness.

On the Sentences, 7 books. On the little Summa of Peter of Spain, 7 books. Because, as the wise man bears witness. On mathematical science, 1 book. As the Philosopher says. On Aristotle's books of the Physics, 8 books. The first part having been completed. On the book On Heaven and the World, 2 books. Nature; here begins the book. On the book On Generation and Corruption, 2 books. On generation; here begins... 3 books. On first things. The book begins. On the books of the Meteors, 1 book. Of good and honorable things. On the book On the Soul, 12 books. The second part having been completed. On the books of the Metaphysics, 10 books. Having been treated compendiously. On the books of the Ethics, 10 books.

And certain other works. He was, moreover, a profound interpreter and most keen defender of the sayings of John Scotus; from whose writings, expounding philosophy, he divided this very work into three parts, mathematical, theological, and ethical, and named it a compendium. He flourished in the times of Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Callixtus III, in the year of the Lord 1455.

Petrus de Unzola, a citizen of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, notable for experience in many matters, especially judicial ones. He wrote, for the use of notaries studying in legal science, an excellent volume on the continuation of the fifth, sixth, and seventh chapters of the Summa of Lord Rolandinus, which he entitled:

The Newest Dawn, 1 book. Of scribes and notaries. Various consultations, 1 book.

He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus de Herph, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, German by nation, of the province of Cologne, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of pontifical law, outstanding in intellect, clear in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people, venerable no less for religious life than for knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote little works of authority not to be rejected, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: a great and distinguished volume.

On the Precepts of the Decalogue, 1 book. I find another law in... Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Behold, your king comes. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Rabbi, where do you dwell? Sermons throughout Advent, 1 book. Who will be able to think. On the Three Parts of Penance, 1 book. No one can serve two masters.

And certain other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Turrecremata, of the Order of Friars Preachers, bishop of Sabina, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, an excellent declaimer of sermons, quick in intellect, clear in eloquence. He wrote many little works of his intellect, by which he made himself known. Of these the following are reported. For Arsenius, monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict, which he himself held in commendam, he composed a great work, not to be rejected.

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book. Since, with the help of our Lord. On the whole Psalter, 1 book. To the most blessed father [unclear]. On the Sunday Gospels, questions, 1 book. To the most sacred and most revered. On holy water, 1 book. Recently the reverend father enjoined me. On the salvation of the soul, 1 book. Divine Scripture teaches us. Sermons on the Season.

And very many other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and the supreme pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Johannes de Mechilinia, German by nation, a man long exercised by study in the divine Scriptures, not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in intellect, distinguished in knowledge, taught theology publicly to many in the school of Cologne, [unclear] some distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a distinguished work.

The Abbot of Sponheim

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Psalter, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. Sermons and Conferences, 1 book. And many other things. He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Dionysius Rykel, otherwise de Leeuwis, German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Bethlehem in Roermond, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through continual practice, not ignorant also of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, and singularly devout in life and conduct, so much so that he was even considered worthy of divine revelations; to him there are extant several letters of Nicholas of Cusa, a most learned cardinal. He wrote so many and such great works that, in the number of his treatises, among the Latins he had no equal except Augustine. He applied himself to contemplation and prayer with such fervor that you would have thought he could never have written anything. Again, in writing and reading he was so diligent that you would have judged that he could nowhere pray or contemplate. He slept very little, was admirable in abstinence from food and drink, and, after the example of blessed Jerome, judged it sweet to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, always either writing something useful or reading, so that prayer often interrupted reading, and sacred reading frequently followed prayer. Of his treatises he himself, in a certain appended little index, listed the following.

On the Sentences, 1 book: “Beloved by God and men.” “All the sermons are just.” On Genesis, 1 book: “Honor the Lord with your...” On Exodus, 1 book: “He who in the number of [unclear].” On Leviticus, 1 book: “Keep the commandments and the law.” On Numbers, 1 book: “Stronger in war [unclear].” “The individual indexes in their own [unclear].” On the book of Joshua, 1 book: “With Saint Jerome as witness.” “Kings shall come forth from you.” On the book of Judges, 1 book: “God made from one man.” “The law of truth was in his mouth.” On the book of Ruth, 1 book: “Nehemiah in memory.” On the book of [unclear], 1 book: “He who is inclined to mercy...” On the [unclear] books, 1 book: “This shall be called woman.” On Chronicles, 1 book: “Like the sun rising in the world.” 1 book: “God said [to] Solomon.” On Ezra, 1 book: “Just as Solomon.” On Nehemiah, 1 book: “The bridegroom will rejoice over...” On Tobit, 1 book: “Learn where wisdom is.” On Judith, 1 book: “All will marvel at the words.” On Esther, 1 book: “Isaiah, a great prophet.” 1 book: On the book of Baruch. On the book of Job, 1 book. On Daniel. On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book: “The wisdom of all the ancients.” On Ecclesiastes, 1 book: “Judah, your brothers will praise you.” On the Song of Songs, 1 book: “David the son of Jesse said.” On the book of Wisdom, 1 book. On Mark, 1 book. On the book of [unclear], 1 book: “I like an aqueduct,” 7 books, [unclear]. On the book of the prophet, 1 book: “Hear me, since concerning your...” On Jeremiah, 1 book. On the canonical epistles. On Ezekiel, 1 book: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit.” On the twelve prophets, 20 books: “Let us examine our ways.” On the book of Maccabees, 1 book: “They proclaim the wisdom of the saints.” On the Psalter, 1 book: “He made a memorial of his wonders.” On Matthew, 1 book: “Whoever shall eat.” On Luke, 1 book: “He who [unclear] in anxiety.” On John, 14 books: “Wisdom is more precious.” On the epistles of Paul, 1 book: “Buy yourselves wine.” On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. On the Apocalypse, 1 book. An Exposition of Hymns, 1 book. On the seven penitential Psalms, 1 book. On authentic documents, 1 book. An Exposition of the Mass, 1 book. A Dialogue on Celebration, 1 book. On Communion, 1 book. A Compendium of Philosophy, 1 book. A Compendium of Theology, 1 book. Dia-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Dialogue of the philosopher and the theologian, one book. On his eleven letters, one book. On Boethius, On the Consolation, five books. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons to religious men for the season, one book. To the same, on the saints, one book. Six sermons on the sacrament, one book. Meditation on the Lord's Passion, one book. On the praises of God, one book. On the praises of Saint Mary, four books. On the fountain of salvation and the paths of life, one book. On the light of Christian theory, one book. On the beauty of the world, one book. On the nature of the eternal and true God, one book. On the divine essence, one book. On the distance between divine and human perfection, one book. On the benefits of God, one book. On the mutual recognition of the saints, one book. On the gifts of the Holy Spirit, one book. A prefatory Cordiale, one book. On joy and inward peace, one book. On the purgative way, one book. Dialogue on the Catholic faith, one book. Dialogue of a Christian and a Saracen, one book. Against magicians and Waldensians, one book. Against superstitions, one book. On vices and virtues, one book. Against ambition, one book. Against the Saracens, one book. On contempt of the world, one book. On the manner of judging and correcting, one book. On remedies for temptations, one book. Mirror of the sinner, one book. On the four last things, one book. On inward reformation, one book. On particular judgment, one book. On the passions of the soul, one book. On the discernment of spirits, one book. On the perfection of charity, one book. Kindling of divine love, one book. On contemplation, one book. On prayer, one book. Sound of the banqueter, one book. On the manner of conducting processions, one book. On the elevation of the mind to God, one book. On the power and jurisdiction of the pope, one book. On the reformation of the Church, one book. Against simony, one book. On the same, one book. On the reformation of cloistered persons, one book. Against plurality of benefices, one book. On the reformation of nuns, one book. On the profession of religious, one book. Exhortation for novices, one book. On the life and governance of prelates, one book. On the institution of the Carthusian order, one book. On the books of Blessed Dionysius, four books. On the book of John Climacus, one book. Summary of the parts of Saint Thomas, one book. “The lips of the priest keep ...” “Holy brothers, callings ...” “Religion is pure ...” [unclear]. Exposition of the Lord's Passion, one book. “O most excellent God ...” “What is this which comes forth ...” “Who is wise, let him understand ...” “Every procession of secondary things ...” “One and the Most High ...” “We know that the Son of God has come ...” On the happiness of the soul, one book. “My soul desires ...” “May the glorious Father give to you ...” “Who will be able [to know] man ...” On the custody of the heart, one book. “As the Apostle says: Foolish ...” “Great wonders ...” “Thus God loved the world ...” “Beware lest you wish to imitate ...” “You shall adore the Lord your God ...” “He who has converted, shall have done sin ...” [unclear]. “The kings of the nations lord it over them ...” On the gravity of sin, one book. “I shall show you,” etc. “A question has been put to me ...” “The life of man is warfare ...” “Turn to the Lord God ...” “A nation without counsel ...” “Christ died for all ...” “The first man from the earth, earthly ...,” one book. On the progress of charity, “What the Lord God ...” “Loving wisdom, from ...” [unclear]. “One must always pray ...” “My thoughts ...” “All who believed were ...” “Zeal for your house ...” On the authority of the pope, one book. On the authority of the council, one book. “Freely you have received, freely ...” “May your money be with you in ...” “Let all things be done honorably ...” On the rules of life of Christians, one book. “Open to me, my sister ...” “A more excellent way [I show] to you ...” “No one putting his hand ...” “Take heed to yourselves ...” On the praises of the same, one book.

Abbot of Sponheim

On the visitation of cloistered persons, book I. On the life of canons, book I. On the discipline of scholars, book I. On the life of soldiers, book I. On virginity, book I. On the office of archdeacons, book I. On the governance of prelates, book I. On the life of nobles, book I. Dialogue between Christ and a prince, book I. On the government of the commonwealth, book I. Dialogue between Jesus and a boy, book I. On the life of widows, book I. On the life of married persons, book I. On the life of famous women, book I. On the office of merchants, book I. On the solitary life, book I. Against the property of monks, book I. Letters to princes, book I. Annotations on his own works, book I. Letters to various persons, book I. And many other works unseen by us. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1471, the fourth indiction, on the eleventh day of the month of March. He was buried, not without a great reputation for holiness, in the common cemetery of the brothers of the aforesaid house of Roermond. Finally, he reduced the books of John Cassian to an easier style for the sake of the simpler brothers; the preface to this work begins thus: Declaration, etc.

Bessarion, Greek by nation, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, commonly called the Cardinal of Nicaea, and patriarch of Constantinople, a man in every respect most learned, a philosopher and orator second to none in both languages. He wrote certain outstanding volumes of his genius, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with great glory. Among these the following are reported: Against Mark, bishop of Ephesus, who held wrong opinions, in the Greek manner, about the Holy Spirit in the Council of Florence. He wrote a distinguished and excellent work which he entitled:

Confutation, book I. In that: Thus I wish him to remain, book I. In praise of Plato’s philosophy, book II. Praises of his homeland, book III. To the Emperor of the Greeks, of consolation, book I. Several orations and letters. And certain other works. He also founded at Venice a distinguished library, most richly furnished with many books both Greek and Latin, over which Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a most learned man, of whom we shall speak later, was placed with no small stipend. At length, full of days, he died while on embassy to the Gauls, under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1473, the sixth indiction.

Johannes Hagen, otherwise de Indagine, German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of the Mount of the Holy Savior near Erfurt, prior at Eisenach and at Stettin, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and excellently instructed in canon law, distinguished in intellect, ready and provident in counsel. In plain speech he wrote many excellent volumes to princes, bishops, and other prelates of churches, having been questioned on various and diverse matters; of these I recall that few have come into our hands. For, as I have learned from the writings of a certain devout father of the same order, he published more than three hundred treatises; of all these I have seen and read only those which I have set down below. A distinguished work, which he entitled:

On the praise of poverty, book I. On the life of religious, book I. On the fall of religion, book I. On the life of young men, book I. On humility and pride, book I. On inner adornment, book I. On access to the new man, book I. On grace and free will, book I. On correction and the grace of God, book I. Cursed is the man who makes. As Aristo. Labor as a good [unclear]. The virgin thinks on the things of the Lord. On the office of a legate, book I. On the life and governance of curates, book I. On the governance of princes, book I. Dialogue between Christ and a princess, book I. Jesus embracing [unclear]. Because he loved chastity. The Lord God said, It is not. How great a multitude. Do not commit iniquity. Dialogue between Christ and a priest, book I. Of an apocalypse made to him, book I. To all princes. By religious and other [unclear]. Three conferences for chapters.

In praise of Plato’s philosophy, book II. To the Emperor of the Greeks, of consolation, book I. Several orations and letters. And certain other works. He also founded at Venice a distinguished library, most richly furnished with many books both Greek and Latin, over which Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a most learned man, of whom we shall speak later, was placed with no small stipend. At length, full of days, he died while on embassy to the Gauls, under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1473, the sixth indiction.

Johannes Hagen, otherwise de Indagine, German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of the Mount of the Holy Savior near Erfurt, prior at Eisenach and at Stettin, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and excellently instructed in canon law, distinguished in intellect, ready and provident in counsel. In plain speech he wrote many excellent volumes to princes, bishops, and other prelates of churches, having been questioned on various and diverse matters; of these I recall that few have come into our hands. For, as I have learned from the writings of a certain devout father of the same order, he published more than three hundred treatises; of all these I have seen and read only those which I have set down below. A distinguished work, which he entitled:

On the praise of poverty, book I. On the life of religious, book I. On the fall of religion, book I. On the life of young men, book I. On humility and pride, book I. On inner adornment, book I. On access to the new man, book I. On grace and free will, book I. On correction and the grace of God, book I. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for. The kingdom of heaven is like. How the city sits alone. I am a young man. I am the way, the truth. All the glory of the king’s daughter. Behold, I make new things. Not I alone, but grace. The righteous man shall correct me in. Of

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On Nature and Grace, one book. On Perseverance, one book. On Spirit, Body, and Soul, one book. On the Commands of Prelates, one book. On Charity, one book. On the Love of God, one book. On Meditation, one book. On the Inquiry into the Highest Good, one book. Against the Errors of the Bohemians, one book. To the Bishop of Ratisbon, against the same, four books. To the Margrave of Brandenburg, one book. To the University of Erfurt, one book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. On Avoiding Foreign Doctrines, one book. On Knowledge of Future Things, one book. On the Vision of Tundal, one book. On the Vision of Daniel, chapter 7. On the Apparition of a Certain Deceased Person, one book. On Future Prodigies, one book. On the Lament of the Solitary, one book. On the Crusade against Heretics, one book. On the Taking Away of the Bridegroom from the Church, one book. On the Time of the Schism, one book. On the Authority of the Pope in a Council, one book. On Ecclesiastical Power, one book. On Fraternal Correction, one book. On Little Children Not Baptized, one book. On a Judge Judging against Conscience, [one book?]. Against the Flagellants, one book. Whether One Is a Religious without Profession, one book. On Fasting on Thursday, one book. On Just and Unjust War, one book. On the Teaching of the Church, one book. On True and False Penitence, one book. On the Mode of Confessing, one book. On Hearing Confessions, one book. On the Spiritual Art of Memory, one book. On the Discernment of Thoughts, one book. On [true?] and False Penitence, one book. On Hearing Masses, one book. On the Spiritual Art of Memory, two books. On the Four Senses of Scripture, one book. On Contemplation, one book. On the Interdict, one book. Five Sermons at a Dedication, one book. To Rudolph, Bishop of Lavant, one book. On Communion under Both Kinds, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. On Kings, in the Fourfold Sense, one book. Finally, he composed elegant commentaries on many books of the Bible, and other treatises and solutions of questions, almost innumerable and distinguished. He flourished under Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

John, abbot of the monastery of Neuberg, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in canon law, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, wrote many and various little works of his talent, by which he transmitted to posterity, with glory, the memory of his most celebrated name. Of these the following are extant: a distinguished and notable work, entitled Concordance of the Bible and the Canons, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. God saw all the things that he had made. He who shall persevere. The apostle Paul, a chosen vessel. So let a man regard us. Strong as death is love. In the law of Moses, after many [unclear]. Happy the soul that humbly [unclear]. Great are you, Lord, and worthy of praise. Prayers in Christ Jesus. Most reverend in Christ. To the illustrious prince and lord. Sincere charity in the Lord. With the Spirit proving whether they are of God. Various and foreign [doctrines]. Announce what things are to come. Concerning the vision of Tundal. It has been asked concerning the things set forth. A certain woman, brought [unclear]. All things in measure, number [unclear]. Who will give to my head [unclear]. Concerning a crusade which [unclear]. In the name of our Lord Jesus. And because they do not want [unclear]. It has been doubted and asked. In the Gospel of Christ [unclear]. Likewise it is asked in fraternal [correction]. It has been doubted and asked. It is doubted whether it is lawful. Note concerning a just war. You are Peter, and upon [this rock]. The wise man says: Son, do all things [unclear]. In the name of Jesus Christ begins [unclear]. If we live by one spirit, by the spirit also [unclear]; Why do you think evil [unclear]. Do penance, [says] the apostle [unclear]. The royal prophet, Psalm [unclear]. Confess to one another. Remember the last things. In the name of Christ and of his [unclear]. This is eternal life. On the willows in the midst [unclear]. Solomon built [unclear]. On False Prophets, one book. Also Various Sermons, one book. In the beginning God created [unclear]. Look and lift up your heads.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Sermons on the saints, one book. In the beginning God created.

Letters and various questions. The rest that he composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Jacobus de Gruytrode, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of All the Apostles near Liege, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, outstanding in talent, sweet in speech. He wrote certain distinguished, devout little works, the reading of which is said not to be unprofitable for religious persons, lovers of their own salvation. Of these the following are reported.

On the True Virtues, three books. On the Seven Deadly Sins, one book.

On the Four Last Things, one book.

On the Life of the Lord Jesus, one book. A bundle of myrrh, beloved.

On Preparation before Mass, one book. On the Definition of the Name Monk, one book.

Meditations on the Passion of the Lord, one book.

A Lectionary by Month, one book. Eat, friends, drink.

Mirror of Prelates, one book. Mirror of Subjects, one book.

Mirror of Priests, one book. Mirror of Secular Men, one book.

Mirror of Old Age, one book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Monk, one book.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Prelate, one book. Deal with me, sweetest Jesus.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Old Man, one book. Do not be angry, I pray.

Colloquy of Jesus and the Hermit, one book. Colloquy of Jesus and the Disciple, one book.

Contemplation of Saint Mary, one book. You have wounded my heart.

Little Crown of Saint Mary.

Dialogue of the Crucified One and the Sinner, one book. Forgive, I pray, most gracious one.

Dialogue of Mary and the Sinner, one book. I have a word for you.

Another Dialogue of Mary and the Sinner.

On the Name of Jesus and Mary, one book. Meditations on the Compassion of Mary, one book.

Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Pontiffs.

Sermons on the Saints, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

And many other things. He died most devoutly under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1472, in the fifth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February.

Jacobus Zenus, a Venetian patrician, bishop of the church of Padua, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent, ready and circumspect in counsel, and distinguished by experience of many things. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Of these there is extant a most elegant work:

On the Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs, one book. And certain other things.

He died, however, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1477, and in the ninth indiction.

Guilhelmus Forleon, a Breton by nation, of the order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in eloquence, who in the Paris gymnasium, by teaching, disputing, and writing, earned great praise for his learning, published certain distinguished little works on the Scriptures. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work:

On the Sentences, one book. Various Questions.

And several other things, one book.

His former hearer and disciple was the most learned man, easily the foremost of the theologians of our age, Master Stephanus, called Brulefer, a Frenchman by nation, of the same order, who taught theology in the Paris convent; afterward, betaking himself to the observance of the order at Mainz in Germany, he began to lecture there on the Sentences, which he continued in the convent of Metz with great praise. This Guilhelmus, however, came to an end under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Albertus de Eybe, a German by nation, canon of the church of Bamberg, chamberlain of Pius II, supreme pontiff, a man zealous and learned in secular letters, and [unclear]. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which the following are extant. To Lord Johannes, duke of Bavaria, bishop of Munster and afterward primate of Magdeburg, a notable work entitled:

The Poetic Pearl, one book. You have very often desired, [unclear].

Likewise On the Matter of Marriage, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And

On Ecclesiastical Writers

And many other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Rodericus, bishop of Zamora, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote some little works of no contemptible authority, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen only one, which he entitled:

The Mirror of Human Life, two books: “Above all human...”

The rest I have not seen. He flourished in the times of Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Ambrosius Choriolanus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St Augustine, prior general, Roman by country, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and distinguished in knowledge of secular letters, excellent in talent, fluent in eloquence, learned and eloquent, wrote certain notable little works, by which he commended his name to immortality. Of these, however, only a few have come to my knowledge by reading; they follow below:

On the Rule of St Augustine, one book: “From the learned parent of all...” A Commendation of the Same Rule, one book: “After blessed Augustine...” On the Second Rule, one book: “Keen in talent, foremost in life...” On the Life of St Augustine, one book: “Very often, when near...” On the Praises of the Same, one book: “Most blessed father, they have been accustomed...” Various Orations, one book. He wrote also many other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Benedictus Stendel of Halle, a town of Saxony, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in talent and clear in speech, taught theology gloriously for many years in the school of Erfurt, and shone forth brightly, renowned both in life and in doctrine. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, from which he regularly lectured in the said university on the following:

On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. Various Sermons, one book. Different Collations, one book.

And certain other things in logic, philosophy, and the other scholastic studies and exercises. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1490.

Sifridus, titled bishop of Cyrene, of the Order of Preachers, German by nation, vicar in pontifical matters of Theodericus, archbishop of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, subtle in talent and clear in speech, an acute disputant and an outstanding preacher of the divine word, ready in counsel, distinguished in life, wrote certain little works worthy of reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are extant, addressed to the aforesaid Archbishop Theodericus:

On the Usury of the Jews, one book: “It is asked in the forum of conscience...” On Rents and Redemption, one book: “It was asked first whether...” Sermons and Collations, one book. Various Questions, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick and the Roman pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1476.

Godescalcus of Meschede, German by nation, Westphalian by country, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, keen in talent, distinguished in life, a profound doctor of most sacred theology, who for many years taught that science gloriously in the school of Erfurt and deserved great praise from all for his learning, wrote and lectured in the same university on certain notable little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, four books. Sermons and Collations, one book. Various Disputed Questions, one book. And many other things.

His brother Theodericus Gresmunt of Meschede, doctor of arts and medicine, a man most learned in every respect, still living, resides at Mainz; he too, among other things, composed an elegant treatise, On the Regimen of Health in Time of Pestilence. He has a son called by the name Theodericus, scarcely completing three lustra of age, whose admirable talent, and singular learning as well as eloquence, far surpass many of advanced age, even doctors. From him there is extant to me a notable book On the Seven Arts. He has also written, both to me and to others, almost

370

The Abbot of Sponheim

innumerable letters, on every kind of subject, most ornate, and various speeches displaying Ciceronian eloquence, so that, like another Adeodatus, formerly the son of the most holy Augustine, by his own talent, readiness in writing and arguing, and skill, he is an object of admiration and astonishment to many, even learned men. Godescalcus, however, was his father’s brother. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1470, and died before this decade.

STEPHAN HOEST of Ladenburg, formerly a canon of the church of Speyer, German by nation, a man learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and orator, keen in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in declaiming sermons to the people, since for some years he held the office of preacher in the castle of Heidelberg. He wrote works not to be despised, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant:

On the books of the Ethics, 10 books. Sermons of collation, 1 book. Certain other poems.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1461, in the fourth indiction.

BERNARD JUSTINIAN, a Venetian by homeland, a very celebrated philosopher and orator, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, who, on account of his singular grace in speaking, was held in esteem not only before his own Venetian senate, but also before the Roman pontiffs, cardinals, the other princes of Italy, and the senates of cities. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote of Lorenzo Giustiniani, patriarch of Venice, his maternal uncle:

His life and most holy manner of life, 1 book. Also Histories, 1 book. Several elegant speeches, 1 book. Letters and certain other things, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1470.

HENRY DE PIRO, German by nation, born from the city of Cologne, of the Carthusian order, professed of the house of Saint Barbara in the same city; before his entry into the order a subtle and famous doctor of both laws, and afterward also practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote certain excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

On the Institutes, 4 books. Annua te mihi [unclear]. Also To Novices, 1 book. Counsels in various cases, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 1 book. Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1490.

NICHOLAS DONIS, German by nation, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man studious and learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher and mathematician, a most vigilant finder and very sagacious restorer of Ptolemy’s Cosmography, outstanding in talent and clear in speech. He wrote volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a remarkable work, with new illustrations and tables most elegantly arranged and most diligently corrected:

On the Cosmography of Ptolemy, To Pope Paul II, 7 books. It does not escape me, blessed [father]. Also On Marvelous Places, 1 book. Since, as Augustine says. Various letters to different persons.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1490.

GEORGE OF PEUERBACH, German by nation, a man most skilled in the knowledge of secular letters, not ignorant of the holy Scriptures, easily the most brilliant philosopher and astronomer of his time, who in the university of Vienna publicly taught philosophy and the science of the stars for a long time; there, among countless other disciples, he instructed Johannes of Regiomontanus, afterward a most learned man. He wrote certain excellent works of a very penetrating talent. Of their number I have seen only:

New Theories of the Planets, 1 book. The sun has three spheres [unclear].

I have as yet seen nothing of the others. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the Roman pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1470.

DOMITIUS CALDERINUS, a Veronese by homeland, a most brilliant rhetorician, perfectly imbued with the disciplines of all the good arts, excellently skilled in Greek and Latin speech, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech. He wrote many excellent works in humane letters

On Ecclesiastical Writers

... little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are cited:

On Juvenal, one book. Two kinds of satires. On Suetonius, one book. On Naso's Ibis, one book. On Cicero's letters, one book. Against Broteus the grammarian, one book. It begins: "Would that, Helius and Marcus." Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations. And many other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, whose secretary he had been, in the year of the Lord 1477, indiction 10.

Johannes Tinctoris, German by nation, from Cologne, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, nobly learned in secular philosophy, acute in intellect, an outstanding disputant, who for a long time publicly taught theology in the gymnasium of Cologne, acquired immense praise for his learning. He wrote little works not to be despised, of which the following are cited:

Disagreements of Thomas and Scotus, one book. It begins: "He began to agree in..." Questions on the Sentences, one book. Also various conferences. And certain other things. He flourished in the aforesaid gymnasium under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Nicolaus Perotus of Sassoferrato, bishop of Siponto, a man most learned in the divine writings and second to none in his time in secular letters, an outstanding theologian and a most eloquent rhetorician, sharp in intellect and distinguished in life, wrote certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survives a notable work, divided into two volumes, on the poet Marcus Valerius Martial, very beautifully comprising all the elegance, method, and exposition of Latin speech; he entitled it A Volume of Commentaries on the Latin Language, or, as it is commonly called,

Cornucopia, one book. On the Kinds of Metres, one book. On the Education of Boys, one book. It begins: "The beard, he flatters." Various orations and letters.

He is said besides to have written many other things, both in divine letters and in humane letters, and to have translated not a few works from Greek into Latin, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the Roman pontiffs Pius and Paul, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Antonius Roselus, Tuscan by nation, an eminent professor of both laws, a most celebrated interpreter, and greatly adorned with the discipline of the other good arts, outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech, who taught law for many years in the gymnasium of Padua, wrote many distinguished little works, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. But I do not remember ever having seen any of them anywhere. His notable work is, however, cited:

On the Monarchy of the World, one book. Various treatises on the laws. And many other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in vigorous old age, and was buried at Padua, in the year of the Lord 1467, indiction 15.

Johannes Beetz, German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man zealous and learned in divine writings, not ignorant of secular literature, an excellent theologian, a subtle philosopher, sharp in intellect, distinguished in life, an outstanding disputant of questions, notable in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain distinguished little works. Of these the following are cited:

On Paul's Epistle to the Romans, one book. A Preceptory of the Divine Law, one book. It begins: "Sacred Scripture of the divine..." On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Various disputed questions, one book.

He published besides some other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV in his convent at [Tenensi?], in the year of the Lord 1476, indiction 9, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Bartholomaeus Cepolla, of Verona by nation, a most celebrated jurist, a notable cultivator of the secular literature of other disciplines, who in the gymnasium of Padua, by lecturing, disputing, and writing in the ordinary course, acquired great praise for his learning, wrote many distinguished little works, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives a truly most subtle work, which he entitled...

The Abbot of Sponheim

Precautions of law in civil cases, one book. On simulated contracts, one book. On the farms of country people, one book. And very many other things. He died in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1477, in the tenth indiction.

Johannes of Regiomonte, a German by nation, formerly a pupil of the astronomer Georgius Burbachius, not inferior to Anaximander of Miletus or Archimedes of Syracuse, most learned in Greek and Latin eloquence, the glory of the Germans, was granted a perpetual stipend on account of astronomy and the other mathematical disciplines by Matthias, king of Pannonia, and by the council and citizens of Nuremberg; he obtained great praise for his learning not only among his own Germans, but also among the Italians and the French. For, when he had been summoned to Rome by Sixtus, the supreme pontiff, to correct the Dionysian computation of Easter, while he was preparing many things for posterity, he died of a destructive disease, not without the very great loss of scholars. He wrote certain excellent little works, of which the following are extant.

A very beautiful Calendar, one book. Ephemerides, that is, [a diary?], one book. Against Gerard of Cremona, one book. After we put forth the index, Of letters and orations, one book. And very many other things.

He died at Rome under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476, in the ninth indiction.

Gerardus of Elten, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, sharp in intellect and distinguished in life. After he had taught theology gloriously for many years in the school of Cologne, holding the vanities of the world in contempt, in his old age he entered the order of preachers for the love of God in the same city of Agrippina, and soon was appointed inquisitor and exterminator of heretical depravity. Among other things, as they report, he wrote:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Disputed Questions, one book. Sermons and collations, one book. Various things also in philosophy, one book. And very many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and the supreme pontiff Sixtus IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1475.

Alexander Tartagnus of Imola, a jurist, studious and learned, and well experienced also in the other institutions of secular disciplines, excellent in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote, for the use of those who keep watch in the study of both laws, certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. On the Clementines also, one book. On the Code also, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books. On the New Digest, twelve books. On the Infortiatum, fourteen books. And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Johannes Soreth, a Norman by nation, the twenty-fifth prior general of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, sweet and dear in eloquence, devout in life and conduct, and singularly religious and holy; the honor, glory, splendor, and reformer of the Carmelite order, such as our ages have rarely seen and future ages will see more rarely; wholly given to God, wholly intent on reading and prayer, despiser of the world, lover, rule, and mirror of monastic conduct, imitator of angelic purity, guardian of virtues, most bitter enemy of vices, wrote many excellent little works of his intellect worthy of commendation, of which the following are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book. On the rule of his order, one book. A larger commentary on the same, one book. He arranged the Constitutions, one book. He wrote also very many other things.

He died at Angers under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the third indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

Theodorus Gaza of Thessalonica, a man excellently learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the holy Scriptures, most learned in Greek and Latin, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote many little works and translated many things from Greek into Latin, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of his own writings nothing anywhere has come to the knowledge of our reading; but of the translated works there are reported:

Theophira-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Theophrastus, On Plants, one book. Aristotle, Problems, one book. The same, On Animals, one book. And certain other things. He died at Rome under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction.

John de Lutria, German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in sacred Scripture, and excellently trained in scholastic philosophy, keen in intellect, illustrious in life, and a very celebrated preacher of sermons, first taught theology gloriously in the university of Erfurt, and afterward energetically carried out the office of preacher in the church of Mainz. He wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books; various sermons, one book; Disputed Questions, one book; and certain works in philosophy, one book. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction.

[Alanus?] de Rupe, German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in sacred Scripture, of the highest reputation in delivering sermons to the people, devoted to God in life and conduct, and a special lover of the blessed Mary ever virgin and a venerable promoter of her rosary and service; by her also he several times merited to be refreshed with the singular gift of heavenly consolation, and now to be sustained in eternal felicity. Among other works of his talent he wrote: Compendium of the Marian Psalter, one book, beginning, 'Because Catholic truth ...'; On the Miracles of the Rosary, one book, beginning, 'Although beautiful praise [unclear]'; likewise various sermons, one book; and certain other things. He died in his convent at Zwolle under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1474, in the seventh indiction, on the vigil of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin Mary. He recalled to the minds and practices of men her rosary and the psalter commemorative of Christ's Passion, which had long since been neglected; in whose honor [unclear]. By fruitfully practicing these, he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of their number the following are extant: On the Monochord, one book, beginning, 'Since, as a certain wise man ...'; On the Method of Singing Well, one book, beginning, 'For the benefit of the whole clergy ...'; On the Ending of the Collects, one book, beginning, 'Although many concerning ...'; many and various sermons, one book; and certain other works. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1470, under Pope Sixtus IV, under whom he also died.

Conradus de Zabernia, German by nation, a man devoted to and practiced in sacred Scripture, and not ignorant of secular literature, especially music, teachable in intellect and exemplary in life, clear and devout in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, in plain speech, certain little works and volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity; of these the following are reported: On the Seven Deadly Sins, one book.

Laurentius Calcaneus of Brescia, a noble man, a knight with the golden spur, and a very celebrated doctor of laws, a philosopher and most lucid historian, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, and a most acute disputant of questions. He wrote certain distinguished works by which he transmitted his name to posterity; among them the following are reported: On the Holy Conception of Mary, one book; also many legal opinions, one book; and certain other small works. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction.

John of Dorsten, German by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man devoted to and learned in sacred Scripture, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, and sufficiently fit for disputing and disentangling questions of Scripture; also of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, who was held in esteem for teaching and preaching in the university of Erfurt. He wrote little works by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these are reported: sermons for the temporal cycle, one book; sermons on the saints, one book.

Angelus Saxo of Brunswick, German by nation, a man learned in sacred Scripture [unclear], under Pope [Sixtus] IV, in the year of the Lord 1475.

The Abbot of Sponheim, 374. Very learned, and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, keen in intellect, distinguished in life, and of a most celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people, since after attaining the mastership of teaching in the gymnasium of Erfurt he held the office of preacher at Mainz for a long time. Among other things he wrote a certain notable work: Various Sermons, one book; Diverse Questions, one book; and certain other things. He died at Strasbourg, buried in the monastery of the Penitents, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1481, indiction 14.

Franciscus Philelfus, born from the ancient town of Tolentino, golden knight and poet laureate, a most celebrated philosopher and orator, once in his youth at Venice a hearer of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, from whom he learned Greek and Latin eloquence most perfectly; a man so studious, and so indefatigable a lover and cultivator of the good arts, that, like another Pliny, amid continual occupations of wars he was always either reading something to himself or dictating to others. For he wrote in both languages, in prose as well as verse, many distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his most celebrated talent. Of these there are extant: Eutyphron, On Piety, one book; On Moral Discipline, two books; Life of Pope Nicholas V, one book, “Since I desire something,” one book; “Of how many laws [unclear],” nine books; Satires in the same meter, ten books; Lyrics in every kind of meter, six books; “If I judged it possible to be done,” sixteen books; “How I regarded nothing among myself,” four books; in Greek verses, by odes, two books; also On Exile, three books. Besides, he translated many things into Latin, of which the following are reported: Aristotle’s Rhetoric to King Alexander, one book; from Plato, [unclear] books; Hippocrates, On Winds and the Passions of the Body, two books; from Plutarch, the lives of Theseus and Galba and Otho. Apophthegms [unclear]. He was his hearer and son-in-law; and when he had become most learned from him, first among the Venetians, afterward among the Florentines, the Sienese, the Bolognese, and finally the Milanese, under four dukes and with an annual pension, he taught Greek and Latin letters to very many with distinction. He died at Bologna, ninety years old and poor, indeed as a philosopher and Christian, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus, in the year of the Lord 1481, indiction 14, in the year after the death of his son Marius. Of the Art of Rhetoric, one book; “I had already decided long since,” one book; Letters to Various Persons, three books; elegant Orations; songs and rhythms. But he also composed many other things in meter and prose, which have not reached me. He died at Mantua under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480, indiction 13.

Theodericus de Herxen, a German by nation, visitor of the order of the brothers, clerics living in common, a devout man, and studious and learned in the divine scriptures, ready in intellect, clear in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, wrote for the edification of simple brothers many devout volumes, with which, usefully exercising his talent, he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Whole Psalter, one book; On the Lord’s Prayer, one book; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; On the Desire of Dying, one book; and many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476.

Dominicus de Dominicis, a Venetian by homeland, first bishop of Torcello and afterward bishop of Brescia, and apostolic referendary, a man learned in the divine scriptures, in

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and most learned in secular letters, excellently adorned with philosophy, dialectic, astronomy, and eloquence; on account of his great virtues he was held in high esteem by the Roman pontiffs Pius, Paul, and Sixtus, and often fulfilled the office of envoy. He wrote several small works of excellent talent, but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. The following elegant works of his, however, are reported:

Orations on various subjects, one book. Also Various Sermons, two books. And many treatises. He died at Brescia, under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixtieth year of his age.

Ludovicus Donatus, a Venetian patrician and bishop of Bergamo, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy, also distinguished for piety, religion, clemency, and gentleness, subtle in talent and renowned in speech, wrote certain lucid small works by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these he deserved to see nothing anywhere. His distinguished work to Paul II is reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Also Various Orations, one book.

He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction. He was buried in the church of Saint Vincent the martyr.

Conradus of Rodenberg, German by nation, abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Rheingau, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a devout and learned man, and an outstanding guardian and lover of regular observance, who previously for many years held the office of prior at Saint Matthias the Apostle in Trier and Saint Martin in Cologne. Since he was a most ardent lover of the blessed Mary ever virgin, he wrote in her honor, in plain discourse, a very celebrated volume, taking the material of praise from each of her members, under the figure of a cluster of grapes, to which he gave the most fitting title:

On the Vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, one book. Its foundations are in the mountains. The Exercise of Novices, one book. Consider your calling, [unclear]. On Preparation before Mass, one book. Our Lord Jesus Christ. On the Ruin of the Order, an oration, one book. The crown of the head has fallen. Catch for us the little foxes. On [unclear], an oration, one book. Blessed is the servant whom [unclear]. On Pastoral Care, an oration, one book. To the thresholds of blessed Peter. And various conferences in chapters.

He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Innocent VIII, pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. He was buried in the right apse of the choir, before the altar of Saint Benedict, toward the ambulatory.

Stephanus of Gaeta, a Neapolitan, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, professor of both laws, a most learned interpreter, acute in talent, well suited for disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures, renowned and orderly in speech, wrote to Giovanni Battista de Bentevogli of Sassoferrato, counsellor of Ferdinand, king of Sicily, a very celebrated work:

On the Sacraments, two books. To the thresholds of blessed Peter.

And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Georgius Molitoris of Nuremberg, German by nation, a man long exercised in the divine Scriptures by study, an outstanding doctor, and not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, keen in talent, distinguished in life, publicly taught theology for many years in the gymnasium at Erfurt and won great praise for his learning. He wrote certain distinguished small works of his talent, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, two books. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Many Sermons, one book. Various Questions.

And many other things. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Bartholomaeus, surnamed Platina, by homeland a Cremonese, formerly an apostolic abbreviator, a man most learned in every respect, a most celebrated philosopher and rhetor, subtle and forceful in talent, eloquent in speech, pleasing, constant and strong in spirit, suffered many calamities from Pope Paul II, so that, stripped of all goods and dignity, after being suspended on the rack he was most cruelly thrust into prison and detained until the death of that Paul. Soon freed by Sixtus, in imitation of Eutrandus Ti-

376 The Abbot of Sponheim [unclear] deacon, having suffered similar things from Berengarius, king of Italy, not without wit noted Paul’s morals and vices through the Antipodosium. For he wrote to Pope Sixtus IV: On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, one book; On the Natures of Things, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; and certain other works. He died at Rome of plague, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1481, indiction 14.

Nicolaus of Wachenheim, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability and distinguished in eloquence, who in the Heidelberg school for almost fifty years, by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, was held in the highest esteem as a prince among theologians, wrote some works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended the memory of his name even to posterity. Of these few have come to me: Questions on the Sentences, one book; many sermons, one book; several conferences and orations, one book; Quia approbante sacri [unclear]; and certain other works. He flourished at Heidelberg under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1470. Already very old, he died under Pope Sixtus IV, about seven years before this.

Michael of Milan, of the Order of Friars Minor, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, for the use of those who devote themselves to preaching, works not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these there are extant: sermons on the season, one book; sermons on the saints, one book; sermons through Advent, one book; sermons on penance, beginning Per quod [unclear], one book; sermons on sins, one book; sermons on the Ten Commandments, one book; and certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480, and died under Pope Innocent VIII.

Sixtus IV, pope, Ligurian by nation, born in the maritime city of Savona, previously called Franciscus, minister general of the Order of Friars, sat after Paul II in the chair of Peter for thirteen years. He was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and an excellent disputant, a lover of the clergy, a promoter of religious, and singular in beneficence, especially toward those whom a life of observance commended. When Pope Paul once heard him disputing, he admired him so greatly that he made him worthy of the honor of the cardinalate. Before his pontificate he wrote certain excellent little works. Among these the following are reported: On Future Contingents, one book; On the Power of God, one book; On the Blood of Christ, one book; and certain other works. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1474, indiction 2.

Johannes Consobrinus, Portuguese by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular literature and canon law, outstanding in ability, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, first in England and then in Portugal gave great and effective barkings against the enemies of the faith. He rejected and refuted very many heresies and errors by disputing, preaching, and writing. At the request of the provost of the royal college of Saint Mary of Amhten [unclear] in England, he wrote a distinguished tripartite work on contracts and exchanges, which he entitled On Commutative Justice, two books; various sermons, one book; and certain other works. He shortened the Conflatum of Franciscus Maro into a pleasing compendium. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1475, and under Pope Sixtus IV died at Lisbon, poisoned for the faith.

Henricus, surnamed Prudens, of the Order of Carthusians, prior of the house of the Valley near Bruges in Flanders, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in ability, devout in life and conduct and singularly devoted to God, wrote for the instruction of religious certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work, most suited to devotion, divided into three parts according to the differences of states, of beginners and of the perfect, in the manner of a dialogue, in which speakers are introduced: an angel and a monk, Jesus and the heavenly Father, Mary, the loving mother-in-law [unclear] of holy souls. He entitled it Tetra-

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

A Tetralogue of devotion, three books. And certain other things. He died in the new [monastery?] of Saint Sophia of Constantinople near Buscunducis, where for some years he held the office of prior, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Franciscus Diedus, a noble Venetian patrician, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician, distinguished for learning and eloquence, a very celebrated interpreter of pontifical and civil law, and an indefatigable lover and guardian of the Venetian republic, wrote certain excellent little works both in verse and prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are reported: The History of Saint Roch the Confessor, one book; Orations and various letters. And certain other things. He died at Verona under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the first indiction.

Rudolphus Agricola of Groningen, by nation a Frisian, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, and not ignorant of the Hebrew language, excellent in ability, eloquent in speech, formerly teacher of Johannes Camerarius of Dalberg, bishop of Worms and a most learned man, easily obtained the first place among all the doctors, even of whatever faculty, by teaching and writing in the Heidelberg gymnasium. He wrote certain most excellent little works of his genius, by which he consecrated his name to immortality and left it to posterity. Of these the following are extant: Life of Francesco Petrarca, one book; Anna, parent of the highest [unclear], three books; various letters and orations, [unclear] books.

Rudolphus Agricola of Groningen, by nation a Frisian, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in speeches, a very celebrated rhetorician and poet, skilled in Greek and Latin, not ignorant of the Hebrew language, [unclear] philosopher, wrote both in verse and prose certain excellent little works, and [unclear] divine devotion, and by writing the first part in this manner: 1. [unclear]. 2. [unclear]. 3. [unclear]. 4. [unclear]. 5. [unclear]. 6. [unclear]. 7. [unclear]. 8. [unclear]. 9. [unclear]. 10. [unclear]. 11. [unclear]. 12. [unclear]. 13. [unclear]. 14. [unclear]. 15. [unclear]. 16. [unclear]. 17. [unclear]. 18. [unclear]. 19. [unclear]. 20. [unclear]. 21. [unclear]. 22. [unclear]. 23. [unclear]. 24. [unclear]. 25. [unclear]. 26. [unclear]. 27. [unclear]. 28. [unclear]. 29. [unclear]. 30. [unclear]. 31. [unclear]. 32. [unclear]. 33. [unclear]. 34. [unclear]. 35. [unclear]. 36. [unclear]. 37. [unclear]. 38. [unclear]. 39. [unclear]. 40. [unclear]. 41. [unclear]. 42. [unclear]. 43. [unclear]. 44. [unclear]. 45. [unclear]. 46. [unclear]. 47. [unclear]. 48. [unclear]. 49. [unclear]. 50. [unclear]. 51. [unclear]. 52. [unclear]. 53. [unclear]. 54. [unclear]. 55. [unclear]. 56. [unclear]. 57. [unclear]. 58. [unclear]. 59. [unclear]. 60. [unclear]. 61. [unclear]. 62. [unclear]. 63. [unclear]. 64. [unclear]. 65. [unclear]. 66. [unclear]. 67. [unclear]. 68. [unclear]. 69. [unclear]. 70. [unclear]. 71. [unclear]. 72. [unclear]. 73. [unclear]. 74. [unclear]. 75. [unclear]. 76. [unclear]. 77. [unclear]. 78. [unclear]. 79. [unclear]. 80. [unclear]. 81. [unclear]. 82. [unclear]. 83. [unclear]. 84. [unclear]. 85. [unclear]. 86. [unclear]. 87. [unclear]. 88. [unclear]. 89. [unclear]. 90. [unclear]. 91. [unclear]. 92. [unclear]. 93. [unclear]. 94. [unclear]. 95. [unclear]. 96. [unclear]. 97. [unclear]. 98. [unclear]. 99. [unclear]. 100. [unclear]. Meditations on the Life of Christ, one book. On the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary, one treatise.

378 The Abbot of Sponheim

On the instruction of novices, one treatise. A dialogue between Jesus and Mary, one treatise. A dialogue on exercises, namely between Saint Margaret and her servant, one treatise. Another dialogue between the same on the cross, one treatise. On the commendation of charity, one treatise. Charity, excellence. On holy humility in the form of a [reason?], one treatise. Humility of the perfect. Again on humility, one treatise. Most dear brothers, humility. Chronicle of the house of the Carthusians in Basel, one treatise.

He happily departed from this life under Frederick III, Roman Emperor, in the year of the Lord 1487.

Jodocus de Calve, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland, a man long practiced in the divine Scriptures through lengthy study, and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy, ready and forceful in intellect, was held in esteem for many years in the Heidelberg school by lecturing and preaching; there also, according to custom, he for some time held the office of preacher in the church of the Holy Spirit. He wrote, as they say, certain treatises not to be rejected, but they have not come to the notice of my reading. There are extant from him on various subjects:

Various sermons, two books. Vocabulary for preachers, two books.

And various treatises. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And under Pope Innocent VIII he died three years ago.

Nicolaus of Kreuznach, a German by nation, from the diocese of Mainz and the county of Sponheim, a man most learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life, an acute disputant and an excellent declaimer of sermons, publicly taught theology for many years in the school of Vienna, and there obtained great praise and reward for his learning both among the scholastics and from Emperor Frederick III. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, two books. Various sermons, two books. Many collations and orations, two books. On the conception of Saint Mary, two books.

And very many other things, which, since he concealed them up to his death, have not yet been able to come to the notice of my reading, though nevertheless they are to come day by day. He died at Vienna in Austria under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, indiction 9.

Petrus Scotus, a German by nation, from Strasbourg by homeland, canon of Saint Peter there, a man practiced in the divine writings, most learned in both laws, and very learned in the other humane arts, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, certain chaste and most elegant little works by which he commended himself to posterity. On Saints John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and John Chrysostom he wrote a beautiful and delightful work:

In elegiac verse, two books. John Gerson [unclear]. Most elegant letters, two books.

Moreover he composed poems, both various and not opposed to the compunction of the reader, but very aptly and suitably fitted to it, in various kinds of meters. He died at Strasbourg and was buried in the church of Saint Peter, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, indiction 9, in the thirty-first year of his age. Being made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many times, and he was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding.

Nicasius de Voerda, of Mechelen, a German by nation, a Brabanter by homeland, deprived of his eyes from the third year of his age, and for that reason naturally altogether ignorant even of all letters, presented, as it were, a great miracle in our time, a second Didymus of Alexandria, when he became most learned in every doctrine and science, both divine and human. For in the school of Cologne, where he also died, he publicly taught law; the books of both laws, which he had never seen, he learned by hearing, retained in his mind, and recited openly. In the university of Louvain he first received the degree of master in arts; afterwards he directed schools for some time in Mechelen; then, having returned to Louvain, in [unclear] theology he was appointed licentiate and, by a singular apostolic dispensation, was ordained priest. He preached publicly, heard confessions, ministered at the altar, and recited the Gospel from [unclear] before everyone, using his mind in place of a book; only he did not celebrate the divine offices at the altar by himself. Finally, in the Academy of Cologne, by the consent of all the doctors, he was made doctor of canon law, and also a cautious interpreter of the imperial laws. He published a very celebrated work, which he read extraordinarily in the same university of Cologne, with many taking it down, On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Institutes, 2 books. “Because those things which well in...” On the Sentences, [4?] books. Various sermons, 1 book. Various questions. He wrote to me certain rather elegant letters, in one of which, quite copious, he wove together the whole story of his fortune; and, when formerly questioned by me, he humbly confessed that he had composed the aforesaid little works. He died at Cologne and was buried in the major church, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1492, in the tenth indiction, on 26 August.
