Christophorus Porsena, a Roman, prior of Saint Albina in the City, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint William, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, highly skilled in the Greek and Latin tongues, since from early youth he drank in those letters in Greece itself and under Greek teachers, so that he seemed to have been born from Greece; subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote, among other things:

Letters to various persons, 1 book. And many other things.

He translated into Latin Origen against the philosopher Celsus, eight books, for Pope Sixtus IV; also the moral sermons of Saint John Chrysostom, twenty-five in number, which he dedicated to Marco Barbo, cardinal of St Mark. But he also converted certain little works of Theophylact, archbishop of Bulgaria, together with other very fine works, and gave them to be read by Latins. He died at Rome, carried off by plague, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1486, in the fourth indiction.

Hermolaus Barbarus, Venetian by nation, patrician by birth, archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, and finally cardinal-bishop of the sacred Roman Church, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, poet, astronomer, and geometer, highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout and distinguished in life and conduct, and most worthy of every ecclesiastical honor, applying zeal and labor from youth to good letters and holy morals, became so great and of such quality that he left no second to himself. Beginning to write from the eighteenth year of his age, he composed many most elegant little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

A very beautiful work, 2 books. [unclear] On celibacy, 1 book. “Because his lucubrations...” Plinian Corrections, 1 book. On the married state, in meter, 1 book. Against the barbarian philosophers, 1 book. The agreement of astronomy and medicine, 1 book. Questions of Geometry, 1 book. Compendium of Philosophy, 1 book. Precepts for writing history, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Compendium of Galen, 1 book. More than twelve poems, 1 book. Multiple orations, 1 book.

And many other things. The Plinian Corrections is a large work, which he began as legate at Rome and completed as patriarch; he dedicated it to Pope Alexander VI, and in it he healed almost five thousand wounds of copyists. When once, in the year of the Lord ’86, he was passing through Cologne on his way to Mainz, at the request of Theoderic Flas of Neuss, a physician, he composed a little book on how much astronomy agrees with medicine. To Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, the historian, he published a book on the precepts of writing history. He interpreted Aristotle’s Rhetoric and the whole Dialectic, and also Dioscorides; he composed elegies, letters, and metrical orations, up to twelve thousand verses, as we have said. He translated into Latin the responsive treatise of the patriarch of Constantinople on the Catholic faith, to the questions of Mehmed, the great Turk. Also Plutarch on Isis and Osiris, and the same author’s Why the Oracles Ceased. To Arnold Bostius, Carmelite of Ghent, once a little work of Dionysius the Areopagite. He translated many other things as well. His work On the Married State contains about six hundred verses, in which he most elegantly disputes whether it is expedient for a wise man to take a wife, concluding that it is not. He died in the year of the Lord 1493, in the thirty-ninth year of his age, in the eleventh indiction.

Junianus Maius, a Parthenopean, Neapolitan, certainly a man most devoted to secular letters and exceptionally learned, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant a large and notable volume addressed to Henry, archbishop of Acerenza, confessor of Ferdinand, king of Naples, and principally to the same king; gathering it from the books of the ancients, he entitled it

The Abbot of Sponheim

On the propriety of the words of the ancients, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I am uncertain whether he is still alive.

Benedict Capra, of Perugia, a man most celebrated for his learning in both laws, well practiced both in the divine Scriptures and in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in intellect and an outstanding disputant, distinguished also by experience of many ancient and new matters, publicly taught law for a long time in the Perugian university and acquired a great reputation for his learning. Among other things he wrote:

On the Decretals, five books. Also several Legal Opinions, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480.

John Andreas, bishop of Aleria, secretary of the apostolic library, formerly a companion of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a jurist and a most eloquent orator, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct, skilled in both Greek and Latin speech, wrote certain little works of no slight authority, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Among their number the following are given:

On the Fourth Book of the Decretals, one book. On the Use of Fiefs, one book. On Appeals, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And very many other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1493, in the eleventh indiction.

John Campeius of Bologna, a most celebrated jurist and not moderately learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, publicly taught law for a long time in the university of Bologna; there, by instructing many very distinguished pupils, he gained great fruit and praise for his knowledge. In that faculty he wrote many excellent commentaries and treatises, as is reported, by which he commended his name to posterity. But none of them has come into our hands. There is reported to be by him an outstanding Treatise on Dowry, one book; On the Conception of Saint Mary, “With no slight grief.” And very fine Legal Opinions, with many other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484. And I do not know whether he is still surviving.

Dominic Bolanus, a Venetian by nation, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician not to be despised, keen and forceful in intellect, composed in speech, published some distinguished little works of his talent, in which he showed himself a devout and faithful worshipper of the Christian name and commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable little work against the detractors of Mary’s purity, which he dedicated to Niccolò Marcello, the seventy-first doge of the Venetians.

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished at Venice under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord [1480?]. I hear that he is still regarded as surviving.

Francis Niger, a Venetian priest, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, a learned professor of the arts and of philosophy, a poet and no trifling orator, excellent in intellect and fluent in speech, wrote various little works of his talent, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a work not to be despised, but to be extolled with great praises, addressed to Leonardo Botta, a Milanese knight:

Entitled Grammar, one book. “From Annaeus Seneca [unclear].” Letters by him are reported, and certain other things.

He flourished at Venice under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. I do not know whether he is still surviving.

Jacob de Stralen, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, who taught theology for many years in the university of Cologne, earned from all great praises for his learning. He wrote many excellent little works, various lectures, and questions:

On the Apocalypse of John, one book. “Jacob saw in sleep.” On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished in Cologne under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490, a very old man, being about eighty years of age. And I believe him still to be alive.

Marsilius Ficinus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by native land, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, highly skilled in both languages, the unique glory, ornament, and crown of Platonic theology, wrote many distinguished little works in prose, in which he showed to posterity the vein of his excellent talent. Of these the following are reported:

A Notable Theology, one book, beginning [unclear]. On Intellect and Intelligence, one book. On Plato’s Symposium, one book, beginning “Plato, chief of philosophers...” Letters, several books.

And many others. From Greek, moreover, he translated many things into Latin. For Pietro de’ Medici of Florence he translated fifty-six treatises of Plato. Also Hermes Trismegistus, On the Power and Wisdom of God. The book of Xenocrates the Platonist On Death, for the same Pietro de’ Medici. For Giovanni Cavalcanti he translated the little works of Speusippus, Alcinous, and Pythagoras. For the same man, the book of Alcinous the Platonist On the Doctrine of Plato. In addition he translated and wrote very many other things which have by no means come to our knowledge through reading. He flourished at Florence under Emperor Frederick III and under Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII, Roman pontiffs, in the year of the Lord 1486. And I believe him still to be among the living.

Rupertus of Liccio, bishop of Aquila, a city of the Marsi or Abruzzi, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, sweet and orderly in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons and famous throughout the whole Christian world, who by word and example converted many from iniquity, wrote for the edification of readers, and especially of preachers of the divine word, certain distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported:

Sermons on the Season, one book, beginning “The night has passed,” etc., words. On the Praises of the Saints, one book, beginning “Let not the wise man glory in...” On Penance through Lent, one book, beginning “There are many...” etc., “on account of...” On Sin also, one book. And certain others.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent, in the year of the Lord 1486. I do not know whether he is still alive.

Johannes Pfeffer of Widenberg, a German by nation, an East Franconian by native land, a man learned by long study in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in talent, devout, gentle, and distinguished in life and conduct, who, sent from the University of Heidelberg, adorned the beginning of the Freiburg academy by his learning, where now for very many years he has gloriously taught theology and has properly instructed many of his hearers, wrote certain distinguished little works, of which there is extant a notable work on the epistles of Paul, which he marked out after it had been read publicly:

Priestly Directory, one book, beginning “Concerning the reading of the epistles...”

And many others. He was still flourishing among the living under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1490. He may still be alive.

Johannes Britannicus, born at Palazzolo, a town in the territory of Brescia, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a famous philosopher, distinguished poet, and clear rhetorician, who among his own Brescian people is today held in esteem, and whom he renders daily more illustrious by inestimable learning, doctrine, and writings, wrote many and various works, by which he made his name known to posterity and venerable to those now living. Of these the following are reported: a very celebrated work of commentaries:

On Persius, one book. On Statius also, one book. On Ovid’s Metamorphoses, one book. Various letters also.

And many others. He flourishes in the city of Brescia and composes various little works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Baptista of Ferrara, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular literature, outstanding in verse and prose, skilled in both languages, of very celebrated and almost divine talent in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made himself useful to those now living and known to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a most lucid work of histories from the times of Christ down to us, which he entitled

382 The Abbot of Sponheim Florida, one book. Chronicles of his order, one book. On the Fall of the Roman Empire, one book. On Mount Sinai, one book. Life of Mechtild, three books. Chronicle of Ferraria, one book. Various sermons, three books.

He has published very many and diverse epigrams, which we hope are to be made public daily. He also translated from Greek into Latin several sermons of blessed John Chrysostom, and many other things unknown to us. He is still living at Ferraria and is writing various works under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Petrus Brutus, a Venetian by nation, bishop of Cathara, a man certainly most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, who for the confirmation of the Christian faith carried through many contests of disputation against the faithless Jews, always as victor. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, to the senate of Vicenza, a very celebrated and notable work, abundantly furnished with the authorities of the holy Scriptures.

Against the Jews, one book, beginning: “As I, reading many [unclear].”

And certain other works. He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1485. And I do not know whether he is still living.

Hubertinus, cleric of Crescentino, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished poet, and most skilled in both languages, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, who in the very celebrated academy of Pavia for seven years read publicly, with the attention and profit of his hearers, on a stipend. He wrote many distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, of which the following are extant.

On the Letters of Cicero, sixteen books, beginning: “The letters of this volume...” On the Offices of the same, three books. On the Metamorphoses of Naso, one book. Also one book of letters. Many poems, one book.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I do not know whether he is still living.

Guilhelmus of Aachen, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in eloquence, distinguished in life and conduct, who formerly held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many commendable little works, by which he commends his memory to posterity. Of these he read certain works publicly in the academy of Erfurt, with the attention and praise of all. He wrote:

On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Canon of the Mass, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book, beginning: “Jesus handed over willingly...” Disputed Questions, one book. Itinerary of the Holy Land, one book. Various sermons, one book. And several other works.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord [1490?] 1485. And I believe that he is still living.

Johannes de Lapide, a German by nation, a monk of the Carthusian order of the house of Basel, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct. Formerly, having obtained the mastership in the faculty of arts in the academy of Paris, he ruled in the same for several years, and, diligently pursuing the study of sacred letters by teaching, reading, and disputing, he deserved to be adorned with the doctoral dignity in the school of theologians. He first brought to the university of Basel the doctrine of those Parisians who are called Realists, and there planted, strengthened, and enlarged it. He was also one of the chief initiators and authors of the study at Tübingen. Finally, after freely resigning several benefices, he was called to a canonry and to the office of preaching in the notable church of Basel, and at last, after a few years had passed, leaving everything for the love of Christ, he put on the habit of the holy Carthusian order. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he made himself useful to the present and memorable to the future. A copy of only a few of these has come to us.

Introduction to Grammar, one book, beginning: “Since grammati...” Dialogue on the Art of Punctuation, one book, beginning: “The disciple, greetings...” On Exponible Propositions, one treatise, beginning: “As by a young man...” On

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the art of dissolving sophistical arguments, one treatise. Explanation of all the books of Aristotle's Logic, one book. Explanation of the books of the same author's Physics, one book. Explanation of the six books of the same author's Metaphysics, one book. On the things required for a worthy priest, one treatise. A resolution of doubts occurring concerning the Mass, one treatise. A summary of the Passion of Jesus Christ, one treatise. On the Ascension of the Lord, among the sermons of Meffret, one sermon. On Meffret's sermons concerning the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin, one treatise. Very many sermons, both to the clergy and to the people, one book. Various orations and letters, one book. Many other works also, of which no mention is made here.

Moreover he divided many books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which what the writer's intention is in them can clearly be known. Among these are Cicero's books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, and On the Dream of Scipio. Likewise Aristotle's books of Logic; the same author's books On the Soul; the books of the Metaphysics. Likewise the books of Ephrem the deacon. The books of John Chrysostom On Compunction of Heart. The books of Saint Augustine On Contrition of Heart. The book of letters of the same author. And nearly all the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop. He is still living in the Charterhouse of Basel, composing various works, and by his own example and writings he greatly summons men to holy studies, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, Alexander VI being supreme pontiff. In the year of the Lord 1494.

Angelus de Clavasio, an Italian by nation, of the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated jurist, outstanding in ability, renowned in speech, devout in life and conduct. He is reported to have fashioned certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known far and wide. Among these there is extant a notable summa on cases, very useful for simple confessors, and nevertheless for learned men who are occupied, necessary and now scattered everywhere, which from the author's name is designated:

The Angelic Summa, one book. It begins: "Angelic spirit." Additions to the same, one book. And certain other works.

He completed this summa under Emperor Frederick III, Sixtus IV being supreme pontiff. And I hear that he is still alive, while Maximilian governs the kingdom of the Roman Germans. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Jason de Mayno, by homeland a Milanese, a ducal senator, a man most learned in both laws, most thoroughly instructed both in the divine Scriptures and in the other secular disciplines, a renowned philosopher, a very celebrated orator, subtle in ability, eloquent in speech, distinguished in counsel and action. He is reported to have written certain excellent little works, in which, exercising his talent, he also commended his memory to posterity. But apart from the oration which he is said to have delivered at Rome before Pope Alexander VI, and which circulates in print, I do not recall that anything [unclear] has come into our hands. But, as I have learned for certain, he wrote elegantly:

On the title De accidentibus in the Institutes, ten books. Also on the Code, one book. On the Digest he wrote various things, fifty books. Orations, letters.

And certain other works. He is renowned today among the princes of Milan, in the highest esteem, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, Alexander VI being supreme pontiff. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493, the eleventh indiction.

Laurentius Butellus, of Dijon, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine writers, excellently taught in secular letters, outstanding in ability, renowned in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote in both genres certain excellent volumes, by which he made his name known. Among these the following are reported: a very celebrated work in praise of Helias, patriarch of the Carmelites, which he entitled:

The Heliad, one book. On the Illustrious Men of His Order, one book.

And many other works. He is still living in great esteem among his own, writing and composing many things under Maximilian, most unconquered king of the Romans, Alexander VI being supreme pontiff. In the year of the Lord 1494.

Christophorus Landinus, an Italian by nation, a citizen of Florence, a man especially learned in secular letters, and not ignorant of philosophy or of the divine page, presided for many years over the chair of the Muses and taught poetry by public office, distinguished in ability. He wrote works held in great esteem among all, especially

384 The Abbot of Spanheim

Commentaries on P. Vergilius Maro. Likewise, commentaries on Q. Horatius. The Camaldolese. Ethics. He is said still to flourish among his own Florentines, whom he adorns with the flowers of all literature.

JACOBUS of Bergamo, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated historiographer. He wrote certain very lucid little works, by which he made posterity indebted to the memorials of himself. Among them there is a work of histories from the beginning of the world down to the year of the Lord 1486, a large and notable volume, which, gathering it with much and long labor from various sources, he entitled:

The Supplement of Chronicles, 15 books. “For [unclear] Cicero of yours.”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He is still living among his own Bergamasques in esteem, nearly sixty years old, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord 1494.

BAPTISTA de Sancto Blasio of Padua, a man most skilled in both laws, distinguished by the learning of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, adorned in eloquence, who in the Paduan academy publicly and excellently taught law, where he educated a great number of disciples. In that faculty he wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he showed the force of his intellect to present and future men. Among these I have read:

On Dowry Privileges, 1 book. “Since concerning dowries many things.” 20 Also On Correlatives, 1 book. “In this work [unclear].” Questions on [unclear], 1 book. “In the name of Christ. [unclear]. Since.” On the First Rubric of the Decretals, 1 book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

He wrote other things. He completed these same works in the Paduan academy, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV. In the year of the Lord 1480, in the thirteenth indiction. And I believe that he is still alive.

MARCUS Antonius Sabellicus, a man most learned on every side, a philosopher, an orator, the most celebrated of all the poets of our time. Adorning Venice with his learning and books, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech, skilled in both languages; to him Hermolaus Barbarus, Venetian archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, once composed a book on the rules for writing history. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, certain distinguished volumes, by which he secured everlasting remembrance for his name among posterity. Of these I have seen the following: three large volumes of histories from the beginning of the world; a most celebrated work addressed to the Venetian senate, containing from the beginning of the city:

The History of the Deeds of the Venetians, 33 books. “I, about to write from the city.” On the Charm of Aquileia, His Fatherland, 1 book. “And if from all writers.” On the Fortification of Fontiacum, a poem, 1 book. “It is poured forth to Illyrian [unclear].” On the Slaughter at Fontiacum, a poem, 1 book. “Whither headlong fortune.” On the Shipwreck of Peter’s Boat, 1 book. “Now, the ropes having been let out, [unclear].” On the Inventors of Things and Arts, 1 book. “The [unclear] fluctuates.” 40 On the Origin of Udine, a poem, 1 book. “Among pleasing suns of study.” In Praise of Saint Mary, 14 elegies. “These things, spread out on the ground.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He is renowned today among the Venetians in the highest esteem, composing many and various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

HUBERTUS Leonardus, bishop of Darien, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in intellect, clear in eloquence, who once taught theology excellently in the Parisian academy, wrote many highly commended little works, by which [unclear] of the deeds of the Franks [unclear]:

To Ludovicus, Bishop of Liège, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, On the Governance of Princes, 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Immunity, 2 books. Against the Heretics of Nivelles, 1 book. Various Sermons, 3 books. A Notable Lenten Sermon Collection, 1 book. And several other things.

When this man was inquisitor of heretical depravity, against certain Nivelles heretics throughout the diocese of Liège, with the sword of the Holy Spirit he confuted and defeated them, writing the aforesaid work

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

A very celebrated work containing twenty-eight propositions, in which, vigorously and eloquently attacking the same number of their erroneous articles, he refuted them. He flourished in Germany, whence he came, under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still alive.

Gabriel Biel, a German by nation, of the order of those who call themselves Brothers of the Common Life, or those living in common, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, who presided for many years over the Tübingen academy from the beginning of its foundation, where he instructed many disciples both in philosophy and in sacred letters, wrote certain little works of no contemptible authority, by which he made his name known. From these he regularly lectured in the aforesaid academy:

On the Canon of the Mass, one book, “Premised in the chamber.” On the Passion of the Lord, he wrote one book. Various sermons also, one book.

And certain other things. He is renowned today, an old man and advanced in age, in the highest esteem with the count of Württemberg; he is said to be writing certain things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Georgius of Gemmingen, a German by nation, provost and canon of the distinguished church of Speyer, a learned nobleman, professor of both laws, a very celebrated interpreter, and excellently skilled in the other disciplines of the good arts, a distinguished philosopher and rhetorician; subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote certain distinguished little works, by which, laudably exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Yet he conceals what he writes, so that he may flee the stamp of empty glory, or may correct what he has written with the file of a more mature examination. Of these, however, the following have become known to us:

On the Method of Duel, one book. On Engines of War, one book. On the Care of Soldiers’ Horses, one book. Certain orations.

In addition he has produced many letters, both to me and to others; from these, how much he is capable of, both in learning and in eloquence and in experience of many things, will easily be perceived by him who reads them. He flourishes in manly age in the city of Speyer, outstanding in sacred letters and devout in conduct, an excellent cultivator of regular observance; he wrote, for the instruction of the simple, little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these [unclear] various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Venetus, of the order of the Carthusians, of the house of St. Andrew the Apostle de Litore near Venice, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, and an excellent cultivator of regular observance, wrote for the instruction of the simple little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a distinguished work, which he entitled:

Know Thyself, one book, “Since nothing [is] more pleasant, nothing…” On Patience and Humility, one book, “Brother most dear in Christ…” The Mirror of the Dying, one book, “In the manner of good parents…” The Crown of the Aged also, one book, “While the human mind…” Various sermons, one book. Several devout letters, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished at Venice under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Sixtus IV, and completed the works written above in the year of the Lord 1480, indiction 13. And I am uncertain whether he still lives.

Johannes of Mylbach, a German by nation; a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in discourse, who formerly taught theology gloriously for a long time in the Erfurt academy and instructed very many disciples in that faculty, wrote several distinguished little works, by which he magnificently exercised his talent and commended the knowledge of himself to posterity. From these he regularly lectured:

On the Epistles of Paul, one book. Various sermons, one book. In Praise of St. Jerome, one book. Various questions.

And certain other things. He is renowned at Erfurt, an old and feeble man, a prebendary in the monastery of St. Peter, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Johannes de Arundine, a German by nation, bishop of [Vsbiten.?], of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, vicar in pontifical matters of David of Burgundy, bishop of Utrecht, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, an excellent declaimer of sermons, subtle in talent, in life

The Abbot of Spanheim. Distinguished in [unclear], he wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported. A notable lecture.

On the Book of Wisdom, one book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book.

On “Blessed are the undefiled,” sermons, one book. Sermons on the season, one book.

Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished at Traiectum, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still alive.

Georgius Valla of Piacenza, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, who, now adorning all Italy with his learning, teaches both languages most brilliantly at Venice. He wrote many excellent volumes, by whose elegance and usefulness he has made all learned men truly indebted to him.

On orthography, two books. On the quantity of syllables, one book.

On the figures of orators and poets, one book. “Long since foreseen by me.”

On Cicero’s On the Universe, one book. Plato’s book which [is called?] Ti[maeus?].

On the same author’s On Fate, one book. “On Cicero’s On Fate.”

On the Topics of the same author, one book. “The observance and especially [unclear].”

On the Rhetoric to Herennium, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

On Juvenal, one book. On the method of disputing, two books.

On Horace’s Poetics, three books. And many other works.

On things to be sought and avoided, one book. The same author’s introduction to medicine. Also four books of the Problems of [Alexander?]. And many other works.

He translated into Latin from Greek a little work of Aristotle On Virtue; likewise two books of his Ethics; also the work of Nemesius, a Christian philosopher, On the Nature of Man; also the little book of Athenagoras, a very acute philosopher, On the Resurrection; also Brisson’s book of dialectic; in addition a treatise of Galen the physician on the sects of physicians; the same author’s introduction to medicine; also four books of the Problems of [Alexander?]. And many other works.

Johannes Camerarius von Dalberg, bishop of Worms, German by nation, a very celebrated jurist, most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters; once a pupil of Rudolf Agricola, a most learned man; skilled in both languages, a most distinguished rhetorician and poet, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, notable for wide experience of affairs, magnificently illustrating the nobility of his family by his character and learning. He has written and writes, both in verse and prose, certain little works of excellent talent, which he has not yet allowed to come to light, because, being occupied with affairs of state, he could not complete them quite as his purpose had been. Of these, however, some have become known to us. A Sapphic poem.

On the death of Rudolf Agricola, one book. Also On Money, one book.

A speech before Pope Innocent VIII. Various poems and speeches; and several very elegant letters. He is distinguished today, in manly age, in the chair of the church of Worms, a bishop worthy of God; he is composing various works, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things about him, 1494.

Battista Guarini of Verona, son of Guarino, a most learned man, of whom we have made mention in his own place; a man certainly not inferior to his father, but most skilled in every branch of literature and in the discipline of good language, very eloquent in both tongues. He wrote and translated many excellent little works, by which he commends the force and keenness of his talent, almost divine, both to those now living and to posterity. Of these the following are reported. A very beautiful work of dialogues.

On the Epicurean sect, one book. “And if, most renowned Mapheus,” one book.

On the order of teaching. On Cicero’s letters, one book.

On administering a kingdom. On Lucan’s Pharsalia, one book.

On the poet Catullus. Letters to various persons, one book.

Also several speeches, and poems of various kinds, one book.

He translated the following into Latin: from Xenophon, the Praise of Agesilaus, which he dedicated to Ermolao Barbaro the elder, bishop of Verona; also certain speeches of Demosthenes and Dio the historian; but also some speeches of Gregory Nazianzen to Christ and Mary. And he published and translated many other works which have not come to my knowledge. He is distinguished even today

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...today at Ferrara, where, succeeding his father, for thirty-three years now he has taught both languages most flourishingly and composes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we are writing these things, 1494, indiction 12. He himself has a son learned in the Greek and Latin languages, following his ancestral discipline.

Angelus Politianus, a man skilled in every respect and a very learned, celebrated grammarian, an outstanding philosopher, orator, and poet; perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, excellent in talent, who for a long time illuminated Italy by his learning and doctrine. He wrote various distinguished volumes, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

One book, On the Errors of the Latin Language, one book. Various letters to different persons, one book.

And he is said to have written certain other works which have not come to my knowledge. Besides these he dared to present Homer’s Iliad for reading in Latin verses. He is still flourishing in Italy, as I have heard, composing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff. In the year of the Lord 1494.

Baptista Mantuanus, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in knowledge of secular letters, doctor of sacred theology, distinguished philosopher, most celebrated poet and orator, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, an ornament of the Latin language, a renowned interpreter of Greek, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote in both styles many excellent volumes, by which he acquired for his name celebrated fame throughout the whole Christian world. Among them let the following be reported:

To His Father, one book. “Brother Baptista, to Peter...” Suburbanum, on Bucolics, one book. “Faustus [unclear]...” One book. “Of holy Palestine [unclear]...” Life of Parthenice, one book. “[unclear]...” One book. On the Life of Ludovicus of Bologna, one book. “Greatest of pontiffs...” Life of Albert the Carmelite, in Sapphic metre, one book. “The month of August returns...” On the Calamity of His Times, one book. “We are compelled by the evils of that...” One book. “The ancients [unclear] of demigods...” Dialogue on the Blessed Life, one book. “Greatest [unclear] of instruction...” One book. “The delightful [unclear] of the sacred spring...” One book. “What you deserve, and fate [unclear]...” One book. “There are those to whom eloquence is given [unclear].” Panegyric of Robert, one book. Apology for Brother Peter, one book. Dream concerning the Same, one book. Most elegant orations, one book. To Falco, epigrams, one book. Poems of various kinds. On Consolation over Death, one book. And many other works. Against Foul-Mouthed Poets, one book. On the Prologue of the Bible, one book. Many conferences to the clergy. On the Conquest of Granada, one book. “Most reverend in Christ...” On the Origin of Religions, one book. Various questions. Introduction to the Subtleties of Scotus, one book. “As I was thinking in former...” Many letters to different persons, one book. And a certain other work.

Under Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we completed these things, 1494.

Johannes Bertram of Nuremberg, a German by nation, once a hearer of Georgius Molitor of Nuremberg, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures; not ignorant of secular philosophy, renowned in talent, scholastic in speech, first at Erfurt, then in the gymnasium of Mainz publicly teaching theology and instructing many. He wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Among them there exists a large work.

One book. He flourishes in mature age in the gymnasium of Mainz, teaching theology in the ordinary course and composing various works, under the most renowned Maximilian, king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we are writing these things, 1494.

Rupertus Ganguinus, a Frenchman by nation, minister general of the Order of the Trinity, distinguished doctor of decrees, most learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, a renowned poet, a most eloquent orator, who often [unclear] the Italians...

388 | Abbot of Sponheim … he rendered by his eloquence, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant: A work in notable verse to Arnoldus Bostius, a Carmelite dwelling at Ghent, against Vincentius de Castronovo, of the Order of Preachers, On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book, “And to me a mind [unclear].” On the same subject, in prose, one book, “No Christian reli[unclear].” On the Wretched Condition of Man, one book, “Among the many things by which he [unclear].” On the Art of Composing Verse, three books, “Those things concerning the making of ver[ses?].” Many very elegant orations, one book. Also a book of letters, one book. And several other things. He is still living at Paris, residing at Saint-Mathurin, and is writing various works day by day to be published, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Harynghus Sifridi Sinnama, from The Hague, of Frisian origin, who is commonly called Hermannus, German by nation, professor of both laws and a most celebrated interpreter, and excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy; subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, ready and steady in counsel, whose authority is held in great esteem among princes and prelates of churches, easily holds the first place in teaching, writing, and giving counsel in the university of Cologne. He wrote, among other things, a large and very celebrated work, explaining legal titles with the utmost clarity, very useful and necessary for all beginning to study in both laws or in either one: On the Titles of the Code, twelve books, “And if verbosity without [unclear].” On the Titles of the Old Digest, twenty-four books, “Although the new pla[unclear].” On the Titles of the New Digest, fourteen books, “It will have to be known here in [unclear].” On the Titles of the Authentics, one book, “Because there are seven parts.” On the Uses of Fiefs, one book, “Although the constitutions [unclear].” On the Peace of Constance, one book, “Because this book of fiefs [unclear].” On the Titles of the Institutes, one book, “Because Emperor Frede[ric?].” On the Titles of the Decretals, four books, “Although from this book.” Certain other works are also extant, “Since, as the Emperor says.” He is living in the vigor of manhood in the city of Cologne, [unclear] that most learned [unclear], and under the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year in which we wrote these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Raphael Regius, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a renowned philosopher, a celebrated poet, and a distinguished orator, skilled in both languages; excellent in talent and eloquent in speech. In the university of Padua he acquired the highest praise for his learning by teaching, disputing, and composing. He is said to have produced many distinguished little works, by which he made his name and talent known with glory. Of these the following are extant: Corrections on Quintilian, one book, “High-minded men are accustomed [unclear].” On the Praises of Eloquence, one book, “If ever anyone of distinguished [unclear].” On one letter of Pliny, one book, “In the inscription of this work.” Against Johannes Calphurnius, one book, “Although with very weighty [unclear].” A dialogue against the same, one book, “Yesterday you disturbed the boys.” Various orations, one book. Also many letters. And several other things. An Introductory Notice to the Fasti, one book. And certain commentaries. He is still living at Padua, as I have learned, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Laurentius Bonincontrius, a philosopher and distinguished astronomer, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of the liberal arts; outstanding in talent and clear in speech, strong in verse and prose. He is said to have produced many distinguished little works, by which he has transmitted his name to the knowledge of many, but up to now I have not been able to see any of them. There is said, however, to be a notable work of his, through the circle of the year.

Johannes de Keisersberg, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, in life and conduct

On Ecclesiastical Writers

renowned for his conduct, a very celebrated preacher of sermons, who for many years has held the office of preacher in the cathedral church of Strasbourg. He wrote some commendable little works, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. His elegant works are reported to be:

Sermons to the People, 1 book. Various Orations to the Clergy, 1 book.

And certain others. At great expense and with long labor he collected the works of Johannes Gerson, many of which at last he brought to us from France, dividing them into three parts in a very handsome order, and making a very useful table; he gave the whole of this to be printed. He is still living in the German city of Strasbourg, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Picus, an Italian by nation, count of Mirandola and lord of Concordia, a man most devoted to every kind of good literature, and, just as he is of illustrious blood, so too most noble in an almost divine talent, surrounded by a great household crowd of all kinds of arts, with whom he practices the arena of Latin studies and letters, and likewise Hebrew and Greek, worthy and most deserving, whose journey the Muses follow, is the most learned philosopher of our age and a very keen disputant. In a most elegant style he wrote some things which the age of our contemporaries will approve and then indeed will hold in the greatest admiration; by these he has not unworthily made the memory of his name and glory everlasting. Of these there have already appeared:

Heptaplus on the Beginning of Genesis.

Also: Nine Hundred Philosophical Conclusions.

Apology. Also On the Psalms, 1 book.

And many other things which have not yet presented themselves to our sight. He is still living today among the company of his gifted young men among the Italians, and he does not cease either to write loftier works or to do good for posterity, under Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, and Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a German by nation, from the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, an outstanding doctor of imperial laws, and counselor of the illustrious count Eberhard of Württemberg, both most eloquent and of the greatest integrity in law and faith, a most diligent investigator of all the most ancient philosophy and literature. Of the three principal languages, namely Hebrew and likewise Chaldaic, and equally Greek and Latin, he is a very skilled interpreter. He is also especially distinguished in French and in our more polished vernacular tongue. And he is most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters. Indeed, in every kind of learning he is foremost in this age, as one who for many years has very earnestly penetrated the secret mysteries of the Greeks. Worthy indeed to devote himself only to letters, and not also to the very noisy popular court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could set against us any equal to this great man. He wrote some works by which he commended the memory of himself to those present and to posterity. To the bishop of Worms, chamberlain Dalberg, he wrote a dialogue in which he explains all the secret words of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy, wondrous words, which he entitled:

Capnion, or On the Wonder-Working Word, 3 books.

On the Preparatory Exercises of the Orator, 1 book.

It is from the ancients.

On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language, 1 book.

A Funeral Oration on the Death of Rudolf Agricola.

Of Epigrams and Elegies, 1 book.

Besides, for our common utility he translated many little works from Greek into Latin: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates, Nestorius the heretic, the Confession of Cyprian, Proclus on the blessed Virgin, some of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead, a dialogue of the same author on the council [unclear] in verse, Epiphanius on the life and death of the prophets, Maximus Tyrius the Platonist [unclear]. That renowned Capnion makes the name more illustrious by his talent. In the year in which we write these things, 1494.

[unclear], monk of the monastery of Maulbronn, of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, excellently taught in secular matters, a philosopher, orator, and poet not to be rejected, skilled, as they report, in the three principal languages, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote in verse and prose some little works by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a volume,

The Abbot of Sponheim

Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations. Many poems. And certain other things.

He lives to this day at Citeaux and persists in the study he has begun, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Conrad Celtis Protucius, German by nation, born from Franconia in Germany, a man in every respect most learned, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent orator, an eminent astronomer and cosmographer, and a poet laureate, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, skilled in both languages, excellent in talent and fluent in speech, wrote certain distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Concerning these he formerly read the following to me:

To Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, on both rhetorics of M. Tullius Cicero, an epitome, that is, a compendium, one book. “Qui in concione quip.” On the praises of eloquence, one book. “Morine aeternis cele.” On the art of versifying, one book. “Accepi illustriss. prin.” On composing letters, one book. “Epistola seu apostolus est.” On the site of Nuremberg, one book. “Cum nuper relaxandi ani.” A Sarmatian journey, one book, to which he gave the name “volu.” Of poems, two books. “Urse doctorum specimen.” Of loves, which he inscribed according to the four sides, four books. “Scribere que nostrae fat alia.” A panegyric to the duke of Bavaria, one book. “Italicas tentare lyres.” On the life of Saint Sebald, in verse, one book. “Regiae stirpis soboles.” The situation of Germany, three books. “Germaniam scripturus.” Various orations, one book.

He published many very elegant letters to various persons, in verse and prose, and diverse epigrams; in cosmography, of which he is most knowledgeable, he wrote various things, which we trust will hereafter come to light. He is still living, thirty-five years of this age, and writes various works under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, and under the supreme pontiff Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Petrus Bonomus of Trieste, protonotary of the imperial court, a man most learned in the Latin language, both very fluent and very practiced in composing every kind of poetry, as one from whose storehouse the tuneful Muses pour forth, and for that reason very celebrated by the fame of a great name, wrote very many works in prose and in verse of various kinds. Of these there are extant especially:

Books of epigrams. An unwearied mass of letters.

Nor does he ever cease to write. He is still living under his king Maximilian, devoted to letters and cultivating his talent with good arts. In the year in which we write these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Sebastian Ticio, otherwise Brandt, of Strasbourg, German by nation, distinguished professor of both laws, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other disciplines of secular literature, by no means unskilled in poetry, subtle in talent, outstanding in speech, counsel, and action, who by his learning and literary labor wonderfully adorns Basel, the renowned city of Germany, wrote certain little works, both in verse and in prose, of by no means contemptible reading, by which he made his name widely known. Of these there are extant:

On the titles of both laws, one book. “Cum difficile.” A Sapphic rosary of divine Mary. “Stirpis humana.” Enigmas in praise of the Virgin, from the Old Testament. “Que parisi.” Proof that the virginal conception was possible. “Huc adez o.” The wonder of Mary when the angel came. “Quid tibi vis.” The salutation of the Angel. “Missus ab excelso.” On the [unclear] places of the blessed Virgin. “Si tu a virgo.” The virginal compassion. “Nare patris.” The consolation of Christ to his mother. “Quid gemis o.” On the blows given to Christ. “Respice que tulerim.” On the ingratitude of those eating manna. “Sorte sub hac.” In praise of Saint Sebastian. “Quid tuas coner.” The life of Saint Onuphrius. “Nostris carminibus.” In praise of Saint Valentine. “Laudibus o presul.” The beginning of a poem: “Vica.”

On Ecclesiastical Writers

The Life of Saint Bernard. In praise of the Carthusian order. On contempt of the world. Praises of blessed Christiana near Basel. Against slanderous advocates. On the captivity of King Maximilian. An elegy on the death of Emperor Frederick. To the divine King Maximilian. Of various epigrams, book 1. Commendatory poems for various printed editions.

He also compiled, with wonderful art and talent, though in the common and vernacular tongue, a certain little book which he called the Ship of Narragonia. In it he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censures the morals of men, and offers certain salutary remedies to each, that he would not rightly have called that work a book of fools, but rather a divine satire. For I do not know whether anything more wholesome or more pleasant could be read for the uses of our age. They say that he is striving greatly so that the same work may come out in Latin as soon as possible, alike in verse and in prose. He is still living at Basel, being 36 years of age, and printers make very great use of his labor and industry in adorning their books. For he writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans, whom he loves in a singular way, and has composed many very sweet poems about him and to him, even secret ones, as they say. In the year in which we write these things, 1494.

Jacob Wimpeling of Schlettstadt, a German by nation, priest of the church of Speyer, a man most learned in divine matters and excellently taught in secular letters, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, orator, and poet, most outstanding among all, first at Erfurt and then in the Heidelberg academy publicly explaining philosophy and sacred scripture, acquired great glory for his learning. A man, I say, most learned from every side, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent both in meter and in prose, he wrote in both kinds certain distinguished little works, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these the following are extant. To Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, he composed a very celebrated work in hexameter and pentameter verse, most elegantly, which he entitled On the Threefold Whiteness.

In praise of the divine Mary, book 1. “Greatest hope of our...” Precepts of rhetoric, book 1. “I do not know whether your, Theoderic...” Praises of the church of Speyer, book 1. “Just as he expects...” On the Holy Spirit, an oration, book 1. “Already eight lustra to be enjoyed...” To the king of France, an oration, book 1. Many poems of various kinds. On the art of poetry, book 1. And certain other things.

He composed many elegant letters, both to me and to others, of which the number is uncertain. At the urging of Ludwig, bishop of Speyer, he composed an office on the compassion of the blessed Mary ever virgin, which is solemnly performed annually throughout that same diocese. To this Jacob we have already long since dedicated the book On the Illustrious Men of Germany. He is living in manly age, being about forty-three years old, in the renowned city of Speyer, and writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Baptista de Salis, of the order of Friars Minor of the province of Genoa, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, and excellently taught both in both laws and in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, and distinguished in observance of the rules of discipline, published certain little works necessary for the instruction of simple priests, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these there is extant a summa on cases in the forum of conscience, very useful, which, according to the author’s name, is called

The Baptista Summa, book 1. He completed this same summa under Frederick III, emperor. And he is still living while his son Maximilian holds the kingdom. In the year of the Lord 1494.

Engelhard Funck of Schwabach, an East Franconian, a German by nation, a learned man and skilled in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, not ignorant of the divine scriptures and pontifical law, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in meter, [unclear]. In elegiac verse.

On the praise of his fatherland, book 1. Various epigrams. Several letters to various persons. And many other things.

392 The Abbot of Sponheim He is distinguished at Rome, as [auditor?] or advocate of causes, and composes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Langer of Bolkenhain, priest of Wroclaw, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, in life and conduct worthy of a priest. He wrote many excellent little works in both kinds of style, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a distinguished work addressed to Georg von Stein, lord of Steynaw, which he entitled:

On [unclear] and [unclear], one book. “Today I am oppressed by a great [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. Many poems. And many other things.

He is still living in Wroclaw and writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Werner Rolevinck, of Laer, a German by nation, by homeland a Westphalian, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, published many excellent little works, by which he made himself useful to the present and memorable to the future. Of these the following survive: a large work on all the epistles of Paul, which he entitled:

The Teaching of Paul, two books. “The teaching of Paul the apostle.” On the Life of Paul, one book. “Just as I was with Moses, so.” On the Value of Masses, one book. On the Rule of Princes, one book. On the Study of Theology, one book. The Bundle of Times, one book. “Generation and genera.” The Paradise of Conscience, one book. “The Lord God took the man.” Many sermons, one book. And many other things.

I once saw in his cell treatises, small indeed, but numerous and useful, whose titles oblivion has now taken from my memory. He is still living in the Cologne Charterhouse, of advanced age, and writing various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Arnold Bostius, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, orator, and poet, acute in talent, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, of whom several letters to me survive. He wrote many excellent little works in verse and prose. Of these the following survive: a distinguished volume written in verse and prose, in which he clearly shows the prerogative origin and progress of his order in view of Marian protection; for that reason it was pleasing that it be entitled:

On the Patronage of Mary, one book. “You asked, most distinguished man.” On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians, one book. “To the venerable and among [unclear].” On the Illustrious Men of His Own Order, one book. “Brother Arnold Bostius.” Against Vincent in the New Castle, one book. “How long always [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. On the Four Last Things, one book. Various poems. And many other things.

He is still living at Ghent, in vigorous age, and composing various works, and by his example and writings he summons many to sacred studies. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Heinrich Euticus, an East Franconian, an excellent professor of both kinds of medicine, has published many things which he prepares for posterity. Also, in a varied and pleasing character of poems, a very beautiful little work which he entitled:

Jests, or Urbane and Witty Jokes of Young Men. In Praise of the Blessed Virgin. And many other things. A Satire against Sophists and Dialecticians and Enemies of the Study of the Humanities.

He is still living, when we wrote these things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Eytelwolf von Stein, a noble man, German by nation and Swabian, a man of great talent and a vigorous emulator of Roman eloquence, and for that reason having obtained great honor with the margrave of Brandenburg. He wrote to Georg von Stein, his maternal uncle, a man most devoted to letters:

On the Praises of Heroes and Illustrious Men, one book. A most polished letter. And

On Ecclesiastical Writers

And other works by which he will win great praise for Germany among cultivators of the Roman tongue. He is still living today under King Maximilian, in the year in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Rudolphus Langius, German by nation, canon of the church of Münster in Westphalia, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, a most learned philosopher, orator, and very celebrated poet, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he spread his name far and wide with immense glory. Of these the following are extant. To Hermann Langius, dean of the same church: On the City of Jerusalem, 2 books, “A certain most splendid [unclear].” To the dean of Cologne, Poems, 1 book, “Clear virtue, whom [unclear].” On the Siege of the City of Neuss, 1 book. A Poem on the Three Magi, 1 book. Several letters to various persons. Various poems also. And many other works.

He is still living, very old, in the city of Münster, composing many works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Sebastianus Murrho of Colmar, German by nation, priest and canon in Colmar, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and most learned in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher, orator, poet, and cosmographer, very skilled in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, celebrated for his knowledge of laws and canons, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole quadrivium, wrote, among other things, to Jacob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, whom we mentioned above, a brief but very beautiful work: Epitome on the Praises of the Germans, 1 book. On the Works of Baptista Mantuanus, 1 book. And certain other works.

He is living today in Colmar, where he is a canon, and is composing various works which we hope will be published day by day, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Carolus Phernandus, German by nation, born at Bruges, a town of Flanders, blind from earliest childhood, and for that reason also wholly ignorant of the elements, presents so great a marvel of himself that, like another Homer, he became a very celebrated poet, musician, philosopher, and orator, and also a most sagacious interpreter of the divine Scriptures, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and most upright in life and conduct. Having been granted a public and perpetual stipend by the king of the French, he taught humane letters with distinction for a long time in the celebrated college of Paris, and explained many authors most beautifully. At length, despising everything, he abandoned the world together with his stipends, and about two years ago entered the order of our holy father Benedict, in a well-reformed monastery called Casale Benedictum, situated in a very dense wood about ten miles distant from the city of Bourges. There he perseveres to this day, burning with great zeal for souls, so much so that, ordained a Levite by apostolic dispensation, he publicly preaches the word of God with the greatest profit and admiration of all. He wrote many very distinguished volumes, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity. Against the metrical contestation of Robert Gaguin on the most pure conception of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, against Vincentius de Castronovo of the Order of Preachers, a most elegant work: Commentaries, 1 book, “We do not doubt from the Apostle.” Praises of the Order of Carmelites, 1 book, “While the Parthian turns his weapons.” Odes in Praise of Christ, 4 books. On the Conception against Vincentius, 1 book. Iambic Poem on the Same, 1 book, “How much he surpasses created things.” Oration on the Conception to the Carthusians, 1 book. Oration on Saint Catherine, 1 book. Many Letters, 2 books. Almost innumerable poems, 1 book. Elegies on Contempt of the World, 1 book. And many other works.

He is living today, blind but most learned, in the aforesaid monastery, composing many and varied works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Johannes Phernandus, brother of the aforesaid Carolus, himself also German by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, very celebrated orator and poet, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, whom the king of the French, granting him a perpetual stipend, took for himself as a musician, wrote many useful little works, suited to devotion, both in verse and in prose, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Of these the following are extant.

394 The Abbot of Sponheim

On Saint John the Baptist, one book. “Seek with the plectrum how ...” Many and varied orations, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Many poems and epigrams, and many other things.

He also wrote the Hours of the Holy Cross and of the compassion of Saint Mary in elegant verse; these, recently printed at Paris, are in circulation. He lives to this day with the king of France in the highest esteem, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Donatus, a Venetian patrician, a most distinguished man, devoted to the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated translator of both languages, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, although he is now distracted by the care of wife and children, nevertheless burns with a wonderful diligence and incredible zeal for letters, writing many things day by day and translating many things from Greek; if another man, even one free from every care, were to compose them, they could be something of a marvel.

An oration to the king of Portugal, one book. Various orations also, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And very many other things.

He translated into Latin John Damascene on the immaculate mysteries; also Dionysius on the Divine Names, and certain letters of his; also the volume On the Soul by Alexander of Aphrodisias the philosopher; and many other things. He lives to this day at Venice, thirty-seven years old, writing and translating various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Jodocus Badius of Ghent, German by nation, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very distinguished philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, who once at Ferrara heard Baptista Guarinus teaching Greek letters, and in that branch of knowledge also became learned. He now adorns Lyons with his learning, and reads the poets publicly and privately, instructing several sons of magnates. He wrote many excellent little works in verse and prose, of which the following are extant. A notable metrical work against vices, which he entitled:

The Moral Grove, one book. “Unhappy Vincent, and ...” Against Vincent also, one book. “What chorus of poets ...” 20 Psalter of Mary in Sapphic verses, one book. Many epigrams, one book. On grammar also, one book. Various letters. And very many other things.

He lives to this day, thirty-two years old, composing many different works under the renowned King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Helias Regnier, a very celebrated jurist, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, cautious in counsel, who for a long time publicly taught law in the school of Poitiers, wrote certain excellent little works by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only the following, a celebrated work which contains:

Cases of the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. “Boniface the Eighth established ...” 40 Cases of the Clementines, two books. “John, bishop, divide ...”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He is still living in the University of Poitiers, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Rutgerus Ventray, German by nation, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, from the monastery of the holy apostle Peter which, situated not far from Worms, is called Heyne; a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote in both kinds certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant. A Tetralogue, which he entitled:

On the Instruction of Boys, two books. “When you notice childish ...” 53 On the Inquiry into the Blessed Life, two books. “In the year in which Ceres ...” Hymns on Saint Mary, two books. “Behold, Mary, mother of God ...” On the Various Use of Letters, two books. “For knowing in verse ...” On a Marvelous Thing, two books. “Very many things to the mind, to the will ...” On New Matters, one book. “Most familiar in Christ ...” On the Kinds of Metres, two books. “This Tetralogue, which concerning ...” A panegyric to me. Various epigrams, one book. “To the reverend father in Christ ...” And certain other things. I hear

On Ecclesiastical Writers

I hear that he is composing for me a work on the calamities of these times, which I have not yet seen. He has written very many letters, both to me and to others, in verse and in prose, not without elegance. He is living to this day and composes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Jodocus Beysselius, a patrician of the royal city of Aachen, a German by nation, a man devoted to the sacred Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, eloquent orator, and notable poet, although he is necessarily distracted by care for his wife and household estate, nevertheless burns with an incredible love of the Scriptures, writing and composing many things every day. Of these the following are extant, by which his name is everywhere spread with great glory. Of these the following are extant:

A very beautiful dialogue addressed to Hermolaus Barbarus, in the manner of the Platonists, On the Best Kind of Musicians, one book. “I have brought you, O Hermo[laus]...”

On Christian Ambition, one book. “Even if all things are at hand for you...”

Epitome of the Goad of Love, one book. “Since through these, Christina...”

On the Rose-like Crown of Mary, one book. “Most august rose-like...”

A Metrical Rosary, one book. “Whoever loves the rose-like...”

On the Mystery of the Rosary, one book. “Go forth, daughters of Sion...”

Rosary on the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “Under this small bread...”

Deeds of the Flemings, one book.

Most elegant orations.

Also many letters. Many poems and epigrams.

And certain other things.

He lives to this day at Aachen, a most distinguished interpreter of both laws, and writes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we were about to write these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Balbus, a man of very celebrated reputation, excellently learned in all the disciplines of the liberal arts, a distinguished philosopher and eloquent rhetorician, outstanding in verse and prose, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, who by teaching, public lecturing, and writing earned great glory among the French and the Parisians. He wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen [unclear], a volume composed with great [unclear] of eloquence, in which he responds to the slanders of a certain Guilhelmus Tardivus, rhetorician, in the form of a dialogue under the names of himself, Carolus Phernandus, Petrus Cohardus, and his accuser himself, to which he gave the title, one book. “Among those duties by which...”

[unclear] of the boastful rhetorician, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord 1494.

I have seen nothing of the others. He still lives in France, writing and composing various works, under Maximilian [unclear] from letters. The rest is unknown to me.

Of Saint Jerome the priest, four books.

He lives to this day in the city of Cambrai, very celebrated in life and doctrine, and [unclear] various compositions, and learned, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, and conspicuous for singular devotion. He published certain excellent works in volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work of all [unclear], by which he made his name known. Of their number [unclear], which with wonderful industry and very beautiful sequence he brought together into one from the letters.

Polish History against the Turk, one book.

Of Loves in Various Metres, two books.

Philippus Callimachus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, secretary of the king of Poland, most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent orator and fluent in speech. He is said to have published many excellent little works, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: an outstanding work on the deeds of Attila, the impious king, which he entitled Attila.

On the Customs of the Tartars, one book.

And very many other things. He lives to this day at the court of the king of the Poles in the highest esteem, and writes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which he was about to write these things, 1490, in the twelfth indiction.

Paulus Niavis, a German by nation, a man excellently learned in humane letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, by teaching and by writing various things in the gymnasium of Leipzig acquired great fame for his name. For he wrote certain excellent little works, whose reading should not be despised. Of these the following are reported:

A Little Work for Religious Novices. “Since I have often thought...”

On the Practice of Latinizing, one book.

396 The Abbot of Spanheim

Vision of a certain hermit, one book: “A huge grove clearly.” Colors of the art of rhetoric, one book: “Once you wished, [unclear].” Dialogue of the idiot, one book: “When I often recalled [unclear].” Short formal letters, one book: “Great force is wont.” Letters to the same, of moderate length, one book: “I promised, good man.” Letters also of greater length, one book: “I conceive a great and [unclear].” And certain other works. He lives to this day in Germany, composing various works under Maximilian, most illustrious King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Bohuslaus of Hassenstein, a German by nation, a noble man and learned on every side, a distinguished orator and poet, who, contrary to the custom of the other nobles of this age, both handles arms and with remarkable zeal cultivates, fosters, and celebrates letters, so that, like a second Pliny, even while serving as a soldier he composes books and poems, wrote certain excellent little works both in verse and in prose, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant:

A distinguished work on the proper inventions of the Germans and Italians, one book. Various letters. Poems also, one book. Various letters. And many other works.

He lives to this day in his castle Hassenstein and writes various works under Maximilian, most excellent King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.
