Henricus of Northeim, a Teuton by nation, a man devoted to and learned in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and fluent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have seen only that distinguished work which he wrote in verse and prose to Frederick, Margrave of Meissen, and the dukes of Saxony, entitled Dimetronachia:

On the conflict of virtues and vices, one book: “Then you, laurel-bearing [unclear].”

Of the other things which he composed, nothing has come to my knowledge. He lives to this day, writing various works, under Maximilian, most illustrious king, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Aquinus, of the order of Friars Preachers, having the origin of his life from Sweden, was devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, a celebrated philosopher and distinguished mathematician, excellent in talent and polished in speech. Imitating Boethius, he wrote a most highly commended work:

On the proportions of numbers and sounds, one book. Certain letters. And certain other works.

He lives to this day among the Bavarian dukes, in esteem with Otto, and writes various works under Maximilian, most unconquered king, in the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Albertus of Prusa, a Pole by nation, a collegian of the university of Krakow, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, also excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, and astronomer. Praised in a poem of Conrad Celtis for his skill in the stars, outstanding in talent and clear in speech, he wrote several little works not contemptible in reading, by which he made his name known. But few of them have come to my knowledge:

Commentaries on the Theoricae of Georgius Burbachius, one book. To the ephemerides of Königsberg, one book. And certain other works.

He still lives in the university of Krakow, composing various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1493, indiction 12.

Theodericus of Osnabrück, a Teuton by nation, of the order of Friars Minor of the province of Cologne, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, a very famous declaimer of popular sermons, whose life all who have known him proclaim at this time to be most holy. In making sermons to the people he is illumined from God with such grace, speaks with such eloquence, and finally affects his hearers with such compunction and sweetness, that he has had no one like him among the Germans. Hence he was appointed general preacher throughout the whole province. Recently, while he was with me at Cologne, he read to me a distinguished little work, fitting for devotion, which he had composed at the instance of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne:

On the Passion of the Lord, one book: “Most reverend in Christ.” Manual of the simple, one book: “Because, as Augustine.” On the inner army, one book: “He who shall have persevered.” And certain other works.

He still lives in the province of Cologne, vigorously pressing on in the office he has begun, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493. Bartho-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

BARTHOLOMAEUS of Cologne, German by nation, a man excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, a distinguished philosopher and poet, whose poems even the most learned poets admire and extol with praises. He wrote in both styles certain little works worthy of notice, by which he made his name known. Of these I have so far seen only a little work on the praises of philosophy, composed in meter, which he entitled:

A Woodland of Poems, book I. “Why [unclear] gold to Pluto.” On the Sect of Diogenes, book I. “Whoever desires [unclear].” A mythological letter.

There is, however, as is said, what he wrote on this book, which bore the sign of the cross, and through him [unclear]. Of the others I have seen nothing. He is still living today at Deventer, composing various works, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

JOHANNES Thurotus, a Hungarian, a man studiously trained in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, excellent in intellect, renowned in eloquence. He is said to have fashioned some little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a volume not to be rejected, which he assembled with much industry, containing:

A Chronicle of Hungary, book II. “In constant leisure in these years [unclear].”

And certain other things. He is said still to be living and composing various works, under King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

HIERONYMUS of Padua, Italian by nation, a man studious in the divine scriptures, excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, excellent, eloquent in speech. He wrote certain little works not of contemptible reading, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there exists a very beautiful little book, entitled Jesuita, addressed in meter to Peter Donatus, bishop of the city of Padua:

On the Passion of the Lord, book I. “Greatest of the heaven-dwellers [unclear].”

Other works of his exist. He is said still to be living and composing various works, under King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

FRANCISCUS Mataracius of Perugia, a man educated in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher, orator, and poet, highly skilled in both languages, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. He wrote certain distinguished works, book I [unclear]. Of these there exists a very celebrated little work addressed to the young man Petrus Paulus Cornelius:

On Composing Verses, book II. “The ancients [unclear] the poetic art.” Letters to various persons, book II. Many epigrams.

And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV.

DOMINICUS Mancinus, a man very learned in the divine scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, excellent in meter and prose, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence. He wrote certain approved little works, by which he spread abroad his name. Of these I have read only that treatise which he composed in elegant meter:

On the Passion of the Lord, book I. “Not the praises of men, nor [unclear].”

He wrote other things. He is said still to be living and writing various works, under Maximilian, most noble king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

LUDOVICUS Brunus, Italian by nation, from the marquisate of Montferrat, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, a poet laureate, philosopher, distinguished orator, and not ignorant of the divine writings, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. He is said to have fashioned many distinguished little works in both kinds of writing, but none of them has come into our hands except that treatise which he described in elegant verse:

On the Coronation of King Maximilian, book II. “Holy through eternity [unclear].”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He is still living, and is said to be writing various works, under the same King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

JACOBUS Sprenger, German by nation, provincial of the Order of Preachers at Cologne, a man studiously learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in intellect and plain in speech, when he had formerly been appointed inquisitor of heretical depravity by Pope Innocent VIII, together with Henricus Institoris, a theologian of the same order, assembled and wrote, with the help of the same colleague, a volume against little women who are witches, instruments of the Devil, for the caution of the simple, which he entitled:

Abbot of Spanheim

The Hammer of Witches, 5 books. He lives to this day in his convent at Cologne, under Maximilian, most clement king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493, indiction 12.

Johannes Tholosus, a German by nation, born in Eastern Francia, which is called Franconia, canon of Regensburg and provost of Forchheim, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of pontifical law, a very celebrated astronomer, cosmographer, and poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote certain excellent little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his talent to posterity. But I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands. Yet those who knew the man well report that he has, on various subjects:

Elegant Letters, 1 book. And certain works in mathematics.

And certain other things. He lives to this day in the city of Regensburg, in the province of the Norici, and writes various works, a very great supporter of learned men, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493, the twelfth indiction.

Adam Werner of Themar, a German by nation, a man excellently instructed in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and no trivial poet, and a most distinguished interpreter of imperial law, outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech, writes various works, playing in verse and prose, by which he has made his talent known far and wide. There are extant many of his writings, and poems addressed to me, 1 book, beginning: “To the reverend father in Christ.”

Also many letters. He composed for me, On Saint Anne, 1 book.

In addition he has written, and daily writes, many other works to be published. He lives to this day at Heidelberg, tutor of young princes, under Maximilian, king, in the year of the Lord in which we composed these things, 1493.

Johannes of Düsseldorf, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, a very celebrated interpreter of the faculty of theology, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in life, is said to write many things, but [unclear]. I saw certain treatises of his, whose titles I have not now been able to recall to memory. He lives to this day at Strasbourg, under Maximilian, most clement king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493, the twelfth indiction.

Theodericus Visenius, a Frisian man of singular learning, persistent in poetry and oratory. Among his works are extant:

Cultivated Elegies. And other epigrams, 1 book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

And many other things which will come down to posterity. He is still living under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Hartmann Schedel of Nuremberg, a German by nation, doctor of arts and medicine, and not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, compiled and wrote, among other little works of his talent, from Jacobus of Bergamo and other historiographers, adding some things, especially concerning German affairs, a great and distinguished work, which contains:

Histories of the Times, 10 books. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He lives to this day at Nuremberg, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494. [unclear]

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the Bishop in Spanheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, a German by nation, a Mosellan by homeland, born from the village of Trittenheim in the diocese of Trier: although I am not worthy for my name to be placed among the ecclesiastical writers, because of the poverty of my intellect, nevertheless, compelled by the urging of friends, I have been forced at the end of this catalogue [unclear] also of my lucubrations [unclear] the priest of Autun, Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who also placed themselves at the end of their treatises published on these same matters. Therefore I wrote, besides this work, also the following. And first, indeed, by command of the presiding officers of the general chapter, I abridged:

The Statutes

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Statutes of the same chapter, one book. “Since for one wishing [to know] each thing...”

On the visitation of monks, one book. “You shall visit your brothers.”

On the manner of keeping chapter, one book. “Since in holding chap[ters]...”

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, two books. “Come, sons, listen to me.”

An exhortation to monks, two books. “Of the Christian warfare [unclear]...”

two books. “The human race through...”

On the life of priests, one book. “You ask me, Nicholas, [unclear]...”

On the vice of property, one book. “All toward eternal life...”

On the misery of this life, one book. “Since the present life is nothing...”

On the ruin of our order, one book. “Since the former [state] of our order...”

On the illustrious men of our order, four books. “As I was thinking and repeatedly...”

Praises of the Carmelite order, two books. “At the prayers and insistence...”

On the praise of writers, one book. “To the venerable father, lord G...”

On the luminaries of Germany, one book. “Since there are some...”

Letters to various persons, one book. “You ask that copies...”

Various sermons, one book.

Conferences, indeed, delivered both in general chapters and in observantine ones, or elsewhere, without fixed number, are partly extant and partly have been taken away, besides those which still remain unfinished in my hands; these I recall having written up to the present, in the thirty-fourth year of my age, the tenth of my assumption of the office of abbot, and the twelfth of my monastic life, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, when Alexander VI was supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which I have now for the third time corrected, enlarged, and completed this catalogue, having labored on it for nearly seven years: 1493, in the twelfth indiction.

Now therefore, after many labors at last, let us put an end to our work, since, even if many men worthy of the catalogue of illustrious writers remain, it was nevertheless impossible for us to find even the names alone of all of them. But those of whom I was able to have certainty I have diligently set down, and I have knowingly omitted no one whose little works, talent, and times I could know. Nor am I unaware how many very learned men survive today, composing various things, of whom I have made no mention: not because I judged them unworthy of our catalogue, but because they either preferred to hide their little works, or they have not yet been so multiplied that they could come to my knowledge. I have done as much as I could, not as much as I wished, since, if it had been permitted, I would have brought together for myself all writers, as many as there are or ever have been. I leave to posterity this province: that they should add from their own vein where I, wearied, have stopped.

Moreover, I beseech you, enrolled fathers, who hold the heavenly kingdoms, who adorn this catalogue of ours with your names, talents, and studies: if we have written things about you that are true, just, worthy, and finally pleasing, pray for us to the tender mercy of almighty God, that he may wash away our faults, grant pardon, strengthen our holy purpose, enlighten our understanding, purify our affection, and graciously make us sharers in your joys. But if in some matters we have been able to do less than the matter itself required, grant us pardon, O most holy ones, because wherever there has been error, it is the fault of ignorance, not of will.

You also, O most distinguished men and writers, who still lead mortal earthly life, I call upon you, I adjure and beseech you: if in this catalogue we have accomplished anything less worthy of your merits, talents, or studies, ascribe it not to our will but to our inexperience, and do not deny the pardon which we ask, because, insofar as we have failed, it was the fault of those who described your little works or talents to us otherwise than the matter stands. Then we admonish and beseech the reader of this catalogue not to be readily moved against us if he finds the names, dignities, native lands, or little works of writers set down otherwise than perhaps he has read elsewhere, since no one has ever been able to reconcile the discordance of histories of a time past. Nor have we written anything that has not been confirmed in many places or by many testimonies. But, as we professed at the beginning of this work, we gladly yield to the opinion of any well-disposed corrector, an opinion which truth has made sound and charity sincere.

Lastly, rivals are indeed to be laughed at by us: those who, barking like dogs from the worst habit, condemn everything, disparage everything, tear apart everything which either they themselves have not made or have found to be contrary to their own opinions. For as soon as they have begun to read even a little, in indignation they say that it is not true, made rash judges before they have become examiners of truth. But what cause have we with those who disparage nothing except the good, praise nothing except the evil? Envious dogs, therefore, are to be despised, not taught. But we...

Additions of Certain Men ...we may consider it glorious to displease the malicious, yet we judge it far more glorious to have pleased good and learned men; by them, if there had been error anywhere, we are gladly corrected, and, once corrected, are more fruitfully amended. Let love of the Scriptures excuse us, for whose sake we have taken this heavy burden upon an intrepid neck. End of the book On Ecclesiastical Writers of Lord Johannes de Trittenheim, Abbot of Sponheim. There follow additions of certain illustrious men.

An addition to the foregoing, of illustrious men, partly excerpted here and there, partly recently inserted.

Marianus, Roman by nation, [Genazzanensis?] by native place, of the order of the hermits of St Augustine, a most skilled theologian and prior general of the whole order, shone forth in this our age, like the morning star and a certain most brilliant sun, by his most exquisite declamations and by a certain new manner of preaching; and, offered to the world as if another vessel of election, he displayed such force of talent and strength in teaching that I would dare to say that no one could ever have been found in this century who [unclear] might be compared with him. Indeed he was of such quality and so great that nothing in any more polished discipline could be vainly desired in him. For in his declamations to the people he was so eloquent and sententious in choice words, and also so suited to the matter by his melodious voice, countenance, and other movements of the body, that you could add nothing to the full measure of praise. How great this man’s learning was, and how great the force and majesty of his eloquence, anyone can clearly gather in part from the sermons and orations most learnedly published by him. For he wrote various sermons; one book of orations; one book of letters. He died, moreover, with great loss to the Christian commonwealth, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Felinus Sandeus, of the most noble family of the Sandei, a native of Ferrara, a most accomplished doctor of both laws and not ignorant of the rest of good letters. First at Ferrara, then at Pisa, in the public university of those cities, he professed canon law to the great admiration of all. Summoned to Rome by Innocent VIII, he was placed in charge of the college of the Rota, where difficult and very important business is handled. Although he was occupied with a thousand affairs, because he was of almost divine and most consummate prudence in both laws, he published many little works and commentaries in it. And these indeed so clearly, so learnedly, so exactly, that he untied all the knots of this discipline, restored obscure matters to the light, and, with right judgment applied to doubtful matters, made them easy and open; in this he brought no small assistance to our jurists. The works which he sent forth are appended: first, on the books of the Decretals of Gregory: On Constitutions; On Rescripts; On the Office of the Ordinary; On Majority and Obedience; On Witnesses; On Compelled Witnesses; On the Credibility of Instruments; On Presumptions; On Oath-taking; On Exceptions; On Prescriptions; On Sentence and Res Judicata; On Appeals; On Accusations and Inquisitions. Additions to the Decretum, to the work begun by the abbot. One treatise On the Right of Patronage. A sermon On Plenary Indulgence, whose theme is: Today you will be with me in paradise, etc. In history, one little book On the Neapolitan Kings. There are also other commentaries of his. He flourished at Rome under Innocent VIII and Alexander VI.

Matthaeus Bossus, a native of Verona, of the order of the regular canons of blessed Augustine, a man excellently learned in every kind of erudition, but still more learned in elegance and gravity of speech, was held in great esteem among all, both from the office of preaching and teaching, in which he was long engaged, and from the various works composed by him, by which he so adorned and polished ecclesiastical dogma with rhetorical embellishments that you would find nothing more refined or more elegant. He wrote the following little works: a Dialogue on Enduring Adversities, divided into two books; On Bearing Office and Cultivating Justice, addressed to Johannes Ludovicus Bossus, jurist and golden knight, one book; Letters to various persons, one book. He also published certain other works, in all of which, since varied learning shines forth, and everywhere [unclear].

Of Illustrious Men.

however brilliant he was, he nowhere breathed out any smoke of arrogance, but, as befits a religious man, was everywhere most devoted to holiness and divine wisdom. He died at Padua, in the year of the Lord 1502.

Antonius Cornazanus, a native of Ferrara, a most brilliant orator and poet, so polished, copious, and pleasing, especially in poetry, that many suppose he received poetry from the mouths of angels. For among other works he sang of the life and death of the Virgin Mother of God so devoutly, piously, copiously, brilliantly, and holily that all proclaim his poetry not mortal but altogether divine. He inscribed and dedicated that work to Hippolita, queen of the Neapolitans, while she was still a maiden.

He published certain elegies and various poems.

He wrote in prose the life of Bartholomaeus Coloneus, the greatest commander of the Venetians.

Commentaries on Juvenal. On Statius and many others.

He published certain centuries. Many books of letters.

He died at Milan, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Georgius Merula, a native of Alessandria, an orator and philosopher most learned in both languages, always served literature well by teaching and writing. He wrote, in many volumes, the deeds of Ludovicus Sporcia and of his ancestors.

Commentaries on Juvenal, book 1.

He published certain centuries.

Also: many letters.

Very many orations as well, and certain other things.

Bernardinus Gadolu, a Brescian, Camaldolese abbot, a man especially learned in good letters, philosophy, and canon law, renowned for holiness of life and religion, left us many monuments of his learning, in which he shows himself most learned.

He wrote commentaries on all the books of the Bible.

On fleeing the world and embracing religion, one treatise.

Against pride and ambition, book 1.

He arranged the works of Jerome in order.

Also: many letters.

He published various sermons of the same man.

Book 1, On the Lives of the Venetian Princes. Book 1.

Works of his are extant, scattered here and there.

And certain other things on the Venetian magistrates.

Having completed his life, he is buried honorably in the Camaldolese monastery.

Rogerus Sanutus, a Venetian patrician, was not only a man learned in good letters, but also skilled in the administration of the commonwealth; he excelled greatly in eloquence, as can easily be recognized from his little works. For he wrote the following.

On the Magistrates of Venice, book 1. On the Accents of the Latins, book 1.

On the Gallic War, certain books, in Latin and in the vernacular.

He wrote certain other things.

Many epigrams to various persons.

Very many letters, both in prose and in verse.

Philippus Beroaldus, a native of Bologna, most skilled in both languages and easily the foremost of all grammarians, rhetoricians, and orators of his age, left no ordinary testimonies of his most fertile talent.

Orations delivered in exposition of various authors.

A panegyric to Lodovicus Sphortia.

One oration On the Marriage of the Bentivoli.

The history of Gisippus and Titus.

Also that of Galesus and Symon.

One proverbial oration.

One little book on the sayings of the seven sages.

Symbols of Pythagoras, book 1.

book 1.

On the best state, book 1.

On happiness

Additions of Certain [Writers]

The declamation of a philosopher, a physician, and an orator. The declamation of a drunkard, a whoremonger, and a gambler. On the Lord's Passion, [unclear]. A poem on Fortune. A poem on two lovers. A poem on Cupid, god of love. A poem against a slanderous woman. Various epigrams. A little work on earthquake and plague, with notes of Galen. Notes on Servius. Notes on civil law. Commentaries on Propertius. On Suetonius. On the Tusculan Questions. On Apuleius. Notes on Titus Livius. On Cicero's Rhetoric. On Horace Flaccus. On Persius. On Silius Italicus.

He also wrote many other works which have not yet come down to us. He died at Bologna, not without great loss to the world of letters, in the year of the Lord 1510.

Ponticus Virunio, by birth, as they say, of Treviso, a most learned philosopher, a student of Latin and Greek literature, by industry, toil, and liveliness of talent, without any help from his parents, advanced so far in learning that, because of his enormous erudition, he was held in great esteem with Ludovico Sforza throughout all Insubria.

He wrote the following works: Commentaries on Claudian. Commentaries on the Sphere of Johannes Sacrobosco. Three books On Obscure Passages in Authors and Corrupt Names. Two books On the Misery of Letters, in verse. One book On the Praises of Beatrice, queen of Milan, in verse. Two books of elegies and epigrams. A commentary on the Chremata of Chrysoloras. A commentary on the Achilleid of Statius. Commentaries on Ovid's Metamorphoses. Commentaries on the works of Virgil. Sixteen books On the Art of Divination. He translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin. Four books of hymns of the same Homer. Six tragedies of Euripides. In medicine he translated Theophilus. On pulses and urines. Likewise Aeneus on pulses and urines. One book of Inventions. One book On Titlings. He translated Apollonius' Argonautica into Latin in four books. He also made and published many other Latin works. He flourished under Ludovico Sforza.

Nicolaus Leonicenus, the most elegant of all orators of his age, most accomplished in philosophy, not ignorant of natural things, treated many matters in medicine elegantly and copiously.

Likewise there is a little work in the same discipline, in which he taught that health and life can be restored and procured for all the sick.

Very many letters of the same man are extant, which display his very great learning and elegance. He flourished at this same time in Italy under Ludovico Sforza.

Ambrosius Calepinus of Bergamo, of the order of Saint Augustine, flourished in this age, a most zealous investigator of divine and human letters. Hence, by his own industry and with great labor, he made common to us a very large work, collected from almost innumerable authors, concerning knowledge of vocabulary and the interpretation of Greek and Latin prepositions, with attestation from the authors. In it not only those words which contribute very much to knowledge of literature, poets, and learned men, but also the words which pertain to physicians and philosophers, and also to ecclesiastical doctors, are explained learnedly enough and elegantly, so that in clearer light than in certain other works, where barbarous men had already made barbarous things, they may become Latin. But those things which among the doctors were being called into doubt now lie open, the cloud of uncertainty having been dispelled.

Petrus Burrus, a Belgian, by birth of Bruges, canon of Amiens, renowned in divine and human letters, flourished at Paris under Charles VIII, king of the French, where his youth, celebrated for good disciplines, virtues, most approved morals, piety, and religion,

Of Illustrious Men [unclear]

...grew up. As very many people, and especially the Gandincourt family, would have wished to have this one man alone as teacher for instructing their children and many other rather noble youths. Nor indeed should one swear it, since he is one among the few in our age who taught how to join eloquence, poetry, and the other good arts with wisdom, and that the arts without morals, but morals without letters, are of no benefit. This, indeed, his works show; in them you would not know what most to admire: the weight of the most serious and most holy thoughts; or the variety of style and poetry; or the elegance of things and words; or the skillful joinings; or the pleasing texture of little words; or the flow and harmony that repeatedly mark the verse; or, finally, six hundred other adornments, so that one might deservedly say that all graces, charms, delights, and beauties of speech have been most abundantly gathered here, although nothing either swollen or inflated is seen. Therefore, if this Burrus had written in Quintilian’s time, he would certainly not have said: “Among lyric poets Horace almost alone is worthy to be read.” For this man is most worthy to be read even by holy nuns. Indeed, since he is wholly chaste and wholly Christian, which that man is not, he sweetly breathes forth the Christian religion. Yet no less than he does this man sometimes rise full of delight, grace, varied figures, and most happily bold words, as it is easy to discern from his works listed below and issued into the light. These, then, are the monuments of that most fertile talent:

Four books of Odes. One book of Hexameters.

One book of Apologues. Two books of Elegies.

One book of Epigrams. Of Moral Poems.

Songs on the two feasts. On the Advent of the Lord.

On the vigil of the Lord. On the Nativity of the Lord.

On the Circumcision of the Lord. On Epiphany.

On fasting. On the Entry into Jerusalem.

On Confession. On the Eucharist. On the Lord’s Supper.

On the praise of the Cross. On the Lord’s Passion. On Easter Communion.

On the feast of blessed Mary. On the Ascension of the Lord.

On the Finding of the Cross. On the Trinity.

On Pentecost. On the Exaltation of the Cross. Hymns on All Saints.

On the Body of the Lord. Hymns on philosophy [unclear].

On the Lord’s Face. [unclear]

On the feast of blessed Mary.

There are certain other things printed by Apianus in the year 1507.

Iacobus Faber Stapulensis, the most celebrated philosopher of our age, the one glory of Belgium, indeed of all France. In our time he was given by a certain divine gift as a remedy for the world of letters. He rescued all parts of philosophy from the shadowy barbarism of certain sophists. And where they had already completely unlearned how to speak Latin and had gone far away from the mind of Aristotle and of the other true philosophers, he restored the majestic dignity of juridical speech and teaching, with such structure and sequence that nothing is lacking to be added, and nothing presents itself that could be removed without fault. So great is the industry, so great the art in all his works, so great the dignity in his speech, that anyone even moderately learned may, together with philosophy, most richly attain eloquence, which previously was not permitted. For he was the first among the Gauls, as Cicero among the Romans, to join philosophy, still raw and unpolished, with eloquence. For when previously he was sojourning at Paris, he endowed it with citizenship. Hence not only untrained philosophers, but even learned men think that they have gained something for speaking and for judging. For in speech he is lofty; in thoughts, weighty; in invention, choice; in composition, careful and exacting; and not only in his own works, but also in those of others. Indeed, he seems to have been born for this one purpose: to take thought for the literary arena, to restore the good arts, and to bring them back to their ancient splendor. Such is this man’s care, such his delight in study; to this all his thinking, to this his mind, to this his spirit is directed. That this might happen more freely, he not only, like Demetrius, gave over to his own people the patrimony which he had at Étaples and which was not to be despised, but he cast aside dignities, offices, benefices, and wealthy honors, thinking with Crates the Theban that such things rarely cling to virtues. Finally, to conclude everything in a short verse:

Faber has enriched our age with wisdom.

What follows are the things composed by him in the liberal arts. The first is:

A Paraphrase on Aristotle’s Logic, worked out with wonderful artistry.

An Introduction to Aristotle’s Physics, and a Paraphrase composed in a style not unlearned.

Some Additions

A paraphrase and introduction on the Ethics of the same author.

A commentary on the Oeconomics. A commentary and introduction on the Politics.

A commentary, with demonstrations, on the Arithmetic of Jordanus.

An epitome on the arithmetic books of Severinus Boethius.

Certain elements on Music.

A commentary on the astronomical introduction of John of Sacrobosco.

An introduction to the six books of Aristotle's Metaphysics; a commentary on the same.

Other and greater works, indeed, are awaited in the faculty of the liberal arts. But, not content with these, the most religious man directed his mind to divine matters and gave himself wholly to them, destined to bring great adornment and assistance to our theologians, the searchers of the divine word, since he explains what is involved, illuminates what is obscure, unties what is knotted, and restores here and there passages that are truncated and mutilated. This can easily be perceived from those things which, in this most sacred discipline of divine wisdom, he either translated, or wrote, or saw to it that they were printed in a more correct and more emended form.

They are the following:

A translation of John of Damascus. Commentaries on Richard.

On the Trinity. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes.

Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul. Scholia on the works of Dionysius the Areopagite.

On the Adornment of Spiritual Nuptials. Commentaries on Hugh of St Victor.

He lives in Paris, daily forging certain new things on his craftsman's anvil.

Guilhelmus Budaeus of Paris, born of the most illustrious family of the Budaei, a historian, poet, philosopher, and most eloquent orator. He is splendidly endowed not only with gifts of fortune but also with gifts of mind. In this our time he is becoming famous throughout all Italy, and not only throughout Gaul, because of his incredible knowledge of all branches of wisdom; day by day he is most learned in both languages, of almost divine talent, grave and serious in speech, most learned in every kind of discipline, and besides his singular learning a man truly most humane, affable, modest, and worthy of great veneration. He wrote very many orations and letters; diverse elegies and epigrams. He published Annotations on twenty-four books of the Pandects, or Digest. He will publish annotations on the remaining books, as he himself testifies in the letter which he writes to Jean de Ganay, great chancellor of France. How great the learning and doctrine of these annotations is, is left for each person to weigh. He lives in Paris, to the great expectation of all; greater works from him will shortly come to light.

Guilhelmus Castellus, or Castalius, a Gaul, a poet and most [unclear] orator of Tours, was born at Tours, his father being Christianus Castellus, a Parisian doctor and royal physician, his mother a woman of Bourges, in the year of the Lord 1468. There, taught the first beginnings of letters, he was sent to Paris, as is the custom, to undertake more fruitful and more solid disciplines, to Johannes Anglicus, his maternal brother, a man exceptionally [unclear] in divine and human letters. Entering the College of Navarre, to use the common word, he was to succeed there, where in liberal studies, through uprightness and learning, he not only equalled those who went before him but even far surpassed them. So great was his thirst for literature, so great his love, so great his care, so great his zeal. Hence, soon known by fame beyond [unclear], he was summoned to the College of Burgundy to instruct the youth in better and more polished letters by Bernhardus Roilletus, a man most richly furnished with all good disciplines and chief rector of the same college, and he was placed over the first class of the humanities. Then, after the contest of dialectic had been endured and his pupils had been presented with the laurel, he returned to the College of Navarre, joining divine studies, for which he had always yearned, to the human disciplines. At length, having obtained the doctorate in the most sacred faculty of theology, he withdrew to Tours, where, honored with honorable ecclesiastical benefices, an archdeaconry and a canonry, he lives among his own, attending to prayer and [unclear], as he has now begun, with many works which he has sent into the light. Their titles are appended below.

A Sibylline poem on the Last Judgment.

An eclogue, whose name is Enmorphis. A poem on the foolish vows of women.

A dialogue in praise of Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples.

One book of elegies.

One book of epigrams.

Letters

10 26 35 49

Of Illustrious Men.

Many and various letters to diverse persons. Far greater things are expected.

JOHANNES Bartholus, Parisian, doctor of medicine, the most excellent of all in this age, and for that reason specially endowed, even by various most devoted and most expert lovers of every discipline, with the name of Apollo and Aesculapius. He is of such authority in learning among all men that you will assuredly find no one whom you could compare with him, whether you seek what belongs to his own profession or what belongs to any other doctrine. For, most accomplished in every kind of discipline, he discusses all things so learnedly, so elegantly, so skilfully and readily, and has so deep an understanding, that he alone seems to have embraced with the greatest zeal all arts, both divine and human.

ANTONIUS Sylviolus, Parisian, notable poet and orator, although he is skilled in many kinds of languages, excels nevertheless in three: French, Latin, and the common Italian tongue. By these he has won for himself, among all men and also among the most learned and noble, especially the foremost and most renowned nobles of the Amboise house of the French nation, such fame and favor as no detraction of the envious can dissolve, no devouring decay of age abolish, since already by this threefold gift of language he has sought immortality for himself, and is regarded among our countrymen as no less in this most charming fluency of the French language than Dante among the Florentines. But how great an eloquence he possesses by labor and by the light of his own talent, by what subtlety of invention he stands out, by what art of arrangement he excels, with what fertility of variety he abounds, and finally with what weight of matter and sententiae he advances, his very splendid works, several serious dialogues, [unclear] most richly. For he wrote many splendid works, especially several comedies in his own vernacular, in which he showed how various, how abundant, how fluent, how elegant, how witty, and finally how urbane he was. In Latin, however, he published the following:

One book of Elegies. One book of Epigrams.

They bear witness. He has written and writes every day other things far greater, by which he may show that the French have their poets and orators, not inferior to the Italians, indeed superior to them. If they were to expend constant and unwearied labor upon these languages, in which every Italian either flatters or catches the breeze, [unclear]. He still lives and feeds on the ethereal air, orator of the reverend father in Christ, Georges d’Amboise, archbishop of Rouen.

GUILHELMUS Copus of Basel, a most learned philosopher and very skilled in Latin and Greek, excels in this our age at Paris in the medical art, of which he is a most eminent doctor and professor. To his house not only Parisians resort as to the single remedy of health, but even those who preside over this our kingdom, having heard the man’s fame, send for him with utmost speed and summon him, and experience his aid. Alone among all the prelates of this profession he has begotten a name for himself, I do not know whether immortal or rather enviable. This Guillelmus is subtle in talent, polished in speech, eloquent in discourse, admirable in learning, to be placed after no one in knowledge of natural things. He lives at Paris under Louis the Twelfth of this name, with great expectation of him among all. For he is forging things for posterity to read, among which we already have:

The Salutary Precepts of Paulus Aegineta, clothed by him in Latin elegance.

The same man’s Prognostics of Hippocrates.

JUDOCUS Clichtoveus of Nieuwpoort, doctor, most accomplished theologian, most polished philosopher, and so notable an orator that he orders the untamed manners of men, indeed the whole mortal race, with eloquence divine rather than mortal. Born for these duties, he directs one ignorant of letters with straight reins and enlightens the foolish with polished speech. Nature the parent has marked this man with dignity, with these most noble gifts of mind, so that whatever he undertakes in this sensible world he adapts to the propagation of literary learning. For he strives with all his might to polish what is rough, foul, gaping, and barbarous, and to restore to philosophy its own brilliance; above all, he resolves in soul and mind to devote his effort to interpreting deeds and sayings. Divine utterances and knowledge of supramundane things so adorn him that, while he is still breathing mortal life on earth, they admit him to the most radiant choirs of the heavenly ones. He has left to us and to future posterity most abundant and outstanding monuments of his learning in a great number of volumes, intending at last to restore greater things. For he wrote the things which are set out in this sequence:

A commentary on the Elegances of Augustinus Dathus.

A commentary on the Introduction to Arithmetic of Severinus Boethius. A compendium On the Practice of Numbering.

A commentary on Johannes Damascenus. An excellent book On True Nobility.

Scholia on the paraphrase of Aristotle’s Physics.

E.I S

Additions Concerning Certain Men

A commentary on the prepared introduction to Aristotle’s Physics.

A commentary on the prepared introduction to the books of Aristotle’s Metaphysics.

A commentary on the elaborated introduction to Aristotle’s Ethics.

CHARLES Bovillus, [of Vermandois?], of Amiens, a man polished with rhetorical fluency, poetic variety, and the most glittering splendor of all philosophy, and an eminent geometer. Nature is believed to have brought him forth to investigate the divine secrets of things and the hidden essences of all beings, rather than that, confined in a mortal body, he should lead a human life. For he was endowed with so refined a sharpness of intellect that he not only brings into the light the natures of earthly beings, previously covered in blind darkness, but, with philosophy as his guide, penetrates most deeply the star-bearing spheres and the open structure of the heavens; by the philosophical proportion of worldly things he shows beforehand the natures of supernatural beings, and by philosophical demonstration and the most unified scrutiny of earthly things exactly prefigures the [ineffable?] Trinity, the number, of the heavenly court. He was altogether so devoted to the contemplation of the highest philosophy and to geometrical abstractions that very often, for nine hours, leaning against the trunk of a tree, with unmoving eyes and motionless body, forgetful of himself, his own, and human sustenance, the mass of his body as it were dissolved, he seemed to dwell in the heavens rather than, bound by human ties, to draw vital breaths in this sensible world. By the keenness of his intellect he discovered many things unknown to former ages. For he worked out the quadrature of the circle by his own geometrical devices, which no philosopher before had discovered with sufficient exactness. With great admiration from all, he wrote a book On Nothing with wondrous ingenuity, and he left to posterity very many other philosophical works which no mortal in past ages had foreseen.

Six introductory books on Geometry. One book On the Quadrature of the Circle. An Introduction to the Science of Perspective. A book On the Divine, Angelic, and Human Intellect. A book On Sense. A book On Nothing. The Art of Opposites. A book On Generation. A book On the Wise Man. A book On the Twelve Numbers. Several philosophical letters.

GUILHELMUS de Quercu, an eminent doctor of theology, in this our age most distinguished among all other mortals in counsel, morals, and sacred eloquence. When that majesty of the French was pressed by the dreadful assault of the supreme pontiff, the English, and the Spaniards, with the cruel apparatus of wars, he alone, by his counsel and the sound judgment of his mind, most kindly came to meet the straitened necessity of the French. Crossing the Alps, he indeed reached the city of [Pisa?], where, in a very great assembly of cardinals and bishops concerning the French affair, disturbed by so great a prodigy of wars, he strengthened it by the sagacity of his mind alone and claimed for himself the more eminent parts of so great a council. Nor does he use lesser eloquence among the people for the undertaking of divine offices. For he is cultivated with such weight of judgments and knowledge of divine counsels that he easily composes the untamed manners of mortals and barbarous peoples with fluent eloquence, and easily leads them back to the bright recognition of the highest Creator by his kindly voice, pleasing eyes, moderated gesture, and delightful comparisons.

RENATUS Garnerius of Luçon, doctor in both laws, most learned in our age, who, because of his brilliance in every kind of discipline, and especially in the distinguished faculty of laws, has spread his fame and distinction through various regions of the earth, and has deservedly and easily claimed for himself everywhere the roles of Lycurgus and Socrates in establishing and interpreting laws. For by a rather polished eloquence of speech and a tested profession he increased the sagacity of his mind, so that he has adorned the [Pictavian?] territories with perpetual honor and daily ennobles all France by his eminence.

CHRISTOPHER Longolius, a Parisian, a most ingenious philosopher and the most distinguished orator of our century. Just as mother Nature adorned him with the greatest gifts of mind, so she most abundantly endowed him with [unclear] by a most pleasing dexterity. He increased [unclear] nature by labor and exercise, so that he emerged as the most distinguished philosopher and most abundant orator of our age. He professed Pliny in the renowned academy of Poitiers with an inexpressible structure, so that he seemed to all without distinction to rely not on mortal eloquence, but rather to be strengthened by a variety of judgments drawn from the innermost places of the heavens. The Parisian academy, nurse of disciplines, instructed him not inelegantly in morals, rhetorical vigor, and philosophical letters; nevertheless, not satisfied with Gallic eloquence, he went with hasty step to Italian homes, supposing that he would attain greater things, where easily, by experience of affairs and by his polished

Of Illustrious Men.

[unclear] in eloquence, at last, retracing his steps, he reached the borders of Gaul, where he produced proofs of his eloquence and learning. For in his twenty-fourth year, consulting posterity with an innumerable variety of volumes, he published monuments of his learning and left them to his followers in this ordered sequence:

An oration on Saint Louis, king of the Franks, and on the praises of the Gallic nation, addressed to Francis of Valois, the Dauphin.

Almost innumerable orations and letters. Various elegies and epigrams.

Commentaries on Pliny, which he publicly interpreted at Poitiers learnedly and elegantly, to the great admiration of all.

Certain works on civil law, while he was publicly teaching it at Poitiers.

Johannes Stephanus flourished in our time, Italian by nation, bishop of Vercelli, cardinal of Bologna, a most exacting cultivator of literary study; the higher fortune raised him by the most eminent dignities, the more nature adorned him with nobler gifts of mind. Indeed, he always set leisure for letters and the refined natures of things above even all the most illustrious summits of dignities. And at last, by his own unwearied labor and industry, he brought it about that Aristotle’s Great Ethics, never known beforehand in earlier ages, became common property for us. Jacobus Faber, the most eminent philosopher of our age and a most vigorous defender of philosophy, arranged these for his printing, which will bring no small benefits to posterity.

Guilhelmus de Mera flourished in this time, a Neustrasian by nation, born from the village of [Constantinus?], of parents of noble lineage and of most holy life.

He is now canon and treasurer of the cathedral church of Coutances, and a distinguished orator and poet. When he was still a boy, the distinguished theologian Doctor Johannes Boucardus, formerly bishop of Avranches and royal confessor, undertook to have him educated in the disciplines because of the excellent gifts of mind that he saw in the boy. Nor did he merely see to it that the boy was instructed by others; when he had leisure, he also taught him himself, taking no small delight in so fertile a cultivation. And he hoped so much from his excellent natural ability that he did not hesitate to endow him at that age with a benefice, and certainly would have given greater things if he had survived. Finally Guilhelmus himself set out for the renowned study of Paris and in a short interval of time reached such a point that no one was regarded as more celebrated than he in the art of oratory or poetry. When the once archbishop of Reims and chancellor of France, [Robert Briçonnet?], heard the reputation of so great a man, he summoned him to himself among his secretaries. When this Robert died, Charles VIII gave this Guilhelmus to his chancellor, Guido de Rochefort. For Charles loved Guilhelmus because of the not inelegant rhymes which he knew how to compose most elegantly in the French tongue, and also because of his skill in writing in every kind of letters, in which he saw no equal. Afterwards the most reverend cardinal of Saint-Malo, Guilhelmus Briçonnet, obtained him from Guido de Rochefort to be his confidential adviser, and he remained with him for a long time. But at last, weary of the misery of courtiers and ill bearing the waste of time, he withdrew to the study of Caen, where he was endowed with the dignity of rector and afterwards with the doctoral laurel in both laws. And in that study he professed the laws for several years. At last he was taken up as canon and treasurer of the cathedral church of Coutances, where he resides, serving himself alone with good letters, with which he is going to enrich posterity.

These are the proofs of his learning that already survive:

Conflictus in Chimeram, addressed to Johannes de Ganay, great chancellor of France, a very excellent and holy work, in which he elegantly attacked those three principal vices by which the whole world is infected and poisoned, namely pride, lust, and avarice.

A little work on the fact of the holy Eucharist, addressed to Guilhelmus, bishop of Coutances.

A paraphrase on Musaeus, concerning Hero and Leander, addressed to Nicolas de Cerisay, dean of Saint-Germain of Paris.

One book On Loves, addressed to the same man. One book On Divine Things.

In addition he wrote many things in [metrical?] discourse which have not yet come to light.

One book On Praises, addressed to Johannes Briçonnet, president of the royal accounts.

One book On Reproaches, addressed to Carolus Guillart, president of the Parlement of Paris.

Of [unclear] and epitaphs.

He flourished, as appears from certain of his writings, around the times of Charles VI of France, [unclear].

When his books had been scattered in quires, Brother Robert Bai[guardus?] gathered them together again.

Matthaeus of Evreux, a Norman, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a most profound investigator of the Scriptures, a man full of [strict?] religion and of letters, produced an excellent postil on the Pentateuch with Isaiah and very many other books of the Old and New Testament. It was placed in the common library of the convent of Evreux of the aforesaid order, of which he had been an alumnus, [unclear]. When his books had been scattered in quires, Brother Bai[guardus?] gathered them together again.

Additions of Certain Men

[unclear]guardus, doctor of theology and confessor of the Most Christian king of the Franks, Charles VII, of the convent of the same order, and he deposited it in the common library of that house.

Guido of Evreux, compiler of excellent sermons, is believed also to have flourished around these times, a brother of the same order; he also, besides the rules of Tyconius, gave certain very apt instructions for grasping the sense of sacred Scripture, showing that through ignorance of four things it often happens that one errs in the exposition of sacred doctrine. These are found collected among the rest of his works in the libraries of certain convents.

Laurentius Gervasius, of the convent of Lisieux of the Order of Preachers in Normandy, in the reign of Louis XI, king of the Franks, was held famous at Paris as a doctor and theologian, a man indeed most renowned for knowledge and doctrine. Because of his outstanding wisdom, since he was especially versed in the doctrine of the most holy doctor Thomas Aquinas, he was sent to reform for the better the study at Cologne. When he had made extraordinary progress there, returning thence, he gave up the spirit at Dijon, a town of Burgundy, and there he was buried with the brothers of his order. He left very useful works, which are called the collected works of Master Laurentius Gervasius, on the whole Summa of Theology of the Angelic Doctor; of that doctrine, indeed, while he lived, he was called the mart.

Silvester of Prierio, of Bologna, of the Order of Friars Preachers, venerable doctor and very famous expositor and likewise most learned defender of Saint Thomas Aquinas, flourished around the times of Innocent VIII, supreme pontiff.

He wrote a defense of the doctrine of Saint Thomas, abridging the writings of John Capreolus, demonstrating more clearly than light the irrefragable doctrine of the most holy doctor, dissolving from his sayings the arguments of all opponents.

He also wrote an Introduction to Logic.

Item, a Summa of Sermons, which is called The Golden Rose.

Item, a Summa on Cases of Conscience.

Item, The Hammer of the Scotists.

Item, on the four books of the Sentences.

He has continued writing even to the present time, dwelling at Bologna, namely up to the year of the Lord 1522.

Dominicus of Flanders, a very famous doctor, of the same Order, of Bologna, at the same times as the preceding man.

He wrote Metaphysical Questions.

Questions on the Soul. Item, on the books of the Posterior Analytics.

He died when Alexander VIII, supreme pontiff, was presiding in the chair of Peter.

Paulus of Soncino, of the same Order, in these times.

He wrote Metaphysical Questions.

Item, on the Predicables and Predicaments.

At the same time, or thereabouts, as the preceding man, he departed this life.

The End.

Appendix

Letter of Master Jacob Wimpheling of Sélestat to the reverend father, Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, concerning the additions to the Catalogue of Germans.

Of Illustrious Men.

You have excerpted a portion of the luminaries of Germany, adding not a few who meanwhile came to your notice; I read it with all the more pleasure because I would have believed all the less that so great an abundance of excellent men had existed in Germany. I myself added, as you will see, even only the bare names of some, since I was not able to search out their works. Let us entrust this burden to posterity, so that, if there shall ever be in Germany men who love the praise and glory of their native nation, they may add from their own vein where we have now stopped, themselves to take up the work hereafter.

For henceforth uncouth and raw barbarism will not reign among the Germans, nor will it always be proclaimed as true what, in Lucan, Cato is once represented as having said: “Let the two battle-lines pierce me; let the barbarous throng of the Rhine attack me with missiles.” For many people, accustomed to magnify their own glory and diminish that of others, suppose that this barbarism of the Rhine or of Germany prevailed from the times of Julius down to our own age. Whether this is true, would that they might understand by meditating on the words of blessed Jerome, who, among the other calamities of the lands, also laments the miserable ruin of Germany, by no means passing over the lofty cities of the Rhine.

“Mainz,” he says, “once a noble city, has been captured and overthrown; in the church many thousands of people were butchered. The Vangiones were destroyed by a long siege. [Nemetae?] (which is now Speyer), Argentoratum (which is now called Argentina), were ravaged.” Surely [unclear]. Would Jerome have mentioned the disaster or destruction of those cities, if he had not known that in them there were then both most devout worshippers of Christ and men outstanding in learning and wisdom? Is it not a very strong and victorious argument that very many learned men once existed in Germany: so overflowing an abundance of very ancient volumes? Were the authors of those same works unlearned, or the scribes, or those who ordered them to be written, or those who used them every day? Or did a man of such piety grieve more that splendid walls, very strongly fortified places, or wealth were laid waste than that, in those same places, the most flourishing talents of very many people miserably perished?

Additions of Certain Persons

... What, then, would they object next? Is God, from whom every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, just as Simonides was falsely believed to begrudge metaphysics or divine knowledge to mortals, so pursuing the Germans alone with some singular envy, not favoring them, nor giving them keenness of mind, lively talent, elevated understanding, eager industry, firm memory, exercises of talent, and courses of the mind in which they may sweat and toil? Far from it; for God is without envy. For there is a pagan poet who sings: "Each man's beginnings will bring his toil and fortune; King Jupiter is the same for all."

I pass over the most learned men of Germany, who in our own time flourish in knowledge of every art and of all kinds of things, both in schools and monasteries, and in churches and the courts of princes: in regular grammar, in all dialectic, in music, in geometry, in the science of the stars, in Aristotelian philosophy, in all the mysteries of natural things, in moral disciplines, in oratory, in poetry, in all humane letters, in the most sacred laws, in pontifical canons, in divine institutions; they are most learned, outstanding in talent. They produce poems in every genre; they know histories and cosmography excellently; they write ornate treatises. I pass over these Germans of ours who are not ignorant of Greek letters. Indeed, Germans survive today who have translated Greek books into the Latin language not inelegantly.

Even if, perhaps, some Germans write sacred, humble, honorable, and most solid sentiments in a lowly style, are they therefore to be held cheap? Far from it. The old jurists, even Italians, are not to be cast aside; nor physicians, nor theologians, who set forth their old and excellent doctrines not with verbal paint and bombast, but in a calm manner of speaking and with moderate Latinity. Is the Italian Bonaventure to be rejected? In written works there is no one greater, no one more profound, no one more devout than he. Is Johannes Andreae to be rejected, or Hostiensis? or Baldus the Sicilian? Are all those men to be rejected as harsh, unpolished, rude, and shapeless, because after the manner of the scholastics they run through their teachings on a pedestrian plain? Or is no one to be judged learned unless he writes most elegantly in the Ciceronian manner? Or are all those who strive to adorn light, slippery, useless, obscene sentiments with a caparisoned style, wantonness of words, and license of composition to be judged most learned? Both are false.

Although that man is certainly more advanced who intermingles the sweetness of honeyed speech with distinguished, weighty, and profound sentiments. But we cannot all be Scipios, nor all like Nestor, from whose tongue, though he was aged and almost decrepit, speech flowed sweeter than honey. Therefore, if some of our countrymen have used not a highly polished but a doctrinal and everyday style of speech, they are not to be despised. For it was enough for them to speak in such a way that they might be understood in honorable matters. Indeed, just as for the farmer not only that land is to be cultivated which produces either the most precious spices or the most excellent gifts of Bacchus, so good men accept not only Ciceronian orations or the more polished works of noble poets, but also embrace middling works; they also read those walking in a humble buskin.

Finally, let them remember, I beseech them, those envious detractors, most bitter censors of our language, that styles of speaking change with the times, and that what is different is not immediately worse; but by the fault of human malice the old is always praised, the present is distasteful. It is sufficiently clear that even Cicero did not lack detractors, to whom he seemed swollen and puffed up, not compressed enough, exulting beyond measure, overflowing, and insufficiently antique. I would believe that our philosophers turned aside from that old and most ornate path of writing not through ignorance of eloquence, but that, after weighing the condition of the times, the subject, and the hearers, they changed the form and appearance of their speech. Let foreigners therefore cease to harass the Germans, who once described very lofty and most sacred matters under a plain and humble style.

What did that censor of the Latin language, Valla, seek? Pluto does not dare to speak Latin words. Jupiter deemed this man worthy of a part of heaven; but he fears him as censor of his own language.

Finally, to come down to the matter itself, reverend father, we add something to your Catalogue, beginning with the German Roman pontiffs, whom we do not think not excellent, nor much inferior to many others. Then we have joined the rest here and there, without order, just as they came to mind, asking pardon from the kindly reader for brevity, confusion, and an undigested, inelegant style. Farewell, most elegant Father, sole glory of the divine order, exemplar of honor, from Sponheim. On the Ides of October, in the year 1492. Pro-

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Of Illustrious Men. Supplement or Addition. Of Illustrious Germans, by Jakob Wimpheling of Sélestat: composed after the Catalogue of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

When recently the reverend father Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, induced by my requests, had published the Catalogue of the illustrious men of Germany and sent it to me, I found that the supreme pontiffs of the city of Rome chosen from among the Teutons were missing, and also [certain?] others, in my judgment worthy of remembrance; and I was grieved, and at once resolved to add those who had been neglected and to commend them to posterity, if only by their names. For our most dutiful father Trithemius had long ago, with my knowledge, adopted this rule: to introduce absolutely no one into his Catalogue unless both the times of his life and the little works of his talent had become certainly known to him. But I, since I believe that no German could have been raised to the height of the supreme pontificate without exceptional learning, although their works have not reached us, shall by no means pass them by.

Stephen, therefore, Pope VIII, born from Germany, is not to be thought to have been able to be elevated to the most holy summit of the Roman see without exceptional excellence both in virtues and in learning, although, harassed by the tyranny of the Romans, he experienced fortune hostile to him with grief, so that he could do nothing magnificent or distinguished or worthy of remembrance. Sebastian Murrho of Colmar also mentions him, in his work on the virtues and magnificence of the Germans. He flourished under Emperor Otto I, in the year of the Lord 942.

Gregory, Pope V, a Saxon by race, by establishing and ordaining the electors of the Roman Empire, to whom the election of the emperor was entrusted with unassailable perpetuity, happily and beneficially provided for the holy Roman Empire with his wondrous prudence, fearing that offspring might at some time degenerate from the virtues of their grandfathers and fathers. He flourished under Otto III, in the year of the Lord 995.

Clement, Pope II, previously called Synderus, crowned Henry II, who compelled the Romans to swear allegiance to him, that he would never hereafter interfere in the election of pontiffs: a very excellent and salutary decree, instituted for the Romans by the pontiff and the prince, both of them, as is allowed, Teutons. He flourished under Henry III, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1047.

Leo, Pope IX, Alsatian by nation, from the counts of Egisheim, famous for holiness, formerly Bruno, bishop of Toul, a monk of the holy father Benedict, deserved to hear a voice from heaven: “I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction.” And of him our [unclear], in his Catalogue of the churches, made mention, and likewise Sebastian Murrho. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1048.

Victor, Pope II, previously called Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, held a great synod at Florence, in which, condemning many bishops for simony and fornication, he deposed them. He ruled and reformed the clergy very well, and did and established many good things. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1054.

Stephen, Pope IX, previously called Frederick, a monk of the order of the holy father Benedict. He immediately took care that the church of Milan, which had withdrawn itself from the Roman church for almost two hundred years, should now obey the same, as truly the mother of all churches. He flourished under Henry of this name the third, in the year [unclear].

And so much concerning the Roman pontiffs chosen; now concerning the rest omitted in the Catalogue, so far as it has been possible for us to gather, let us briefly write something.

Bruno, founder of the Carthusian order, then a theologian, rector and governor of the scholars of Paris, when he was considered most excellent in Gaul in lecturing, disputing, and writing, left behind the world and its pomps and, with seven most learned men, withdrew into the wilderness of Chartreuse; and, a monastery having been built, he happily established this very order. Among his disciples was Urban, Pope II. Bruno flourished around the year of the Lord 1085.

Hugh of Saint-Victor at Paris, a German by nation, was originally from Saxony, and therefore is rightly to be counted among our own. How much he wrote, our Trithemius did not leave unsaid in his Catalogue of ecclesiastical writers. He flourished at the same time as Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Johannes, originally from Turghem, a village of Swabia, first of Eichstätt, then of Argenti-

bishop of [Argentinensis?], a man most learned and most acute in all, and especially in divine, letters, is not to be passed over without remembrance and praise, although none of his own works has come down to us. We have seen a Bible and the Decretum, which he wrote with his own hand and which today are extant at Molsheim. He died in the year of the Lord 1328.

Johannes Buridanus, a very great philosopher, first taught philosophy gloriously for many years in the school at Paris, and afterward instructed many in the same faculty at the University of Vienna in Austria, not without the admiration of all. Among many little works of his talent he wrote Questions on Aristotle's Ethics, solid, [unclear], profound, as Johannes de Gerson bears witness; he composed many other things, which do not now come to our notice.

Apollonius, a most eminent and very penetrating physician of Erfurt, who in [unclear] established perpetual stipends for learned men in philosophy, which he endowed magnificently. In his profession he wrote some little works, which, however, have as yet by no means come into our hands.

Sigismund, Emperor of the Romans, a man distinguished both for learning and for knowledge of many languages, delivered a Latin oration at the great Council of Constance, full of all religious piety and true Christian religion, which Johannes Gerson relates that he heard with his own ears, not without pious compunction. Nor did he hesitate to compare him with most holy David.

Johannes, called Sonnemannus, that is, Man of the Sun, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, Doctor of Sacred Theology, of the convent of Kassel in Hesse, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent interpreter of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, a most eloquent declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote On the Ten Commandments, one book; On the Apostles' Creed, one book; On the Preparation of the Heart, one book; On Superstitions, one book; On Contracts, one book; Cases against the redemption of rents, one book; Sermons for the season and on the saints, two books. He also published some other things that have not come to my notice. He flourished in his convent at Kassel, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1460.

Gerardus de Castris, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Mainz, a learned and erudite man, outstanding in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout also in life and conduct, and a very celebrated cultivator of regular observance, an excellent declaimer of sermons. He wrote On the Passion of the Lord, one book; Sermons for the season and on the saints, two books; and other things not to be scorned. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Gregorius Heimburgius, no ordinary jurist and orator, did not depart from Italy, especially from the Venetians, without praise for his speeches. Although his admirable talent, trained not merely in the empty windiness of words but also well instructed in the most sacred laws, procured for him the envy of others. For envy seeks the highest things; the winds blow upon the loftiest. He wrote various speeches and letters in defense of Sigismund, duke of Austria, and an appeal from the sentence of the supreme pontiff, and other things.

Johannes Simlerus of Strasbourg, a very celebrated jurist, outstanding in intellect, eloquent in speech, supreme in prudence, wrote many very elegant letters, both to me and to others, and certain other little works not to be despised, in which he exercised his lively intellect. He died under Pope Innocent VIII.

You now have from me, candid reader, the Prosthesis which I promised, that is, an addition of certain men outstanding in talent to the famous Catalogue of the reverend father Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, in which he described the illustrious men of our Germany with the greatest eagerness. Nor do we doubt that there remain almost countless men of whom we have made no mention, because their names and little works are wholly unknown to us. But let each man after us add those whom he finds, and the glory of the Germans, ever increased, will become known to all foreigners. For we, as much as was permitted us, have labored with a most ready mind for the praise of our nation.

Clodoveus received the Christian faith from Remigius, 40.53. Clodomirus, king of the Franks, how many years he reigned, 47.9.

Christianus, monk and priest: what he wrote, and when [unclear]. He despoils the churches of the Christians, ibid. 1; from [unclear] he takes the Christian Clotildis as wife, ibid. 19. He conquers the Alamanni in war, 45. He is baptized by Bishop Remigius, 41.2. He orders all the noblest men of the Franks to be killed, 41.15.

Clodophorus, count palatine of the Rhine, died without children, 119.12.

Chunibertus, chancellor of the kingdom in Austrasia, 53.42. The kingdom of Sigebert, with all its treasures, he receives into his own power, ibid. 47. He kills King Caracalus with [unclear], ibid. 50. Ruacharius, [unclear], he cuts down with his own hand, 53. He slaughters almost all his kinsmen, 42.3. He assigned Burgundy to the tribute and subjection of the Franks, ibid. 14; when he died, ibid. 16.

Claudius, bishop of Vienne: what he wrote and when, 17.

Clodulfus, bishop of Metz, 53.10.

[unclear] to reign. He captures the city of Cambrai, ibid. 24. He subjects Gaul as far as the river Saône to his kingdom, ibid. 26; when [unclear].

Clodarius X, duke of the Eastern Franks: how many years he reigned, and when he died, ibid. 3.

Cleodoner, wife of the king: when [unclear], 247.35.

[unclear] 24.2. He is killed in battle, ibid. 14. XVIII.1: how many years [unclear].

Clemens, king XLIV: how many years he reigned, 35.37. He entrusts Coma to be raised among the Franks, ibid. 42; he was called “the long-haired,” ibid. 45. He moves an army into Thuringia, ibid. 57. Having conquered the Thuringians, he makes them tributaries, 36.9.

King of the Franks XXXII: how many years he reigned, 21.5; when he died, ibid. 3.

Caesar of the Romans subjects Britain and the Orkney Islands to the Romans, 16.34.

King of the Franks XLV: how many years he reigned, 35.37. He entrusts Coma to be raised among the Franks, ibid. 48; he was called “the long-haired,” ibid. 45. He moves an army into Thuringia, ibid. 57. Having conquered the Thuringians, he makes them tributaries, 30.9. He devastates the region of the Tungri, ibid. 12. He sends scouts into Gaul, ibid. 17. He captures the city of Cambrai, ibid. 27. He subjects the city of Tournai to himself, ibid. 33. He receives a great part of Gaul, as far as the sea, into his power, ibid. 35; when he died, ibid. 44.

Clodoaldus, son of King Clodomirus, becomes a cleric, 43.25.

Clodomer, duke of the Eastern Franks I: how many years he reigned, and when he died, 79.53. The king’s brother, after the king had been killed, dressed in his arms, defeats the Romans and Gauls, 24.8.

Cleromirius R.: letter to the Gallic princes, 9.39; speech to the Thuringians, 25.22.

Cleromirus, king of the Franks XXVII: how many years he reigned, ibid. 56.

Cleromiris, son of Clodoneus, reigns at Orléans for 7 years, 43.17; by whom his sons were killed, ibid. 24. Duke of the Eastern Franks XVI: how many years he reigned, and when he died, 80.9. King of the Franks XXXVI: how many years he reigned, 24.21; when he died, 27.26. [unclear] of the Franks [unclear]: how many years he reigned, 9.20.

Clodomirus, son of Basanus: he is appointed king by his father, 9.5. King of the Franks XIII: how many years he reigned, 11.56.

Clodomerus, king of the Franks LVII: how many years he reigned, 58.37; he dies, ibid. 54. LVIII: how many years he reigned, 57.38; he dies, ibid. 48. Clodomerus is born from Basina in the year of Christ 463, 39.8. What he was ordered to adore and burn when he was baptized, 69.10. King of the Franks LIII: how many years he reigned, 53.28; he died mad and demented, 55.37; he complains about his kinsmen who had been killed, 42.7. The king is baptized by Saint Remigius, 41.2. He vows that he will be a Christian, 40.40. The first Christian king of the Franks, born in adultery, 86.44; on what occasion he was converted to the Christian faith, 86.7. Duke of the Eastern Franks XVIII: how many years he reigned, 80.13.

Clodomirus, king of the Franks, 47: how many years he reigned, 9. He despoils the churches of the Christians, ibid. 1; from [unclear] he takes the Christian Clotildis as wife, ibid. 19. He lays waste the region of the Thuringians with fire and sword, ibid. 28. He defeats Alaric, king of the Visigoths, 30. On what occasion he was made a Christian, ibid. 40. He conquers the Alamanni in war, 45. He is baptized by Bishop Remigius, 41.2. He orders all the noblest men of the Franks to be killed, 15. He slaughters almost all his kinsmen, 42.3. He assigned Burgundy to the tribute and subjection of the Franks, ibid. 14; when he died, ibid. 16.

The counts of Dachau, eighteen in number, are all called by the name Conrad, 105.42.

The kings of Dacia and Norway submit themselves to the kingdom of Britain, 39.2. Dagobert kills all the Saxons who exceed the length of his sword, 90.3. King of the Franks, how many years he reigned, 23.40; he cultivates justice, ibid.43; he dies, ibid.57. Interrex or duke of the Franks, how many years he reigned, 31.48; he dies, 33.13. Son of King Lothar, he is made king of Austrasia, 50.10; he is wounded by Bertulf, duke of the Saxons, ibid.21. King of the Franks, how many years he reigned, 50.39; he founded the monastery of St. Denis in Gaul, ibid.48; he repudiates his wife Gertrude because of sterility, ibid.57. He is excessively luxurious, 51.1. He makes the Slavs, or Bohemians, tributary to the Franks, 51.10. He is the founder of the monastery of Wissembourg, ibid.23. He makes Sigebert, his seven-year-old son, king of Austrasia, 53.5; he conquers the Wends and makes them tributary, ibid.17; he remits the tribute of Saxony, ibid.20; he died, ibid.22.
